card_event_aans.name: card_event_aans
card_event_aans.title: NZANS
card_event_aans.text: Your HQ gets +3 defense. Gain 1 extra kredit slot.
card_event_aans.flavorText: NZANS refers to the New Zealand Army Nursing Service, whose members served far from home during WWII. Between 1939 and 1948, 680 New Zealand nurses served in different theatres of war, while many more women served in medical and support roles through the New Zealand Women’s Army Auxiliary Corps. New Zealand nurses worked in military hospitals in the Middle East, the Pacific, and later with J Force in occupied Japan. Their duties ranged from routine ward care to treating men wounded in battle, often under difficult conditions and strict wartime censorship. In 1940, a New Zealand nurse recorded a Christmas radio message from Egypt, reassuring listeners at home that patients would still receive small gifts on Christmas morning. Some nurses experienced the danger of war directly. Matron Eva Mackay led a party of New Zealand Army nurses out of Greece and Crete in 1941 as the Allied campaign collapsed. Her group took cover during air attacks and escaped by truck and ship to the Middle East. After the war, nurses continued their service in Japan, helping care for New Zealand personnel while witnessing the early years of occupation and rebuilding.

card_event_anzac_spirit.name: card_event_anzac_spirit
card_event_anzac_spirit.title: THE ANZAC SPIRIT
card_event_anzac_spirit.text: Deal 2 damage to all enemies. Draw 2 cards. Gain 2 extra kredit slots.
card_event_anzac_spirit.flavorText: The Anzac spirit is a shared idea in Australian and New Zealand memory, shaped by the 1915 Gallipoli campaign. It is often associated with courage, endurance, initiative, good humour, and mateship. Early reports from Anzac Cove praised the Australians and New Zealanders for landing under fire and pushing inland despite confusion and danger. Australian official historian Charles Bean helped turn these stories into a wider legend. For many, the Anzac spirit came to describe ordinary soldiers facing hardship while supporting their mates. The idea has been debated by historians, but it remains central to Anzac Day remembrance and to the close wartime bond between Australia and New Zealand.

card_event_corps_command.name: card_event_corps_command
card_event_corps_command.title: CORPS COMMAND
card_event_corps_command.text: Your left and right-most cards in hand get: "Destroy a random enemy unit when played."
card_event_corps_command.flavorText: During WWII, a corps headquarters coordinated the operations of several divisions, directing large formations across a broad front while managing planning, logistics, communications and the allocation of supporting forces. For Australia, I Corps became the main operational corps for much of WWII, commanding Australian and other Allied formations in several theatres. From 1940 to 1942, I Corps operated in the Mediterranean and Middle East, overseeing forces in North Africa, Greece and Syria–Lebanon. During the Greek campaign in 1941, its headquarters moved to Greece as part of Operation Lustre. Because it controlled the New Zealand 2nd Division alongside Australian, British and Greek formations, I Corps was officially renamed ANZAC Corps on 12 April, under Lieutenant General Thomas Blamey. The campaign was short-lived, and the corps headquarters was evacuated later that month. After Japan entered the war, I Corps was transferred to the South West Pacific. From late 1942 onward, it commanded Allied frontline formations in New Guinea, and it later oversaw operations in Borneo in 1945, making corps-level command central to Australia’s war effort across multiple theatres.

card_event_forward_base_anzac.name: card_event_forward_base_anzac
card_event_forward_base_anzac.title: FORWARD BASE
card_event_forward_base_anzac.text: Discard your left-most card. Deal damage to target unit equal to its cost.
card_event_forward_base_anzac.flavorText: A forward base is an advanced military position established close to an active combat zone. It allows troops to receive supplies, reinforcements, medical support and communications without relying entirely on support from distant rear bases. In the Pacific, where operations were often separated by mountains, jungle and long stretches of ocean, forward bases were essential for keeping forces supplied and maintaining pressure on the enemy. Australian and New Zealand forces made extensive use of them during WWII. In New Guinea, locations such as Port Moresby and Milne Bay became vital centres for air operations, logistics and troop movements. In 1942, at Milne Bay, Allied engineers built airfields that allowed aircraft to operate close to Japanese positions and supported Australian troops defending the area. As Allied forces advanced farther along the New Guinea coast, new bases and airfields were established closer to the front. These positions provided food, ammunition, fuel and medical care while giving aircraft and ground forces a staging point for the next operation. Forward bases therefore became a crucial part of the Allied advance through the Southwest Pacific.

card_event_guerilla_warfare_school.name: card_event_guerilla_warfare_school
card_event_guerilla_warfare_school.title: GUERILLA WARFARE SCHOOL
card_event_guerilla_warfare_school.text: Costs 1 less if right-most in hand. Retreat a random enemy unit.
card_event_guerilla_warfare_school.flavorText: The Guerrilla Warfare School at Tidal River trained Australian and New Zealand soldiers for irregular warfare in the Pacific. Its courses taught men how to operate in small commando groups, behind enemy lines, without the support expected by normal infantry. The aim was to raid, scout, sabotage, and disappear before a stronger enemy could react. Training focused on practical tactics. Trainees learned ambush drills, night movement, camouflage, silent patrols, map reading, and how to set up hidden observation posts. They practiced cutting communications, blowing bridges with timed charges, and attacking supply routes. Demolition work used explosives such as gelignite, while close-range fighting involved firearms like Bren guns, Thompson submachine guns, grenades, and mortars. The school also taught survival and self-reliance. Men trained to cross rivers, move through swamps, climb rough ground, forage, and keep operating with little food or equipment. Coastal raids were practiced with collapsible boats, while signals training taught small patrols how to report information without exposing themselves. Graduates took these skills into the Pacific, where Independent Companies and later commando units used them for reconnaissance, raids, ambushes, and harassment operations in places such as Timor, New Guinea, and New Britain.

card_event_hmas_warramunga.name: card_event_hmas_warramunga
card_event_hmas_warramunga.title: HMAS WARRAMUNGA
card_event_hmas_warramunga.text: Choose a card in hand. Move it all the way to the left. Reduce its cost by 1 if it is an ANZAC card.
card_event_hmas_warramunga.flavorText: HMAS Warramunga was a Tribal-class destroyer of the Royal Australian Navy, built at Cockatoo Island Dockyard in Sydney. She was commissioned in late 1942 and first served on convoy escort duty between Queensland and New Guinea. In 1943, she joined the joint Australian and US Task Force 74, supporting Allied operations across the South West Pacific. Warramunga took part in a busy series of amphibious operations. She helped cover the landings at Kiriwina and Woodlark Islands, escorted the damaged cruiser HMAS Hobart after a Japanese torpedo hit, and later supported landings at Arawe and Cape Gloucester. In 1944, she supported the landings in the Admiralty Islands, at Tanamera Bay, Wakde Sarmi, Biak, Morotai, and Leyte. During the Battle of Leyte, she escorted damaged Allied cruisers back to safety. In 1945, Warramunga supported the landings at Lingayen Gulf, Tarakan, and Wewak. She was present in Tokyo Bay when Japan surrendered in September 1945. She was decorated with five battle honours for its service during WWII : Pacific, New Guinea, Leyte Gulf, Lingayen Gulf, and Borneo.

card_event_repel_the_attack.name: card_event_repel_the_attack
card_event_repel_the_attack.title: REPEL THE ATTACK
card_event_repel_the_attack.text: All enemy units Retreat. End the turn unless played from right-most in hand.
card_event_repel_the_attack.flavorText: In August 1942 at Milne Bay, Australian forces faced a determined Japanese attempt to seize newly-built Allied airfields on the eastern tip of New Guinea. The Japanese badly underestimated the strength of the garrison, expecting only a few companies of defenders, while the Allies had reinforced the area with thousands of troops. The first line of defence was held largely by the Australian 7th Infantry Brigade, including the 9th, 25th and 61st Battalions. Despite being pushed back in several hard-fought engagements, these Militia troops slowed the Japanese advance and helped hold the approaches to the airfields. Veteran troops of the 18th Infantry Brigade, part of the 7th Division, were then committed to the fighting and launched counterattacks that steadily forced the Japanese eastward. RAAF Kittyhawks from Nos. 75 and 76 Squadrons also played a crucial role, attacking Japanese troops, landing craft and supply lines. By 7 September, the Japanese had withdrawn. The victory at Milne Bay became the first full-scale defeat of Japanese land forces in the Pacific theater during WWII and provided an important boost to Allied morale.

card_event_task_force_44.name: card_event_task_force_44
card_event_task_force_44.title: TASK FORCE 44
card_event_task_force_44.text: Forecast. Deal 2 damage to a unit. Deal 3 damage instead if this card was left-most in hand.
card_event_task_force_44.flavorText: Task Force 44 was an Allied naval force made up of US Navy and Royal Australian Navy warships operating during WWII. It was created in 1942 from the ANZAC Squadron and was tasked with defending northeast Australia, New Guinea, and nearby sea routes from Japanese attacks. Its first commander was Rear Admiral John Gregory Crace of the Royal Australian Navy. It was later commanded by Rear Admiral Victor Crutchley of the British Royal Navy. The force’s best known action came during the Battle of the Coral Sea. In May 1942, Crace led HMAS Australia, HMAS Hobart, USS Chicago, and several US destroyers toward the Jomard Passage to block any Japanese ships moving toward Port Moresby, the capital city of Papua New Guinea. Japanese aircraft attacked the force with torpedoes and bombs, but none of the ships were hit. A later mistaken attack by US aircraft also failed to damage the ships. Task Force 44 later helped escort Allied convoys around Australia, New Guinea, and the Coral Sea. It also supported the early Guadalcanal campaign and took part in the Battle of Savo Island. In 1943, it was redesignated Task Force 74 and served under the US Seventh Fleet.

card_event_the_double_sunrise.name: card_event_the_double_sunrise
card_event_the_double_sunrise.title: THE DOUBLE SUNRISE
card_event_the_double_sunrise.text: Give a random friendly unit on the battlefield and in hand +2+1.
card_event_the_double_sunrise.flavorText: The Double Sunrise was a wartime air service run by Qantas, Australia’s airline company, with RAAF personnel during WWII. It was created in 1943 to restore the air link between Australia and England after the fall of Singapore had cut the old route. The flights used Consolidated PBY Catalina flying boats between Western Australia and Lake Koggala in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). The route flew over more than 3,500 nautical miles of the Indian Ocean and was then the longest nonstop airline service in the world. The flights were slow, lonely and difficult. Crews flew without radio navigation and relied on compass work and stars. Departures were timed so the aircraft crossed Japanese occupied areas in darkness. Westbound flights lasted between 27 and 33 hours, long enough for passengers and crew to see sunrise twice, which gave the service its name. The Catalinas carried heavy fuel loads, so each flight usually took only a few passengers and a small amount of urgent mail. Between 1943 and 1945, the service made 271 crossings, carried 860 passengers, and helped keep Australia connected to Britain.

card_event_z_special_unit.name: card_event_z_special_unit
card_event_z_special_unit.title: Z SPECIAL UNIT
card_event_z_special_unit.text: Deal 4 damage to a unit. If played from left-most in hand, your HQ gains +5 defense.
card_event_z_special_unit.flavorText: Z Special Unit was a joint Allied special forces unit formed in 1942 to operate behind Japanese lines in Southeast Asia. Although most were Australian, it also included British, Dutch, New Zealander, Timorese, and Indonesian members. Its missions included reconnaissance, sabotage, raids, intelligence gathering, and guerrilla operations, often in areas controlled by Japanese forces. Teams were inserted by submarine, parachute, or small landing craft, and the unit carried out a total of 81 covert operations in the South West Pacific during its service.Training was spread across secret sites in Australia, including Refuge Bay near Sydney, Fraser Island, Garden Island, and the Z Experimental Station near Cairns. Men learned small boat handling, demolition, close combat, parachuting, jungle warfare, and how to survive with limited support. The unit’s best known success was Operation Jaywick in 1943, when 14 commandos reached Singapore Harbour aboard MV Krait, a captured Japanese fishing vessel, and used folding kayaks to place limpet mines on Japanese ships. The raid sank or badly damaged several of them. A later raid, Operation Rimau, ended in disaster, with all 23 commandos killed or executed after capture. Z Special Unit was disbanded after the war, but its methods influenced later Australian special forces.

card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade_vet.name: card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade_vet
card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade_vet.title: 16th INFANTRY BRIGADE
card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade_vet.text: Your units get +2+2 after you play a Rain or a Storm card.

card_unit_6th_brigade_nz_vet.title: 6th BRIGADE NZ
card_unit_6th_brigade_nz_vet.text: Deal 1 damage to a random enemy when a friendly unit becomes Veteran.

card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac_vet.title: 7th BRIGADE
card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac_vet.text: When this unit becomes Veteran, draw 2 cards.

card_unit_raaf_walrus_vet.name: card_unit_raaf_walrus_vet
card_unit_raaf_walrus_vet.title: RAAF WALRUS
card_unit_raaf_walrus_vet.text: Units to the left of this unit operate for 1 less.

card_unit_the_silent_seventh_vet.name: card_unit_the_silent_seventh_vet
card_unit_the_silent_seventh_vet.title: THE SILENT SEVENTH
card_unit_the_silent_seventh_vet.text: Your left-most card costs 2 less, to a minimum of 1.

card_unit_14th_brigade_nz.name: card_unit_14th_brigade_nz
card_unit_14th_brigade_nz.title: 14th BRIGADE NZ
card_unit_14th_brigade_nz.text: Deployment: Gain an extra kredit slot if deployed from left-most in hand.
card_unit_14th_brigade_nz.flavorText: The 14th Brigade NZ was an infantry brigade of New Zealand’s 3rd Division, which served in the Pacific during WWII. Formed in 1942, the brigade trained in New Zealand and New Caledonia before moving to Guadalcanal in 1943. From there, it took part in operations in the Solomon Islands under US command, with New Zealand ground troops supported by Allied naval and air forces. The brigade’s first major operation was on Vella Lavella in September 1943. Landing after US forces had secured a foothold, the 14th Brigade was ordered to clear Japanese troops from the north of the island so radar installations and motor torpedo boat bases could be established. Its battalions advanced along both coasts, trapping the defenders in a small pocket, though many Japanese troops later escaped by sea. In February 1944, the reinforced brigade landed on Nissan Island in the Green Islands. The Japanese garrison resisted strongly but was ultimately overwhelmed, and organized resistance ended within days. Soon after, New Zealand’s manpower shortage forced the 3rd Division’s disbandment, ending the brigade’s service in the Pacific.

card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade.name: card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade
card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade.title: 16th INFANTRY BRIGADE
card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade.text: Becomes Veteran after you play a Rain or a Storm card.
card_unit_16th_infantry_brigade.flavorText: The 16th Infantry Brigade was part of the 6th Australian Division during WWII. It was raised in 1939 as part of the Second Australian Imperial Force and was one of the first Australian volunteer formations ready for overseas service. After training in Australia, it sailed for the Middle East in 1940 and entered combat in the Western Desert campaign. Its first major engagement came at Bardia in January 1941, followed by service around Tobruk. In Greece, the brigade resisted against the German advance. Its battalions helped cover the retreat through Veria Pass, Tempe Gorge, and Larissa before being evacuated. Some elements reached Crete, where the 2/1st Battalion was largely destroyed while defending Retimo airfield. After Japan entered the war, the brigade shipped to the Pacific. In 1942, it crossed the Owen Stanley Range in Papua New Guinea during the Kokoda campaign, fought around Eora Creek and Oivi Gorari, then advanced toward the Japanese beachheads at Sanananda. Later, after rebuilding in Australia, the brigade returned to New Guinea for the Aitape-Wewak campaign, conducting patrols and small actions until the end of the war.

card_unit_17th_infantry_brigade.name: card_unit_17th_infantry_brigade
card_unit_17th_infantry_brigade.title: 17th INFANTRY BRIGADE
card_unit_17th_infantry_brigade.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to a unit. If you do, draw a card if deployed from left-most in hand.
card_unit_17th_infantry_brigade.flavorText: The 17th Infantry Brigade was part of the 6th Australian Division during WWII. It was raised in 1939 as part of the Second Australian Imperial Force, with its main battalions recruited in Victoria. After training in Australia, the brigade shipped to the Middle East in 1940 and first saw action in the Western Desert campaign. At Bardia, it supported the main assault, then helped capture Italian positions as the conflict moved through Tobruk, Barce and Marsa Brega. In 1941, the brigade was sent to Greece during the German invasion. Its battalions fought delaying actions near Larissa and Domokos before evacuation. Some men reached Crete, where the 2/7th Battalion took part in the fierce bayonet attack at 42nd Street alongside the Māori Battalion. The brigade later fought in the Syria-Lebanon campaign, including the advance toward Damour and Beirut. After Japan entered the war, the 17th Brigade was sent to the Pacific theater. In New Guinea, it fought at Wau, Mubo, Bobdubi, Lababia Ridge, Nassau Bay, and Mount Tambu during the Salamaua Lae campaign. Its final engagement  was the Aitape-Wewak campaign in 1944 and 1945.

card_unit_27th_mg_battalion.name: card_unit_27th_mg_battalion
card_unit_27th_mg_battalion.title: 27th MG BATTALION
card_unit_27th_mg_battalion.text: Units you deploy get Blitz if they were left-most in hand, Shock if they were right-most.
card_unit_27th_mg_battalion.flavorText: The 27th Machine-Gun Battalion was an infantry unit of the 2nd New Zealand Division during WWII. Raised at Burnham in 1939, it counted about 700 men, equipped with Vickers machine guns, which gave the division sustained fire support. Its companies also included signals, transport, administration, and anti-aircraft support. After training in New Zealand, the battalion was sent to Egypt in early 1941. The battalion first saw action in Greece, where it fought during the long withdrawal to the Peloponnese, including the rearguard battles at Vevi and Mount Olympus. It was then sent to Crete and fought at Maleme and Galatas during the German airborne invasion. In North Africa, it served in Operation Crusader, at El Alamein, during the advance into Tunisia, and the flanking move around the Mareth Line. It also supplied men to the Long Range Desert Group. In Italy, the battalion crossed the Sangro River early and was heavily engaged, firing nearly nine million rounds during the campaign. It was converted to infantry in 1945 and ended the war at Trieste.

card_unit_2_2nd_pioneers.name: card_unit_2_2nd_pioneers
card_unit_2_2nd_pioneers.title: 2/2nd PIONEERS
card_unit_2_2nd_pioneers.text: Your other units get +1+1 when you Forecast.
card_unit_2_2nd_pioneers.flavorText: The 2/2nd Pioneer Battalion was an Australian unit raised in 1940 as part of the Second Australian Imperial Force. Pioneer battalions were trained to support infantry with practical battlefield work, such as building tracks, digging positions, clearing obstacles, and handling smaller engineering tasks. In combat, they could also fight as infantry when needed. The 2/2nd was assigned to the 7th Division and first served in the Middle East. During the Syria-Lebanon campaign in 1941, it fought mainly as infantry, including costly engagements around Merdjayoun, El Mtolle, and Damour. In 1942, the battalion was sent back to Australia but got diverted to Java after Japan entered the war. There, it joined Blackforce, a 3.000 man pioneer infantry unit named after its commander, Brigadier Arthur Blackburn, and fought briefly before the Allied force surrendered. More than 800 men were captured, and 258 later died in captivity. The battalion was rebuilt in Australia and sent to New Guinea in 1943. It helped build an airfield after the landing at Nadzab, fought toward Lae, and later served in the Finisterre Range around Shaggy Ridge. Its final campaign was in Borneo in 1945.

card_unit_3_7_inch_mountain_howitzer.name: card_unit_3_7_inch_mountain_howitzer
card_unit_3_7_inch_mountain_howitzer.title: 3.7 inch MOUNTAIN HOWITZER
card_unit_3_7_inch_mountain_howitzer.text: This unit also deals damage to enemies to the left of the enemy it attacks.
card_unit_3_7_inch_mountain_howitzer.flavorText: The QF 3.7-inch mountain howitzer was a lightweight artillery piece designed for use in terrain where conventional field guns were difficult to move. It could be broken down into eight separate loads for transport and, with a trained crew, reassembled and made ready to fire in about two minutes. Its high elevation and adjustable suspension made it particularly useful in steep or uneven country. During WWII, the weapon saw service with Commonwealth forces in several theatres, including the Kokoda Campaign in New Guinea. For Australian troops fighting through the mountains and jungles of Papua, the howitzer’s portability allowed artillery support to be brought into positions that heavier guns could not easily reach. Its 20-pound shells could be fired to a maximum range of about 5,900 yards (5.4 km). Australian gunners in Papua New Guinea even used the normally restricted fifth propellant charge for emergencies, giving it the nickname “O’Hara’s charge.” Ultimately, the 3.7-inch mountain howitzer proved well-suited to the difficult terrain faced by Australian forces in the Southwest Pacific.

card_unit_4th_brigade_nz.name: card_unit_4th_brigade_nz
card_unit_4th_brigade_nz.title: 4th BRIGADE NZ
card_unit_4th_brigade_nz.text: Deployment: If you have less than 3 cards in hand, draw until you have 3.
card_unit_4th_brigade_nz.flavorText: The 4th Infantry Brigade served as part of the 2nd New Zealand Division, New Zealand’s main expeditionary formation during WWII. Re-raised in 1939, the brigade consisted of the 18th, 19th and 20th Battalions and was one of the division’s three infantry brigades. Its first major campaign with the division came in Greece in 1941. The 2nd New Zealand Division fought alongside the Australian 6th Division against the German invasion, with the 4th Brigade defending the Aliakmon Line and later Servia Pass, before withdrawing to Thermopylae. The brigade was then evacuated to Crete, where it served as a reserve formation around Galatas. Later, the brigade rejoined the 2nd New Zealand Division in North Africa. In July 1942, it attacked Ruweisat Ridge, where a German counterattack inflicted severe losses on the 19th and 20th Battalions. The brigade was rebuilt soon afterwards and, in October 1942, converted into the 4th New Zealand Armoured Brigade, continuing to serve within the 2nd New Zealand Division.

card_unit_6th_brigade_nz.name: card_unit_6th_brigade_nz
card_unit_6th_brigade_nz.title: 6th BRIGADE NZ
card_unit_6th_brigade_nz.text: Deployment: Becomes Veteran if deployed from right-most in hand.
card_unit_6th_brigade_nz.flavorText: The 6th Infantry Brigade was part of the 2nd New Zealand Division during WWII. The brigade was formed in 1940, shipped to the Middle East and trained in Egypt before joining the 2nd Division’s first major operations. In Greece, the brigade held positions on the Aliakmon Line, then withdrew through Olympus Pass as German forces advanced. It helped cover the Allied evacuation and embarked from Monemvasia in April 1941. In North Africa, the brigade fought in Operation Crusader and was heavily engaged around Sidi Rezegh. Its battalions attacked Point 175 and suffered severe losses when surrounded during the fighting near Tobruk. The brigade later served at El Alamein, where it held defensive positions before taking part in the wider Eighth Army offensive. It pushed west through Libya and Tunisia, fighting  in battles such as El Agheila and the Tebaga Gap. In Italy, the brigade crossed the Sangro River, fought around Orsogna, and attacked Cassino in 1944. During the final 1945 offensive, it crossed several northern Italian rivers before reaching the Trieste area. It was disbanded in late 1945.

card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac.name: card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac
card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac.title: 7th BRIGADE
card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac.text: Becomes Veteran when your hand is empty. Deployment: Discard your left-most card.
card_unit_7th_brigade_anzac.flavorText: Australia’s 7th Brigade was a Militia formation that played an important role in the Pacific theater during WWII. Initially responsible for defending South East Queensland, it was fully mobilised after Japan entered the war, and by mid-1942 consisted of the 9th, 25th and 61st Battalions. In July 1942, the brigade was sent to Milne Bay in New Guinea, where it fought alongside elements of the 7th Division. In August, Australian forces repelled a Japanese landing aimed at capturing the strategically important Allied airfields, inflicting to Japan its first major defeat on land in the Pacific War. In March 1943, the 7th Brigade was reassigned to the 11th Division and served as part of New Guinea Force’s reserve. It later returned to combat on Bougainville Island, taking part in the battles of Pearl Ridge and Slater’s Knoll.

card_unit_anzac_hurricane_ii_c_trop.name: card_unit_anzac_hurricane_ii_c_trop
card_unit_anzac_hurricane_ii_c_trop.title: RAAF HURRICANE TROP
card_unit_anzac_hurricane_ii_c_trop.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 and Blitz if deployed from right-most in hand.
card_unit_anzac_hurricane_ii_c_trop.flavorText: The Hawker Hurricane served with the RAAF mostly overseas, rather than for home defence in Australia. In 1941 and 1942, No. 3 Squadron RAAF, No. 450 Squadron RAAF, and No. 451 Squadron RAAF all used RAF numbered Hurricanes in the Middle East. These aircraft were not Australian-built or uniquely marked RAAF machines, but they were flown and maintained by Australian units in active service. No. 3 Squadron RAAF converted to Hurricanes in North Africa in early 1941. The squadron used them as fighters and for ground attack during the desert campaign, before changing to P-40 Tomahawks later. No. 450 Squadron RAAF also used Hurricanes while forming an operational squadron in the Middle East. No. 451 Squadron RAAF had a detachment that operated Hurricanes during the Siege of Tobruk, including reconnaissance work. Only one Hurricane served on Australian soil. It was a tropicalised Hurricane Mk I given to Australia by Britain in 1941, numbered V7476. It received the RAAF serial A60-1 and was used for familiarization, communications, public demonstrations, and testing Professor Frank Cotton’s anti-G suit at Laverton base in 1942.

card_unit_coastwatchers.name: card_unit_coastwatchers
card_unit_coastwatchers.title: COASTWATCHERS
card_unit_coastwatchers.text: Your weather cards cost you 1 less. Deployment: Forecast.
card_unit_coastwatchers.flavorText: The Coastwatchers were Allied intelligence operatives stationed on remote Pacific islands during WWII. Many were Australians, New Zealanders and Pacific Islanders citizens, with various jobs such as planters, traders, missionaries, and local police. Their task was not to seek battle, but to watch quietly, report Japanese ship and aircraft movements, and help rescue stranded Allied personnel. Lieutenant Commander Eric Feldt led the Australian coastwatching organization for much of the war and gave it the code name Ferdinand, a reference to Ferdinand the Bull, as a reminder that coastwatchers were meant to stay hidden and gather information, not draw attention. Their reports were especially valuable during the Guadalcanal campaign. Hidden observers in the Solomon Islands warned Allied forces about Japanese warships, aircraft, and troop movements. In November 1942, coastwatchers Jack Read and Paul Mason, based on Bougainville, sent early warnings of Japanese movements toward US forces in the Solomons. Admiral William Halsey later credited the coastwatchers with helping save Guadalcanal. Coastwatchers also guided rescues. After PT 109 was sunk, Australian coastwatcher Arthur Evans sent Solomon Islander scouts Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana to find the survivors, helping rescue future US president John F. Kennedy and his crew.

card_unit_dingo_armored_car.name: card_unit_dingo_armored_car
card_unit_dingo_armored_car.title: DINGO
card_unit_dingo_armored_car.text: When this unit attacks the enemy HQ, your HQ gets +1 defense and you draw a card.
card_unit_dingo_armored_car.flavorText: The Dingo scout car was a light armoured vehicle built in Australia during WWII. Australia had entered the war with few armoured vehicles and could not rely on large deliveries from the United Kingdom, whose factories were focused on urgent needs in Europe. This forced Australian industry to design and build vehicles from local resources. Ford produced 245 Dingo Scout Cars in 1942. The Dingo was based on a commercial Ford 30 cwt chassis, shortened and fitted with a Marmon Herrington all-wheel drive kit. It used either an 85 or 95 hp Ford V8 engine and had an armoured body made from Australian bulletproof plates by Victorian Railways. The two-man crew consisted of a commander and driver. Protection was 30 mm at the front, and 10 mm on the sides and rear. Its armament was a .303 Bren light machine-gun, and it also carried a Wireless Set No. 19 radio. The Dingo could reach 90 km/h, but its weight limited off-road mobility.

card_unit_flaming_matilda_anzac.name: card_unit_flaming_matilda_anzac
card_unit_flaming_matilda_anzac.title: MATILDA FROG
card_unit_flaming_matilda_anzac.text: Deals double damage to infantry and HQ. Units to the left of this unit have +2 attack.
card_unit_flaming_matilda_anzac.flavorText: The Matilda “Frog” was an Australian flamethrower version of the British Matilda II infantry tank, developed for jungle warfare in the Pacific. In 1943, the Australian Army asked for a tank-mounted flame weapon, and Major A.E. Miller helped shape the final design. A prototype was completed in 1944, and production of 25 units was approved. The first tank was ready by July 1944 and was demonstrated to General Thomas Blamey at Monegeetta Proving Grounds. The Frog replaced the Matilda’s 2-pounder gun with a flame projector hidden inside a tube, so the tank still looked much like a normal gun tank. Its fuel and pressure system were carried inside the vehicle rather than in a trailer. The turret held an 80-gallon fuel tank and pressure equipment, which left room for only one man there. Extra fuel tanks could be fitted inside and outside the hull. The flamethrower could fire about 90 yards, but needed around 30 seconds to build pressure between shots. Matilda Frogs were used on Borneo, where they proved effective against fortified Japanese positions.

card_unit_maori_battalion.name: card_unit_maori_battalion
card_unit_maori_battalion.title: MAORI BATTALION
card_unit_maori_battalion.text: Gets +2+2 when a friendly unit becomes Veteran.
card_unit_maori_battalion.flavorText: The 28th Māori Battalion was a light infantry battalion of the New Zealand Army which was part of the 2nd New Zealand Division during WWII. It was formed in 1940 after pressure from Māori leaders and organisations who wanted a distinct Māori unit for overseas service. The battalion, counting about 3,600 men in its ranks,r became one of New Zealand’s most decorated units of the war. It first served in Greece, where it fought at Petra Pass and helped cover the Allied withdrawal. In Crete, it took part in hard fighting after the German airborne landings, including a bayonet charge at the Battle of 42nd Street alongside the Australian 2/7th Battalion. In North Africa, it fought at Sollum, Gazala, Minqar Qaim, El Alamein, Tebaga Gap, and Takrouna. Second Lieutenant Moana-Nui-a-Kiwa Ngarimu received the Victoria Cross for his actions at Point 209. In Italy, the battalion fought at Orsogna, Cassino, Florence, Faenza, and during the final river crossings toward Trieste. It was disbanded in 1946 after returning to New Zealand.

card_unit_raaf_walrus.name: card_unit_raaf_walrus
card_unit_raaf_walrus.title: RAAF WALRUS
card_unit_raaf_walrus.text:
Deployment: Forecast. 
Becomes Veteran at the end of turn.
card_unit_raaf_walrus.flavorText: The RAAF Walrus, originally called the Supermarine Seagull V, was a ship-based amphibious aircraft designed to meet an Australian requirement. The RAAF ordered 24 aircraft in 1933, for use as spotter and reconnaissance aircraft aboard Royal Australian Navy cruisers. Deliveries began in 1935, with most aircraft first sent to Point Cook for seaplane crew training. The type later served from HMAS Australia, Canberra, Sydney, Perth, and Hobart. In Australian service, the aircraft was launched by catapult, landed on the sea, and was lifted back aboard by crane. It was used for patrols, scouting, gunnery support, and general naval duties. In August 1940, a Walrus from HMAS Hobart attacked Italian headquarters at Zeila in British Somaliland with bombs and machine guns. The RAAF also used the type with No. 5 Squadron, No. 9 Squadron, No. 11 Squadron, and No. 101 Flight. The Royal New Zealand Navy also used Walruses aboard HMNZS Achilles and HMNZS Leander, while the RNZAF operated the type with No. 5 Squadron and its Seaplane Training Flight.

card_unit_the_silent_seventh.name: card_unit_the_silent_seventh
card_unit_the_silent_seventh.title: THE SILENT SEVENTH
card_unit_the_silent_seventh.text: Once per turn, draw a card when you play your left-most card. Becomes Veteran after the third time.
card_unit_the_silent_seventh.flavorText: The 7th Australian Division was an infantry formation of the Second Australian Imperial Force during WWII. It became known as the Silent Seventh because many felt its achievements received less attention than those of other Australian divisions. One reason was wartime censorship around its hard fighting in the Syria-Lebanon campaign of 1941. The division was one of the few Australian formations to serve in both the Middle East and the South West Pacific theaters. In the Middle East, the 7th Division fought at Giarabub, Tobruk, and in Syria and Lebanon, where it advanced through difficult terrain toward Beirut. After Japan entered the war, the division was recalled to defend Australia. Elements were lost in Java, but most of the division returned home, before being sent to New Guinea. In Papua, the division fought on the Kokoda Track, at Milne Bay, Buna Gona, and later in the Markham and Ramu valleys. It helped capture Lae and fought through the Finisterre Range, at the Battle of Shaggy Ridge in particular. In 1945, the division took part in its final campaign at Balikpapan in Borneo, before disbanding in 1946.

card_brawl_history_card.name: card_brawl_history_card
card_brawl_history_card.title: SKIRMISH EVENT
card_brawl_history_card.flavorText: Theaters of War Special rule or event.

card_brawl_test1.name: card_brawl_test1
card_brawl_test1.title: Special Rule
card_brawl_test1.text: Djebel Abiod was the first town in Tunisia taken by the British, after a hard fight on November 17th 1942.

card_event_burning_fields_skirm.name: card_event_burning_fields_skirm
card_event_burning_fields_skirm.title: BURNING FIELDS
card_event_burning_fields_skirm.text: Distribute 1 damage five times among enemies.

card_event_espionage_skirm.name: card_event_espionage_skirm
card_event_espionage_skirm.title: ESPIONAGE
card_event_espionage_skirm.text: Copy 2 random cards in the enemy hand.

card_event_firestorm_skirm.name: card_event_firestorm_skirm
card_event_firestorm_skirm.title: FIRESTORM
card_event_firestorm_skirm.text: Deal 2 damage to all enemy units.

card_event_foreign_support_skirm.name: card_event_foreign_support_skirm
card_event_foreign_support_skirm.title: FOREIGN SUPPORT
card_event_foreign_support_skirm.text: Add a random 1, 2 and 3 cost units to your support line

card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union_sk.name: card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union_skirm
card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union_sk.title: HEROES OF THE SOVIET UNION
card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union_sk.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite Soviet units to add to your hand.

card_event_lost_cause_skirm.name: card_event_lost_cause_skirm
card_event_lost_cause_skirm.title: LOST CAUSE
card_event_lost_cause_skirm.text: Take control of an enemy unit with cost 3 or less.

card_event_soul_of_old_japan_skirm.name: card_event_soul_of_old_japan_skirm
card_event_soul_of_old_japan_skirm.title: SOUL OF OLD JAPAN
card_event_soul_of_old_japan_skirm.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite Japanese units to add to your hand.

card_event_aerial_reconaissance.name: card_event_aerial_reconaissance
card_event_aerial_reconaissance.title: AERIAL RECONNAISSANCE
card_event_aerial_reconaissance.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, reduce the cost of all orders in your hand by 1, to a minimum of 1.
card_event_aerial_reconaissance.flavorText: In 1928 the RAF developed an electrical heating system for aerial cameras which allowed reconnaissance aircraft to take pictures at a high altitude without the camera parts freezing. At the start of WWII the RAF developed high speed Spitfire PR variants that had their armament replaced with 5 cameras and could take photographs from up to 30,000 feet. Other aircraft were also adapted for photo-reconnaissance missions, such as the British Mosquito, the American P-38 Lightning and P-51 Mustang.

card_event_grounded.name: card_event_grounded
card_event_grounded.title: GROUNDED
card_event_grounded.text: Put a unit on top of owner's deck.
card_event_grounded.flavorText: During WWII not all aircraft could take off when needed as various factors could interfere, such as weather conditions, engine or technical failures and damage inflicted by the enemy. In 1944 almost the entirety of the Luftwaffe’s air force was grounded due to the fact that its oil supply ran dry. This meant that the Luftwaffe's role was reduced to anti-aircraft roles and many of its men were transferred to infantry units.

card_event_lend_lease.name: card_event_lend_lease
card_event_lend_lease.title: LEND LEASE
card_event_lend_lease.flavorText: The Lend-Lease program, formally titled “An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States”, was a program where the United States supplied the Allied nations with food, oil, materials and weaponry between 1941 and 1945. For most part the aid was free, but some hardware such as ships were returned after the war. A total of $50.1 billion ($697 billion today) worth of supplies were shipped, most of it going to Britain and the Soviet Union

card_event_merchant_navy.name: card_event_merchant_navy
card_event_merchant_navy.title: THE MERCHANT NAVY
card_event_merchant_navy.text: When an enemy unit attacks, Retreat it instead.
card_event_merchant_navy.flavorText: The British Merchant Navy kept the United Kingdom and their Allies supplied with arms, ammunition, fuel, food and raw materials necessary to the nation and its fighting forces throughout WWII. Up to 185,000 men and women from many nations served in the British Merchant Navy during the war, these were seamen from the age of 14 up to their late 70s. The Merchant Navy Seamen suffered greater casualties and more hardship than almost every other branch of the armed services. A total of 47,176 men and women lost their lives or were wounded or captured in the services for the Merchant Navy during the war.

card_event_raid.name: card_event_raid
card_event_raid.title: RAID
card_event_raid.text: Cards in enemy hand cost 2 more next turn.
card_event_raid.flavorText: Many raids were conducted by the British armed forces during WWII, mostly by the British commando forces. Most of the raids were against the Atlantic Wall, which was an extensive defense system and fortifications built by the Axis along the coast of continental Europe and Scandinavia. A total of  57 raids were conducted between 1940 and 1944 by the commandos, most of them against targets in France, but also Norway, the Channel Islands, Belgium and the Netherlands. Many of the raids resulted in the capture or death of all commandos involved, but many were successful, for example, Operation Chariot which was a raid against dock installations at Saint-Nazaire in France and has since been called “The Greatest Raid of All Time”.

card_event_resolute_defense.name: card_event_resolute_defense
card_event_resolute_defense.title: RESOLUTE DEFENSE
card_event_resolute_defense.flavorText: On September 15, 1940, now known as “Battle of Britain Day”, the Luftwaffe launched its largest attacks on London, but were defeated by RAF Fighter Command. That day RAF pilot Ray Holmes was flying his Hawker Hurricane fighter when he spotted a formation of three Dornier Do 17 bombers lining up to attack the royal residence of Buckingham Palace. Holmes managed to shoot one of them down and chase another one away, but a third Dornier was still heading towards the palace. When Holmes went in for the attack his machine guns failed to fire, but not giving up, he decided to ram the bombers rear and by this he managed to cut off the rear tail section of the enemy aircraft and the Dornier went down. After the ramming Holmes lost control of his Hurricane, but managed to bail out to safety before it crashed. This incredible event was caught on film and afterwards it became one of the defining moments of the Battle of Britain.

card_event_secret_operatives.name: card_event_secret_operatives
card_event_secret_operatives.title: SECRET OPERATIVES
card_event_secret_operatives.text: Counter an order that targets a friendly unit. Give the unit +2 defense.
card_event_secret_operatives.flavorText: The Special Operations Executive (SOE) was a British organization formed at the start of WWII. Very few people knew of SOE’s existence, but those who were a part of it were also known as “Churchill’s Secret Army”, “The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare” or “Baker Street Irregulars”, named after the location of their London HQ. The SOE operated behind enemy lines in all territories occupied by the Axis and the organization counted 13,000 operatives, both men and women. The purpose of the SOE was to conduct sabotage, espionage, reconnaissance and to aid local resistance movements in the occupied countries. The most famous operations executed by SOE were perhaps the assassination of SS-Obergruppenführer Reinhard Heydrich in Czechoslovakia and the heavy water sabotage in Norway.

card_event_shelling.name: card_event_shelling
card_event_shelling.title: SHELLING
card_event_shelling.text: Deal 1 damage to all enemy units and pin them. Enemy loses a kredit slot.
card_event_shelling.flavorText: A shell is usually a projectile that contains explosives, and shelling in war is heavy fire, usually from artillery, tanks or ships, on an area rather than a specific target. Shelling of enemy positions is common practice in warfare and was frequently utilized in WWII.

card_unit_111th_indian_brigade.name: card_unit_111th_indian_brigade
card_unit_111th_indian_brigade.title: 111th INDIAN BRIGADE
card_unit_111th_indian_brigade.text: When your HQ gains defense, it gains 1 extra defense.
card_unit_111th_indian_brigade.flavorText: The 111th Indian Infantry Brigade was part of the Chindits 3rd Indian Infantry Division of the Indian Army during WWII. The brigade was formed in 1943 in India as part of the Long Range Penetration Brigade which was a special operations unit of the British and Indian armies. The Chindits saw action in the Burma Campaign and during the Pacific War where they participated in raiding operations against the Imperial Japanese Army. The division often operated deep behind enemy lines and was tasked with attacking enemy forces, facilities and lines of communications. Four members of the Chindits were awarded the Victoria Cross for their services in WWII.

card_unit_1st_airborne.name: card_unit_1st_airborne
card_unit_1st_airborne.title: 1st AIRBORNE
card_unit_1st_airborne.text: At the start of your turn, -1 operation cost if Mobilized.
card_unit_1st_airborne.flavorText: The 1st Parachute Brigade was part of the 1st Airborne Division of the British Army during WWII and participated in numerous operations and battles during the war. The first missions was in 1942, a parachute drop in France during Operation Biting, followed by a successful glider mission into Norway where they sabotaged Germany’s Heavy Water production. That same year the brigade was sent to North Africa where they fought as an independent unit, both as paratroopers and as normal infantry on the front line. This is where they earned their nickname the Red Devils. In 1943 the brigade participated in the Allied invasion of Sicily where they sustained heavy casualties in combat and were therefore held in reserves for the next couple of operations in Italy. In 1944 the brigade participated in the Battle of Arnhem as part of Operation Market Garden, and after heavy fighting and casualties the remaining members of the brigade were forced to surrender to the Axis forces. When the war ended they joined the 6th Airborne Division for security duties in Palestine.

card_unit_4_5_inch_medium_gun.name: card_unit_4_5_inch_medium_gun
card_unit_4_5_inch_medium_gun.title: BL 4.5" MEDIUM GUN
card_unit_4_5_inch_medium_gun.flavorText: The BL 4.5 inch Medium Gun was a British gun used by British and Canadian field artillery in WWII. The 4.5inch gun was operated by a crew of 10 men and could fire up to 18.75 km, which matched the German 10.5 cm and 150 mm howitzer in range and firepower. The gun was first issued in 1938 and withdrawn from field service in 1945, but used for training purposes until 1959.

card_unit_blenheim_mk_iv.name: card_unit_blenheim_mk_iv
card_unit_blenheim_mk_iv.title: BLENHEIM Mk IV
card_unit_blenheim_mk_iv.flavorText: The Bristol Blenheim was a British light bomber/fighter designed and built by the Bristol Aeroplane Company. The aircraft was originally designed and produced as the fastest commercial aircraft in Europe, but its performance impressed the Air Ministry who ordered a modified design as the Type 142M for the Royal Air Force. The name was soon after changed to Blenheim Mk IV. The Blenheim became one of the first British aircraft with an all-metal stressed-skin construction, retractable landing gear, flaps, a powered gun turret and variable-pitch propellers. It was used by the RAF until 1944 and by then a total of 4,422 aircraft had been built.

card_unit_coldstream_guards.name: card_unit_coldstream_guards
card_unit_coldstream_guards.title: COLDSTREAM GUARDS
card_unit_coldstream_guards.text: Deployment: Add a NAVAL SUPPORT to your hand.
card_unit_coldstream_guards.flavorText: The Coldstream Guards are a part of the Guards Division of the British Army, and as the oldest regiment in the army it has participated in conflicts since the English Civil War in 1642. During WWII the battalions of the Coldstream Guards saw action in most theaters of the war. At the start of the war the 1st and 2nd battalions were part of the British Expeditionary Force in France, while the 3rd battalion was stationed in the Middle East. During the war two additional battalions were formed, the 4th and 5th, and they fought with the Guards Armored Division as dismounted infantry, first in North Africa and later in Europe. The 4th and 5th battalions were disbanded after the war.

card_unit_cromwell_mk_iv.name: card_unit_cromwell_mk_iv
card_unit_cromwell_mk_iv.title: CROMWELL Mk IV
card_unit_cromwell_mk_iv.text: When an enemy unit is pinned, Suppress it.
card_unit_cromwell_mk_iv.flavorText: The Cromwell was a British Cruiser tank used during WWII by the British Army. The Mk IV variant had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader/radio operator, driver, front gunner), 76 mm front armor and 20 mm armor at the back, a main armament of a QF 75 mm gun (6 Pounder) Mk V ROQF and a secondary armament of 2 x 7.92 mm Besa machine guns. The British Army started to use the Mk IV in 1943, but it first saw action during the Battle of Normandy in 1944 and later in Operation Market Garden. The tank had less firepower than similar sized German tanks, but the reduced thickness in armor made it more fast and maneuverable but at the same time more vulnerable. The Cromwell Mk IV became the most produced variant, with 1,935 tanks manufactured.

card_unit_lancashire_fusiliers.name: card_unit_lancashire_fusiliers
card_unit_lancashire_fusiliers.title: LANCASHIRE FUSILIERS
card_unit_lancashire_fusiliers.flavorText: The Lancashire Fusiliers was a line infantry regiment of the British Army that was active from 1688 to 1968. At the outbreak of WWII the regiment was stationed in British India and their first engagement was during the Burma Campaign where the 1st Battalion fought with the 77th Indian Infantry Brigade. The 2nd Battalion joined the British Expeditionary Forces and fought in Belgium and France before it was evacuated from Dunkirk. Parts of the 2nd Battalion participated in the Normandy landings during Operation Overlord and would later participate in two operations on French soil. In 1943 members of the Lancashire Fusiliers participated in the Italian Campaign and saw heavy fighting on the Gothic Line. In early 1945 parts of the regiment were sent to Palestine were they served for the rest of the war.

card_unit_manchester_ia.name: card_unit_manchester_ia
card_unit_manchester_ia.title: MANCHESTER IA
card_unit_manchester_ia.text: Deployment: Add a PRECISION BOMBING to your hand.
card_unit_manchester_ia.flavorText: The Avro 679 Manchester was a British twin-engine medium bomber developed and manufactured by the Avro aircraft company. The aircraft was the forerunner of the famous four-engine Avro Lancaster, but due to various failures it was not manufactured in great numbers and production was terminated early on in the war. Many technical issues with the aircraft were encountered, and although variants were produced in order to address these issues, the Manchester was considered too unreliable and it was withdrawn from operations in mid 1942. Due to the many technical issues, Bomber Command was often unable to raise significant numbers of the aircraft to participate in large scale bombing missions. For example, out of a force of over 400 bombers sent on a mission to bomb Berlin in November 1941, only 15 were Manchesters.

card_unit_no43_commando.name: card_unit_no43_commando
card_unit_no43_commando.title: No. 43 COMMANDO
card_unit_no43_commando.text: After you give an order, deal 2 damage to a random enemy.
card_unit_no43_commando.flavorText: Originally Commando units were all from the British army but in 1942 the Royal Marines were asked to organize their own Commando units. Around 6,000 men from the Royal Navy volunteered for the positions and in 1943, No. 43 Commando was formed, a unit of 450 men. The No. 43 Commandos and three other commando units formed the 2nd Special Service Brigade. From 1943 to 1945 the No. 43 Commando served in Italy, Yugoslavia and Greece.

card_unit_qf_40mm_mk_iii.name: card_unit_qf_40mm_mk_iii
card_unit_qf_40mm_mk_iii.title: QF 40mm Mk III
card_unit_qf_40mm_mk_iii.text: Deployment: Duplicate this unit if you have damaged the enemy HQ this turn.
card_unit_qf_40mm_mk_iii.flavorText: The QF 40mm Mk III gun, also referred to as the Bofors gun, was a Swedish made anti-aircraft auto-cannon designed in the 1930s. During WWII it was used in most theatres by the Allies, but also to some extent by the Axis powers. The QF 40 mm Mark III variant (QF stood for quick firing) was the standard light AA weapon of the British Army and considered vital in the defense of Britain and the Commonwealth countries after the fall of France. By the end of the war over 19,000 units had been produced and a small number of these weapons remain in service to this day.

card_unit_royal_ulster_rifles.name: card_unit_royal_ulster_rifles
card_unit_royal_ulster_rifles.title: ROYAL ULSTER RIFLES
card_unit_royal_ulster_rifles.text: When your HQ is damaged, deal that amount of damage to this unit instead.
card_unit_royal_ulster_rifles.flavorText: The Royal Ulster Rifles was an infantry rifle regiment of the British Army and saw service in the Second Boer War, WWI, WWII and the Korean War. When WWII started the regiment was serving in India with 31st Independent Brigade Group which was trained in mountain combat. The brigade was returned to the UK and converted into a glider-borne unit and the name was changed to 1st Airlanding Brigade, a subordinate of the 1st Airborne Division. The brigade participated in the D-Day landings, the Battle of Normandy and later the Rhine Crossing in 1945 as part of the 21st Army Group.

card_unit_tempest_mk_v.name: card_unit_tempest_mk_v
card_unit_tempest_mk_v.title: TEMPEST Mk V
card_unit_tempest_mk_v.flavorText: The Hawker Tempest was a British fighter aircraft used by the RAF and its Allies during WWII. The aircraft was originally known as Typhoon II and was an improved version of the Hawker Typhoon, designed to improve combat performance at high altitude. However, after considerable alterations from the Typhoon it was decided to rename the aircraft to Tempest, which came to be one of the most powerful fighters of WWII. When the Tempest entered service in 1944 it was used as a low-level interceptor against the V-1 flying bomb and the jet-propelled ME 262, and also as a ground attack aircraft in Operation Market Garden. Later it was also used in combat against Japan in South-East Asia as part of the Commonwealth Tiger Force. A total of 1,702 aircraft were built, including variants.

card_unit_typhoon_mk_ib.name: card_unit_typhoon_mk_ib
card_unit_typhoon_mk_ib.title: TYPHOON Mk IB
card_unit_typhoon_mk_ib.text: When a ground unit retreats, draw a card.
card_unit_typhoon_mk_ib.flavorText: The Hawker Typhoon, also nicknamed Tiffy by RAF pilots, was a British fighter-bomber produced by Hawker Aircraft. It was originally intended as a medium to high altitude interceptor, but it never took on that role due to several design problems. When the Typhoon came into service in 1941 it was the only aircraft that could catch up with the German Focke-Wulf and as a result it took on a role as a low-altitude interceptor. Later it established itself as a night time intruder and long-range fighter. From 1942 to 1943 bombs and later RP-3 rockets were added to its arsenal, and along with its 4 x 20mm Hispano autocannons it became the most powerful ground-attack aircraft of WWII.

card_unit_valentine_mk_iii.name: card_unit_valentine_mk_iii
card_unit_valentine_mk_iii.title: VALENTINE Mk III
card_unit_valentine_mk_iii.flavorText: The Valentine Mk III was a British made infantry tank, developed by Vickers and used during WWII. More than 8,000 Valentines were produced, from 1 up to 11 Marks, including many variants which made it account for almost a quarter of all British tanks produced during the war. The tank was supplied in large numbers to the USSR and other Allies, and it  proved to be both strong and reliable. The Mk III had a crew of 4 (commander, gunner, driver and a loader), main armament of a QF 2-pounder (40 mm) and secondary armament of a 7.92 mm BESA machine-gun. There are several explanations for the name and according to the most popular one is that the design was presented to the War Office on St. Valentine's Day, February 14, 1940.

card_unit_welsh_guards.name: card_unit_welsh_guards
card_unit_welsh_guards.title: WELSH GUARDS
card_unit_welsh_guards.flavorText: The Welsh Guards are a part of the Guards Division and one of the Foot Guards Regiment of the British Army. The regiment grew from 1 to 3 battalions during WWII and throughout the war they served in various theaters. The 1st Battalion fought in numerous campaigns in Western Europe, first as part of the British Expeditionary Force in Belgium and France, and later with 2nd Battalion as part of the Guards Armoured Division in Operation Overlord and Operation Market Garden. The 3rd Battalion fought in the North African Campaign, the Tunisia Campaign and lastly in the Italian campaigns of 1943.

card_event_aa_barrage.name: card_event_aa_barrage
card_event_aa_barrage.title: AA BARRAGE
card_event_aa_barrage.text: Target air unit must retreat. Give your HQ +2 defense.
card_event_aa_barrage.flavorText: The purpose of an AA barrage is to direct a heavy curtain of artillery fire at the sky in order to shoot down, or prevent enemy aircraft from completing their attacking objectives.

card_event_atlantic_convoy.name: card_event_atlantic_convoy
card_event_atlantic_convoy.title: ATLANTIC CONVOY
card_event_atlantic_convoy.text: Add one random US unit with cost 3 or less to the support line and another to hand.
card_event_atlantic_convoy.flavorText: As an island, the United Kingdom was highly dependent on imported goods from their allies in order to continue the fight. The Atlantic convoys that supplied the British war effort came mainly from North America and were protected for the most part by the British and Canadian navies and air forces.

card_event_blockade.name: card_event_blockade
card_event_blockade.title: BLOCKADE
card_event_blockade.text: Deal 2 damage to each enemy unit. Deal 3 instead if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_event_blockade.flavorText: The Blockade of Germany during WWII, also known as the Economic War, was an effort conducted by the United Kingdom to restrict supplies required by Germany for their war efforts. This blockade is what the Axis and Allies fought over in the Battle of the Atlantic, the longest military campaign in WWII.

card_event_carpet_bombing.name: card_event_carpet_bombing
card_event_carpet_bombing.title: CARPET BOMBING
card_event_carpet_bombing.text: Deal 3 damage to all enemy units.
card_event_carpet_bombing.flavorText: Carpet bombing is an aerial bombing conducted to inflict damage in every part of a selected area of land. This was done by both the Allies and the Axis, and used against civilian, industrial and military targets.

card_event_close_air_support.name: card_event_close_air_support
card_event_close_air_support.title: CLOSE AIR SUPPORT
card_event_close_air_support.text: Target friendly British air unit and its adjacent units get +1+1.
card_event_close_air_support.flavorText: Close air support is a military tactic that uses aircraft to attack hostile targets that are operating close to friendly forces. The CAS tactics developed by the British during the campaign in North Africa was the basis for the Allied system used later in the war.

card_event_convoy_175.name: card_event_convoy_175
card_event_convoy_175.title: CONVOY HX 175
card_event_convoy_175.flavorText: In order to protect their merchant fleet and vital supplies, the British adopted a convoy system that was used throughout WWII. Each convoy consisted of 30 to 70 ships, mostly unarmed merchant ships combined with armed support. Each convoy had its code name, and CONVOY HX 175 was part of the HX convoys, sailing from Halifax Canada to Liverpool and back.

card_event_cup_of_tea.name: card_event_cup_of_tea
card_event_cup_of_tea.title: CUP OF TEA
card_event_cup_of_tea.flavorText: Besides representing an important feature of British culture, the act of making and drinking tea was also a time for bonding, raising morale and courage, plus it was a good way to keep soldiers hydrated and refreshed. The "Keep Calm And Carry On" slogan is from a motivational poster produced by the British government in preparation for WWII.

card_event_daylight_bombing.name: card_event_daylight_bombing
card_event_daylight_bombing.title: DAYLIGHT BOMBING
card_event_daylight_bombing.text: Deal 2 damage to any target. The enemy loses a kredit slot.
card_event_daylight_bombing.flavorText: Daylight bombing is an aerial bombing of a target while there is still light of day.

card_event_desert_rats.name: card_event_desert_rats
card_event_desert_rats.title: THE DESERT RATS
card_event_desert_rats.text: Deal 1 damage to an enemy unit and Pin it.
card_event_desert_rats.flavorText: The Desert Rats was a nickname for the 7th Armored Division of the British Army. The Division earned its nickname after their distinguished service in the North Africa Campaign, where the British and Allies fought and won against the Italians and the notorious German Afrika Korps led by General Erwin Rommel. The Desert Rats also fought in the Italian Campaign and landed in Normandy on D-Day from where they fought their way across Europe.

card_event_finest_hour.name: card_event_finest_hour
card_event_finest_hour.title: FINEST HOUR
card_event_finest_hour.text: Give an air unit +1+1 and Blitz.
card_event_finest_hour.flavorText: "Finest Hour" originates from a speech delivered by Winston Churchill to the House of Commons in 1940 during the Battle of France.

card_event_fortification.name: card_event_fortification
card_event_fortification.title: FORTIFICATION
card_event_fortification.flavorText: From 1940-1942 Britain was under threat of a German invasion and as part of an anti-invasion plan both the military and civilians were mobilized into building field fortifications across the United Kingdom, and large areas, especially in southern England, were transformed into a prepared battlefield.

card_event_for_precision_bombing.name: card_event_for_precision_bombing
card_event_for_precision_bombing.title: PRECISION BOMBING
card_event_for_precision_bombing.text: Reduce cost by the highest attack on a bomber you control. Destroy an enemy unit.
card_event_for_precision_bombing.flavorText: Precision bombing is an attempt at highly accurate aerial bombing of a legitimate military target, with the aim of limiting collateral damage.

card_event_for_the_king.name: card_event_for_the_king
card_event_for_the_king.title: FOR THE KING
card_event_for_the_king.text: Deal 5 damage to an enemy tank.
card_event_for_the_king.flavorText: George VI (Albert Frederick Arthur George; December 14, 1895 – February 6, 1952) was King of the United Kingdom and the Dominions of the British Commonwealth during WWII. He reigned from December 11, 1936 until his death and was the last Emperor of India and the first Head of the Commonwealth.

card_event_hms_illustrious.name: card_event_hms_illustrious
card_event_hms_illustrious.title: HMS ILLUSTRIOUS
card_event_hms_illustrious.text: Add two SWORDFISH MK I to your support line. Give them Blitz.
card_event_hms_illustrious.flavorText: HMS Illustrious was a British aircraft carrier built before the war and launched in 1939. The ship carried 36 aircraft and was used in the frontline throughout the war. Its most notable achievement was when it sank an Italian battleship and damaged two others in the Battle of Taranto in 1940. The carrier was last used in combat in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, but was sent home early due to mechanical failure. HMS Illustrious was decommissioned and sold for scrap in 1956.

card_event_interception.name: card_event_interception
card_event_interception.title: INTERCEPTION
card_event_interception.text: Counter an enemy order that targets a friendly target.
card_event_interception.flavorText: An interceptor aircraft, or simply interceptor, is a type of fighter aircraft designed to attack enemy aircraft, particularly bombers and reconnaissance aircraft, as they approach. During WWII, British fighters such as the Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane developed an impressive reputation as interceptors, especially during the Battle of Britain.

card_event_mi_5.name: card_event_mi_5
card_event_mi_5.title: MI5
card_event_mi_5.text: Your enemy puts a random card in hand on top of their deck. You draw a card.
card_event_mi_5.flavorText: The MI5 (Military Intelligence, Section 5) is the United Kingdom's domestic counter-intelligence and security agency. During WWII its major wartime success was the so-called "double-cross" system, which placed emphasis on turning captured spies into British double agents and using them to mislead enemy.

card_event_monty.name: card_event_monty
card_event_monty.title: MONTY
card_event_monty.text: Pin target unit and adjacent units. Draw a card.
card_event_monty.flavorText: Field Marshal Bernard Law Montgomery, 1st Viscount Montgomery of Alamein, nicknamed "Monty" and "The Spartan General". He commanded the British Eighth Army in the North African campaign, the Allied invasion of Sicily and the Allied invasion of Italy. Later, he was in command of all Allied ground forces during Operation Overlord and continued in command of the 21st Army Group in the campaign in North West Europe.

card_event_national_fire_service.name: card_event_national_fire_service
card_event_national_fire_service.title: NATIONAL FIRE SERVICE
card_event_national_fire_service.text: When your HQ receives damage this turn, reduce the damage to 1.
card_event_national_fire_service.flavorText: The National Fire Service (NFS) was a fire service created in Great Britain during WWII. The NFS had full-time and part-time members, male and female, and were often called to attend the aftermath of German bombing raids and coastal shelling from France, often while these attacks were still ongoing.

card_event_naval_power.name: card_event_naval_power
card_event_naval_power.title: NAVAL POWER
card_event_naval_power.text: Pin an enemy unit. Give your HQ +3 defense.
card_event_naval_power.flavorText: The British Royal Navy was far more powerful than the German Kriegsmarine throughout WWII and their navy supremacy played a vital role in winning the war. The Royal Navy was responsible for protecting friendly ports, trade and supply routes, and it enabled the deployment of Allied troops in remote parts of the world such as North Africa, the Mediterranean and the Far East. The Royal Navy also played a vital role in blocking Axis supply routes, for example, to North-Africa and Malta.

card_event_naval_support.name: card_event_naval_support
card_event_naval_support.title: NAVAL SUPPORT
card_event_naval_support.text: Change the attack on target unit to be equal to its defense.
card_event_naval_support.flavorText: During WWII, battleships, cruisers and destroyers were often used to bombard shore installations in an attempt of reducing fortifications and wearing down the opposing forces. Naval gunfire support was both used for defensive and offensive purposes and often used to supplement land-based artillery.

card_event_night_raid.name: card_event_night_raid
card_event_night_raid.title: NIGHT RAID
card_event_night_raid.text: Copy random order from enemy deck. Add a No. 10 COMMANDO to support line.
card_event_night_raid.flavorText: British and Allied commandos served in all the theaters of war and their operations ranged from small groups of men landing from the sea or by parachute, to a brigade of assault troops spearheading the Allied invasions. Operation Frankton was a commando raid conducted in 1942, and by night against the vessels in Bay of Biscay’s Bordeaux port in France, which was occupied by the Germans. The plan involved taking 12 men on six canoes, by submarine, and to paddle from the Gironde Estuary area to Bordeaux by night. Although only 2 of 12 men survived the mission, the raid was considered a success and Winston Churchill believed it to have shortened the war by 6 whole months.

card_event_radar_alert.name: card_event_radar_alert
card_event_radar_alert.title: RADAR ALERT
card_event_radar_alert.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, add a random British air unit of similar cost.
card_event_radar_alert.flavorText: The British radar air defense system was code-named Chain Home and served as the backbone in their defense during the Battle of Britain. The system consisted of a ring of coastal radar installations, each with a maximum range of 322 km (200 miles), which meant they could detect German formations all the way to their bases in occupied France. This provided the RAF with nearly a half hour of lead time which could be used to gather squadrons of fighters to intercept threats. Each radar installation sent out a stream of short-pulse radio waves which scattered upon striking an object, such as an aircraft, and some of the energy returned as an echo that was displayed on a cathode-ray tube. The time between transmission and echo reception was used to calculate the distance to the reflecting object.

card_event_rescue_mission.name: card_event_rescue_mission
card_event_rescue_mission.title: RESCUE MISSION
card_event_rescue_mission.text: When a friendly unit is destroyed, add two copies of it to your hand.
card_event_rescue_mission.flavorText: The RAF Air Sea Rescue Services (ASRS) were formed in 1941 to rescue surviving aircrew who were shot down over sea during the Battle of Britain. Their motto was "The sea shall not have them". Prior to its establishment, 200 pilots and aircrew had been lost to the sea during the battle. The air-sea rescue squadrons of the ASRS flew a variety of aircraft, usually ones that had been withdrawn from front line services. The role of aircraft in the ASRS, was mainly to locate downed airmen and to keep them alive, by dropping them survival equipment and supplies until they were picked up by an amphibious aircraft or the Royal Navy's Naval Sea Rescue Services. By the end of WWII, more than 8,000 aircrew and 5,000 civilians had been rescued from the sea.

card_event_supply_drop.name: card_event_supply_drop
card_event_supply_drop.title: SUPPLY DROP
card_event_supply_drop.text: Give a tank or infantry +4 defense and Guard. Smokescreen is removed.
card_event_supply_drop.flavorText: A supply drop, or airdrop, is a way of delivering supplies via military transport aircraft. This was a method developed during WWII and used to resupply otherwise inaccessible troops.

card_event_tactical_withdrawal.name: card_event_tactical_withdrawal
card_event_tactical_withdrawal.title: TACTICAL WITHDRAWAL
card_event_tactical_withdrawal.text: Retreat a friendly unit in the frontline and fully repair it. It can operate again this turn.
card_event_tactical_withdrawal.flavorText: When a defending force is outmatched or fighting on disadvantageous ground, the situation may call for a tactical withdrawal. This means that the defending forces withdraw, but the aim is to cause as much damage to the enemy as possible and to slow down their advance. This can be conducted with various tactics, for example, setting booby traps or mines, obstacles or fortifications, luring the enemy into a prepared artillery barrage, or using scorched earth tactics. Perhaps the most famous retreat in British military history is when 338,000 British, French and Belgian troops were evacuated from the French coast of Dunkirk. The Allied troops were cornered and facing imminent destruction by the advancing German forces, but when Adolf Hitler halted the advance of his Panzer tanks, the British Expeditionary Force was able to fortify the port of Dunkirk and initiate a frantic retreat codenamed Operation Dynamo.

card_event_the_commonwealth.name: card_event_the_commonwealth
card_event_the_commonwealth.title: THE COMMONWEALTH
card_event_the_commonwealth.text: Deal 20 damage to target HQ if your HQ has 30 or more defense. Draw 4 cards.
card_event_the_commonwealth.flavorText: Forces from the countries of the British Commonwealth were involved in all major theaters of the war. There were self-governing Dominions of Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa. Then there were those Dominions that were wholly or partly governed from London, including India as well as the West Indies and British colonies in Africa and the Far East. At the outbreak of war in 1939, India and the other colonial Dominions of the Empire had no choice and automatically joined in the war on the side of Britain. The Dominions made their own decision to enter the war on the British side. The Irish Free State decided on neutrality.

card_event_the_empire.name: card_event_the_empire
card_event_the_empire.title: THE EMPIRE STRIKES
card_event_the_empire.text: Deal damage to each enemy equal to 1 plus the number of bombers you control.
card_event_the_empire.flavorText: In 1939 the United Kingdom controlled numerous crown colonies, protectorates and the Indian Empire. It also maintained close ties to four nations; Australia, Canada, South Africa, and New Zealand that all were part of the Commonwealth. The British Commonwealth had direct or political and economic control of 25% of the world's population, and 30% of its land mass, and was considered global super power at the outbreak of WWII.

card_event_ultra.name: card_event_ultra
card_event_ultra.title: ULTRA
card_event_ultra.text: Counter an enemy order and draw a card.
card_event_ultra.flavorText: ULTRA was a codename the Allies used to describe German coded messages they had managed to intercept and decode. This included the famous decryption of the Enigma, a cryptography machine used by the Germans.

card_event_unexpected_resistance.name: card_event_unexpected_resistance
card_event_unexpected_resistance.title: UNEXPECTED RESISTANCE
card_event_unexpected_resistance.text: Pin a unit that moves to the frontline. If it has Blitz, destroy it instead.
card_event_unexpected_resistance.flavorText: During WWII, the British often fought against the odds, being outnumbered or fighting in the harshest conditions. The most famous defensive battle of WWII is the Battle of Britain, where the RAF defended the United Kingdom against large-scale attacks by the German Luftwaffe. Another incident worth mentioning happened during Operation Market Garden in September 1944. Although the operation was a military disaster for the Allies, the heroic fight put up by the British 1st Airborne Division and the 1st Polish Parachute Brigade during the Battle of Arnhem is remembered as an example of courage and endurance. Greatly outnumbered by the Germans, trapped and unable to be relieved, the British and Polish troops put up a heavy resistance and fought for several days. Their story is told in the 1977 cinematic masterpiece "A Bridge Too Far".

card_unit_17_pounder.name: card_unit_17_pounder
card_unit_17_pounder.title: 17 POUNDER
card_unit_17_pounder.text: Deployment: Pin target enemy unit. Draw a card if it is a tank.
card_unit_17_pounder.flavorText: The 17 pounder, also known as Ordnance Quick-Firing 17-pounder, was a British made 76.2 mm (3 inch) gun used in WWII. It was used as an anti-tank gun and could penetrate all but the thickest German armor. The gun was also mounted on a number of British tanks, such as the Sherman Firefly and the Cruiser Mark VIII Challenger.

card_unit_1st_airlanding_brigade.name: card_unit_1st_airlanding_brigade
card_unit_1st_airlanding_brigade.title: 1st AIRLANDING BRIGADE
card_unit_1st_airlanding_brigade.text: Deployment: Retreat a unit in the frontline. If it is empty, gets Blitz.
card_unit_1st_airlanding_brigade.flavorText: The 1st Airlanding Brigade was an airborne infantry brigade of the British Army during WWII and the glider infantry formation assigned to the 1st Airborne Division. The brigade only participated in combat on two occasions, in Operation Ladbroke during the Allied invasion of Sicily in 1943, and in Operation Market Garden in 1944. During Operation Market Garden the 1st Airlanding Brigade along with the rest of 1st Airborne Division held out against overwhelming German odds and suffered heavy losses. Of the 2,526 men of 1st Airlanding Brigade that left England for Operation Market Garden 230 were killed, 476 evacuated and 1,822 were missing or prisoners of war. After the surrender of Germany in 1945, the brigade was sent to Norway to disarm a German garrison and shortly after it was disbanded.

card_unit_22nd_guards_brigade.name: card_unit_22nd_guards_brigade
card_unit_22nd_guards_brigade.title: 22nd GUARDS BRIGADE
card_unit_22nd_guards_brigade.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of its third turn on the battlefield.
card_unit_22nd_guards_brigade.flavorText: The 22nd Guards Brigade was a British infantry unit known for its distinguished service during WWII. It was converted to the 200th Guards Brigade in 1942 and then to the 201st Guards Motor Brigade Group in 1942.  The brigade saw extensive active service in the North African Campaign but was forced to surrender in June 1942 when Tobruk was captured by German and Italian forces. The Brigade was reformed in August 1942 and trained as motorized infantry before being sent to Syria. The Brigade was attached to the XXX Corps of the British Eighth Army and participated in numerous battles and military campaigns, including the Tunisian Campaign and the Italian Campaign. Due to heavy casualties and lack of guards replacements, the brigade was sent back to Britain in 1944 where it became a training brigade for the whole Brigade of Guards for the rest of the war.

card_unit_25_pounder.name: card_unit_25_pounder
card_unit_25_pounder.title: 25 POUNDER
card_unit_25_pounder.flavorText: The Ordnance QF 25-pounder, or also called 25 pounder or 25-pdr, was the major British field gun and howitzer used during WWII and in later conflicts. It was introduced just before the war started, combining high-angle and direct-fire, relatively high rates of fire, and a reasonably lethal shell in a highly mobile piece.

card_unit_2_pounder.name: card_unit_2_pounder
card_unit_2_pounder.title: 2 POUNDER
card_unit_2_pounder.flavorText: The Ordnance QF 2-pounder (QF for "quick firing") was a 40 mm British anti-tank and vehicle-mounted gun that was used by the Allies in WWII. The 2-pounder was a typical main armament on armored cars, such as the Daimler, but also a common main gun on British tanks early in the war. However, as Axis tank armor improved the gun was gradually replaced by the 6-pounder, but some remained in service until the end of the war.

card_unit_3_7_inch_aa_gun.name: card_unit_3_7_inch_aa_gun
card_unit_3_7_inch_aa_gun.title: 3.7” ANTI-AIR GUN
card_unit_3_7_inch_aa_gun.text: Deployment: Pin all enemy air units.
card_unit_3_7_inch_aa_gun.flavorText: The QF 3.7 inch anti-air gun was British made and was the primary heavy AA gun used by the British and Commonwealth forces in WWII.
