It was equivalent to the German 88 flak gun, and also had a secondary role as an anti-tank gun, but since it was two tonnes heavier than the German counterpart, it was less suitable for the role. The 3.7 inch anti-air gun was used in all major theaters of WWII, except the Eastern front.

card_unit_5th_brigade.name: card_unit_5th_brigade
card_unit_5th_brigade.title: 5th BRIGADE
card_unit_5th_brigade.flavorText: The 5th Infantry Brigade was a part of the 2nd Division of the British Army during WWII. The Brigade was sent to France in 1939 and served at the Franco-Belgian border until it was evacuated at Dunkirk in May 1940. In 1942, the 5th Brigade served in the Burma Campaign and the Battle of Kohima.

card_unit_6_pounder.name: card_unit_6_pounder
card_unit_6_pounder.title: 6 POUNDER
card_unit_6_pounder.flavorText: The 6 pounder, also known as Ordnance Quick-Firing 6-pounder 7 cwt, was a British 57 mm gun which was mainly used as an anti-tank gun by the British Army and the Allies during WWII. The 6 pounder was also used as a main armament a number of Allied tanks and other armored vehicles.

card_unit_85_pioneer_company.name: card_unit_85_pioneer_company
card_unit_85_pioneer_company.title: 85 PIONEER COMPANY
card_unit_85_pioneer_company.text: The first order you play each turn costs 1 less.
card_unit_85_pioneer_company.flavorText: The 85th Pioneer Company served under the Royal Pioneer Corps of the British Army during WWII. On D-Day in 1944 the 85th Company served with the 6th Beach Group assisting the units landing on Sword Beach. Pioneer units performed a variety of tasks during WWII, and in all theaters of war, including stretcher-bearing, handling all types of stores, laying prefabricated track on beaches or airfields, and working various logistical operations.

card_unit_albacore.name: card_unit_albacore
card_unit_albacore.title: ALBACORE Mk I
card_unit_albacore.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to an enemy ground unit and pin it.
card_unit_albacore.flavorText: The Fairey Albacore was a British made carrier-borne biplane, designed and built for the Royal Navy Fleet Air Arm and used during WWII. The Albacore had a three-man crew and was used for spotting and reconnaissance as well as level bombing, dive bombing and torpedo bombing. It was designed and built to replace the Fairey Swordfish, but it proved less popular than its predecessor as the pilots considered it less maneuverable and it suffered from reliability problems when it was first introduced. The aircraft was used in a combat role from 1940 to 1944, but from 1943 the Fleet Air Arm service started replacing it with the Barracuda.

card_unit_argyllshire_highlanders.name: card_unit_argyllshire_highlanders
card_unit_argyllshire_highlanders.title: ARGYLLSHIRE HIGHLANDERS
card_unit_argyllshire_highlanders.text: Gets +1+1 when you deploy or add a Guard unit.
card_unit_argyllshire_highlanders.flavorText: The Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders was an  infantry regiment of the British Army and was created in 1881. The regiment was expanded to fifteen battalions during WWI (1914–1918) and nine during WWII (1939–1945) which between them participated in all theaters of the war.

card_unit_baluch_regiment.name: card_unit_baluch_regiment
card_unit_baluch_regiment.title: BALUCH REGIMENT
card_unit_baluch_regiment.flavorText: The 10th Baluch or Baluch Regiment was part of the British Indian Army from 1922 to 1947. During WWII the regiment participated in numerous battles and had acquired a distinguished war record by the end of the war. The 10th Baluch raised in total 18 battalions in WWII, but most of them were disbanded in 1945.

card_unit_black_watch.name: card_unit_black_watch
card_unit_black_watch.title: BLACK WATCH
card_unit_black_watch.text: Orders in enemy hand cost 2 more.
card_unit_black_watch.flavorText: The Black Watch is a name of an infantry battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland that was created in 1881. During WWII the Black Watch battalions of the regiment served in most major theaters of the war, including North Africa, Italy, North West Europe and Burma. It's uncertain where the "Black Watch" name comes from but it may originate from the uniform plaids of dark tartan which the companies were provided and wore as part of its everyday uniform until 1940.

card_unit_british_sherman_firefly.name: card_unit_british_sherman_firefly
card_unit_british_sherman_firefly.title: M4 FIREFLY
card_unit_british_sherman_firefly.text: Deployment: Deal 5 damage to an enemy tank.
card_unit_british_sherman_firefly.flavorText: The Sherman Firefly was a tank used by the British and the Allies in WWII that was put into production in early 1944. It was based on the US M4 Sherman, but fitted with the British 17-pounder anti-tank gun as its main weapon. The M4 Firefly had a crew of 4 (Commander, gunner, loader/radio-operator, driver) and for secondary armament it had a 0.50 Browning M2 machine gun mounted on the turret and a coaxial .30 in (7.62 mm) Browning M1919 machine gun which was generally not mounted.  Approximately 2200 units were built during the war and it performed well on the battlefield, with enough firepower to knockout Tigers and Panthers at long range, as well as tanks like the Panzer IVs and StuGs.

card_unit_churchill.name: card_unit_churchill
card_unit_churchill.title: CHURCHILL Mk IV
card_unit_churchill.flavorText: The Mark IV Churchill was a British made heavy infantry tank. It was one of the heaviest tanks used by the Allies in WWII, with a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader/radio operator, driver, co-driver/hull gunner), and several variations were produced throughout the war. It was slow, but had the ability to cross difficult ground and several variations were produced. The tank was named after British Prime Minister Winston Churchill.

card_unit_coastal_gun.name: card_unit_coastal_gun
card_unit_coastal_gun.title: 9.2” COASTAL GUN
card_unit_coastal_gun.text: Damage dealt by this unit adds equal defense to your HQ.
card_unit_coastal_gun.flavorText: The 9.2 inch coastal gun, also known as BL 9.2-inch Mk IX or Mk X, was a British coast defense gun in service from 1899 to the 1950s. Approximately 43 guns were deployed in fixed defenses of ports throughout the British Empire during WWII, and their role was to defeat enemy ships attacking the ships in a port. The 9.2 inch coastal gun fired 170 kg shells and had a maximum firing range of 26.7 km (29,200 yd).

card_unit_comet1.name: card_unit_comet1
card_unit_comet1.title: A34 COMET
card_unit_comet1.text: When this unit deals damage to enemy HQ, draw a card.
card_unit_comet1.flavorText: The A34 Comet was a British cruiser tank, developed and used during the late stages of WWII. The A34 Comet was considered one of the best British tanks and proved very effective against late German tanks. It had a crew of 5 (Commander, gunner, loader/operator, driver, hull gunner) and a main armament of 77 mm HV gun and a secondary armament of 2 x 7.92 mm Besa machine guns.

card_unit_commandos.name: card_unit_commandos
card_unit_commandos.title: No. 10 COMMANDO
card_unit_commandos.text: After you give a British order, deal 1 damage to a random enemy.
card_unit_commandos.flavorText: The commandos were an elite light infantry or special operations force unit, often specializing in amphibious landings, parachuting or abseiling. No. 10 (Inter-Allied) Commando was a unit of the British Army during WWII and included volunteers from France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark, Poland and Yugoslavia, but also Germans and Austrians. No. 10 Commando served in most theaters, primarily in small numbers attached to other formations, never as a complete unit.

card_unit_crusader_mk_ii.name: card_unit_crusader_mk_ii
card_unit_crusader_mk_ii.title: CRUSADER Mk II
card_unit_crusader_mk_ii.text: When you give a British order, draw a card.
card_unit_crusader_mk_ii.flavorText: The Crusader Mk II was an A15 Crusader variation, a British cruiser tank used during WWII. It had a crew of 4-5 men and was fitted with a 2 pounder gun and 1 or 2 × Besa machine guns. After the North African Campaign, the tank was no longer used in the front-lines and was replaced with the US-supplied M3 Grant and Sherman medium tanks.

card_unit_daimler_mk_ii.name: card_unit_daimler_mk_ii
card_unit_daimler_mk_ii.title: HUMBER Mk II
card_unit_daimler_mk_ii.flavorText: The Humber Mk II was a British armored reconnaissance car, used by the British and their Allies in WWII. It had a crew of 3 (driver, gunner, commander), a main armament of Mk I-III 15 mm Besa machine gun and a secondary armament of 7.92 mm Besa machine gun.

card_unit_gladiator.name: card_unit_gladiator
card_unit_gladiator.title: GLADIATOR Mk I
card_unit_gladiator.flavorText: The Gloster Gladiator (or Gloster SS.37) was a British biplane fighter. It was used by both the Royal Air Force (RAF) and the Fleet Air Arm (FAA) (as the Sea Gladiator variant). Although the Gladiator was the last biplane fighter aircraft put in service by the RAF it was used throughout WWII and saw action in almost all theaters of the war.

card_unit_gladiator_escort.name: card_unit_gladiator_escort
card_unit_gladiator_escort.title: GLADIATOR ESCORT
card_unit_gladiator_escort.text: Damage to STIRLING Mk I S3 is dealt to this unit instead.

card_unit_grenadier_guards.name: card_unit_grenadier_guards
card_unit_grenadier_guards.title: GRENADIER GUARDS
card_unit_grenadier_guards.flavorText: The Grenadier Guards is an infantry regiment of the British army and can be traced back to year 1656. At the start of WWII they were part of the British Expeditionary Force, but after the defeat in the Battle of Dunkirk they took on defensive duties in the UK. In 1944 the 1st, 2nd and 4th battalions were sent to serve in the North West Europe Campaign while the 3rd, 5th and 6th Battalions were sent to serve in the North African Campaign, the Italian Campaign and the final stages of the Tunisia Campaign. The Battalions of the Grenadier Guards saw action in most major military operations and battles from 1944 to 1945.

card_unit_hampden.name: card_unit_hampden
card_unit_hampden.title: HAMPDEN Mk I
card_unit_hampden.flavorText: The Hampden Mk I, full name Handley Page HP.52 Hampden, was a British twin-engine medium bomber used by the Royal Air Force during WWII. Early on the British realized that the aircraft was no match to the Luftwaffe fighters, and was therefore mostly used for nighttime operations. In 1942 the Hampden was withdrawn from Bomber Command, but it was used as a long-range torpedo bomber and reconnaissance aircraft to some extent after that.

card_unit_hudson.name: card_unit_hudson
card_unit_hudson.title: HUDSON Mk III
card_unit_hudson.text: When Hudson destroys a unit, it gets Fury until end of turn.
card_unit_hudson.flavorText: The Lockheed Hudson was an American light bomber and coastal reconnaissance aircraft specially built for the Royal Air Force at the start of WWII. The aircraft was used by the Allies throughout the war, mostly in maritime operations but also in transport and training roles as well as delivering agents into occupied France.

card_unit_hurricane.name: card_unit_hurricane
card_unit_hurricane.title: HURRICANE Mk I
card_unit_hurricane.flavorText: The Hawker Hurricane was a British single-seat fighter aircraft used by the Royal Air Force (RAF) and British Allies. The Hurricane was used in all the major theaters of WWII, and during the battle of Britain the Hurricane inflicted 60 percent of the losses sustained by the Luftwaffe in the engagement. It was slow, but maneuverable and could take a lot of damage, and even though it was not equal to the German BF 109 fighter or the British Spitfire in 1on1 dogfights, it did a very good job in taking down the German bombers.

card_unit_hurricane_vs2.name: card_unit_hurricane_vs2
card_unit_hurricane_vs2.title: HURRICANE Mk IIA
card_unit_hurricane_vs2.flavorText: The Hurricane Mark IIA was a British fighter aircraft, built in 1940 and used by the Allies throughout WWII. The aircraft was a Hawker Hurricane variant where they first experimented with fitting cannons, first with two 20 mm (.79 in) Oerlikon cannons, one under each wing, and later with four 20 mm (.79 in) Hispano Mk II cannons, two under each wing.

card_unit_lancaster.name: card_unit_lancaster
card_unit_lancaster.title: LANCASTER Mk I
card_unit_lancaster.flavorText: The Avro Lancaster was a British four-engine heavy bomber used by the Royal Air Force (RAF) during WWII. The aircraft had a standard crew of 7 men, and it had the greatest bomb carrying capacity of all WWII bombers, which meant it could carry the biggest bombs the RAF had in their arsenal. The Lancaster was first used in the strategic bombing offensive over Europe in 1942 and after that it operated in almost every major bombing raid in the European conflict.

card_unit_lancaster_biii.name: card_unit_lancaster_biii
card_unit_lancaster_biii.title: LANCASTER B.III
card_unit_lancaster_biii.text: When this unit damages a HQ, cards in enemy hand cost +1 kredit.
card_unit_lancaster_biii.flavorText: The Avro Lancaster B.III (Special) was a British heavy bomber variant used by the Allies during WWII. This variant was built to carry the "Upkeep" bouncing bomb for dam busting raids. The bomb bay doors were removed and the dam busting bomb was mounted under the aircraft. A chain driven by a hydraulic motor gave the bomb its backspin when it was dropped. In total 23 aircraft of this type were built.

card_unit_mathilda_mk_ii.name: card_unit_mathilda_mk_ii
card_unit_mathilda_mk_ii.title: MATILDA Mk II
card_unit_mathilda_mk_ii.text: Units damaged by MATILDA Mk II are pinned.
card_unit_mathilda_mk_ii.flavorText: The Infantry Tank Mark II, better known as Matilda, was a British tank used in WWII. With its heavy armor it served well as an infantry support tank despite it having limited speed and armament. The Matilda had a crew of 4 (driver, gunner, loader, commander) and had a mounted 2 pounder (40 mm) and a 7.92 mm Besa machine gun.

card_unit_mosquito.name: card_unit_mosquito
card_unit_mosquito.title: MOSQUITO FB Mk VI
card_unit_mosquito.text: Deployment: Deal 4 damage to an enemy unit.
card_unit_mosquito.flavorText: The de Havilland DH.98 Mosquito, also known as "Mossie", was a British twin-engine shoulder-winged multi-role combat aircraft. The aircraft had a crew of two (pilot and navigator) sat side by side. It was used during and after the WWII by the British and the Allies and served as light bomber, fighter-bomber, night fighter, maritime strike aircraft and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.

card_unit_p38_lightning_raf.name: card_unit_p38_lightning_raf
card_unit_p38_lightning_raf.title: RAAF LIGHTNING F-4
card_unit_p38_lightning_raf.flavorText: The Lockheed P-38 Lightning was an American fighter aircraft manufactured and used by the Allies during WWII. The British ordered variants of the P-38 (named Lightning I and II) through the Lend Lease program and used it extensively as a long-range bomber escort. The P-38 was used for various other purposes, such as interception, dive bombing, level bombing, ground attack, night fighting, photo reconnaissance, radar and visual path-finding for bombers and evacuation missions.

card_unit_p40_kittyhawk.name: card_unit_p40_kittyhawk
card_unit_p40_kittyhawk.title: P-40 KITTYHAWK
card_unit_p40_kittyhawk.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to an enemy ground target.
card_unit_p40_kittyhawk.flavorText: The P-40 Kittyhawk, also known as Curtiss P-40 Warhawk, was an American all-metal fighter and ground-attack aircraft that was produced and used in WWII by the Allies. The P-40s was first used in combat by the British Commonwealth squadrons in the Middle East and North African campaigns. The British and the Soviets named the aircraft Kittyhawk, but the Americans used the name Warhawk.

card_unit_royal_engineers.name: card_unit_royal_engineers
card_unit_royal_engineers.title: 26 ENGINEER REGIMENT
card_unit_royal_engineers.text: Deployment: Give all other friendly units +2 defense.
card_unit_royal_engineers.flavorText: The 26th Engineer Regiment was attached to the Corps of Royal Engineers, better known as the Royal Engineers (RE) or as the Sappers of the British Army. During WWII they disposed of bombs and maintained railways, roads, water supply, bridges, transportation, buildings and defensive structures etc. Their motto was “ubique”, meaning everywhere.

card_unit_royal_west_kents.name: card_unit_royal_west_kents
card_unit_royal_west_kents.title: ROYAL WEST KENTS
card_unit_royal_west_kents.text: Your other Guard units have +2 attack and Blitz.
card_unit_royal_west_kents.flavorText: The Queen’s Own Royal West Kent Regiment was an infantry regiment of the British Army based in the county of Kent. The bulk of the regiment was part of the British Expeditionary Force in France at the outset of the war and suffered heavy losses in the retreat from Dunkirk. In 1943 it participated in the later stages of the Tunisian Campaign, again suffering severe losses. In 1944 it fought in Italy against the Germans, for instance at Monte Cassino.

card_unit_sexton.name: card_unit_sexton
card_unit_sexton.title: SEXTON
card_unit_sexton.text: Deployment: Pin an enemy unit. At the start of your turn, pin that unit again.
card_unit_sexton.flavorText: The 25pdr SP, tracked, Sexton was a Canadian built self-propelled artillery vehicle used by the British and other Allied forces in WWII. Two variants were made, the Sexton I with its design based on the Canadian Ram tank hull and the chassis of the American Medium Tank M3, and then the Sexton II design which was based on the Grizzly (M4A1 Sherman) hull. Both versions used a QF 25 pounder gun-howitzer as its main armament and for secondary armament it used two 0.303 (7.7 mm) Bren light machine guns.The British forces used the Sexton for indirect supporting fire and kept them back from the front line and used forward observers to direct fire onto a target. The Sexton was produced from 1943 to 1945 with a total of 2000 units put into service.

card_unit_skua_mk_ii.name: card_unit_skua_mk_ii
card_unit_skua_mk_ii.title: BLACKBURN SKUA Mk II
card_unit_skua_mk_ii.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to an enemy. If the enemy is a unit, pin it.
card_unit_skua_mk_ii.flavorText: The Blackburn B-24 Skua was a British, carrier-based, two-seater dive bomber and fighter aircraft operated by the British Fleet Air Arm during WWII. The aircraft did fairly well against Axis bombers, but was no match against contemporary modern fighters such as the Bf 109, and by 1941 most of them were withdrawn from frontline service.

card_unit_spitfire.name: card_unit_spitfire
card_unit_spitfire.title: SPITFIRE Mk Ia
card_unit_spitfire.flavorText: The famous Supermarine Spitfire was a British fighter aircraft used by the RAF and the Allies, during and after WWII. The aircraft was very agile, but traded its range with speed and maneuverability. This meant that it did not do well as an offensive aircraft, but it served its purpose exceptionally well as a defensive aircraft, especially during the Battle of Britain. Many variants of the Spitfire were built and it was produced in greater numbers than any other British aircraft.

card_unit_spitfire_v.name: card_unit_spitfire_v
card_unit_spitfire_v.title: SPITFIRE Mk V
card_unit_spitfire_v.flavorText: Late in 1940, the RAF predicted a high altitude bombing offensive by the Luftwaffe, in which case a development of a pressurized version of the Spitfire was needed to counter this, with a new version of the Merlin engine. As a result, the Spitfire Mk V was designed and produced in 1941 and it was a Mk I with the Merlin 45 series engine. Three versions of the Mk V were produced and several sub-series.

card_unit_stirling.name: card_unit_stirling
card_unit_stirling.title: STIRLING Mk I S3
card_unit_stirling.text: Deployment: Add a GLADIATOR ESCORT fighter to the support line.
card_unit_stirling.flavorText: The Short Stirling was a British heavy bomber used by the RAF in WWII. It was the first four-engined bomber to be used in service by the Royal Air Force. The Stirling was used as a bomber until 1943, but took on second line duties when more capable heavy bombers, such as Handley Page Halifax and Avro Lancaster, became increasingly available for the strategic bombing of Germany.

card_unit_swordfish.name: card_unit_swordfish
card_unit_swordfish.title: SWORDFISH Mk I
card_unit_swordfish.flavorText: The Fairey Swordfish was a British biplane torpedo bomber used by the Royal Air Force, the Royal Navy and the Allied forces during WWII. Despite being outdated by the start of the war it was used in the front line until 1945, and caused more destruction of Axis shipping than any other Allied aircraft. The Swordfish was also involved in the bombing and sinking of the Bismarck.

card_event_breakout.name: card_event_breakout
card_event_breakout.title: BREAKOUT
card_event_breakout.text: Give a Veteran unit Fury and Shock.
card_event_breakout.flavorText: A breakout is a military operation to end a situation where troops are surrounded by the enemy, by launching assaults that achieve a breakthrough: escape from confinement. Encircled forces face annihilation unless they are relieved or they manage to break out. In the fluid combat of WWII, it was common for large forces to get surrounded, like at Dunkirk, Stalingrad, Korsun or Falaise. Breakout attempts were dangerous and desperate affairs, but they were often the only hope of survival for a surrounded unit. Such desperation could lead to heroic and furious actions. British General Bernard Montgomery used breakout tactics most famously during the Battle of El Alamein in late 1942. This was a turning point in the North African Campaign of World War II. Montgomery concentrated his forces and firepower on a narrow front, breaking through German and Italian lines to perform a breakout. Montgomery was thus able to wear down Field Marshal Erwin Rommel's Afrika Korps, eventually forcing an Axis retreat.

card_event_creeping_barrage.name: card_event_creeping_barrage
card_event_creeping_barrage.title: CREEPING BARRAGE
card_event_creeping_barrage.text: Pin target unit. When the Pin is removed, Retreat it.
card_event_creeping_barrage.flavorText: A creeping barrage is an artillery tactic where a line of artillery fire gradually advances forward in coordination with infantry, providing a protective "curtain" of explosions that suppresses enemy forces directly ahead of the troops. First developed during WWI, it continued to be used in WWII, especially in large-scale offensives. Creeping barrages were used in several major Allied operations, including the Normandy Campaign and the Italian Campaign, where coordinated artillery fire helped troops advance by neutralizing enemy defenses, reducing exposure to machine gun fire, and disorienting opposing forces. The technique required precise timing and coordination as troops had to follow closely behind the barrage without getting too close to the impact zone. Creeping barrages became an essential part of combined arms tactics, effectively blending artillery support with infantry movement.

card_event_desert_dust.name: card_event_desert_dust
card_event_desert_dust.title: DESERT DUST
card_event_desert_dust.text: Pin target unit. Add two GARRISON units to your support line.
card_event_desert_dust.flavorText: Visual deception played a key role in Allied operations in North Africa during WWII. When Italy invaded Egypt in 1940, both sides faced the challenge of open desert terrain, leaving little natural cover. Camouflage and disguise became vital tools.In 1941, filmmaker Geoffrey Barkas was appointed Director of Camouflage at the British General Headquarters in Cairo. His team, which included artists and set designers, used creative tactics to mislead the enemy. One notable trick during the defense of Tobruk consisted in making an essential water purification building look bombed when it was undamaged. They also made airfields look damaged in order to fool reconnaissance aircraft flying over. As the deception proved effective, large-scale dummy equipment such as tanks, artillery, and soldiers were produced, along with fake railheads and pipelines. Sunshields, canvas covers that disguised tanks as trucks, were also developed. These techniques, especially at El Alamein, misled German forces into overestimating British strength and contributed to the Allied victory.

card_event_echelon.name: card_event_echelon
card_event_echelon.title: ECHELON
card_event_echelon.text: Your units get: "Gets +1+1 if another of your units is attacked."
card_event_echelon.flavorText: An echelon is a military formation in which its units are arranged diagonally. This gives the units excellent fields of vision and overlapping fields of fire. It is used by air, land and naval forces. The first recorded use of an echelon formation was in the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BC.

card_event_entanglement.name: card_event_entanglement
card_event_entanglement.title: ENTANGLEMENT
card_event_entanglement.text: When a friendly unit is attacked, give it +2 defense before damage. Add a GARRISON to your support line.
card_event_entanglement.flavorText: When defending a position, military units set up extensive barriers, typically made of barbed wire, mines, obstacles and ditches. They are intended to impede enemy infantry or vehicles. For the defenders, a strong prepared position is a force multiplier. Any attacking unit caught in an entanglement is at a serious disadvantage.

card_event_kangaroo_transport.name: card_event_kangaroo_transport
card_event_kangaroo_transport.title: KANGAROO TRANSPORT
card_event_kangaroo_transport.text: Give a British infantry Blitz and +1 Heavy Armor.
card_event_kangaroo_transport.flavorText: The Kangaroo was an improvised Canadian armored personnel carrier (APC) which was created by converting a tank chassis. It was so successful that it was widely used by British and Commonwealth forces during WWII. It was developed in 1944 to improve infantry mobility and protection during assaults, particularly following the heavy casualties suffered in Normandy. The Kangaroo was originally converted from obsolete or damaged tanks, such as Canadian Ram tanks and M7 Priest self-propelled guns, and offered a new way to transport infantry safely across battlefields by providing shielding from small arms fire and shell fragments. Kangaroos played a crucial role in operations in Europe, where they helped troops advance alongside tanks.

card_unit_70th_brigade.name: card_unit_70th_brigade
card_unit_70th_brigade.title: 70th BRIGADE
card_unit_70th_brigade.text: At the start of your turn, draw a card and gain +2 HQ defense if this unit was not attacked last turn.
card_unit_70th_brigade.flavorText: The 70th Infantry Brigade was a brigade of the British Army which participated both in WWI and WWII. The brigade was disbanded in 1919 after WWI, but reformed in 1939 in the Territorial Army. Despite being very poorly trained and equipped, it joined the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) and served in the Battle of France in May 1940, and was then evacuated from Dunkirk. After the ordeal in France the brigade was reformed as an independent formation and redesignated 70th Independent Infantry Brigade. In September it was sent to Iceland where it served as garrison force until December 1941, when it was sent back to the UK to join the 49th Division, nicknamed “The Polar Bears”. The 70th Brigade landed in Normandy on 14 June 1944 as part of the 49th Division where it participated in the Battle of Normandy. In France the brigade saw heavy combat, but withdrew from the frontline in August and disbanded in order to fill the gaps in other infantry formations. In October 1944 the brigade ceased to exist and most of its men were posted to battalions of the 50th (Northumbrian) and the 51st (Highland) Infantry Divisions.

card_unit_black_prince.name: card_unit_black_prince
card_unit_black_prince.title: BLACK PRINCE
card_unit_black_prince.text: Only 2 units can occupy the frontline. Deployment: Retreat all units in it.
card_unit_black_prince.flavorText: The Black Prince was a British experimental heavy tank developed during the final stages of WWII. The tank was named after Edward, the Black Prince, son of Edward III and heir to the English throne, but it was officially known as Tank, Infantry, Black Prince (A43). It was designed as a continuation of the Churchill tank series, but equipped with a more powerful armament. The primary goal of the Black Prince was to mount a QF 17-pounder gun, which was highly effective against German armor, including the Panther and Tiger tanks. It was very similar to the Churchill tank design, including its thick armor. However, the larger 17-pounder gun called for a larger turret which made the tank much heavier and less mobile. The Black Prince also used the same engine as the Churchill, which resulted in a top speed of only 10.5 mph (17 km/h), far slower than other tanks of the time. Six prototypes were built by 1945, but the Black Prince never saw combat. By the time its development was completed, some faster, more versatile tanks such as the Centurion were emerging, which made the slow and heavily armored Black Prince obsolete. Consequently, the project was discontinued after the war.

card_unit_bloody_eleventh.name: card_unit_bloody_eleventh
card_unit_bloody_eleventh.title: BLOODY ELEVENTH
card_unit_bloody_eleventh.flavorText: The Devonshire Regiment, nicknamed "The Bloody Eleventh," was a British Army regiment active from 1685 to 1958, which participated in many wars and conflicts such as the Napoleonic Wars, the Second Boer War, World War I and World War II. In May 1942, the 1st Battalion of the Devonshire Regiment was stationed in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) after a local troop uprising. It was then sent to Burma in July 1943, where it served with the 20th Indian Infantry Division until the end of the war. In 1938, the 2nd Battalion was stationed in Malta, where it was involved in the Siege of Malta, before later serving in Sicily and Italy in 1943. In 1944, it took part in the D-Day landings in Normandy and fought through the North West Europe campaign, up to the crossing of the Rhine, finishing the war near Hamburg. The 50th (Holding) Battalion, raised in 1940 and later renumbered as the 12th Battalion, initially served in home defense but was trained for airborne operations in 1943. It landed in Normandy by glider in June 1944, participated in the Rhine crossing, and finished the war in Germany. The Devonshire Regiment also raised the 7th, 8th, and 9th Territorial Army battalions, in addition to the 4th, 5th, and 6th. The 5th Battalion was converted into an anti-tank unit before the war, and while the others were part of the 45th Infantry Division, only the 4th Battalion saw active service outside the UK. Most battalions were used for home defense, training, or supplying reinforcements. The 4th Battalion was sent to Gibraltar in 1940, returned to the UK in 1943, and served with various divisions until the end of the war.

card_unit_chesire_regiment.name: card_unit_chesire_regiment
card_unit_chesire_regiment.title: CHESHIRE REGIMENT
card_unit_chesire_regiment.text: At the start of your turn, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ if this unit was not attacked last turn.
card_unit_chesire_regiment.flavorText: The Cheshire Regiment was an infantry regiment of the Prince of Wales’s Division of the British Army, active from the year 1689 to 2007. During WWII the 2nd Battalion of the Cheshires first served in France in 1940 with the British Expeditionary Force, and was evacuated after the Battle of Dunkirk. The 2nd battalion then fought in North Africa from 1941 to 1943 and Sicily and Italy from 1943 to 1944. It landed in Normandy on D-Day and fought in the North West Europe campaign. The 1st Battalion fought at Tobruk in North Africa in 1941-1942 and later participated in the crossing of the Rhine in March 1945. The 6th and 7th Battalions fought in the Italian Campaign from 1943 to 1945. The 5th Battalion stayed in the UK throughout the war, where it provided machine gun support to the 38th Infantry (Reserve) Division, the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division, and the 80th Infantry (Reserve) Division.

card_unit_frontier_force.name: card_unit_frontier_force
card_unit_frontier_force.title: FRONTIER FORCE
card_unit_frontier_force.text: Deployment: Add a GARRISON unit to your hand.
card_unit_frontier_force.flavorText: The 12th Frontier Force Regiment was formed in 1922 as part of the British Indian Army. During WWII the regiment was raised from 5 regular battalions to 15 battalions and saw service in East Africa, North Africa, the Middle East, Italy, India, Malaya and Burma.The 1st battalion served in Iraq and Syria before it was sent to fight in the Italian Campaign on 24 September 1943. The 2nd battalion fought during the Battle of Malaya until it was forced to surrender with the rest of the Allied forces in Singapore on 15 February 1942. The 3rd battalion was part of the 5th Indian Infantry Division and served in East Africa and the Western Desert Campaigns. The 4th battalion served throughout the war in the Burma Campaign, while the 5th battalion was on garrison duties in Iraq as part of the 6th Indian Infantry Division. The Regiment's casualties in the war totalled 1,444 dead and 3,503 wounded.

card_unit_garrison.name: card_unit_garrison
card_unit_garrison.title: GARRISON
card_unit_garrison.text: At the start of your turn, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ if this unit was not attacked last turn.

card_unit_humber_mk_iv.name: card_unit_humber_mk_iv
card_unit_humber_mk_iv.title: HUMBER Mk IV
card_unit_humber_mk_iv.flavorText: The Humber Mk IV was a British armored car used extensively during WWII. The Humber was manufactured by the Rootes Group, and the Mk IV variant was the final and most developed version of the Humber series, following the Mk I, Mk II, and Mk III. It was introduced in 1943 and featured several improvements based on the earlier models’ performance in combat. It was fitted with the US M5 or M6 37 mm high-velocity gun, which replaced the earlier 15 mm Besa machine gun. Because the larger gun took up more space, the third crew member located in the turret, the wireless operator, was removed. The turret hatches were also rearranged to accommodate the new gun and crew setup. Around 2,000 units of the Mk IV were produced and it saw widespread use by British and Commonwealth forces, particularly in reconnaissance roles, but also in infantry support roles.

card_unit_matilda_mk_iv.name: card_unit_matilda_mk_iv
card_unit_matilda_mk_iv.title: MATILDA Mk IV
card_unit_matilda_mk_iv.text: Becomes Veteran after it Shock attacks.
card_unit_matilda_mk_iv.flavorText: The Infantry Tank Mark II is better known as the Matilda. Its design began as the A12 and it was meant to be a gun armed counterpart to the machine gun armed Infantry Tank Mark I, also known as the Matilda. It was heavily armored and turned out to be a good infantry tank despite limitations in armaments and speed. It was used on most fronts early in the war, such as France, North Africa, Soviet Union and in the Pacific. The Mk IV variant used a QF 3-inch howitzer instead of the QF 2-pounder. The QF 3-inch gun fired high explosives and smoke shells and was much favored in the Pacific.

card_unit_slashers.name: card_unit_slashers
card_unit_slashers.title: SLASHERS
card_unit_slashers.text: When a friendly unit survives combat, add a GARRISON unit to your support line.
card_unit_slashers.flavorText: The Gloucestershire Regiment, nicknamed Glosters or Slashers, was an infantry regiment of the British Army active between 1881 and 1994. At the outbreak of WWII the regiment was composed of four battalions (1st, 2nd, 5th and 7th), but later the 10th Battalion was added. The 2nd and 5th Battalions were deployed in France as part of the British Expeditionary Force, and both participated in the Battle of France before retreating to Dunkirk, where they were evacuated. In 1942 the 1st Battalion saw action in Burma, where it provided rearguard for the British retreat from Rangoon during the Japanese conquest of Burma. After heavy losses the battalion was sent to India to rest and recuperate, and it spent the remainder of the war there. In 1944 the 2nd Battalion participated in the Normandy landings and fought in the Battle of Normandy as part of the 56th Independent Infantry Brigade. From there it advanced into Belgium and the Netherlands, and ended the war in Germany where some of the men served as guards during the Nuremberg trials. The 10th Battalion of the Gloucestershire Regiment, assigned to the 72nd Brigade in the 36th Infantry Division, also fought in Burma. Despite lacking jungle warfare training, they engaged in key battles such as the relief of the Admin Box, the capture of Mayu tunnels, and the fierce fighting at Pinwe. The battalion faced significant losses, particularly from sickness and combat, losing many officers during intense engagements. After a controversial battle at Myitsone in February 1945, which led to the dismissal of their commanding officer, the battalion reached Mandalay, then returned to India in May, and was disbanded in December 1945.

card_unit_the_rangers.name: card_unit_the_rangers
card_unit_the_rangers.title: THE RANGERS
card_unit_the_rangers.text: Increase the non-combat, non-attack damage dealt by your units by 1.
card_unit_the_rangers.flavorText: The Rangers was a British volunteer unit first formed in 1860 which served in the Second Boer War, and saw intensive action on the Western Front during the First World War. At the outbreak of WWII both battalions of the Rangers were part of the 3rd London Brigade, but from March 1941 they served with the 20th Armoured Brigade, and became the 9th Battalion, King's Royal Rifle Corps (The Rangers). They trained as Motorised Infantry and were sent to Greece and Crete in 1941. They later served in North Africa in the desert war around the siege of Tobruk. When Tobruk fell to the Germans, they withdrew to Egypt. The depleted Battalion was disbanded in September 1942 and the remaining men re-allocated to other units.

card_event_active_sonar.name: card_event_active_sonar
card_event_active_sonar.title: ACTIVE SONAR
card_event_active_sonar.text: Pin all enemy units. Increase cost of all cards in enemy hand by 3.

card_event_advanced_royal_research.name: card_event_advanced_royal_research
card_event_advanced_royal_research.title: ADVANCED ROYAL RESEARCH
card_event_advanced_royal_research.text: Choose one - add ACTIVE SONAR to your hand OR add BLETCHLEY PARK to your hand.

card_event_airdrop.name: card_event_airdrop
card_event_airdrop.title: AIRDROP
card_event_airdrop.text: Retreat an enemy unit in the frontline. If it is now empty, add two 2nd PARACHUTE to it.
card_event_airdrop.flavorText: Winston Churchill was so impressed by the performance of Germany’s paratroopers in the first two years of WWII that he called for the formation of a British equivalent. By the end of 1941, No 2 Commando had been retrained as parachutists and they soon proved their worth, which led to further expansion. By 1944 there were five British parachute brigades consisting of 17 battalions. They fought in most of the major theatres of the war, with 1st Airborne Division, 6th Airborne Division and the independent 2nd Parachute Brigade.

card_event_bletchley_park.name: card_event_bletchley_park
card_event_bletchley_park.title: BLETCHLEY PARK
card_event_bletchley_park.text: All enemy cards with cost 5 or less in hand and on the battlefield are put on top of enemy's deck.

card_event_critical_damage.name: card_event_critical_damage
card_event_critical_damage.title: CRITICAL DAMAGE
card_event_critical_damage.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. If it doesn't have any adjacent units, deal 2 instead.
card_event_critical_damage.flavorText: By 31 October 1940, the date on which the Battle of Britain is generally considered to have ended, the Allies had lost 1,547 aircraft and suffered 966 casualties. The Axis casualties, mostly Germans, included 1,887 aircraft, and 4,303 aircrew. Most of the Luftwaffe aircraft that were shot down were bombers.

card_event_dowding_system.name: card_event_dowding_system
card_event_dowding_system.title: DOWDING SYSTEM
card_event_dowding_system.text: Counter an enemy order with cost 4 or more.
card_event_dowding_system.flavorText: The Dowding System was an elaborate air defence network that was built by RAF before WWII and gave the British a critical advantage during the Battle of Britain. The system was the first ground controlled interception network that could cover such a large area. It used the British telephone network to collect information from radar stations and the Royal Observer Corps which enabled the RAF Fighter Command to establish a clear overview of the airspace over Britain. The Dowding System was not only used to control the fighter force, but also anti aircraft guns, searchlights and barrage balloons against the attacking Luftwaffe.

card_event_evasive_action.name: card_event_evasive_action
card_event_evasive_action.title: EVASIVE ACTION
card_event_evasive_action.text: Trigger this card when the enemy deploys a unit with a deployment effect. Cancel the effect.
card_event_evasive_action.flavorText: The “Corkscrew” was a defensive maneuver developed to help bombers to defend against attacking fighters, mostly against night fighters. The manoeuvre involved a high speed spiral, turning and diving, sometimes 600-1000 ft, followed by a steep climb and then to roll and repeat the manoeuvre. The dive was intended to pull enough G-force that it would tear off the wings of a fighter. Another evasive maneuver was the “Barrel Roll” which involved slowing down the forward motion by doing a Helical Roll around a straight flightpath. This would often force an attacking fighter to overshoot the bomber and fly out in front.

card_event_expanded_royal_research.name: card_event_expanded_royal_research
card_event_expanded_royal_research.title: EXPANDED ROYAL RESEARCH
card_event_expanded_royal_research.text: Choose one - add SYNTHETIC RUBBER to hand OR add ADVANCED ROYAL RESEARCH to hand.

card_event_fog_of_war.name: card_event_fog_of_war
card_event_fog_of_war.title: FOG OF WAR
card_event_fog_of_war.text: Remove target unit from the battlefield. Put two copies on top of owner's deck.
card_event_fog_of_war.flavorText: “Fog of war” is a phrase used to describe the complexity and uncertainty in military conflicts. Military forces use intelligence in an attempt to reduce this uncertainty. “Fog of war” phrase is often attributed to the Prussian military analyst Carl von Clausewitz, but is actually a paraphrase of what he said:  “War is the realm of uncertainty; three quarters of the factors on which action in war is based are wrapped in a fog of greater or lesser uncertainty.”

card_event_long_range_desert_group.name: card_event_long_range_desert_group
card_event_long_range_desert_group.title: LONG RANGE DESERT GROUP
card_event_long_range_desert_group.text: Your units get: "When this unit deals damage to a unit, destroy it."
card_event_long_range_desert_group.flavorText: The Long Range Desert Group (LRDG) was a special operations unit of the British Army during WWII. This was an elite unit that specialized in long range reconnaissance missions, intelligence gathering and raiding operations. The unit was founded in Egypt in 1940 and was only made up of volunteers who were recruited from all the Commonwealth forces. The unit consisted of 14 patrols, 15-20 men in each, and each patrol usually operated in Chevrolet 30 cwt unarmored trucks and a Willy Jeep for the commanding officer. The LRDG was part of the Western Desert Force Eighth Army between 1940-43 and their area of operations stretched about 1500 km over the Sahara desert. Their mission was to provide critical intelligence to Allied commanders and finding new paths for Allied armor for flank maneuvers, but they were perhaps better known for their cooperation with the newly established SAS that were operating behind enemy lines. In 1943 the LRDG was retrained for mountain warfare and for the remainder of the war they operated in Italy and the Balkans where they continued to support the Allied onslaught against the Axis.

card_event_radar.name: card_event_radar
card_event_radar.title: RADAR
card_event_radar.text: Draw a card. Your HQ gains +4 defense.

card_event_royal_research.name: card_event_royal_research
card_event_royal_research.title: ROYAL RESEARCH
card_event_royal_research.text: Choose one - add RADAR to hand OR add EXPANDED ROYAL RESEARCH to hand.
card_event_royal_research.flavorText: Britain made some huge technological advances during WWII, some that would have a great impact on civilian life after the war. The “Bombe” was an electromechanical device developed in 1939 by Alan Turing and a team of scientists at Bletchley Park. The “Bombe” was used to speed up the cracking of Enigma code. In 1943 the British codebreakers developed Colossus, the world's first electronic digital programmable computer. The British would also perfect radar technology, which helped them to detect incoming air raids during the Battle of Britain in 1940. Further development in radar technology led to the invention of the H2S radar, the first airborne radar used to aid bomb targeting. Other British military inventions during WWII was the bouncing bomb, the high-explosive squash head, also known as "high explosive plastic" and the Bailey Bridge, a portable truss bridge that was used by Allied military engineers.

card_event_sea_patrol.name: card_event_sea_patrol
card_event_sea_patrol.title: SEA PATROL
card_event_sea_patrol.text: Deal 3 damage to an enemy. Costs 1 less for each friendly air unit.
card_event_sea_patrol.flavorText: In WWII maritime patrol aircraft used by the RAF were often older biplanes or converted bombers or airliners. Other maritime aircraft were also used such as the Short Sunderland flying boat and the Consolidated PBY Catalina. During the war there were also major developments in sonar and radar technology which helped the aircrafts to find and destroy enemy submarines.

card_event_second_chance.name: card_event_second_chance
card_event_second_chance.title: SECOND CHANCE
card_event_second_chance.text: Draw two random orders from your deck.
card_event_second_chance.flavorText: At the beginning of WWII the British were ill prepared in saving aircrews that were downed over sea and RAF relied on its coastal defense force to rescue the crewmen, which was an uncoordinated effort and not very efficient. Following the heavy losses of aircrew in the Battle of Britain, RAF established their own Air Sea Rescue Services and rescue operations became increasingly efficient throughout the remainder of WWII. Aircrews were trained in techniques that would help to maximize their chances of survival and supplied with survival equipment such as inflatable dinghies copied from the German Luftwaffe. The air-sea rescue squadrons of the RAF flew a variety of aircraft, usually those that had been rejected or withdrawn from front line service. Spitfires and Boulton Paul Defiants were used to look for downed aircrew and Avro Ansons to drop supplies. Supermarine Walrus and Supermarine Sea Otter amphibious aircraft were used to pick up aircrew from the water.

card_event_synthetic_rubber.name: card_event_synthetic_rubber
card_event_synthetic_rubber.title: SYNTHETIC RUBBER
card_event_synthetic_rubber.text: Target unit gets +4 defense, then set its attack equal to its defense.

card_unit_avro_anson1.name: card_unit_avro_anson1
card_unit_avro_anson1.title: AVRO ANSON
card_unit_avro_anson1.text: When you attack with a Spitfire, draw a card.
card_unit_avro_anson1.flavorText: The Avro Anson was a British twin engined aircraft used in various roles during WWII by RAF, and other Allied air forces. The aircraft was initially developed for maritime reconnaissance, but at the outbreak of war it had been realized that it had limited capabilities for this role and was replaced with the American Lockheed Hudson. The Avro Anson was after that pulled from front line service, some were used as a transporter, but mostly as trainers which became its most successful role. The aircraft was  very suitable to use in preparing pilots in flying multi engine bombers, such as the Avro Lancaster.

card_unit_cruiser_mk_iii.name: card_unit_cruiser_mk_iii
card_unit_cruiser_mk_iii.title: CRUISER Mk III
card_unit_cruiser_mk_iii.flavorText: The Cruiser tank, also known as A13 Mark I, was a British cruiser tank used by the British Army during WWII. The Mk I and Mk II versions were first developed in the mid 1930s and it was the first British cruiser tank to use the Christie suspension system which gave it high speed and good off road performance. The Mk III variant came into service in 1939, it had a crew of 4 (commander, gunner, loader, driver), weighed 14 tons and had a top speed of 48 km/h. For main armament it used a QF 2-pounder gun and a .303 Vickers machine gun for secondary armament. The Cruiser Mk III did live up to its speed requirements, but it was mechanically unreliable and the armor was insufficient which made it vulnerable in combat. Only 65 Mk III’s were produced.

card_unit_irish_guards.name: card_unit_irish_guards
card_unit_irish_guards.title: IRISH GUARDS
card_unit_irish_guards.flavorText: The Irish Guards were formed in 1900 and are a regiment of the Guards Division of the British Army, one of two Irish regiments in the army. In WWII the regiment grew from 1 battalion to 3 in size and the battalions fought separately in many of the major Allied military operations; the Norwegian Campaign, in France prior to the evacuation at Dunkirk, the Tunisian Campaign, the Italian Campaign, the Normandy Campaign, Operation Market Garden and the Rhineland Campaign.

card_unit_no_3_commando.name: card_unit_no_3_commando
card_unit_no_3_commando.title: No. 3 COMMANDO
card_unit_no_3_commando.text: Units with 4 or more attack cannot attack.
card_unit_no_3_commando.flavorText: No. 3 Commando was a battalion sized unit of the 1st Special Service Brigade that was formed in 1940 and was the first unit to carry the “Commando” title. Their first operation was a failed raid on the German occupied Channel island of Guernsey, but in 1941 Nr. 3 took part in successful raids on Lofoten Islands and Vaagso in Norway. In 1942 Nr. 3 was involved in the Allied Dieppe raid, which was a failed amphibious assault on the port of Dieppe in Northern France. The year after the unit was shipped to North Africa from where they participated in the Allied invasion of Sicily, but afterwards they were sent back to Britain to prepare for Operation Overlord. On D-Day in 1944 Nr. 3 Commando landed on Sword Beach where they were tasked with linking up with the 6th Airborne Division. By then the unit was no longer used for small scale raiding missions and was mostly deployed as an elite infantry assault unit, and as such they would fight with the Allied forces on the Western Front until the war in Europe ended. After the German surrendered Nr. 3 was tasked with occupational duties before being sent home to Britain in 1946 and disbanded.

card_unit_raf_ground_crew.name: card_unit_raf_ground_crew
card_unit_raf_ground_crew.title: RAF GROUND CREW
card_unit_raf_ground_crew.text: Your Spitfires cost 2 less to deploy and get +1+1 when deployed.
card_unit_raf_ground_crew.flavorText: During WWII every pilot and aircrew in RAF depended on the ground crews to get into the air and to engage the enemy. The Controllers were in direct contact with the aircraft and guided them into battle based on radar technology and Observer Corps info. During the Battle of Britain the Women's Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) received reports of enemy aircraft movement and updated the map in the Ops Room to give the Controllers an overall picture of the situation who then coordinated the squadrons in the air. Once the enemy aircraft was spotted the commanders in the air took over and were in charge of how the enemy should be attacked. Engineers worked frequently on aircraft, repairing damage after missions and carrying out maintenance to get them ready for flight. Armourers were responsible for bombs, defensive ammunition and flares at the airfields plus arming aircraft guns and fusing and loading bombs onto the aircraft. Riggers and fitters prepared aircraft for mission, wheeling them into position, checking them over and warming the engines before a flying mission.

card_unit_royal_scots.name: card_unit_royal_scots
card_unit_royal_scots.title: ROYAL SCOTS
card_unit_royal_scots.text: If in hand or on the battlefield, random effects always choose this unit.
card_unit_royal_scots.flavorText: The Royal Scots Regiment was first raised in 1633 and existed until 2006 when it became the Royal Scottish Borderers. At the start of WWII the 1st Battalion of the Royal Scots was part of the British Expeditionary Force and fought in the Battle of France prior to being evacuated at Dunkirk. After Dunkirk the 1st Royal Scots worked on home defense preparations, but in 1942 they were sent to British India from where they would fight in the Burma Campaign. The 2nd Battalion was in Gibraltar in 1943 from where it was moved to Italy to participate in the Italian Campaign in 1944. The 2nd Royal Scots saw action in the Battle of Anzio and on the Gothic Line.  The 7th/9th Battalion was moved to the Netherlands in 1944 and participated in the  Battle of the Scheldt and later Operation Bluecoat followed by the advance across the Rhine and to Bremen by the end of the war. The 8th Battalion remained in the UK until it participated in the Normandy landings in 1944 and fought in a series of offensive battles and operations, from Paris to the Rhine, and were advancing to Hamburg when the war ended.

card_unit_seaforth_highlanders.name: card_unit_seaforth_highlanders
card_unit_seaforth_highlanders.title: SEAFORTH HIGHLANDERS
card_unit_seaforth_highlanders.text: Has +3 attack on the enemy turn.
card_unit_seaforth_highlanders.flavorText: The Seaforth Highlanders is an infantry regiment of the British Army, mainly associated with the northern Highlands of Scotland. The regiment existed from 1881 to 1961 and fought in WWI and WWII, plus other minor conflicts. During WWII the Seaforth Highlanders were split into 7 battalions which served separately in various theaters of the war. The 1st was deployed in Malaya in 1940 and served in the Burma Campaign. The 2nd and 4th Battalions were captured in the Battle of France in 1940. The 2nd was reformed and fought in the Second Battle of Alamein, the Tunisian Campaign and the Italian Campaign. Later the battalion participated in Operation Overlord and the Allied invasion of Germany. The 5th and 6th Battalions served in the Italian campaign and was then deployed in North-West Europe. The 7th Battalion fought in Operation Epsom in France in 1944 and then served in North-West Europe.

card_unit_short_sunderland.name: card_unit_short_sunderland
card_unit_short_sunderland.title: SUNDERLAND Mk V
card_unit_short_sunderland.text: At the end of your turn, draw a random Navy card from your deck.
card_unit_short_sunderland.flavorText: The Short Sunderland was a British flying boat patrol bomber, used in anti-shipping strikes and reconnaissance- and rescue missions, used by RAF and other Allied air forces during WWII. The aircraft played a vital role against German U-boats and in anti-shipping strikes during the Battle of the Atlantic, as well as being in high demand for convoy escort roles due to its ability to land on water and rescue crews from torpedo hit ships. Due to its excellent endurance and armament the Sunderland became notorious among German sea and air crews who gave it the nickname “Flying Porcupine”. The aircraft was produced from 1938 to 1946 and 749 of them were built, including a few variants.

card_unit_short_wellington.name: card_unit_short_wellington
card_unit_short_wellington.title: WELLINGTON
card_unit_short_wellington.text: If in your hand, this unit costs 2 less each time you give an order.
card_unit_short_wellington.flavorText: The Vickers Wellington was a British medium bomber that was used by RAF and other Commonwealth air forces during WWII. The aircraft was first introduced in the mid 1930s and at the outbreak of WWII the first RAF bomb attack on German targets involved Wellington’s as well as Blenheim bombers. At that time the Wellingtons flew bomber missions unescorted, and in daytime, but when RAF realized how vulnerable they were against defending fighters they quickly switched them to night operations. Throughout the war the Wellingtons were mainly used in night operations and mainly to bomb Axis communications and industrial targets  instead of military targets. Coastal Command also used the Wellingtons variants, mainly in anti-submarine and anti-shipping warfare, but also to perform reconnaissance missions. A total of 11,464 Wellingtons were built, including many variants and prototypes that were used for various purposes.

card_unit_spitfire_mk_ii.name: card_unit_spitfire_mk_ii
card_unit_spitfire_mk_ii.title: SPITFIRE Mk II
card_unit_spitfire_mk_ii.flavorText: The Supermarine Spitfire was a British fighter aircraft that was first introduced in 1938 and was used by the Royal Air Force and the Allied air forces during WWII. The Mk II varied from the Mk I as it used the Merlin XIII engine, which gave it an increase of 120 horsepower over the engines used in the Mk I. Another main difference was that it was produced in a new giant factory at Castle Bromwich in Southampton where a total of 920 Mk IIs were built. The Mk II came into service in time for the Battle of Britain in 1940, but the Mk I and Mk II were more or less phased out in 1941 and replaced with the Mk V.

card_event_close_call.name: card_event_close_call
card_event_close_call.title: CLOSE CALL
card_event_close_call.text: Counter an order or deployment effect that targets a friendly unit.
card_event_close_call.flavorText: One of the remarkable stories from the London Blitz is that of St. Paul's Cathedral. Despite being a prime target for bombing, St. Paul's survived the Blitz almost completely unscathed. This was due in large part to the efforts of the firefighters who risked their lives, on Churchill's orders, to save the iconic building. They worked tirelessly to put out fires started by the bombing and used innovative methods such as water pumped from the nearby Thames river to prevent the flames from spreading. St Paul's Survives is the photograph shown here and it is taken in London during the night air raid of 29–30 December 1940, the 114th night of the Blitz. It shows St Paul's Cathedral, illuminated by fires and surrounded by the smoke of burning buildings and has become a symbol of British resilience and courage, and is considered one of the iconic images of the Blitz.

card_event_committed_crew.name: card_event_committed_crew
card_event_committed_crew.title: COMMITTED CREW
card_event_committed_crew.text: Until end of turn, Spitfires cost 0 to deploy and get +3+3 when deployed.
card_event_committed_crew.flavorText: RAF ground crews were essential to air operations and often had to work while under fire during WWII. This was particularly true during air raids on RAF airfields and during bombing missions against enemy targets. RAF airfields were frequently targeted by enemy aircraft, and ground crew had to be ready to repair and refuel aircraft even during air raids. In addition, the ground crew often accompanied aircraft on missions to provide maintenance and support, and they were often exposed to enemy fire during these missions. For example, during the famous "Dambusters" raid in 1943, ground crew members flew in Lancaster bombers alongside the pilots and aircrew to maintain the aircraft and equipment during the mission. These ground crew members were exposed to enemy fire and several of them were killed or injured. RAF ground crew also worked under difficult and dangerous conditions in remote locations, such as in North Africa and the Middle East. In these locations, ground crew had to maintain aircraft and equipment in extreme heat and harsh desert conditions while under threat from enemy air and ground attacks. Many ground crew members were awarded medals for their bravery and service during WWII.

card_event_desert_raid.name: card_event_desert_raid
card_event_desert_raid.title: DESERT RAID
card_event_desert_raid.text: All units deal 1 combat damage until your next turn.
card_event_desert_raid.flavorText: The Raid on Sidi Haneish Airfield was a military operation carried out by the British Special Air Service (SAS) during WWII, specifically on the night of December 26-27, 1942. The objective of the raid was to disrupt enemy air operations and destroy aircraft at the airfield, which was located in Libya and was being used by German and Italian forces. The operation was conducted by a force consisting of the Long Range Desert Group (LRDG) and the Special Air Service (SAS). The LRDG provided the vehicles and navigation expertise and the SAS carried out the actual raid on the airfield. The raid was carried out with 18 jeeps that drove through the night in formation without headlights, each carrying 3-4 British or French commandos and mounted Vickers K machine guns. On arrival the SAS stormed the airfield in V formation and used their mounted machine guns to fire on and destroy the parked German aircraft on the airfield. The Germans fired back using machine guns and anti-aircraft weapons but were only able to disable one jeep and one SAS was shot and killed. The raid was a success, with the SAS destroying at least 30 enemy aircraft, damaging several others, and causing significant damage to the airfield infrastructure. Afterwards the raiders escaped through the desert and were able to return safely to Allied lines. The Raid on Sidi Haneish Airfield was significant because it demonstrated the effectiveness of special operations forces in disrupting enemy operations and causing damage with minimal casualties. It also highlighted the importance of intelligence gathering and navigation expertise in planning and executing successful raids.

card_event_escort_group.name: card_event_escort_group
card_event_escort_group.title: ESCORT GROUP
card_event_escort_group.text: Choose one - shuffle MATERIALS OR ARMAMENTS into your deck.
card_event_escort_group.flavorText: The British Escort Group protocol was a naval tactic used by the Royal Navy during WWII to protect merchant convoys from German U-boat attacks. The protocol involved the use of a group of warships, consisting of a mix of destroyers, frigates, and corvettes, to escort the merchant ships. The escort group would operate in a tight formation around the convoy, using a combination of radar, sonar, and visual lookout to detect and track enemy submarines. If a U-boat was detected, the escort ships would work together to attack it with depth charges, guns, and torpedoes. The British Escort Group protocol was highly effective in reducing the number of merchant ships lost to U-boat attacks. By the end of the war, the Royal Navy had developed a range of tactics and technologies to counter the submarine threat, including improved sonar equipment, better communication systems, and new anti-submarine weapons.

card_event_hms_hermes.name: card_event_hms_hermes
card_event_hms_hermes.title: HMS HERMES
card_event_hms_hermes.text: Fill your support line with SWORDFISH Mk I.
card_event_hms_hermes.flavorText: HMS Hermes was a British aircraft carrier and the first ship to be designed as an aircraft carrier, although it took so long for it to be built that during its construction that in the meantime the Japanese Navy built and launched the Hōshō. HMS Hermes was commissioned in 1924, and at the time of her launch was the largest aircraft carrier in the world. During the interwar years, she was involved in a number of operations and was often used to showcase British naval power around the world. When WWII broke out, HMS Hermes was immediately put to use. In 1939, she operated in the western Atlantic, where she helped to prevent German U-boats from attacking British shipping. In 1940, she was sent to the Indian Ocean, where she continued to support British and Allied operations. Despite being outdated and vulnerable, HMS Hermes performed admirably well and her aircraft were able to inflict significant damage on Japanese troops and shipping, and helped to slow the Japanese advance. However, on April 9, 1942, she was caught by surprise and attacked by Japanese carrier-based aircraft in the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). The attack was devastating, and within minutes HMS Hermes was hit by several bombs and torpedoes. The damage was catastrophic, and the ship quickly sank, taking over 300 men with her. Her loss was a major blow to the British war effort in the Far East, and marked the first time in history that an aircraft carrier had been sunk by enemy aircraft while at sea.

card_event_partnership.name: card_event_partnership
card_event_partnership.title: PARTNERSHIP
card_event_partnership.text: Add a random US Elite unit to your support line.
card_event_partnership.flavorText: The first combined British and American operation was Operation Torch which was launched in late 1942. This was the invasion of French North Africa with the objective of securing Allied victory in North Africa and to give the American armed forces the chance to engage Axis forces on a limited scale. This was the first mass involvement of US troops in the North African Theater, and involved the first major airborne assault carried out by the United States. The success of Torch was followed by Operation Husky, the invasion of Sicily, and Operation Avalanche, the invasion of southern Italy.

card_event_refit_bia.name: card_event_refit_bia
card_event_refit_bia.title: REFIT
card_event_refit_bia.text: Choose one - draw a Spitfire from your deck OR give a Spitfire Blitz.
card_event_refit_bia.flavorText: During the Battle of Britain, a key difference in engineering between the German Messerschmitt 109 and the British Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane was their fuel delivery systems. The German fighters had a direct fuel injection, allowing them to perform extreme negative G maneuvers without starving the engine of fuel. This gave the ME-109 an advantage in quickly diving away from combat. On the other hand, the British fighters used direct carburetors, which were sensitive to engine cut-outs due to fuel flooding during negative G maneuvers. To work around this issue, British pilots developed the tactic of flipping their aircraft in a half-roll before diving, converting the maneuver into a positive G one and avoiding engine cut-outs. This problem persisted in British planes until 1941 when Miss Tilly Shilling introduced a simple but effective solution using a washer-type device to help alleviate the fuel and float level fluctuations that caused the engine to cut out. While it didn't completely solve the problem, it considerably improved the situation.

card_event_sincerely_yours.name: card_event_sincerely_yours
card_event_sincerely_yours.title: SINCERELY YOURS
card_event_sincerely_yours.text: Give your HQ +6 defense. Draw 2 cards.
card_event_sincerely_yours.flavorText: During WWII, Vera Lynn was one of the most popular singers in the UK, and her music played an important role in boosting the morale of British troops fighting overseas. Lynn's songs were broadcast on the radio and played at military bases, giving soldiers a sense of comfort and home. In 1941 she became widely popular because of her weekly 30 minute radio programme called “Sincerely Yours”, described as “to the men of the forces – a letter in words and Music”. Some of her most famous songs from this time include "We'll Meet Again" and "The White Cliffs of Dover". In addition to her music, Lynn also visited military hospitals and entertained wounded soldiers, becoming a familiar face to those fighting on the frontlines. She also toured extensively, performing for troops in various locations, including Egypt, India, and Burma. Lynn's work during the war made her a beloved figure in the UK and earned her numerous accolades. She was awarded the Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 1969 and the Order of the Companions of Honour in 2016.

card_event_stiff_upper_lip.name: card_event_stiff_upper_lip
card_event_stiff_upper_lip.title: STIFF UPPER LIP
card_event_stiff_upper_lip.text: Draw a card. Draw another if you control a Guard.
card_event_stiff_upper_lip.flavorText: According to many outsiders, the Brits are reserved, resilient and self-controlled, and the so-called “Blitz Spirit” of WWII, and slogans “Keep calm, carry on” and “London can take it” are a showcase of that. The term "Blitz spirit" refers to the resilience and determination shown by the British people during the intense bombing raids carried out by the German Luftwaffe on British cities during WWII, particularly during the period known as the Blitz from September 1940 to May 1941. The term has become a symbol of the strength and resilience of the British people during one of the most difficult times in their history. However, the reality behind the “Blitz Spirit” was far less rosy than history books have led us to believe. Of course people carried on as there was little else to do in the situation, but they lived in constant fear for their life during the bombings, crime rose by 57%, as looting, ration card theft and black-market profiteering increased substantially. Even cases of murder increased by 22%.

card_event_strong_bond.name: card_event_strong_bond
card_event_strong_bond.title: STRONG BOND
card_event_strong_bond.text: Friendly ground unit gets Guard and: "Add a US 3-cost unit to your support line at the start of your turn."
card_event_strong_bond.flavorText: After the American Revolution in 1783 the UK recognized American independence and the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1785. Ever since the UK and the US have remained close partners. The UK-US relations at the start of WWII were complex as the Americans were divided on what the role of the nation should be in the war, or if it should interfere at all. However, public opinion changed, especially during the Battle of Britain, as it showed that the German war machine was not invincible, and by April 1941 a public poll showed that the majority of Americans were in favor of joining the war against the Axis. Finally the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, ended the debate once and for all and shortly after the US was at war with the Axis powers.

card_unit_185th_brigade.name: card_unit_185th_brigade
card_unit_185th_brigade.title: 185th BRIGADE
card_unit_185th_brigade.flavorText: The 185th Infantry Brigade of the British Army was formed in September 1942 and started as a Home Defense formation in the northern part of the UK. In 1943 it was assigned four frontline battalions: 2nd Battalion - Royal Warwickshire Regiment, 1st Battalion of the Royal Norfolk Regiment, 2nd Battalion of the King’s Shropshire Light Infantry and the 1st Battalion of the Highland Light Infantry. At first the brigade was a part of the 79th Armored Division, but as of April 1943 it was transferred to the 3rd Infantry Division and started training for Operation Overlord. On D-Day, June 1944, the 3rd Infantry Division was set to land at Sword beach which was the responsibility of the British Army and a naval bombardment force provided by the British Royal Navy plus Polish, Norwegian and other Allied navies. Sword beach was the smallest of the D-Day landing beaches and only wide enough for a brigade sized landing (ca. 5000 men). The goal was to get enough troops ashore and link up with the Canadians at Juno, and from there they were supposed to push inland and capture Caen. By the end of D-day, 29,000 men had been successfully landed at the beach, and 630 casualties had been taken in the fight, mostly during the only German counteroffensive that was made on June 6. However, the major objective which was the capture of Caen was still out of reach and what followed was 6 weeks of fierce fighting for the city known as the Battle for Caen. After that, the 185th Brigade engaged in combat at Bourguébus, Mont Pinçon, the Nederrijn, the Rhineland, and on the other side of the Rhine. By the end of the war the 185th Brigade had lost more soldiers than the other two infantry brigades of the 3rd Infantry Division and received two Victoria Crosses for its act of bravery during the conflict.

card_unit_6th_airlanding_brigade.name: card_unit_6th_airlanding_brigade
card_unit_6th_airlanding_brigade.title: 6th AIRLANDING BRIGADE
card_unit_6th_airlanding_brigade.text: When a friendly unit would deal 1 combat damage, it deals 3 instead.
card_unit_6th_airlanding_brigade.flavorText: The 6th Airlanding Brigade was an airborne infantry brigade of the British Army during WWII. The brigade was created in 1943 and was assigned to the 6th Airborne Division, nicknamed Red Devils, along with the 3rd and 5th Parachute Brigades. The 6th Airlanding Brigade was unique among British airborne units in that it was composed entirely of glider-borne troops. The brigade consisted of three battalions of infantry, as well as supporting units such as engineers, medics, and anti-tank troops. The brigade saw action in several major operations during the war, including the Normandy landings in June 1944 and the Battle of Arnhem in September 1944. During the Normandy landings, the brigade was tasked with securing the eastern flank of the invasion area and capturing several key bridges. At Arnhem, the brigade was tasked with securing the landing zones and holding bridges over the Rhine River. The 6th Airlanding Brigade suffered heavy losses during both operations, with many of its troops killed, wounded, or captured. However, the brigade's actions were critical in the success of these operations. After the war, the 6th Airlanding Brigade was disbanded.

card_unit_blenheim_mk_i.name: card_unit_blenheim_mk_i
card_unit_blenheim_mk_i.title: BLENHEIM Mk I
card_unit_blenheim_mk_i.text: Deals double damage if the frontline is empty.
card_unit_blenheim_mk_i.flavorText: The Bristol Blenheim was a British light bomber, heavy fighter and night fighter and it first came into service in 1937 as the first British aircraft with an all metal skin construction. By the outbreak of WWII the Blenheim had become more or less obsolete, but was used during the Battle of France for shorter bomber missions against German targets where it performed poorly and many aircraft were lost to enemy aircraft and anti aircraft artillery. The Blenheim’s saw more success as an early type of night fighter, but by 1941 the Blenheim was deemed inadequate for current operations and was phased out by more capable aircraft such as the Beaufighters and later the De Havilland Mosquitos. By 1944 a total of 4,422 aircraft had been built, including variants.

card_unit_green_howards.name: card_unit_green_howards
card_unit_green_howards.title: GREEN HOWARDS
card_unit_green_howards.text: Draw a card when a unit becomes Veteran.
card_unit_green_howards.flavorText: During WWII, the Green Howards, or the Yorkshire Regiment, fielded 12 battalions that saw action across various theaters. The 1st Battalion fought in Sicily and Italy with the 5th Division, while the 2nd Battalion operated in Burma as part of the 26th Indian Infantry Division and the 82nd (West Africa) Division. The 4th and 5th Battalions were captured during the Battle of Gazala in North Africa, serving with the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division. The 6th and 7th Battalions were duplicates formed for the Territorial Army, joining the 69th Brigade in France, North Africa, Sicily, and Northwest Europe. The 8th Battalion was initially formed for home defense, merging with the 13th Battalion and later becoming the 30th Battalion. It served in Italy and French North Africa. The 9th and 10th Battalions were initially for training and home defense but later participated in the Normandy campaign and operations in Northwest Europe. The 11th, 12th, and 13th Battalions were formed in 1940. The 12th Battalion transformed into an armored unit and later joined the Reconnaissance Corps, providing reinforcements to the 43rd Reconnaissance Regiment. After WWII the Green Howards continued to serve with the British Army until 2006, when it was merged into the Royal Yorkshire Regiment (14th/15th, 19th and 33rd/76th Foot) along with all other Yorkshire based regiments.

card_unit_hurricane_mk_ii_c_trop.name: card_unit_hurricane_mk_ii_c_trop
card_unit_hurricane_mk_ii_c_trop.title: HURRICANE Mk II-C TROP
card_unit_hurricane_mk_ii_c_trop.text: Becomes Veteran when it survives combat.
card_unit_hurricane_mk_ii_c_trop.flavorText: The Hurricane Mk II variant first saw service in 1940, with a more powerful engine and gradually improved armament. The Hurricane's main advantage over the Spitfire was that it was easier to fly, which was useful because squadrons were full of inexperienced pilots, and its gun platform was easier to handle than the Spitfire's. The unprotected fuel tank in front of the cockpit, on the other hand, could rupture and cause serious burn injuries to the pilot if hit. The wooden and fabric rear fuselages were also more prone to catching fire than metal fuselages. Despite its flaws, the Hurricane shot down the vast majority of enemy aircraft claimed by the RAF. The Hawker Hurricane and other aircraft were tropicalized, or "trop" for use in North Africa. They were given engine dust filters as well as a desert survival kit for the pilots.

card_unit_kings_own_scottish.name: card_unit_kings_own_scottish
card_unit_kings_own_scottish.title: KING'S OWN SCOTTISH
card_unit_kings_own_scottish.text: Pincer: Damage dealt to this unit is dealt to its Pincer partner instead.
card_unit_kings_own_scottish.flavorText: The King’s Own Scottish Borderers (KOSBs) was an infantry regiment of the British Army that was first raised in 1689 and stayed active until 2006 when it was merged with the Royal Scots Battalion to form the Royal Scots Borderers. Between the wars the battalions of the regiment were in service all over the British Empire, but were called back home when WWII started in 1939. The 1st Battalion was sent to France to serve in the British Expeditionary Force as part of the 9th Brigade of the 3rd Infantry Division and took part in the Dunkirk evacuation in June 1940. The 1st and the 6th Battalion would later serve in the Normandy landings in 1944 and the following Battle for Caen. The 2nd Battalion was sent to Burma as part of the 89th Brigade of the 7th Indian Infantry Division and participated in the Battle of the Admin Box and the Battle of Imphal in the Burma Campaign.  The 4th and 5th Battalion were sent to Saint-Malo in France as part of the 155th Brigade of the 52nd (Lowland) Division to service in the British Expeditionary Force, and were evacuated from Cherbourg in 1940. In 1944 they took part in the Operation Infatuate which successfully cleared the seaway to Antwerp port for the Allied forces, and in 1945 they took part in capturing the city Bremen.  The 7th Battalion participated in the failed Operation Market Garden as part of the 1st Airlanding Brigade of 1st Airborne Division, where the battalion suffered 90% casualties during the Battle of Arnhem while defending the perimeter in Oosterbeek against the 2nd SS Panzer Corps.

card_unit_vildebeest.name: card_unit_vildebeest
