card_unit_vildebeest.title: VILDEBEEST
card_unit_vildebeest.text: When a friendly unit deals 1 combat damage, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_vildebeest.flavorText: The Vickers Vildebeest was a large two to three seated single engined biplane that was used by the RAF as a light bomber, torpedo bomber and in army cooperation roles. The Vildebeest flew its first flight in 1928 and was used in service up until 1942. At the outbreak of WWII the aircraft was considered obsolete, but 101 still remained in service although they were all scheduled to be replaced by aircraft such as the Bristol Beaufort. However, two squadrons based in Singapore were still waiting for their Beauforts when Japan invaded Malaya in 1941 and they had no choice but to send the obsolete biplanes against the attackers. During these attacks the Vildebeests had no fighter escort and suffered heavy losses from Japanese fighters. On January 26, 1942,  two squadrons with 12 Vildebeests were sent against the Japanese landing forces at Endau, which was only 250 miles from Singapore, and despite being escorted by Brewster Buffalo and Hawker Hurricane fighters, 5 Vildebeests were lost. The attack was repeated that same day, this time with 8 Vildebeests and 3 Fairey Albacores, but this resulted in 6 more Vildebeests being lost plus 3 Albacores. The surviving Vildebeests were withdrawn to Java where they continued operating against the Japanese forces to some success, but by March 1942 the last Vildebeests in RAF service was retired. By this time it had been replaced by more modern aircraft such as the Bristol Blenheim and Vickers Wellesley bombers. A total of 209 Vildebeests were manufactured, including quite a few variants.

card_event_baker_street_irregulars.name: card_event_baker_street_irregulars
card_event_baker_street_irregulars.title: BAKER STREET IRREGULARS
card_event_baker_street_irregulars.text: Develop a British special force unit. If you control a Commando, also Develop a British order.
card_event_baker_street_irregulars.flavorText: The Baker Street Irregulars was a nickname given to the Special Operations Executive (SOE), a British special forces organization. Founded in 1940, the SOE played a crucial role in conducting espionage, sabotage, and subversion operations behind enemy lines in occupied Europe and other theaters of war. The SOE recruited and trained agents from various backgrounds, including military personnel, civilians, and members of resistance movements. These agents were deployed in occupied territories to gather intelligence, organize and support resistance networks, and carry out acts of sabotage against enemy targets. The organization employed more than 13,000 people, about 3,200 of whom were women.The SOE operated covertly, often working in collaboration with local resistance fighters and partisan groups to undermine enemy morale and disrupt Axis military operations. The SOE also conducted several deception operations aimed at misleading the Axis forces, most notably Operation Mincemeat, prior to the Allied invasion of Sicily in 1943, and Operation Titanic prior to D-Day in 1944. The organization was nicknamed  "Baker Street Irregulars" because it operated from a building on Baker Street in London, and its members used unconventional methods similar to those of the fictional character Sherlock Holmes and his group of streetwise helpers known as the Baker Street Irregulars. Other nicknames were "Churchill's Secret Army" and "Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare".

card_event_commando_raid.name: card_event_commando_raid
card_event_commando_raid.title: COMMANDO RAID
card_event_commando_raid.text: Deal 1 damage. Add two No. 10 COMMANDO units to your support line.
card_event_commando_raid.flavorText: A notable example of a British commando raid during WWII was the Saint-Nazaire Raid, also known as Operation Chariot, which took place on March 28, 1942. The objective of the raid was to disable the heavily fortified dry dock at Saint-Nazaire, France, which was used for repairing and refitting German warships, particularly battleships and U-boats. By disabling the dry dock, the British hoped to disrupt German naval operations in the Atlantic and weaken their ability to threaten Allied shipping lanes. The raiding force, led by Commando units under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Charles Newman, included sailors from the Royal Navy, Royal Marines and Army commandos. The force embarked on the nighttime assault using a converted destroyer, HMS Campbeltown, which was packed with explosives and disguised to resemble a German vessel. Under the cover of darkness and a diversionary bombardment, the Campbeltown rammed the gates of the dry dock, which allowed the commandos to disembark and engage in fierce close combat with German defenders. Despite heavy casualties and intense resistance, the commandos succeeded in achieving their objective by detonating the explosives aboard the Campbeltown and rendering the dry dock unusable. Although the raid inflicted significant damage on the Saint-Nazaire port, it came at a high cost and many commandos were killed, wounded, or captured by the Germans.

card_event_first_responders.name: card_event_first_responders
card_event_first_responders.title: FIRST RESPONDERS
card_event_first_responders.text: At the end of the enemy turn, add a 5th BRIGADE to your support line. Give it +3+3 if enemy has 3 or more units.
card_event_first_responders.flavorText: The Battles of Kohima and Imphal in 1944, part of the Burma Campaign during WWII, were the turning point of the Japanese U-Go offensive into India, and a notable example of Allied logistical superiority at the time. The battles took place from April 4 to June 22- 1944, in the vicinity of Kohima, now the capital of Nagaland in Northeast India, and near the city of Imphal. Despite having numeral superiority, the Japanese underestimated the Allies’ defensive skills, and their ability to bring up reinforcements. The Allied reinforcements started to arrive on April 14th and from then on the battle turned in their favor. During the battle, the RAF managed to airlift the 5th Indian Division and its equipment from Arakan to Imphal (525 km) in only two days, and to evacuate around 13,000 casualties from the battle. The Japanese suffered a bitter defeat, with 53,000 men dead or missing, most being the result of starvation, disease and exhaustion. Despite their victory the Allies also suffered heavy losses, 4,000 casualties at Koshima and another 12,500 at Imphal.

card_event_hms_talbot.name: card_event_hms_talbot
card_event_hms_talbot.title: HMS TALBOT
card_event_hms_talbot.text: If your HQ is about to receive lethal damage, give it +6 defense first.
card_event_hms_talbot.flavorText: HMS Talbot, also known as the 10th Submarine Flotilla, was the name of the Royal Navy's submarine base at Manoel Island, Malta, from 1941 to 1943. The base hosted submarines from both the Royal Navy and the Polish Navy, and the flotilla never counted more than 12 submarines at the time. Despite its small size, it managed to sink 412,575 tons of Axis shipping between 1941 and 1942. The base was a priority target for Axis aerial attacks and was heavily bombed in 1942, which forced a withdrawal of the flotilla from Malta to Alexandria, where the ships of the Mediterranean Fleet had already moved.

card_event_infiltrate.name: card_event_infiltrate
card_event_infiltrate.title: INFILTRATE
card_event_infiltrate.text: Each friendly Commando deals damage to a random enemy equal to known enemy cards.
card_event_infiltrate.flavorText: Operation Biting was a daring commando raid undertaken by British forces against a German radar installation at Bruneval, France, in February 1942. Led by members of No. 12 Commando, supported by paratroopers from the British Army's 1st Airborne Division, the operation aimed at capturing key components of the German Würzburg radar system for analysis. Under the cover of darkness, the commandos infiltrated the enemy position, engaging in fierce close-quarters combat against defending German troops. Despite encountering heavy resistance, the commandos successfully secured the radar components and evacuated via landing craft. The raid provided valuable intelligence on German radar technology, contributing to the Allies' understanding of enemy capabilities and aiding in the development of countermeasures.

card_event_lure.name: card_event_lure
card_event_lure.title: LURE
card_event_lure.text: When the enemy gives the second order this turn, counter it.
card_event_lure.flavorText: During WWII the British military employed paradummies, also known as lures, as part of their deceptive tactics. These dummy paratroopers were made from burlap and filled with straw or green waste, and designed to resemble real soldiers when dropped from aircraft. The purpose of these paradummies was to lure enemy forces into believing that a larger airborne assault was underway, thereby diverting their attention and resources from the actual objectives. These decoys were often equipped with simple parachutes to simulate a real drop and were strategically dropped to confuse enemy reconnaissance and intelligence efforts. The paradummies were used during the Normandy landings in 1944, and some were also fitted with a timed detonator to ensure they exploded on landing, destroying evidence of the trick. This gave the illusion that the supposed paratrooper had burned his parachute upon landing and was now avoiding detection.

card_event_sea_embargo.name: card_event_sea_embargo
card_event_sea_embargo.title: SEA EMBARGO
card_event_sea_embargo.text: Give target unit +1+1. If its an air unit, Develop a British air unit with 2 or less attack.
card_event_sea_embargo.flavorText: During WWII, the Allied naval blockade of Germany from 1939 to 1945 became a major component of the Allied strategy. The blockade was primarily enforced by the British Royal Navy, which used its naval superiority to intercept ships and prevent goods and resources from reaching enemy territories by sea. By disrupting supply lines and depriving Germany, and later Italy, of essential resources such as food, fuel, and raw materials, the blockade significantly hampered the Axis war effort. This economic strangulation led to widespread shortages, rationing, and a decline in living conditions for civilians in Germany. Despite Germany's attempts to evade the blockade through domestic production increases and alternative supply routes, the sustained pressure played a crucial role in undermining Germany's military capabilities and ultimately contributed to the Allied victory in WWII.

card_event_wave_after_wave.name: card_event_wave_after_wave
card_event_wave_after_wave.title: WAVE AFTER WAVE
card_event_wave_after_wave.text: Deal 2 damage to all enemy units. If this is the second order you give this turn, deal 4 instead.
card_event_wave_after_wave.flavorText: During WWII, the British Royal Navy conducted several air raids from aircraft carriers. One notable example is the raid on the German Battleship Tirpitz in April 1944, where carrier-based aircraft from the British Home Fleet, including aircraft from HMS Victorious, conducted a series of air raids against the Tirpitz, which was anchored in a Norwegian fjord. The attacks inflicted significant damage on the Tirpitz, ultimately leading to its destruction in November 1944.

card_unit_10th_para_battalion.name: card_unit_10th_para_battalion
card_unit_10th_para_battalion.title: 10th PARA BATTALION
card_unit_10th_para_battalion.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 and Blitz if you have given an order this turn.
card_unit_10th_para_battalion.flavorText: The 10th Battalion was an airborne infantry battalion of the Parachute Regiment of the British Army during WWII. The battalion was originally raised around volunteers from the Royal Sussex Regiment in Egypt and assigned to the 4th Parachute Brigade. The battalion saw its first action in Operation Slapstick, which was part of the Allied invasion of Italy in 1943. It was then held as reserve during the Normandy landings, but saw action again during Operation Market Garden in September 1944. On the second day of the Battle of Arnhem, they landed but failed to reach their designated target. Over the course of two days of intense combat, the battalion was gradually destroyed. Those who survived retreated to the divisional position at Oosterbeek, and after bravely holding their ground within the perimeter, the remaining few were evacuated south of the River Rhine. Unfortunately, the battalion never fully recovered from the significant losses suffered during the battle and was disbanded. The surviving soldiers were reassigned to various battalions within the 1st Parachute Brigade.

card_unit_15th_recon_regiment.name: card_unit_15th_recon_regiment
card_unit_15th_recon_regiment.title: 15th RECCE
card_unit_15th_recon_regiment.text:
Deployment: Target a unit. 
15th RECCE gets +1+1 and Guard when the targeted unit deals damage.
card_unit_15th_recon_regiment.flavorText: The 15th Scottish Reconnaissance Regiment was a unit of the 15th (Scottish) Infantry Division, active during WWII. The division was formed in 1939 as part of the Territorial Army and it remained in the United Kingdom for training and home defense duties. In June 1944, they landed in Normandy shortly after D-Day and participated in Operation Epsom and the capture of Caen as part of the British 21st Army Group. They continued to fight through France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, where they participated in Operation Veritable and Operation Plunder. The 15th (Scottish) Infantry Division was disbanded on April 10th, 1946, after suffering over 11,000 casualties, including over 1,500 killed in action over 11 months of fighting. The division was highly regarded and considered one of the best-led infantry divisions in the 21st Army Group.

card_unit_7th_scottish_borderers.name: card_unit_7th_scottish_borderers
card_unit_7th_scottish_borderers.title: 7th SCOTTISH BORDERERS
card_unit_7th_scottish_borderers.text: Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ for each excess Intel you get.
card_unit_7th_scottish_borderers.flavorText: The 7th Battalion was a unit of the King's Own Scottish Borderers, an infantry regiment of the British Army that was first raised in 1689 and stayed active until 2006 when it was merged with the Royal Scots Battalion to form the Royal Scots Borderers. During the interwar period the battalions of the regiment were in service all over the British Empire, but they were called back home when WWII started in 1939. Between 1939 and 1943, the 7th Battalion was stationed in Great Britain on home defense duties, but in July 1943 it was transferred to the 1st Airlanding Brigade and started training as an airborne unit. On September 17th, 1944, the 7th Battalion participated in Operation Market Garden and landed in gliders at Arnhem, where they fought fiercely against a larger German force before withdrawing across the Lower Rhine. After Arnhem, the battalion joined Operation Doomsday to oversee the German surrender in Norway, but tragically lost four men in a plane crash during the journey. The battalion was disbanded on November 28th, 1945, with its members dispersed to other units.

card_unit_beaufighter_vi_f.name: card_unit_beaufighter_vi_f
card_unit_beaufighter_vi_f.title: BEAUFIGHTER VI F
card_unit_beaufighter_vi_f.text: British air units you deploy get +2+2.
card_unit_beaufighter_vi_f.flavorText: The Bristol Beaufighter was a British multi-role aircraft introduced into service in 1940 during the Battle of Britain and used by the Royal Air Force (RAF), the Commonwealth Air Forces and the United States Army Air Forces (USAAF) throughout WWII. The Beaufighter was originally designed as a heavy fighter and proved to be a very effective night fighter as it was able to carry heavy armament and early airborne interception radar without it affecting its performance. The Beaufighter VI variant was introduced in 1942, and the Beaufighter VI F variant was equipped with AI Mark VIII radar which greatly enhanced its performance as a night fighter. However, in late 1942 the faster de Havilland Mosquito became the main night fighter, but the heavier Beaufighter made a valuable contribution in other areas such as anti-shipping, long range interdiction and ground attack roles, and it came to great use in every major theater of operations.

card_unit_cameronians.name: card_unit_cameronians
card_unit_cameronians.title: CAMERONIANS
card_unit_cameronians.text: Draw 2 cards when you give your second order in a turn.
card_unit_cameronians.flavorText: The Cameronians (Scottish Rifles) was a rifle regiment of the British Army which was formed in 1881 and served in the Second Boer War, WWI and later WWII. At the outbreak of WWII, the 1st Battalion was stationed in India, but in 1942 it was deployed in Burma and saw combat in the Burma Campaign as part of the 39th Indian Division. The 2nd Battalion was deployed to France in 1939 as part of the British Expeditionary Force, and after the Dunkirk evacuation in 1940 it participated in the Allied invasion of Sicily and later the Allied invasion of Italy. After serving in the Italian Campaign from 1943 to1944, the battalion participated in the North West Europe Campaign in 1945. The 6th and 7th Battalions were deployed to France as part of the 52nd (Lowland) Infantry Division to provide cover for the Allied withdrawal at Dunkirk, before returning to Britain. After the Normandy Landings in June 1944, the battalions took part in the North West Europe Campaign from 1944 to 1945. The 9th Battalion participated in the Normandy landings in 1944 as part of the 15th (Scottish) Infantry Division and saw action in the North West Europe Campaign from 1944 to 1945. After the war the regiment was reduced to one battalion and would serve in the British Army until it was disbanded in 1968.

card_unit_no_9_commando.name: card_unit_no_9_commando
card_unit_no_9_commando.title: No. 9 COMMANDO
card_unit_no_9_commando.text: Deployment: Set the defense of target enemy unit to 1.
card_unit_no_9_commando.flavorText: No. 9 Commando was a battalion sized unit raised from volunteers by the British Army during WWII.  Their first raid, Operation Sunstar, took place on the night of 22/23 November- 1941 on the French coast at Houlgate and was concluded successfully with no casualties. In March 1942, No. 9 Commando participated in the Saint-Nazaire Raid, providing demolition support alongside other commando units, such as No. 2 Commando. Later that year they reinforced the Gibraltar garrison during Operation Torch, the Allied landings in French North Africa. Following this, they conducted raids on the Italian islands of Tremiti and Pianosa. During the Allied invasion of Italy, as part of the 2nd Special Service Brigade, they engaged in Operation Partridge in December 1943 around the Garigliano River. Then they took part in Operation Shingle, the Anzio landings, and saw combat at Monte Ornito, which led to their withdrawal to Naples in March 1944. Later that year, No. 9 Commando participated in Operation Darlington in May, aimed at rescuing Allied POWs located in Italy, and Operation Gradient in August, which involved demolishing a bridge in the Northern Adriatic. They later operated in Greece before returning to Italy, engaging in Operation Roast, the crossing of Comacchio Lagoon, and finally the battle of the Argenta Gap in April 1945. After the end of WWII, the unit was disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_shark_mk_iii.name: card_unit_shark_mk_iii
card_unit_shark_mk_iii.title: SHARK Mk III
card_unit_shark_mk_iii.text: Deployment: Deal damage to target enemy equal to other friendly air units.
card_unit_shark_mk_iii.flavorText: The Blackburn Shark was a biplane torpedo bomber used by the British Royal Navy Fleet Air Arm during WWII. The aircraft was introduced in the mid-1930s and served primarily as a carrier-based reconnaissance and torpedo bomber aircraft. Despite its obsolescent design compared to contemporary monoplane aircraft, the Blackburn Shark played a significant role in maritime operations during the early years of the war. It saw action in various theaters, including the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic Ocean, where it was used in reconnaissance missions, anti-submarine patrols and torpedo attacks against enemy shipping. While the Blackburn Shark was gradually phased out of frontline service as more advanced aircraft became available, it remained in use for training purposes and coastal defense duties throughout the war. A total of 269 Blackburn Shark’s were manufactured, including a few variants.

card_event_combined_chiefs_of_staff.name: card_event_combined_chiefs_of_staff
card_event_combined_chiefs_of_staff.title: COMBINED CHIEFS OF STAFF
card_event_combined_chiefs_of_staff.text: Your British and US units get +2+3.
card_event_combined_chiefs_of_staff.flavorText: The Combined Chiefs of Staff (CCS) was formed in 1942 and became the central command body for Anglo-American military planning during WWII. Operating from Washington, it brought together senior US and British military leaders to harmonize strategy across all theaters. The CCS played a decisive role in shaping Allied operations, overseeing war production priorities, logistics, and theater command appointments. One of its earliest achievements was the "Germany First" strategy, which prioritized defeating Nazi Germany before focusing on Japan. The CCS also approved Operation Torch, the first major Allied amphibious assault in North Africa, and later coordinated the invasions of Sicily and Italy. Perhaps its most critical contribution came with Operation Overlord. The CCS selected General Eisenhower as Supreme Commander and directed the build-up for the 1944 Normandy landings. In the Pacific, the CCS established a division of responsibility: the US led operations in the central and south-west Pacific, while British forces focused on Southeast Asia. This division allowed for coordinated offensives that overwhelmed Japanese defenses on multiple fronts. Meeting frequently throughout the war and in close contact with political leaders, the CCS ensured unity of command and purpose. Its coordinated approach was unprecedented and critical to the eventual Allied victory.

card_event_forward_observers.name: card_event_forward_observers
card_event_forward_observers.title: FORWARD OBSERVERS
card_event_forward_observers.text: Deal 2 damage to all enemy units. If you deployed a British infantry last turn, draw a card.
card_event_forward_observers.flavorText: During WWII, Forward Observation Officers (FOOs) became vital to British artillery operations. As indirect fire gradually allowed for increased engagement distances, FOOs acted as the eyes of their batteries, embedded with infantry or tank units at the front. Positioned in forward posts or in armored carriers or tanks like the Stuart or Sherman, they identified targets, coordinated fire missions, and communicated directly with their artillery units. FOOs had the authority to call in fire from their own battery, and from mid-war, some could command fire from their entire regiment. Select officers designated as Commander’s Representatives could even access divisional or corps artillery. This decentralized control allowed for rapid, localized responses in fast-moving operations. Often attached to a company or squadron, FOOs developed quick fire plans involving multiple coordinated targets to support limited offensives. These plans were crucial in assaults and defensive actions, blending artillery firepower with frontline maneuvering. By integrating with supported units and adapting to evolving battlefield demands, FOOs played a central role in the success of British artillery throughout the war.

card_event_home_guard.name: card_event_home_guard
card_event_home_guard.title: HOME GUARD
card_event_home_guard.text: Deal 2 damage to target unit. Add a GARRISON to your hand.
card_event_home_guard.flavorText: Formed in May 1940 as the Local Defence Volunteers, the Home Guard quickly became a vital part of Britain's defensive strategy during WWII. It was made up of over 1.5 million men who were too old, too young or medically unfit for regular service, as well as those in reserved occupations (exempt from military service). Their main task was to resist a German invasion by delaying enemy forces long enough for the regular army to respond. Volunteers were initially given only armbands marked "LDV" and received little equipment. Many units improvised weapons or used donated civilian firearms. Eventually, they were issued standard rifles and uniforms. The Home Guard guarded factories, bridges and airfields and manned roadblocks and observation posts. During the Blitz, they were also tasked with guarding unexploded bombs, a role that cost over 1,000 lives. By 1942, the Home Guard took over some coastal artillery and anti-aircraft duties, freeing up regular troops for overseas deployment. Although unpaid, the service attracted widespread support, with entire platoons formed from workplaces or social clubs. The Home Guard represented a massive volunteer effort to protect Britain from within. It officially stood down in late 1944 and was disbanded a year later.

card_event_national_service_home.name: card_event_national_service_home
card_event_national_service_home.title: NATIONAL SERVICE
card_event_national_service_home.text: For each British card in your deck, give it +2 defense if a unit, otherwise reduce the cost by 1.
card_event_national_service_home.flavorText: Britain’s National Service during WWII extended far beyond the battlefield. The National Service (Armed Forces) Act, passed in 1939, introduced conscription for men aged 18 to 41, and it was later expanded to include younger and older groups. From 1941, unmarried women aged 20 to 30 were also called up. While many conscripts served in the military, others were directed into essential civilian roles.The Bevin Boys were among those assigned to industrial work. Named after Minister of Labour Ernest Bevin, these young men were randomly selected to work in coal mines instead of joining the armed forces. Their labor was critical to keeping Britain’s war industries running but earned little recognition at the time. Women were conscripted into services like the Auxiliary Territorial Service (ATS), where they served as clerks, drivers, mechanics and radar operators. Others joined the Women’s Royal Naval Service or the Air Transport Auxiliary. National Service also directed thousands into factories, farms, and shipyards, filling shortages in vital industries. Whether in uniform or overalls, conscripts formed the backbone of Britain's wartime manpower, helping sustain the war effort on all fronts.

card_event_the_land_girls.name: card_event_the_land_girls
card_event_the_land_girls.title: THE LAND GIRLS
card_event_the_land_girls.flavorText: First created in 1917, the Women’s Land Army (WLA) was reformed in 1939 to safeguard British food production as war was imminent. With the regular agricultural workforce depleted by military conscription, the government turned to women to keep farms running. By 1944, the WLA had grown to nearly 80,000 members, nicknamed “Land Girls”. Recruits came from all backgrounds, including cities, and underwent short training courses before being assigned to farms across Britain. Their tasks were varied and often strenuous: cultivating crops, managing livestock, maintaining machinery, and even felling trees. Pay was low and the work physically demanding, yet Land Girls quickly proved their value, earning respect from initially doubtful farmers. Many lived on-site in hostels or with farming families. Despite limited comforts, the WLA fostered strong morale through shared purpose and the novelty of rural life. The government supported recruitment with posters and films showing Land Girls as patriotic heroines vital to the war effort. Their contribution was crucial in avoiding severe food shortages during the war.

card_event_your_courage.name: card_event_your_courage
card_event_your_courage.title: YOUR COURAGE
card_event_your_courage.text: Reduce the cost of cards with Bond in hand by 1. Then your Bond units everywhere get +1+1.
card_event_your_courage.flavorText: In 1939, as Britain prepared for war, the Ministry of Information launched a poster campaign to bolster civilian morale. The first two designs were quickly printed: “Your courage, your cheerfulness, your resolution will bring us victory” and “Freedom is in peril. Defend it with all your might.” The goal was to maintain public confidence during expected air raids and hardships. These posters appeared across shop windows, public transport, and official buildings in the early months of the war. The bold red backgrounds and serif white lettering beneath a stylized crown projected authority and calm. “Your courage” aimed to show unity between the government and the people, placing the burden of perseverance not on soldiers alone but on every British citizen. Unlike “Keep calm and carry on,” which was held in reserve and never widely released, “Your courage” was among the most visible wartime slogans in Britain during 1939 and 1940. Despite its wide distribution, public response was mixed. Some saw it as inspiring, others as patronizing. But it remains a striking example of how wartime British propaganda used simple design and direct language to prepare the homefront for the trials ahead.

card_unit_baltimore_mk_iii.name: card_unit_baltimore_mk_iii
card_unit_baltimore_mk_iii.title: BALTIMORE Mk III
card_unit_baltimore_mk_iii.text: Deployment: Deal 3 damage to an enemy unit if you deployed a British infantry last turn.
card_unit_baltimore_mk_iii.flavorText: The Baltimore Mk III was a British-operated variant of the American-built Martin 187 Baltimore light bomber, employed extensively in the Mediterranean and Middle East during WWII. Built by the Glenn L. Martin Company, the Mk III incorporated several improvements over earlier versions, including upgraded Wright R-2600-19 engines and better defensive armament. This variant retained the twin .50 caliber machine guns in the dorsal turret and added enhanced armor and self-sealing fuel tanks for better survivability in combat. Deployed by the Royal Air Force thanks tor the Lend-Lease program, the Baltimore Mk III served in bomber and reconnaissance roles. It gained a reputation for ruggedness and reliability, particularly in desert operations. The RAF used it in tactical bombing missions over North Africa, Sicily, and Italy, often flying at low to medium altitudes to target enemy supply lines, airfields, and defensive positions. Despite initial concerns about visibility from the cockpit and handling characteristics, crews came to appreciate the Baltimore’s durability and payload capacity. The aircraft’s performance was particularly valued during the Tunisian campaign, where its speed and maneuverability made it difficult for Axis fighters to intercept. In total, 1,575 Baltimores were built, with a significant portion being Mk III variants.

card_unit_britain_25_pounder_home.name: card_unit_britain_25_pounder_home
card_unit_britain_25_pounder_home.title: 25 POUNDER Mk I
card_unit_britain_25_pounder_home.text: At the start of your turn, this and adjacent ground units get +1+1.
card_unit_britain_25_pounder_home.flavorText: The Ordnance QF 25-pounder Mk I served as Britain’s primary field gun at the onset of WWII. It started as an emergency measure, created by mounting a new 25-pounder barrel onto the carriage of the obsolete 18-pounder field gun. Commonly known as the '18/25-pounder,' this hybrid was a compromise design. Although not perfect, it allowed artillery units to rearm quickly in the late 1930s. First issued in 1939, the Mk I was deployed with the British Expeditionary Force in France and saw action during the early desert campaigns in North Africa. It fired a 25-pound (11.3 kg) shell and offered both high-explosive and smoke rounds, along with a solid-shot anti-tank capability. However, unlike the later versions, the Mk I utilized a split-trail carriage rather than a platform, which limited its traverse and restricted it to a maximum range of roughly 11,500 yards (due to the inability to use maximum propellant charges). While it was soon replaced by the robust Mk II, which featured a dedicated carriage, muzzle brake, and 360-degree firing platform, the Mk I played a crucial role in bridging Britain’s artillery gap. Approximately 400 units were produced, providing essential firepower during the early war's most critical moments.

card_unit_defiant_mk_i.name: card_unit_defiant_mk_i
card_unit_defiant_mk_i.title: DEFIANT Mk I
card_unit_defiant_mk_i.text: Has +2 attack on your turn if you deployed a British infantry last turn.
card_unit_defiant_mk_i.flavorText: The Boulton Paul Defiant Mk I was a unique British "turret fighter" introduced in 1939. Designed to combat unescorted bombers, it was notable for lacking forward-firing guns. Instead, it relied on a powered dorsal turret located behind the pilot, armed with four .303 Browning machine guns. This concept proved effective briefly during the Dunkirk evacuation, as Luftwaffe pilots often mistook the aircraft for a Hawker Hurricane and attacked from the rear, flying directly into the gunner's sights. However, once the Germans adapted their tactics, the Defiant suffered heavy losses in daylight operations. Outclassed by faster, more agile enemy fighters, the Mk I was withdrawn from day combat and reassigned to night fighting. Equipped with airborne interception radar, the Defiant found a new niche role, achieving moderate success during the Blitz, between September 1940 and May 1941, before being superseded by faster twin-engine aircraft like the Beaufighter and Mosquito. The Mk I remained in service for training, air-sea rescue, and electronic warfare roles. Over 700 Mk I units were produced before the improved Mk II entered service. Though short-lived as a frontline fighter, the Defiant filled a critical gap during a period of RAF vulnerability and remains notable as one of the few operational turret fighters of WWII.

card_unit_hampshire_regiment.name: card_unit_hampshire_regiment
card_unit_hampshire_regiment.title: HAMPSHIRE REGIMENT
card_unit_hampshire_regiment.text: Deployment: Develop CONVOY HX 175, THE DESERT RATS or FORTIFICATION.
card_unit_hampshire_regiment.flavorText: The Hampshire Regiment served in numerous theatres during WWII, continuing a long tradition dating back to its formation in 1881. By 1939, it fielded multiple regular and Territorial Army battalions. The 1st Battalion was deployed to North Africa where it fought in the Tunisia Campaign, and then participated in the Allied invasion of Sicily in 1943. After that, it landed at Salerno during the Italian Campaign and fought northward through arduous mountain battles. The 2nd Battalion, originally stationed in India, was later sent to Burma where it took part in the Arakan operations against Japanese forces. Territorial battalions were deployed across various fronts. Notably, the 7th Battalion landed in Normandy shortly after D-Day, fought through the bocage and took part in the advance into Germany. The regiment earned numerous battle honours, in particular for its role at El Alamein, Monte Cassino and in the Rhine crossings. In 1946, the regiment was granted the “Royal” prefix in recognition of its wartime service. The Royal Hampshire Regiment eventually merged with the Queen's Regiment in 1992 to form the Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment.

card_unit_kings_african_rifles.name: card_unit_kings_african_rifles
card_unit_kings_african_rifles.title: KING'S AFRICAN RIFLES
card_unit_kings_african_rifles.text: Deployment: Choose a unit in hand. Give it +1+1 and Bond. +3+3 instead if it already has Bond.
card_unit_kings_african_rifles.flavorText: The King’s African Rifles (KAR) was a multi-battalion regiment of African soldiers under British command, drawn from Britain’s East African colonies. At the start of WWII, the regiment consisted of only six battalions. Wartime expansion saw it grow to 43 battalions by 1943, including support units like engineers, signals, and medical detachments. Recruits came from Kenya, Tanganyika, Uganda, Nyasaland, and Northern Rhodesia. KAR units fought in the East African Campaign against Italian forces in Ethiopia and Somaliland, conducting mountain warfare in challenging terrain. In 1942, the regiment took part in the invasion of Madagascar, helping to remove the Vichy French presence. Later, KAR formations were sent to Burma. The 11th (East African) Division, formed largely from KAR units, fought in the Arakan and across central Burma. African soldiers of the KAR crossed the Irrawaddy River, helped take Mandalay, and advanced on Rangoon. They proved adept at jungle warfare, often using machetes instead of bayonets, and showed strong discipline and adaptability despite racial inequities in pay and rations. By the end of the war, over 100,000 African troops had served in the KAR, making it one of the largest African formations in the British Empire.

card_unit_layforce.name: card_unit_layforce
card_unit_layforce.title: LAYFORCE
card_unit_layforce.text: Your non-British cards cost +1. Gets +1+1 when the enemy targets or attacks it.
card_unit_layforce.flavorText: Layforce was a temporary commando formation created in early 1941 to strike Axis positions across the Mediterranean. Named after its commander, Colonel Robert Laycock, the unit drew men from several British commando battalions, including No. 3, No. 7, No. 8 (Guards), No. 11 (Scottish), No. 50 and No. 52 Commandos. Initially intended for raids on enemy-held islands like Rhodes, Layforce instead found itself pressed into more conventional roles as the Allied situation worsened. In March 1941, elements of Layforce took part in the Bardia raid in Libya. In May, they were rushed to Crete where they fought fiercely during the German airborne invasion but suffered heavy casualties. Later that summer, they supported regular troops in the Syria-Lebanon campaign and helped defend Tobruk, notably participating in a daring assault known as the Twin Pimples raid. In August 1941, the unit was disbanded, its survivors moving on to other special forces like the SAS and the Special Boat Section. Though short-lived, Layforce proved the value of unconventional troops in the Mediterranean theater.

card_unit_london_irish_rifles.name: card_unit_london_irish_rifles
card_unit_london_irish_rifles.title: LONDON IRISH RIFLES
card_unit_london_irish_rifles.text: When you play a card with Bond, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_london_irish_rifles.flavorText: The London Irish Rifles were formed in 1859 as a volunteer rifle corps in London, reflecting the city’s Irish community and military tradition. In WWII, the regiment expanded to two battalions under the Territorial Army. The 1st Battalion took part in the Battle of Graveney Marsh in 1940, the last recorded ground engagement with a foreign enemy on the British mainland. Both battalions were later deployed to the Mediterranean theater. They fought in Tunisia, joined the Allied landings in Sicily, and advanced through Italy. In 1944, they endured prolonged shelling and enemy counterattacks while holding a critical beachhead at Anzio. They later went on to help liberate Rome and fought through the Apennines into northern Italy. Throughout the campaign, the London Irish Rifles were noted for their combat effectiveness, earning a solid reputation within the 8th Army.

card_unit_middlesex_regiment.name: card_unit_middlesex_regiment
card_unit_middlesex_regiment.title: MIDDLESEX REGIMENT
card_unit_middlesex_regiment.text: Deployment: Add a GARRISON to your hand.
card_unit_middlesex_regiment.flavorText: The Middlesex Regiment’s nickname was "The Die Hards". It inherited it from the 57th Regiment of Foot, whose men stood firm under Colonel Inglis at the 1811 Battle of Albuera. During WWII, the regiment played a diverse and significant role. The 1st Battalion was stationed in Hong Kong when Japan launched its December 1941 attack. Despite being cut off and outnumbered, they resisted for 17 days before surrendering. Meanwhile, the 1/7th Battalion, part of the 51st (Highland) Division, operated as a machine gun unit across Europe. The 1/8th, later redesignated as the 8th Battalion, supported the 43rd (Wessex) Division throughout the Normandy Campaign and the Battle for Caen. The Middlesex Regiment was one of the few infantry units converted entirely to a machine gun role, providing fire support across various theatres. Its wartime organization also included duplicate Territorial battalions formed before the outbreak of war.

card_unit_raf_mustang.name: card_unit_raf_mustang
card_unit_raf_mustang.title: RAF MUSTANG
card_unit_raf_mustang.text: Your non-British cards cost +2. Draw a card when the enemy targets or attacks this unit.
card_unit_raf_mustang.flavorText: The RAF Mustang I was the first British-operated version of the American-designed North American P-51 Mustang. It entered service in 1942 and was powered by an Allison V-1710 engine that performed best at low altitudes. This made it ideal for tactical reconnaissance and ground attack missions, roles where its speed, range, and low-level agility were fully utilized. The RAF employed the Mustang I extensively for operations over France, the Low Countries, and occupied Europe. Flying low to evade radar and intercept German troop movements, its pilots gathered valuable intelligence and struck targets behind enemy lines. Its range allowed it to fly deep into enemy territory, supporting bombing missions and disrupting supply routes. Although it struggled at higher altitudes compared to fighters like the Spitfire or Bf 109, the Mustang I filled a critical gap in British tactical air power. Its success in these missions encouraged further development. Later versions, fitted with Rolls-Royce Merlin engines, would transform the Mustang into one of the most effective high-altitude escort fighters of the war. But it was the Mustang I that proved the concept in combat.

card_unit_the_bleeders.name: card_unit_the_bleeders
card_unit_the_bleeders.title: THE BLEEDERS
card_unit_the_bleeders.text: Gets +1+1 when you play a card with Bond.
card_unit_the_bleeders.flavorText: The Somerset Light Infantry, nicknamed “The Bleeders,” traced its origins to 1685, having been raised in response to the Monmouth Rebellion. By the outbreak of WWII, the regiment had already fought in numerous major conflicts. During the early years of the war, its battalions served across India, Burma, and the Middle East. The 1st Battalion saw extensive combat in the Burma Campaign, enduring some of the most punishing conditions of the war. Deployed in 1942 to counter the Japanese advance into India, it later participated in the critical battles of Kohima and Imphal, helping to halt the Japanese offensive. The regiment’s light infantry training made it particularly well-suited for the region's mountainous terrain and dense jungles. Meanwhile, the 7th Battalion served with distinction in North Africa and Italy. The 10th Battalion, originally a hostilities-only unit, was converted into the 7th Parachute Battalion in 1943. It went on to fight in Normandy, the Ardennes, and across the Rhine during the final Allied push into Germany. Finally, the 30th Battalion, part of the 43rd Infantry Brigade under the British First Army, saw active service in both Tunisia and Italy.

card_unit_the_polar_bears.name: card_unit_the_polar_bears
card_unit_the_polar_bears.title: THE POLAR BEARS
card_unit_the_polar_bears.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 if you deployed a British infantry last turn.
card_unit_the_polar_bears.flavorText: The 49th (West Riding) Infantry Division earned the nickname "The Polar Bears" during their deployment to Iceland in 1940. Tasked with garrison duties to prevent German occupation, they adopted the polar bear as their divisional insignia. After returning to Britain in 1942, the division underwent extensive training before joining the Normandy campaign in June 1944. Attached to I Corps, they were initially tasked with securing the left flank of the Allied beachhead, fighting around Caen and advancing through the Bocage. The Polar Bears played a key role in Operation Martlet and the costly battles for Rauray and Fontenay-le-Pesnel. In the final push into the Low Countries and Germany, they participated in clearing the Scheldt estuary and crossed the Rhine in March 1945. Under the command of Major General Evelyn Barker, the division developed a reputation for discipline and toughness in battle. By war's end, they had advanced deep into northwestern Germany, contributing significantly to the Allied victory in Europe.

card_unit_the_pompadours.name: card_unit_the_pompadours
card_unit_the_pompadours.title: THE POMPADOURS
card_unit_the_pompadours.text: While in hand, your HQ gets +1 defense each time you play a card with Bond.
card_unit_the_pompadours.flavorText: The Essex Regiment existed from 1881 to 1958 and served with distinction throughout WWII. The regiment’s battalions were deployed in various roles across multiple theaters. In 1940 the 2nd battalion was attached to the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division and served with the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1940. The battalion was evacuated from Dunkirk after the short but fierce Battle of Dunkirk and remained stationed in the UK for home defense duties before joining the 3rd Infantry Division to take part in Operation Overlord. It landed on Sword Beach during the Normandy invasion on 6 June 1944. In the weeks that followed, the battalion was engaged in intense fighting to secure Caen and push through German defenses in northern France. Other battalions of the Regiment served in the Middle East and Italy, contributing to key operations including the North African campaign and the advance through Italy. The Essex Regiment had purple facings, which were rare and distinctive. This color became closely associated with their identity and led to their nickname, "The Pompadours", a reference to Madame de Pompadour, who favored purple.

card_unit_valentine_mk_ii.name: card_unit_valentine_mk_ii
card_unit_valentine_mk_ii.title: VALENTINE Mk II
card_unit_valentine_mk_ii.text: Deployment: Gets Blitz if you deployed a British infantry last turn.
card_unit_valentine_mk_ii.flavorText: The Mk II was the first version of the Valentine tank to be fitted with a diesel engine, replacing the petrol engine used in the Mk I. Based on the AEC Comet commercial vehicle’s engine, the diesel was chosen for better range and reliability. Introduced in 1940, the Mk II kept the same compact hull and 2 pounder gun in a two-man turret, but the change of engine significantly improved operational performance. The Mk II was rushed into production without prototype trials, as British industry scrambled to rearm after the evacuation at Dunkirk. By September 1940, over 100 had already been built. It began service in armoured divisions in Britain and arrived in North Africa in June 1941. Although undergunned by contemporary standards, the Mk II’s excellent mechanical reliability made it a favorite in desert conditions. During the advance from El Alamein to Tunisia, some Valentines covered more than 3,000 miles.The Mk II was also supplied in large numbers to the Soviet Union through the Lend Lease program. Crews valued its sturdy armor and dependable engine, even if the 2 pounder gun quickly became obsolete in frontline combat.

card_event_against_the_odds.name: card_event_against_the_odds
card_event_against_the_odds.title: AGAINST THE ODDS
card_event_against_the_odds.text: When a unit attacks, pin it afterwards. Draw a card.
card_event_against_the_odds.flavorText: In August 1940, during the Battle of Britain, Flight Lieutenant Peter Brothers was leading a flight of 8 fighters and came into contact with 100 Luftwaffe bombers and fighter escorts. Despite being so heavily outnumbered Lieutenant Brothers led his flight against the enemy, but was soon attacked by a number of Bf 109 fighters. Despite this he managed to shoot down a Dornier 215 bomber, a Bf 109 fighter and escape unharmed. This one of many stories of RAF pilots that Winston Churchill referred to as “The Few”.

card_event_ats.name: card_event_ats
card_event_ats.title: ATS
card_event_ats.text: The enemy HQ gets: "If this HQ has taken 3+ damage this turn, you draw a card."
card_event_ats.flavorText: The Auxiliary Territorial Service (ATS) was formed in 1938 and was the women's branch of the British Army.  At the time women were not allowed to serve in battle, but instead they took over many supporting roles, such as being radar operators, military police, searchlight operators, crews of anti aircraft guns and many served with the Royal Corps of Signals. By 1945 there were over 190,000 women serving in the ATS.

card_event_double_strength.name: card_event_double_strength
card_event_double_strength.title: DOUBLE STRENGTH
card_event_double_strength.text: Shuffle a copy of a random order in your hand into your deck.
card_event_double_strength.flavorText: Ground attack aircraft were often converted air-superiority fighters such as Spitfires, P-38 Lightnings, P-51 Mustangs and Mosquitos. In their attacks they would fly very low, at treetop level, in order to avoid radar detection and bomb and strafe military targets on land or sea. The P-51’s that were used to escort bombers into Germany, would on their way back to England often fly low and freely attack any ground targets they spotted on the way.

card_event_emergency_measures.name: card_event_emergency_measures
card_event_emergency_measures.title: EMERGENCY MEASURES
card_event_emergency_measures.text: Choose and discard a Spitfire to add a RAF GROUND CREW to the support line.
card_event_emergency_measures.flavorText:
During the Battle of Britain there were several instances where pilots used their aircraft to ram into enemy aircraft. This was most of the time used as a last resort, when the ammo had run out or the guns were jammed, and many pilots never lived to tell the tale. There were three types of ramming: 

> Using the whole aircraft to ram directly into the enemy aircraft, this was of course the most dangerous option. 
> Using the propeller to chop off the controls in the tail of the enemy aircraft.
> Using the wings, either to damage the enemy aircraft or to make it lose control.

Another method, which is not exactly ramming, was used by British pilots when intercepting the German V1 rockets and is called the “wing tipping”. Instead of trying to shoot at the V1 rocket, which involved the risk of being incinerated in the blast, the pilot would dive from high altitude in order to gain enough speed to catch up with the rocket, then fly beside it and tip the wing into in order to knock it off its course.

card_event_overrun.name: card_event_overrun
card_event_overrun.title: OVERRUN
card_event_overrun.text: Attacking ground units deal damage equal to their defense this turn.
card_event_overrun.flavorText: In military terms, the verb “overrun” is to defeat and occupy enemy positions in a decisive manner.

card_event_resourcefulness.name: card_event_resourcefulness
card_event_resourcefulness.title: RESOURCEFULNESS
card_event_resourcefulness.text: Draw a random Commando unit from your deck.
card_event_resourcefulness.flavorText: Many Allied prisoners of war believed that it was their duty to try to escape and to rejoin the fight again. However, fewer than 1,200 of the 170,000 British and Commonwealth POWs in Germany managed to escape successfully and to make it home. One of the most famous breakouts is the “Great Escape” in 1944, lead by Squadron Leader Roger Bushell, from Stalag Luft III camp which held Allied aircrew. Preparations for the escape started in 1943, with three tunnels being dug by the POWs, but they only managed to finish one. On the night of the breakout 76 men climbed out of the tunnel, but of those only 3 made it home. The rest of the men were captured by the Germans and 50 of them were executed on Hitlers orders. This breakout was immortalized in the 1963 film “The Great Escape” although characters and events were altered.

card_event_timely_supplies.name: card_event_timely_supplies
card_event_timely_supplies.title: TIMELY SUPPLIES
card_event_timely_supplies.text: Draw a card. It costs 2 less this turn.
card_event_timely_supplies.flavorText: In 1940 the US was still a neutral country but nevertheless they started to provide the Allies with significant supplies, most of them going to the United Kingdom. At the time the majority of Americans opposed direct participation in the war, and although President Roosevelt was willing to help the Allied cause, he could simply not provide them with supplies as a gift. Instead he initiated the Lend-Lease program, which meant that the US would “lend” supplies to the United Kingdom and other Allies, but would not insist on being paid back immediately. Throughout the war the US would provide over 30 countries with aid through the Lend-Lease program, in the approximate amount of 50 billion dollars.

card_unit_1st_gurkha_rifles.name: card_unit_1st_gurkha_rifles
card_unit_1st_gurkha_rifles.title: 1st GURKHA RIFLES
card_unit_1st_gurkha_rifles.text: Gets +1 attack when you give an order.
card_unit_1st_gurkha_rifles.flavorText: The 1st Gurkha Rifles, also known as The Malaun Regiment, was first formed in 1815 and has since then participated in many conflicts, including WWI and WWII, and is today a regiment of the Indian Army. During WWII the regiment grew from 2 to 5 battalions in size who all participated in fierce fighting against the Japanese forces, mostly in Malaya and Burma. The Gurkhas have a reputation for military valor and skill and are often associated with the kukri, a machete that is curved forward, and is used both as a melee weapon or a cutting tool.

card_unit_5th_parachute_brigade.name: card_unit_5th_parachute_brigade
card_unit_5th_parachute_brigade.title: 5th PARACHUTE BRIGADE
card_unit_5th_parachute_brigade.flavorText: The 5th Parachute Brigade was raised by the British Army during WWII, and along with the 3rd Parachute and the 6th Airlanding Brigade it was assigned to the 6th Airborne Division. The brigade participated in their first airborne operation in June 1944, Operation Tonga, which was part of Operation Overlord and the D-Day landings in Normandy. The next engagement the 5th Brigade participated in was during the Battle of the Bulge, which was followed by Operation Varsity, a successful airborne operation over Germany and the last Allied airborne operation during WWII. When the war ended the brigade was involved in disarming Japanese forces in South Asia before rejoining the 6th Airborne Division in Palestine where the brigade was disbanded in late 1945.

card_unit_barracuda_21.name: card_unit_barracuda_21
card_unit_barracuda_21.title: BARRACUDA
card_unit_barracuda_21.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to an enemy. If the enemy is a unit, pin it.
card_unit_barracuda_21.flavorText: The Fairey Barracuda was a British carrier-borne torpedo and dive bomber that was used by the Royal Navy Fleet Air Arm (FAA) during WWII. The Barracuda entered service in 1943 as a replacement Fairey Albacore biplane, and after the retirement of the Blackburn Skua, it was the only British naval aircraft fit for dive bombing, even though it was primarily designed for torpedo bombing. Later models such as the Mk II and Mk III were radar-equipped and mostly used in anti-submarine operations. The Barracuda was used in numerous operations during the war, most famously in the attack on Tirpitz in Operation Tungsten, and was deployed in the Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. A total of 2,602 aircraft were built from 1941-1945, including variants.

card_unit_beaufighter_tf_mk_x.name: card_unit_beaufighter_tf_mk_x
card_unit_beaufighter_tf_mk_x.title: BEAUFIGHTER TF Mk X
card_unit_beaufighter_tf_mk_x.text: Any unit that attacks this unit takes 3 damage first.
card_unit_beaufighter_tf_mk_x.flavorText: The Bristol Beaufighter was a British heavy fighter aircraft that was introduced in 1940 and used by the RAF and the air forces of the British Commonwealth during WWII. The Beaufighter was slow and heavy, but rather maneuverable, and had space for radar which made it an excellent night fighter to counter German night time bombing raids. The aircraft would take on a variety of roles throughout the war and was used in anti-shipping, ground attack and long-range interdiction.  The Beaufighter TF Mk X variant was called “Torbeau”, and was a two seated torpedo fighter aircraft that had a Hercules XVII engine with cropped superchargers, which improved its low-altitude performance. A total of 5,928 Beaufighters were built, 2,231 of the TF Mk X variant.

card_unit_british_buffalo.name: card_unit_british_buffalo
card_unit_british_buffalo.title: RAF BUFFALO Mk I
card_unit_british_buffalo.flavorText: The Brewster Buffalo Mk I was the British designation of the American Brewster F2A Buffalo, a fighter aircraft that was introduced in 1939 and used in service by the US and Allied air forces early in WWII.  At the start of the war the British and Commonwealth forces were in desperate need of fighter aircraft and ordered the Buffalo to use in the Far East only as it was deemed unfit for service in the West. The Buffalo was considered both unstable and overweight in comparison to the Axis aircraft, especially the Japanese Mitsubishi A6M Zero, and would soon make way for the Hawker Hurricane which was a great improvement over the Buffalo. From 1942 most Buffalo’s in British service were pulled from the frontline and for training purposes.

card_unit_churchill_mk_iii_avre.name: card_unit_churchill_mk_iii_avre
card_unit_churchill_mk_iii_avre.title: CHURCHILL Mk III AVRE
card_unit_churchill_mk_iii_avre.text: Deployment: All enemy ground units must Retreat.
card_unit_churchill_mk_iii_avre.flavorText: The Churchill AVRE (Assault Vehicle Royal Engineers) was a converted Churchill tank, Mk III or IV, that was designed to protect engineers during frontline battlefield operations. The Churchill AVRE had the 6 pounder gun replaced with a 290 mm petard spigot mortar that was used to destroy defenses such as roadblocks, bunkers, pillboxes and other concrete, brick or earthen obstacles. The AVRE could also be equipped with other devices such as the Canadian Indestructible Roller Device (CIRD) that protected the tank against mines, and the Small Box Girder bridge that could be laid over narrow ditches or rivers. The first Churchill AVRE’s were deployed in Normandy during D-Day and a total of 754 tanks were produced before the end of the war.

card_unit_intel_fusiliers.name: card_unit_intel_fusiliers
card_unit_intel_fusiliers.title: INNISKILLING FUSILIERS
card_unit_intel_fusiliers.text: When you play a card with Intel, deal 3 damage to a random enemy.
card_unit_intel_fusiliers.flavorText: The Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers was an Irish regiment of the British Army and was active from 1881 to 1968. During WWII the regiment was raised from 2 battalions to 5, the 1st, 2nd, 5th, 6th and 70th. The 1st Battalion was stationed in British India when the war broke out and fought in the British colony of Burma against the Japanese forces. The 2nd Battalion was part of the British Expeditionary Forces in France before being evacuated at Dunkirk in 1940. In 1942 the battalion was sent to Madagascar where it fought the Vichy French. In 1943 the 2nd participated in the Invasion of Sicily, followed by the advance into Italy, as part of the British Eighth Army. The 5th Battalion served as a home defense formation in the UK where it spent the war. The 6th Battalion was formed in 1940 and was later redesignated 38th (Irish) Infantry Brigade, which fought with the 6th Armoured Division in the Invasion of Sicily, Italy and the Tunisian Campaign. The 70th Battalion was raised early in the war and was for young volunteers who had not reached the age to be conscripted. The 70th was disbanded in 1943 without seeing active service.

card_unit_m3_grant_brit.name: card_unit_m3_grant_brit
card_unit_m3_grant_brit.title: M3 GRANT
card_unit_m3_grant_brit.text: Deployment: Gets +1+2 if your HQ has defense over 20.
card_unit_m3_grant_brit.flavorText: The M3 Grant was a British variant of the M3 Lee, an American medium tank that was produced and used by the Allies during WWII. The version of the M3 tank that the British and Commonwealth forces used was slightly smaller than the American version because it had the commander's cupola removed. The first M3 Grant’s started to arrive on the battlefield in 1942 and they saw action for the first time during the North African Desert campaign. At the start they were superior to the enemy tanks, both in armor and firepower, but this did not last long. With the introduction of the German Panther, Tiger and the long barreled 75 mm Panzer MkIV, the British M3 tanks became easy targets due to their high profile and would soon be replaced with the M4 Sherman. The M3 Grant had two guns, a 75 mm Gun M2/M3 in the hull and a  37mm Gun M5/M6 in the turret, and needed a crew of 6 (driver, 2x gunners, loader, machine gun operator and commander).

card_location_alam_el_halfa.name: card_location_alam_el_halfa
card_location_alam_el_halfa.title: ALAM EL HALFA
card_location_alam_el_halfa.text: During the Battle of Alam el Halfa in 1942 the British forces halted a major Axis assault.
card_location_alam_el_halfa.flavorText: The Battle of Alam el Halfa took place from August 30th to September 5th, 1942, near El Alamein in Egypt. German and Italian forces, led by General Erwin Rommel, attempted to break through British defenses to seize the Suez Canal. However, the British, under General Bernard Montgomery, anticipated the attack and established strong defensive positions on higher ground. Despite intense fighting, the British forces held their lines, forcing Rommel to retreat. This battle marked a turning point in the North African Campaign, as it was the last major offensive by Axis forces in the region.

card_location_london_waw.text: The capital of the British Empire and the center of the British and Allied war effort in Europe.
card_location_london_waw.flavorText: London, the capital city of the UK, was hit hard by German bombing in the so called “Blitz” that lasted from September 1940 to May 1941, and from 1944 to 1945 the V1 bomb and V2 rocket attacks caused massive casualties and damage. During the war London was also the home of several governments in exile and hosted large numbers of overseas personnel, which put it at the center of the Allied war effort in Europe.
