card_location_tunis_city.title: TUNIS CITY
card_location_tunis_city.text: The capture of Tunis City in 1943 saw all of North Africa in Allied hands.
card_location_tunis_city.flavorText: Tunis City, the capital of Tunisia was one of the Allied objectives in Operation Torch, the Allied landings in North Africa in 1942. The Tunisian Campaign lasted from November 17, 1942 to May 13, 1943 and was a series of battles that took place in French Tunisia between the Axis and the Allies. The Allied coalition consisted of British, Greek, American and French forces versus the German and Italian forces on the Axis side. The campaign ended with an Allied victory and the ejection of the Axis forces from North Africa.

card_event_bpf.name: card_event_bpf
card_event_bpf.title: BPF
card_event_bpf.text: Develop BLAST, PLAN or PRODUCTION, then Develop a British Navy card.
card_event_bpf.flavorText: The British Pacific Fleet (BPF) was a Royal Navy force that fought against Japan during World War II. It was created in November 1944 and included aircraft carriers, warships, submarines, and supply ships from the Royal Navy and other Commonwealth navies. After forming in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), the fleet first carried out attacks on Japanese resources in Sumatra. It then moved to Australia, setting up its main base in Sydney and a forward base on Manus Island near Papua New Guinea. In March 1945, the BPF supported the invasion of Okinawa by targeting Japanese air bases on the Sakishima Islands. Despite facing strong Japanese air attacks, the fleet’s armored carriers and modern fighter aircraft provided strong defense. Its submarines also played a crucial role in disrupting Japanese supply lines and naval operations. In July 1945, the fleet helped bombard the Japanese mainland. By the war’s end the BPF had four battleships, six fleet carriers, fifteen smaller carriers, and over 750 aircraft.

card_event_chain_home.name: card_event_chain_home
card_event_chain_home.title: CHAIN HOME
card_event_chain_home.text: Change the attack of a friendly unit to be equal to its defense. It fights a random enemy unit.
card_event_chain_home.flavorText: Chain Home was the code name for the British early warning radar system developed before and during WWII. It was the first operational radar network in the world and became a key component of the United Kingdom’s air defense system. Construction began in the 1930s, and by the outbreak of war in 1939, a chain of radar stations had been established along the British coastline. These stations used high-frequency radio waves to detect incoming enemy aircraft at long range. Information from the radar was sent to filter rooms and command centers, where it was used to direct RAF fighter aircraft to intercept enemy bombers. Chain Home played a vital role in the defense of Britain against aerial attacks and was especially important during the Battle of Britain in 1940, as it allowed the RAF to effectively manage its limited fighter resources. The system remained operational throughout the war and was continually expanded and upgraded.

card_event_dilemma.name: card_event_dilemma
card_event_dilemma.title: DILEMMA
card_event_dilemma.text: Swap the attack and operation cost of target unit.
card_event_dilemma.flavorText: The cracking of the German Enigma code, codenamed Program Ultra by the Allies, was one of the most closely guarded secrets of WWII and a turning point in the Allied campaign. The first breakthroughs came from Polish mathematicians, who succeeded in reconstructing early Enigma machines and passed their knowledge to British and French intelligence just before the war. Building on this foundation, the codebreakers at Bletchley Park achieved what many thought impossible, breaking the complex ciphers that directed German military operations. Ultra intelligence gave the Allies a decisive edge, revealing enemy plans across land and sea. But this success came with a painful dilemma. To protect the Ultra secret and keep the Germans unaware that their codes were compromised, British commanders sometimes allowed friendly ground forces, convoys and ships to be attacked, even when forewarned by decrypted messages. These sacrifices were a heavy burden, but it preserved the vital flow of Ultra intelligence for the rest of the war.

card_event_hms_belfast.name: card_event_hms_belfast
card_event_hms_belfast.title: HMS BELFAST
card_event_hms_belfast.text: Put a unit on top of owner's deck. Shuffle the deck if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_event_hms_belfast.flavorText: HMS Belfast was a British Royal Navy light cruiser launched in 1938 which played a significant role during WWII. Early in the war, the ship was damaged by a German mine and spent over two years undergoing repairs. She returned to action in 1942, equipped with advanced radar and heavy artillery, and at first her main role was to escort Arctic convoys to the Soviet Union where vital supplies were delivered for the Allied war effort on the Eastern Front. In December 1943, Belfast took part in the Battle of North Cape where she helped to sink the German battlecruiser Scharnhorst. Later it participated in Operation Tungsten, which was a major Fleet Air Arm strike on the German battleship Tirpitz. Most famously, HMS Belfast was one of the first ships to open fire on D-Day, bombarding German positions to support Allied landings on the beaches of Normandy. After the war, HMS Belfast served in Korea before being retired. Today, she is preserved as a museum ship on the river Thames in London where her wartime service is commemorated.

card_event_hms_formidable.name: card_event_hms_formidable
card_event_hms_formidable.title: HMS FORMIDABLE
card_event_hms_formidable.text: Change the attack of a friendly unit to be equal to its defense. It fights all enemy units in random order.
card_event_hms_formidable.flavorText: HMS Formidable was an Illustrious-class aircraft carrier of the British Royal Navy, commissioned in 1940. She was built with an armored flight deck designed to withstand heavy air attacks, which was a critical feature during the intense naval battles of WWII. HMS Formidable first saw action in the Mediterranean where it launched strikes against Italian targets and played a key role in the Battle of Cape Matapan in 1941. She later supported operations in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, including air raids against Japanese positions in Sumatra and the invasion of Okinawa. In May 1945, she was hit directly by a kamikaze attack, but thanks to her armored design, took only limited damage and was back in action within hours. Throughout the war, Formidable's aircraft flew thousands of sorties and provided vital support to Allied naval and ground forces. After the war, HMS Formidable was used to transport former POWs and military personnel across the British Empire. Her final troop transport mission concluded in February 1947. She was then decommissioned in 1953 and sold for scrap.

card_event_hms_spectre.name: card_event_hms_spectre
card_event_hms_spectre.title: HMS SCEPTRE
card_event_hms_spectre.text: Counter an enemy order then Convert it to PLAN and return it to hand.
card_event_hms_spectre.flavorText: HMS Sceptre was an S-class submarine of the Royal Navy commissioned in 1943. It was built by Scotts Shipbuilding and Engineering Company, and deployed primarily in the North Sea and Norwegian waters. Sceptre conducted patrols and offensive operations against German naval and merchant vessels, including laying mines and launching torpedo attacks. Sceptre played a role in Operation Source in 1943, supporting attacks against German battleships in Norwegian fjords, though she did not participate directly in the X-craft midget submarine attacks. Another of her notable missions involved the sinking of a couple German merchant ships and damaging others during convoy attacks in the Bay of Biscay in May 1944. Throughout her service in WWII, HMS Sceptre completed multiple patrols and contributed to the disruption of Axis maritime activity in northern European waters. She remained in service until the end of the war and was eventually scrapped in 1949.

card_event_protected_convoy.name: card_event_protected_convoy
card_event_protected_convoy.title: PROTECTED CONVOY
card_event_protected_convoy.text: Add a PRODUCTION and a PLAN to your hand.
card_event_protected_convoy.flavorText: During WWII, British and Allied convoys transported essential supplies such as food, fuel, and equipment across oceans. These groups of merchant ships, escorted by warships, faced constant threats from German U-boats, aircraft, and surface raiders. Convoys operated in key regions such as the North Atlantic, Arctic, and Mediterranean, where they ensured the flow of essential resources to Allied forces and civilian populations. To counter attacks, convoys relied heavily on coordinated tactics. Escort ships used sonar and depth charges to detect and engage submarines. Aircraft patrols, including long-range bombers, reduced U-boat effectiveness by forcing them to submerge. Intelligence from decoded German communications (designated Ultra) allowed convoys to reroute away from U-boat "wolf packs". New weapons such as the Hedgehog mortar improved anti-submarine accuracy, and decoy ships, disguised as civilian vessels, lured U-boats into range of hidden guns. By 1943, improved technology, air coverage, and convoy organization significantly reduced losses. These measures, combined with Allied industrial production and codebreaking, secured Allied control of sea routes by 1945.

card_unit_40_royal_marine.name: card_unit_40_royal_marine
card_unit_40_royal_marine.title: 40 ROYAL MARINE
card_unit_40_royal_marine.text:
Deployment: Fight target enemy unit. 
Destruction: If this unit isn't Navy, put on top of your deck with the Navy type.
card_unit_40_royal_marine.flavorText: The 40 Royal Marine Commando was formed in 1942 and was the first Royal Marines unit established for commando operations during WWII. Initially designated as 'A' RM Commando, it was later renamed 40 RM Commando in October 1942. The unit comprised volunteers from Royal Marine battalions and underwent rigorous commando training. Their first major engagement was the Dieppe Raid on 19 August 1942. Tasked with operations in the port area, they faced intense German resistance. Out of 370 officers and men, 76 were lost, including their commanding officer, and the second-in-command, Robert Houghton, was captured. In July 1943, they participated in Operation Husky, landing near Pachino, Sicily. They later saw action at Pizzio in September and at Termoli in October, where their commanding officer, Lt. Col. 'Pops' Manners, was killed during a German counterattack. In September 1944, during Operation Mercerised, 40 Commando landed at Sarande, Albania, facing a larger-than-expected German force. Despite the odds, they captured the town and took 1,000 prisoners. They then moved to Corfu to accept the German surrender and remained there until February 1945 to maintain order. Their final WWII operation was Operation Roast in April 1945 at Lake Comacchio, Italy. They conducted a feint attack to the south, crossing the Reno River and clearing its north bank. The subsequent action, Operation Impact Plain, was costly, with 27 killed and 45 wounded, but they succeeded in taking their objectives.

card_unit_buffs.name: card_unit_buffs
card_unit_buffs.title: BUFFS
card_unit_buffs.text: Gets +1+1 when it is targeted by an order or deployment effect.
card_unit_buffs.flavorText: The Buffs, officially known as the Royal East Kent Regiment, was an infantry regiment of the British Army with a long history dating back to 1572. During WWII, the Buffs played an active role across multiple theatres of combat as the regiment's battalions were mobilized and deployed extensively. The 1st Battalion fought in the North African Campaign, where they engaged Axis forces during crucial battles, including Operation Crusader and the fierce fighting around Tobruk and El Alamein. Following their success in North Africa, the battalion participated in the Italian campaign, where it faced fierce resistance at Monte Cassino and contributed significantly to the Allied advance. Meanwhile, the 2nd Battalion experienced intense combat in the Far East, defending Malaya against the Japanese invasion in 1941. They suffered heavy losses, and many troops endured years of harsh captivity as prisoners of war after the fall of Singapore. The 4th Battalion served in France in 1940, and after being evacuated at Dunkirk it was transferred to Malta where it defended against the Axis siege of the island. After the end of the siege, the battalion fought in the Battle of Leros, Greece, in 1943 where it surrendered after intense fighting. The 5th Battalion was also heavily involved in the Battle of France in 1940, where it fought bravely during the defense of key positions but suffered substantial casualties before being evacuated from Dunkirk. Later the 5th was reformed and saw further action in North Africa and Italy. Territorial battalions of the Buffs served with distinction as well, primarily within the British Isles and later in Northwest Europe after D-Day.

card_unit_gordon_highlanders.name: card_unit_gordon_highlanders
card_unit_gordon_highlanders.title: GORDON HIGHLANDERS
card_unit_gordon_highlanders.text: Deployment: Choose an order in hand. Set its cost to 0 and put it on top of your deck.
card_unit_gordon_highlanders.flavorText: The Gordon Highlanders was a regiment of the British Army which was active from 1881 to 1994. During WWII its battalions fought in nearly every theater. The 1st Battalion came to France with the BEF in September 1939.  It joined the 51st (Highland) Division in May 1940, but most of the division was captured at Saint-Valéry-en-Caux in June. The 1st battalion was later reformed and fought in North Africa, Sicily, and Northwest Europe, ending the war in Germany. The 2nd Battalion, stationed in Malaya, was captured by the Japanese at Singapore in 1942, and suffered more losses during captivity than in battle. Reformed later that year, it fought in Normandy, the Netherlands, and Germany. The 4th Battalion served as a machine gun unit before becoming the 92nd Anti-Tank Regiment. The 5th and 7th Battalions were united and saw combat in North Africa and Normandy. The 6th Battalion fought in France, North Africa, Italy, and ended the war in Palestine. The 8th Battalion converted to artillery, while the 9th became an armored unit. Both served in Burma.

card_unit_lovat_scouts.name: card_unit_lovat_scouts
card_unit_lovat_scouts.title: LOVAT SCOUTS
card_unit_lovat_scouts.text: Your cards have the Navy type while on top of your deck.
card_unit_lovat_scouts.flavorText: The Lovat Scouts, originally a Scottish Highland regiment, was a unit which served with the British Army from 1900 to 1969. They were the first military unit known to wear a ghillie suit and were recognized for their advanced reconnaissance skills. In 1916, the Lovat Scouts became the British Army’s first official sniper unit, called "sharpshooters." The regiment served in many conflicts, including WWI and WWII. During the early stages of WWII they were stationed in the Faroe Islands, guarding against a German invasion. In December 1943, the regiment was sent to Canada for specialist ski and mountain training in Jasper National Park, focusing on cross-country movement, survival in cold climates, and mountain ascents. After completing their training and returning to the UK, the Scouts deployed to Italy in July 1944. There, they participated in the later stages of the Italian campaign until the German surrender in May 1945. Following the war, the Lovat Scouts advanced through the Brenner Pass into Austria and Bavaria to locate senior Nazi and SS personnel.

card_unit_mosquito_bomber.name: card_unit_mosquito_bomber
card_unit_mosquito_bomber.title: MOSQUITO B Mk IV
card_unit_mosquito_bomber.text: At the end of turn, Convert into MOSQUITO F Mk II.
card_unit_mosquito_bomber.flavorText: The de Havilland DH.98 Mosquito was a British twin-engined, multirole combat aircraft that was introduced during WWII. Its airframe was constructed mostly of wood, hence its nickname "Wooden Wonder", or "Mossie". When it became operational in 1941 it was the fastest operational aircraft in the world. The B Mk IV series of the Mosquito were bomber variants that came into service in 1942 and 273 were built. The 1st series of the variant had a payload of four 110 kg bombs, but the 2nd series increased the payload to four 230 kg bombs. In April 1943, a decision was made to modify a B Mk IV to carry a 1,800 kg Blockbuster bomb, commonly referred to as "cookie." Several Mosquito B Mk IVs were also modified to carry the Highball bouncing bomb, a smaller version of the one used in the “Dambusters” raid, and intended for attacks on enemy ships. Early missions of the B Mk IV variant included raids over Germany and German occupied territories with the intent of straining enemy morale. The Mosquito’s bombing capabilities were also demonstrated in a raid on the Gestapo headquarters in Oslo in September 1942.

card_unit_mosquito_fighter.name: card_unit_mosquito_fighter
card_unit_mosquito_fighter.title: MOSQUITO F Mk II
card_unit_mosquito_fighter.text: At the end of turn, Convert into MOSQUITO B Mk IV.
card_unit_mosquito_fighter.flavorText: The de Havilland Mosquito F Mk II was a fighter variant of the iconic British multirole aircraft, introduced in 1941. It  was designed as a night fighter, featured an AI (Air Interception) Mk IV radar operated by a second crewmember and was armed with four 20mm Hispano cannons in the nose and four .303-inch Browning machine guns in the fuselage. The F Mk II’s speed (over 612 km/h) and agility made it effective against German bombers like the Heinkel He 111 and Junkers Ju 88. Early models were modified to carry external fuel tanks for extended range during so-called "Intruder" missions, aimed at disrupting enemy airfields and night operations. The F Mk IIs also defended British airspace during the Baedeker Blitz, a series of bombing raids by the Luftwaffe on the UK in 1942, and conducted nighttime raids over occupied France. Some were later adapted for training or radar calibration. This variant’s success laid groundwork for improved Mosquito night fighters such as the NF Mk XII, which integrated more advanced radar systems.

card_unit_queens_own.name: card_unit_queens_own
card_unit_queens_own.title: QUEEN'S OWN
card_unit_queens_own.text: Deployment: Put target unit on top of its owner's deck.
card_unit_queens_own.flavorText: The Queen’s Own Cameron Highlanders was a Scottish infantry regiment, renowned for its Highland heritage and service in British military campaigns from 1793 to 1961. During WWII the regiment’s battalions fought in every major theater. The 1st Battalion began the war in France with the British Expeditionary Force, endured the retreat and evacuation at Dunkirk, and then redeployed to Burma, where it played a vital role in the intense campaigns at Kohima, Mandalay, and the Irrawaddy River. The 2nd Battalion, stationed in North Africa at the war’s outbreak, fought in Operation Battleaxe before being captured at Tobruk. After reforming in the UK, they went on to serve in Tunisia, Italy, and Greece. The 4th Battalion, after being captured at Saint-Valéry-en-Caux in France, was reformed in the UK and helped rebuild the 2nd Battalion, with some members serving garrison duty in Bermuda. The 5th Battalion saw action at El Alamein, Sicily, Normandy, and in the pivotal battles of Caen, the Falaise Gap and the Bulge. The 7th Battalion transformed into a parachute unit. The regiment’s legacy also extended to the Australian 61st Battalion, which became the “Queensland Cameron Highlanders” and fought in the Pacific.

card_unit_royal_fusiliers.name: card_unit_royal_fusiliers
card_unit_royal_fusiliers.title: ROYAL FUSILIERS
card_unit_royal_fusiliers.text: After you give an order, swap the attack and operation cost of this unit.
card_unit_royal_fusiliers.flavorText: The Royal Fusiliers (City of London Regiment) was a British Army infantry regiment with a distinguished history dating back to 1685. During WWII, its battalions served across multiple theaters, demonstrating versatility and resilience. The 1st Battalion, initially stationed in India, was deployed to Egypt in 1939. It participated in the East African Campaign in Abyssinia and later in Syria, where it was captured in 1941. After reformation in Palestine, the battalion served in Iraq and subsequently in Italy, contributing to the Allied efforts in the Mediterranean. The 2nd Battalion was part of the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1939. Following the retreat to Dunkirk, it was evacuated to the UK and later saw action in North Africa and Italy, in particular in the Battle of Monte Cassino and operations along the Gothic Line. The 8th and 9th Battalions, Territorial Army units, were involved in the North African Campaign and the Italian Campaign. They participated in the Salerno landings, the crossing of the Volturno River, and the Battle of Monte Cassino. Both battalions also fought at Anzio and advanced through the Gothic Line. While some battalions remained in the UK for home defense and training, the Royal Fusiliers active units played significant roles in key operations across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East during WWII.

card_unit_sherwood_foresters.name: card_unit_sherwood_foresters
card_unit_sherwood_foresters.title: SHERWOOD FORESTERS
card_unit_sherwood_foresters.text: Deployment: Put a copy of target unit on top of owner's deck.
card_unit_sherwood_foresters.flavorText: The Sherwood Foresters Regiment was a unit of the British Army, active from 1881 to 1970, which participated in both WWI and WWII. During WWII, some of the regiment’s battalions served in the Norwegian Campaign, the Battle of France, the North African Campaign and the Italian Campaign. Others saw action in the Far East. The 1st Battalion fought in the North African and Western Desert Campaigns before remaining in the UK for the remainder of the war. The 2nd Battalion served with the 1st Infantry Division throughout the war, seeing action in France, Tunisia, and Italy. The 1/5th and 2/5th Battalions were deployed to Malaya, where they defended Singapore against the Japanese. After the fall of Singapore, many of their men became prisoners of war and were forced to work on the infamous Burma Railway. Several battalions were raised for home defense and did not see combat. A few served as anti-aircraft units, participating in the defense during the Blitz and the Battle of Britain, and later operating on the European mainland. Of the nearly 27,000 men who served in the regiment’s 17 battalions during WWII, approximately 1,500 officers and men were killed in action.

card_event_area_bombardment.name: card_event_area_bombardment
card_event_area_bombardment.title: AREA BOMBARDMENT
card_event_area_bombardment.text: Add a LANCASTER Mk I to your support line. Shuffle it into your deck at the end of turn.
card_event_area_bombardment.flavorText: Area bombardment became a central part of RAF Bomber Command’s night war against Germany. Early hopes of striking individual factories or military targets often failed due to darkness and poor weather. The 1941 Butt Report used photographs to measure results and showed how often crews missed their aiming points. Many bombs fell far from the intended target, which pushed the RAF toward attacks on wider industrial areas rather than single buildings. This did not mean the RAF gave up trying to improve accuracy. In 1942 it created the Pathfinder Force, made up of selected crews who flew ahead of the main bomber group. Their job was to locate the target and mark it with flares and target indicators. They also received navigation systems such as Gee, Oboe, and H2S earlier than many other units. In 1943, the force was redesignated No. 8 Group, with the motto “We Guide to Strike”. The Pathfinders helped concentrate area bombardment and reduced the waste caused by scattered bombing.

card_event_colossus.name: card_event_colossus
card_event_colossus.title: COLOSSUS
card_event_colossus.text: Copy three random orders in the enemy deck and shuffle them into yours. They get: "Draw a card."
card_event_colossus.flavorText: Colossus was a secret British codebreaking computer built for Bletchley Park during WWII. It was designed to attack the Lorenz cipher, a German high level teleprinter system used for messages between the German High Command and army commands in occupied Europe. Unlike the better known Bombe, which helped against Enigma, Colossus worked on the “Tunny” traffic produced by Lorenz machines. The design came from the work of Max Newman’s section and was built by General Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers with his team at Dollis Hill. The first Colossus was operational in December 1943 and reached Bletchley Park in early 1944. The faster Mark 2 first ran on 1 June 1944, just in time for the Normandy landings. It used thousands of thermionic valves, read punched paper tape at high speed, and tested possible cipher wheel settings through switches and plug panels. By the end of the war, ten Colossus machines were operating. Their existence remained secret for decades, which delayed public recognition of their role in early electronic computing.

card_event_pams.name: card_event_pams
card_event_pams.title: PAMS
card_event_pams.text: Develop a British order costing 4 or less. Add it to your deck with a cost of 0.
card_event_pams.flavorText: During the Blitz, Britain’s Police Auxiliary Messengers, universally known as the PAMs, carried vital information through streets where normal communications had broken down. Women and boys under the age of eighteen helped local police forces during and after air raids, delivering messages when telephone lines had been cut by bombing, power failures, or fallen wires. The PAMs received basic training in first aid and the use of stirrup pumps, and they had to learn the locations of police and civil defense posts by heart. Their work could mean delivering messages through blackout conditions, rubble-strewn streets, and ongoing enemy attacks. In heavily bombed cities such as Coventry, PAMs also assisted rescue services and dealt with fires caused by incendiary bombs. Several were decorated for exceptional bravery, including messengers who continued carrying urgent dispatches despite blast injuries and falling bombs. The service remained active until 1945, when wartime restrictions were lifted and the PAMs were effectively replaced by Police Cadets.

card_event_planned_attack.name: card_event_planned_attack
card_event_planned_attack.title: PLANNED ATTACK
card_event_planned_attack.text: Choose One - deal 2 damage and add a PLAN to hand OR draw a card and add a BLAST to hand.
card_event_planned_attack.flavorText: Operation Thursday took place from March to August 1944 and was the second and largest Chindit expedition in Burma. The Chindits, officially named Long Range Penetration Groups, were British and Indian Army  units assembled by Orde Wingate to operate deep behind Japanese lines. Their columns included British, Indian, Gurkha, Burmese, and West African soldiers. They were trained for jungle warfare , demolition, raiding, and survival far from normal supply routes. The plans for Operation Thursday changed several times before the final attack. Wingate shifted from long marches into Burma toward a bolder plan based on air power. Chindit units would be flown deep into enemy-held territory, build fortified bases with airstrips, and send out mobile columns to cut roads, railways, and supply lines. The US 1st Air Commando Group provided gliders, Dakota transports, supply drops, evacuation, and air support. Landing zones were selected by aerial reconnaissance and given code names such as Piccadilly, Broadway and Chowringhee. The operation disrupted Japanese communications, but diseases, exhaustion, monsoon rain, and heavy fighting made the cost severe.

card_event_seac.name: card_event_seac
card_event_seac.title: SEAC
card_event_seac.text: Draw a card from your deck that did not start there. Duplicate it.
card_event_seac.flavorText: South East Asia Command, known as SEAC, was created by the Allies in 1943 to direct operations against Japan in the South-East Asian Theatre. Its first Supreme Allied Commander was Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten, with US General Joseph Stilwell serving as his deputy. SEAC was formally created in November 1943 and later moved its headquarters to Kandy in Ceylon. The command faced a difficult task. Southeast Asia was a secondary theatre while Allied resources were focused first on Germany and then on the Central Pacific. SEAC had to coordinate British, Indian, American, Chinese, and Commonwealth forces across a vast region. Its main wartime focus became the Burma campaign, where the Fourteenth Army, Chinese formations, American-led forces and various Allied air and naval units all had to be fitted into one strategy. By 1945, SEAC had helped support the reconquest of Burma and was preparing for operations toward Malaya when Japan surrendered. After the war, its role shifted to overseeing the Japanese surrender, recovering prisoners, restoring order, and managing occupied territories. SEAC was disbanded in 1946.

card_event_the_rock_of_gibraltar.name: card_event_the_rock_of_gibraltar
card_event_the_rock_of_gibraltar.title: THE ROCK OF GIBRALTAR
card_event_the_rock_of_gibraltar.text: Develop a card in the enemy deck, then in your deck.
card_event_the_rock_of_gibraltar.flavorText: The Rock of Gibraltar held enormous strategic importance during WWII. Guarding the entrance to the Mediterranean, Gibraltar allowed Britain to protect vital shipping routes and maintain a strong naval and air presence close to North Africa and southern Europe. After war broke out in 1939, much of Gibraltar’s civilian population was evacuated so the territory could be transformed into a heavily fortified military base. By 1942, more than 30,000 British soldiers, sailors, and airmen were stationed on the Rock. Its existing network of tunnels was greatly expanded to provide protected accommodation, storage, communications, and defensive positions deep inside the limestone. Britain even prepared for the possibility of Gibraltar being captured. Under the secret Operation codenamed Tracer, a small team was ready to be sealed inside hidden tunnels to observe and report enemy movements. The plan was never needed, and Gibraltar remained firmly in British hands throughout the war.

card_unit_2nd_west_africa.name: card_unit_2nd_west_africa
card_unit_2nd_west_africa.title: 2nd WEST AFRICA
card_unit_2nd_west_africa.text: Deployment: Draw the cheapest order from your deck. Repeat if it did not start there.
card_unit_2nd_west_africa.flavorText: The 2nd (West Africa) Infantry Brigade was a British Army formation made up of battalions of the Royal West African Frontier Force. Originally formed as the 4th (Gold Coast) Infantry Brigade, it fought in the East African Campaign, advancing from Kenya into Italian Somaliland and Ethiopia as part of the 2nd (African) Division. After returning to West Africa in late 1941, the formation was reorganized and renamed the 2nd (West Africa) Infantry Brigade. In 1944, it joined the 82nd (West Africa) Division and was deployed to Burma. During the Third Arakan Campaign, the brigade advanced through the Kalapanzin Valley and crossed difficult, jungle-covered mountain terrain toward Myohaung. Its advance, together with other West African forces, helped force the Japanese to abandon the Mayu Peninsula. The brigade continued pressing south along the coast and captured the port of Gwa shortly before Japanese forces withdrew from Burma.

card_unit_46th_indian_brigade.name: card_unit_46th_indian_brigade
card_unit_46th_indian_brigade.title: 46th INDIAN BRIGADE
card_unit_46th_indian_brigade.text: Deployment: Draw a card from your deck that did not start there. Get +1+1 and Blitz if you do.
card_unit_46th_indian_brigade.flavorText: The 46th Indian Infantry Brigade was formed at Ahmednagar in India in 1941 and assigned to the 17th Indian Infantry Division. Its primary units included the 3rd Battalion, 7th Gurkha Rifles; the 7th Battalion, 10th Baluch Regiment; and the 5th Battalion, 17th Dogra Regiment. Like much of the British Indian Army in early WWII, the brigade was soon pulled into a fast-moving campaign where time, transport, and equipment were in short supply. In 1942, the Japanese advance into Burma forced the 17th Indian Division into a difficult retreat toward the Sittang River. The 46th Brigade suffered heavy casualties during this withdrawal and was caught up in the crisis around Sittang Bridge. The bridge was a vital escape route, but confusion and Japanese pressure threatened to trap the division on the wrong side of the river. After the battle, the brigade was broken into scattered groups and ceased to exist as an effective formation. It was not rebuilt and was officially disbanded in February 1942.

card_unit_meteor.name: card_unit_meteor
card_unit_meteor.title: METEOR
card_unit_meteor.text: Remove after this unit attacks. Add a copy to your deck with double attack and defense.
card_unit_meteor.flavorText: The Gloster Meteor was Britain’s first operational jet fighter and the only Allied jet aircraft to fly combat missions in WWII. It was built by the Gloster Aircraft Company around turbojet work pioneered by Frank Whittle and Power Jets. The Meteor first flew in 1943 and entered RAF service with No. 616 Squadron in July 1944. A total of 3,947 Meteors were built. Early Meteors were kept under strict secrecy and were first used over Britain against V-1 flying bombs. On 4 August 1944, Meteor pilots claimed their first V1s. The RAF did not initially allow the aircraft to fly over German-held territory, to prevent a crashed jet from being captured. In 1945, Meteor F.3s joined the Second Tactical Air Force in Belgium and later moved into Germany. They flew armed reconnaissance and ground attack missions, but never fought German jets in the air. The Meteor was not as fast or heavily armed as the German Me 262, yet it gave the RAF valuable experience with jet aircraft. It also became an important postwar fighter and test aircraft.

card_unit_no_46_commando.name: card_unit_no_46_commando
card_unit_no_46_commando.title: No. 46 COMMANDO
card_unit_no_46_commando.text: Deployment: Add a BLAST and a PLAN to your hand.
card_unit_no_46_commando.flavorText: No. 46 Royal Marine Commando was formed in August 1943 as the Royal Marines Division was being turned into commando units. Led by Lieutenant Colonel Campbell Hardy, it trained for the demanding role of light assault infantry. Like other commandos, its men passed through the course at Achnacarry in the Scottish Highlands, where they practiced forced marches, weapons handling, map reading, climbing, small boat work, and demolitions. The unit landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944 and fought on the Orne River bridgehead beside the British 6th Airborne Division. It entered Douvres-la-Délivrande two days later, a moment captured in a wartime photograph showing local civilians watching the commandos move through the village. Heavy losses in Normandy forced No. 46 Commando back to Britain for refitting in late 1944. It returned to mainland Europe in January 1945, guarded Antwerp, then j participated in river-crossing assaults during the advance into Germany. After being assigned to occupation duties, it was disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_royal_sussex_regiment.name: card_unit_royal_sussex_regiment
card_unit_royal_sussex_regiment.title: ROYAL SUSSEX REGIMENT
card_unit_royal_sussex_regiment.text:
Your BLASTS deal +1 damage.
Your PLANS draw +1 card.
Your PRODUCTIONS give +1 kredit.
card_unit_royal_sussex_regiment.flavorText: The Royal Sussex Regiment was a British line infantry regiment formed in 1881 from the 35th Royal Sussex Regiment of Foot and the 107th Regiment of Foot. In WWII, its battalions served across several theatres. The 1st Battalion was stationed in Egypt and Palestine before joining the 4th Indian Infantry Division. It fought in the Western Desert, then in Italy, where it endured hard fighting at Monte Cassino, before moving to Greece in late 1944. The 2nd Battalion fought with the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1940 and was evacuated from Dunkirk. It later served in North Africa, including Alam el Halfa and El Alamein. In 1943, men from the 2nd, 4th, and 5th Battalions helped form the 10th Parachute Battalion, which was engaged at Taranto and later at Arnhem. The 9th Battalion took a different route. After briefly converting to armour, it returned to infantry and fought in Burma with the 36th Division. It saw action in the Arakan, was airlifted into Myitkyina, and advanced toward Mandalay in 1945.

card_unit_stirling_mk_iii.name: card_unit_stirling_mk_iii
card_unit_stirling_mk_iii.title: STIRLING Mk III
card_unit_stirling_mk_iii.text: Deployment: Shuffle a CARPET BOMBING into your deck.
card_unit_stirling_mk_iii.flavorText: The Short Stirling was the RAF’s first four-engine heavy bomber to enter service in WWII. Designed by Short Brothers to meet Air Ministry requirements, it carried a large bomb load and was praised by crews for its handling. Its main weakness was a low operational ceiling, caused partly by the restricted wingspan required in the original specification. This made it more vulnerable than later heavy bombers such as the Halifax and Lancaster. The Mk III variant appeared in 1943 and became the main improved version of the Stirling. It used more powerful Bristol Hercules VI or XVI engines, raising maximum speed from about 255 to 270 mph. It also replaced the earlier dorsal turret with a fully-glazed FN.50 turret like the one used on the Lancaster, giving the gunner better space and visibility. Later Mk III aircraft carried electronic aids and countermeasures, including H2S radar, Monica rear warning radar, Mandrel jamming equipment, and chaff for confusing German radar. A total of 2,371 Stirlings were built. By late 1943, the type was leaving front line bombing service, but many Mk III aircraft were converted for glider towing and airborne support.

card_unit_the_biscuit_boys.name: card_unit_the_biscuit_boys
card_unit_the_biscuit_boys.title: THE BISCUIT BOYS
card_unit_the_biscuit_boys.text: Your HQ gets +1 defense when you play a neutral card.
card_unit_the_biscuit_boys.flavorText: The “Biscuit Boys” was the nickname of the Royal Berkshire Regiment, whose depot was at Brock Barracks in Reading. In WWII, the regiment fought in France, Burma, Sicily, Italy, and Normandy. The 1st Battalion served with the British Expeditionary Force in 1939 and was evacuated from Dunkirk in 1940. It was later sent to India with the 2nd Infantry Division and fought in Burma under the Fourteenth Army. At Kohima in 1944, B Company helped relieve the 4th Royal West Kents during the siege. The battalion then fought for weeks in difficult conditions, before joining operations around Meiktila and Mandalay later. The 2nd Battalion was already in India when the war began and also served in Burma, notably during the final capture of Mandalay Hill in 1945. The 10th Battalion fought with the 56th London Infantry Division in Sicily and at Anzio, where the fighting became a bitter static struggle. Heavy manpower shortages led to the battalion being disbanded in 1944, with its men sent as reinforcements to other units.

card_unit_the_holy_boys.name: card_unit_the_holy_boys
card_unit_the_holy_boys.title: THE HOLY BOYS
card_unit_the_holy_boys.text: Once per turn, give your units +1+1 after you play a neutral card.
card_unit_the_holy_boys.flavorText: The Royal Norfolk Regiment inherited the nickname “The Holy Boys” from its predecessor, the 9th Regiment of Foot. During the Peninsular War, a Spanish soldier reportedly mistook the figure of Britannia on the regiment’s cap badge for the Virgin Mary, giving rise to this unusual nickname. The regiment received its “Royal” title in 1935 and went on to serve extensively during WWII. It fought in France in 1940, where the 2nd Battalion helped cover the retreat towards Dunkirk. In 1944, the 1st Battalion landed on Sword Beach on D-Day and fought through Normandy and the North West Europe campaign. Other battalions served in the Far East, notably at Singapore and in the Burma campaign. Five members of the regiment received the Victoria Cross during the war, reflecting the distinguished service of the “Holy Boys” across several theatres.

card_unit_the_tigers.name: card_unit_the_tigers
card_unit_the_tigers.title: THE TIGERS
card_unit_the_tigers.text: Gets +1+1 when you play a card that did not start in your deck.
card_unit_the_tigers.flavorText: "The Tigers" was the nickname of the Leicestershire Regiment, a British infantry regiment that served on several fronts during WWII. Its 1st Battalion was in the Far East when Japan entered the war, fighting in the Malayan Campaign starting in December 1941. After suffering heavy losses, it was amalgamated with the 2nd Battalion, East Surrey Regiment, to form the "British Battalion". This combined unit was later captured at the Fall of Singapore in February 1942, and its surviving men spent the rest of the war as Prisoners of War (POWs). Other Leicestershire battalions fought in North Africa, Italy, and Burma. The 2nd Battalion served at Sidi Barrani, Bardia, Crete, and Tobruk before moving to Ceylon and India, later joining the Chindits in the Burma Campaign. The 7th Battalion, raised after Dunkirk, was also sent to India and became one of the few non-Regular units selected for the Chindits. During Operation Thursday in 1944, it attacked Japanese rear areas and supply lines, but losses were so severe that the battalion was disbanded at the end of the year.

card_unit_universal_carrier.name: card_unit_universal_carrier
card_unit_universal_carrier.title: UNIVERSAL CARRIER
card_unit_universal_carrier.text: Your PLANS cost 1 less. When you play a PLAN, add a BLAST to your hand.
card_unit_universal_carrier.flavorText: The Universal Carrier was one of the most common British armoured vehicles of WWII, with around 113,000 units built. It was developed from earlier Bren Gun and Scout Carriers, but the Universal design introduced in 1940 gave the British Army a single flexible tracked vehicle suited for many roles. It was small, open-topped, lightly armoured, and powered by a Ford V8 engine. Its usual crew included three or four men, with space for weapons, ammunition, stores, or passengers. The carrier was not meant to be a tank. Its value came from mobility and practicality. British and Commonwealth units used it to move Bren guns, Boys anti-tank rifles, PIATs, mortars, radios, and observation teams. In infantry battalions, carrier platoons gave commanders a fast way to shift support weapons across the battlefield. Reconnaissance units also used carriers beside scout cars. The vehicle appeared in nearly every theatre, from the Western Desert to Burma and Northwest Europe. Many variants were built, including mortar carriers, artillery observation vehicles, and the Wasp flamethrower version. Its simple design made it easy to adapt, which explains why it served long after WWII.

card_event_armaments_eg.name: card_event_armaments_eg
card_event_armaments_eg.title: ARMAMENTS
card_event_armaments_eg.text: Deal 4 damage to any target. Deal 8 if this card spent 4+ turns in your deck.
card_event_armaments_eg.flavorText:
The bomb loads of four-engine British bombers during WWII varied depending on the type of aircraft, the target, and the mission. However, here are some examples of the bomb loads of some of the most common four-engine bombers used by the Royal Air Force:

Avro Lancaster: The Lancaster had a maximum bomb load of up to 22,000 pounds (9,980 kg), although the typical bomb load for most missions was around 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg) of bombs.

Handley Page Halifax: The Halifax had a maximum bomb load of up to 14,500 lb (6,600 kg), although the typical bomb load for most missions was ca.5,800 pounds (2,600 kg).

Short Stirling: The Stirling had a maximum bomb load of up to 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg) of bombs, although the typical bomb load for most missions was around 8,000 pounds (3,600 kg).

Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress (used by the RAF's No. 100 Group): The B-17 had a maximum bomb load of  8,000 pounds (3,600 kg) , although the typical bomb load for most missions was around 4,000-pound (1,800-kg).

It's worth noting that the weight and type of bombs used by these bombers varied depending on the mission and the target. For example, bombers on night bombing missions tended to carry more incendiary bombs, while those on daylight precision bombing missions often carried heavier high-explosive bombs.

card_event_materials_eg.name: card_event_materials_eg
card_event_materials_eg.title: MATERIALS
card_event_materials_eg.text: Draw 4 cards. Draw 8 if this card spent 4+ turns in your deck.
card_event_materials_eg.flavorText: During WWII, Britain relied heavily on imports to support its war effort and ensure that its population had enough food and other essentials to survive. The country imported a range of goods including food, oil, raw materials, machinery and equipment, medical supplies, and arms and ammunition. These imports were critical to keep Britain's factories and transportation systems running and to support its own war production efforts. Britain's imports were heavily regulated by the government, which prioritized the needs of the war effort, and the country relied heavily on imports from its Allies, particularly the United States.

card_event_air_power.name: card_event_air_power
card_event_air_power.title: AIR POWER
card_event_air_power.text: Choose one - destroy target tank OR deal 2 damage to an enemy.
card_event_air_power.flavorText: The Desert Air Force (DAF), known under various different names throughout the period it was active, was an Allied tactical air force that was created under RAF command in North Africa in 1941. In 1942 the DAF had over 1,500 combat aircraft under its control, mostly RAF units, but also Australian, South African, American, Polish and other Allied units. The Axis desert air force had less than half that amount of aircraft.

card_event_delaying_tactics.name: card_event_delaying_tactics
card_event_delaying_tactics.title: DELAYING TACTICS
card_event_delaying_tactics.text: All units in the frontline must Retreat.
card_event_delaying_tactics.flavorText: A delaying tactic is intended to slow an enemy force down, generally called “Defense in depth” or “Elastic Defense” in military terms. This tactic is often used when facing an enemy with superior numbers, and the goal is to minimize your own losses while reducing, eliminating or slowing down the enemy. This tactic was used in various forms by most fighting nations during WWII, but most notably by Germany and Japan.

card_event_his_majesty_chosen.name: card_event_his_majesty_chosen
card_event_his_majesty_chosen.title: HIS MAJESTY'S CHOSEN
card_event_his_majesty_chosen.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite British units to add to your hand.
card_event_his_majesty_chosen.flavorText: The British Eight Army was the formation of the British Army that fought in North Africa and Italy from 1941-1945. The units came from all over the Commonwealth, but also from Greece, the Free French Forces, mostly from the French colonies, and the Polish II Corps. The Eighth Army was awarded battle honors for its victory against the Axis forces in the Second Battle of El Alamein. By then the army consisted of 10 divisions and several independent brigades, counting over 220,000 men.

card_event_rule_britannia.name: card_event_rule_britannia
card_event_rule_britannia.title: RULE BRITANNIA
card_event_rule_britannia.text: Give your British units +2 defense, then their attack becomes equal to their defense.
card_event_rule_britannia.flavorText: “Rule Britannia” is a poem written by James Thomson (1700-1747), but is better known as a British patriotic song composed by Thomas Arne in 1740. The text to the  main chorus is as follows: Rule, Britannia! Britannia rule the waves: Britons never will be slaves. The song was played by the Allies in 1945 during the surrender ceremony of the Japanese Imperial Army in Singapore.

card_unit_east_surray_regiment.name: card_unit_east_surray_regiment
card_unit_east_surray_regiment.title: EAST SURREY REGIMENT
card_unit_east_surray_regiment.flavorText: The East Surrey Regiment was first formed in 1881 and participated in The Second Boer War, WWI and WWII. In 1939 the 1st Battalion of the East Surrey Regiment was part of the 11th Infantry Brigade of the 4th Infantry Division which was sent to France as part of the British Expeditionary Force. After the evacuation from Dunkirk the regiment spent two years in the UK on home defense duty, preparing for a German invasion. In 1942 the regiment and the rest of the 11th Brigade became part of the 78th Battleaxe Infantry Division which participated in Operation Torch and landed in Algiers as part of the British First Army. In 1943 they fought with the British Eight Army in the Italian Campaign and participated in the Battle of Termoli and saw combat at the Barbara Line and River Sangro. In 1944 the division participated in the fourth and final battle of Monte Cassino and in the winter they participated in Operation Olive where they fought against the German forces in the Apennine Mountains. Finally the regiment fought with the 78th Division in the spring offensive of 1945 and ended the war in Austria.

card_unit_m3a3_honey_desert.name: card_unit_m3a3_honey_desert
card_unit_m3a3_honey_desert.title: M3A3 HONEY
card_unit_m3a3_honey_desert.text: When you draw a card, your HQ gains +1 defense.
card_unit_m3a3_honey_desert.flavorText: The M3A3 Honey was a Stuart V tank, an American light tank that was produced during WWII. The tank was manufactured between 1941-1944 and a total of 22,744 units were built, including variants and its successor the M5. The tank was called Stuart after the Civil War Confederate General J.E.B. Stuart, but the crews nicknamed it Honey due to its smooth ride. The M3A3 had an improved hull (copied from M5 to the M3 series), and a new turret that could fit a SCR-508 radio. The M3A3 had a crew of 4 (commander, gunner, driver and assistant driver), a main armament of a 37 mm gun M6 and a secondary armament of 3 x .30 caliber (7.62 mm) Browning M1919A4 machine guns.

card_unit_no1_commando.name: card_unit_no1_commando
card_unit_no1_commando.title: No. 1 COMMANDO
card_unit_no1_commando.text: Units dealt combat damage by this unit are destroyed.
card_unit_no1_commando.flavorText: The No. 1 Commando was a battalion sized unit of the British Army during WWII. The unit was formed in 1940 by men that were cherry picked from every army regiment to participate in special assignments, often behind the enemy lines where they risked being shot if captured. During the war the No. 1 Commando participated in operations in France from 1941 to 1942, but was then assigned to Operation Torch in November 1942 where it participated in the Allied landings in North Africa. The unit continued to operate in North Africa and fought in the first battle of Sedjenane in the Tunisia Campaign in 1943. In 1944 it fought as part of a Commando brigade in Burma and the Arakan, but was later withdrawn and prepared to participate in the invasion of Malaysia in 1945. However the war ended before that and the unit participated in the liberation of Hong Kong instead.

card_event_bomber_run_brit.name: card_event_bomber_run_brit
card_event_bomber_run_brit.title: BOMBER RUN
card_event_bomber_run_brit.text: Deal 2 damage to target unit. Deal 5 instead if you control a bomber with 5+ attack.
card_event_bomber_run_brit.flavorText: Operation Hydra, carried out by RAF Bomber Command on the night of August 17th 1943, targeted a German research center in Peenemünde. Group Captain John Searby led the operation; it was Bomber Command's first use of a master bomber to direct the attack. This mission marked the beginning of the Crossbow campaign against the German V-weapon program. Even though it resulted in the loss of 215 crew members and 40 bombers for the British, and casualties among enslaved workers in a nearby forced labor camp, it also inflicted damage on the Luftwaffe, causing delays in V-2 rocket testing and production. However, its overall effectiveness in slowing down German V-weapon production has been debated as the Germans had already dispersed V-2 manufacturing to other locations by 1942.

card_event_cobelligerents.name: card_event_cobelligerents
card_event_cobelligerents.title: CO-BELLIGERENTS
card_event_cobelligerents.text: Target enemy unit is shuffled into your deck.
card_event_cobelligerents.flavorText: In WWII, various nations and resistance movements, such as those from occupied countries or exiled governments, acted as co-belligerents, actively engaging in the fight without being formal parties of an alliance. Just as there were co-belligerents who aligned themselves and fought alongside the Allied powers (e.g. Free France, Poland, Norway, The Netherlands,Yugoslavia and Greece) there were also co-belligerents who sided with or supported the Axis powers, for exemple Finland, which switched sides and fought with the Allies against Germany from 1944. Similarly, Italy, Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria, all former allies of Germany, would later switch sides and join the Allies in the war against the nazi regime. It should also be mentioned that the pact between Germany and the Soviet Union against Poland in 1939 has been described as co-belligerent.

card_event_enemy_contact.name: card_event_enemy_contact
card_event_enemy_contact.title: ENEMY CONTACT
card_event_enemy_contact.text: Pin target unit. Draw a card.
card_event_enemy_contact.flavorText: The first significant battle where British forces participated during WWII was the Battle of France, which began in May 1940. While there were minor skirmishes and engagements on the Western Front before this, the Battle of France marked the first major and sustained combat operations involving British forces in the war. The Battle of France opposed British, French, and other Allied forces to the German Wehrmacht, which employed blitzkrieg tactics to rapidly advance through France and Belgium. This campaign led to the Dunkirk evacuation (Operation Dynamo) in late May and early June 1940, where British and Allied forces were evacuated from the beaches of Dunkirk as they faced encirclement by German forces.

card_event_entrenched.name: card_event_entrenched
card_event_entrenched.title: ENTRENCHED
card_event_entrenched.text: Give a friendly Guard unit +3 attack, Fury and Salvage.
card_event_entrenched.flavorText: While trench warfare was a defining characteristic of WWI, it was not the primary form of warfare in WWII. However, there were instances where trench-like defenses were used in specific locations during WWII, particularly in some defensive positions, sieges, and specific battles. F.ex. during the North African Campaign, Tobruk was subjected to a prolonged siege by the Axis forces in 1941, which lasted 241 days. During this time both sides dug extensive trench networks to defend and attack positions, similar to the trench warfare of WWI. The Siege of Tobruk was finally lifted when the British Eighth Army launched Operation Crusader and managed to break through the Axis lines and relieve the pressure on Tobruk.

card_event_ingenuity.name: card_event_ingenuity
card_event_ingenuity.title: INGENUITY
card_event_ingenuity.text: Develop a British or US bomber.
card_event_ingenuity.flavorText: The so-called “Butt Report” was a report initiated by Lord Cherwell, a friend of Churchill and chief scientific advisor to the Cabinet, but commonly referred to by the name of its author, Archibald Butt, a civil servant who worked for the Statistical Section of the Admiralty during WWII. The report was published in August 1941 and revealed the widespread failure of RAF Bomber Command aircraft to hit their targets. Following this highly critical report, Bomber Command was reorganized with new aircraft, new navigational aids, new tactics and new leadership. In February 1942 Air Marshal Arthur Harris was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Bomber Command and the implementation of electronic navigational tools such as GEE, Oboe, G-H, and ground-mapping radar H2S increased bombings precision significantly. Furthermore, the creation of the Pathfinder Force also improved the accuracy of bombing raids. This was a specialized force within the RAF that was responsible for marking targets and guiding bomber formations to those.

card_unit_3rd_canadian_division.name: card_unit_3rd_canadian_division
card_unit_3rd_canadian_division.title: 3rd CANADIAN DIVISION
card_unit_3rd_canadian_division.text: Your Salvaged units cost 2 less to deploy.
card_unit_3rd_canadian_division.flavorText: The 3rd Canadian Division was formed in 1915 as a formation of the Canadian Army. The division fought in WWI, after which it was deactivated. It was reactivated in 1941 and sent to the UK, where it spent three years in garrison and training duties, before landing on Juno Beach on D-Day in June 1944 as part of the British Second Army. The division faced intense German resistance, but managed to advance inland despite suffering heavy casualties. They continued to fight through the Normandy Campaign and played a key role in the Battle of Caen and the liberation of Falaise. Later the division became part of the First Canadian Army and was involved in the clearing of the French channel ports and the following Battle of Boulogne. In October 1944 the division fought in the Battle of the Scheldt in Belgium, where they earned the nickname “Water Rats” in recognition of the poor terrain conditions they were forced to fight in. After that they kept fighting in France and were involved in the liberation of Boulogne-sur-Mer and Calais. After the war the 3rd served as part of the Canadian Army Occupation Force in Germany, until 1946 when it was sent back to Canada where the division was disbanded shortly after.

card_unit_halifax.name: card_unit_halifax
card_unit_halifax.title: HALIFAX B Mk I
card_unit_halifax.text: Bombers you deploy (including this) deal their attack in damage to a random enemy.
card_unit_halifax.flavorText: The Handley Page Halifax was a four-engine heavy bomber used by the RAF and the Commonwealth air forces during WWII. The Halifax entered service in 1940 and made its operational debut in March 1941, participating in a daylight bombing raid on German captured port of Le Havre in France. Later that year, due to increased fighter opposition and a high casualty rate, the Halifax was withdrawn from daylight bombing operations and became part of the Pathfinder Force, marking routes and targets for the Main Force bombers. It played a core role in the bombing offensive against Germany, and at its peak, Bomber Command operated 76 Halifax-equipped squadrons. The early-built Halifax models faced performance issues, primarily due to the underpowered Merlin engines. However, with the introduction of the Halifax Mk III, powered by Bristol Hercules radial engines, it started to demonstrate superior performance against German fighter defenses. Following the invasion of Europe in 1944, the Halifax resumed daylight bombing operations, conducting strikes against enemy targets such as troop concentrations, gun emplacements, and the Atlantic Wall defenses. The Halifax was also used by Coastal Command for anti-submarine warfare, reconnaissance, and mine deployment. It served in various support roles, including glider tug, electronic warfare and special operations. The Halifax flew its last major operation in April 1945, and after the war it remained in service with RAF Coastal Command and Transport Command, Royal Egyptian Air Force, and the French Armée de l'Air until early 1952.

card_unit_ox_and_bucks.name: card_unit_ox_and_bucks
card_unit_ox_and_bucks.title: OX AND BUCKS
card_unit_ox_and_bucks.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to an enemy unit.
card_unit_ox_and_bucks.flavorText: The Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry, known as the Ox and Bucks, was a British Army regiment which was active from 1881 to 1958. At the start of WWII the 1st and 4th Battalions of the Ox Bucks were part of the British Expeditionary Force and they saw action during the Battle of France. The 1st Ox and Bucks was eventually evacuated from Dunkirk but the 4th Ox and Bucks surrendered in Belgium after being encircled by the German forces. Members of the 2nd Ox and Bucks participated in the Normandy landings and were the first British troops to land on D-Day on June 6th 1944. As part of the 6th Airborne Division they were dropped by Horsa Glider to secure road bridges across the river Orne and the Caen Canal. During this operation they captured the Pegasus Bridge, an operation that was immortalized in the film “The Longest Day”. Later that year, the 1st Battalion took part in Operation Market Garden. The 2nd Battalion was again dropped by glider during the Rhine Crossings in 1945. The regiment's Territorial battalions fought in North Africa, Italy and the Far East. Two companies from the battalion joined the T-Force, a British-American unit sent to capture German scientists and to secure research and industrial technologies late in the war.

card_unit_raf_mitchell.name: card_unit_raf_mitchell
card_unit_raf_mitchell.title: RAF MITCHELL
card_unit_raf_mitchell.flavorText: The North American B-25 Mitchell was an American medium bomber which was introduced in 1941 and used by many Allied air forces and in every theater of WWII. The Royal Air Force (RAF) acquired the B-25 Mitchell bombers through the Lend-Lease program, for a total of 700 aircraft delivered before the end of the war. The initial batch was designated Mitchell I and arrived in August 1941, and later the B-25 Cs and Ds were designated Mitchell II. By the end of 1942, the RAF had received 93 Mitchells (Marks I and II), with some deployed to No. 2 Group RAF. After the European invasion, RAF Mitchell squadrons moved to bases in France and Belgium in support of the Allied ground forces. Additionally, the Polish No. 305 Squadron which fought alongside RAF operated Mitchell IIs before transitioning to the de Havilland Mosquito, and various second-line RAF units used B-25s for reconnaissance missions.

card_unit_sdf.name: card_unit_sdf
card_unit_sdf.title: SDF
card_unit_sdf.text: Your other units have +1 attack for each of your Guard units.
card_unit_sdf.flavorText: During WWII, Sudan was under British and Egyptian joint control, known as the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. The Sudan Defence Force was formed in 1925 and was a locally raised military force composed of Sudanese personnel, but led by the British. During WWII the SDF was expanded to 25,000 officers and men, and from 1940, they participated in the East African Campaign. They defended against Italian forces in Sudan and contributed to the successful invasion of Eritrea in 1941. The SDF also played a crucial role in the Western Desert Campaign where they were used to resupply the Free French and the Long Range Desert Group (LRDG) in Libya. In 1942 during the North African Campaign, the SDF was successfully used in operations aimed at intercepting German Brandenburger commando’s infiltration into Egypt. After the Allied victory in the Tunisian Campaign, the SDF continued patrolling and countering German efforts behind enemy lines. By the war's end, the SDF had evolved into an experienced military unit, and Sudanese officers began replacing British officers in the years leading up to the country's independence.

card_unit_the_glamour_boys.name: card_unit_the_glamour_boys
card_unit_the_glamour_boys.title: THE GLAMOUR BOYS
card_unit_the_glamour_boys.flavorText: The 48th Highlanders of Canada, nicknamed “The Glamour Boys”, is a regiment of the Canadian Army. The regiment has been active from 1891 to the present day and has fought in the Second Boer War (1899-1901), WWI, WWII and the War in Afghanistan. In 1939 the regiment was sent to France as part of the Second British Expeditionary Force, but was soon ordered back to Britain. In 1943 the 48th Highlanders, as part of the 1st Canadian Infantry Division, landed in Sicily during Operation Husky, where it engaged in heavy fighting against the defending Axis forces. The 48th Highlanders then fought its way up the Italian peninsula, where it participated in the Battle of Ortona and the breaching of the Hitler Line defenses south of Rome. In March 1945, the regiment moved with the remainder of the I Canadian Corps to North-West Europe, where it fought until the end of the war.

card_unit_welsh_regiment.name: card_unit_welsh_regiment
card_unit_welsh_regiment.title: WELCH REGIMENT
card_unit_welsh_regiment.flavorText: The Welch Regiment was an infantry regiment of the British Army that existed from 1881 to 1969, and fought on multiple fronts during WWII.. The 1st battalion of the regiment was stationed in Palestine in connection to the Arab revolt (1936-1939) when the war broke out. Their first engagement happened during the Western Desert Campaign in 1940, but later that year they were sent to take part in the defense of Crete, where they suffered heavy losses and were finally evacuated. After being re-formed in Egypt, the battalion joined the 5th Indian Infantry Brigade and returned to the Western Desert where it was involved in heavy fighting. In 1943 it became part of the 34th (Welch) Beach Brick and landed in Sicily during the invasion with the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division. After being replaced in 1944, it joined the 168th (London) Infantry Brigade in Italy. The 2nd Battalion of the Welch Regiment was sent to Burma in 1944, where it engaged in intense fighting along the Taungoo-Mawchi Road. The 4th Battalion faced fierce battles in Caen, the Falaise Pocket, the Ardennes, and the Reichswald Forest during the liberation of Europe. The 1/5th Battalion transferred to the 158th Infantry Brigade and distinguished itself in the North West Europe Campaign. Around 1,100 officers and other ranks of the Welch Regiment lost their lives during World War II, with many more wounded.

card_event_monsoon_rot.name: card_event_monsoon_rot
card_event_monsoon_rot.title: MONSOON ROT
card_event_monsoon_rot.text: The defense of each enemy unit is set to 1.
card_event_monsoon_rot.flavorText: The Burma Campaign (1941-1944) was very much affected by the geographical characteristics of the region and the tropical climate was particularly extreme during the 1940s. From May to November the heat was blistering and painful, and then the monsoon season came with extreme thunderstorms that soaked the soldiers and their equipment, followed by insects that attacked them ruthlessly and tropical diseases that spread like wildfire among the troops. This made logistics extremely difficult for both friends and foe, but this hit the Japanese harder than the Allies and by 1944 the Japanese forces suffered their greatest military defeat up to that point. In total the Japanese suffered 200,000 casualties and losses in Burma, and some claim that 78% of these losses were from non-combat causes such as starvation and disease.

card_event_observer_corps.name: card_event_observer_corps
card_event_observer_corps.title: OBSERVER CORPS
card_event_observer_corps.text: Choose a card with cost 5 or more in your hand. Reduce its cost by 2.
card_event_observer_corps.flavorText: The Observer Corps was an organization that was active from 1925 to 1995 and acted as the “Eyes and Ears” of the Royal Air Force (RAF). The members of the organization were mainly volunteers that were trained in aircraft recognition and their role was to spot enemy aircraft flying inland and to estimate their height and formation. This information was then used by the Fighter Command's operations to intercept the attacking formations. During WWII some 30,000 members of the Observer Corps were on active duty and control centers and observation posts across the UK were manned continuously, from 3 September 1939 to 12 May 1945, four days after VE day. The organization played a crucial role during the Battle of Britain, and in recognition for its services it became the Royal Observer Corps in 1941.

card_event_pound.name: card_event_pound
card_event_pound.title: POUND
card_event_pound.text: Deal damage to a ground unit equal to the total attack of your air units.
card_event_pound.flavorText: RAF Fighter Command played a crucial role in defending Britain and maintaining air superiority during WWII. Formed in 1936, it rose to prominence during the Battle of Britain in 1940 when it repelled the Luftwaffe's efforts to gain control of British airspace. Using a network of radar stations and ground observers, Fighter Command coordinated quick responses to incoming raids. Its primary aircraft, the Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane, helped secure victory despite being outnumbered. After the battle, Fighter Command shifted to offensive operations over occupied Europe, escorting bombers and carrying out fighter sweeps. It also adapted to changing needs, eventually forming part of the 2nd Tactical Air Force to support ground operations after the Normandy landings. By the war's end, it had flown hundreds of thousands of sorties and claimed over 15,000 enemy aircraft. Fighter Command’s integration of radar, flexible tactics, and skilled pilots made it a model for modern air defense. Its success in 1940 prevented a German invasion and ensured Britain remained a base for Allied operations throughout the war.

card_event_supply_shortage.name: card_event_supply_shortage
card_event_supply_shortage.title: SUPPLY SHORTAGE
card_event_supply_shortage.text: Enemy units get: "Receives 1 damage at the start of owner's turn."
card_event_supply_shortage.flavorText: A key contributor to the Allied victory in the North African Campaign was Ultra; the Allied intelligence project which allowed them to decrypt high level enemy communications. Ultra provided valuable information about the times and routes of Axis supply shipments across the Mediterranean to Africa and this information was used to intercept and destroy them. It is estimated that 40% to 60% of Axis supply shipping was located and destroyed due to decrypted information. This gave a crippling blow to the Afrika Korps as it was denied essential supplies for the war effort, from fuel to equipment ranging from tanks and guns all the way down to food and uniforms.

card_unit_1st_london_brigade.name: card_unit_1st_london_brigade
card_unit_1st_london_brigade.title: 1st LONDON BRIGADE
card_unit_1st_london_brigade.text: Your other British ground units have +2 attack.
card_unit_1st_london_brigade.flavorText: The 1st London Brigade was a formation of the British Territorial Army and saw service in WWI and WWII. From 1939 to 1943 the brigade remained in the UK, preparing for the expected German invasion, but in 1943 it was sent to Egypt. By then the formation had been renumbered to the 167th London Brigade and was now part of the 56th (London) Infantry Division which was under the command of the X Corps of the British Eighth Army. The brigade saw minimal service in the Tunisia Campaign and would after that participate in the Italian Campaign where it saw heavy fighting in numerous operations and battles, including the Battle of Anzio, the Battle of Salerno, and finally the Allied Spring 1945 offensive in Italy, codenamed Operation Grapeshot. The 167th London Brigade ended the war in Austria with the British Eighth Army.

card_unit_2nd_para_c.name: card_unit_2nd_para_c
card_unit_2nd_para_c.title: 2nd PARA C
card_unit_2nd_para_c.text: Pincer: Units dealt combat damage by this unit are destroyed.
card_unit_2nd_para_c.flavorText: The 2nd Parachute C was a company sized unit of the 2nd Battalion, the Parachute Regiment (2 PARA) of the British Army, but would later become part of the Army Air Corps. The battalion was formed in 1941 and early 1942 it participated in its first mission which was Operation Biting, a raid on a German radar installation in Bruneval, France. After its first mission the C Company of the battalion took the nickname “C (Bruneval) Company” in honor of the operation. The battalion became part of the 1st Parachute Brigade of the 1st Airborne Division and participated in British airborne operations in North Africa, Sicily and Italy, and lastly and most famously in the Battle of Arnhem during Operation Market Garden in September 1944.

card_unit_oxford.name: card_unit_oxford
card_unit_oxford.title: OXFORD
card_unit_oxford.text: When you deploy or add a Guard unit, give it +1+3.
card_unit_oxford.flavorText: The Airspeed Oxford, nicknamed “Ox-box”, was a British twin engined monoplane that was used to train British Commonwealth aircrews during WWII and after. The aircraft was mainly used to prepare bomber aircrews for combat and it could simultanously train pilots, bomb aimers, navigators, gunners and radio operators. Although the Oxford was mostly used as a trainer during the war it provided valuable service as an air ambulance, in anti-submarine roles, in communications and for anti-aircraft cooperation duties. A total of 8,751 aircraft were built, including a few variants, and a great number of them were converted for civilian transportation after the war.

card_unit_rnzaf_kittyhawk.name: card_unit_rnzaf_kittyhawk
card_unit_rnzaf_kittyhawk.title: RNZAF KITTYHAWK
card_unit_rnzaf_kittyhawk.text: When a unit is deployed, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ and gain +1 HQ defense.
card_unit_rnzaf_kittyhawk.flavorText: The Curtiss P-40 Kittyhawk was the backbone of Royal New Zealand Air Force fighter squadrons from 1942 to 1944 when they were replaced by Corsairs. 297 Kittyhawks equipped eight squadrons of the RNZA during WWII, mostly in operations in the South West Pacific. By the end of the war, there were only 124 Kittyhawks remaining, 20 were lost in combat, 152 were lost in accidents overseas and in New Zealand. During the time  the RNZAF Kittyhawks were used in front line service they accounted for at least 99 Japanese aircraft destroyed in air combat.

card_unit_spitfire_mk_iia.name: card_unit_spitfire_mk_iia
card_unit_spitfire_mk_iia.title: SPITFIRE Mk IIa
card_unit_spitfire_mk_iia.text: Deployment: Gets +2+2 if your enemy controls an air unit. Gets Fury if not.
card_unit_spitfire_mk_iia.flavorText: The Spitfire Mk II variant was a modification of the Mk I and came with factory fitted armour and a Merlin Mk XII powerplant that made it more powerful and faster than its predecessor. The Mk IIa was fitted with eight .303 Browning machine guns and the Mk IIb was fitted with four .303 Brownings and twin 20mm Hispano cannons. Some early Mk II’s were used in the Battle of Britain in 1940, but most were used during the Allied offensive in Europe, until superseded by the Mk V. A total of 921 Mk II’s were built, some were converted into MK V’s and 50 of them were converted for air-sea rescue work.

card_unit_tiger_moth.name: card_unit_tiger_moth
card_unit_tiger_moth.title: TIGER MOTH
card_unit_tiger_moth.text: Deployment: Give a friendly unit +1 defense, then change its attack to equal its defense.
card_unit_tiger_moth.flavorText: The de Havilland Tiger Moth was Britain’s standard trainer aircraft throughout WWII. First flown in 1931, it entered service in the RAF in 1932 and quickly became the cornerstone of Allied pilot training. Over 8,000 were produced in Britain, Canada, Australia and other countries, and thousands of pilots from across the Commonwealth earned their wings in this plane. Although it was designed for basic flight instruction, the Tiger Moth took on unexpected wartime roles. In 1939, RAF Coastal Command organized “scarecrow patrols” using unarmed Tiger Moths to deter German U-boats and force them to dive. Lacking radios, crews carried homing pigeons for emergencies. A few were even armed with small bombs, though none were confirmed used in combat. After the 1940 campaign in France, Britain prepared for possible invasion. Around 350 Tiger Moths were fitted with bomb racks to serve as emergency light bombers under Operation Banquet. Some were tested with scythe-like devices intended to slash parachutes mid-air. Others were equipped to disperse toxic dust like Paris green against enemy troops. Despite its fragile appearance, the Tiger Moth proved surprisingly adaptable. It played no direct combat role, but it proved to be a vital link in the Allied air effort worldwide, from training fields to improvised defensive missions.

card_unit_whirlwind.name: card_unit_whirlwind
card_unit_whirlwind.title: WHIRLWIND
card_unit_whirlwind.text: When the enemy targets or attacks this unit, deal 3 damage to their HQ.
card_unit_whirlwind.flavorText: The Westland Whirlwind was Britain’s first single-seat, twin-engine fighter and the first RAF aircraft armed with four 20 mm cannons. Introduced in 1940, it excelled at low-level attack missions thanks to its speed, firepower, and agility. Only 114 were built due to engine production limits, yet it served effectively with two RAF squadrons. The Whirlwind was first used by 263 Squadron for convoy patrols and coastal defense, before shifting to offensive operations across the English Channel. It hunted German aircraft, strafed trains and sank enemy ships. In 1941, 137 Squadron was formed to exploit the aircraft’s precision and power in attacking railways and other transport targets. Armed with two 500 lb bombs, the “Whirlibomber” version flew cross-channel sorties, often returning with multiple kills. Pilots praised the Whirlwind’s heavy nose-mounted cannon, superb low-altitude performance and toughness. It was fast enough to contend with enemy fighters and rugged enough to survive crash landings. However, the unreliable Rolls-Royce Peregrine engine ended its career. By late 1943, the Whirlwind was retired in favor of the Hawker Typhoon.

card_event_breaking_point.name: card_event_breaking_point
card_event_breaking_point.title: BREAKING POINT
card_event_breaking_point.text: Destroy a Suppressed or Pinned unit.
card_event_breaking_point.flavorText: The breaking point of the Winter War between Finland and the Soviet Union was when the Finns successfully repelled the Soviet offensive at the Battle of Suomussalmi and the Battle of Raate Road in December 1939. The Finnish forces used guerrilla tactics and took advantage of the harsh winter conditions to outmaneuver the larger and better-equipped Soviet troops, causing significant losses for the Soviets and ultimately leading to a strategic setback. These battles demonstrated Finland's effective resistance and the difficulties faced by the Soviet Union, eventually contributing to the Soviet decision to seek peace negotiations in March 1940.

card_event_cold_trap.name: card_event_cold_trap
card_event_cold_trap.title: COLD TRAP
card_event_cold_trap.text: When an enemy unit attacks, add a SISSI as defender.
card_event_cold_trap.flavorText: The winter during the Winter War of 1939-40 was extraordinarily harsh, with the Karelian Isthmus experiencing a frigid weather with up to -43°C in January 1940. The Finnish forces maximized the advantages offered by the cold and forested landscape to conduct effective defensive operations and hinder the progress of the Soviet forces.
