For concealment, Finnish soldiers adopted layered clothing, while ski troopers wore lightweight white snow capes, effectively rendering themselves nearly invisible for executing guerrilla tactics against Soviet units. The Finnish forces ensured their comfort and hygiene in the harsh winter conditions by providing warm tents and dugouts with heating from hot stoves. They also had the luxury of saunas to keep them warm and to maintain their personal cleanliness. In contrast, the Soviets dug snow holes which were their main shelters, their tanks were painted in standard olive drab and the troops wore conventional khaki uniforms. They didn’t adapt to the winter environment until late January 1940, when they started painting their equipment white and distributing snowsuits to their infantry.

card_event_dark_deeds.name: card_event_dark_deeds
card_event_dark_deeds.title: DARK DEEDS
card_event_dark_deeds.text: Add a SISSI to your support line. Draw a card. Discard it at the end of your next turn.
card_event_dark_deeds.flavorText: As the Soviets were planning to invade Finland in late 1939, the Finnish military prepared for a harsh winter, which ultimately became the coldest in over a century. The Finns spent most of the autumn destroying infrastructure like bridges, roads, houses and barns that had taken decades to build. Their goal was to deny the Soviets any shelter or resources during their advance. This scorched earth strategy left abandoned villages and towns in ruins, making them inhospitable even to the enemy. Finns set booby traps everywhere: mines were hidden in haystacks, under outhouse seats, in abandoned sleds, and even inside dead animals. They poisoned wells or, when time and resources were limited, contaminated them with horse manure. Floating mines were placed under newly-frozen lakes to detonate under Soviet troops as they advanced across the ice.

card_event_decoy_tactics.name: card_event_decoy_tactics
card_event_decoy_tactics.title: DECOY TACTICS
card_event_decoy_tactics.text: Give a unit Ambush, Shock and: "Enemy discards a random card when they target or attack this unit."
card_event_decoy_tactics.flavorText: In February 1944, the Soviet Union launched three large-scale bombing raids against Helsinki, aiming to cripple Finnish morale and force the country into abandoning its alliance with Germany. The raids, approved at the 1943 Tehran Conference with British and American support, targeted the Finnish capital on the nights of February 6-7, 16-17, and 26-27. Soviet air forces deployed over 2,100 bombers and dropped more than 16,000 bombs during these operations. Anticipating such attacks, Finnish defenses implemented a sophisticated deception strategy. Fires were set on outlying islands and searchlights were activated only east of the city to mislead Soviet pathfinder aircraft. These tactics convinced the Soviet crews that they were striking central Helsinki, while in reality most bombs fell outside the urban core. The result was remarkably effective. Only 530 bombs hit the city itself, causing significantly fewer casualties than similar raids elsewhere in Europe. Finland also spread disinformation via Swedish channels, falsely claiming Helsinki had been devastated. When Soviet officials visited after the war, they were stunned to find the city largely untouched. Stalin, furious at the failure and deception, dismissed Marshal Golovanov, commander of the Soviet Strategic Air Force.

card_event_depot_raid.name: card_event_depot_raid
card_event_depot_raid.title: DEPOT RAID
card_event_depot_raid.text: Send target enemy unit to hand. Add a Salvaged copy to your hand.
card_event_depot_raid.flavorText: Following the Winter War, Finland secretly reinforced its guerrilla forces, forming specialized long-range scout patrols called Kaukopartiojoukot (e. Remote patrol forces). These patrols were composed of physically and mentally fit volunteers who were tasked with conducting reconnaissance and guerrilla strikes deep behind enemy lines. During the Continuation War these forces operated in small groups, they infiltrated Soviet territory to gather intelligence, sabotage infrastructure, and attack targets like convoys, officers, and supply lines. While primarily focused on reconnaissance, they were authorized to conduct raids, placing mines and intercepting communications. Occasionally, these patrols were reinforced for larger-scale operations targeting high-value targets such as supply centers and transportation routes, like the Murmansk railway and the Stalin White Sea–Baltic Canal.

card_event_friendly_fire_fin.name: card_event_friendly_fire_fin
card_event_friendly_fire_fin.title: FRIENDLY FIRE
card_event_friendly_fire_fin.text: When an enemy unit attacks, its attack damage goes to a random other enemy.
card_event_friendly_fire_fin.flavorText: Friendly fire, the unfortunate and unintended harm inflicted upon one's own forces, was a recurring problem during WWII, and in almost every conflict before and after. During WWII instances of friendly fire occurred in all theaters of the war and affected all branches of the military. Soldiers were mistakenly shot or shelled by their own comrades, pilots bombed or strafed friendly positions, and naval vessels fired upon allied ships. Friendly fire incidents deeply affected morale and despite attempts to prevent it through better communication and training, it remained a frequent and tragic occurrence throughout the war.

card_event_frozen_assets.name: card_event_frozen_assets
card_event_frozen_assets.title: FROZEN ASSETS
card_event_frozen_assets.text: Add a SISSI adjacent to a friendly unit. It has Blitz and Salvage.
card_event_frozen_assets.flavorText: The Winter War started on 30 November 1939 and ended on 13 March 1940, three and a half months later, with the Moscow Peace Treaty, which ceded 11% of Finland's territory to the Soviet Union. Early on the Finns managed to repel Soviet attacks successfully, but finally the Soviet forces broke the stalemate and the Finns were forced to sue for peace. Despite the Soviet Union being the victor of the Winter War, the Red Army suffered devastating losses: 168,000 soldiers were killed, 207,538 wounded and frostbitten, while 1,000 aircraft, 2,300 tanks and armored cars and an enormous amount of other war materials were lost. Finland's losses were limited to 25,904 dead or missing and 43,557 wounded.

card_event_heartland_defense.name: card_event_heartland_defense
card_event_heartland_defense.title: HEARTLAND DEFENSE
card_event_heartland_defense.text: When your HQ receives damage, add a SISSI to your support line. Give it +X+X where X is the damage dealt.
card_event_heartland_defense.flavorText: During WWII, Finland fought hard to defend its heartland from Soviet invasion. The Soviet Union aimed to annex Finnish territory, but Finland’s determined resistance became a symbol of national resilience. In the Winter War, though outnumbered, Finnish forces used the terrain and harsh winter to stall the Soviet advance. Defending the Mannerheim Line and using guerrilla tactics, the Finns inflicted heavy losses and forced the Soviets to settle for limited territorial gains in the 1940 peace treaty. In the Continuation War, Finland allied with Germany to regain lost lands, but focused on protecting its own territory rather than pushing deep into the Soviet Union. The Soviet summer offensive of 1944 led to battles like Tali-Ihantala, the largest in Finnish and Nordic history, where Finnish troops held their ground against overwhelming odds. This success allowed Finland to negotiate an armistice and preserve its independence. Finland’s wartime goal was survival, not conquest, and its steadfast defense ensured sovereignty despite immense pressure.

card_event_lotta_svard.name: card_event_lotta_svard
card_event_lotta_svard.title: LOTTA SVÄRD
card_event_lotta_svard.text: Your units get +1 defense and -1 operation cost.
card_event_lotta_svard.flavorText: Lotta Svärd was a Finnish voluntary auxiliary paramilitary organization for women, formed originally in 1918 in support of the White Guard during the Finnish Civil War. During WWII, it was mobilized in order to replace men conscripted into the army. The women of Lotta Svärd mainly served in hospitals, at air raid warning positions, and other auxiliary tasks in close cooperation with the army. The women were officially unarmed except for a voluntary anti-aircraft battery in Helsinki in the summer of 1944. This unit was also issued rifles for self-protection, making them the only armed female military unit in the Finnish Defence Forces history. The Lotta Svärd organization was disbanded after WWII.

card_event_molotov_cocktail_fin.name: card_event_molotov_cocktail_fin
card_event_molotov_cocktail_fin.title: MOLOTOV COCKTAIL
card_event_molotov_cocktail_fin.text: Deal 2 damage. The enemy discards a card. Discard at the end of your turn.
card_event_molotov_cocktail_fin.flavorText: During the Winter War between Finland and the Soviet Union in 1939-1940, Molotov cocktails played a significant role in Finland's defense against the larger and better-equipped Soviet forces. These makeshift incendiary weapons, essentially glass bottles filled with flammable liquid and a cloth wick, were named by the Finns as a mocking reference to Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov. Finnish soldiers used Molotov cocktails effectively to disrupt and destroy Soviet tanks and vehicles, earning a reputation for tenacity in the face of overwhelming odds. Note that not all Molotov cocktails were improvised in the field. During the Winter War, they were mass-produced by the Alko corporation at a distillery in southern Finland, 45 km from Helsinki, where the bottled mixture of ethanol, tar and gasoline was bundled with matches. The production totalled 450,000 Molotov Cocktails throughout the war.

card_event_motti_tactic.name: card_event_motti_tactic
card_event_motti_tactic.title: MOTTI TACTIC
card_event_motti_tactic.text: Destroy target unit. Add a copy of it to your hand.
card_event_motti_tactic.flavorText:
"Motti" is Finnish military slang for completely encircling an enemy unit. The tactic, known as "motitus," involves trapping the enemy. It's related to the idea of a small, manageable unit.
Finnish forces used this tactic effectively in the Winter War and Continuation War, especially against Soviet mechanized units. Skilled Finnish troops would split the enemy columns into smaller segments in the forests, then attack from all sides. A "motitus" is a double envelopment maneuver, encircling enemies on a road with mobile troops. Despite being outnumbered, Finnish forces could immobilize larger enemy groups by dividing and surrounding them. If an encircled unit was too strong, it would be left to weaken due to a lack of supplies and ammunition. The Battle of Suomussalmi is a notable example where Finnish regiments surrounded and defeated two Soviet divisions and a tank brigade on a road.

card_event_order_of_the_day.name: card_event_order_of_the_day
card_event_order_of_the_day.title: ORDER OF THE DAY
card_event_order_of_the_day.text: Add two SISSI units to the support line. Your SISSI get: "It costs the enemy +1 kredits to target or attack this unit."
card_event_order_of_the_day.flavorText: The Sword Scabbard Declaration was a speech made by Finnish Commander-in-Chief Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim on July 23rd, 1941, during WWII. At the time, Finland was engaged in the Continuation War against the Soviet Union in an effort to reclaim territories lost to the USSR in the Winter War of 1939-1940. In his speech, Mannerheim declared that he would not "sheathe his sword" until Finland had reclaimed all lost lands. The speech became symbolic and rallied the Finnish people to support the war effort, and it remains one of Mannerheim’s most famous wartime statements.

card_event_prolonged_siege.name: card_event_prolonged_siege
card_event_prolonged_siege.title: PROLONGED SIEGE
card_event_prolonged_siege.text: Draw 4 cards. Discard them at the end of your next turn.
card_event_prolonged_siege.flavorText: During WWII, Finland participated in the Siege of Leningrad (now St. Petersburg) as part of its alliance with Germany during the Continuation War (1941–1944). At the time Finland fought to regain territories lost to the Soviet Union after the Winter War (1939–1940), including the Karelian Isthmus and the city of Viipuri (Vyborg). In 1941, Finnish forces advanced to the pre-1940 Soviet-Finnish border north of Leningrad, cutting off land routes and contributing to the blockade of the city. However, Finland halted its advance at the historic border, refusing to push further into Soviet territory or directly bombard Leningrad. This decision stemmed from political caution and a focus on defensive goals rather than total warfare. While Finnish troops blockaded Leningrad’s northern approaches, they avoided active direct participation in the brutal urban siege conducted by the German forces. The Finnish front remained static until 1944, when Soviet breakthroughs in the Vyborg–Petrozavodsk Offensive forced Finland to retreat and eventually negotiate an armistice with the Soviet Union.

card_event_salpa_line.name: card_event_salpa_line
card_event_salpa_line.title: SALPA LINE
card_event_salpa_line.text: Add a SISSI to your support line, then give all your SISSI units +3 defense.
card_event_salpa_line.flavorText: The Salpa Line was Finland’s great eastern defensive line, built after the Winter War to guard against a possible new Soviet invasion. Its official name was Suomen Salpa, meaning Finland’s latch. Construction began in 1940 during the Interim Peace, the period between the Winter War and the Continuation War, first with volunteers and then with men who were not eligible for front line service. At its peak in 1941, about 35,000 workers were involved. The line stretched over roughly 1,200 kilometres from the Gulf of Finland to Petsamo. Its strongest section laid between the Gulf of Finland and the Lake Saimaa waterway system, where lakes, marshes, islands, rivers and rocky ground were built into the defence plan. The fortifications included 728 concrete installations, 315 kilometres of wire obstacles, 225 kilometres of anti-tank obstacles, 130 kilometres of anti-tank ditches, more than 3,000 entrenchments, and 254 concrete infantry shelters. Work stopped after the Continuation War began, but resumed in 1944 as the front moved closer to Finland’s old borders. The Salpa Line was never tested in battle, since the Soviet offensive was stopped farther east, but its existence strengthened Finland’s position in the peace talks.

card_event_scrap_metal.name: card_event_scrap_metal
card_event_scrap_metal.title: SCRAP METAL
card_event_scrap_metal.text: Choose and discard a unit to draw a card. Gain 4 kredits if the unit was Salvaged.
card_event_scrap_metal.flavorText: Finland, like many other countries during WWII, used scrap metal for war production. The Finnish government and industry recognized the importance of conserving and recycling resources during the war, including metal, to support their military efforts. It is worth noting that Finland did not produce much of its own heavy equipment during the war, mainly due to industrial limitations. They did produce aircraft in limited numbers, such as the VL Myrsky and VL Pyry fighters, and a variety of small arms such as the Suomi KP/-31 submachine and Lahti-Saloranta M/26 light machine gun. When it came to tanks and armored vehicles, Finland was fully reliant on foreign powers and had to either purchase them or to use captured vehicles from the Red Army.

card_event_sisu.name: card_event_sisu
card_event_sisu.title: SISU
card_event_sisu.text: When your HQ is to take damage, the enemy HQ takes the damage instead.
card_event_sisu.flavorText: The word “sisu” originates from ‘sisus’, which literally means “guts” or “the intestines” in Finnish. According to Finnish understanding, “sisu” is a metaphor for a stoic determination that is reserved for really tough times, similar to “gutsy” in English, and it has been described as the word that explains Finland and Finns. The Finnish people feel that “sisu” constitutes their national character and culture, and it certainly is a metaphor for their perseverance during the Winter War.

card_event_ski_troops.name: card_event_ski_troops
card_event_ski_troops.title: SKI TROOPS
card_event_ski_troops.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, suppress it, then add a SISSI to your support line.
card_event_ski_troops.flavorText: When the Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939, Finnish ski troops quickly emerged as one of the defining forces of the Winter War. Outnumbered and lacking heavy equipment, they leveraged their skis, white winter camouflage, and deep knowledge of the forests to run circles around road-bound Soviet formations. This extreme mobility was the cornerstone of the Finnish motti tactics. Ski troops would strike the front and rear of long, vulnerable Soviet columns, chopping them into isolated pockets. Once trapped, these pockets were systematically dismantled using sniper fire, mortars, submachine guns, and Molotov cocktails. Beyond their physical toll, these sudden strikes inflicted heavy psychological damage. Gliding silently through the dense woods, Finnish soldiers would ambush camps and supply lines, melting back into the forest before the Soviets could even mount a response. At major engagements like the Battle of Suomussalmi, these hit-and-run tactics allowed vastly outnumbered Finnish forces to annihilate massive mechanized units, proving that speed and terrain mastery could overcome overwhelming numerical superiority.

card_event_strike_from_the_forest.name: card_event_strike_from_the_forest
card_event_strike_from_the_forest.title: STRIKE FROM THE WOODS
card_event_strike_from_the_forest.text: Pin target unit. Add a SISSI to your support line.
card_event_strike_from_the_forest.flavorText: The Battle of Tolvajärvi, fought on 12 December 1939 in Ladoga Karelia, was the first large offensive victory for Finland during the Winter War. The Finnish side had 4,000 men (16th Infantry Regiment, 4 separate battalions and one artillery battalion) against 20,000 Soviet soldiers of the 139th Rifle Division (9 infantry battalions, 60 artillery pieces, one scout battalion, one signal battalion, one sapper battalion, 30 tanks, and 376 aircraft), and despite being outnumbered 5 to 1, the Finns won a convincing victory. The Finnish side lost over 100 soldiers, with 250 others injured, while the Soviet Union suffered significant losses, with an estimated 5,000 soldiers killed and the capture of many of their weapons and equipment, including artillery pieces, tanks, and machine guns. This battle was a big win for the Finnish forces and lifted the morale of the entire Finnish Army. After this successful counter-attack, there were no major battles in this area, and only infrequent gunfire occurred. The Finnish troops held their position there until the end of the Winter War.

card_event_through_the_ice.name: card_event_through_the_ice
card_event_through_the_ice.title: THROUGH THE ICE
card_event_through_the_ice.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit and each other unit with the same name.
card_event_through_the_ice.flavorText: During the Winter War (November 1939 - March 1940), numerous lakes in Finland were covered by a thick layer of ice. This offered the Soviet invading forces extensive areas to move troops safely away from the sniper-laden forests. Finnish engineers used to embed mines beneath the ice, in order to help guard frozen rivers and lakes during winter time. These mines were detonated when enemy formations crossed the ice, often sending Soviet soldiers and equipment to a watery grave. As a result, Red Army commanders stopped moving large numbers of troops across frozen lakes. Instead they moved their troops through nearby forests where Finnish snipers and machine gunners would patiently await their targets.

card_event_white_death.name: card_event_white_death
card_event_white_death.title: THE WHITE DEATH
card_event_white_death.text: Suppress all enemy units. Add a SISSI to your support line with Blitz.
card_event_white_death.flavorText: Simo Häyhä, known as "The White Death," was a Finnish sniper during WWII, specifically the 1939–1940 Winter War against the Soviet Union. He used a Finnish M/28-30 rifle and a Suomi KP/-31 submachine gun. Häyhä is credited with over 500 kills during this conflict, making him the deadliest sniper in any major war. He chronicled his experiences in a private memoir titled "Sotamuistoja" (War memoirs) written in 1940, shortly after being wounded. This memoir, hidden for many years, was discovered in 2017. The name "White Death" has been suggested to originate entirely in Finnish propaganda, rather than having been given to Häyhä by Soviet soldiers, to whom at the time "White Death" generally referred to a severe frost in the deep forests of Finland. Häyhä having the nickname "White Death" first appeared in the Finnish Winter War literature of the late 1980s, but during the war, the "White Death" was one of the leading themes of Finnish propaganda. Finnish newspapers frequently featured the invisible Finnish soldier, thus creating a hero of mythical proportions. But even though Simo Häyhä’s nickname can be debated, he is widely regarded as the most skilled and successful sniper there ever was.

card_unit_sissi.name: card_unit_sissi
card_unit_sissi.title: SISSI
card_unit_sissi.text: Units dealt combat damage by this unit are destroyed.

card_unit_coastal_battalion_7.name: card_unit_coastal_battalion_7
card_unit_coastal_battalion_7.title: COASTAL BATTALION 7
card_unit_coastal_battalion_7.text: Units you deploy get +1+1 for each combat keyword they have.
card_unit_coastal_battalion_7.flavorText: The 7th Coastal Infantry Battalion is best known for being involved in the Battle of Suursaari, recapturing Gogland Island in the Gulf of Finland in the spring of 1944. The island held high strategic value due to its location between Finland, the Soviet Union and Estonia. Though previously abandoned, the Soviets had reoccupied and fortified it with over 1,000 troops. The 7th Coastal Infantry Battalion, led by Captain Esko Laaksonen, played a central role in the assault, landing under fire and pushing inland in close-quarter combat. The battalion had to overcome difficult terrain and strong resistance to secure key positions on the island. The operation concluded after seven days of fighting, with Finnish forces regaining control of Gogland, defending it for the rest of the Continuation War.

card_unit_detached_battalion_4.name: card_unit_detached_battalion_4
card_unit_detached_battalion_4.title: DETACHED BATTALION 4
card_unit_detached_battalion_4.text: Deployment: Destroy target enemy unit with cost 2 or less.
card_unit_detached_battalion_4.flavorText: Detached Battalion 4 (Erillinen Pataljoona 4 or ErP4) served as a special force of the Finnish Army during the Continuation War and Lapland War. In the beginning the detachment had as few as 14 soldiers, but as the war progressed, their ranks were increased up to 40–60 men who carried out missions aimed at disrupting enemy operations and gathering intelligence. In 1944, a special operations aviation unit was established, equipped with  amphibious Heinkel He 115 aircraft to support the battalion with mission insertions and extractions. During its short lived service the battalion participated in over 350 long-range reconnaissance patrols and played an important role in the Battle of Ilomantsi where it disrupted Soviet supply lines.

card_unit_fiat_g_50_fi.name: card_unit_fiat_g_50_fi
card_unit_fiat_g_50_fi.title: FIAT G.50 FI
card_unit_fiat_g_50_fi.text: Has +3 attack against units with higher attack.
card_unit_fiat_g_50_fi.flavorText: The Fiat G.50 Freccia ("Arrow") was an Italian fighter aircraft which was used by the Regia Aeronautica (the Italian Air Force) and their allies during WWII. When it entered service in 1938, it was widely regarded as being an extremely maneuverable aircraft and was often considered to be one of Italy's best fighters. In November 1939 Finland purchased 35 Fiat G.50s from Italy. Only fourteen were delivered by the end of the "Winter War". All thirty-five had arrived and were ready for service by the time the "Continuation War" started and they were assigned to Lentolaivue 26 (Flying Squadron 26), where they replaced the squadron's aging Fokker XXIs and Gloster Gladiators. The G.50s were in service until they were replaced in May 1944 by Brewster Buffalos. The G.50 proved to be an effective fighter in the hands of Finnish pilots who achieved a remarkable kill/loss ratio of 33 to 1.

card_unit_finnish_boys.name: card_unit_finnish_boys
card_unit_finnish_boys.title: FINNISH BOYS
card_unit_finnish_boys.flavorText: Infantry Regiment 200, also known as the "Finnish Boys" (Soomepoisid), was a Finnish Army unit mainly made up of Estonian volunteers. Formed in early 1944 during the Continuation War under Field Marshal Mannerheim’s command, the regiment fought in the defensive battles on the Karelian Isthmus and near the Bay of Viipuri as part of the Finnish 10th Division. After Finland signed an armistice with the Soviet Union in September 1944, the Estonian volunteers faced a difficult situation. Many returned to Estonia, where they were often persecuted by the Soviet regime, while others fled to Sweden or joined other military units. Many fought against the Red Army with the 20th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS, despite initially escaping to Finland to avoid such service. The Finnish Boys' story reflects the challenges faced by Estonians caught between Soviet and German forces during WWII.

card_unit_fokker_finland.name: card_unit_fokker_finland
card_unit_fokker_finland.title: FOKKER D.XXI
card_unit_fokker_finland.flavorText: The Fokker D.XXI was a Dutch fighter that saw its most extensive service with the Finnish Air Force. Finland first acquired the aircraft in 1937, and later produced 93 under license at the State Aircraft Factory in Tampere between 1939 and 1944. Designed as a rugged and affordable monoplane with a fixed undercarriage, the D.XXI proved well suited for operations in Finnish conditions, and could be converted to skis for winter use. At the outbreak of the Winter War in 1939, 41 Finnish D.XXIs were in service. On December 1st, one of them claimed the type’s first kill by downing a Soviet Tupolev SB. Though increasingly outclassed as newer Soviet fighters entered the war, the Fokker D.XXI's maneuverability and sturdy construction earned it the respect of enemy pilots. It remained in frontline use during the Continuation War, where pilots like Jorma Sarvanto achieved Ace status flying this type. The highest-scoring airframe, FR-110, achieved 10 victories and is preserved today at the Central Finland Aviation Museum. Finnish D.XXIs served until 1949, long after the aircraft had been retired elsewhere.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_11.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_11
card_unit_infantry_regiment_11.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 11
card_unit_infantry_regiment_11.flavorText: The 11th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 3rd Division of the Finnish Army during the Continuation War (1941 to 1944). In 1941 the division participated in Operation Arctic Fox which was a joint offensive by German and Finnish forces against the Soviet defenses at Salla, a municipality located in northern Finnish Lapland. Operation Arctic Fox was part of a larger operation codenamed Operation Silver Fox, which aimed to capture the port of Murmansk. Even though they managed to capture Salla, the operation did not meet its goal and it ended in November 1941 when both sides dug in at their positions. In 1944, the 3rd Division was sent to the Karelian Isthmus, engaging in Finland's defense against the Soviet Vyborg–Petrozavodsk offensive where the Soviets forces managed to capture East Karelia and southern Karelian Isthmus. After the Moscow Armistice (19 September 1944), the division fought in the Lapland War against Germany until it was disbanded in October 1944.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_13.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_13
card_unit_infantry_regiment_13.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 13
card_unit_infantry_regiment_13.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 for each enemy unit.
card_unit_infantry_regiment_13.flavorText: The 13th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 5th Division of the Finnish Army during the Winter War. This division was part of the II Corps (II AK), and along with the III Corps (III AK), it formed the Army of the Isthmus, which was the largest formation of the Finnish Army during the Winter War. The 5th Division's primary deployment was along the Mannerheim Line, a defensive system of fortifications against the Soviet Union that was positioned between Lake Muolaanjärvi and Kuolemajärvi. The  Army of the Isthmus managed to halt the Soviet advance for two months, but finally the Soviet forces pierced the Mannerheim Line, and the rest of the Finnish defenses fell in turn.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_2.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_2
card_unit_infantry_regiment_2.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 2
card_unit_infantry_regiment_2.text: Your Salvaged units destroy any unit they damage.
card_unit_infantry_regiment_2.flavorText: The 2nd Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 5th Division of the Finnish Army of Karelia during the Continuation War, which was the conflict between Finland and the Soviet Union during WWII. The 5th Division operated mainly in Karelia and participated in the Battle of Nietjärvi in 1944. It fought several defensive battles during the Soviet Karelian Offensive where it suffered heavy losses.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_25.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_25
card_unit_infantry_regiment_25.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 25
card_unit_infantry_regiment_25.text: Your HQ gets +2 defense when you attack with a unit with 2 or more combat keywords.
card_unit_infantry_regiment_25.flavorText: Infantry Regiment 25 served under the Finnish 4th Division as part of II Corps during the Continuation War. In the autumn of 1941, the regiment took part in the Karhumäki-Povetsa offensive in East Karelia. This operation aimed to secure the Maaselkä Isthmus, a strategic land corridor between Lake Onega and Lake Seesjärvi. Advancing under the command of General Taavetti Laatikainen, II Corps moved deep into Soviet territory, following earlier successes near Lake Ladoga. The corps attacked north of Petrozavodsk and pushed toward Karhumäki. The town, situated on low ground and surrounded by hills, fell by late November. After securing key positions such as the Krivi railway station and Suurlahti, the Finnish forces established defensive lines as ordered by High Command. Following this advance, II Corps remained stationed in the region and transitioned into trench warfare. From 1942 to 1944, the corps was known as Maaselkä Group and faced repeated Soviet attacks. Despite supply difficulties and morale issues, it held its ground, anchoring Finland’s eastern front until Soviet offensives resumed in 1944.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_36.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_36
card_unit_infantry_regiment_36.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 36
card_unit_infantry_regiment_36.text: Deployment: Draw a card. Discard it at the end of your next turn.
card_unit_infantry_regiment_36.flavorText: The 36th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 12th Division of the Finnish Army. The division fought in the Winter War (1939–1940) and the Continuation War (1941–1944). It is most famously associated with the Battle of Kollaa in 1940 which was a pivotal engagement in the Winter War. The division was tasked with defending the Kollaa River region in Ladoga Karelia and it managed to repel repeated Soviet assaults despite severe numerical and material disadvantages. It is worth noting that the legendary Finnish sniper Simo Häyhä, nicknamed "The White Death", would see his first battle on the Kollaa front. After the Winter War, the 12th Division was re-formed in 1941 from the 3rd Brigade and integrated into Finland’s offensive operations during the Continuation War, where it fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union. The division’s activities at this time are less well known, but it remained part of Finland’s order of battle until the armistice with the Soviet Union in 1944.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_56.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_56
card_unit_infantry_regiment_56.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 56
card_unit_infantry_regiment_56.text: Deployment: Add a SISSI to your support line, then give your SISSI units +3+3.
card_unit_infantry_regiment_56.flavorText: The 56th Infantry Regiment was a regiment of the 1st Division of the Finnish Army during the Continuation War (1941-1944). Composed primarily of Finnish soldiers, it played a significant role in the Finnish advance into Soviet-held territories to reclaim lands lost in the Winter War. The division participated in the invasion of East Karelia as part of the Finnish VII Corps which captured the city of Petrozavodsk.The division was involved in various battles, mainly engagements on the Karelian Isthmus. Facing overwhelming Soviet forces, the 1st Division fought a series of defensive battles in an attempt to secure Finland's borders before the armistice was signed in September 1944.

card_unit_infantry_regiment_61.name: card_unit_infantry_regiment_61
card_unit_infantry_regiment_61.title: INFANTRY REGIMENT 61
card_unit_infantry_regiment_61.flavorText: The 61st Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 17th Division of the Finnish Army during the Continuation War (1941-1944). The 17th Division operated primarily in the Karelian Isthmus and along the Svir River and engaged in numerous defensive and offensive operations throughout the war, including the Battles of Svir and Jandeba in 1941 and the Battle of Tienhaara in June 1944, where it successfully defended against the Soviet offensive. The men and officers of the regiment didn’t speak Finnish as this regiment recruited exclusively among Swedish-speaking Finns. This formation also included no small number of Swedish volunteers. The 61st Infantry Regiment went down in Finnish history books as the Sextiettan, meaning “61” in Swedish.

card_unit_i_stridsgruppan.name: card_unit_i_stridsgruppan
card_unit_i_stridsgruppan.title: I. STRIDSGRUPPEN
card_unit_i_stridsgruppan.text: Has +2 attack against units with higher attack.
card_unit_i_stridsgruppan.flavorText: The I. Stridsgruppen was an infantry battalion of the Swedish Volunteer Corps (Swedish: Svenska frivilligkåren) which consisted of 9,640 officers and men. Despite Sweden having declared itself "non-belligerent" during the conflict, the Corps was utilized by Finland and actively engaged in combat. These Swedish volunteers fought on the front lines and encountered significant casualties during the Battle of Salla (30 November 1939 – 13 March 1940): 33 dead, 10 missing, 50 wounded, and 130 disabled due to frostbite. Additionally, the Swedish Voluntary Air Force, F19, deployed 25 aircraft, while volunteers defended Turku with an anti-aircraft battery. By the war's end, the Volunteer Corps comprised 8,260 Swedes, along with 725 Norwegians and 600 Danes, showcasing a strong Nordic unity reflected in their emblem, the "four brother hands," symbolizing Finland, Sweden, Norway, and Denmark.

card_unit_jager_battalion_2.name: card_unit_jager_battalion_2
card_unit_jager_battalion_2.title: JÄGER BATTALION 2
card_unit_jager_battalion_2.text: Deployment: Add a SISSI to your support line.
card_unit_jager_battalion_2.flavorText: The 2nd Jäger Battalion was a unit of the Armored Division of the Finnish Army during the Continuation War (1941-1944). The division was formed in 1942 and consisted of a newly formed Armored Brigade and the elite Jaeger Brigade which was created in 1921. It is still active today. In 1944 the division also consisted of the 14th Heavy Artillery Battalion, 6th Signals Battalion, 2nd Pioneer Battalion and the Separate Armour Company which operated BT-42 assault guns. In addition to the many captured T-26 variants, the division also possessed a number of obsolete T-28s, a small number of captured T-34s armed with a 76mm cannon and 2 tanks of the hulking KV1 series. During the Continuation War, the Finnish Armored Division was mostly located at Petrozavodsk (which is now the Republic of Karelia in the Russian Federation) but in 1944 it was moved to the Karelian Isthmus. This year the division took part in the Battle of Kuuterselkä, the Battle of Tali-Ihantala and the Battle of Vuosalmi. In October 1944 it participated in the Lapland War and fought in the Battle of Rovaniemi against the German Twentieth Mountain Army. The Armored Division was disbanded during the Lapland War on 30 December 1944.

card_unit_light_detachment_15.name: card_unit_light_detachment_15
card_unit_light_detachment_15.title: LIGHT DETACHMENT 15
card_unit_light_detachment_15.text: Gets +1 attack when a unit with higher attack is deployed.
card_unit_light_detachment_15.flavorText: Light Detachment 15 was part of the 7th Division (7. Divisioona) of the Finnish Army, nicknamed the "Sword Division," and was active during the Continuation War (1941–1944). It was formed with men from the Northern Savonia and North Karelia civil guard districts and was part of the VII Corps under the Army of Karelia. In July 1941, the division advanced to the Matkaselkä Railway and it captured Sortavala on August 8. It continued eastward, aiding in the capture of Petrozavodsk and reaching the Svir River by October. In July 1944, during the Soviet Svir-Petrozavodsk Offensive, the division fought a delaying action from the Svir River to Petrozavodsk and eventually to the Sortavala region. The 7th Division suffered 12,384 casualties during the war, the second-highest among Finnish divisions.

card_unit_me_bf_109_fin.name: card_unit_me_bf_109_fin
card_unit_me_bf_109_fin.title: ME BF 109 G FI
card_unit_me_bf_109_fin.text: When this unit attacks the enemy HQ, draw a card from the enemy deck. Discard it end of turn.
card_unit_me_bf_109_fin.flavorText: Finland acquired its first Bf 109 aircraft in March 1943 under a German-Finnish agreement, initially receiving 48 Bf 109 G-2s, followed by 111 G-6s and three G-8s (reconnaissance variant) by 1944. A total of 162 Bf 109s were procured for Finland, though three were lost during delivery. The Finnish Air Force used the Messerschmitt Bf 109 as its primary fighter aircraft during the Continuation War (1941–1944) against the Soviet Union. Finnish pilots found the Bf 109 to be a highly effective interceptor, with its superior speed, climb rate, and firepower making it a match against Soviet fighters like the Yak-9 and La-5. The aircraft played a key role in defending Finnish airspace, achieving aerial superiority in many battles. Finnish Bf 109 pilots were credited with shooting down over 600 enemy aircraft while suffering relatively low losses. After the war, Finland retained the Bf 109 in service until 1954, making it one of the last countries to operate the aircraft.

card_unit_pak_36_fl.name: card_unit_pak_36_fl
card_unit_pak_36_fl.title: PAK 36 FI
card_unit_pak_36_fl.text: When this unit attacks, it deals 1 damage to a random enemy.
card_unit_pak_36_fl.flavorText: The 3.7 cm Pak 36, also known as the Panzerabwehrkanone 36, was a German anti-tank gun and one of the primary anti-tank weapons used by the German military during the early stages of WWII. It was known for its effectiveness against the lightly armored and smaller tanks of the time, such as the early war French and Soviet tanks. The Pak 36 guns were widely used among German allies, including Finland, and approximately 200 were delivered to the Finnish Army between 1940 and 1941.

card_unit_ryhma_susi.name: card_unit_ryhma_susi
card_unit_ryhma_susi.title: RYHMÄ SUSI
card_unit_ryhma_susi.text: At the start of your turn, lose 1 kredit and draw a card.
card_unit_ryhma_susi.flavorText: Ryhmä Susi (e. Wolf Group) was a Finnish Army formation during the Winter War, operating under the North Finland Group. Led by Lieutenant Colonel Paavo Susitaival, a veteran of the 27th Jäger Battalion and a member of Parliament, the group was tasked with defending the northern flank of the Suomussalmi front. In December 1939, Ryhmä Susi engaged Soviet forces advancing along the Kuusamo-Suomussalmi road. Their objectives included defeating Soviet troops, securing the Kiannanniemi area, and cutting off enemy retreat routes near Lake Kianta. While they achieved several of these goals, they were unable to completely sever the Soviet withdrawal paths. The group comprised units such as the 6th Cycling Battalion, Separate Battalion 16, and the 1st Battalion of the 65th Infantry Regiment. Employing guerrilla tactics and leveraging their knowledge of the terrain, Ryhmä Susi effectively disrupted Soviet supply lines and communications. Their actions contributed significantly to the Finnish victory at the Battle of Suomussalmi, where outnumbered Finnish forces managed to encircle and defeat larger Soviet units. Following the conclusion of the Winter War in March 1940, Ryhmä Susi was disbanded as part of the broader demobilization of Finnish forces.

card_unit_sissiosasto_5d.name: card_unit_sissiosasto_5d
card_unit_sissiosasto_5d.title: SISSIOSASTO 5.D
card_unit_sissiosasto_5d.text: Gets +1+1 when an enemy unit is added, deployed or destroyed.
card_unit_sissiosasto_5d.flavorText: Sissiosasto/5.D (5th Division Sissi Detachment) was a specialized Finnish Army unit established during the Continuation War under the Lynx Division (5th Division, Finnish VI Corps). The unit was raised in 1941 and it focused on reconnaissance, sabotage, and guerrilla operations behind enemy lines. Led by Second Lieutenant V.I. Laajoki and comprising 51 volunteers from the 5th Division's sub-units, SissiOs./5.D conducted reconnaissance patrols in newly captured territories near the Svir River in late 1941. From early 1942, they engaged in longer reconnaissance missions independently and collaboratively with other Sissi units (light infantry units). In April 1942, an ad hoc squad, Osasto Uimonen, was formed to destroy a Soviet logistics center. Divided into two groups, the squad faced unexpected challenges and, despite significant losses, engaged in a fierce battle against a large enemy force. After the failed mission and the loss of their officers, SissiOs./5.D was reassigned to Kevyt osasto 19 (English: Light Division 19) and participated in frontline battles in the Šemenski-Pertjärvi area, contributing to a Finnish defensive victory.

card_unit_stug_iii_g_fin.name: card_unit_stug_iii_g_fin
card_unit_stug_iii_g_fin.title: STURMI
card_unit_stug_iii_g_fin.text: It costs the enemy +2 kredits to target or attack this unit.
card_unit_stug_iii_g_fin.flavorText: The Sturmgeschütz III (StuG III), nicknamed “Sturmi" by the Finns, was a German assault gun manufactured during WWII. The official Finnish designation for these vehicles was Stu-40, but they were widely referred to as "Sturmi". Finland purchased 30 StuGs from Germany in 1943 and another 29 were bought in 1944, and all were used during the Continuation War against the Soviet Union. The first 30 Sturmis were armed with the long barreled 75mm StuK 40 L/48 gun, which was an excellent anti-tank weapon capable of penetrating all but the heaviest Soviet armor. The Finns modified their Sturmis by adding extra armor and storage to improve survival and self-sufficiency during long front-line operations. These changes, along with their unique camouflage, made them look different from German StuGs. The Sturmi stayed in Finnish service for more than a decade following the 1944 truce with the Soviet Union.

card_unit_t_26_fl.name: card_unit_t_26_fl
card_unit_t_26_fl.title: T-26 FI
card_unit_t_26_fl.text: Has +2 attack against units with higher attack.
card_unit_t_26_fl.flavorText: The T-26 was a Soviet light tank used in various conflicts during the Interwar period and WWII. The underlying T-26 design came from the British Vickers 6-Ton tank and it stood out as one of the most effective tank designs of the 1930s. The Finnish Army used captured T-26s of different models, mainly during the Continuation War, and some tanks served in Finland for various non-combat purposes until 1961. The Finnish experience with captured T-26 tanks was versatile, with the tanks generally considered agile in steering, with reasonable road speed and terrain mobility. However, the suspension system created challenges when it came to accurate aiming while the tank was in motion, and enemy detection proved somewhat difficult. In comparison to captured BT-series tanks, the T-26 tanks were considered more practical and dependable in Finnish conditions, but engine-related problems persisted and efforts to replace it with a more powerful alternative did not materialize.

card_unit_uusimaa_regiment.name: card_unit_uusimaa_regiment
card_unit_uusimaa_regiment.title: UUSIMAA REGIMENT
card_unit_uusimaa_regiment.text: Your SISSI units deal +4 damage to HQs. At the end of your turn, add a SISSI to the same front.
card_unit_uusimaa_regiment.flavorText: The Uusimaa Regiment was the interwar name of the unit that later became Finland’s Nyland Brigade. Its roots reached back through the 3rd Jaeger Regiment of 1918 and the older Nyland and Tavastehus Cavalry Regiment, which had traditions dating to 1626. During the Winter War, the Uusimaa Regiment helped form the new 13th Brigade, which then became Infantry Regiment 13 during the Continuation War. During that time it fought with the 5th Division on the Karelian Isthmus, as part of the Army of the Isthmus. The brigade later carried these traditions into Finland’s coastal forces. Based at Dragsvik near Raseborg, it became known as Nyland Brigade and eventually joined the Finnish Navy. The unit has a unique language tradition. It is the only formation in the Finnish Defence Forces where training is given in Swedish, one of Finland’s two national languages, while the command language remains Finnish. Its modern coastal jaegers continue the unit’s focus on fighting in difficult shoreline terrain.

card_unit_white_guard.name: card_unit_white_guard
card_unit_white_guard.title: WHITE GUARD
card_unit_white_guard.text: Units dealt combat damage by this unit are destroyed.
card_unit_white_guard.flavorText: The White Guard, officially known as the Suojeluskunta, was a voluntary Finnish militia that played a decisive role in securing Finland’s independence during the turbulent years following the Russian Revolution. Formed from local citizen militias amid the collapse of imperial authority in 1917, the White Guard became the backbone of the White Army during the Finnish Civil War of 1918, fighting under the leadership of General C. G. E. Mannerheim and defeating the socialist Red Guard. After the civil war, the White Guard was integrated into Finland’s national defense system. While remaining a voluntary organization, it trained reservists, supported mobilization plans, and helped build Finland’s defensive preparations in the interwar years. During the Winter War and Continuation War, its members formed a significant and well-trained part of the Finnish field army, serving both at the front and on home defense duties. Disbanded in 1944 under the terms of the Moscow Armistice, the White Guard left behind a complex legacy. It is remembered both for its central role in Finland’s fight for independence and for shaping the country’s strong tradition of national defense and civilian preparedness.

card_event_ambush.name: card_event_ambush
card_event_ambush.title: FIERY AMBUSH
card_event_ambush.text: Deal 3 damage to a unit. If the enemy now has no units, deal 3 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_event_ambush.flavorText: In June 1944, as part of the preparations for the upcoming D-Day invasion, the Francs-tireurs et partisans (FTP), an armed resistance organization created by leaders of the French Communist Party, was actively engaged in sabotage and disrupting German supply lines. On that day, a convoy of German troops, including soldiers and vehicles, was passing through Tulle. The local Resistance fighters seized the opportunity and launched an ambush on the convoy. The ambush resulted in chaos and confusion among the German forces. The Resistance fighters targeted the vehicles, causing damage and casualties. They specifically focused on disabling the German tanks and armored vehicles, aiming to neutralize their firepower advantage. The surprise attack by the Resistance fighters caught the Germans off guard and delayed their progress. It also boosted the morale of the local population and inspired others to join the resistance movement. The Tulle ambush showcased the effectiveness of guerrilla tactics employed by the French Resistance, demonstrating their ability to strike at German forces and disrupt their operations. However, the German response to the ambush was brutal. In reprisal for the Resistance attack, the Germans carried out a series of severe reprisals, including the burning of the town of Tulle and the execution of numerous civilians. The reprisals served as a grim reminder of the risks faced by those involved in Resistance activities.

card_event_arming_resistance.name: card_event_arming_resistance
card_event_arming_resistance.title: ARMING THE RESISTANCE
card_event_arming_resistance.text: Deal 5 damage to target unit. Add a RESISTANCE card to the enemy deck for each excess damage.
card_event_arming_resistance.flavorText: Resistance in France began as soon as the Germans invaded and occupied the country in 1940. At first people acted alone, but gradually organized groups were formed. The Resistance groups were supported with weapons and training by the British, but pre-war weapons were also used as well as weapons stolen and captured from German or Vichy armories. After the Normandy landings the Resistance grew rapidly and became more organized and from June to October their strength grew from 100,000 to 400,000 men and women.

card_event_call_to_the_colonies.name: card_event_call_to_the_colonies
card_event_call_to_the_colonies.title: CALL TO THE COLONIES
card_event_call_to_the_colonies.text: Choose one - your HQ gains +8 defense OR draw 2 cards.
card_event_call_to_the_colonies.flavorText: During WWII the Vichy government of France fought for control over the colonies against the Allied Free French, who were most of the time supported by the British. Approximately 300,000 men, mostly from the French colonies in North Africa, fought with the Free French forces and helped liberate France from the German occupation.

card_event_chasing_shadows.name: card_event_chasing_shadows
card_event_chasing_shadows.title: CHASING SHADOWS
card_event_chasing_shadows.text: Target unit moves into the frontline, if possible.
card_event_chasing_shadows.flavorText: During the German occupation of France the French resistance groups developed an “underground railroad” system that was used to smuggle downed Allied airmen to the front lines or back to Britain. Later this same underground system was used to send messages between the resistance groups and Allied command. It also came to use during Operation Jedburgh in 1944 where Allied special operatives used the underground network to reach the groups and towns in France where they were to operate. The mission was to assist Allied forces in the upcoming invasion with sabotage, guerrilla warfare or by leading the resistance forces against the Germans.

card_event_compromise.name: card_event_compromise
card_event_compromise.title: COMPROMISE
card_event_compromise.text: Choose One - Draw a card and gain +3 HQ defense OR do this twice for both players.
card_event_compromise.flavorText: Free France’s military input in the total Allied war effort was fairly modest in comparison with Britain and the USA, and de Gaulle’s influence on his allies' decisions was limited. From 1940 to 1944, he insisted on having the Free French troops involved in many operations alongside the larger Allied forces, in the North African and the Italian campaigns. Political and military cooperation on the ground were achieved, because it was agreed France needed to earn its place amongst the victors, even if only up to its small means at the time. But de Gaulle took offense when Churchill summoned him to London, on June 4th 1944, to inform him about D-Day. He was also told no French troops were to be involved. In the meantime, Allied preparation to liberate Europe from German occupation also included planning for a new currency to be used for military purchasing in combat zones, and for the restoration of monetary order in liberated regions. The Allies landed in Normandy carrying “Allied Military francs”, printed in the USA, and authorized by General Eisenhower, but de Gaulle denounced these as “counterfeit currency”. This illustrates how, even amongst Western Allies, partnership wasn’t always an “Entente Cordiale”, given the huge stakes at play following liberation, over the political and economical control of liberated areas. Each side pushed strongly for their own interests, and ultimately they had to negotiate and to compromise. France wasn’t really involved in D-Day (only 209 French infantry soldiers landed that day), but managed to safeguard its monetary sovereignty.

card_event_cross_of_lorraine.name: card_event_cross_of_lorraine
card_event_cross_of_lorraine.title: CROSS OF LORRAINE
card_event_cross_of_lorraine.text: Costs 1 less for each card in the enemy hand. Deal 3 damage to an enemy.
card_event_cross_of_lorraine.flavorText: The Cross of Lorraine (French: Croix de Lorraine) is a cross with one vertical and two horizontal bars which was used as a symbol for Free France led by Général Charles De Gaulle, the Free French Forces and the French resistance during WWII. The cross is known in French history as the Cross of Anjou and dates back to the 15th century, but the use of the double cross symbol can be traced to the middle ages and can also be found in the coat of arms of Hungary, Slovakia, Belarus and Lithuania. It became, through the course of history, an emblem of Lorraine in Eastern France. After the defeat in the Franco-Prussian war in 1871, Alsace and part of Lorraine were annexed by Germany until 1918. During that period, the Cross served as a rallying point for French ambitions to recover its lost provinces and became a symbol of French patriotism. When the same thing happened in 1940, Capitaine de corvette Thierry d'Argenlieu suggested the Cross of Lorraine as the symbol of the Free French Forces. The Cross was displayed on the flags of Free French warships, on the fuselages of aircrafts and on the tanks. The medal of the Order of Liberation bears the Cross of Lorraine. De Gaulle himself is memorialized by a 43 meter (141 ft) high Cross of Lorraine in his home village of Colombey-les-Deux-Églises.

card_event_defend_in_depth.name: card_event_defend_in_depth
card_event_defend_in_depth.title: DEFEND IN DEPTH
card_event_defend_in_depth.text: Deal damage to target unit equal to cards in the enemy hand.
card_event_defend_in_depth.flavorText: Defense in depth, also known as elastic defense, is a military strategy which aims at delaying the attackers advance rather than trying to stop it altogether. Rather than having one line of defense, the defense in depth tactic focuses on having multiple lines of fortified defenses, each protecting the other, and aims at weakening the enemy over time. The French had built the Maginot line in the 1930s, which was an elaborate chain of concrete fortifications along the German border. However, since the defenses did not cover the French-Belgian border, the Germans bypassed it by invading Belgium first and from there they crossed over to France.

card_event_defend_the_empire.name: card_event_defend_the_empire
card_event_defend_the_empire.title: DEFEND THE NATION
card_event_defend_the_empire.text: Draw the top non-French card of your deck, then shuffle your deck.
card_event_defend_the_empire.flavorText: During WWII, faced with German occupation and the collaboration of the Vichy regime, many French citizens took up arms in the shadows to defend their homeland. The emerging resistance networks were initially independent and fragmented. In 1942, General de Gaulle tasked Jean Moulin with unifying these movements under the banner of Free France. Under Moulin's leadership, three major resistance groups of the Southern Zone joined to form the “Armée Secrète” (Secret Army) in September 1942, later consolidating into the “Mouvements Unis de la Résistance” (MUR, United Resistance Movements) in January 1943. Following the creation of the “Conseil National de la Résistance” (National Council of the Resistance) in May 1943 and Moulin's arrest, the MUR and a few Northern Zone groups united as the “Mouvement de Libération Nationale” (MLN, National Liberation Movement) in January 1944. The MLN organized clandestine operations (sabotage, intelligence, underground press) and, after its integration into the Forces Françaises de l'Intérieur (FFI, French Forces of the Interior) in February 1944, coordinated with Allied forces to prepare for Liberation. This unification granted the Resistance military effectiveness, critical to France's role in its own liberation, and political legitimacy, ensuring the nation could determine its postwar future itself. Beyond the fight for freedom, it laid the foundation for France's democratic rebirth.

card_event_escaut_plan.name: card_event_escaut_plan
card_event_escaut_plan.title: ESCAUT PLAN
card_event_escaut_plan.text: Target unit moves into the frontline, if possible. Give it Ambush, if this is the first order this turn.
card_event_escaut_plan.flavorText: The Escaut Plan was an operation planned by the French Army as a response if Germany invaded Belgium. It was an alternative to the Dyle Plan, in case Belgium didn’t allow the French troops to enter its territory quickly enough. It was adopted in October 1939 but never put into action. Motivated by military, economic and political reasons for the French and the British, both those plans aimed at stopping the German offensive in Belgium rather than on the French border. The Escaut Plan’s objective was to set up, in coordination with the Belgian Army, a defensive line along the Scheldt river (named Escaut in French), a river crossing Belgium from North to South, to defend the western part of the country. For that purpose, the fastest Allied troops were gathered in northern France: the British Expeditionary Force (partially motorized), and the French Light Mechanized Divisions (armored), Cavalry Divisions (part on horseback and part motorized) and Motorized Infantry Divisions. This plan was updated in November 1939 in order to also plan an intervention in the South of Netherlands, following intel collected by the Allies indicating the Germans intended to invade the country. When the German forces crossed the Belgian and Dutch borders on May 10th, 1940, the Belgian and Dutch governments immediately called the French for help, and the Dyle Plan was therefore launched.

card_event_fortified_position.name: card_event_fortified_position
card_event_fortified_position.title: FORTIFIED POSITION
card_event_fortified_position.text: Pin an enemy unit. If it is in the frontline, it Retreats.
card_event_fortified_position.flavorText: Prior to WWII the French had built the heavily fortified Maginot Line along the German borders. Although the bulk of the invading German forces managed to bypass the defenses of the Maginot Line, they did attack a few of its fortified positions. The German 16th Army attacked a fortified sector called “petit ouvrage” La Feré, southeast of Sedan, and backed up by heavy artillery fire they managed to take the fortification in 4 days. Another attack was made near Wissembourg, which the French defenders managed to stop, but for most parts there were only small skirmishes along the Maginot Line. In the end all the defenders of Maginot Line were ordered out and taken as prisoners of war.

card_event_frappe.name: card_event_frappe
card_event_frappe.title: FRAPPE
card_event_frappe.text: If you control a unit with Mobilize, destroy a unit with 3 or less defense.

card_event_free_french_navy.name: card_event_free_french_navy
card_event_free_french_navy.title: FREE FRENCH NAVY
card_event_free_french_navy.text: Draw the top unit of your deck with an operation cost of 3. Your HQ gains +3 defense.
card_event_free_french_navy.flavorText: The Free French Navy (Forces Navales Françaises Libres, FNFL) played a significant role in WWII after the fall of France in 1940. The Free French Navy began with a small force of about 3,600 sailors and 50 vessels, led by Vice-Admiral Émile Muselier who was the only flag officer of the French Navy to join the Free French Forces. As the war progressed its ranks and fleet grew, as more sailors and ships aligned with De Gaulle’s Free France joined from overseas colonies. The Free French Navy operated in various theaters, from the North Atlantic to the Mediterranean, and supported key operations such as the Battle of the Atlantic, the Normandy and Provence landings, and the liberation of French territories.

card_event_french_alliance.name: card_event_french_alliance
card_event_french_alliance.title: WESTERN ALLIES
card_event_french_alliance.text: Add the top non-French unit from your deck to your support line.
card_event_french_alliance.flavorText: The Free French were the government in exile, led by Charles De Gaulle, who continued to fight against the Axis as one of the Allies after the fall of France. The Free French fought Axis and Vichy regime troops and served on battlefronts everywhere from the Middle East to Indochina and North Africa during WWII.

card_event_honor_and_loyalty.name: card_event_honor_and_loyalty
card_event_honor_and_loyalty.title: HONOR AND LOYALTY
card_event_honor_and_loyalty.text: Shuffle target friendly unit into your deck, then draw 2 cards.
card_event_honor_and_loyalty.flavorText: The French Foreign Legion, whose motto is “Honneur et Fidélité” (French for “Honor and loyalty”),  was involved in several campaigns during WWII, including the Norway Campaign, the North African Campaign and the Syria-Lebanon Campaign. The 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion engaged in the Norwegian campaign in May 1940, where they suffered heavy losses at the Battle of Narvik. On June 4th they landed in Brittany, but they were forced to withdraw during the debacle and managed to board a ship bound for Scotland on June 21st, the day prior to the French Armistice. Afterwards the 13th Demi-Brigade was deployed in North Africa and in 1942 it participated in the Battle of Bir Hakeim as part of the British 8th Army. While Germany incorporated German legionnaires into the Wehrmacht's 90th Light Infantry Division in North Africa, many legionnaires answered General Charles de Gaulle's call to join the Free French Forces. However, some legionnaires were also loyal to the Vichy government and in the Battle of Damascus, during the Syria–Lebanon Campaign, one engagement at Kadem on June 20th saw legionnaires fighting legionnaires , resulting in one killed and one wounded. Nonetheless, later in the war thousands of Vichy legionnaires joined the Free French forces and would see combat in numerous operations and campaigns, both in North Africa and Europe.

card_event_liberation.name: card_event_liberation
card_event_liberation.title: LIBERATION
card_event_liberation.text: Add 3 RESISTANCE cards to the enemy deck. Your HQ gains +6 defense.
card_event_liberation.flavorText: On August 25, 1944, Paris was liberated from German occupation by Allied forces, including the Free French Forces lead by Charles De Gaulle. That day De Gaulle led a liberation march down the Champs d'Élysées, and in the afternoon General Dietrich von Choltitz, the last commander of Nazi-occupied Paris, formally surrendered to the Free French Forces.

card_event_maginot_line.name: card_event_maginot_line
card_event_maginot_line.title: MAGINOT LINE
card_event_maginot_line.text: Give target ground unit +3+4 and "Cannot retreat or be suppressed."
card_event_maginot_line.flavorText:
Built between the two World Wars, the Maginot Line was one of the most ambitious defensive systems ever constructed. Stretching over 400 kilometers from Switzerland to Luxembourg, it was designed to shield France from a future German invasion. Named after French Minister of War André Maginot, the line featured a network of underground fortresses, bunkers, artillery casemates, and supply tunnels. Each major fortification, or “ouvrage”, could house hundreds of soldiers and came equipped with retractable turrets, machine guns, and anti-tank weapons. Deep underground, these forts contained living quarters, power plants, command centers, and even electric railways to transport ammunition. The goal was to delay or block any direct assault on France’s eastern border, buying time for full mobilization.
The Maginot Line reflected the trauma of World War I and France’s desperate desire to avoid another devastating invasion. It stood as a symbol of national resilience and engineering prowess, intended to turn the eastern frontier into an impenetrable wall. While the defense strategy would later be bypassed, the construction itself remains a remarkable feat of military planning.

card_event_national_resistance_council.name: card_event_national_resistance_council
card_event_national_resistance_council.title: RESISTANCE COUNCIL
card_event_national_resistance_council.text: Pin target unit. Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ. Add a RESISTANCE card to the enemy deck.
card_event_national_resistance_council.flavorText: Created by Jean Moulin at the request of General de Gaulle, the National Council of the Resistance (French: Conseil National de la Résistance, or CNR) was the body that unified the various French Resistance movements under German occupation, encompassing all political tendencies. It met for the first time on May 27, 1943, in Paris, bringing together around the same table representatives of the eight major resistance movements, the two most important pre-war trade unions, and the six main political parties of the French Third Republic. The primary mission of the CNR was to put an end to the fragmentation and rivalries that could weaken the Resistance from within. It became the sole and legitimate interlocutor for General de Gaulle's Free France, based in London. The Council coordinated intelligence, the clandestine press, sabotage actions, and the armed struggle across the entire country. In March 1944, the CNR adopted a fundamental document: its programme. This document did not only plan for the national insurrection at the time of the D-Day landings. It also outlined the "Jours Heureux" (happy days), a project of economic and social reforms for post-war France, including social security and nationalizations, which durably marked the country's reconstruction. The unifying action of the CNR allowed for the integration of the French Forces of the Interior into the regular army during the Liberation. Its legacy, both military and political, enabled France to take its place among the victors and regain its full sovereignty.

card_event_phoney_war.name: card_event_phoney_war
card_event_phoney_war.title: PHONEY WAR
card_event_phoney_war.text: Both players draw until they have 8 cards in hand.
card_event_phoney_war.flavorText: The Phoney war began with the declaration of war by Britain and France against Germany in September 1939. What followed was an 8 month period with almost no fighting on the Western Front. Meanwhile the French and British were making defensive war plans and enforcing a naval blockade on Germany, while the Germans were preparing further military conquests. On 10 May 1940, Germany launched attacks on France and the low countries, bringing the stalemate on the Western Front to an end.

card_event_plan_d.name: card_event_plan_d
card_event_plan_d.title: PLAN D
card_event_plan_d.text: Choose one - your units get +2 attack this turn OR they get +2 defense.
card_event_plan_d.flavorText: Plan D, also known as the Dyle Plan, was a military strategy devised by the French high command in the late 1930s as a response to the growing threat of German aggression. The plan was primarily designed to defend against a potential German invasion along the Belgian border. It was based on the assumption that Germany would launch a similar offensive as it did during World War I, moving through Belgium to attack France. Plan D aimed to halt the German advance by establishing a defensive line along the Dyle River in Belgium, extending from Antwerp to the French border. The French Army, along with British and Belgian forces, would concentrate their troops in this region to counter the German invasion. The plan emphasized the importance of cooperation with the Belgian army and relied on the strong fortifications along the Franco-Belgian border. However, when Germany launched its invasion of France in May 1940, it did so through the Ardennes Forest, a heavily wooded and less fortified area that was considered impassable by the French high command. This unexpected maneuver bypassed the defenses established under Plan D and ultimately led to the swift defeat of France. In hindsight, the reliance on Plan D and its failure to account for the Ardennes offensive has been criticized as a strategic miscalculation that contributed to the rapid collapse of the French defenses and the subsequent occupation of the country by German forces.

card_event_provence_landing.name: card_event_provence_landing
card_event_provence_landing.title: PROVENCE LANDING
card_event_provence_landing.text: Units you deploy this turn move into the frontline if possible.
card_event_provence_landing.flavorText: On August 15, 1944, the Allied forces launched Operation Dragoon, the landing in Provence. A fleet of nearly 2,000 ships gathered off the French Riviera. The first operations began during the night of August 14-15. French commandos neutralized the coastal batteries. Simultaneously, 5,000 American and British paratroopers were dropped behind the lines. At dawn, naval bombardments pummeled the shore. At 8 a.m., the first American assault waves landed on the beaches of Cavalaire, Saint-Tropez and Saint-Raphaël. The weak German defenses were quickly overwhelmed with the help of the local Resistance. On August 16, the French 1st Army of General de Lattre de Tassigny landed. Its first mission was to liberate Toulon and Marseille. After fierce street fighting, the German forces in Toulon capitulated on August 26, and Marseille fell on August 28. These two major ports became operational again within a few weeks, allowing the Allies to unload tons of supplies there. The Allied forces then advanced up the Rhône valley and joined with the troops coming from Normandy on September 12 near Dijon. This success accelerated the liberation of France and forced the German troops to withdraw toward the Vosges mountains and Alsace.

card_event_rally_caledonia.name: card_event_rally_caledonia
card_event_rally_caledonia.title: RALLY CALEDONIA
card_event_rally_caledonia.text: Add a ROUTED TROOPS to your support line with Blitz and +1+1 for each enemy unit.
card_event_rally_caledonia.flavorText: The announcement of the Armistice of 22 June 1940 plunged New Caledonia into uncertainty. Cut off from the now-occupied mainland France, the local population was in favor of continuing the war alongside the British, echoing De Gaulle's Appeal of 18 June. The "Vergès Manifesto," signed by many New Caledonians, symbolizes this refusal to accept defeat. In reaction, on 4 September, the Vichy Government replaced Governor Georges Pélicier, whose behavior was deemed equivocal, with Lieutenant-Colonel Denis, a supporter of the regime. Henri Sautot, resident-commissioner in the New Hebrides, who had already rallied that territory to Free France on 20 July 1940, received orders from General de Gaulle to travel to New Caledonia. He arrived in Nouméa, escorted by the Australian cruiser Adelaide, on 19 September 1940. Greeted by an enthusiastic crowd and supported by the General Council, he had Lieutenant-Colonel Denis arrested and proclaimed the colony's definitive rallying to Free France. This allowed Free France to maintain a strategic presence in the Pacific, with New Caledonia becoming an essential base for the Allies against the Japanese threat. 300 New Caledonian volunteers later participated in the creation of the Pacific Battalion in 1940, which distinguished itself at Bir Hakeim in June 1942, then in Tunisia, Italy, and during the landing in Provence. In recognition of this commitment, New Caledonia received the Resistance Medal in April 1946.

card_event_resistance.name: card_event_resistance
card_event_resistance.title: RESISTANCE
card_event_resistance.text: Choose one - deal 1 damage to your HQ OR remove the top card of your deck.

card_event_saar_probe.name: card_event_saar_probe
card_event_saar_probe.title: SAAR OFFENSIVE
card_event_saar_probe.text: Deal 7 damage to target unit. Add CROSS OF LORRAINE to hand if this is the first order given this turn.
card_event_saar_probe.flavorText: The Saar Offensive was a military operation by the French Army in German territory, which took place between September 7th and October 17th, 1939, at the beginning of the “Phoney War.” After Germany invaded Poland on September 1st, 1939, the Allies declared war on Germany on September 3rd. Four days later, the French Army crossed the border between Moselle and Saarland. The civilians had already been evacuated, and a large number of anti-personnel and anti-tank mines had been deployed. As soon as the French arrived, the Germans detonated the bridges. Initially, they offered little resistance and chose to retreat behind the Siegfried Line. Only a few skirmishes took place, resulting in minimal casualties. The French advanced 8 kilometers into German territory and stopped 4 kilometers short of the Siegfried Line, staying out of reach of German heavy artillery. After Soviet forces invaded Poland on September 17th, French operations halted, and the frontline was fortified. The order to retreat to the Maginot Line was given on September 21st. Following Poland’s defeat, German divisions were transferred to the Western Front, allowing the German 1st Army to launch a counter-offensive into French territory from October 16th to 24th.In the end, the Saar Offensive and the subsequent German counterattack resulted in approximately 2,000 French casualties and 700 German casualties. The situation then remained unchanged until May 10th, 1940. This operation is sometimes considered a missed opportunity for the French to defeat Germany at a time when it was vulnerable and before the conflict escalated into a full-scale European war.

card_event_sabotage.name: card_event_sabotage
card_event_sabotage.title: SABOTAGE
card_event_sabotage.text: Choose 1 of 3 cards in the enemy hand. Discard it and add a copy to your hand.
card_event_sabotage.flavorText: Men and women from the French resistance planned, coordinated and executed many acts of sabotage against the German occupation troops and the Vichy government. Favorite targets were railways, phone lines and power supplies, anything that caused a disturbance for the occupying forces. Prior to D-Day 1944 the French Resistance executed a sabotage plan at the request of the British S.O.E.. The aim of the operation was to delay the transport of German troops and ammunition to the front, and in two days, 98 locomotives had been destroyed by the French Resistance.

card_event_sally.name: card_event_sally
card_event_sally.title: SALLY
card_event_sally.text: Target unit is pinned if a tank, suppressed if an infantry, destroyed if an artillery and retreats if an air unit.
card_event_sally.flavorText: During WWII, French aircraft played a limited but determined role in ground attack missions, particularly during the Battle of France in 1940. The most notable was the Bréguet Br.693, a twin-engine assault aircraft designed specifically for low-level attacks against enemy troops and armor. Entering service only shortly before the German invasion, around 200 units were built. Armed with machine guns, cannons and bombs, the Br.693 was used in desperate attempts to slow down the German advance. Despite their courage, crews faced intense anti-aircraft fire and high losses. Other aircraft, such as the Loire-Nieuport LN.411 and the Potez 633, also saw brief service in ground attack roles, though in smaller numbers. Many missions had to be improvised due to limited aircraft and poor coordination between air and ground forces. The French Air Forces also suffered from insufficient standardization and shortages of spare parts for their many different types of aircraft. After the armistice, a number of surviving planes were used by the Vichy regime or repurposed by Germany. Later in the war, Free French pilots flew Allied aircraft in North Africa and Europe.

card_event_sortie.name: card_event_sortie
card_event_sortie.title: SORTIE
card_event_sortie.text: Choose one - Give a friendly unit Mobilize OR add a FRAPPE to your hand.
card_event_sortie.flavorText: A sortie (French meaning “exit”) is an attack made from a strongpoint or a defensive position, and in military aviation, a sortie is a combat mission carried out by an individual aircraft, starting when it takes off. During WWII a couple of French heavy bomber squadrons were formed at RAF Elvington in England. Their names were 346 “Guyenne” Squadron and 347 “Tunisie” Squadron and they were the only French Air Force heavy bomber squadrons in operation during WWII. Around 2,300 French airmen and ground crew would eventually be part of these units. Throughout the war these units flew 2,834 sorties where they dropped 8,621 tons of bombs as well as ferrying 627,000 liters of petrol to the 2nd Army in Brussels.

card_event_test_resistance2.name: card_event_test_resistance2
card_event_test_resistance2.title: VIVE LA RESISTANCE!
card_event_test_resistance2.text: Add 2 RESISTANCE cards to the enemy deck. Draw a card.
card_event_test_resistance2.flavorText: The militant arm of the French resistance was called Maquis. These were rural guerilla groups that fought against the Nazi occupation of France and the Vichy government. At first the groups were scattered, but in 1943, a man named Jean Moulin managed to merge them into a single movement called Conseil National de la Resistance (CNR). After Jean Moulin was captured by the Gestapo and tortured to death Henri Giraud and Charles de Gaulle took over control of CNR. The CNR and other resistance groups worked closely with the Allies conducting sabotage, providing intelligence and performing armed resistance operations both before and after the Allied invasion in Normandy.

card_event_campaign_tunis1_french_reinfo.name: card_event_campaign_tunis1_french_reinforcement
card_event_campaign_tunis1_french_reinfo.title: FRENCH REINFORCEMENT
card_event_campaign_tunis1_french_reinfo.text: Add a 2e RMT to your hand with cost of 5.

card_event_campaign_tunis3_french_artill.name: card_event_campaign_tunis3_french_artillery
card_event_campaign_tunis3_french_artill.title: FRENCH ARTILLERY
card_event_campaign_tunis3_french_artill.text: Add a FRENCH 75 to your support line with Blitz.

card_event_fortified_position_cam1.name: card_event_fortified_position_cam1
card_event_fortified_position_cam1.title: FORTIFIED POSITION
card_event_fortified_position_cam1.text: Pin target unit. Increase its operation cost by +2.
