card_event_resistance_new.name: card_event_resistance_new
card_event_resistance_new.title: RESISTANCE
card_event_resistance_new.text: Play for free when drawn. Lose 1 kredit. Take 1 HQ damage. Pin a friendly unit. Draw a card.

card_unit_48e_regiment_cam1.name: card_unit_48e_regiment_cam1
card_unit_48e_regiment_cam1.title: 3e RÉGIMENT DE ZOUAVES
card_unit_48e_regiment_cam1.text: Has Guard when it doesn't have Mobilize.

card_unit_french_expedition_campaign.name: card_unit_french_expedition_campaign
card_unit_french_expedition_campaign.title: EXPEDITIONARY CORPS
card_unit_french_expedition_campaign.flavorText: The French Expeditionary Corps, also known as the French Expeditionary Corps in Italy, was a force of 112,000 Free French soldiers, 60% were Maghrebis (mostly Morroccan) and 40% Pied-Noirs (people of French and other European origin, born in Algeria under French rule). The corps fought with the U.S. Fifth Army in the Italian Campaign during WWII under the command of Général de Corps d'Armée Alphonse Juin. The FEC fought in the First Battle of Monte Cassino in January 1944. In May 1944 the FEC fought in the battle for the Gustav Line, which it managed to penetrate in less than two days of fighting and thrust forward in what is considered one of the most brilliant and daring advances of the war in Italy. After the Italian Campaign the soldiers were withdrawn to Africa where they joined France’s 1st Army which landed in southern France after Operation Dragoon.

card_unit_110e_regiment_motorize.name: card_unit_110e_regiment_motorize
card_unit_110e_regiment_motorize.title: 110e RÉGIMENT MOTORISÉ
card_unit_110e_regiment_motorize.text: Give your other units +1+1 the first time you shuffle your deck each turn.
card_unit_110e_regiment_motorize.flavorText: The 110th Motorized Infantry Regiment is a French Army unit established in 1792 during the Revolution. At the start of WWII, it was part of the 1st Motorized Infantry Division (1st DIM), attached to the 7th Army, and advanced into Belgium according to the Dyle plan, or plan D. Between May 11 and 15, 1940, the 110th Regiment took part in one of the rare French victories against the Wehrmacht during the Battle of France, repelling assaults by the 3rd Panzer Division near Gembloux, Belgium, despite lacking tanks and air support and suffering heavy casualties. Following the German breakthrough at Sedan further south, the 1st DIM was forced to retreat and became encircled in the Lille Pocket, where it fought fiercely until running out of ammunition, buying crucial time for the Allied evacuation at Dunkirk. After France’s surrender, soldiers from the 110th Regiment formed Resistance groups in Northern France. The regiment was first revived in October 1944 during the Siege of Dunkirk, then officially reestablished on January 1, 1945, to fight in Germany.

card_unit_13e_dragons.name: card_unit_13e_dragons
card_unit_13e_dragons.title: 13e DRAGONS
card_unit_13e_dragons.text: Cannot be deployed if you have deployed a unit this turn.
card_unit_13e_dragons.flavorText: The 13th Dragons Regiment is a unit of the French Army formed in 1791 during the French Revolution. Formerly a cavalry unit, it was transformed into an armored unit in 1936, during the mechanization of the French cavalry. Its motto is “Beyond what’s possible”. At the beginning of WWII, the 13e Dragons was equipped with Hotchkiss H35 and Somua S35 tanks, and was part of the 2nd Light Mechanized Division. They crossed the Belgian border on May 10th 1940 when the Dyle Plan was launched. Between 12 and 14 May, they fought the German XVI Motorized Corps at the Battle of Hannut, the largest tank battle in History at that time, where 400 French tanks faced 600 German tanks. The 13e Dragons kept fighting in Belgium and northern France during the second half of May. Surrounded at Dunkirk, they evacuated to England at the end of May, leaving their equipment behind. They quickly came back to France and reformed the 2nd Light Mechanized Division, charged with covering the retreat until the Armistice was signed on June 22nd, 1940. The 13e Dragons was disbanded in July, after suffering 90% casualties. It was reformed on 16 October 1944 at Orléans, and took part in the fighting against the remaining German pockets of resistance on the Atlantic coast. They notably participated in the liberation of Royan and Oléron, and the siege of La Rochelle. They were sent to Germany in May 1945, where they remained stationed until April 1946.

card_unit_152e_regiment.name: card_unit_152e_regiment
card_unit_152e_regiment.title: 152e RÉGIMENT
card_unit_152e_regiment.text: Cannot be deployed unless you have 6 or more kredit slots.
card_unit_152e_regiment.flavorText: The 152nd Infantry Regiment is a unit of the French Army formed in 1794 during the French Revolution. It is famous notably for having fought at the Battle of Hartmannswillerkopf in the Vosges mountains during WWI, where the Germans gave it the nickname “Teufels Regiment”, meaning Devil’s Regiment. It also bears the name “First of the French Regiments” for being the first recipient of the Légion d’Honneur decoration. It has been stationed in Colmar, Alsace, since 1919 and their motto is “Do not suffer”. During WWII, the regiment was first engaged in the Battle of France with the 14th Infantry Division, led by General de Lattre de Tassigny. The division fought in the Ardennes region, especially at Rethel, where it managed to halt the German advance on the river Aisne from May 14th to June 9th. After that, it retreated orderly towards central France, and kept resisting until the Armistice was signed on June 22nd. The 152nd Regiment was then part of the Armistice Army (Vichy France), but it was disbanded in 1942 when the German forces invaded the “Zone libre”, the unoccupied part of France. Many officers and soldiers joined the Resistance in the Auvergne region at that time, where they organized numerous sabotage operations between 1942 and 1944. During the campaign for the liberation of France, they joined the First Army, and took part in the offensive on the sector of Belfort and southern Alsace. On February 8th, 1945, six days after liberating Colmar, they were back in their old quarters. They also participated in the invasion of Germany, and they were the first to enter Stuttgart on April 21st. They ended the war near Lake Constance, in Radolfzell, where they remained in charge of occupation duties until April 1946.

card_unit_155_c_model_1917.name: card_unit_155_c_model_1917
card_unit_155_c_model_1917.title: 155 C MODÈLE 1917
card_unit_155_c_model_1917.text: Deployment: Get +2 attack for each friendly Mobilized unit.
card_unit_155_c_model_1917.flavorText: The Canon de 155 C model 1917 Schneider, often abbreviated as the C17S, was a French howitzer designed by Schneider and had a maximum firing range of 11.3 km. The gun was used during WWI and then widely exported after the war, which meant that many countries were using it at the start of WWII. In 1939, 2043 guns were still in service in France, but those that were captured by the Germans were designated as the 15.5 cm sFH 414(f).

card_unit_18e_regiment.name: card_unit_18e_regiment
card_unit_18e_regiment.title: 18e RÉGIMENT
card_unit_18e_regiment.text: On turn end, set operation cost to 0 if this was the only unit you deployed.
card_unit_18e_regiment.flavorText: The 18th Infantry Regiment is a unit of the French Army formed in 1791 during the French Revolution, from a French royal regiment dating back to 1587. It took part in the American Revolutionary War, notably in the decisive siege of Yorktown in 1781. It also participated in numerous battles during the Napoleonic Wars and it fought on all major French battlefields during World War I: the Marne, the Aisne River, the Somme and Verdun. When World War II broke out, the regiment, which was part of the 36th Infantry Division, was transferred to the Maginot Line, in the Moselle area. In September and October 1939, at the beginning of the “Phoney War”, it was involved in the Saar Offensive, a French military operation in German territory, launched in response to the German invasion of Poland. In May and June 1940, during the Battle of France, the Division fought in the French Ardennes at Attigny, repelling the German assaults for 25 days, despite being outnumbered and outgunned. The 18th Regiment lost a third of its men during those fierce combats, with 300 dead and 700 wounded. The regiment and several of its members were decorated for their bravery during this battle. After the Armistice, the 18th Regiment was reformed as part of the Armistice Army, but it was disbanded in November 1942 following Operation Anton, the German invasion of Vichy France. Many officers and soldiers of the 18th then joined the “maquis” (the underground) and formed the Pommiès Free Corps, leading resistance operations in all South-West of France as part of the Army Resistance Organization, until June 1944. They later took part in the general insurrection and the liberation of France with the French Forces of the Interior, until they were incorporated in the French Army in February 1945 after the liberation of Alsace, and named 49th Infantry Regiment. The 49th Regiment participated in the crossing of the Rhine and the capture of Stuttgart, where it ended the war.

card_unit_1er_bcp.name: card_unit_1er_bcp
card_unit_1er_bcp.title: 1er BCP
card_unit_1er_bcp.text: Draw a card when the enemy draws a RESISTANCE order.
card_unit_1er_bcp.flavorText: Created in 1840, the 1er Bataillon de Chasseurs à Pied (1er BCP) belonged to the French Army's 43rd Infantry division at the start of WWII. During the Battle of France, it fought in northern France at La Longueville and La Bassée, before falling back towards Dunkirk, from where it was evacuated during Operation Dynamo. It returned to France a few days later in an attempt to re-establish a front in Normandy, before being taken prisoner on the day of the armistice. Disbanded in November 1942, it was reformed a first time in September 1944 during the liberation of France, as part of the Swiss Groupe Mobile d'Alsace (GMA), with Alsatians who had refused forced conscription or deserted from the Wehrmacht, having taken refuge in Switzerland. It took part in the fighting to liberate southern Alsace, notably around Seppois-le-Bas where it repelled, alongside the 152e Régiment d’infanterie, a counter-attack by the Wehrmacht's 198th Infantry division on November 25th. In December, the Alsatians were released from their military obligations, but many members of the Swiss GMA enlisted in the new 31e BCP to continue the fight. The 1er BCP was reformed a second time on January 1st, 1945 and took part in the fighting in the Saint-Nazaire pocket, until the German capitulation.

card_unit_1er_hussards.name: card_unit_1er_hussards
card_unit_1er_hussards.title: 1er HUSSARDS
card_unit_1er_hussards.text: At the end of your turn, draw a card if the enemy has no units on the battlefield.
card_unit_1er_hussards.flavorText: The 1st Hussar Regiment was a cavalry unit of the French Army during WWII. It was established in 1791, during the Revolution, from a previous royal cavalry regiment dating back to 1719. The name Hussar comes from their function and uniform, both similar to Hungarian Huszárs which are units of light cavalry. In May 1940, as part of the 1st Light Cavalry Division, it was tasked with delaying the German advance in the Belgian Ardennes, and covering the following retreat of the Allied troops. During the Battle of Stonne (15-27 May 1940), 400 hussars of the 1st Regiment defended the village of Mont-Dieu and held back 5 German battalions for 3 days. They managed to withdraw safely, however the Wehrmacht launched an offensive on Tannay on May 23rd, defeated the 1st Hussar and captured the village. The regiment lost 190 men, killed, wounded or MIA, during the Battle of France. It was disbanded after the Armistice of June 22nd 1940, and refounded later by the Resistance in 1945, under the name Reconnaissance Regiment of the 25th Division. In 1946 it evolved into a paratrooper unit, still active to this day, named 1st Parachute Hussar Regiment.

card_unit_1er_marins_commandos.name: card_unit_1er_marins_commandos
card_unit_1er_marins_commandos.title: COMMANDOS KIEFFER
card_unit_1er_marins_commandos.text: Deal 1 damage to a random enemy when your HQ gains defense.
card_unit_1er_marins_commandos.flavorText: The 1er Bataillon de Fusiliers Marins Commandos, aka Commandos Kieffer, was a battalion sized commando unit that was formed in 1942 by the Free French Navy. The battalion was split into three troops, designated 1, 8 and 9. Members of Troop 1 took part in the Operation Jubilee, or the Dieppe Raid in 1942, and that same year they participated in a night raid on a bridge at Plouézec in France. In February 1944 they participated in the raid on the beach of Wassenaar in the Netherlands, which was the launch site of the German V-2 rockets. On 6 June 1944, D-Day, the battalion participated in the Normandy landings and disembarked on Sword Beach, and with No.4 Commando they supported the landings of the British 3rd Infantry Division. Despite heavy losses they managed to capture a 50 mm AT gun and a fortified artillery position. That same day the 1er Marins linked up with the British 6th Airborne Division at Pegasus Bridge (aka Bénouville Bridge) where more fighting took place. By the evening of 6 June the battalion had lost 25% of its men (27 KIA and many wounded), but they managed to hold their position. For the next couple of months Commandos Keiffer fought in Normandy, but in November 1944 they took part in the Allied landings on the island of Walcheren in the Netherlands where the city of Flessingue was captured. After WWII the unit was returned to French control and is still serving as part of the Naval Commandos of the French Navy.

card_unit_1er_regiment_etranger.name: card_unit_1er_regiment_etranger
card_unit_1er_regiment_etranger.title: 1er RÉGIMENT ÉTRANGER
card_unit_1er_regiment_etranger.text: Deployment: Choose One - Gain Blitz and draw a card OR gain Guard and your HQ gets +4 defense.
card_unit_1er_regiment_etranger.flavorText: The 1st Foreign Regiment was first formed in 1841 and it still exists although it only performs administrative duties today. In 1940 the regiment was sent to France and engaged the invading German forces in May 1940 at the Somme. After the Battle of France the 1st Foreign Regiment was on garrison duty in Tunisia, but in 1943 it was refitted with US weapons and armor and joined the Free French Foreign Legionnaires as part of the 5th Armored Division. The regiment engaged Axis forces in Tunisia in 1943 and in 1944 it landed in France and participated in the Liberation of France.

card_unit_1e_bfl.name: card_unit_1e_bfl
card_unit_1e_bfl.title: 1re BFL
card_unit_1e_bfl.text: Deployment: Deal damage to the enemy HQ equal to the number of non-French units you control.
card_unit_1e_bfl.flavorText: The 1re BFL was a brigade of the 1st Free French Division (French 1re Division Française Libre, 1re DFL) during WWII. Led by General Charles de Gaulle, the 1re Free French Division initially consisted of volunteers from various French colonies and territories, as well as French soldiers who had escaped from occupied France. The division saw action in several major campaigns and battles throughout the war and played a key role in liberating French territories in North Africa and later Europe. In the North African Campaign the division participated in the Battle of Bir Hakeim from 26 May – 11 June 1942, then in the Second Battle of El Alamein, and in both battles the 1re BFL distinguished itself. In 1943, the 1re Free French Division participated in the Italian campaign, fighting in battles such as the Battle of Monte Cassino. The division continued to engage in combat across Italy, contributing to the Allied advance and the liberation of Rome. During the invasion of France in 1944, the 1re Free French Division played a crucial role in the liberation of Paris. They were among the first units to enter the French capital, symbolizing the restoration of French sovereignty and the end of German occupation. The division went on to fight in other significant battles, including the Battle of Alsace and the Battle of Authion, as part of the Allied efforts on the Western Front. They also participated in the final offensive in Germany, contributing to the ultimate victory in Europe.

card_unit_27e_dia.name: card_unit_27e_dia
card_unit_27e_dia.title: 27e DIA
card_unit_27e_dia.text: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ when the enemy draws a RESISTANCE order.
card_unit_27e_dia.flavorText: When war was declared in 1939, the French Army's 27e Division d’Infanterie Alpine (27e DIA) was part of the 6th Army, tasked with defending the Alpine front. In early 1940, several of its battalions of Chasseurs Alpins, forming the 27e Demi-Brigade de Chasseurs Alpins, were assigned to the French Expeditionary Corps in Scandinavia. They took part in the Norwegian Campaign following the German invasion and notably participated in the Battle of Narvik, the first military victory of the Allied forces in WWII. After the start of the Battle of France, they re-embarked to fight on French soil. The remainder of the division was attached to the 7th Army Corps of the 8th Army, tasked with defending a sector of the Maginot Line in north-eastern France. It was engaged in violent fighting on Mont-de-Soissons on June 8th. Following the disbanding of the Armistice army in 1942, many mountain soldiers joined the resistance. During the Liberation, the 27e DIA was the first major unit reconstituted from the Maquis, in September 1944. It was first tasked with protecting the liberated valleys, and later took part in the offensive in the Alps from March 23rd to April 28th, 1945, pushing back the Germans who still held the passes and advancing into Italy.

card_unit_2e_brigade.name: card_unit_2e_brigade
card_unit_2e_brigade.title: 2e BRIGADE
card_unit_2e_brigade.text: At the start of your turn, give +1+1 if Mobilized.
card_unit_2e_brigade.flavorText: The 2nd Brigade was part of the 1st Free French Division during WWII and consisted of soldiers from mainland France and the French colonies. The division was formed in the summer of 1940 and was one of the first French units to rally to De Gaulle and Free French forces. The 2nd Brigade fought with the 1st Free French Division in numerous battles and campaigns throughout the war, both in North Africa and Europe, for which it became one of the most decorated French divisions of WWII.

card_unit_2e_rima.name: card_unit_2e_rima
card_unit_2e_rima.title: 2e RIMa
card_unit_2e_rima.text: At the end of your turn, give adjacent units Mobilize.
card_unit_2e_rima.flavorText: The 2nd Marine Infantry Regiment (French: 2e Régiment d'Infanterie de Marine or 2e RIMa) is a regiment of the Troupes de marine in the French Army which has been active from 1831 to the present day. During WWII, the regiment took part in the Battle of France and resisted the German invasion forces at Amiens, but was dissolved following the fall of France in 1940. The 2e RIMa was restored by the Free French Forces in 1941 and participated in the Battle of Keren during the East African Campaign, as part of the Free French Brigade of the Orient. In 1942 the regiment joined the 2nd Free French Brigade, which in 1943 became part of the 1st Free French Division (1re Division Française Libre or 1re DFL). They were involved in operations and campaigns in Libya and Tunisia, including the Battle of El Alamein and the Battle of Takrouna. The 1re DFL joined the Italian Campaign in April 1944 where it fought in the Battle of Pontecorvo, and landed in Provence during Operation Dragoon, which was the Allied landing in Southern France. Finally in 1945, as part of the French First Army, the division fought German forces in the Colmar Pocket and participated in the city’s liberation.

card_unit_2e_zouaves.name: card_unit_2e_zouaves
card_unit_2e_zouaves.title: 2e ZOUAVES
card_unit_2e_zouaves.text: Gets +2+2 if it is moved into the frontline.
card_unit_2e_zouaves.flavorText: The 2nd Zouaves Regiment is an infantry unit of the French Army created in 1852 in Algiers, under the Second Empire. It was decorated multiple times for its actions during the Crimean Campaign and the First World War. In September 1939, it was stationed in Oran and was sent to Lebanon, where it was disbanded in November 1940. Following the Allied landing in North Africa in November 1942, the zouaves corps was re-formed and became mixed to compensate for the lack of manpower, recruiting Muslim North African soldiers. The 2nd Zouaves Regiment joined the 1st Armored Division upon its creation on May 1, 1943, then it was transformed into 3 independent motorized battalions. Embarked in half-tracks and operating in close coordination with the division's tanks, they took part in the Provence landings and the liberation of France, advancing from the Mediterranean to the Vosges mountains. The 1st Armored Division reached Alsace first, where it saw intense fighting during a harsh winter from November 1944 to February 1945. It then entered Germany and was first again to reach the Danube, where it ended the war. During this campaign, the zouaves suffered heavy losses, with 72% of their troops killed or wounded. The 2nd Zouaves Regiment was awarded the Croix de Guerre for its bravery.

card_unit_31e_algiers.name: card_unit_31e_algiers
card_unit_31e_algiers.title: 31e ALGÉRIENS
card_unit_31e_algiers.flavorText: The 31st Regiment of Tirailleurs Algerians (31e RTA) was part of the 7th North African Infantry Division ( 7e DINA) of the French Army during WWII. The division was composed primarily of regiments from French North Africa, including Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco, except for the 97th Reconnaissance Group which was a motorized cavalry unit composed of members of the French Foreign Legion. The division saw action while trying to defend positions near the Somme in 1940, but suffered such heavy losses that it was disbanded shortly after. It is worth mentioning that during WWII, approximately 290,000 Algerian soldiers fought with the Allies in the French Expeditionary Corps between 1943 and 1945, participating in the Italian campaign of 1943 and the invasion of southern France in 1944.

card_unit_43e_regiment_motorise.name: card_unit_43e_regiment_motorise
card_unit_43e_regiment_motorise.title: 43e RÉGIMENT MOTORISÉ
card_unit_43e_regiment_motorise.text: When this unit loses Mobilize, fully repair your units.
card_unit_43e_regiment_motorise.flavorText: The 43rd Infantry Regiment was a unit of the French Army that was active from 1638 to 2010. It was originally created as the Régiment Royal des Vaisseaux, a regiment that was set to serve on ships and in the colonies, hence its name, meaning The Royal Regiment of Vessels. It was the first marine troops regiment in the French army. During WWI, the regiment fought relentlessly on all major battlefields (the Marne, the Somme, Verdun, etc.) for 4 years. In 1939 the regiment became part of the 1st Motorized Infantry Division and was redesignated as the 43rd Motorized Infantry Regiment, a unit comprising 3000 men. During the "Phoney war" it was stationed in Oise in Northern France, up until May 1940 when it was sent to Belgium where it participated in heavy fighting against the German forces. Despite fierce resistance the regiment experienced heavy casualties and was forced to retreat to Lille, and later to Dunkirk where they continued the fight but were ordered to lay down arms after losing 231 killed and 600 wounded. After the Armistice was signed, the regiment was redesignated 43rd Alpine Infantry Regiment and was stationed in Marseille and Digne, but in 1942 it was disbanded. In 1945 the regiment was restored and would later participate in the Indochina War (1947-1948) and the Algerian War (1956-1962). In 2010 the 43rd Infantry Regiment was disbanded.

card_unit_48e_regiment.name: card_unit_48e_regiment
card_unit_48e_regiment.title: 48e RÉGIMENT D'INFANTERIE
card_unit_48e_regiment.text: Has Guard when it doesn't have Mobilize.
card_unit_48e_regiment.flavorText: The 48th Infantry Regiment was part of the 21st Infantry Division of the Seventh French Army. When Germany invaded France the Seventh Army was under the command of General Henri Giraud. When combat commenced it became the 1st Army Group and was deployed to northern Belgium where it participated in heavy fighting against the German forces. The 1st Army Group retreated to France, where it again became the Seventh Army and continued the fighting until the armistice on June 25, 1940.

card_unit_4e_brigade.name: card_unit_4e_brigade
card_unit_4e_brigade.title: 4e BRIGADE
card_unit_4e_brigade.text: Deployment: Gets +1 attack for each non-French unit you control.
card_unit_4e_brigade.flavorText: The 4th Brigade was part of the 1st Free French Division, one of the principal units of the Free French Forces (FFL) during WW2. It was formed in London by men who decided to keep fighting after the fall of France, and it consisted of personnel from both France and its colonies. They were the first to join the FFL and participated in numerous battles and campaigns against the Axis forces in Africa, Middle East, Italy and France, and became the most decorated French division of WW2 alongside the 3rd Algerian Infantry Division. The division most notably distinguished itself during the Battle of Bir Hakeim which took place in an oasis in the Libyan desert south and west of Tobruk, between May 26 and June 11, 1942. During the battle, Général de brigade Marie-Pierre Kœnig and 3,700 his men defended the position against Panzerarmee Afrika commanded by General Erwin Rommel, a ten times larger force. The delay imposed on the Axis offensive by the defense of Bir Hakeim influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta, and allowed the British forces, to retreat, regroup and prepare for the following confrontation, the First Battle of Alamein, which would be a decisive victory for the Allies.  Later, in 1944, the 1st Free French Division was part of the Italian campaign and the Allied landing in Provence. They fought their way through German defenses on the French territory, until they reached Alsace and liberated Colmar. They ended the war crossing the Italian border in the Alps.

card_unit_51e_regiment.name: card_unit_51e_regiment
card_unit_51e_regiment.title: 51e RÉGIMENT
card_unit_51e_regiment.text: Deployment: Choose One - Gain +3 attack and Blitz OR gain +3 defense and Guard.
card_unit_51e_regiment.flavorText: The 51st Infantry Regiment is a unit of the French Army created in 1791, under the Revolution. It took part in several major battles against the enemies of France throughout History, notably during the Napoleonic Wars, the Crimean War, the Second French intervention in Mexico and the Great War. At the dawn of World War 2, the regiment was part of the 3rd Motorized Infantry Division and used as backup for the French Second Army, which was charged with preventing the Germans from outflanking the Maginot Line at the South of the Belgian border. During the German invasion, they participated in the Battle of Stonne, one of the largest fights in the Battle of France, sometimes referred to as “1940’s Verdun”. From May 15th to May 27th, 42,500 French soldiers and 130 French tanks, facing 90,000 German soldiers and 300 German tanks, fought violently in and around the village of Stonne, located on a crest dominating the German breakthrough’s spearhead at Sedan. The village changed hands 17 times in only 3 days. Largely outnumbered, and despite managing to inflict significant losses and to slow down the Germans, the French lost the battle and ultimately failed in their attempt to stop the enemy moving forward to the sea and cutting their forces in half. After the fall of France, the 51st Infantry Regiment became part of the Armistice Army (or Vichy French Army) until its dissolution in November 1942 when the German forces invaded the Free Zone and occupied all of France. The unit was reformed after the Allies landed in Provence, and was engaged in the Dunkirk Pocket, where 10,000 heavily equipped and determined German soldiers resisted from September 1944 to the German surrender in May 1945.

card_unit_5e_cuirassier.name: card_unit_5e_cuirassier
card_unit_5e_cuirassier.title: 5e CUIRASSIERS
card_unit_5e_cuirassier.text: Deployment: If this is the first unit you deploy this turn, add a 18e RÉGIMENT to hand.
card_unit_5e_cuirassier.flavorText: The 5th Cuirassiers Regiment is a cavalry unit of the French Army formed during the French Revolution from a French royal regiment dating back to 1653. It took part in the campaigns of the Kingdom of France, the Napoleonic Wars, the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and World War I. Its motto is “Nec pluribus impar” (meaning “unmatched” in Latin). At the beginning of World War II, it participated in the Battle of France. On May 10th, 1940, as part of the 2nd Light Cavalry Division, the 5th Cuirassiers fought the invading German troops at the Belgian border. They kept fighting in the French Ardennes after the German breakthrough at the Battle of Sedan. The division received the order to cease fire on June 12th after suffering heavy losses, and had to surrender to Erwin Rommel’s 7th Panzerdivision. On this occasion, Rommel paid homage to the French cavalry. After the end of WWII, the 5th Cuirassiers Regiment took part in the Indochina War as part of the French Far East Expeditionary Corps from 1946 to 1954. After being disbanded in 1992, it was reformed in June 2016.

card_unit_5r_chasseurs.name: card_unit_5r_chasseurs
card_unit_5r_chasseurs.title: 5e CHASSEURS
card_unit_5r_chasseurs.text: Deployment: Target unit moves into the frontline if possible.
card_unit_5r_chasseurs.flavorText: The 5th Foot Rifle Battalion is a unit of the French Army created in 1840. They became famous for participating in some of the harshest battles which took place during the early years of the Great War, in the Vosges mountains, notably on the Linge battlefield in 1915. It was renamed 5th Motorized Rifle Battalion in 1937 and became part of the 1st Armored Division when it was created in January 1940, joining 4 tanks battalions and one artillery regiment. This was the largest and most powerful unit in the French Army when the war broke out, but it lacked training, having only recently been formed. During the Battle of France, the Division first joined the French 9th Army in Belgium in May 1940, facing the 7. and 9. Panzerdivision. They suffered heavy casualties and had to be reformed at the end of the month. They kept fighting after the Germans invaded France, but ultimately faced the same difficulties plaguing the whole French Army at the time: late orders, poor fuel supply, lack of anti-aircraft support and communication issues. It was disbanded after the fall of France in June 1940. In 1945, during the liberation of France, around 200 members of the maquis reformed the unit within the French Forces of the Interior. They participated in the liberation of Vieux-Thann in Alsace, and then moved to Redon, Brittany, to take part in the siege of the Saint-Nazaire pocket, where 30,000 Germans soldiers resisted until May 1945.

card_unit_73e_regiment_infanterie.name: card_unit_73e_regiment_infanterie
card_unit_73e_regiment_infanterie.title: 73e RÉGIMENT D'INFANTERIE
card_unit_73e_regiment_infanterie.text: Gets +1+1 when your HQ gains defense.
card_unit_73e_regiment_infanterie.flavorText: The 73rd Infantry Regiment of the French Army was raised in 1673 and has fought in numerous conflicts, including WWI. During WWII the regiment was attached to the 2nd Infantry Division, the oldest division in the French Army, which joined the French Colonial Army Corps in May 1940 and fought with the 4rd French Army in the Battle of France.

card_unit_8e_tirailleurs_marocains.name: card_unit_8e_tirailleurs_marocains
card_unit_8e_tirailleurs_marocains.title: 8e MAROCAINS
card_unit_8e_tirailleurs_marocains.text: When you deploy another unit, your HQ gains defense equal to its operation cost.
card_unit_8e_tirailleurs_marocains.flavorText: The 8th Regiment of Moroccan Tirailleurs was part of the 2nd Moroccan Division (French: 2e Division d'Infanterie Marocaine, 2e DIM), formed in 1943 after the Allied liberation of French North Africa, and part of the Army of Africa (French: Armée d'Afrique). It was the first French division to land in Italy, where it fought in the Monte Cassino campaign. The unit participated in several key battles, including San Michele de Pantano, Mainarde, and Monte Croce. On May 11th, 1944, the division captured Monte Majo in the Battle of Garigliano, and later marched through Rome on June 15th. The division then advanced to Siena and Florence. Though it missed the initial invasion of Southern France, it arrived in late August 1944, liberating Briançon and Modane. It broke through German defenses at the Belfort Gap, captured several towns, and entered Belfort. After reaching the Doller and Thur Valleys, it helped eliminate the Colmar Pocket, crossed the Rhine in March 1945, and continued into Germany, entering Karlsruhe, Pforzheim, and later Austria. The 2nd Moroccan Division was deactivated in August 1945 after being decorated numerous times for its actions during the war.

card_unit_bloch_mb_150.name: card_unit_bloch_mb_150
card_unit_bloch_mb_150.title: BLOCH MB.152
card_unit_bloch_mb_150.text: Deployment: If this is the first unit you deploy this turn, draw a card.
card_unit_bloch_mb_150.flavorText: The Bloch MB.151 was a French all metal fighter aircraft used during WWII by the French Air Force and later the Axis. The first variant, MB.150 made its first flight in 1937 and after a series of service trials and modifications, 25 aircraft were ordered. However, none of them were delivered due to many technical problems with the design. The aircraft was redesigned which led to the parallel design and production of the MB.151.01 and MB.152.01 variants. By the outbreak of WWII 120 of the new variants had been delivered to the French Air Force. However, most of them were non-operational as they were either missing a propeller or gunsight, or both. When the Germans attacked in May 1940, eight pursuit groups of the French Air Force were equipped with Bloch 151 or 152 fighters, and although the aircraft was sturdy and could withstand heavy punishment it was no match to the Messerschmitt Bf 109E and the Bf 110 and the Bloch groups suffered heavy losses. Following the Armistice in 1940 further variants of Bloch were produced by the Axis powers and were used in the service of the Vichy French Air Force, Luftwaffe and the Royal Romanian Air force. A total of 663 Bloch aircraft were produced throughout the war.

card_unit_b_26_bretagne.name: card_unit_b_26_bretagne
card_unit_b_26_bretagne.title: B-26 GROUPE BRETAGNE
card_unit_b_26_bretagne.text: The first order you give each turn deals damage equal to its cost to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_b_26_bretagne.flavorText: The Martin B-26 Marauder was an American medium bomber used by the Free French Air Force and the Allied air forces during WWII. During Operation Torch, the Allied invasion of North Africa in 1942, three squadrons of the Free French Air Force were equipped with Marauders for medium-bombing operations in Italy and the Allied invasion of France. During the last phase of the war seven of the nine French Groupes de Bombardement used B-26’s for their bombing missions.

card_unit_char_b1_bis.name: card_unit_char_b1_bis
card_unit_char_b1_bis.title: CHAR B1 bis
card_unit_char_b1_bis.text: Deployment: Gets Blitz if this is the first unit you deploy this turn.
card_unit_char_b1_bis.flavorText: The Char B1 bis was a French heavy tank manufactured by Renault. The Char B1 was first manufactured in 1935, but from 1937 to 1940 the Char B1 bis version was manufactured. The tank had a crew of 4, a main armament of 47 mm SA 35 gun and a secondary armament of 2 x 7.5 mm Reibel machine guns. The tank was placed in use by the French forces from 1936-1940, and then again by the Free French Forces from 1944-1945. A total of 774 units were built, including variants.

card_unit_dewoitine_520.name: card_unit_dewoitine_520
card_unit_dewoitine_520.title: DEWOITINE D.520
card_unit_dewoitine_520.flavorText: The Dewoitine D.520 was a French fighter aircraft that came into service in 1940 and was used by the French Air Force during WWII. The D.520 was a modern aircraft for its time, it had good firepower and a powerful engine, and was close to being a match to the German Messerschmitt BF 109. However, the D.520 did not have a real impact since production had just started in 1940 and only 79 were in service when the Battle of France began. Following the fall of France in 1940 the D.520 continued to be used, both by the Free French and the Vichy Air Force. The aircraft was retired in 1953 and by then 900 units had been built.

card_unit_farman_222.name: card_unit_farman_222
card_unit_farman_222.title: FARMAN F.222
card_unit_farman_222.text: When this unit deals damage to the enemy HQ, draw a card.
card_unit_farman_222.flavorText: The Farman F.222 was a French twin-engine bomber aircraft that was produced from 1935-1938 and used to some extent by both the Free French and the Vichy Regime during WWII. By the outbreak of WWII the Farman bomber was already outdated, it was slow, with poor maneuverability and only one 7,5 mm gun, but it had an extra long range which would become very useful in one of its most famous missions. On June 7, 1940, a single and unescorted French Navy Farman F.222 bomber variant, named "Jules Verne," attacked Berlin on a night raid, and this was the first aerial attack on Berlin in WWII, and in history. To avoid detection during the raid, the French bomber flew a simulated landing approach to Tempelhof airport before releasing its bombs on the Siemens factory and other targets, causing only minimal damage. The aircraft had racks for the demolition bombs but none for the incendiaries, so the crew simply opened the passenger door and tossed them out by hand. The raid triggered German air defenses, but despite that the crew managed to fly the aircraft back to safety to France, and 3 days later the raid was repeated. These raids were not widely reported, possibly due to embarrassment among German leaders, and were largely overshadowed by the imminent threat posed from the German forces that were rapidly advancing through France and the Low Countries. After the night raids on Berlin the Farman bombers were transferred to North Africa where they were mainly used in transporting roles both by the Free French and the Vichy Regime.

card_unit_french_75.name: card_unit_french_75
card_unit_french_75.title: FRENCH 75
card_unit_french_75.text: The first unit you deploy each turn gets +1+1.
card_unit_french_75.flavorText: The French 75 mm field gun was a quick-firing field artillery, produced from 1897 to 1940. Officially the gun was called Matériel de 75mm Mle 1897, but commonly known as the French 75, simply the 75 and Soixante-Quinze (French for "seventy-five"). The gun was designed as an anti-personnel weapon, delivering large volumes of time-fused shrapnel shells on enemy targets. Large numbers of 75’s were still in use in 1939, 4,500 of them in France alone. Many of the guns were captured by the Germans who used a modified anti-tank version named 7.5 cm Pak 97/38, which was mainly used in 1942 against the Soviet T-34 and KV tanks.

card_unit_french_expedition.name: card_unit_french_expedition
card_unit_french_expedition.title: EXPEDITIONARY CORPS
card_unit_french_expedition.text: Deployment: Add a RESISTANCE card to the enemy deck.
card_unit_french_expedition.flavorText: The French Expeditionary Corps, also known as the French Expeditionary Corps in Italy, was a force of 112,000 Free French soldiers, 60% were Maghrebis (mostly Morroccan) and 40% Pied-Noirs (people of French and other European origin, born in Algeria under French rule). The corps fought with the U.S. Fifth Army in the Italian Campaign during WWII under the command of Général de Corps d'Armée Alphonse Juin. The FEC fought in the First Battle of Monte Cassino in January 1944. In May 1944 the FEC fought in the battle for the Gustav Line, which it managed to penetrate in less than two days of fighting and thrust forward in what is considered one of the most brilliant and daring advances of the war in Italy. After the Italian Campaign the soldiers were withdrawn to Africa where they joined France’s 1st Army which landed in southern France after Operation Dragoon.

card_unit_french_p_36.name: card_unit_french_p_36
card_unit_french_p_36.title: H75-C1
card_unit_french_p_36.text: Deployment: Give a friendly unit Mobilize.
card_unit_french_p_36.flavorText: The Curtiss P-36 Hawk, also known as the Curtiss Hawk Model 75, was an American fighter aircraft used by the Allied air forces during WWII. The French designated the aircraft as Curtiss H75-C1, leaving Hawk out of the name, and 316 were delivered to France before the German occupation. The French Air Force utilized the H75-C1 very successfully during the Battle of France. Only 12.6% of the French air force was made up of H75’s, but still the aircraft was responsible for a third of all their air victories. Most of the French H75 equipped squadrons were evacuated to North Africa before the armistice to avoid them from being captured by the Germans, but there they were used by the Vichy Government against the British during the Battle of Mers El-Kebir and the Battle of Dakar.

card_unit_hotchkiss_35.name: card_unit_hotchkiss_35
card_unit_hotchkiss_35.title: HOTCHKISS H35
card_unit_hotchkiss_35.text: Gets +1 attack when you deploy a non-French unit.
card_unit_hotchkiss_35.flavorText: The Hotchkiss H35 (French: Char Léger model 1935 H) was a French light Cavalry tank in French service from 1936 to 1940. The H35 had a crew of 2, a main armament of a 37 mm SA 18 gun and a secondary armament of a 7.5 mm MAC31 Reibel machine gun. After the fall of France in 1940, production was halted, and by then 1200 Hotchkiss tanks had been produced. For the rest of WWII, the Axis powers used captured Hotchkiss H35s and made several modifications to them.

card_unit_ii_rmt.name: card_unit_ii_rmt
card_unit_ii_rmt.title: 2e RMT
card_unit_ii_rmt.text: At the start of your turn, each non-French unit you control gets +1+1.
card_unit_ii_rmt.flavorText: The 2e RMT, or Régiment de marche du Tchad, was a mechanized unit of the French Army who joined the WWII Allies in their fight against the Axis forces in North Africa. The regiment had approximately 1,200 personnel and was organized into 9 companies during the war. The regiment fought in several campaigns in North Africa and Europe, and continued to fight until Germany surrendered in 1945. The RMT participated in the Liberation of Paris and was the first Allied unit to reach Hitler’s Eagle Nest in the German Alps. The regiment received several decorations after the war for its exemplary performance.

card_unit_la_division_leclerc.name: card_unit_la_division_leclerc
card_unit_la_division_leclerc.title: LA DIVISION LECLERC
card_unit_la_division_leclerc.text: Gets +3+3 the first time you shuffle your deck each turn.
card_unit_la_division_leclerc.flavorText: La Division Leclerc refers to the troops of the Free French Forces regrouped under the command of General Leclerc. It was initially named Leclerc Column, and won its first victory against the Italians at the Battle of Kufra, Libya, in February 1941. At the end of the battle, the French made the “Oath of Kufra”, swearing to “not lay down our arms until our colors, our beautiful colors, fly over Strasbourg Cathedral." The Column distinguished itself in Libya and during the Tunisian campaign in 1942 and 1943, and was expanded and transformed into the 2nd Armored Division (French: 2e Division Blindée, or 2e DB) in August 1943, and equipped with modern American military equipment. They fought in the Battle of Normandy from August 1944, and they were the first Allied unit to enter Paris, on August 24. Then they took part in fierce fighting in Lorraine and Alsace, and liberated Strasbourg on 23 November 1944, fulfilling their oath. The Division Leclerc pushed the offensive into Germany and ended the war at the “Eagle’s Nest”, at Berchtesgaden in the Bavarian Alps.

card_unit_ms_460.name: card_unit_ms_460
card_unit_ms_460.title: M.S.406
card_unit_ms_460.flavorText: The M.S.406 was a French fighter aircraft developed by Morane-Saulnier in 1938. At the start of WWII over 1,000 M.S.406s were in French service, which made it France’s most numerous fighter and one of two French fighters capable of 400 km/h. During the Battle for France the aircraft provided mixed results. The aircraft was highly maneuverable, but there were technical setbacks and it had very low firepower. In some cases the M.S.406 was effective, even against the German BF 109, but overall the losses were high (approx. 150 aircraft were lost in combat), and the aircraft is considered to be the least effective French fighter in service during the Battle of France. Many M.S.406s were captured by the Germans after the fall of France, some were used for training purposes while others were sold.

card_unit_potez_63_11.name: card_unit_potez_63_11
card_unit_potez_63_11.title: POTEZ 63.11
card_unit_potez_63_11.text: When you add or deploy a unit with Mobilize, draw a card and your HQ gains +2 defense.
card_unit_potez_63_11.flavorText: The Potez 63.11 was a variant of the Potez 630 aircraft, a heavy fighter developed for the French Air Force in the 1930s and used in WWII, both by the Vichy French Air Force and Free French Air Forces. The 63.11 was the most numerous variant, with 730 units being manufactured. The 63.11 didn’t have the same speed and maneuverability as previous variants which made it vulnerable in the air. It was designed with a light bomber capability and came with a small bomb bay which could carry 8 x 10kg bombs and 2 x 50kg bombs could be carried under the wings. It was armed with 3 x MAC 1934s under the nose and some had additional guns in the wing gondolas.

card_unit_somoa_s35.name: card_unit_somoa_s35
card_unit_somoa_s35.title: SOMUA S35
card_unit_somoa_s35.text: The first unit you deploy each turn gets +1+1 and -1 operation cost.
card_unit_somoa_s35.flavorText: The SOMUA S35 was a French cavalry tank which was used at the beginning of World War II in the Battle of France, and later as a salvaged vehicle in the German and Italian armies, and the Free French Forces during the liberation. In 1940, it was considered the best French tank available, alongside the B1 Bis heavy tank, and it was in service in the French Light Mechanized Divisions. The French cavalry tanks aimed at offering a good compromise between firepower, protection and mobility, to fit the needs of modern cavalry on the battlefield. They were to be used in both anti-personnel and anti-tank roles. Thanks to its speed, its solid armor and its efficient cannon for that time, the SOMUA S35 proved to be a valuable asset on battlefields such as Hannut in Belgium, the first large tank battle of World War II. The thickness and inclination of its armor offered solid protection against shells from Panzer III and Panzer IV tanks, while its own 47mm cannon could in theory pierce their armor. It was also armed with a 7.5mm coaxial machine gun, and was manned by three crew members. However, it suffered from low visibility and the lack of a radio in each vehicle (only the platoon leader had one). And its worst flaw, like many other French tanks, was its “one-man turret” design. The tank commander had to man the gun and reload it, on top of fulfilling its own role (target acquisition, giving instructions, etc.) which seriously hindered the tank’s rate of fire and general efficiency. Nonetheless, the SOMUA S35 allowed the French Light Mechanized Divisions to accomplish their mission and to delay the German advance in May 1940. 430 were built between 1936 and 1940.

card_event_joint_operation.name: card_event_joint_operation
card_event_joint_operation.title: JOINT OPERATION
card_event_joint_operation.text: Deal damage to target unit equal to 1 plus the number of unit types you control.
card_event_joint_operation.flavorText: German military tactics during WWII focused on combined arms in their operations and played a fundamental part in their Blitzkrieg doctrine. Their tactics were highly dependent on radio communications that were used to coordinate their combined air-ground attacks. The Blitzkrieg doctrine proved less successful against the Soviet defenses, and by 1943 Germany was forced into a defensive war on all fronts.

card_event_kriegsmarine.name: card_event_kriegsmarine
card_event_kriegsmarine.title: KRIEGSMARINE
card_event_kriegsmarine.text: Deal damage to enemy HQ equal to cards in enemy hand, then enemy discards a card.
card_event_kriegsmarine.flavorText: The Kriegsmarine was the German navy from 1935 to 1945. After WWII the remaining ships of the Kriegsmarine were divided between the Allied powers and used for various purposes. In 1956 West Germany established a navy called Bundesmarine (e. Federal Navy) and East Germany had its navy called Volksmarine (e. People's Navy). After the reunification of Germany in 1990 it was decided to use the name Deutsche Marine (German Navy).

card_event_lurking_danger.name: card_event_lurking_danger
card_event_lurking_danger.title: LURKING DANGER
card_event_lurking_danger.text: Draw two random countermeasures from your deck.
card_event_lurking_danger.flavorText: Early in the war commanders of the Kriegsmarine believed that an effective submarine warfare strategy could bring Britain to its knees. A tactic called Rudeltaktik was implemented (also known as “wolfpack”) where submarines would spread across a projected course of a convoy and attack them “en masse” when sighted. This tactic changed how submarines were used in warfare, but prior to WWII they had been seen as lone ambushers, or as fleet attachments and to be used as destroyers. Most navy commander also thought that submarine warfare was dishonorable compared to other types of fleet engagements. Nevertheless, the Rudeltaktik proved successful early in the war and German U-boat commanders were seen as heroes in Germany, but nevertheless they failed to stop supplies from reaching the Allies and to knock Britain out of the war. Some historians believe that the German U-boat arm was close to win the Battle of the Atlantic, while others believe that they were far from it.

card_event_retaliation.name: card_event_retaliation
card_event_retaliation.title: RETALIATION
card_event_retaliation.text: After your HQ receives damage, deal equal damage to the enemy HQ.
card_event_retaliation.flavorText: During WWII combat operations sometimes lacked military or tactical importance but were executed anyway out of vengeance.  Operation Steinbock was a strategic bombing campaign conducted by the Luftwaffe in 1941 and lasted from January to May 1944. The campaign is sometimes referred to as the Baby Blitz as it was performed on a much smaller scale than the Blitz campaign against the UK in 1940-41. The campaign became the last strategic air offensive of the Luftwaffe, and even though they lacked resources, they wanted to conduct revenge for the Allied bombing of German cities, and while doing such, attempt to disrupt Allied preparations for the invasion of France. The campaign had very little effect, and instead the Luftwaffe suffered heavy losses and had very little offensive power remaining when the Allied invasion began in June 1944.

card_event_rush_production.name: card_event_rush_production
card_event_rush_production.title: RUSH PRODUCTION
card_event_rush_production.text: When you deploy a German unit this turn, it gets +2-1.
card_event_rush_production.flavorText: As the situation worsened for Germany in WWII, new weapon designs were often rushed into production which often led to poor and disappointing results on the battlefield. There were a few examples of successful new weapons that were rushed to production, such as the V-2 rocket, the StG 44 assault rifle and the jet aircraft, but they came too late to have a decisive impact. An example of a failed new “superweapon” that was rushed to production was the Panzer VIII Maus, a 188 tonne steel monster with a top speed of 3 km/h. It was considered to be a useless mountain of steel that drained material and resources that could be used to produce many working tanks.

card_event_spoils_of_war.name: card_event_spoils_of_war
card_event_spoils_of_war.title: SPOILS OF WAR
card_event_spoils_of_war.text: Choose and draw a card from the top 3 of your deck, put rest on bottom of deck.
card_event_spoils_of_war.flavorText: During WWII the Nazi party and military units known as the Kunstschutz (e. art protection) conducted systematic plundering of valuables from minorities they suppressed and every territory they occupied. Everything of value was taken, from gold, silver and currency, to art or cultural and religious objects. Even today, Nazi plunder is identified and returned to the rightful owners, but there is still much unaccounted for.

card_event_stranglehold.name: card_event_stranglehold
card_event_stranglehold.title: STRANGLEHOLD
card_event_stranglehold.text: When a unit is deployed, the enemy loses remaining kredits.
card_event_stranglehold.flavorText: What started as an Allied blockade of Germany, and a subsequent German counter-blockade of Allied shipping routes, came to be the longest campaign of WWII, the Battle of the Atlantic. During this time the German Kriegsmarine avoided large fleet engagements and instead they used their large fleet of submarines, and small groups of cruisers and battleships, to disrupt the logistics of the enemy by attacking Allied merchant ships. The Battle of the Atlantic ended with an Allied victory, but at a great cost. From 1939 until the war ended in 1945, the Allies lost 3,500 merchant ships and 175 warships while Germany lost 783 U-boats and 47 warships.

card_event_suppression_fire.name: card_event_suppression_fire
card_event_suppression_fire.title: SUPPRESSION
card_event_suppression_fire.text: Suppress target unit. Draw a card if you have an air unit.
card_event_suppression_fire.flavorText: Suppression fire, more commonly called covering fire, is a military tactic where the enemy positions are fired upon in order to suppress or prevent the enemy forces from performing their mission, whether it’s defending or attacking a position.

card_event_u_99.name: card_event_u_99
card_event_u_99.title: U-48
card_event_u_99.text: The enemy cannot deploy units next turn.
card_event_u_99.flavorText: U-48 was a German Type VIIB U-boat submarine that was in service of the Kriegsmarine during WWII. The U-48 was launched in 1939 and when the war started it was positioned in the North Atlantic where it immediately started to operate against Allied shipping. The U-48 participated in numerous operations and her crew managed to sink a total of 55 Allied before being withdrawn from frontline service in 1943. In May 1945 the remaining crew scuttled her in the Bay of Lübeck in order to prevent her from being captured by the Allies.

card_unit_141_gebirgsjager.name: card_unit_141_gebirgsjager
card_unit_141_gebirgsjager.title: 141. GEBIRGSJÄGER
card_unit_141_gebirgsjager.text: Cannot be targeted by enemy orders.
card_unit_141_gebirgsjager.flavorText: The 141st Gebergjäger Regiment (e. 141st Mountaineer Regiment) was part of the 6. Gebirgs Division (e. 6th Mountain Division) of the Wehrmacht during WWII. In 1940 the division was deployed in France, and later Poland for occupation duties. In 1941 the division participated in Operation Marita, which was the invasion of Greece, and that same year it was relocated to Lapland (northern Finland). In 1942 the 6. Gebirgs Division became part of the 20th Mountain Army that operated along the Arctic coast. In 1944 the division withdrew into Norway where it surrendered to the British at the end of the war in 1945.

card_unit_25_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_25_panzergrenadier
card_unit_25_panzergrenadier.title: 25. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_25_panzergrenadier.text: Gets Guard when it moves into the frontline.
card_unit_25_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 25th Panzergrenadier Regiment was originally part of the 2nd Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht that participated in the invasion of Poland and France. The division was reorganized as a panzer division in 1940 and renamed to 12th Panzer Division. In 1941 the division participated in Operation Barbarossa and fought in several battles and campaigns on the Eastern Front. The division participated in the Siege of Leningrad, the Battle of Kursk and finally it surrendered to the Red Army in the Courland Pocket in 1945.

card_unit_adler_command_vehicle.name: card_unit_adler_command_vehicle
card_unit_adler_command_vehicle.title: GREIF
card_unit_adler_command_vehicle.text: Your other tanks operate for 1 less.
card_unit_adler_command_vehicle.flavorText: The Sd.Kfz. 250 was a light armored half track used by the Wehrmacht during WWII. The most common version of the vehicle was used as a basic troop carrier, but the 250/3 and 250/5 were command variants that had fewer seats and were equipped with long-range radios. Rommel used a couple of custom made 250/3 variants in the North Africa campaign called “GREIF” and ADLER”.

card_unit_flammpanzer.name: card_unit_flammpanzer
card_unit_flammpanzer.title: FLAMMPANZER
card_unit_flammpanzer.text: Deployment: Destroy target enemy unit with cost 1 or less.
card_unit_flammpanzer.flavorText: The German Pz.Kpfw III (fl), or Flammpanzer III, was a Panzer III medium tank variant with a mounted 14mm flamethrower nozzle. In order to disguise the tank’s role it had a fake barrel installed that was 1.5 meters long. The tank could carry 1020 liters of flammable liquid and the flame gun, which was fired via a foot pedal, had a range of up to 60 meters. In order to protect the tank and the flammable liquids inside it had 20 mm of extra armor and additionally it had a 30 mm plate added to the upper and lower hull front. For protection the tank also carried 5 fire extinguishers, 3 on the inside and 2 on the tank’s exterior. The Flammpanzer III first saw action in 1943 and was used on the Eastern Front and in the Italian Campaign. A total of 100 Flammpanzer IIIs were produced.

card_unit_heinkel_he_219.name: card_unit_heinkel_he_219
card_unit_heinkel_he_219.title: HEINKEL HE 219
card_unit_heinkel_he_219.flavorText: The Heinkel He 219 Uhu (e. Eagle Owl) was a German night fighter in service during WWII. The He 219 was introduced in 1943 and the design was advanced for its time, equipped with an airborne Lichtenstein intercept radar and the first aircraft that had an ejection seat installed. The He 219 could obtain the speed of 580 km/h which made it capable of hunting down several enemy bombers in a single sortie. Some aircraft had their excess weight removed which allowed it to obtain a speed of 650 km/h. The He 219 was a very capable night fighter, but did not play a significant role in the war since only a limited number of aircraft were built (approx. 300) and they saw limited service.

card_unit_henschel_hs_126.name: card_unit_henschel_hs_126
card_unit_henschel_hs_126.title: HENSCHEL HS 126
card_unit_henschel_hs_126.text: Deployment: Give a friendly tank +1+1 for each non-tank unit type in the same line.
card_unit_henschel_hs_126.flavorText: The Henschel Hs 126 was a German reconnaissance aircraft, used during WWII by the Luftwaffe and the Axis allies. The aircraft was two seated and carried a pilot seated in the front of the cockpit and a gunner in the rear. The Hs 126 first entered service in 1938 and it was used early in the war by the Luftwaffe, but by then it was superseded by more advanced reconnaissance aircraft and was mainly retired from front line services in 1942. Later in the war the aircraft was used in night ground attacks and for glider towing. In 1943 ten Henschel Hs 126’s were used to tow DFS 230 attack gliders on a raid to rescue the imprisoned Benito Mussolini.

card_unit_hummel.name: card_unit_hummel
card_unit_hummel.title: HUMMEL
card_unit_hummel.text: Deployment: If you control a tank, target enemy unit must retreat.
card_unit_hummel.flavorText: The Hummel (e. Bumblebee), full name “Panzerfeldhaubitze 18M auf Geschützwagen III/IV (Sf) Hummel, Sd.Kfz. 165”,  was a German self propelled gun use by the Wehrmacht during WWII. The Hummel was based on the chassis of Geschützwagen III/IV, manned by a crew of 6 (a driver and 5 man gun crew), and featured a main armament of a 15 cm sFH 18/1 L/30 howitzer gun and a secondary armament of a 7.92 mm Maschinengewehr 34. The Hummel was introduced in 1943 and was first used in large scale combat in the Battle of Kursk where 100 served in the artillery battalions of the Panzer divisions. Because the Hummel could carry a limited amount of ammunition, special Hummel Ammunition Carriers (Munitionsträger Hummel) were developed. Basically this was a Hummel without the 15 cm howitzer, and it could be fitted with the gun when necessary. A total of 714 Hummels were manufactured, plus 150 Hummel ammunition carriers.

card_unit_ju_87_b2.name: card_unit_ju_87_b2
card_unit_ju_87_b2.title: Ju 87 B2
card_unit_ju_87_b2.text: Deployment: Add a DIVE BOMBING to your hand.
card_unit_ju_87_b2.flavorText: The Junkers Ju 87 B2, most commonly known as Stuka, was a German dive bomber used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. The B series became the first mass produced variant, and after testing in Spain some 336 aircraft were ready for operations at the start of WWII. The variant came with general improvements, a redesigned fuselage and landing gear and the later B1 version was the first version with the "Jericho Trumpets" installed, named for its signature sound. Other changes from B1 to B2 were not significant, except that the B2 had various ski equipped versions produced and others with a tropical operation kit called the Ju 87 B-2 trop.

card_unit_panther_a.name: card_unit_panther_a
card_unit_panther_a.title: PANTHER A
card_unit_panther_a.text: When this unit moves into the frontline, the enemy does not draw a card next turn.
card_unit_panther_a.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen V Panther was a German medium tank that was used by the Wehrmacht during WWII. The tank came into service in 1943 and the Panther A variant was the second in line with 2,200 tanks produced between September 1943 and August 1944. This variant included an improved turret, with increased turret traverse speed, and a new commander cupola. Like its predecessors the Panther A had a crew of 5 (driver, radio-operator/hull machine gunner, commander, gunner, loader), a main armament of a 7.5 cm KwK 42 L/70 and a secondary armament of 2 x 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns.

card_unit_panzer_iii_h.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_h
card_unit_panzer_iii_h.title: PANZER III-H
card_unit_panzer_iii_h.text: Deployment: Choose and draw a card from the top 3 of your deck, put rest on bottom.
card_unit_panzer_iii_h.flavorText: The Panzer III-H was a German medium tank in service during WWII and one of many variants in the Panzerkampfwagen III series, a German light tank that was used by the Axis from 1939 to 1945. The Panzer III-H came into service in 1941, it was manned by a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/machine gunner), a main armament of a 5 cm KwK 38 L/42 and a secondary armament of 2-3 x  7.92 mm machine guns. A total of 5,774 Panzer III tanks were built from 1939 to 1943, with approximately 286 of them being of the H variant.

card_unit_panzer_ii_c.name: card_unit_panzer_ii_c
card_unit_panzer_ii_c.title: PANZER II-C
card_unit_panzer_ii_c.text: Your units get +2+1 when they become Veteran.
card_unit_panzer_ii_c.flavorText: The Panzer II-C was a variant in the Panzerkampfwagen II series (abbreviation PzKpfw II), a German light tank that was used by the Axis from 1937 to 1945. The tank had a crew of 3 (commander/gunner, driver and loader), a main armament of 1 x 2 cm KwK 30 L/55 and a secondary armament of 1 x 7.92 mm Maschinengewehr 34 (e. machine gun 34). A total of 1,113 units were built of the Panzer II A, B and C series  from 1937 to 1940. By the end of 1942 the Panzer II was primarily removed from front line services, however the turrets from Panzer I and IIs were reused for defensive purposes in bunkers, particularly in the Atlantic Wall.

card_unit_stug_iii_g.name: card_unit_stug_iii_g
card_unit_stug_iii_g.title: STUG III-G
card_unit_stug_iii_g.text: Damage from this unit ignores Heavy Armor.
card_unit_stug_iii_g.flavorText: The StuG III Ausf G, full name Sturmgeschütz III Ausführung G, was a German self propelled assault gun in service from 1940 to 1945, and Germany’s second most produced armored combat vehicle during WWII. The Stug III-G was built on the chassis of the Panzer III but the turret was replaced with a fixed superstructure that enabled it to mount a 75 mm M3 gun. The Stug III was initially designed as a mobile assault gun for infantry support, but it would later take on the role of a tank destroyer. The Stug III-G was manned by a crew of 4 (driver, commander, gunner, loader) and for secondary armament it used 1 x 7.92 mm MG34 machine gun. A total of 10,086 StuG III’s were built.

card_unit_tiger_i_e.name: card_unit_tiger_i_e
card_unit_tiger_i_e.title: TIGER I-E
card_unit_tiger_i_e.text: Cannot be targeted by enemy orders.
card_unit_tiger_i_e.flavorText: The Tiger I was a German heavy tank used by the Wehrmacht during WWII. The Tiger was built from 1942 to 1944 and was the first tank to mount the 8.8 cm KwK 36 gun, but despite its outstanding design it was a good example of German over-engineering and this high maintenance tank would be haunted by various failures and vulnerabilities throughout the war. The Tiger I would see a few small upgrades throughout the war but there was no significant change between the H and E variants. The Tiger I E had the cupola replaced with a lower profile design and an extra 100 mm armor was added in front of the gunner. The tank had a crew of 5 ((commander, gunner, loader, driver, assistant driver) and a secondary armament of 2 x 2× 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns. A total of 1,347 Tiger I tanks were produced, but only seven survive today.

card_event_admiral_hipper.name: card_event_admiral_hipper
card_event_admiral_hipper.title: KM ADMIRAL HIPPER
card_event_admiral_hipper.text: Send a unit to hand. Enemy does not gain a kredit slot or draw a card next turn.
card_event_admiral_hipper.flavorText: Admiral Hipper was the lead ship of the Admiral Hipper class of heavy cruisers which served with the German Kriegsmarine during WWII. The ship was launched in 1937 and entered into service in 1939, shortly after the outbreak of the war. Admiral Hipper was used in the Battle of the Atlantic and saw a significant amount of action. The ship sank the British destroyer HMS Glowworm in 1940 and several merchant ships in 1941 before returning to Germany. The ship was then transferred to Northern Norway where it participated, with some success, in operations against Allied convoys sailing to the Soviet Union in 1942. In 1943 the ship returned to Germany for repairs and never returned to active service after that time.

card_event_airstrike_new.name: card_event_airstrike_new
card_event_airstrike_new.title: AIRSTRIKE
card_event_airstrike_new.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, return it to hand. Enemy discards a random card.
card_event_airstrike_new.flavorText: The German Luftwaffe performed well between 1939–41, using mainly Stuka dive bombers to support their advancing troops. However, the Luftwaffe was poorly coordinated and was lacking in radar technology which meant that it never reached the size and scope needed to gain total air supremacy during the later stages of the war. Advanced German aircraft designs came too late to make an impact, the Messerschmitt Me 262 jet fighter did not come to use until July 1944, and the Heinkel He 162 appeared only during the last months of the war in Europe.

card_event_air_blitz.name: card_event_air_blitz
card_event_air_blitz.title: AIR BLITZ
card_event_air_blitz.flavorText: The main bombers in the German arsenal were the Heinkel He-111, Dornier Do-17, and the Junkers Ju-88. The Luftwaffe doctrine was to provide close tactical support to the army. This proved to be a great success for Germany early in the war, but their lack of long range bombers proved disastrous in the long run.

card_event_annihilation.name: card_event_annihilation
card_event_annihilation.title: ANNIHILATION
card_event_annihilation.text: Destroy an enemy unit that costs 5 or less. Enemy discards a card at random.
card_event_annihilation.flavorText: A battle of annihilation is a military strategy where the goal is to defeat the opposing forces in a single decisive battle. The image comes from an anti allied propaganda poster. A knife with the Wehrmacht insignia stabs through a clawed Allied hand over the Northern French coast.

card_event_bismarck.name: card_event_bismarck
card_event_bismarck.title: KM BISMARCK
card_event_bismarck.flavorText: The Bismarck was a battleship built and used by Nazi Germany's Kriegsmarine in WWII. It was named after Chancellor Otto von Bismarck and was, along with her sister ship Tirpitz, the largest battleships ever built by the Germans, and among the two largest ships built by any European power. The battleship was used in WWII for only 8 months and was sunk by the British Navy in the North Atlantic in 1941.

card_event_blackout.name: card_event_blackout
card_event_blackout.title: BLACKOUT
card_event_blackout.text: Pin target enemy air unit and draw a card.
card_event_blackout.flavorText: In 1944 German authorities ordered a full blackout in all cities at the sounding of an alert. During other nights they allowed lighting to the equivalent of moonlight and this was conducted in order to obstruct navigation and visibility for Allied bombers during night raids. The day Hitler died, on April 30, 1945, full lighting on the streets of German cities was permitted again.

card_event_blitzkrieg.name: card_event_blitzkrieg
card_event_blitzkrieg.title: BLITZKRIEG
card_event_blitzkrieg.text: Friendly units in the frontline have +3 attack and operate for one less until end of turn.
card_event_blitzkrieg.flavorText: Blitzkrieg (e. lightning war) was a military tactic used by the Germans. The strategy was to use a highly mobile form of infantry, armor and air superiority, using speed and surprise to encircle the enemy and win a swift victory.

card_event_breakthrough.name: card_event_breakthrough
card_event_breakthrough.title: BREAKTHROUGH
card_event_breakthrough.text: Deal 3 damage to target unit. If it is destroyed, your units operate for 1 less this turn.
card_event_breakthrough.flavorText: In military terms a breakthrough is an assault through and past enemy lines.

card_event_careless_talk.name: card_event_careless_talk
card_event_careless_talk.title: CARELESS TALK
card_event_careless_talk.text: When your enemy deploys a unit, deal 3 damage to it.
card_event_careless_talk.flavorText: Anti gossip campaigns were launched by all fighting parties in WWII. The aim was to discourage talking about sensitive material where it could possibly be overheard by spies. Careless talk did indeed have an impact on the Nazi Germany war effort, and perhaps from where they least expected. As an example, Poles were used as forced laborers across the continent of the Nazi Reich, which put them in a unique position to spy on their enemy. It is believed that 48 percent of all reports received by British secret services during the war had come from these sources. The reports included advanced warnings of Operation Barbarossa, Operation Edelweiss, the German Caucasus Campaign and first intelligence on the Holocaust.

card_event_combined_arms.name: card_event_combined_arms
card_event_combined_arms.title: COMBINED ARMS
card_event_combined_arms.text: Give a friendly tank +1+1 for each unit type you control.
card_event_combined_arms.flavorText: At the start of WWII German armor enjoyed the advantage of having radios, allowing them to communicate and coordinate faster than their counterparts. In every tank there was at least one radio and in some command tanks as many as four conversations could take place on them simultaneously through the use of carrier telephony. The Germans were the first to use this type of radio technology, but the British and the U.S. forces soon followed their example.

card_event_dive_bombing.name: card_event_dive_bombing
card_event_dive_bombing.title: DIVE BOMBING
card_event_dive_bombing.text: Deal 1 damage to an enemy unit. Set its attack to 0 until your next turn.
card_event_dive_bombing.flavorText: A dive bomber is an aircraft that dives directly at the targets in order to provide greater accuracy for the bomb it drops. It is difficult to say how dive bombing originated, but the tactic was developed and used during WWI and the interwar era, but during WWII dive bombing was utilized by all sides. Dive bombers used by the Luftwaffe during WWII were the Arado Ar 81, Heinkel He 50, Heinkel He 118, Henschel Hs 132 (prototype) and Junkers Ju 87 (Stuka).

card_event_eagle_claws.name: card_event_eagle_claws
card_event_eagle_claws.title: EAGLE CLAWS
card_event_eagle_claws.text: Deal 2 damage to all units in the enemy support line.
card_event_eagle_claws.flavorText: The eagle was the national symbol of the Third Reich, where eagle's claws were to grasp a wreath of oak leaves surrounding a swastika. However, this particular card refers to the air superiority of the fast advancing German army.

card_event_encirclement.name: card_event_encirclement
card_event_encirclement.title: ENCIRCLEMENT
card_event_encirclement.text: Duplicate a friendly unit in the frontline with a cost of 3 or less and give it Blitz.
card_event_encirclement.flavorText: Encirclement is a military term for the situation when a force or target is isolated and surrounded by enemy forces. When the Axis nations invaded the Soviet Union in Operation Barbarossa they managed to encircle large portions of the Red Army during the early stages of the campaign. The most famous examples are the Battle of Białystok–Minsk and the First Battle of Kiev which both took place in the summer of 1941. In both battles the Red Army lost over a million men (killed or captured), including 12,000 guns and mortars, 4,863 tanks and 1,177–1,669 aircraft.

card_event_enigma.name: card_event_enigma
card_event_enigma.title: ENIGMA
card_event_enigma.text: Draw cards until you have as many cards in your hand as the enemy.
card_event_enigma.flavorText: The Enigma Machine was a cipher machine used by the Germans to encrypt and protect commercial, diplomatic and military communication. With the help of Alan Turing (father of theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence) and others, the Allies finally managed to crack the Enigma Code.

card_event_fast_heinz.name: card_event_fast_heinz
card_event_fast_heinz.title: FAST HEINZ
card_event_fast_heinz.flavorText: Heinz Wilhelm Guderian was a German general during WWII and was a specialist in motorized tactics and armored formations. He successfully lead the German Panzer units in Poland and France, later during the invasion of the Soviet Union, which was not as successful. After the defeat at the Battle of Moscow in 1941 he was transferred to the reserves and ended the war as Chief of the General Staff.

card_event_from_the_deep.name: card_event_from_the_deep
card_event_from_the_deep.title: FROM THE DEEP
card_event_from_the_deep.text: When your enemy deploys a unit, destroy it.
card_event_from_the_deep.flavorText: At the start of WWII the German Kriegsmarine had the largest submarine fleet in the world and U-boat warfare became a major component during the Battle of the Atlantic, and throughout the war. At first the U-Boat tactics were somewhat civil, they would find a target, surface and advise the crew to abandon ship before bringing it down with deck guns or explosives (torpedoes were expensive and only used when absolutely necessary). However, when the Allies began arming merchant ships the Germans began firing without a warning. Throughout the war the German U-boats managed to sink 5,000 Allied ships.

card_event_iron_from_the_north.name: card_event_iron_from_the_north
card_event_iron_from_the_north.title: IRON FROM THE NORTH
card_event_iron_from_the_north.text: If you control the frontline, gain 3 additional Kredits
card_event_iron_from_the_north.flavorText: During WWII Germany was in much need of iron-ore for its military production and a large portion of it was imported from Sweden. The iron-ore came from the Swedish northern mining districts surrounding the towns of Gallivare and Kiruna, and were shipped from the Baltic sea ports of Lulea and Oxelosund. However, when the Baltic sea froze over in the winter the Germans began shipping the Swedish iron ore from the Norwegian port of Narvik. The Allies put much effort into stopping this trade, and finally through diplomatic pressure, Sweden decided to end its trade with Germany by November 1944.

card_event_missing.name: card_event_missing
card_event_missing.title: MISSING
card_event_missing.text: When a unit moves into the frontline, destroy it.
card_event_missing.flavorText: Missing in action is a classification of those combatants that are reported missing during wartime or ceasefire. They may have been killed, wounded, captured, or deserted. The combat environment itself could increase the likelihood of missing combatants such as in submarine warfare, jungle warfare or air-crashes in remote locations, or at sea.

card_event_reichsbank.name: card_event_reichsbank
card_event_reichsbank.title: REICHSBANK
card_event_reichsbank.text: Next turn, you gain 5 additional kredits and cannot give orders.
card_event_reichsbank.flavorText: The Reichsbank was the central bank of Germany from 1876 to 1945.

card_event_reinforcements.name: card_event_reinforcements
card_event_reinforcements.title: REINFORCEMENTS
card_event_reinforcements.text: Fully repair all friendly units and draw a card.
card_event_reinforcements.flavorText: A reinforcement in military terms is when additional troops or material are sent to support a military action.

card_event_sky_barons.name: card_event_sky_barons
card_event_sky_barons.title: SKY BARONS
card_event_sky_barons.text: Destroy an air unit. Draw a card.
card_event_sky_barons.flavorText: The majority of flying aces during WWII were pilots of the Luftwaffe, with 105 of them having more than 100 aerial victories. The top scoring ace was Erich Hartmann who had 352 aerial victories. The first Allied pilot to hit the list, number 231, was Ivan Kozhedub of the Soviet Air Force with 66 aerial victories.

card_event_sudden_strike.name: card_event_sudden_strike
card_event_sudden_strike.title: SUDDEN STRIKE
card_event_sudden_strike.text: Destroy a unit that costs 2 kredits or less.
card_event_sudden_strike.flavorText: The Luftwaffe only contributed a small amounts of forces to naval use from 1940 to 1944. They used mainly long-range reconnaissance planes, first the Focke-Wulf Fw 200 and later the Junkers Ju 290 maritime patrol aircraft, and early on their naval arm successfully claimed 365,000 tonnes of shipping.
