However, following the defeats on the Eastern Front, in North Africa and the ever-increasing Allied bombing raids on Germany ensured that the Luftwaffe's naval arm was denied the necessary resources to combat Allied air and naval superiority over the Atlantic.

card_event_tactical_strike.name: card_event_tactical_strike
card_event_tactical_strike.title: TACTICAL STRIKE
card_event_tactical_strike.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit. Deal 4 damage if the unit is in a support line.
card_event_tactical_strike.flavorText: The Luftwaffe performed well in 1939 to 1941, with their air force flying in close coordination with the fast advancing land forces, and the Stuka dive bombers terrifying the enemy infantry units. However, as the war dragged on the Luftwaffe didn't have the size or scope to conquer the skies, both due to lack of aircraft production and shortage of fuel.

card_event_u_375.name: card_event_u_375
card_event_u_375.title: U-375
card_event_u_375.text: Your enemy discards a random card with cost 5 or less.
card_event_u_375.flavorText: The U-375 was a Type VIIC German submarine used by the Kriegsmarine in WWII. The submarine sailed 10 patrols, sank 9 merchant ships and damaged one warship. The U-375 sunk in 1943 after being depth charged by USN submarine chaser PC-624. All hands were lost.

card_event_wolfpack.name: card_event_wolfpack
card_event_wolfpack.title: WOLFPACK
card_event_wolfpack.text: Send target unit to hand. The enemy discards a random card.
card_event_wolfpack.flavorText: Wolfpack, or “Rudeltaktik” as the Germans called it, was a tactic used by the German U-boats of the Kriegsmarine against convoys during the Battle of the Atlantic. The idea was to form a pack of U-boats, and to delay an attack until all boats were in position to conduct a massed organized attack. This tactic had a devastating effect on Allied shipping.

card_unit_10_5_cm_lefh.name: card_unit_10_5_cm_lefh
card_unit_10_5_cm_lefh.title: 10.5 cm leFH
card_unit_10_5_cm_lefh.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_10_5_cm_lefh.flavorText: The 10.5 cm leFH 18/40 was a German light howitzer used in WWII by the Wehrmacht and the Axis forces of Finland and Romania. The 10.5 cm leFH had an effective firing range of 12,325 meters (13,479 yds).

card_unit_158_nachschub.name: card_unit_158_nachschub
card_unit_158_nachschub.title: 158. NACHSCHUB
card_unit_158_nachschub.text: Once per turn, gain 2 kredits when an enemy unit is destroyed during your turn.
card_unit_158_nachschub.flavorText: The 158. Nachschub was a German supply battalion attached to the 58th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division took part in the Battle of France in 1940, and then Operation Barbarossa in 1941 and after that it was constantly engaged on the Eastern Front until the end of the war in 1945.

card_unit_15_cm_autokanone.name: card_unit_15_cm_autokanone
card_unit_15_cm_autokanone.title: 15 cm AUTOKANONE
card_unit_15_cm_autokanone.text: When you deploy a unit, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_15_cm_autokanone.flavorText: The 15 cm Autokanone M. 15/16 was a heavy field gun that was designed and manufactured by Skoda for the Austrian Empire in WWI. They were taken into the service of the German Wehrmacht after the annexation of Austria and the occupation of Czechoslovakia, but due to their unique ammunition they weren't used much, and mainly for coast-defenses.

card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment
card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment.title: 1. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 1st Infantry Regiment was attached to the 1st Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht and served throughout WWII. The division participated in the invasion of Poland and France, and later as part of the 18th Army with Army Group North in Operation Barbarossa. In 1945, after the capitulation of Konigsberg, the remains of the division surrendered to the Soviet Army.

card_unit_22_infantry.name: card_unit_22_infantry
card_unit_22_infantry.title: 22. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_22_infantry.text: If you control the frontline at the end of your turn, draw a card.
card_unit_22_infantry.flavorText: The 22nd Infantry Regiment was attached to the 1st Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht and served throughout WWII. The division participated in the invasion of Poland and France, and later as part of the 18th Army with Army Group North in Operation Barbarossa. In 1945, after the capitulation of Konigsberg, the remains of the division surrendered to the Soviet Army.

card_unit_33_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_33_panzergrenadier
card_unit_33_panzergrenadier.title: 33. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_33_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 33rd Panzergrenadier Regiment was formed in 1942 and was attached to the 4th Panzer Division of the Wehrmacht. The regiment fought on the Eastern Front and took part in many battles and military campaigns, including Operation Barbarossa, the Battle of Moscow and the Battle of Kursk. In 1944 the division was moved to northern Lithuania where they supported the defenses against the Soviet offensive until the end of the war.

card_unit_3_fallschirmjager.name: card_unit_3_fallschirmjager
card_unit_3_fallschirmjager.title: 3. FALLSCHIRMJÄGER
card_unit_3_fallschirmjager.text: At the start of your turn, gets +1 attack for each tank in the same line.
card_unit_3_fallschirmjager.flavorText: The 3. Fallschirmjager Regiment was formed in 1940 as part of the 1st Parachute Division, initially named 7th Air Division for secrecy. It took part in the invasion of Crete in 1941 and later that year was sent to the eastern front, seeing heavy combat near Leningrad, Vitebsk and Smolensk over the next couple of years. In 1943 it was sent to Sicily to defend against the Allied invasion of the island and spent the remainder of the war slowly retreating up the Italian peninsula from one defensive position to another.

card_unit_4_pioneer.name: card_unit_4_pioneer
card_unit_4_pioneer.title: 4. PIONEER BATTALION
card_unit_4_pioneer.text: Deployment: Give all friendly ground units in the frontline +1 defense.
card_unit_4_pioneer.flavorText: German combat pioneers (German: Sturmpioniere) were foremost assault troops and tasked with overcoming man-made and natural obstacles and to support the infantry as specialist assault troops. This included attacking fortified positions with demolitions and flamethrowers. Their job was also to construct fortifications and shelters, place obstacles, lay minefields, plant booby traps, maintain supply routes etc. The 4th Pioneer Battalion was attached to the 13th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht and first saw combat in the Polish Campaign. They fought in France and on the Eastern Front until they finally surrendered to the American Army in Herford Germany in 1945.

card_unit_88_mm_flak.name: card_unit_88_mm_flak
card_unit_88_mm_flak.title: 88 mm FLAK
card_unit_88_mm_flak.text: Deals double damage against air and tank units.
card_unit_88_mm_flak.flavorText: The 8.8 cm Flak 18/36/37/41 (mostly called the eighty-eight) was a German 88 mm gun, originally manufactured and used as an anti-aircraft gun but also used as anti-tank artillery gun. It was widely used by Germany in WWII and was one of the most recognized German weapons in the conflict.

card_unit_arado_ar_196.name: card_unit_arado_ar_196
card_unit_arado_ar_196.title: ARADO AR 196
card_unit_arado_ar_196.text: Deployment: If you have equal or less units on the battlefield, draw an order.
card_unit_arado_ar_196.flavorText: The Arado Ar 196 was a German made seaplane and was mainly used for reconnaissance missions. It was a standard aircraft of the Kriegsmarine (German Navy) and was used by the Axis forces throughout WWII. The aircraft was considered best of its class and served its purpose well in reconnaissance missions and submarine hunts, but it was no match against enemy fighters. The Finnish Air Force used it for transporting and supplying special forces behind enemy lines as it had the ability to land on small lakes in remote locations.

card_unit_comet.name: card_unit_comet
card_unit_comet.title: KOMET
card_unit_comet.text: At the end of your turn, return KOMET to your hand.
card_unit_comet.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet was a German rocket-powered interceptor aircraft. It's the only rocket-powered fighter aircraft ever to have been operational and the first piloted aircraft to exceed 1000 km/h in level flight. Over 300 Komets were built, and although the design was revolutionary they were considered a tactical failure. Me 163 fighters began operations in May 1944 and their speed overwhelmed Allied fighters. However, the rocket engines soon became the aircrafts biggest weakness, due to the rocket's short fuel life which only allowed for a short time to attack. Allied pilots soon learned to simply wait until the rocket fuel ran out before beginning their attacks.

card_unit_dornier_do_217.name: card_unit_dornier_do_217
card_unit_dornier_do_217.title: DORNIER DO 217
card_unit_dornier_do_217.text: When DORNIER DO 217 destroys a unit, the enemy must discard a card at random.
card_unit_dornier_do_217.flavorText: The Dornier DO 217 was a German heavy bomber used by the Luftwaffe during WWII.  The aircraft was designed in 1938 to replace the Dornier Do 17 and first saw combat in late 1940. Early variants had greater speed, range and bomb load capacity than the contemporary Heinkel He 111 and Junkers Ju 88, and although it was designed as an heavy bomber it took on many roles. The Dornier DO 217 was operated as a strategic bomber, torpedo bomber and reconnaissance aircraft, and later in the war as night fighters, but did not perform particularly well in that role. In total 1,905 were been built, including variants.

card_unit_fallschirmjager.name: card_unit_fallschirmjager
card_unit_fallschirmjager.title: 8. FALLSCHIRMJÄGER
card_unit_fallschirmjager.flavorText: The Fallschirmjager's were the paratroopers of the German Luftwaffe before and during WWII. They were the first paratroopers conducting the first airborne infantry assaults in history, but throughout the war they mainly fought on the ground as elite infantry rather than airborne units. They were called the "green devils" by the Allies and were known as fierce and resilient opponents. The 8th Fallschirmjager Regiment was attached to the 3rd Parachute Division of the Luftwaffe, which was formed in 1943. The regiment fought with its division in Normandy and in the Arnhem area before participating in the Battle of the Hurtgen Forest in Germany. They surrendered to the Americans in Rhur in April 1945.

card_unit_flak_37_spg.name: card_unit_flak_37_spg
card_unit_flak_37_spg.title: 3.7cm FLAK 37
card_unit_flak_37_spg.flavorText: The 3.7 cm Flak 18/36/37/43 was a series of anti-aircraft cannons produced by Germany and used by the Axis forces during WWII. The cannon was fully automatic and effective against aircraft flying at altitudes up to 4,200 m and was produced in both towed and self-propelled versions. A total of 20,243 weapons of these series were built, most of which were of the Flak 36 and Flak 37 variant design.

card_unit_fw_190.name: card_unit_fw_190
card_unit_fw_190.title: FW 190 A
card_unit_fw_190.flavorText: The FW 190 A was a Focke-Wulf Fw 190 variant, a German fighter aircraft used by the Luftwaffe and the Axis allies in WWII. It took on a variety of roles and was used as a day fighter, fighter-bomber, ground-attack aircraft and night fighter. The FW 190 was well-liked by its pilots and a number of German fighter aces claimed many aerial victories while flying it.

card_unit_grenadier_245.name: card_unit_grenadier_245
card_unit_grenadier_245.title: 980. VOLKSGRENADIER
card_unit_grenadier_245.flavorText: The 980th Volksgrenadier Regiment fought under the 272nd Volksgrenadier Division and participated in numerous battles on the Western Front until it was largely encircled in what is known as the Battle for the Ruhr Pocket in April 1945. Volksgrenadier was a name given to German Army divisions that were formed in the autumn of 1944 after a series of military defeats against the Allies. These divisions participated in the final stages of the war, including the Battle of the Bulge, the defense of the Eastern Front and Siegfried Line, and in the final battles in Germany.

card_unit_henschel_hs_123.name: card_unit_henschel_hs_123
card_unit_henschel_hs_123.title: HENSCHEL HS 123
card_unit_henschel_hs_123.flavorText: The Henschel Hs 123 was a single-seat biplane dive bomber first used by the German Luftwaffe during the Spanish Civil War, and although the production was stopped in 1940, it was used up until 1944, but then it was pulled from the frontline and assigned to secondary duties such as conducting supply drops and glider towing.

card_unit_jagdpanther.name: card_unit_jagdpanther
card_unit_jagdpanther.title: JAGDPANTHER
card_unit_jagdpanther.flavorText: Jagdpanther (meaning "hunting panther" in German) was a German tank destroyer. The G2 variant was first produced in 1945 and used until the end of WWII, both on the Eastern and Western Fronts. The tank destroyer had a crew of 5, a main armament of 1x 8.8 cm Pak 43/3 or 43/4 L/71 and a secondary armament of 1x 7.92 mm Maschinengewehr 34. Only 415 Jagdpanther's were produced and placed into service.

card_unit_junkers_ju_188.name: card_unit_junkers_ju_188
card_unit_junkers_ju_188.title: JUNKERS JU 188 E
card_unit_junkers_ju_188.flavorText: The Junkers Ju 188 was German medium bomber used by the Luftwaffe in WWII. A few versions were made and it was a perfect example of the "bullet nose" design that most German bombers had from Heinkel He 111P and onwards. The Ju 188 was a high performance aircraft but it appeared too late to make any significant impact on the war. Only 1,234 of the Ju 188 were built,  and this was both due to tactical and logistical reasons, the Luftwaffe focusing more on building fighters and the effect the heavy Allied bombing had on German industries.

card_unit_junkers_ju_88.name: card_unit_junkers_ju_88
card_unit_junkers_ju_88.title: JUNKERS JU 88 A
card_unit_junkers_ju_88.flavorText: The Junkers Ju 88 was a German twin-engine multi-role combat aircraft used in WWII by the Luftwaffe and the Axis powers. Many variants of the aircraft were produced and it served as a bomber, dive bomber, night fighter, torpedo bomber, reconnaissance aircraft, heavy fighter, and as a flying bomb by the end of the war. Due to its multiple roles, the Ju 88 became one of the most important aircraft for the Luftwaffe and it was produced nonstop from 1936 to 1945.

card_unit_ju_87_stuka.name: card_unit_ju_87_stuka
card_unit_ju_87_stuka.title: JU 87 B STUKA
card_unit_ju_87_stuka.text: The enemy must discard a card each time Stuka deals damage to their HQ.
card_unit_ju_87_stuka.flavorText: The Junkers Ju 87 or Stuka, which is abbreviation of Sturzkampfflugzeug which is German for "dive bomber", was a German dive bomber and ground-attack aircraft. The aircraft was easily recognized by its inverted wings and undercarriage and the wailing sound of the Jericho-Trumpets when it made its dive. The Stuka was the main aircraft used for close air support in the Luftwaffe and was first used in combat in the Spanish Civil War in 1937 and served the Axis forces throughout WWII.

card_unit_marder_iii_h.name: card_unit_marder_iii_h
card_unit_marder_iii_h.title: MARDER III H
card_unit_marder_iii_h.text: When a friendly unit destroys an enemy unit, draw a random unit.
card_unit_marder_iii_h.flavorText: The Marder III H was a German tank destroyer that was produced from 1942 to 1944 and served at the frontline until the end of WWII. The Marder III H variant mounted a 7.5 cm Pak 40 German anti-tank gun on a slightly modified Panzer 38(t) Ausf. H chassis and also carried a 7.92 mm machine gun in the hull. This tank destroyer type was considered mechanically reliable and it carried enough firepower to take out the majority of enemy tanks on the battlefield.

card_unit_me_262_schwalbe.name: card_unit_me_262_schwalbe
card_unit_me_262_schwalbe.title: ME 262A SCHWALBE
card_unit_me_262_schwalbe.text: Deployment: Destroy all enemy air units.
card_unit_me_262_schwalbe.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Me 262, nicknamed Schwalbe (German: "Swallow"), was the world's first operational jet-powered fighter aircraft. The Me 262's roles included light bomber, reconnaissance and experimental night fighter versions, and it was faster and more heavily armed than any Allied fighter. Me 262 pilots claimed to have shot down 542 Allied aircraft, but some claim the number was higher. However, despite being the most advanced military aircraft design at the time it had an insignificant impact on the course of the war, both due to its late introduction and the small numbers put into operational service. In total 1,430 ME 262's were built and after the war they were no longer used by the Germans, however the Czechoslovak Air Force the operated the aircraft until 1951.

card_unit_me_bf_109_g.name: card_unit_me_bf_109_g
card_unit_me_bf_109_g.title: ME BF 109 E
card_unit_me_bf_109_g.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Bf 109, was the main German WWII fighter aircraft of the Luftwaffe. The Bf 109 was first used in service during the Spanish Civil War (1939) and was still in service at the end of WWII by Germany and its Axis partners.  It was one of the most advanced fighters of the era, and conducted more aerial kills than any other aircraft during WWII.

card_unit_me_bf_110.name: card_unit_me_bf_110
card_unit_me_bf_110.title: ME BF 110
card_unit_me_bf_110.text: At the end of your turn, give ME BF 110 +1+1 if you control the frontline.
card_unit_me_bf_110.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Bf 110 was a twin-engine heavy fighter and fighter-bomber developed by the Germans in the 1930s and used by the Luftwaffe during WWII.  It was armed with two MG FF 20 mm cannons, four 7.92 mm (.312 in) MG 17 machine guns, and one 7.92 mm (.312 in) MG 15 machine gun or twin-barrel MG 81Z for defense. The aircraft served successfully in the early campaigns, however it lacked agility in the air which was a vulnerability that was exploited by the Allies during the Battle of Britain. After the Battle of Britain the Bf 110 served successfully as an air superiority fighter and strike aircraft, but by 1944 it was no match against American air supremacy.

card_unit_nebelwerfer.name: card_unit_nebelwerfer
card_unit_nebelwerfer.title: NEBELWERFER 42
card_unit_nebelwerfer.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to an enemy unit.
card_unit_nebelwerfer.flavorText: The 21 cm Nebelwerfer 42 (e. smoke mortar) was a German multiple rocket launcher used in WWII. It was used by special units called Nebeltruppen which were tasked with delivering chemical weapons and high explosives during the war. The Nebelwerfer 42 had five barrels, and the rockets were electrically fired to a maximum range of 7.85 km.

card_unit_pak_36.name: card_unit_pak_36
card_unit_pak_36.title: PAK 36
card_unit_pak_36.text: When your enemy deploys a tank unit, deal 1 damage to it.
card_unit_pak_36.flavorText: The 3.7 cm Pak 36 was a German anti-tank gun used from 1936 and throughout WWII by the Axis powers. By 1940 it had become ineffective against modern tanks of the era and production was halted in 1942. The PAK 36 had a crew of 5 (Commander, gunner, loader, two ammunition bearers) and an effective range of 5,484 meters, and due to its light weight and maneuverability it was often used by German paratroopers.

card_unit_pak_38_vs_2.name: card_unit_pak_38_vs_2
card_unit_pak_38_vs_2.title: PAK 38
card_unit_pak_38_vs_2.flavorText: The 5 cm Pak 38 (L/60) (5 cm Panzerabwehrkanone 38 (L/60)) was a German anti-tank gun of 50 mm caliber developed in 1938 and used by the Axis powers in WWII. The gun was first used in 1941 as a successor to the PAK 36, Pak 37 had been designed in 1935, but never used due to its low capabilities. The gun remained in service until the end of the war and was one of the few early guns capable of penetrating the 45 mm sloped armor of the T-34's hull at close range. It could also be equipped with Panzergranate 40 APCR ammunition with a hard tungsten core against the heavy KV-1 tank.

card_unit_panther.name: card_unit_panther
card_unit_panther.title: PANTHER G
card_unit_panther.text: Cannot be targeted by enemy orders.
card_unit_panther.flavorText: The Panther G was a medium tank built and used by the Germans in WWII from 1943 to 1945. The tank was built to counter the Soviet T-34 and is today considered the best tank of WWII, both for its firepower and protection. The Panther G had a crew of 5 (driver, radio-operator/hull machine gunner, commander, gunner, loader),  a main armament of 1x 7.5 cm KwK 42 L/70 and a secondary armament of 2x 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns.

card_unit_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_panzergrenadier
card_unit_panzergrenadier.title: 59. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_panzergrenadier.text: 59. Panzergrenadier can move and attack during the same turn.
card_unit_panzergrenadier.flavorText: Panzergrenadier is a German term for a motorized or mechanized infantryman and a term that was first adopted in 1942. The Panzergrenadier Divisions were combined arms formations, usually with two or three regiments of truck-mounted infantry, a battalion of tanks, artillery support, reconnaissance units, combat engineers, anti-tank and anti-aircraft artillery, etc. The 59th Panzergrenadier Regiment was attached to the 20th Panzer Division of the Whermacht which fought on the Eastern Front and took part in the battles of Moscow and Kursk. They surrendered with their division to the US and Soviet forces in Czechoslovakia in May 1945.

card_unit_panzerzug_6.name: card_unit_panzerzug_6
card_unit_panzerzug_6.title: PANZERZUG 61 BP42
card_unit_panzerzug_6.text: Deployment: Add to your support line two 59. PANZERGRENADIER with Blitz.
card_unit_panzerzug_6.flavorText: The BP42 and BP44 were the standardized armored trains of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The trains had a symmetrical layout and the rail cars had the same setup in front and rear, with an armored locomotive in the middle. The following setup was common: 2x control flatcars (front and rear), 2x flatcars for tanks, 2x AA Cars with Flak vierling and 7.62cm gun, 2x Armoured Command/infantry Cars, 2x Tender and the armored locomotive in the middle.

card_unit_panzer_35_t.name: card_unit_panzer_35_t
card_unit_panzer_35_t.title: PANZER 35(t)
card_unit_panzer_35_t.text: Deployment: Reduce operation cost by 1 if you control an infantry.
card_unit_panzer_35_t.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen 35(t), commonly known as Panzer 35(t) was a Czechoslovakian light tank manufactured by Skoda, but mainly used by the German Wehrmacht during WWII. Only 434 units were built and of these the Germans seized 244 when they occupied Bohemia-Moravia in 1939. The Panzer 35 was used early in the war during the invasion of Poland, the Battle of France and the invasion of the Soviet Union, but retired from frontline services in 1942. The tank had a crew of 3 to 4 men, a main armament of 3.7 cm (1.5 in) KwK 34(t) gun and a secondary armament of 2 x 7.92 mm MG 37(t) machine guns.

card_unit_panzer_38_t.name: card_unit_panzer_38_t
card_unit_panzer_38_t.title: PANZER 38(t)
card_unit_panzer_38_t.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen 38(t) was originally a Czechoslovak tank but taken over by Germany after their invasion of Czechoslovakia and adopted to the German Army. The PANZER 38 (t) saw service in the invasions of Poland, France and the USSR, but production was halted in 1942 since its armament was deemed inadequate.

card_unit_panzer_iii_e.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_e
card_unit_panzer_iii_e.title: PANZER III-L
card_unit_panzer_iii_e.text: Has +1 attack for each non-tank unit type you control.
card_unit_panzer_iii_e.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen III-L was a Panzer III variant, a German medium tank produced from 1939 to 1943. It was manufactured by Daimler-Benz and was used in all major theaters by the Germans and the Axis powers. The Panzer III-L was a re-designated III-J tank equipped with long 5 cm gun, 20 mm stand-off armor plates on hull and turret front.

card_unit_panzer_iii_j.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_j
card_unit_panzer_iii_j.title: PANZER III-J
card_unit_panzer_iii_j.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen III-J was a Panzer III variant, a German medium tank produced from 1939 to 1943. It was manufactured by Daimler-Benz and was used in all major theaters by the Germans and the Axis powers. The Panzer III-J had a main armament of a 1x 5 cm KwK 38/39 gun and a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner).

card_unit_panzer_iii_l.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_l
card_unit_panzer_iii_l.title: PANZER III-E
card_unit_panzer_iii_l.text: Other friendly tanks with Blitz have +2 attack.
card_unit_panzer_iii_l.flavorText: The Panzer III-E was the fifth version of the German Panzer III medium tank. This version had a 30 mm armor all-round, except for the rear, which made it heavier than its predecessors. The suspension was redesigned and used six road wheels per side instead of five and a 300 PS HL 120 engine. The Panzer III-E had a main armament of a 1x 3.7 cm KwK 36 gun and secondary armament of  2–3x 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns. This variant was first introduced in 1939 with 96 units being manufactured.

card_unit_panzer_ii_a.name: card_unit_panzer_ii_a
card_unit_panzer_ii_a.title: PANZER II-A
card_unit_panzer_ii_a.flavorText: Panzer II is a name used for a series of German tanks used in WWII, and PANZER II-A, or Panzerkampfwagen II Ausf.A (Sd.Kfz.121), was one of the early models in these series. It had an armament of a 2 cm Kw.K.30 gun and had a crew of 3 (commander/gunner, driver, loader). The tank played an important role in the Polish and French Campaigns, but was also used in North Africa and on the Eastern Front.

card_unit_panzer_iv_f2.name: card_unit_panzer_iv_f2
card_unit_panzer_iv_f2.title: PANZER IV F2
card_unit_panzer_iv_f2.flavorText: The PANZER IV F2 was a German Panzer IV (Panzerkampfwagen IV) variant, a medium tank used by the Axis powers throughout WWII. The tank had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner), a main armament of 7.5 cm (2.95 in) KwK 40 L/48 and secondary armament of 2 × 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns.

card_unit_panzer_iv_g.name: card_unit_panzer_iv_g
card_unit_panzer_iv_g.title: PANZER IV-G
card_unit_panzer_iv_g.flavorText: The Panzer IV-G was a German Panzer IV (Panzerkampfwagen IV) variant that was produced between March 1942 to June 1943. The Panzer IV was a medium tank used by the Axis powers throughout WWII and 8,553 units of numerous variants were manufactured throughout the war. The IV-G variant had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner), a main armament of 7.5 cm (2.95 in) KwK 40 L/48 and secondary armament of 2 × 7.92 mm MG 34 machine guns.

card_unit_railway_gun_leopold.name: card_unit_railway_gun_leopold
card_unit_railway_gun_leopold.title: LEOPOLD
card_unit_railway_gun_leopold.text: Deployment: Send all enemy units to hand.
card_unit_railway_gun_leopold.flavorText: The Leopold was a Krupp K5 gun (named Leopold by its crew), a railway gun used by Germany throughout WWII. With its 25 meter long barrel it had a maximum range of 64 km and it fired shells that weighted 243 kg. Two K5 guns, "Leopold" and "Robert", were shipped to Italy to help counter the American landing at the town of Anzio in 1944. The gun fired a few rounds but since it couldn't be evacuated due to its immense size during the German retreat, it was destroyed by its crew.

card_unit_sd_kfz222x.name: card_unit_sd_kfz222x
card_unit_sd_kfz222x.title: Sd KFz 222
card_unit_sd_kfz222x.flavorText: The Sd KFz 222 (Leichter Panzerspähwagen) was a light armored reconnaissance vehicle used by the Germans in WWII. It had a crew of three and was armed with a 2 cm KwK 30 L/55 autocannon and a 7.92 mm MG 13 machine gun.

card_unit_stug_iii.name: card_unit_stug_iii
card_unit_stug_iii.title: STUG III-F
card_unit_stug_iii.flavorText: The STUG III-F (abbreviation of Sturmgeschütz III) was a German assault gun built on the chassis of the Panzer III tank. This was Germany's most produced armored fighting vehicle during WWII and used by the axis forces, mostly as a tank destroyer, but also as an assault gun. For main armament it had a 1× 7.5 cm StuK 40 L/48 gun and 1 × 7.92 mm MG34 machine gun as a secondary armament.

card_unit_stug_iv.name: card_unit_stug_iv
card_unit_stug_iv.title: STUG IV
card_unit_stug_iv.flavorText: The STUG IV (abbreviation of Sturmgeschütz IV) was a German assault gun variant of the Panzer IV tank. 1,108 units were built during the war and additional 31 were converted from battle-damaged Panzer IV hulls. The STUG IV had a crew of 4 (Commander, Gunner, Loader, Driver), a main armament of 1 x 7.5 cm StuK 40 L/48 and a secondary armament of 1 x 7.92 mm MG34 machine gun.

card_unit_tiger_i.name: card_unit_tiger_i
card_unit_tiger_i.title: TIGER I-H
card_unit_tiger_i.flavorText: The Tiger I-H (also Panzerkampfwagen VI Tiger Ausf. H) was a TIGER I variant, a German heavy tank used in WWII by the axis forces. The Tiger I had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, assistant driver) and was the first tank that mounted a 8.8 cm KwK 36 gun. The Tiger I was an outstanding design of its time but the production and the maintenance was very expensive and only 1347 were built.

card_unit_wirbelwind.name: card_unit_wirbelwind
card_unit_wirbelwind.title: WIRBELWIND
card_unit_wirbelwind.text: While in frontline, enemy air units enter the battlefield pinned.
card_unit_wirbelwind.flavorText: The Flakpanzer IV "Wirbelwind" (e. Whirlwind) was a German self-propelled anti-aircraft gun mounted on Panzer IV tank chassis. It was developed in 1944 and had a main armament of 4 × 2 cm Flak 38 guns and 1 × 7.92 mm MG 34 Panzerlauf as a secondary armament. The Wirbelwind had a crew of 5 (commander/gunner, two loaders, driver, radio operator).

card_event_aunt_frieda.name: card_event_aunt_frieda
card_event_aunt_frieda.title: AUNT FRIEDA
card_event_aunt_frieda.text: Give a friendly infantry +1+1. Add TANK MANEUVER to your hand.
card_event_aunt_frieda.flavorText: The German field manual “Truppenführung” was notable for its clarity. It consisted of a two-part pocket sized manual which was issued to all commissioned officers and senior NCOs. It contained all the basic military doctrine for the German forces and introduced concepts like Command and Battle of the Combined Arms and Mission Command. Rather than a set of rules, it provided guidelines that could be consulted for any situation. It insisted on the importance of delegating operational command and that all subordinates had to understand the commander's intent so they could act on their own initiative. This way of thinking gave the German army an advantage over their enemies while they updated their own tactics and command structure. The manual was affectionately called “Tante Frieda”. A modified form is still used today by the German Army.

card_event_buzz_bomb.name: card_event_buzz_bomb
card_event_buzz_bomb.title: BUZZ BOMB
card_event_buzz_bomb.text: Deal 1 damage to an enemy. Draw a card if it is the HQ.
card_event_buzz_bomb.flavorText: The German "Buzz Bomb," officially known as the V-1 flying bomb, was an early cruise missile and one of the world’s first guided weapons, used by Germany during World War II. It was developed as part of Hitler's "vengeance weapons" program to retaliate against Allied bombings. Launched primarily from sites in northern France and Belgium due to its limited range, the V-1 targeted London and other cities in southeast England, causing significant destruction and civilian casualties. The V-1 earned the nickname "Buzz Bomb" or "Doodlebug" because of the loud, distinctive buzzing noise made by its jet engine. This sound struck fear into the population below, as the buzzing would suddenly stop just before the bomb descended and exploded. In total, over 9,000 V-1 bombs were launched, causing thousands of casualties and leaving a lasting mark on the cities they targeted. The V-1’s development marked a significant step in the evolution of modern missile technology.

card_event_case_blue.name: card_event_case_blue
card_event_case_blue.title: CASE BLUE
card_event_case_blue.text: Deal 4 damage to target enemy for each unit with 4 or more attack you control.
card_event_case_blue.flavorText: Case Blue (Fall Blau) was a major German military campaign during WWII, launched in the summer of 1942 on the Eastern Front. Its primary goal was to capture the oil fields of the Caucasus and secure economic resources in order to sustain the German war effort. The operation followed the failure to decisively defeat the Soviet Union in 1941 and aimed to destroy Soviet forces in southern Russia. The offensive began in June 1942, with German forces advancing rapidly and capturing key cities like Voronezh. However, the campaign became overstretched, particularly as part of the German Army advanced toward Stalingrad. This led to the eventual encirclement and destruction of the 6th Army during the Battle of Stalingrad, marking a turning point in the war. The failure of Case Blue not only weakened Germany's military strength but also signaled the beginning of the Soviet counteroffensive that would eventually lead to Germany's defeat.

card_event_crossfire.name: card_event_crossfire
card_event_crossfire.title: CROSSFIRE
card_event_crossfire.text: Deal 1 damage to each enemy unit. Repeat this effect if any unit is destroyed.
card_event_crossfire.flavorText: Crossfire is a military tactic in which two or more positions direct intersecting fields of fire on an enemy, creating a deadly zone where advancing troops are exposed from multiple angles. This setup makes it difficult for the enemy to find cover and disrupts their movement, often causing heavy casualties. During WWII, German forces effectively used crossfire to defend strategic points and slow down enemy advances. For example,during the Allied landings in Normandy, German machine gun positions were set up in overlapping fields of fire to cover key approaches, creating kill zones that inflicted significant losses on Allied troops.

card_event_glide_bombing.name: card_event_glide_bombing
card_event_glide_bombing.title: GLIDE BOMBING
card_event_glide_bombing.text: Target unit has 0 attack until your next turn. Draw a card if it is destroyed this turn.
card_event_glide_bombing.flavorText: Glide bombing was an alternative tactic to dive bombing and it involved the use of heavier aircraft which had difficulties recovering from near vertical approaches. This required the use of more sophisticated bombsights and aiming techniques and relied on specialized bomb aimers amongst the aircrew. During WWII the German Luftwaffe used glide bombing tactics with multi-engine aircraft such as the Junkers Ju 88 and the Heinkel He 177.

card_event_run_the_battlefield.name: card_event_run_the_battlefield
card_event_run_the_battlefield.title: RUN THE BATTLEFIELD
card_event_run_the_battlefield.text: For each of your units with 4 or more attack, randomly gain 3 kredits, give it +2+2 or draw a card.
card_event_run_the_battlefield.flavorText: Overall, German generals were often characterized by their aggressiveness, adaptability and frontline presence, which contrasted with the more methodical, organized, and often remote command styles of Allied generals. This approach contributed to early German successes but also led to high casualty rates among German leadership as the war progressed. Notable examples include commanders like Erwin Rommel and Walter Model, who frequently exposed themselves to enemy fire to rally their troops and strengthen defenses. This hands-on leadership style not only boosted soldier morale but also allowed these generals to make rapid, situational adjustments. However, it placed them in greater personal danger and resulted in irreplaceable losses within the German command structure as the war wore on.

card_event_tank_frieda.name: card_event_tank_frieda
card_event_tank_frieda.title: TANK MANEUVER
card_event_tank_frieda.text: Give a friendly tank +2+1. Add AIR SUPPORT to your hand.

card_unit_110_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_110_panzergrenadier
card_unit_110_panzergrenadier.title: 110. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_110_panzergrenadier.text: Your ground units with 4 or more attack deal +3 damage.
card_unit_110_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 110th Panzergrenadier Regiment was part of the 11th Panzer-Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in August 1940 and saw its first action during the Invasion of Yugoslavia in 1941, where it participated in the capture of Belgrade, the capital and largest city of Serbia. The 11th Division was then sent to the Eastern Front where it took part in the Battle of Kiev and the Battle of Moscow as part of the Army Group South. Finally their advance came to a halt and during the Soviet counter-offensive in December 1941 the division had to retreat and fought in defensive operations. In June 1942 the 11th Panzer Division was involved in Case Blue, a failed German strategic offensive with the objective of capturing the oil fields of Baku (Azerbaijan SSR), Grozny and Maikop. After this, the division participated in the failed relief attempt at Stalingrad and defended Rostov, helping German forces retreat from the Caucasus. In July 1943 the division fought in the Battle of Kursk and the defensive operations during the following German retreat. After being trapped in the Korsun-Cherkassy Pocket in February 1944, the division was almost entirely destroyed during its breakout from the pocket. The remains of the division were then sent to France where they fought with Army Group G against the Allied invasion of southern France. The survivors finally surrendered to the US forces in Czechoslovakia in 1945.

card_unit_113_schutzen.name: card_unit_113_schutzen
card_unit_113_schutzen.title: 113. SCHÜTZEN
card_unit_113_schutzen.flavorText: The 113th Schützen-Regiment (riflemen regiment in English) was a unit belonging to the 1st Panzer Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. It was renamed 113th Panzergrenadier-Regiment in 1941. The division participated in the annexation of Austria and the occupation of the Sudetenland in 1938. In 1939, it took part in the invasions of Czechoslovakia and Poland. In 1940, the 1st Panzer Division fought in the Battle of France, seeing combat in Sedan and Dunkirk, and later it participated in the assault on the Weygand Line in northern France. In June 1941, the division joined Operation Barbarossa as part of Army Group North, engaging in intense fighting during the advance towards Leningrad. By October 1941, it was reassigned to Army Group Center to support the advance on Moscow, reaching within 32 km of the city before retreating due to Soviet counterattacks. Throughout the winter of 1942–43, the division participated in defensive operations on the Eastern Front, suffering heavy losses, until it was eventually sent to France for refitting. After an uneventful period in France and later in Greece, the 1st Panzer Division returned to the Eastern Front, where it fought in Kiev, Zhitomir, and Cherkassy. Severely weakened by March 1944, it retreated west, engaging in Poland and Hungary, including an unsuccessful attempt to relieve Budapest. In May 1945, the division surrendered to US forces in southern Bavaria, avoiding Soviet capture.

card_unit_304_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_304_panzergrenadier
card_unit_304_panzergrenadier.title: 304. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_304_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Gets +2+2 if the enemy HQ has taken damage this turn.
card_unit_304_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 304th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a regiment of the 2nd Panzer Division, an armored division of the German Wehrmacht that played a significant role in multiple campaigns during WWII. It was involved in the invasion of Poland in 1939, marking the beginning of the war. In 1940, the division took part in the Battle of France, pushing through the Ardennes and helping encircle Allied forces at Dunkirk. In 1941, it participated in Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the Soviet Union, fighting as part of Army Group Center and advancing deep into Soviet territory. The division saw heavy combat around Moscow but had to retreat in the winter of 1941–42. In 1943, it fought at Kursk, the largest tank battles in history, where it suffered significant losses. Later in the war, the division was transferred to Western Europe to prepare for the Allied invasion. After the D-Day landings in June 1944, it was engaged in the Normandy campaign, fighting against the Allies in France. Later, in late 1944, the division participated in the Battle of the Bulge, a German counteroffensive in the Ardennes which failed to break through Allied lines. By early 1945, the division was heavily depleted but it kept fighting defensively as it retreated into Germany. It ultimately surrendered to US forces in May 1945 as the war came to an end in Europe. The 2nd Panzer Division, like many other German armored divisions, was noted for its aggressive tactics and experienced heavy losses throughout the war.

card_unit_62_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_62_infantry_regiment
card_unit_62_infantry_regiment.title: 62. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_62_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Reduce the operation cost on a friendly unit by 1.
card_unit_62_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 62nd Infantry Regiment was a regiment belonging to the 7th Infantry Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. In 1939 the division was stationed in the Slovak Republic in preparation for the Invasion of Poland. In 1940, it took part in the Battle of France, where it saw action across Belgium and northern France. In June 1941, the 7th Infantry Division joined Operation Barbarossa as part of Army Group North in its push towards Leningrad, but it was later attached to Army Group Center in defensive operations. Over time, the division suffered heavy losses due to continuous Soviet attacks and the harsh winter conditions, but it remained engaged in defensive and retreat actions as German forces were pushed westward. In 1944–45, the division was involved in rear-guard actions as the Soviet Army advanced through Eastern Europe. During the Soviet summer offensive of 1944, the division narrowly escaped destruction when Army Group Center fell apart. It retreated through Poland to the Vistula River line. In January 1945, Soviet forces cut it off during their winter offensive, isolating the division on the Hel Peninsula near Danzig. The division surrendered there on May 8th, 1945.

card_unit_feldhernhalle_rifles.name: card_unit_feldhernhalle_rifles
card_unit_feldhernhalle_rifles.title: FELDHERRNHALLE RIFLES
card_unit_feldhernhalle_rifles.text: Once per turn, gain 2 kredits when you deploy another unit with 4 or more attack.
card_unit_feldhernhalle_rifles.flavorText: The Panzergrenadier Division Feldherrnhalle was a semi-armored formation of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in September 1943 in France and soon after it participated in the forced disarmament of the 8th Italian Army following Italy’s armistice with the Allies. In December 1944 the Feldherrnhalle Division was sent to the Eastern Front where it joined the 3rd Panzer Army of the Army Group Centre, and took up defensive positions near the city of Vitebsk. In February 1944 the division participated in the Battle of Narva, but in May that same year it returned to Army Group Centre where it defended against the Soviet Mogilev Offensive, which was part of Operation Bagration, the Soviet Byelorussian strategic offensive operation. The Feldherrnhalle Division was destroyed in July 1944 during the Soviet Minsk Offensive, then reformed in September 1944 in Hungary, where it was renamed as Panzer-Division Feldherrnhalle. The division was destroyed a second time during the Battle of Budapest, but once again it was recreated as Panzer-Division Feldherrnhalle 1. The remnants of the division surrendered to the Soviets in May 1945 in Czechoslovakia.

card_unit_maus.name: card_unit_maus
card_unit_maus.title: MAUS
card_unit_maus.text: Deployment: Destroy all units with cost 3 or less. Deal 2 damage to an enemy for each.
card_unit_maus.flavorText: Panzerkampfwagen VIII Maus is the heaviest fully enclosed armored fighting vehicle ever built. Weighing 188 tons, it had up to 220mm thick armor. Its main armament was a 128 mm gun firing a 28 kg shell, with a coaxial 75 mm gun as well as a machine gun. Initially it was named Mammut, then it was changed to Mäuschen (little mouse) and finally to Maus. Meaning the largest tank ever built was called mouse. On paper this was a battle winning weapon. Yet it was fraught with problems. The primary issue was to develop an engine and drivetrain powerful enough for such a large and heavy tank, and still fit inside it. The solution was a hybrid drive, using an internal combustion engine to produce electricity powering the motor units driving the tracks. Its top speed was 22 km/h. The second concern was that the Maus immense weight made it unable to use most bridges, which meant it had to ford or submerge in rivers to a depth up to 8 m using a snorkel. In the end only two prototypes were built before all work was stopped in August 1944. After the war the Soviets captured the first hull and mated it with the turret of the second Maus. The sole remaining Maus is now on display at the Kubinka tank Museum.

card_unit_panzer_iii_j_late.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_j_late
card_unit_panzer_iii_j_late.title: PANZER III-J LATE
card_unit_panzer_iii_j_late.text: Becomes Veteran when the enemy HQ has taken 4 or more damage.
card_unit_panzer_iii_j_late.flavorText: The Panzer III Ausf. J was the most common variant of the Panzer III, a German medium tank widely used in WWII. Initially designed as an anti-tank vehicle, it was armed with a 50 mm KwK 38 L/42 gun. Later models were upgraded with a more powerful 50 mm KwK 39 L/60 gun to meet evolving battlefield demands. However, as the war progressed and Germany encountered heavier Soviet tanks like the T-34 and KV-1, the Panzer III-J began to struggle. By 1943, it was largely outclassed on the Eastern Front due to its relatively light armor and limited firepower, especially compared to newer German tanks like the Panzer IV and Panther. As a result, many Panzer III-J tanks were either phased out or relegated to secondary roles, such as infantry support or training. Production of the Panzer III ended in 1943, but the Sturmgeschütz III assault gun, developed from the Panzer III chassis, continued to be manufactured until the end of the war.

card_unit_panzer_iv_h.name: card_unit_panzer_iv_h
card_unit_panzer_iv_h.title: PANZER IV-H
card_unit_panzer_iv_h.text: Deployment: Fight target enemy unit. Becomes Veteran if the enemy unit is destroyed.
card_unit_panzer_iv_h.flavorText: The Panzer IV (Panzerkampfwagen IV) was the main workhorse of the German armored forces during World War II. It fought on every front and was the only German tank in production from the beginning to the end of the war. It saw continuous development and went through a series of upgrades. The Panzer IV-H was the pinnacle of the series as later versions had to be simplified to speed production and due to lack of raw materials.

card_unit_panzer_i_dak.name: card_unit_panzer_i_dak
card_unit_panzer_i_dak.title: PANZER I DAK
card_unit_panzer_i_dak.text: Gets Shock when it moves into the frontline.
card_unit_panzer_i_dak.flavorText: The Panzer I was originally designed as a light training tank in the early 1930s, and its use in combat was limited due to its light armor and weak armaments (two 7.92mm MG13 machine guns). By the time the Afrika Korps was deployed to North Africa in 1941, the Panzer I was considered obsolete as a frontline combat vehicle. Some were converted into mobile artillery units by removing their turret. These mobile artillery units were called Panzerjäger I and equipped with various caliber heavy cannons and some were even used in an anti-tank role. However, a few Panzer I tanks were still used by the Deutsches Afrikakorps (DAK), primarily in a supporting role early in the campaign. These tanks were involved in reconnaissance missions, supply runs, and other non-frontline duties because their armor and firepower were inadequate for direct tank battles, especially against more powerful British and Allied tanks like the Matilda II. The Panzer I's light weight made it relatively mobile in the desert environment, but its combat effectiveness was very limited. It was soon replaced by more advanced tanks like the Panzer III and Panzer IV, which were far better suited to the rigors of desert warfare and the stronger Allied armor they faced.

card_event_advanced_reich_research.name: card_event_advanced_reich_research
card_event_advanced_reich_research.title: ADVANCED REICH R&D
card_event_advanced_reich_research.text: Choose one - add TYPE XXI U-BOAT to hand OR add URANPROJEKT to hand.

card_event_entrapment.name: card_event_entrapment
card_event_entrapment.title: ENTRAPMENT
card_event_entrapment.text: When a unit attacks, destroy it. Your units get +1+1.
card_event_entrapment.flavorText: During the opening stages of WWII the German Blitzkrieg operations focused on breaking through the enemies line of defence by using short, fast and powerful attacks by motorized force. The aim was to knock holes in the enemy defensive lines, to set up objectives in the rear and encircle the enemy. During the early phases of the war this proved to be a successful tactic and resulted in the entrapment of large pockets of Allied troops and equipment which could easily be finished off. These tactics proved successful in the Invasion of Poland, the invasion of the low countries and France. At the start of Operation Barbarossa Blitzkrieg tactics resulted in huge encirclements that ended in heavy losses for the Red Army, with nearly 3.5 million prisoners of war being taken along with masses of equipment.

card_event_expanded_reich_research.name: card_event_expanded_reich_research
card_event_expanded_reich_research.title: EXPANDED REICH R&D
card_event_expanded_reich_research.text: Choose one - add SYNTHETIC OIL to hand OR add ADVANCED REICH R&D to hand.

card_event_lightning_strike.name: card_event_lightning_strike
card_event_lightning_strike.title: LIGHTNING STRIKE
card_event_lightning_strike.text: When the enemy draws an extra card, deal 4 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_event_lightning_strike.flavorText: The Battle of Britain began in 1940 and the Germans started with air attacks on British shipping, ports and military installations. Luftwaffe’s aim was to destroy RAF, which they came close to doing several times in the summer of 1940, not least when they attacked the visible and vital radar masts at key airfields. Hitler had ordered that London should not be bombed except on his orders, but due to a mistake bombs were dropped on the capital. In retaliation the British bombed Berlin and from then on the Luftwaffe started daily raids on British cities. The Blitz had started. Some historians argue that this change in strategy turned the tides in the Battle of Britain, the attacks on airfields halted and this gave RAF the breathing space it needed to establish air superiority over Britain.

card_event_rally.name: card_event_rally
card_event_rally.title: RALLY
card_event_rally.text: Your units get +1 attack this turn. Remove Pin on them. Draw a card.
card_event_rally.flavorText: By 1944 it was clear that Germany had lost the war, but for several reasons the soldiers kept on fighting. For Hitler and millions of his countrymen, unconditional surrender against the Allies was not an option and this is what kept many fighting. Blind loyalty to the nazi leadership was a reason for many to fight, some even believed in a final German victory. Others fought for their comrades or to protect civilians, but many were also affected by tireless propaganda, directed by Goebbels, about the potential horrors of a Bolshevik occupation. The German soldiers were also very much aware of the atrocities they and their comrades had committed on the Eastern Front. Fears of Soviet reprisal against prisoners of war kept them fighting. During the final days of the war there were also rumours spreading among the nazi leadership and the German armed forces that Britain and US would change sides and join their fight against Soviet Union, but this was sheer fantasy.

card_event_rapid_engagement.name: card_event_rapid_engagement
card_event_rapid_engagement.title: RAPID ENGAGEMENT
card_event_rapid_engagement.text: Remove a friendly unit from the battlefield, then return it and give it Blitz.
card_event_rapid_engagement.flavorText: According to his opponents, Rommel seemed to anticipate his enemy’s actions, and his lightning-fast offensives caught them completely off balance. Even though Rommel’s reputation as a military genius is questioned today, it is a fact that he managed to lead the Afrika Korps to victory on several occasions in the North Africa Campaign, despite numerical inferiority. He repeatedly managed to outflank his British and Commonwealth opponents and managed to push them across the vast North African desert, from Libya to the Egyptian frontier, in a series of audacious assaults.

card_event_reich_research.name: card_event_reich_research
card_event_reich_research.title: REICH RESEARCH
card_event_reich_research.text: Choose one - add V-1 FLYING BOMB to hand OR add EXPANDED REICH R&D to hand.
card_event_reich_research.flavorText: At the start of WWII Germany had a leading edge in industrialized and technological warfare. At the start of the war they had also been researching nuclear energy for the war effort, but in 1941, they decided to abandon its nuclear program and focus on the development of other new technologies that had a more immediate impact. This included the Sturmgewehr 44, the first mass produced assault rifle, the V-1 flying bomb, the Me 262 and the Arado 234 jet engined aircraft, but with all these it was a case of “too little, too late” and didn’t really affect the outcome of the war. Furthermore, as the war prolonged chemistry research and development became vital as Germany became increasingly isolated from raw materials during WWII. Chemists started developing techniques for producing synthetic alternatives to rubber and petrol and Chemical expertise was required to set up and run factories for these products.

card_event_sea_hunters.name: card_event_sea_hunters
card_event_sea_hunters.title: NIGHT HUNTERS
card_event_sea_hunters.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, destroy it. Draw a card.
card_event_sea_hunters.flavorText: Intercepting bombers at night was a demanding and risky mission during WWII. It required carrying heavy armament and a primitive radar, plus being fast enough to catch the enemy aircraft, which could only be done with two engines aircraft.  The German Luftwaffe deployed a few night fighters during the war,  the Messerschmitt Bf-110G, the Junker Ju-88G6, the Dornier Do-217J and the Heinkel He-219A Uhu (Owl). Towards the end of the war, a night fighting version of the Me-262 was used.

card_event_synthetic_oil.name: card_event_synthetic_oil
card_event_synthetic_oil.title: SYNTHETIC OIL
card_event_synthetic_oil.text: Gain 10 additional kredits and draw an extra card next turn.

card_event_type_xxi_boat.name: card_event_type_xxi_boat
card_event_type_xxi_boat.title: TYPE XXI U-BOAT
card_event_type_xxi_boat.text: Destroy target unit. Enemy discards 2 cards.

card_event_uranium_club.name: card_event_uranium_club
card_event_uranium_club.title: URANPROJEKT
card_event_uranium_club.text: Destroy all enemy units. Gain 1 kredit for each unit destroyed.

card_event_u_16.name: card_event_u_16
card_event_u_16.title: U-16
card_event_u_16.text: Retreat target unit. Draw a card if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_event_u_16.flavorText: The U-16 was a Type IIB u-boat that was launched in 1936 and used by the German Kriegsmarine during WWII as part of the 3rd U-boat Flotilla. In 1939 the submarine took part in laying mines in and around the English Channel and managed to sink a couple of merchant ships. In October 1939 the U-16 was attacked by the Royal Navy in the Dover Strait, and while trying to escape depth charges from both ships it ran aground on a sandbank in the North Sea and was lost with all hands.

card_event_v1_flying_bomb.name: card_event_v1_flying_bomb
card_event_v1_flying_bomb.title: V-1 FLYING BOMB
card_event_v1_flying_bomb.text: Destroy target unit with cost 3 or less.

card_unit_54_jager_regiment.name: card_unit_54_jager_regiment
card_unit_54_jager_regiment.title: 56. JÄGER REGIMENT
card_unit_54_jager_regiment.flavorText: The 56th Jäger Regiment, formally known as 56th Infantry Regiment, was formed in France 1941. The regiment was placed under the 5th Light Division and then in July 1942 the name was changed to 5th Jäger Division. The division fought on the Eastern Front from where it would retreat back to Germany in 1944. In 1945 the division fought in defensive battles in Germany and surrendered to the Red Army near Oder River during the Battle of Berlin. Jäger divisions (Jäger means hunter in German) of the Wehrmacht were highly trained and used to operate where smaller units were needed, in rough terrain, foothills, urban areas, and were more heavily equipped than mountain divisions. At the start of the war Jäger divisions had three regiments, but by 1942 they were downsized to two.

card_unit_5_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_5_panzergrenadier
card_unit_5_panzergrenadier.title: 5. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_5_panzergrenadier.text: Pincer: After this unit attacks and survives combat, your other units with an active Pincer get +1+1.
card_unit_5_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 5th Panzergrenadier regiment was part of the 12th Panzer Division which was an armored division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. In 1941 the division participated in Operation Barbarossa, and as part of Army Group North it participated in the drive towards Leningrad where it suffered heavy casualties in the Soviet Counteroffensive of 1941-42. The division participated in the Battle of Kursk in 1943 and was eventually entrapped in the Courland Pocket during Operation Bagration in 1944, where it surrendered to the Red Army in May 1945.

card_unit_81_infanterie_regiment.name: card_unit_81_infanterie_regiment
card_unit_81_infanterie_regiment.title: 81. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_81_infanterie_regiment.text: Has +3 attack against HQs and units with Guard.
card_unit_81_infanterie_regiment.flavorText: The 81st Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 15th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht that was formed in 1934 and stayed active until the end of WWII. The division fought in the Battle of France and in 1941 it was transferred to the Eastern Front where it joined the XXXV Army Corps of Army Group Centre. After that the 15th Infantry Division fought in numerous battles and campaigns on the Eastern Front, including the Battle of Smolensk, the Battle of Moscow, the Third Battle of Kharkov, and finally in Romania during the Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive of 1944 where the division was destroyed. The division was reformed in 1944 and fought the remainder of the war in Hungary and in Slovakia where they finally surrendered to Soviet troops.

card_unit_87_grenadier.name: card_unit_87_grenadier
card_unit_87_grenadier.title: 87. GRENADIER
card_unit_87_grenadier.text: Give +2+2 when the enemy triggers your countermeasure.
card_unit_87_grenadier.flavorText: The 87th Grenadier Regiment was a unit of the 36th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division participated in the invasion of France and later in Operation Barbarossa as part of the XXXXI Panzer Corps of the Army Group North. The division participated in various battles and operations on the Eastern Front and in the summer of 1944 during Operation Bagration the division was largely destroyed. The division was reformed in France later that year, and renamed to 36th Volksgrenadier Division, and would defend against the Allied advance in France, Luxembourg and the Saarland. The division ended the war defending against Patton’s 3rd Army in central Germany.

card_unit_bloom_and_voss.name: card_unit_bloom_and_voss
card_unit_bloom_and_voss.title: BLOHM & VOSS BV 138
card_unit_bloom_and_voss.text: Draw a card when the enemy triggers your countermeasure.
card_unit_bloom_and_voss.flavorText: The Blohm & Voss BV 138 Seedrache (e. Sea Dragon) was a German flying boat that was used by the Luftwaffe during WWII as a naval patrol and reconnaissance aircraft. The aircraft was produced in 1938-1943 and the standard variants had an armament of two 20 mm MG 151/20 cannons, up to three 7.92 mm MG 15 machine guns and finally a 13 mm MG 131 machine gun. Some had specialized roles such as a minesweeping variant that carried a magnetic field generating degaussing equipment and an anti-shipping variant that was fitted with a maritime search radar. A total of 297 aircraft were built, including a few variants.

card_unit_fw_190_f.name: card_unit_fw_190_f
card_unit_fw_190_f.title: FW 190 JAGDBOMBER
card_unit_fw_190_f.text: Deployment: Send an enemy ground unit to hand.
card_unit_fw_190_f.flavorText: The Fw 190 A Jagdbomber, aka Jabo, was a German fighter-bomber variant of the Fw 190 Würger fighter. The Fw 190 A series included many variants, but the first Jagdbomber was the Fw 190 A-3/U3 which could carry up to 500 kg of bombs or a standard Luftwaffe drop tank. The Jagdbombers were also heavily armed, with a 7.92 mm MG 17 in the fuselage and two 20 mm MG 151 cannons mounted in the wings. In 1942, the first Jagdbombers were operating over Britain and they reached the Eastern Front in time to bomb Soviet positions in Stalingrad and later they were used successfully in the Battle of Kursk.

card_unit_fw_200_condor.name: card_unit_fw_200_condor
card_unit_fw_200_condor.title: FW 200 CONDOR
card_unit_fw_200_condor.text: Deployment: Cannot attack the enemy HQ this turn.
card_unit_fw_200_condor.flavorText: The Focke-Wulf Fw 200 Condor was a German four engined aircraft, developed as a long range airliner in 1937. During WWII military versions were put into service by the Luftwaffe and the Japanese Navy Air force as a long range reconnaissance aircraft, but also as an anti-shipping, maritime patrol bomber and transport aircraft. The FW 200 was also known to the Allies as the Courier and Churchill called it the "Scourge of the Atlantic" due to its contribution to the heavy Allied shipping losses during the Battle of Atlantic. The aircraft was manufactured between 1937-1944 and 276 were built, including quite a few variants.

card_unit_me_410_hornisse.name: card_unit_me_410_hornisse
card_unit_me_410_hornisse.title: ME 410 HORNISSE
card_unit_me_410_hornisse.text: At the start of your turn, draw a card. Deal damage equal to its cost to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_me_410_hornisse.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Me 410 Hornisse (e. Hornet) was a German heavy fighter, used by the Luftwaffe in WWII. The aircraft was produced from 1943 to 1944 and was an improved version of the Me 220 that was renamed to Me 410. Shortly after the Me 410 came into service it was used against British aircraft and was moderately successful against unescorted bombers. Later it would be used as a bomber destroyer but it proved to be extremely vulnerable against British and American fighters. In 1944 production ceased and the Me 410 would be used in reconnaissance missions only. In total 1,160 units were produced, including a few variants.

card_unit_pak_40.name: card_unit_pak_40
card_unit_pak_40.title: PAK 40
card_unit_pak_40.text: Deployment: Destroy target enemy unit that costs 2 or less. Draw a card if it is a tank.
card_unit_pak_40.flavorText: The 7.5 cm Pak 40 was German anti-tank gun that was used by the Wehrmacht and their allies during WWII. The gun was produced from 1942 to 1945, with 23,303 units built, and it became the main German anti-tank gun for the latter part of WWII. It was mostly towed or used on a number of tank destroyers, but a variant was made that could be vehicle-mounted. The Pak 40 was very effective against almost every Allied tank, and could fire up to 14 rounds per minute, but it had some problems with penetrating some of the Allied late war heavy tanks.

card_unit_panzer_35t_commander.name: card_unit_panzer_35t_commander
card_unit_panzer_35t_commander.title: Pz. BEFEHLSWAGEN 35t
card_unit_panzer_35t_commander.text: If this unit is in hand, add it to the frontline when you take it.
card_unit_panzer_35t_commander.flavorText: The Panzerbefehlswagen 35(t) was a command tank variant of the Panzer 35(t) light tank, which was a Czechoslovakian design, but mainly used by the Germans during WWII. The tank had a crew of 4, a main armament of a 3.7 cm (1.5 in) KwK 34(t) gun and 2 x 7.92 mm MG 37(t) machine guns a secondary armament. The German command tank version carried less ammunition to make room for an extra radio and a gyrocompass and it could be recognized by the radio antenna mounted on the rear deck that looks like a fence. 434 Panzer 35(t) tanks were built between 1936-1940.

card_unit_panzer_iii_f.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_f
card_unit_panzer_iii_f.title: PANZER III-F
card_unit_panzer_iii_f.text: Your German tanks have Blitz. Deployment: Your other tanks get +1+1.
card_unit_panzer_iii_f.flavorText: The Panzer III, or Panzerkampfwagen III, was a German medium tank that was used by the Axis during WWII. The tank was first used in service in 1939 and used throughout the war, but production was halted in 1943 when more powerful anti tank guns were needed against the Soviet T-34 tank. The Panzer III-F was one of many variants and was the first one to be mass produced, with 450 tanks built, and was used in all theaters of the war. The tank had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner), a secondary armament of  2–3 × 7.92 mm Maschinengewehr 34 and a main armament of a 3.7 cm KwK 36 gun, but later models were mounted with a 5 cm KwK 38 gun.

card_unit_stug_iii_g_schurzen.name: card_unit_stug_iii_g_schurzen
card_unit_stug_iii_g_schurzen.title: STUG III G SCHÜRZEN
card_unit_stug_iii_g_schurzen.flavorText: The Stug III, full name Sturmgeschütz III, was a German assault gun built on the chassis of the Panzer III tank and the second most produced German armored vehicle during WWII, after the Sd.Kfz. 251 half-track. It was designed as a mobile assault gun for infantry support, but with later modifications it was also used as a tank destroyer. The Stug III G variant had an improved superstructure design and the addition of side-mounted armor (Schürzen) for protection against anti-tank rifles and hollow-charge ammunition. In early Stug III versions armor was retrofitted, but this proved inadequate and later versions would have an improved side-mounted armor.

card_event_maelstrom.name: card_event_maelstrom
card_event_maelstrom.title: MAELSTROM
card_event_maelstrom.text: Deal 4 damage to each non-Veteran unit.
card_event_maelstrom.flavorText: In a military context, a "maelstrom" is a chaotic and violent situation characterized by intense fighting and confusion. The term is often used to describe a battle or conflict where opposing forces are engaged in close-quarters combat, with soldiers and equipment moving rapidly and unpredictably in all directions. A good example is the Battle of Kursk which was a massive tank battle that took place in the summer of 1943, and was a major turning point in WWII. The Germans launched a major offensive against the Soviet Union, but the Red Army was prepared for the attack. The resulting battle involved thousands of tanks and other armored vehicles, and was characterized by intense fighting and confusion as both sides tried to gain the upper hand. Additionally the air-to-air and air-to-ground combat was intense, with the Soviet air force successfully defending against the German bombing campaign, resulting in chaotic low-altitude air battles. The battle ended with Soviet victory and the Germans were eventually forced to withdraw from the region, which marked a significant turning point in the Eastern Front.

card_event_momentum.name: card_event_momentum
card_event_momentum.title: MOMENTUM
card_event_momentum.text: Add two PANZER I-B to the frontline if it is not enemy controlled.
card_event_momentum.flavorText: During the early stages of WWII, Germany experienced significant military momentum, achieving several swift and decisive victories on the European continent. In 1939, Germany invaded Poland, prompting Britain and France to declare war. In 1940, Germany launched a series of lightning offensives, conquering Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium, and France in just a few months. Of course losing the Battle of Britain was a major blowback for the German war machine, but up until that moment they seemed to be invincible and their tactics were characterized by speed, surprise, and a devastating combination of tanks, infantry, and air power. However, Germany's early successes would ultimately be unsustainable as they faced increasing resistance from allied forces and were eventually defeated.

card_event_protect_the_pocket.name: card_event_protect_the_pocket
card_event_protect_the_pocket.title: PROTECT THE POCKET
card_event_protect_the_pocket.text: Draw 4 cards. If you have 4+ units with active Pincer, end the next enemy turn immediately.
card_event_protect_the_pocket.flavorText: In military context, the term "pocket" is often used to describe a situation where a group of enemy forces become encircled and cut off from their main force, or are trapped in a confined geographic area, often resulting in their capture or defeat. For example, in 1944, the Allied forces in Europe were able to create a pocket around German forces in the Falaise region of Normandy, France, by encircling them and preventing them from escaping. Earlier Hitler had refused to allow the German forces to withdraw and instead ordered him to conduct Operation Lüttich, a counter-offensive at Mortain against the US. Despite objections from his generals, Hitler insisted on the attack, but the four depleted panzer divisions involved were insufficient to defeat the Allied armies. As a result, the Germans were driven deeper into the Allied envelopment, ultimately leading to their defeat  The battle of the Falaise pocket resulted in the destruction of most of the German Army Group B west of the Seine, which opened the way to Paris and the Franco-German border.

card_event_rout.name: card_event_rout
card_event_rout.title: ROUT
card_event_rout.text: Convert target unit with cost 2 or less into ROUTED TROOPS.
card_event_rout.flavorText: Some notable examples of Germany routing their enemies in WWII happened in the early stages during the Invasion of Poland (1939), France and the Low Countries (1940), the Balkan Campaign (1941)  and the early stages of the invasion of the Soviet Union (1941). Throughout the war it is estimated that the Germans took as many as 5.7 million prisoners of war plus large quantities of military equipment. The captured equipment was used to supplement their own military forces and equip their allies, but as the war progressed, it became increasingly difficult to maintain and repair, and many pieces of equipment fell into disuse or were abandoned.

card_event_support_column.name: card_event_support_column
card_event_support_column.title: SUPPORT COLUMN
card_event_support_column.text: Give a unit: "Adjacent ground units have +1 attack and operate for 1 less."
card_event_support_column.flavorText: In a military context, a support column typically refers to a convoy of vehicles and personnel that provide logistical support to troops engaged in combat operations. The support column may transport supplies, ammunition, food, water, fuel, and medical equipment to the troops in the field. The support column is a critical element of military operations because it ensures that troops have the resources they need to sustain themselves and carry out their missions. Without a reliable support column, troops may become vulnerable to enemy attacks and may not be able to operate effectively for an extended period of time.

card_unit_101_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_101_infantry_regiment
card_unit_101_infantry_regiment.title: 101. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_101_infantry_regiment.text: Pincer: Gets +1+1 when this unit attacks.
card_unit_101_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 101st Infantry Regiment was a component of the 14th Infantry Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. In 1939 the division was deployed to Poland during the invasion. After the Polish campaign, the division was transferred to the Western Front, where it participated in the invasion of France in 1940. In 1941 the division was assigned to the Ninth Army and Army Group Centre and during Operation Barbarossa, the division was involved in the encirclement of Minsk. In 1943 the division suffered heavy losses during the Battles of Rzhev and during the defense against the Soviet summer counter-offensive called Operation Suvorov.. In 1944, the division was transferred to 3rd Panzer Army and was used as a reserve formation by Army Group Centre. The division was rushed into the line in a desperate attempt to hold back the breakthrough of several Soviet divisions during Operation Bagration, where again it suffered heavy losses and only a handful of troops were able to retreat to the German lines. By the end of the year, the remainder of the division was transferred to the Second Army and were in the area of Ostrolenka, Poland. During the Soviet East Prussian Offensive of January 1945, the rebuilt 14th Infantry Division was pushed north and trapped in the Heiligenbeil pocket, where it attempted a breakout before falling back on Braunsberg. The division was eventually destroyed in the fighting, with most of its surviving troops entering Soviet captivity, while a few were evacuated via the Frisches Haff.

card_unit_119_grenadier.name: card_unit_119_grenadier
card_unit_119_grenadier.title: 119. GRENADIER
card_unit_119_grenadier.text: Becomes Veteran if you control 35. GRENADIER.
card_unit_119_grenadier.flavorText: Both the 35th and 119th Panzergrenadier Regiments were part of the 25th Panzergrenadier Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. Originally formed as the 25th Infantry Division, it participated in the Polish Campaign and the Battle of France. In 1940, it was reorganized as the 25th motorized infantry division and joined Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the Soviet Union. After two years of fighting in the Soviet Union, it became the 25th Panzergrenadier Division in 1943. The division faced heavy losses during battles, including the near destruction near Minsk in 1944. Survivors were reorganized as the 107th Panzer Brigade, which participated in Operation Market Garden. In November 1944, the brigade regained divisional status and became the 25th Panzergrenadier Division again. It fought a delaying action against the US Third Army in France and defended the Maginot Line fortifications. The division also took part in Operation Nordwind which was the last major German offensive on the Western Front. After the failed German offensive the division was sent to defend against the Soviet attack on the Oder north of Berlin. Afterwards many survivors of the division managed to escape to the west and surrender to British or American forces.

card_unit_35_grenadier.name: card_unit_35_grenadier
card_unit_35_grenadier.title: 35. GRENADIER
card_unit_35_grenadier.text: Becomes Veteran if you control 119. GRENADIER.
card_unit_35_grenadier.flavorText: Both the 35th and 119th Panzergrenadier Regiments were part of the 25th Panzergrenadier Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. Originally formed as the 25th Infantry Division, it participated in the Polish Campaign and the Battle of France. In 1940, it was reorganized as the 25th motorized infantry division and joined Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the Soviet Union. After two years of fighting in the Soviet Union, it became the 25th Panzergrenadier Division in 1943. The division faced heavy losses during battles, including the near destruction near Minsk in 1944. Survivors were reorganized as the 107th Panzer Brigade, which participated in Operation Market Garden. In November 1944, the brigade regained divisional status and became the 25th Panzergrenadier Division again. It fought a delaying action against the US Third Army in France and defended the Maginot Line fortifications. The division also took part in Operation Nordwind which was the last major German offensive on the Western Front. After the failed German offensive the division was sent to defend against the Soviet attack on the Oder north of Berlin. Afterwards many survivors of the division managed to escape to the west and surrender to British or American forces.

card_unit_39_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_39_panzergrenadier
card_unit_39_panzergrenadier.title: 39. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_39_panzergrenadier.text: Has +2 attack while in the frontline. Deployment: Swap a position with a friendly unit.
card_unit_39_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 39th Panzer Grenadier Regiment was a unit of the 17th Panzer Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in November 1940 from the 27th Infantry Division, The division unit participated in Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, and during the harsh winter of 1941-1942, it played a crucial role in the Battle of Moscow. In November 1942, the division was deployed to the southern sector of the Eastern Front, taking part in Operation Winter Storm, a failed attempt to relieve the encircled troops at Stalingrad. Remaining in reserve during the Battle of Kursk in 1943, the division subsequently conducted a strategic retreat through Ukraine and Poland, eventually concluding the war in Czechoslovakia.

card_unit_50_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_50_infantry_regiment
card_unit_50_infantry_regiment.title: 50. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_50_infantry_regiment.text: Becomes Veteran when it moves into the frontline.
card_unit_50_infantry_regiment.flavorText: At the start of WWII the 50th Infantry Regiment was part of the 3rd Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht which took part in the invasion of Poland in 1939 and the invasion of France in 1940. In 1941 the regiment was transferred to the 111th Infantry Division to participate in Operation Barbarossa as part of Army Group South. The division fought around Kiev where it helped to trap and destroy the Soviet 37th Army before pushing eastwards. After the capture of Russian city Rostov-on-Don in 1941 they were forced to retreat and take up defensive positions. After some rest the 111th Infantry Division joined operation Case Blue with the 17th Army, which was a German summer offensive in 1942 with the goal of securing the Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus. Case Blue was a failure and ended with the withdrawal of the German forces and the 111th Division took up defensive positions which lasted until July 1943. After the German defeat at the Battle of Kursk in the summer of 1943 the division gradually rolled back to the west, defending various areas until it was eventually destroyed while defending Crimea. The last remnants were evacuated by ship in May 1944, and the division was disbanded.

card_unit_7_schutzen.name: card_unit_7_schutzen
