card_unit_7_schutzen.title: 7. SCHÜTZEN
card_unit_7_schutzen.text: Becomes Veteran when it attacks and destroys a unit.
card_unit_7_schutzen.flavorText: The 7th Schützen Regiment was an infantry regiment of the 7th Panzer Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division achieved notable victories in France in 1940 under Rommel's command, and later in the Soviet Union in 1941 under the command of Generalmajor Hans von Funck. However, in May 1942, it was withdrawn from the Soviet Union and sent back to France for replenishment and rearmament after suffering losses. Following the defeat at Stalingrad, the division returned to the Eastern Front and played a crucial role in defensive battles as part of Army Group Don, under General Erich von Manstein. It also participated in the counterattack at Kharkov. The 7th Panzer Division faced significant challenges during the unsuccessful offensive at Kursk in the summer of 1943, resulting in heavy casualties and equipment losses. The subsequent Soviet counteroffensive further weakened the division's strength. From 1944 to 1945, the division remained understrength and engaged in a series of defensive battles along the eastern front. It was forced to evacuate twice by sea, abandoning its remaining heavy equipment each time. After engaging in defensive actions across Prussia and Northern Germany, the surviving soldiers eventually sought refuge in the forest and surrendered to the British Army northwest of Berlin in May 1945.

card_unit_list_regiment.name: card_unit_list_regiment
card_unit_list_regiment.title: LIST REGIMENT
card_unit_list_regiment.text: Deployment: If you control the frontline, target enemy unit must retreat.
card_unit_list_regiment.flavorText: The 19th Grenadier Regiment, given the honorific title “Infanterie-Regiment List '' in 1944, was an infantry regiment of the 7th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. In 1938, the 7th Division participated in the occupation of Austria. During the 1939 Polish Campaign, it fought under XVII Army Corps, engaging Polish forces and advancing eastwards. In the French campaign of 1940, the division served as a diversionary force against the French and British. It fought against the British Expeditionary Force and took up positions on the eastern section of the German lines near Lille. After the Dunkirk Pocket was eliminated, the division was placed in reserve. During Operation Barbarossa, the division fought in the siege of Mogilev and participated in the unsuccessful thrust towards Moscow in December 1941. It spent 1942 in the central sector of the Eastern Front and joined the Kursk offensive in July 1943. In 1944, it conducted a fighting retreat through Poland to the Vistula line. In January 1945, it found itself isolated on the Hela peninsula and surrendered to the Allied forces on May 8, 1945.

card_unit_me_bf_109_brothers.name: card_unit_me_bf_109_brothers
card_unit_me_bf_109_brothers.title: ME BF 109 G
card_unit_me_bf_109_brothers.text: Pincer: When this unit attacks and destroys a unit, gain a kredit and draw a card.
card_unit_me_bf_109_brothers.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Bf 109 G was a German fighter aircraft that was primarily used during WWII. It was an improved version of the earlier Bf 109 F model and was introduced into service in 1942. The Bf 109 G was powered by a Daimler-Benz DB 605 engine, and a GM-1 nitrous oxide power boost, which produced up to 1,475 horsepower. It had a top speed of around 685 km/h (426 mph) and a range of approximately 850 km (528 miles). The armament of the Bf 109 G variant typically included one MG 151/20 20mm cannon and two 7.92mm MG 17 machine guns. Some later variants of the Bf 109 G also included additional armament, such as rockets or an underwing gondola cannon kit. One of the notable features of the Bf 109 G was its improved aerodynamics and performance, which made it faster and more agile than earlier versions. It was also equipped with advanced radio and navigation equipment, which made it well-suited for both bomber escort and ground-attack missions. The Bf 109 G saw extensive service on all fronts of the war and was flown by some of the top German aces of the war, including Erich Hartmann and Gerhard Barkhorn. It remained in service until the end of the war, and over 33,000 Bf 109s of all variants were produced, making it one of the most successful fighter aircraft in history.

card_unit_me_bf_110_brothers.name: card_unit_me_bf_110_brothers
card_unit_me_bf_110_brothers.title: ME BF 110 E
card_unit_me_bf_110_brothers.text: Deployment: Gets Blitz if you control the frontline.
card_unit_me_bf_110_brothers.flavorText: The Bf 110 E Zerstörer 4 was a variant of the Messerschmitt Bf 110 twin-engine heavy fighter aircraft used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. It was a development of the Bf 110C variant and was introduced into service in 1941. The Bf 110E Zerstörer 4 was designed as a long-range fighter-bomber, capable of engaging both ground targets and enemy aircraft. It was armed with two 20mm MG FF/M cannon and four 7.92mm MG 17 machine guns, and up to 1,200 kg (2,650 lb) bombload. The Bf 110 E was powered by two Daimler-Benz DB 601 engines which allowed the aircraft to achieve a top speed of around 560 km/h (348 mph) at 6,000 meters (19,685 feet) altitude. One of the main differences between the Bf 110 E series and earlier Bf 110 variants was the improved armor protection for the pilot and crew, as well as for the engines and fuel tanks. The aircraft also had an improved cockpit layout, which provided better visibility for the pilot. The Bf 110 E was used extensively in the ground-attack role, particularly in the Eastern Front where it was used to attack Soviet armored columns and ground targets. It was also used for long-range fighter missions, including bomber escort duties. Overall, the Bf 110 was a versatile and capable aircraft that played an important role in the Luftwaffe's arsenal during WWII. Its combination of heavy firepower and long range made it a formidable opponent for both ground and air targets, and it is still considered an iconic aircraft of the war.

card_unit_panzer_i_brothers.name: card_unit_panzer_i_brothers
card_unit_panzer_i_brothers.title: PANZER I-B
card_unit_panzer_i_brothers.text: Becomes Veteran when it damages the enemy HQ.
card_unit_panzer_i_brothers.flavorText: The Panzer I-B, aka Panzerkampfwagen I Ausf.B,  was a light tank developed by Germany in the 1930s, and it was an improved version of the Panzer I-A tank. The Panzer I-B was armed with a 7.92mm machine gun and had a crew of two. It had a top speed of 40 km/h (25 mph) and a range of around 150 km (93 mi). The Panzer I-B was produced between 1934 and 1935, with approximately 400 units built, including variants. It saw action in the Spanish Civil War and the early stages of WWII. However, due to its light armor and inadequate armament, it was quickly outdated and outclassed by newer tank designs. As a result, the Panzer I-B was gradually phased out of service and replaced by more advanced tanks such as the Panzer II. Overall, the Panzer I-B played a limited role in WWII, but it was an important step in the development of German tank technology and helped pave the way for future designs.

card_unit_stuka_brothers.name: card_unit_stuka_brothers
card_unit_stuka_brothers.title: STUKA 87G
card_unit_stuka_brothers.text: Becomes Veteran after an enemy ground unit is destroyed.
card_unit_stuka_brothers.flavorText: The Ju 87G was a variant of the Junkers Ju 87 Stuka dive bomber that came into service in 1943 and was used by the German Luftwaffe throughout WWII. The G variant was primarily designed as an anti-tank aircraft and it featured two Bordkanone BK 3,7 cannons mounted under the wings in gun pods. These cannons fired high-explosive armor-piercing rounds that were primarily effective against lightly armored or unarmored targets. The gun's effectiveness was limited against heavily armored tanks, but to compensate for this the pilots often attacked tanks from above or from the rear, where the armor was usually thinner. The gun pods were removable and could be replaced with ordinary bomb racks that could carry a 1,000 kg (2,200 lb) bomb load, which meant that the G variant could be used in other ground attack roles. In addition the G variant came with an enhanced armor protection that safeguarded the crew against ground fire. This was copied from the Soviet made Ilyushin Il-2 Sturmovik.

card_event_blitz_doctrine.name: card_event_blitz_doctrine
card_event_blitz_doctrine.title: BLITZ DOCTRINE
card_event_blitz_doctrine.text: Develop a German light tank. Add CONTEST DOCTRINE to your hand.
card_event_blitz_doctrine.flavorText: The Aufklärungsabteilung units of the German Wehrmacht, or reconnaissance battalions, were the eyes and ears of the advancing German forces and a vital part of the blitzkrieg doctrine.These units were equipped with armored cars, motorcycles, and sometimes light tanks, and they were tasked with scouting ahead of the main force to gather vital intelligence on enemy positions, troop movements, and terrain features. Their operations allowed the German command to make informed decisions in real-time and to adjust their strategies and exploit weaknesses in the enemy lines. The intelligence provided by these units were key to the Blitzkrieg's success, as it enabled the Germans to rapidly concentrate their forces at decisive points and to achieve breakthroughs in their attacks.

card_event_bridge_too_far.name: card_event_bridge_too_far
card_event_bridge_too_far.title: A BRIDGE TOO FAR
card_event_bridge_too_far.text: At the end of the enemy turn, add a PANZER III-J to the frontline if possible. Otherwise, destroy all units there.
card_event_bridge_too_far.flavorText: “A bridge too far” is an idiom inspired by Operation Market Garden, which refers to the act of overreaching, made popular by the 1977 movie of the same name. Operation Market Garden was an ambitious Allied attempt to secure key bridges in the Netherlands and open a route into Germany, but it failed due to a combination of factors. The Germans, despite being outnumbered and surprised by the initial airborne landings, were able to regroup and mount a fierce defense. The terrain, with its rivers and canals, hindered the Allied advance and allowed the Germans to concentrate their forces. Furthermore, communication breakdowns and logistical issues hampered the Allies ability to reinforce their paratroopers, who were eventually defeated by the German counterattack at Arnhem. The German defense, and the tactical errors on the Allied side, resulted in a costly defeat and prolonged the war in Europe.

card_event_contest_doctrine.name: card_event_contest_doctrine
card_event_contest_doctrine.title: CONTEST DOCTRINE
card_event_contest_doctrine.text: Develop a German medium or heavy tank. Your HQ gets: "Tanks you deploy this battle get +1+1."

card_event_foiled_plans.name: card_event_foiled_plans
card_event_foiled_plans.title: FOILED PLANS
card_event_foiled_plans.text: When the enemy gives an order, deal damage to the enemy HQ equal to its cost.
card_event_foiled_plans.flavorText: The Battle of Kursk in July 1943 marked a turning point on the Eastern Front. Germany had hopes for a decisive victory in Operation Citadel, an offensive proposed by Generalfeldmarschall Manstein, which aimed at encircling and destroying Soviet forces in Kursk. However, Soviet intelligence, aided by Britain, had intercepted German communications, decrypted messages and uncovered the German intentions months in advance. The Red Army prepared extensive defenses which included minefields, fortifications, artillery fire zones and anti-tank strong pointsthat covered approximately 300 km. When the offensive began, the Germans faced a formidable obstacle. The supposed element of surprise was quickly lost, and the battle turned into a brutal war of attrition. Though the Germans made some gains, they were unable to achieve a breakthrough. The Soviets eventually launched a counteroffensive, pushing the Germans back and inflicting heavy losses.

card_event_hit_the_drop_point.name: card_event_hit_the_drop_point
card_event_hit_the_drop_point.title: HIT THE DROP POINT
card_event_hit_the_drop_point.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, suppress it. Can affect a Covert unit.
card_event_hit_the_drop_point.flavorText: In preparation for a potential Allied invasion, the German forces started undertaking several measures long before D-Day in June 1944. They started constructing the Atlantic Wall in 1942, a 2,400-mile network of bunkers, pillboxes, mines and landing obstacles along the European coastline. In addition, obstacles like “Rommel's asparagus” (stakes in fields to hinder glider landings) were placed in potential landing fields. Although millions of these wooden poles were placed in fields, their effect on the Allied invasion was inconsequential. Once Allied troops were on the ground, some German units used the “Rommel's asparagus” for defense by cutting them down and using the logs to reinforce their positions.

card_event_recuperation.name: card_event_recuperation
card_event_recuperation.title: RECUPERATION
card_event_recuperation.text: Give a unit +2 attack. If it is pinned, remove the pin and give it +4 attack instead.
card_event_recuperation.flavorText: After their defeat in World War I, the Treaty of Versailles imposed strict restrictions on Germany's military and effectively grounded the once mighty Luftstreitkräfte (German air force). However, despite the restrictions, the Germans started building their air force in secrecy. Under the guise of civilian aviation clubs and glider training programs, and thanks to covert collaborations with foreign countries, German pilots were trained and engineers developed new aircraft designs. By the time Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, a revived air force was already in place. The Luftwaffe was officially established in 1935, revealing a modern and powerful aerial force that had been secretly rebuilt in defiance of the treaty. This catched the world off guard and played a crucial role in Germany's aggressive expansion leading up to WWII.

card_event_shifting_attack.name: card_event_shifting_attack
card_event_shifting_attack.title: SHIFTING ATTACK
card_event_shifting_attack.text: Send a friendly unit to hand. It costs 0 kredits to deploy this turn.
card_event_shifting_attack.flavorText: As the war progressed, Germany would often redeploy units to new fronts and weaken existing ones. This was especially true in anticipation of the Allied landings in France. In early 1944 the German Western Front was significantly weakened by personnel and materiel being transferred to the Eastern Front. For instance, the entire II SS Panzer Corps was relocated from France to the Eastern Front to face the Soviet Dnieper-Carpathian Offensive. This included two elite SS Panzer Divisions (the 9th and 10th), an infantry division, a heavy tank battalion, and two assault gun brigades. Overall, this removed nearly 46,000 soldiers and over 360 armored vehicles from France, which severely impacted Germans defensive capabilities on the Western Front. This was a major change in German strategy, as previous orders had restricted such large transfers from the west to the east.

card_event_tip_of_the_spear.name: card_event_tip_of_the_spear
card_event_tip_of_the_spear.title: TIP OF THE SPEAR
card_event_tip_of_the_spear.text: Destroy target unit with cost 3 or less. Can target Covert units.
card_event_tip_of_the_spear.flavorText: While the Luftwaffe and infantry played crucial roles, the Panzer divisions were the most symbolic and effective representation of the German war machine's aggressive and relentless drive for conquest during the early stages of WWII. Their speed, firepower, and shock value made them the spearhead of the German advance, carving a path for the rest of the army to follow.

card_unit_15_aufklarungs.name: card_unit_15_aufklarungs
card_unit_15_aufklarungs.title: 15. AUFKLÄRUNG
card_unit_15_aufklarungs.flavorText: The 15th Aufklärungs-Abteilung was a reconnaissance detachment of the 15th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division participated in the Invasion of Poland in 1939 and the Battle of France in 1940. In 1941 the 15th Division was transferred to the Eastern Front and fought with Army Group Centre in the Battle of Smolensk, and later that year against the Soviet Yelnya Offensive. The division participated in the Battle of Moscow but was withdrawn to France after heavy losses. In 1943 the 15th Division returned to the Eastern Front where it joined Army Group South in the Third Battle of Kharkov, and it kept fighting in Ukraine for the next several months before starting to retreat in front of the Soviet advance. In 1944 the division fought in Romania and was destroyed in the Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive against the Soviet forces in August. The division was formed again in October 1944 and fought in Hungary as part of the Hungarian II Corps of 8th Army, but in 1945 it retreated into Czechoslovakia where it finally surrendered to the Soviet forces at the end of the war.

card_unit_171_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_171_infantry_regiment
card_unit_171_infantry_regiment.title: 171. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_171_infantry_regiment.text: Has +4 attack if this is your only unit.
card_unit_171_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 171st Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 56th Infantry Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in 1939 and spent a short time on occupation duty in Poland before seeing combat for the first time in 1940 during the Battle of France. After that the 56th Division spent the remainder of the war on the Eastern Front where it participated in the Battle of Moscow and the Battle of Kursk, where it suffered heavy losses. It was disbanded shortly after. The division was reformed in East Prussia in September 1944 but was again destroyed during the Soviet East Prussian Offensive in early 1945.

card_unit_342_fusiliers.name: card_unit_342_fusiliers
card_unit_342_fusiliers.title: 342. FÜSILIERS
card_unit_342_fusiliers.text: When this unit moves into the frontline, units there get +2 attack.
card_unit_342_fusiliers.flavorText: The 342nd Füsilier Battalion was a battalion of the 342nd Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was deployed in France in 1940 as part of the occupation forces, but in 1941 it was sent to Belgrade in Yugoslavia and assigned to counterinsurgency operations in the occupied territory of Serbia. In 1942 the division was sent to the Eastern Front where it fought in the Battles of Rzhev. They retreated after the Battle of Kursk as part of the Army Group Centre. In 1944 the 342nd Division fought at Kovel in Ukraine, during the withdrawal across eastern Poland and at the Baranov bridgehead on the Vistula. During the Vistula-Oder Offensive, in 1945, the division suffered significant losses and was nearly destroyed. However, it kept fighting until it was trapped in the Halbe pocket during the Battle of Berlin. A few members of the division managed to break through the encirclement and surrendered to the United States Army in Travemünde, near Lübeck, on the Baltic Sea.

card_unit_738_jager_regiment.name: card_unit_738_jager_regiment
card_unit_738_jager_regiment.title: 738. JÄGER REGIMENT
card_unit_738_jager_regiment.text:
Deployment: Target a unit. 
Draw a card when it is destroyed.
card_unit_738_jager_regiment.flavorText: The German Jäger divisions were light divisions specially trained for combat in difficult terrain. They were smaller than the standard infantry divisions, and more heavily armed than mountain divisions, but not as much as larger infantry formations, especially when it came to artillery support. The 738th Jäger Regiment was a unit of the 118th Jäger Division of the German Wehrmacth. The division was formed in 1941 as the 718th Infantry Division, and redesignated 118th Jäger Division in 1943. In 1941 the division was transferred to Yugoslavia and was mainly assigned to anti-partisan and internal security operations. In 1943 it participated in the Battle of the Sutjeska against the Yugoslav Partisan force and later saw fighting again in Bosnia and Croatia. During the final stages of the war it fought against the Soviet Red Army in the Vienna offensive, before retreating and surrendering to the British in May 1945.

card_unit_96_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_96_infantry_regiment
card_unit_96_infantry_regiment.title: 96. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_96_infantry_regiment.text: When you deploy another unit, destroy this unit.
card_unit_96_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 96th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 32nd Infantry Division of the German Wehrmacht. The division was formed in 1936 and first saw combat during the Invasion of Poland in 1939, followed by the Battle of France in 1940. The 32nd Division was then relocated to the Cherbourg peninsula in preparation for Operation Sea Lion, the planned invasion of the United Kingdom which never happened. In 1941 the division was transferred to the Eastern Front where it was encircled by the Soviet Red Army in the Demyansk Pocket along with elements of the 16th Army, just south of Leningrad. The encirclement in the Demyansk Pocket was relieved, but by that time the 32nd had suffered heavy losses. The remainder of the division was withdrawn to the Courland Pocket where it saw heavy combat again during the winter of 1944-45. Finally the remnants of the division surrendered to the Red Army in Poland on May 8th, 1945.

card_unit_dornier_do_18g.name: card_unit_dornier_do_18g
card_unit_dornier_do_18g.title: DORNIER DO 18G
card_unit_dornier_do_18g.text: Units you deploy move into the frontline, if possible.
card_unit_dornier_do_18g.flavorText: The Dornier Do 18G was a German flying boat used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. The aircraft was designed as a long-range maritime patrol aircraft, but it was also used in search and rescue and weather reconnaissance missions. By the start of the war, the Dornier Do 18 was already outdated, but being the only military flying boat available, 62 of them were distributed across five Coastal aviation groups, each receiving a squadron for North Sea reconnaissance duties. However, by 1941 only one squadron still operated on Do 18 aircraft, while others had been replaced with the Blohm & Voss BV 138. A total of 170 Do 18 were built, including civilian variants. Notably, a Do 18 holds the unfortunate distinction of being the first German aircraft downed by the British during the war.

card_unit_kurmark_aufklarungs.name: card_unit_kurmark_aufklarungs
card_unit_kurmark_aufklarungs.title: KURMARK AUFKLÄRUNG
card_unit_kurmark_aufklarungs.text: Deployment: Choose a countermeasure in hand. Activate it at the end of your turn.
card_unit_kurmark_aufklarungs.flavorText: The Kurmark Aufklärungs-Abteilung was a battalion in the Panzergrenadier Division Kurmark, also known as Panzer Division Kurmark, which was an armored unit of the German Army formed in January 1945 in preparation for the Battle of Berlin. The division was named after the Kurmark region in the province of Brandenburg, and established in Frankfurt on the Oder from remains of the Panzergrenadier Division "Großdeutschland", an elite combat unit of the German army. It was understaffed and lacked sufficient motorized transport from the start, forcing some soldiers to use bicycles and horses. The division later found itself encircled with other Wehrmacht units southeast of Berlin. After exhausting their fuel, they were forced to abandon and destroy their remaining King Tiger tanks on April 30th, 1945. The surviving members of the Panzergrenadier Division Kurmark managed to escape and eventually surrendered to the US Army in Jerichow on the Elbe River in May 1945.

card_unit_sturm_brigade_rhodos.name: card_unit_sturm_brigade_rhodos
card_unit_sturm_brigade_rhodos.title: STURM-BRIGADE RHODOS
card_unit_sturm_brigade_rhodos.text: If in your hand, this unit costs 2 less each time your countermeasure triggers.
card_unit_sturm_brigade_rhodos.flavorText: Sturm-Brigade Rhodos was an assault brigade of the German Wehrmacht which was formed from elements of the 22nd Infantry Division. The brigade included four infantry companies and an anti-tank company. In 1943 the brigade was reformed into the Grenadier Regiment Rhodos as part of Assault Division Rhodos, but the regiment was destroyed near Belgrade in Yugoslavia in 1944, and the remaining soldiers were moved to the Panzergrenadier Division Brandenburg which were the German special forces during WWII.

card_event_front_and_homeland.name: card_event_front_and_homeland
card_event_front_and_homeland.title: FRONT AND HOMELAND
card_event_front_and_homeland.text:
Draw from your deck on turn 4.
Reduce the cost of German cards with odd cost in your deck by 1.
card_event_front_and_homeland.flavorText: Throughout WWII, German propaganda worked tirelessly to link the front lines with the civilian population. The concept of “Front und Heimat” (e. front and homeland) emphasized unity between soldiers and those supporting the war effort at home. Soldiers were portrayed as selfless defenders of the nation, while civilians, especially women, were called to maintain production, morale and to support rationing. The regime promoted this connection through newspapers, radio, and cinema, depicting shared sacrifice and mutual reliance. Packages from home, letters, and news from the front helped sustain this illusion. But as the war progressed, the hardships grew both at home and on the front. While German industry shifted to total war production by 1943 under Albert Speer, cities suffered devastating Allied bombing campaigns. Civilian life grew harsher, with widespread shortages and destruction. On the front, soldiers endured brutal winters, extended deployments, and mounting casualties. Still, the idea of “Front und Heimat” remained central to Nazi propaganda, used to justify hardship and rally support long after military momentum had turned against Germany.

card_event_kettenkrad_home.name: card_event_kettenkrad_home
card_event_kettenkrad_home.title: KETTENKRAD
card_event_kettenkrad_home.text: Send a friendly unit to hand. Your German units everywhere get +1 attack.
card_event_kettenkrad_home.flavorText: The Kettenkrad, officially designated Sd.Kfz. 2, was a unique German half-track motorcycle developed before WWII. Built by NSU Motorenwerke, it combined motorcycle agility with the off-road capabilities of tracked vehicles. Weighing just over 1.5 tons, it was light enough to be transported inside a Junkers Ju 52 aircraft, making it suitable for airborne operations. First deployed during the 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, the Kettenkrad served as a gun tractor, cable layer, and general utility vehicle. It could carry two passengers behind the driver and reach speeds up to 70 km/h. Steering involved both a front wheel and track braking, and the wheel could be removed entirely for better performance on rough terrain. Its compact size and versatility made it ideal for reconnaissance, airfield maintenance, and even towing aircraft in muddy conditions. Production continued until 1948, with around 8,000 units built. Though not a frontline combat vehicle, the Kettenkrad’s adaptability ensured it remained in use across various theaters throughout the war.

card_event_minor_nation_conquest.name: card_event_minor_nation_conquest
card_event_minor_nation_conquest.title: CONQUEST
card_event_minor_nation_conquest.text: Draw a card for each unit type you control.
card_event_minor_nation_conquest.flavorText: Seeking to secure its position in Europe, Germany began subduing neighboring states in 1938. This started with the annexation of Austria and the subsequent occupation of Czechoslovakia. On 1 September 1939, Germany’s invasion of Poland triggered a global conflict, drawing in major Western powers France and Great Britain, who declared war in defense of their ally. Following the fall of Poland and a campaign in Scandinavia, the conflict reached a turning point in May 1940. Germany launched a massive offensive against the West. Despite possessing one of the most formidable militaries in the world, the French and their British allies were outmaneuvered by a high-speed armored breakthrough through the Ardennes. After weeks of intense, large-scale combat that saw the collapse of the Allied front, German forces captured Paris. By late June, France was forced to sign an armistice.

card_event_night_attack.name: card_event_night_attack
card_event_night_attack.title: NIGHT ATTACK
card_event_night_attack.text: Remove a unit from the battlefield, then return it with Blitz and Shock. Send it to hand end of turn.
card_event_night_attack.flavorText: Though German doctrine emphasized swift daytime offensives, their forces made calculated use of night for tactical advantage. Darkness offered cover from Allied airpower, especially in the later stages of the war, and was often used for troop movements, resupply, and redeployment. Night was also critical for reconnaissance. German patrols frequently crossed into enemy territory under cover of darkness, sometimes triggering tripflares set by US Rangers. While rare, some full-scale German attacks did occur at night. The Battle of the Bulge began before dawn on December 16, 1944, with a 90-minute artillery barrage followed by ground assaults through fog and early morning darkness. German infantry doctrine allowed for night attacks under special conditions, emphasizing stealth, coordinated machine gun placement and confusion among enemy ranks. Defensive positions were often adjusted or abandoned at night to avoid detection and counter air superiority. Despite preferring daylight for blitzkrieg-style assaults, the German army used night as a flexible tool for survival, deception and surprise when conditions favored such actions.

card_event_second_front.name: card_event_second_front
card_event_second_front.title: SECOND FRONT
card_event_second_front.text: Remove a German ground unit. Return it at the end of the next enemy turn, then duplicate it.
card_event_second_front.flavorText: The Allied landings in Normandy on 6 June 1944 opened a second front in Europe, posing a strategic nightmare for Germany. The Wehrmacht now had to fight on two major fronts against numerically and logistically superior enemies. Hitler insisted on holding the Atlantic Wall at all costs, ordering divisions like the 19th Panzer Division to stand their ground rather than maneuver. German commanders such as Rommel and Rundstedt disagreed on tactics, but both faced severe limitations due to Allied air superiority and fuel shortages. In response to the landings, Germany rushed reinforcements from other theaters. Units were transferred from Italy and Scandinavia, and dozens of divisions were pulled from the Eastern Front, weakening defenses against the advancing Red Army. In the weeks following D-Day, Soviet forces launched Operation Bagration, one of the largest offensives of the war. German lines in the East collapsed, losing hundreds of thousands of men and exposing Poland and the Baltics. The opening of the Western Front did not just split Germany’s forces; it accelerated the downfall of Germany’s empire on both sides of the continent.

card_event_tactical_retreat.name: card_event_tactical_retreat
card_event_tactical_retreat.title: TACTICAL RETREAT
card_event_tactical_retreat.text: When a friendly unit is attacked, send it to hand before damage.
card_event_tactical_retreat.flavorText: Tactical or strategic retreats were a key feature of German military doctrine, refined during campaigns on the Eastern Front. Facing overwhelming Soviet offensives, German units often executed planned withdrawals to shorten supply lines, regroup, and avoid encirclement. These tactics, known as mobile defense, were most effectively used in 1943 and 1944 after the defeat at Stalingrad. A textbook example came during the Third Battle of Kharkov in 1943. German forces allowed the Soviets to overextend, then struck back with concentrated armored formations. The counterattack, led by Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, encircled and destroyed several Soviet spearheads. This approach, known as the “backhand blow”, aimed to trade ground for time and to bleed the enemy in costly engagements. By using flexible defense and local superiority, German forces were able to restore much of the lost front. While not a path to victory, tactical retreats gave the Wehrmacht time to delay collapse on the Eastern Front.

card_unit_169_grenadiers.name: card_unit_169_grenadiers
card_unit_169_grenadiers.title: 169. GRENADIERS
card_unit_169_grenadiers.text: The enemy discards a card at random after giving an order.
card_unit_169_grenadiers.flavorText: The 169th Grenadier Regiment was part of the 68th Infantry Division, a German unit formed in Guben on August 26, 1939. It became operational in time for the invasion of Poland, crossing from German-held territory into southern Poland and advancing through Sandomierz and Janów. After the campaign ended, the division served as an occupation force in Poland until November. In early 1940, it was moved west to Germany near Trier, and later took part in the invasion of France. During the second phase of that campaign, it advanced from the Sedan region into eastern France, reaching Épinal, before being sent back east. By mid-1940, the division was stationed in occupied Poland for border security. It joined Operation Barbarossa on June 22, 1941, advancing from southeastern Poland into the Soviet Union as part of Army Group South. It pushed through western Ukraine, passing Lviv and Vinnytsia, and reached the outskirts of Cherkasy in central Ukraine. In late 1941 it advanced to Poltava and Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine, where it endured harsh winter fighting until early 1942. In summer, it reached Voronezh in western Russia, but had to withdraw in 1943 through areas like the Oskol River and Sumy in northeastern Ukraine. After heavy losses, it was reconstituted in Poland and returned to the front in 1944, fighting in western Ukraine near Lviv. The division then retreated across the Carpathian Mountains into southern Poland, later pulling back into Upper Silesia and finally into Moravia, present-day Czech Republic, where it surrendered to Soviet forces in 1945.

card_unit_18_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_18_infantry_regiment
card_unit_18_infantry_regiment.title: 18. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_18_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Moves into the frontline if possible.
card_unit_18_infantry_regiment.flavorText: Formed in Bielefeld in 1934, the 18th Infantry Regiment became one of three main infantry regiments within the German 6th Infantry Division. Initially composed of three battalions, the 18th Regiment contributed men and officers to other formations as the war progressed. In late 1940, its headquarters and third battalion were transferred to help form the 106th Infantry Division, a common practice as the German Army expanded its frontlines. The 6th Infantry Division itself was one of the Wehrmacht’s early peacetime formations, mobilized in August 1939 for the invasion of Poland. Alongside the 18th, it included the 37th and 58th Infantry Regiments, supported by Artillery Regiment 6. The division fought across Europe and later on the Eastern Front, enduring heavy losses. By 1942, all German infantry regiments were redesignated as “Grenadier” regiments, but this change had no effect on their actual structure or role. In October 1943, the division was reorganized into a leaner “neuer Art” format, reflecting reduced manpower. In June 1944, it was encircled and destroyed during the Soviet Union’s massive Operation Bagration. The 6th Infantry Division was officially dissolved shortly after.

card_unit_27_fusiliers.name: card_unit_27_fusiliers
card_unit_27_fusiliers.title: 27. FÜSILIERS
card_unit_27_fusiliers.text: When a German unit enters your hand, reduce its cost by 1, to a minimum of 1.
card_unit_27_fusiliers.flavorText: The 27th Fusilier Regiment was part of the German 12th Infantry Division, a unit formed in 1934 and based in Schwerin. It originated under the cover name Infanterieführer II to conceal German rearmament, receiving its official designation when the Wehrmacht was created in 1935. Built from Pomeranian recruits, the division took part in the invasion of Poland in 1939 as part of I Army Corps, 1st Army. In 1940, it participated in the campaign through the Low Countries and France, helping repel an Anglo-French counterattack during their retreat through Belgium. The division remained stationed in Western Europe until May 1941, then joined Operation Barbarossa under Army Group Center. On the Eastern Front, it endured heavy combat and attrition, and was destroyed in mid-1944 during the Soviet summer offensive, Operation Bagration. In September 1944, a new formation under the same name was raised and deployed on the Western Front, where it fought until its final surrender in April 1945.

card_unit_36_kradschutzen.name: card_unit_36_kradschutzen
card_unit_36_kradschutzen.title: 36. KRADSCHÜTZEN
card_unit_36_kradschutzen.text: When a friendly German unit moves into the frontline, give it +1 attack and -1 operation cost.
card_unit_36_kradschutzen.flavorText: Kradschützen-Bataillon 36 was formed on 9 November 1940 by renaming Machine Gun Battalion 11, which had been based in Lahr, in Wehrkreis V military district. The battalion became part of the 36th Infantry Division (motorized) and served with it during the invasion of the Soviet Union beginning in June 1941. As motorcycle infantry, Kradschützen units were used for rapid movement, reconnaissance, and mobile infantry support, especially during fast-paced operations in the early years of the war. On 15 March 1942, the remnants of Reconnaissance Detachment 36 were absorbed into the battalion. This reorganization provided a new headquarters and added three companies. In March 1943, a plan to rename the unit as Panzer Reconnaissance Detachment 136 was canceled when the entire 36th Division was ordered to give up its vehicles. The battalion was eventually renamed Divisional Fusilier Battalion 36 on 1 January 1944 following a directive issued in November 1943. Replacement troops for Kradschützen-Bataillon 36 were initially supplied by Motorcycle Replacement Battalion 6, and later by Battalion 7, from June 1942.

card_unit_40_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_40_panzergrenadier
card_unit_40_panzergrenadier.title: 40. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_40_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Send a unit to hand. Draw a card if it is friendly.
card_unit_40_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 40th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a key infantry component of the 17th Panzer Division, created from Schützen-Regiment 40 in 1942. It was structured to fight alongside tanks, providing mobile infantry support in fast-moving operations. The regiment was active from the division’s early campaigns on the Eastern Front through to the final months of the war. In 1941, the 17th Panzer Division launched its offensive with Army Group South during Operation Barbarossa, pushing into Ukraine and capturing key cities like Smolensk and Bryansk. The 40th Regiment took part in these rapid advances, often engaging Soviet forces in fierce encounters around river crossings and fortified positions. In 1942, the regiment fought near Stalingrad as the division attempted to relieve the 6th Army. Though it avoided encirclement, it suffered significant losses. Throughout 1943 and 1944, the 40th Panzergrenadier Regiment was heavily engaged in defensive actions across southern Russia and later in Poland. It was continuously weakened by Soviet offensives and shortages of equipment. By 1945, the regiment had been reduced to scattered remnants as the division retreated into Czechoslovakia, where it surrendered in May.

card_unit_43_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_43_infantry_regiment
card_unit_43_infantry_regiment.title: 43. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_43_infantry_regiment.text: At the end of your turn, draw the top card of your deck if it has even cost.
card_unit_43_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 43rd Infantry Regiment was part of the German 1st Infantry Division, formed in 1935 from elements of the old Reichswehr. Stationed in Insterburg, East Prussia, it drew its recruits largely from this region and inherited a strong Prussian identity. The division participated in the 1939 invasion of Poland, seeing action at Mława and during the siege of Warsaw. In 1940 it fought in the Battle of France, and it was later committed to Operation Barbarossa, advancing into the Soviet Union in 1941. It took part in the siege of Leningrad and remained active on the Eastern Front throughout the war. The 1st Infantry Division endured repeated Soviet offensives, including the encirclement at Kamenets-Podolsky in 1944. Despite heavy casualties, it continued to operate until the division’s final surrender in May 1945.

card_unit_74_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_74_panzergrenadier
card_unit_74_panzergrenadier.title: 74. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_74_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Send a friendly unit to hand. Gets +1+1 if you do.
card_unit_74_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 74th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 19th Panzer Division, formed in late 1940. The division participated in Germany's push into the Soviet Union during Operation Barbarossa in 1941. By the end of the first summer, the division had suffered such losses that one of its three tank battalions was disbanded. Throughout the war, the division fought in grueling battles, including Moscow in 1941 and Kursk in 1943. During the harsh winter of 1941-42, further losses reduced the division's armored strength. As the frontlines shifted, the division was redeployed to support Axis defenses along the Don in 1942 and during the brutal retreat westward through Ukraine and Poland. In 1944, its units were briefly pulled back to the Netherlands for refitting. By 1945, the division was fighting in the desperate defense of Germany, including the Vistula-Oder and Prague offensives. It finally surrendered to Soviet forces in Czechoslovakia in May 1945.

card_unit_92_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_92_infantry_regiment
card_unit_92_infantry_regiment.title: 92. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_92_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Develop BLITZKRIEG, SKY BARONS or TACTICAL STRIKE.
card_unit_92_infantry_regiment.flavorText: During WWII; the 92nd Infantry Regiment served within the German 2nd Infantry Division, which was restructured into the 2nd Motorized Infantry Division in 1940. Originally formed in 1934 and based in Cottbus, the division drew its manpower largely from central Germany. It first saw combat during the invasion of Poland in 1939, where it participated in rapid advances as part of Army Group South. The unit then shifted westward for the 1940 campaign in France, moving through Belgium and into northern France with Army Group A. Following the French armistice, the division was reorganized into a motorized formation, enhancing its speed and operational flexibility. As the 2nd Motorized Infantry Division, it took part in Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 under Army Group Centre. It advanced deep into Soviet territory, fighting at key locations like Smolensk and later near Moscow. The division suffered severe losses during the Soviet winter counteroffensive. The relentless fighting on the Eastern Front wore down its strength, leading to its withdrawal and conversion into the 12th Panzer Division in 1942. This marked a further shift toward mechanization as the Wehrmacht adapted to the demands of mobile warfare on the vast Soviet front.

card_unit_ace_of_spades.name: card_unit_ace_of_spades
card_unit_ace_of_spades.title: ACE OF SPADES
card_unit_ace_of_spades.text:
Deployment: Deal 3 damage to an enemy. 
Becomes Veteran at the start of your turn.
card_unit_ace_of_spades.flavorText: The 206th Infantry Division, nicknamed “Pik-As” or "Ace of Spades" for its divisional insignia, was raised in East Prussia in August 1939. Initially a reserve unit for Army Group North, it joined the invasion of Poland that same year. Like most German infantry divisions, it lacked motorization and relied heavily on horses for mobility. In late 1941, the division took part in Operation Typhoon, the German offensive aimed at capturing Moscow. Positioned under XXIII Corps of the Ninth Army, it endured the brutal Soviet counterattacks during the winter. The following year, during Operation Mars, it faced intense assaults by the Soviet 39th Army in the Rzhev salient, a sector marked by high casualties and stagnant frontlines. In 1943, the division was equipped with Marder I tank destroyers and remained on the Eastern Front. In June 1944, during Operation Bagration, it was tasked with holding Vitebsk. While other German units were permitted to withdraw, the 206th was ordered to defend the city to the last man. Encircled and overwhelmed, the division was destroyed by 26 June. Its final stand marked one of the many desperate defensive efforts during the collapse of Army Group Center.

card_unit_armored_car_home.name: card_unit_armored_car_home
card_unit_armored_car_home.title: Sd Kfz 250/9
card_unit_armored_car_home.text: Gets +2 attack until end of turn when you draw a card.
card_unit_armored_car_home.flavorText: The Sd Kfz 250/9 was a reconnaissance variant of Germany’s light armored half-track series, introduced to replace wheeled scout cars which struggled on the Eastern Front. Based on the Sd Kfz 250 chassis, the 250/9 featured a fully enclosed roof and a small turret mounting a 2 cm KwK 38 autocannon alongside a coaxial MG34 machine gun. This turret was initially adapted from the Sd Kfz 222 armored car. Prototype vehicles were tested on the Eastern Front in mid-1942. Following favorable feedback, series production began in late 1942 using the earlier Ausf. A chassis. These early models remained in use until early 1944. From spring 1944, production shifted to the improved Ausf. B chassis. These later variants were equipped with a new Hängelafette 38 turret, which had reinforced 30 mm frontal armor and was shared with the 8-wheeled Sd Kfz 234/1. The Sd Kfz 250/9 offered better off-road mobility and protection than its predecessors, making it a valuable asset for Panzer reconnaissance units operating in challenging conditions across Europe and the Soviet Union.

card_unit_dornier_do_17.name: card_unit_dornier_do_17
card_unit_dornier_do_17.title: DORNIER DO 17Z
card_unit_dornier_do_17.text: Once per turn, gain 2 kredits and draw a card when an undestroyed unit leaves the battlefield.
card_unit_dornier_do_17.flavorText: Nicknamed the "flying pencil" for its slender fuselage, the Dornier Do 17 was one of the Luftwaffe’s primary light bombers in the early years of WWII. Designed in the early 1930s as a fast bomber capable of outrunning enemy fighters, the Do 17 entered Luftwaffe service in 1937 and soon saw combat in the Spanish Civil War. Crews favored its handling, particularly at low altitudes, where it proved harder to hit than its contemporaries. The most produced version, the Do 17Z, featured a glazed nose for improved visibility and typically carried a payload of 1,000 kilograms of bombs. Powered by twin Bramo 323 radial engines, it could reach speeds up to 410 km/h. The Do 17Z served in major campaigns including Poland, France, the Battle of Britain, and the early stages of Operation Barbarossa. However, its limited range and bomb load reduced its effectiveness as the war progressed. By late 1941, the Do 17 was largely removed from frontline duties and reassigned to secondary roles such as training, reconnaissance, and glider towing. A total of 2,139 Do 17s were built before production ended in 1940.

card_unit_panzer_iv_home.name: card_unit_panzer_iv_home
card_unit_panzer_iv_home.title: PANZER IV-J
card_unit_panzer_iv_home.text: Increase the operation cost by 1 after each time this unit attacks.
card_unit_panzer_iv_home.flavorText: The Panzer IV Ausführung J was the final production model of Germany’s most widely used medium tank of WWII. Introduced in early 1944, the J variant emphasized simplified construction to speed up manufacturing as Germany faced mounting battlefield losses and industrial strain. Key changes included the removal of the electric turret traverse motor, replaced by a manual crank, and the addition of a new 16-speed gearbox that allowed for smoother operation in difficult terrain. The J retained the long-barreled 75 mm KwK 40 L/48 gun, capable of engaging most Allied tanks effectively at medium range. Armor was slightly increased, and later models featured skirt armor plates for better protection against anti-tank rifles and shaped charges. To compensate for the weight and power limitations, a secondary fuel tank was added to extend operational range, reflecting the growing importance of mobile defense. Nearly 3,000 Panzer IV Js were built, forming the backbone of many panzer divisions until the end of the war. Despite being increasingly outmatched by newer Allied tanks, the Panzer IV J remained in frontline service across every theater where German forces fought. Its continued presence reflected the vehicle’s adaptability, robust design, and the limits of Germany’s late-war production capacity.

card_unit_panzer_i_a.name: card_unit_panzer_i_a
card_unit_panzer_i_a.title: PANZER I-A
card_unit_panzer_i_a.text: Deployment: Draw a card if you control an infantry.
card_unit_panzer_i_a.flavorText: The Panzer I Ausf. A was Germany’s first mass-produced tank, developed in secret during the early 1930s to train armored troops and jumpstart domestic tank production. Originally known under code names like "Agricultural Tractor", it entered service in 1934. It was manned by a crew of two and equipped with twin 7.92 mm MG13 machine guns. Armor was limited to just 13 mm at its thickest, sufficient only against small arms fire. Powered by a Krupp M305 four-cylinder air-cooled engine delivering 60 horsepower, the Ausf. A could reach 37 km/h on roads but suffered from suspension issues and engine overheating. Although not intended for combat, the Panzer I-A was pressed into front-line service due to Germany's limited armored forces. It fought in the Spanish Civil War, Poland, France, and the early stages of Operation Barbarossa. In Spain, it proved vulnerable to Soviet-supplied T-26 tanks, which prompted attempts to up-gun or replace it .A total of 1,190 combat Panzer I Ausf. A tanks were built across three production series. Despite its shortcomings, the Panzer I-A laid the foundation for Germany’s later armored warfare doctrine and played a crucial role in training the first panzer crews.

card_event_enemy_sighted.name: card_event_enemy_sighted
card_event_enemy_sighted.title: ENEMY SIGHTED
card_event_enemy_sighted.text: Destroy target unit with cost 3 or less. Draw a card.
card_event_enemy_sighted.flavorText: A nose gunner or front gunner on WWII bombers was the crewman that operated the guns in the front, or in the nose of the aircraft. For most parts this crewman had more than one role and would primarily act as a navigator or bombardier, the secondary role would be to act as a gunner.

card_event_envelop.name: card_event_envelop
card_event_envelop.title: ENVELOP
card_event_envelop.text: When a unit moves into the frontline, destroy all units there.
card_event_envelop.flavorText: To envelop means to mount an attack on the enemy's flank, a military tactic that has been widely used in warfare throughout history.

card_event_gathering_storm.name: card_event_gathering_storm
card_event_gathering_storm.title: GATHERING STORM
card_event_gathering_storm.text: Draw a random infantry, tank, artillery and fighter from your deck.
card_event_gathering_storm.flavorText: Many Germans realized that the war was lost by 1943, following the surrender at Stalingrad, but the Nazi propaganda machine kept beating the war drums. It probably wasn’t until 1944 when most Germans realized that the war was lost. One of the few persons that was unwilling to accept the reality of the situation was the one who was able to stop the war. That person was Adolf Hitler.

card_event_lost_convoy.name: card_event_lost_convoy
card_event_lost_convoy.title: LOST CONVOY
card_event_lost_convoy.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, give it -2 attack.
card_event_lost_convoy.flavorText: Convoy PQ-17 was an Allied convoy that was located through German signals intelligence and cryptanalysis, shadowed for days and continuously attacked by the German Kriegsmarine and Luftwaffe. The convoy was the first large joint Anglo-American naval operation under British command and the ships were sailing from Hvalfjord in Iceland to Arkhangelsk in the Soviet Union with vital supplies for the war effort on the Eastern Front. At first PQ 17 had a strong escort of warships, but when the British Admiralty got word that the Bismarck-class battleship Tirpitz was on its way to intercept the convoy, the order was given to scatter since they didn’t want to risk losing their warships. They believed that scattering the convoy would make it harder for the Germans to sink the ships, but what happened was the exact opposite. Contrary to what the British believed, the Tirpitz was not heading towards the convoy, and the merchant ships became easy targets for the German submarines and aircraft which managed to sink 24 ships out of 35.

card_event_propaganda.name: card_event_propaganda
card_event_propaganda.title: PROPAGANDA
card_event_propaganda.text: Choose and discard a Countermeasure from hand to deal 3 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_event_propaganda.flavorText: The Nazi Party propaganda used in the years leading up to and during WWII was a vital instrument in implementing anitsemetic Nazi policies and maintaining power and support for the German war effort. Headed by Joseph Goebbels, the head of Nazi Germany's Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, the aim was to make sure that the Nazi message was communicated through all media available at the time, through  art, music, theater, films, books, radio, educational materials and the press.

card_event_ride_of_the_valkyries.name: card_event_ride_of_the_valkyries
card_event_ride_of_the_valkyries.title: RIDE OF THE VALKYRIES
card_event_ride_of_the_valkyries.text: The enemy HQ gets: "If this HQ has taken 3+ damage this turn, you gain 2 kredits."
card_event_ride_of_the_valkyries.flavorText: Ride of the Valkyries, or simply the “Ride”, is a popular term for the prelude to the 3rd act in Wagner's opera The Ring of the Nibelungs. The score was famously used in Francis Ford Coppola's film Apocalypse Now.

card_event_through_the_breach.name: card_event_through_the_breach
card_event_through_the_breach.title: THROUGH THE BREACH
card_event_through_the_breach.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. Deal 2 damage instead if the unit is in a support line.
card_event_through_the_breach.flavorText: Penetration is a military tactic that focuses on breaching the enemies defensive lines and moving past them, much like the German Blitzkrieg strategy of WWII. The tactic is much similar to the pincer movement except that it is carried out as part of a frontal attack and the aim is to penetrate and go through the enemy lines, instead of focusing on the flanks. And once through, the attacking force turns and attacks the rear.

card_unit_104_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_104_panzergrenadier
card_unit_104_panzergrenadier.title: 104. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_104_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Reduce the operation cost by 1 if you control a tank.
card_unit_104_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 104th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 15th Panzergrenadier Division, which was a mobilized division of the Wehrmacht. The division was formed in 1943 out of the former Sicily Division and remnants of the 15th Panzer Division. Shortly after being formed the division participated in fighting in Sicily against the invading US forces, which ended in retreat and evacuation from the island. The division would later participate in the Italian Campaign and defend against the Allied forces in the Battle of Monte Cassino and the Battle of Anzio. The 15th Division spent the rest of the war on the Western Front where they fought in the Battle of the Bulge before surrendering to the British when the war ended.

card_unit_1097_volksgrenadier.name: card_unit_1097_volksgrenadier
card_unit_1097_volksgrenadier.title: 1097. VOLKSGRENADIER
card_unit_1097_volksgrenadier.text: Deployment: Gets +2 defense and Guard if the enemy controls a Blitz unit.
card_unit_1097_volksgrenadier.flavorText: The 1097th Volksgrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 549th Volksgrenadier Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in 1944 and fought on the Eastern Front and was nearly destroyed by the Red Army during the East Prussian Offensive in 1945. The survivors retreated to the west and surrendered to American troops when the war ended.

card_unit_136_gebirgsjager.name: card_unit_136_gebirgsjager
card_unit_136_gebirgsjager.title: 136. GEBIRGSJÄGER
card_unit_136_gebirgsjager.flavorText: The 136th Mountain Infantry Regiment was a regiment of the 2nd Mountain Division of the Wehrmacht which was formed in 1938 and trained in operating in mountainous terrain and cold weather. The division was formed with personnel from the 6th Division of the Austrian Alpenkorps and most men serving in it came from the Salzburg and Tyrol regions of Austria. During WWII the division served in Norway and the northern sectors near the Arctic on the Eastern Front before being moved to the Western Front by the end of the war. The division fought with Army Group South during the Invasion of Poland in 1939 and in the Norwegian Campaign in 1940. During Operation Barbarossa the 2nd Mountain Division fought with Mountain Corps Norway alongside the Finnish Army against the Red Army in the Arctic region where it continued to serve until the hostilities between Finland and USSR ended in 1944. The division ended the war on the Western Front where it surrendered to the Western Allies.

card_unit_28_jager_regiment.name: card_unit_28_jager_regiment
card_unit_28_jager_regiment.title: 28. JÄGER REGIMENT
card_unit_28_jager_regiment.text: Gains Ambush when it moves into the frontline.
card_unit_28_jager_regiment.flavorText: The 28th Jäger Regiment was part of the 8th Infantry Division of the Wehrmachtand was formed in 1934. The division took part in the Invasion of Poland, the Battle of France and Operation Barbarossa. In 1942 the division was redesignated as the 8th Jäger Division and their main purpose was to fight in rough terrain or urban areas on the Eastern Front. The division surrendered to the Red Army in Moravia in 1945.

card_unit_gebirger_pionier_95.name: card_unit_gebirger_pionier_95
card_unit_gebirger_pionier_95.title: GEBIRGS-PIONIER 95
card_unit_gebirger_pionier_95.text: At the start of your turn, gain 1 additional kredit.
card_unit_gebirger_pionier_95.flavorText: The Gebirgs-Pionier 95 was a battalion sized unit of the 5th Gebirgs-Division that was formed in 1940 and specialized in mountain warfare. The division took part in the invasion of Greece and the island of Crete where it fought its most significant battle in May 1941. In 1942 the division was deployed to the Eastern Front where it joined Army Group North in its offensive towards Leningrad. In 1943 it was redeployed in Italy where it fought for the remainder of the war. The 5th Gebirgs-Division surrendered to the US forces in May 1945.

card_unit_heinkel_he_115_inv.name: card_unit_heinkel_he_115_inv
card_unit_heinkel_he_115_inv.title: HEINKEL HE 115
card_unit_heinkel_he_115_inv.text: When this unit attacks, add a SPOILS OF WAR to your hand.
card_unit_heinkel_he_115_inv.flavorText: The Heinkel He 115 was a German seaplane that was in the service of the Luftwaffe during WWII. The He 115 was first introduced in 1939 and was used as a torpedo bomber in anti-shipping operations, but also as a reconnaissance and minelaying aircraft. The He 115 was lightly armed and served best in its operations against the Allied Arctic convoys since they didn’t have air cover, but this did not last long. Once the convoys started to appear with escort carriers and long range heavy fighters such as the Petlyakov Pe-3bis the Luftwaffe lost its air superiority over the convoys. A total of 138 Heinkel He 115’s were built, including quite a few variants.

card_unit_ju_88_g6.name: card_unit_ju_88_g6
card_unit_ju_88_g6.title: JU 88 G6
card_unit_ju_88_g6.text: When this unit destroys a unit, add a copy of the destroyed unit to your hand.
card_unit_ju_88_g6.flavorText: The Junkers Ju 88 was a German aircraft that was used by the Luftwaffe in various roles during WWII and served as a bomber, dive bomber, torpedo bomber, night fighter, heavy fighter and reconnaissance aircraft. The Ju 88 G6 variant served as a night fighter and was fitted with a MHz frequency radar and some were fitted with “Schräge Musik” which was the name for upwards firing autocannons or machine guns that were used against bombers. A total of 15,183 Junkers Ju were built throughout the war, including many variants.

card_unit_me_bf_109_v2.name: card_unit_me_bf_109_v2
card_unit_me_bf_109_v2.title: BF 109E-7 TROP
card_unit_me_bf_109_v2.text: Deployment: +1+1 if you control a tank or infantry. +3+3 if you control both.
card_unit_me_bf_109_v2.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Bf 109 was one of the main German fighter aircraft during WWII. A total of 33,984 aircraft were produced from 1937 to 1945 and the BF 109E-7 Trop was one of many variants made. Apart from the tropical color scheme a number of modifications were made to the standard Bf 109 in order to make it suitable for tropical climates and the desert sand. The E-7 was very similar to the previously made E-4 Trop variant except that it had an option 300 L drop tank.

card_location_ardennes_waw.name: card_location_ardennes_waw
card_location_ardennes_waw.title: ARDENNES
card_location_ardennes_waw.text: The Germans used the hilly Ardennes to launch several offensives during the war.
card_location_ardennes_waw.flavorText: The Ardennes, also known as the Forest of Ardennes or the Ardennes Forest, is a region of rough terrain, hills and extensive forest. Ardennes is a region in southeast Belgium and extends into Luxembourg, Germany and France, and its strategic position has made it a European battleground for centuries. The Germans have used the region to stage three major battles in the 20th century, in WWI it was the Battle of the Ardennes (1914), and twice during WWII, the Battle of France (1940) and the Battle of the Bulge (1944–1945).

card_location_ardennes_waw_event.name: card_location_ardennes_waw_event
card_location_ardennes_waw_event.title: ARDENNES
card_location_ardennes_waw_event.text: The Germans used the hilly Ardennes to launch several offensives during the war.
card_location_ardennes_waw_event.flavorText: The Ardennes, also known as the Forest of Ardennes or the Ardennes Forest, is a region of rough terrain, hills and extensive forest. Ardennes is a region in southeast Belgium and extends into Luxembourg, Germany and France, and its strategic position has made it a European battleground for centuries. The Germans have used the region to stage three major battles in the 20th century, in WWI it was the Battle of the Ardennes (1914), and twice during WWII, the Battle of France (1940) and the Battle of the Bulge (1944–1945).

card_location_arnhem.name: card_location_arnhem
card_location_arnhem.title: ARNHEM
card_location_arnhem.text: The Battle of Arnheim was fought in 1944 over strategically important bridges over the Rhine.

card_location_berlin.name: card_location_berlin
card_location_berlin.title: DANZIG
card_location_berlin.text: The Free City of Danzig was captured by German forces at the start of the war.
card_location_berlin.flavorText: The Battle of Westerplatte in the harbor of Danzig was one of the first battles in Germany's invasion of Poland, marking the start of World War II in Europe. Germany held the city until at the end of the war when it was liberated by Polish and Soviet forces.

card_location_el_alamein.name: card_location_el_alamein
card_location_el_alamein.title: EL ALAMEIN
card_location_el_alamein.text: El Alamein was the furthest the Afrikakorps got in Egypt.
card_location_el_alamein.flavorText: El Alamein (Arabic: The two flags) is a town in the North of Egypt where two major WWII battles were fought between the Axis, under the command of Rommel, and the Allied forces in the Western Desert Campaign. The First Battle of El Alamein (1–27 July 1942) ended in a stalemate, but the Allies managed to halt the Axis advance on Alexandria. The Second Battle of El Alamein (23 October – 11 November 1942) ended in a decisive Allied victory and broke the grip the Axis had on North Africa.

card_location_villers_bocage.name: card_location_villers_bocage
card_location_villers_bocage.title: VILLERS-BOCAGE
card_location_villers_bocage.text: The Battle of Villers-Bocage was a 1944 tank battle between German and British forces.
card_location_villers_bocage.flavorText: The Battle of Villers-Bocage occurred on June 13th, 1944, shortly after the D-Day landings in Normandy, and was part of the larger Battle for Caen. This intense tank battle involved British and German forces, with German commander Michael Wittmann leading a counterattack using Tiger tanks against British armored units. Wittmann achieved early success by ambushing British forces and destroying several tanks. The battle resulted in heavy casualties on both sides and in the retreat of the British forces. This allowed the Germans to take control of the town for a brief period.

card_location_ai_german_unlock1.title: STALINGRAD
card_location_ai_german_unlock1.text: The Battle of Stalingrad is often identified as the turning point on the Eastern Front.
card_location_ai_german_unlock1.flavorText: The Battle of Stalingrad is often identified as the turning point on the Eastern Front. It was the largest confrontation of World War II, in which Germany and its Allies fought the Soviet Union for control of the city of Stalingrad (now Volgograd) in Southern Russia.
