card_event_capitulation.name: card_event_capitulation
card_event_capitulation.title: CAPITULATION
card_event_capitulation.text: All enemy units are Converted into ROUTED TROOPS.
card_event_capitulation.flavorText: During the early years of WWII, the German military achieved a series of rapid victories that forced multiple countries and armies to surrender. In 1939, Poland was divided after both German and Soviet attacks. In 1940, Denmark capitulated within hours, followed by Norway, which surrendered after two months of resistance. Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg also fell quickly. France, after a swift and devastating German campaign, signed an armistice in June 1940, leading to occupation. Later, Yugoslavia and Greece were overrun in the Balkans campaign of 1941, each surrendering after brief, intense fighting. Numerous other forces, including parts of the Soviet army during Operation Barbarossa, also capitulated during the German advance. Each surrender expanded German control across Europe, setting the stage for the next phases of the war. The wave of capitulations demonstrated both the power of the German military and the vulnerability of countries caught unprepared for modern warfare.

card_event_fliegerfuhrer_atlantik.name: card_event_fliegerfuhrer_atlantik
card_event_fliegerfuhrer_atlantik.title: ATLANTIC COMMAND
card_event_fliegerfuhrer_atlantik.text: Move two random Navy cards in your deck to the top.
card_event_fliegerfuhrer_atlantik.flavorText: The Atlantic Command (German: Fliegerführer Atlantik) was a Luftwaffe command formed in 1941 to support German naval operations in the Atlantic during WWII. Its main role was to locate and attack Allied convoys and assist U-boats by spotting targets from the air. The command was based in occupied France and initially operated long-range aircraft such as the Focke-Wulf Fw 200 Condor, later expanding its fleet to include types such as the Heinkel He 177 and Junkers Ju 290. Early on, it helped boost U-boat success, but as Allied air defenses, radar, and escort carriers improved, its effectiveness dropped sharply. The unit suffered heavy losses and struggled to operate as the Allies gained control of the skies and sea lanes. After the Allied invasion of France in 1944 and the loss of key bases, Fliegerführer Atlantik could no longer function effectively and was disbanded later that year.

card_event_happy_time.name: card_event_happy_time
card_event_happy_time.title: HAPPY TIME
card_event_happy_time.text: Choose 1 of 3 cards in the enemy hand. Copy it, then Convert both into PLAN.
card_event_happy_time.flavorText: The Happy Time (German: Die Glückliche Zeit) refers to a period from July 1940 to early 1941 when German U-boats inflicted severe losses on Allied shipping in the Atlantic. After France fell in June 1940, Germany gained access to Atlantic ports like Lorient and Brest, allowing U-boats to operate farther west and remain at sea longer. Operating primarily against poorly defended merchant convoys, U-boats sank ships at an alarming rate. At the peak of this campaign, Allied shipping losses reached over 300,000 tons per month. German commanders like Günther Prien, Otto Kretschmer, and Joachim Schepke became national heroes. Kretschmer alone sank over 200,000 tons during this phase, often by surfacing at night and attacking with deck guns to conserve torpedoes. The British were hampered by a lack of escort vessels and effective convoy tactics. Radar and sonar were limited, and air cover did not extend far enough into the Atlantic to protect convoys. The tide began to turn by early 1941 as the Royal Navy improved its escort systems and tactics. The entry into service of more escort ships and the breaking of German naval codes helped reduce shipping losses, bringing an end to what German U-boat crews referred to as "the Happy Time".

card_event_old_hares.name: card_event_old_hares
card_event_old_hares.title: OLD HARES
card_event_old_hares.text: Target infantry or tank gets +5 attack until end of turn.
card_event_old_hares.flavorText: In the German Army during WWII, the term "alter Hase" (literally "old hare") was an expression used to describe a veteran soldier, someone with significant combat experience, usually from earlier campaigns or even WWI. It carried a tone of respect and implied that the person was seasoned, knowledgeable, and dependable in battle. These "old hares" often acted as informal leaders or mentors to younger, less experienced troops, especially in infantry units where survival often depended on battlefield intuition and experience. The phrase is similar in meaning to English terms like "old hand" or "battle-hardened veteran”.

card_event_prinz_eugen.name: card_event_prinz_eugen
card_event_prinz_eugen.title: KM PRINZ EUGEN
card_event_prinz_eugen.text: When the enemy deploys a unit, put it on top of their deck and Convert it into PRODUCTION.
card_event_prinz_eugen.flavorText: The Prinz Eugen was a German heavy cruiser of the Admiral Hipper class which served in the Kriegsmarine during WWII. She was named after Prince Eugene of Savoy, a notable 18th-century general of the Austrian Habsburg dynasty. In May 1941, Prinz Eugen participated in Operation Rheinübung, accompanying the battleship Bismarck in an attempt to disrupt Allied shipping in the Atlantic. During the Battle of the Denmark Strait on 24 May, the two ships engaged British forces, resulting in the sinking of HMS Hood and damage to HMS Prince of Wales. In 1942, she took part in Operation Cerberus, a daring dash through the English Channel alongside Scharnhorst and Gneisenau to return to Germany. After that, she was deployed to Norway but suffered significant damage from a torpedo attack by the British submarine HMS Trident, necessitating extensive repairs. Later in the war, Prinz Eugen provided artillery support on the Eastern Front, assisting German forces during their retreat. After Germany's surrender in May 1945, the ship was handed over to the British as a war prize, and then transferred to the US Navy. She was renamed USS Prinz Eugen (IX-300) and subjected to nuclear testing during Operation Crossroads at Bikini Atoll. She survived the blasts, and was eventually towed to Kwajalein Atoll where she capsized and sank in December 1946. Today, parts of her wreck remain visible above the water.

card_event_tirpitz.name: card_event_tirpitz
card_event_tirpitz.title: KM TIRPITZ
card_event_tirpitz.text: Deal 4 damage to the enemy HQ. The enemy cannot deploy units next turn.
card_event_tirpitz.flavorText: The Tirpitz was the second of two Bismarck-class battleships built for Germany's Kriegsmarine during WWII. It was named after Grand Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz. The ship was commissioned in February 1941 and at the time she was the heaviest battleship ever built for a European Navy, weighing over 52,000 tons at full load. In 1941 Tirpitz briefly served in the Baltic Fleet to prevent a possible breakout by the Soviet Baltic Fleet. In early 1942, she was deployed to Norway to deter an Allied invasion and to intercept Arctic convoys supplying the Soviet Union. Although she attempted to engage Allied convoys, during Operation Rösselsprung in July 1942 for instance, these missions were largely unsuccessful. Nevertheless, her presence tied down significant British naval resources. Tirpitz's only offensive action occurred in September 1943, when she, alongside the battleship Scharnhorst, bombarded Allied positions on the island of Spitzbergen. Soon after, she suffered damage from a British midget submarine attack and was subjected to multiple air raids. On 12 November 1944, British Lancaster bombers equipped with 12,000-pound "Tallboy" bombs struck Tirpitz, causing her to capsize rapidly. The attack resulted in the deaths of between 950 and 1,204 crew members. Between 1948 and 1957, the wreck was salvaged by a joint Norwegian and German operation.

card_unit_108_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_108_panzergrenadier
card_unit_108_panzergrenadier.title: 108. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_108_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Convert target enemy unit with cost 4 or less into ROUTED TROOPS, then Retreat it.
card_unit_108_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 108th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 14th Panzer Division during WWII. The 14th Panzer Division was formed in 1940 from elements of the 4th Infantry Division and the 4th Panzer Division, and combined infantry and armored units. The 108th Panzergrenadier Regiment, alongside the 103rd, provided the division's mechanized infantry strength. In April 1941, the division participated in the invasion of Yugoslavia where it advanced swiftly to Sarajevo. Soon after it returned to Germany to prepare for Operation Barbarossa, and as part of Army Group South, it took part in the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. The division engaged in continuous combat throughout the year and during the harsh winter on the Eastern Front. In early 1942, the division advanced through the Kharkov and Don regions as part of the German summer offensives. Later that year, the 14th Panzer Division was transferred to the 6th Army, which became encircled at Stalingrad. By February 1943, the division was destroyed in the battle. It was later reformed in Brittany, France, and by November 1943, it returned to the Eastern Front. The division continued to fight in various engagements until it became trapped in the Courland Pocket in early 1945, where it remained until Germany's surrender in May 1945.

card_unit_2_marine_division.name: card_unit_2_marine_division
card_unit_2_marine_division.title: 2. MARINE DIVISION
card_unit_2_marine_division.text: Once per turn, deal 3 damage to the enemy HQ when you play a Navy card.
card_unit_2_marine_division.flavorText: The 2nd Marine Division of the German Kriegsmarine was formed in March 1945 in Schleswig-Holstein from excess naval personnel and hastily assembled troops. Most of its members were poorly trained and lacked combat experience, far from the standards of a regular army unit. The division was short on heavy weapons and relied mainly on small arms and panzerfausts. Key support elements, including engineer and supply units, were never fully established due to equipment shortages. Declared ready for action in early April, the division was rushed into the defense of the Weser-Aller line, south of Bremen. It engaged in scattered battles along the Aller River, notably at Verden and Rethem, losing all of its anti-aircraft batteries during the fighting. Casualties mounted rapidly under Allied pressure and by April 21, only 3,000 of the original 13,000 men remained. The remnants continued delaying actions near Cuxhaven and Meldorf, eventually falling back behind the Kaiser Wilhelm Canal. Reduced to a few hundred men, the unit acted as a local alarm force before surrendering to British troops at Bunsoh in early May 1945.

card_unit_4_fallschirmjager.name: card_unit_4_fallschirmjager
card_unit_4_fallschirmjager.title: 4. FALLSCHIRMJÄGER
card_unit_4_fallschirmjager.text: Deployment: Choose a unit in hand with a cost of 2 or less. Set its cost to 0.
card_unit_4_fallschirmjager.flavorText: The 4th Fallschirmjäger Regiment was part of the 1st Fallschirmjäger-Division which was the German Luftwaffe's premier airborne unit during WWII. Under General Kurt Student, it executed the daring 1940 assault on Belgium's Fort Eben-Emael, using gliders to assault and neutralize the fortress. The division also participated in the Battle of Crete in 1941, suffering heavy losses that led Hitler to limit future large-scale airborne operations. After Crete, the division served on the Eastern Front near Leningrad and Stalino (named Donetsk today). In 1943, it was redeployed to Italy, engaging in battles at Ortona and Monte Cassino. Throughout the Italian Campaign, the division was noted for its tenacity, delaying Allied advances despite being outnumbered. In April 1945, it retreated across the Po River and surrendered in early May. The division's structure included three parachute regiments, an artillery regiment, and support units like anti-aircraft and engineer battalions. It was commanded by officers such as Richard Heidrich and Karl-Lothar Schulz. As the war neared its end, the division retreated across northern Italy and ultimately surrendered in May 1945.

card_unit_957_volksgrenadier.name: card_unit_957_volksgrenadier
card_unit_957_volksgrenadier.title: 957. VOLKSGRENADIER
card_unit_957_volksgrenadier.text: Deployment: Add a PRODUCTION to your hand.
card_unit_957_volksgrenadier.flavorText: The 957th Volksgrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 363rd Volksgrenadier Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII, active from 1944 to 1945. The division was created in September 1944 by renaming the 566th Volksgrenadier Division, thus replacing the original 363rd Infantry Division which had been destroyed in the Falaise Pocket. The division was commanded by August Dettling and included the 957th, 958th and 959th Grenadier Regiments, as well as the 363rd Artillery Regiment. The division first saw action in the Netherlands, where it suffered heavy losses during a failed German attack near Nijmegen in October 1944. After being re-equipped, it fought along the Roer River before being encircled and destroyed in the Ruhr Pocket in April 1945.

card_unit_bergmann_battalion.name: card_unit_bergmann_battalion
card_unit_bergmann_battalion.title: BERGMANN BATTALION
card_unit_bergmann_battalion.text: Once per turn, draw a card when you Convert one or more cards.
card_unit_bergmann_battalion.flavorText: The Bergmann Battalion was a special German unit formed in 1942, composed of volunteers and Soviet prisoners of war from the Caucasus region, including Georgians, Armenians, Azerbaijanis, and other ethnic minorities. Organized by the Abwehr, Germany’s military intelligence, the battalion drew heavily from anti-Soviet exiles as well as POWs who agreed to serve in exchange for better conditions and the chance to fight against the Soviet regime. Trained for reconnaissance, sabotage, and mountain warfare, the Bergmann Battalion was used for difficult commando missions behind Soviet lines and anti-partisan operations. Their knowledge of local languages and terrain made them useful in the Caucasus, Crimea, and the Balkans, where they served during the German advance and later in defensive battles as the war situation worsened for Germany. The unit suffered heavy losses, and its history reflects both the complex loyalties and harsh realities faced by foreign volunteers and POWs in German service during WWII.

card_unit_fw189.name: card_unit_fw189
card_unit_fw189.title: FW 189
card_unit_fw189.text: Once per turn, add a PRODUCTION to your hand when you play a Navy card.
card_unit_fw189.flavorText: The Focke-Wulf Fw 189 Uhu (nicknamed “Owl” or "Eagle Owl") was a German twin-engine, twin-boom tactical reconnaissance aircraft developed in the late 1930s to replace the Henschel Hs 126. It featured a distinctive central crew gondola and a glazed stepless cockpit providing excellent visibility for its three-man crew. Powered by two Argus As 410 engines, the Fw 189 had a maximum speed of approximately 355 km/h and a range of about 670 km. It was armed with multiple 7.92mm machine guns and could carry up to four 50 kg bombs. The Fw 189 first entered service in 1940 and was primarily used by the Luftwaffe for short-range reconnaissance missions, especially on the Eastern Front. Its agility and excellent field of view made it effective in its role, earning it the nickname "Fliegendes Auge" (Flying Eye) among German forces. Soviet troops referred to it as "Rama" (Frame) due to its unique shape. A total of 864 Fw 189 aircraft were produced until mid-1944, with manufacturing taking place in Germany, occupied France, and Czechoslovakia. While primarily a reconnaissance aircraft, variants of the Fw 189 were adapted for roles such as ground attack and night fighting. Despite its relatively slow speed, the Fw 189's maneuverability and design allowed it to perform effectively in its intended roles throughout its service.

card_unit_fw_190_f8.name: card_unit_fw_190_f8
card_unit_fw_190_f8.title: FW 190 F-9
card_unit_fw_190_f8.text: At the end of each enemy turn, deal 4 damage to their HQ if they did not deploy a unit.
card_unit_fw_190_f8.flavorText: The Focke-Wulf Fw 190 F-9 was a late-war German ground-attack aircraft, developed as the final variant in the Fw 190 F-series. Introduced in early 1945, it was based on the Fw 190 A-9 airframe but incorporated several enhancements tailored for close air support missions. Similar to F-8s and A-8s variants, it was fitted with a bulged canopy enhancing the pilots visibility, which was a critical factor during low-altitude operations. The aircraft was equipped with four underwing bomb racks allowing it to carry a substantial bomb load for ground-attack roles. While exact production numbers are uncertain, records indicate that 147 F-9s were built in January 1945, with additional units likely produced until the war's end, although documentation for subsequent months is incomplete. The Fw 190 F-9 served on both the Eastern and Western Fronts and provided crucial support to German ground forces during the final months of WWII. Its robust design and effective armament made it a formidable opponent in the ground-attack role, despite the challenging conditions faced by the Luftwaffe in 1945.

card_unit_jagdpanzer_iv.name: card_unit_jagdpanzer_iv
card_unit_jagdpanzer_iv.title: JAGDPANZER IV
card_unit_jagdpanzer_iv.text: When you attack and destroy an enemy unit, Convert a random card in the enemy hand into PRODUCTION.
card_unit_jagdpanzer_iv.flavorText: The Jagdpanzer IV was a German tank destroyer developed during World War II, based on the Panzer IV chassis. Designed to provide a low-profile, heavily armored vehicle for anti-tank operations, it was produced from December 1943 to April 1945, with approximately 2,000 units built. Initially, the Jagdpanzer IV was armed with a 7.5cm PaK 39 L/48 gun. Later versions, known as the Panzer IV/70, were equipped with the more powerful 7.5cm PaK 42 L/70 gun. The vehicle featured sloped armor up to 80 mm thick and had a four-man crew. Its low silhouette and strong frontal armor made it effective in ambush roles. The Jagdpanzer IV served on both the Eastern and Western Fronts, participating in battles such as Normandy and the Ardennes Offensive. While effective as a tank destroyer, it performed less well when used as a substitute for tanks or assault guns, roles for which it was not originally intended.

card_unit_sd_kfz_10_38.name: card_unit_sd_kfz_10_38
card_unit_sd_kfz_10_38.title: Sd Kfz 10 PAK 38
card_unit_sd_kfz_10_38.text: Gets +1 attack until end of turn if another card increases the attack of this unit.
card_unit_sd_kfz_10_38.flavorText: The Sd.Kfz. 10 PaK 38 was a German half-track adapted during WWII to mount the 5cm PaK 38 anti-tank gun, giving infantry units a mobile anti-tank capability. The Sd.Kfz. 10 chassis was originally designed to tow light artillery, but this field modification involved fitting the more powerful PaK 38 gun directly onto the vehicle. The Sd.Kfz. 10 was powered by a 6-cylinder Maybach engine and equipped with half-tracks for improved off-road performance. It retained space for a small crew and ammunition, making it well-suited for hit-and-run attacks and mobile defense. While not a standardized production model, the Sd.Kfz. 10 PaK 38 reflected the German Army’s adaptability in addressing the growing threat of better-armored Allied tanks.

card_event_claim_objective.name: card_event_claim_objective
card_event_claim_objective.title: CLAIM OBJECTIVE
card_event_claim_objective.text: Your units get +1 attack for each kredit spent operating this turn.
card_event_claim_objective.flavorText: During Operation Weserübung in 1940, Germany seized Norway and Denmark before the Allies could threaten the iron ore route from Sweden and use Norwegian ports as naval bases. The plan depended on speed, surprise, and warships carrying troops directly to key cities. Oslo was one of the main objectives, and the heavy cruiser Blücher led the naval group sent up the Oslofjord with 2,000 troops, supported by Lützow, Emden, torpedo boats, minesweepers, and whalers. In the early hours of 9 April, Blücher entered the narrow waters of Drøbak Sound. At Oscarsborg Fortress, Norwegian gunners opened fire after the cruiser was illuminated by searchlights. Two old 280 mm Krupp guns, nicknamed Moses and Aron, hit the ship at close range. Shore-launched torpedoes then struck Blücher, leaving her badly damaged and unable to manoeuvre. Within two hours the cruiser sank, with heavy casualties. The delay gave Norway’s royal family, cabinet, parliament members, and national treasury time to escape Oslo. Germany still occupied Norway, but the failed dash through the fjord changed the opening day of the campaign.

card_event_detailed_recon.name: card_event_detailed_recon
card_event_detailed_recon.title: DETAILED RECON
card_event_detailed_recon.text: Cost is reduced by the amount spent operating this turn. Draw a card, reduce its cost by the same amount.
card_event_detailed_recon.flavorText: The Allied Convoy PQ 17 sailed from Iceland in 1942 with 35 merchant ships carrying tanks, aircraft, vehicles, ammunition, and other supplies for the Soviet Union. German forces found the convoy on 1 July, then shadowed it with submarines and aircraft. The Luftwaffe had Ju 88 bombers, He 111 torpedo bombers, He 115 floatplanes, Fw 200 Condors, BV 138 flying boats, and other reconnaissance aircraft ready for Arctic operations, based in northern Norway. The German plan, called Operation Rösselsprung, involved the battleship Tirpitz, heavy cruisers Admiral Scheer, Lützow and Admiral Hipper, and destroyers. Their possible sortie caused deep concern in the British Admiralty. On 4 July, believing a surface attack was imminent, Admiral Dudley Pound ordered the Allied cruiser force to withdraw and the convoy to scatter. The German battleships never reached the convoy, but the scattered merchant ships lost their protection. Luftwaffe aircraft and U-boats then attacked the isolated ships across the Barents Sea. Only 11 merchant ships reached Soviet ports. The losses included 24 ships, 430 tanks, 210 aircraft, and 3,350 vehicles.

card_event_german_counterattack.name: card_event_german_counterattack
card_event_german_counterattack.title: COUNTERATTACK
card_event_german_counterattack.text: Your Veteran units get +2+2. Then each friendly unit fights a random enemy unit.
card_event_german_counterattack.flavorText: After the German defeat at Stalingrad, Soviet armies pushed west across Ukraine in early 1943. Their advance created deep salients and stretched supply lines, while German forces fell back in disorder. Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, commanding Army Group South, chose not to defend every position. Instead, he pulled mobile units back, waited for the Soviet spearheads to overextend, and prepared a counterattack. In February and March 1943, German panzer and infantry formations struck the exposed Soviet flanks around Kharkov. German forces cut off several forward Soviet units, retook some lost ground, and forced the Red Army to abandon positions taken during its winter offensive. Kharkov was recaptured in March after hard fighting in and around the city. The counterstrike restored part of the German front in southern Ukraine and delayed further Soviet advances until summer. It also showed that German mobile warfare could still be dangerous when used against an overstretched enemy, even after the disaster at Stalingrad.

card_event_sustained_pressure.name: card_event_sustained_pressure
card_event_sustained_pressure.title: SUSTAINED PRESSURE
card_event_sustained_pressure.text: Deal damage to a unit equal to kredits spent operating this turn.
card_event_sustained_pressure.flavorText: During WWII, Stalingrad was a major Soviet industrial city on the Volga, with factories, rail links, fuel stores, and river traffic that supported the front. In August 1942, Luftflotte 4, one of the primary divisions of the German Luftwaffe  concentrated much of its strength there as German ground forces closed on the city. Fliegerkorps VIII was ordered to support the 6th Army and 4th Panzer Army, which saw Stalingrad as central to the wider German drive toward the Caucasus oilfields. On 23 August, German aircraft carried out one of the heaviest air attacks yet seen on the Eastern Front. Ju 87 dive bombers, Fw 190 ground attack aircraft, He 111s, and Ju 88s struck Soviet positions and then the city itself. Around 1,600 sorties were flown that day, dropping about 1,000 tons of bombs. Fires spread through factories, schools, homes, oil tanks, and docks, while smoke rose high above the Volga. The pressure did not end with the first raid. Stalingrad was bombed block by block for days, and Luftflotte 4 kept flying repeated missions against Soviet troops, airfields, river crossings, and industrial districts through the battle.

card_event_tank_wedge.name: card_event_tank_wedge
card_event_tank_wedge.title: TANK WEDGE
card_event_tank_wedge.text: Target friendly German tank and its adjacent units get +1+1.
card_event_tank_wedge.flavorText: The Panzerkeil, or “tank wedge,” was a German armoured tactic developed on the Eastern Front in response to increasingly dense Soviet anti-tank defenses. Tanks advanced in a wedge-shaped formation, with the heaviest and best-protected vehicles at the tip and lighter tanks spread along the flanks. At the Battle of Kursk in 1943, Tiger I tanks led the formations, with Panthers behind them and Panzer III and IV tanks forming the wings. This arrangement forced Soviet anti-tank gunners to constantly adjust their range as the formations advanced, while the heavier vehicles absorbed much of the incoming fire. The tactic met with mixed success. During Operation Citadel, elements of the 4th Panzer Army used the Panzerkeil to penetrate parts of the Soviet defensive system, while other German formations failed to break through and suffered heavy losses. Minefields posed a serious threat, often requiring combat engineers to advance ahead of the tanks and clear a path.

card_unit_102_grenadier.name: card_unit_102_grenadier
card_unit_102_grenadier.title: 102. GRENADIER
card_unit_102_grenadier.flavorText: During WWII, the 102nd Grenadier Regiment was part of the German 24th Infantry Division, alongside the 31st and 32nd Grenadier Regiments. The division was formed at Chemnitz in 1935 and first saw combat in Poland in 1939. It fought as part of 8th Army and suffered heavy losses in the fighting along the Bzura river, where Polish resistance hit the division hard. In 1940, the 24th Infantry Division took part in the campaign in France, notably the combat around Stonne. The next year it joined Army Group South for the invasion of the Soviet Union and fought in Ukraine, particularly the battles around Uman and Kiev. It then moved to Crimea under the 11th Army. During the final assault on Sevastopol in 1942, the division captured key positions, including Mekenziyevy Mountain station and Fort Stalin, but lost about 30 percent of its strength. Later in 1942, the division was sent north to the Leningrad sector. It was engaged in the difficult battles on the Volkhov Front, then retreated west during the Soviet offensives of 1944. It ended the war trapped in the Courland Pocket.

card_unit_14_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_14_panzergrenadier
card_unit_14_panzergrenadier.title: 14. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_14_panzergrenadier.text: Becomes Veteran when you deploy a tank.
card_unit_14_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 14. Panzergrenadier Regiment served as one of the two panzergrenadier regiments of the 5th Panzer Division on the Eastern Front. It had previously appeared in the division’s 1940 organization as Schützen-Regiment 14 before becoming a mechanized infantry formation supporting the division’s tanks. The division was formed in 1938 and fought in Poland, France and the Balkans before being sent East for Operation Barbarossa. It advanced to within 34 km of Moscow before being forced back by the Soviet counteroffensive. For the remainder of the war, the division fought mainly defensive battles on the Eastern Front and earned a formidable reputation. Soviet commanders regarded the 5th Panzer Division as one of Germany’s best formations and, until July 1944, the Soviet High Command reportedly advised avoiding direct engagement with it whenever possible. The division survived Operation Bagration and continued fighting through Poland, Courland and East Prussia before its remnants surrendered in Danzig in April 1945.

card_unit_182_landwehr.name: card_unit_182_landwehr
card_unit_182_landwehr.title: 182. LANDWEHR
card_unit_182_landwehr.text: Becomes Veteran after you have operated units three times.
card_unit_182_landwehr.flavorText: The Landwehr Infantry Regiment 182 was part of the 14th Landwehr Division, raised in Wehrkreis V military district during Germany’s general mobilization in 1939. The regiment came from Müllheim and served beside Landwehr Infantry Regiments 40 and 59, with Landwehr Infantry Regiment 33 joining later. These Landwehr formations drew heavily on older reservists, although the army later tried to replace older soldiers with younger men. The division first held defensive positions on the Upper Rhine under 7th Army. On 1 January 1940, it was redesignated as the 205th Infantry Division. Its former Landwehr regiments became Infantry Regiments 335, 353, and 358. After occupation duty in France and a period of demobilization, the division was recalled and sent east in 1942. On the Eastern Front, the 205th Infantry Division fought around Velizh and Velikiye Luki. Heavy losses forced reductions in 1943, but the division was later rebuilt with three grenadier regiments. During the Soviet summer offensives of 1944, it was pushed back with Army Group North through Polotsk, Daugavpils, and Livonia. It ended the war trapped in the Courland Pocket.

card_unit_30_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_30_infantry_regiment
card_unit_30_infantry_regiment.title: 30. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_30_infantry_regiment.text: Reduce operation cost by 1 after you operate a German unit.
card_unit_30_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 30th Infantry Regiment was part of the 18th Infantry Division, a formation whose wartime service stretched from the opening campaigns of 1939 to the final battle in Berlin. Mobilized in August 1939, the 18th Infantry Division took part in the invasion of Poland before fighting in the Battle of France in 1940. Following the French campaign, the division was motorized and redesignated the 18th Motorized Infantry Division. From June 1941 it fought on the Eastern Front, first in the central sector and later in the North. In June 1943, the formation became the 18th Panzergrenadier Division. It continued fighting on the Eastern Front but was devastated during the Soviet summer offensive of 1944. Its surviving members later fought in East Prussia and ultimately in the Battle of Berlin. When Berlin surrendered on 2 May 1945, they attempted to fight their way out of the encircled city.

card_unit_3_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_3_panzergrenadier
card_unit_3_panzergrenadier.title: 3. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_3_panzergrenadier.text: Gets +1+1 after you operate a German unit.
card_unit_3_panzergrenadier.flavorText: Panzer Grenadier Regiment 3 was part of the 3rd Panzer Division, serving alongside Panzer Grenadier Regiment 394 in the division’s 1943 Eastern Front organization. The 3rd Panzer Division was one of Germany’s first three tank divisions, formed in 1935 and headquartered in Berlin. It fought in Poland in 1939, where it was the strongest German panzer division by tank numbers, with 391 tanks. In 1940 it advanced through Belgium toward Brussels and into France. Afterward, one of its two tank regiments was removed to help form new panzer divisions, and the division gained more infantry. Panzer Grenadier Regiments were formed to fill the motorized infantry role that German panzer divisions needed after losing some armored strength and reorganizing for a longer war. In 1941 the 3rd Panzer division joined Operation Barbarossa. It fought first in the central sector, then in Ukraine during the Battle of Kiev, and later drove toward Tula during the Battle of Moscow. In 1942 it advanced toward the Caucasus during Case Blue, but suffered heavy losses near Mozdok. It later fought at Kursk and remained on the Eastern Front until 1945, ending the war in Styria where it surrendered to US forces.

card_unit_blue_legion.name: card_unit_blue_legion
card_unit_blue_legion.title: BLUE LEGION
card_unit_blue_legion.text: After you operate a unit, give it +1+1 for each kredit spent to operate it.
card_unit_blue_legion.flavorText: The Blue Legion was the nickname of the Spanish Volunteer Legion, a small infantry force that remained on the Eastern Front after Spain withdrew most of the Blue Division in 1943. Spanish leader Francisco Franco had begun negotiations with the Allies, making the continued presence of a large Spanish formation in German service politically difficult. Around 2,133 Falangist volunteers stayed behind at first, officially organized into two battalions under German Army command. Later estimates place the number of Spaniards connected to the legion at over 3,000. The unit was active from November 1943 to April 1944 and fought during the later stages of the war on the Eastern Front, including the Leningrad Novgorod offensive. Its soldiers wore a sleeve patch representing a shield in Spain’s red and yellow colors, marked with the word ESPAÑA, which distinguished them from German troops while still showing their place in German service. Some Spanish volunteers refused repatriation even after the Blue Legion was dissolved. Small groups were absorbed into other German units, and a few later fought in Pomerania, Brandenburg, and Berlin in 1945.

card_unit_fw_190_ta_152.name: card_unit_fw_190_ta_152
card_unit_fw_190_ta_152.title: FW TA 152
card_unit_fw_190_ta_152.text: Becomes Veteran when it attacks and destroys a unit.
card_unit_fw_190_ta_152.flavorText: The Focke-Wulf Ta 152 was the final development of the Fw 190 line, redesigned by Kurt Tank to fight at altitudes where earlier German fighters struggled. The original Fw 190 was strong at medium flight level, but Allied heavy bombers and long-range escorts operated at increasingly higher altitudes than its BMW 801 engine could handle well. The Ta 152 answered this issue with a longer fuselage, larger tail, pressurized cockpit, improved radio equipment and, on the H model, a greatly extended wing for high altitude control. The Ta 152H entered Luftwaffe service in January 1945, far too late to affect the air war. Only 69 were built. Its Junkers Jumo 213E engine used MW 50 water methanol boost at lower altitudes and GM 1 nitrous oxide boost higher up. The H 1 carried one 30 mm MK 108 cannon and two 20 mm MG 151 cannons, giving it heavy firepower against bombers. The aircraft served mainly with Jagdgeschwader 301. Pilots praised its speed and handling, but fuel and parts shortages, and Germany’s collapsing production system kept it rare in combat.

card_unit_heinkel_he_59.name: card_unit_heinkel_he_59
card_unit_heinkel_he_59.title: HEINKEL HE 59
card_unit_heinkel_he_59.text: Once per turn, when a friendly unit becomes Veteran, draw a card and gain a kredit.
card_unit_heinkel_he_59.flavorText: The Heinkel He 59 was a large twin-engine biplane floatplane built for roles forbidden to Germany when its design began in 1930. Officially presented as a civil aircraft, it had in reality been developed for the Reichsmarine as a torpedo bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. The first landplane prototype flew in 1931,  but only the floatplane version went into production. A total of 142 were built. The He 59 was easy to fly, but its weak engines, short range, limited load, and light armament made it outdated by WWII. Even so, it found use in coastal reconnaissance, minelaying, torpedo training, transport, and air-sea rescue. During the early war it supported German operations in Norway and the Netherlands, then became closely linked with the Seenotstaffeln, the Luftwaffe air-sea rescue units. He 59 crews searched the Channel for downed German airmen during the Battle of Britain. British forces argued that some rescue aircraft also performed reconnaissance, making them valid targets despite their Red Cross markings. Later, in 1943, Finland later rented four He 59s for long range patrol and transport, before returning them to Germany.

card_unit_katzmann.name: card_unit_katzmann
card_unit_katzmann.title: KATZMANN REGIMENT
card_unit_katzmann.text: Increase operation cost by 1 until end of turn each time you play another card.
card_unit_katzmann.flavorText: Regiment Katzmann was a short-lived formation within the rebuilt German 84th Infantry Division. The division had first gone to France with only two grenadier regiments, 1051 and 1052, a weakness typical of the 25th deployment wave raised from Ersatzheer (literally Replacement Army) manpower in 1944. The 84th Infantry Division had been deployed in February 1944 and fought in France during Operation Overlord. Its first formation was destroyed on 20 August in the Falaise Pocket. It was reformed near Kleve with a third regiment. This new unit was first known as Katzmann, but on 24 December 1944 it received the formal designation Regiment 1062. The rebuilt division then faced the Western Allies on the lower Rhine. It was again destroyed at the Wesel bridgehead during Operation Varsity in 1945. A further rebuilding was planned in the Lüneburg Heath, but the war ended before it could take shape.

card_unit_panther_a_zimm.name: card_unit_panther_a_zimm
card_unit_panther_a_zimm.title: PANTHER A ZIMMERIT
card_unit_panther_a_zimm.text: After this unit operates, increase all its stats by how often it has operated.
card_unit_panther_a_zimm.flavorText: The Panther was one of Germany’s main medium tanks in the late-war period, but even before it entered widespread service there were concerns that its armor might prove insufficient against future Soviet tank guns. In early 1943, this led to work on the more heavily armored Panther II, which was expected to weigh around seven tons more than the standard Panther. Zimmerit was a protective coating applied to German armored vehicles to prevent infantry from attaching magnetic anti-tank mines to their hulls. The idea emerged after Germany introduced its own magnetic Hafthohlladung grenade in 1942 and feared that the Allies might develop similar weapons. Following experiments with several solutions, Zimmer AG developed the specialized coating in 1943. Application to Panther tanks began in September 1943. Around 160 kg of Zimmerit could be required for a Panther, with the paste spread across vertical and sloped armor before being hardened and shaped into distinctive patterns. On 9 September 1944, Germany ordered the Zimmerit application to stop after rumors claimed it could catch fire when hit. Later tests disproved the danger, but production never resumed.

card_unit_windhund_division.name: card_unit_windhund_division
card_unit_windhund_division.title: WINDHUND DIVISION
card_unit_windhund_division.text: Can operate again after it attacks and destroys a unit.
card_unit_windhund_division.flavorText: The 116th Panzer Division was known as the Windhund Division, or Greyhound Division. It was formed in western Germany in 1944 from the remnants of the 16th Panzergrenadier Division and the 179th Reserve Panzer Division. Its motto praised speed and toughness, fitting a formation created during a year when Germany needed mobile reserves against the growing Allied threat in the west. The division entered combat after the Normandy landings and fought during the Battle of Normandy. After the Allied breakout, it was caught in the Falaise Pocket. Along with the 2nd SS Panzer Division, it helped keep an escape route open for other German units, but it escaped with only about 600 infantry men and 12 tanks still intact. After refitting, the Windhund Division fought at Aachen and in the Hürtgen Forest, where it helped retake the town of Schmidt from the US 28th Infantry Division. It later joined the Ardennes offensive, but damaged bridges, resistance, and fuel problems slowed its advance. In 1945, it fought west of the Rhine, then was trapped in the Ruhr Pocket. Most of the division surrendered to the US Ninth Army in April.

card_event_campaign_alamein1_flanking_ma.name: card_event_campaign_alamein1_flanking_maneuver
card_event_campaign_alamein1_flanking_ma.title: FLANKING MANEUVER
card_event_campaign_alamein1_flanking_ma.text: Deal 2 damage to an enemy unit.

card_event_campaign_alamein1_iron_fist.name: card_event_campaign_alamein1_iron_fist
card_event_campaign_alamein1_iron_fist.title: IRON FIST
card_event_campaign_alamein1_iron_fist.text: Target enemy unit must retreat. At the end of turn, your units are fully repaired.

card_event_campaign_alamein3_head_to_hea.name: card_event_campaign_alamein3_head_to_head
card_event_campaign_alamein3_head_to_hea.title: HEAD TO HEAD
card_event_campaign_alamein3_head_to_hea.text: Deal damage to an enemy tank unit equal to friendly tank units. Draw cards equal to damage dealt.

card_event_campaign_alamein3_riding_the_.name: card_event_campaign_alamein3_riding_the_storm
card_event_campaign_alamein3_riding_the_.title: RIDING THE STORM
card_event_campaign_alamein3_riding_the_.text: Remove pin from your units. They cannot be pinned this turn.

card_event_combined_arms_cam1.name: card_event_combined_arms_cam1
card_event_combined_arms_cam1.title: COMBINED ARMS
card_event_combined_arms_cam1.text: Give a friendly tank +1+1 for each unit type you control.

card_event_joint_operation_cam1.name: card_event_joint_operation_cam1
card_event_joint_operation_cam1.title: JOINT OPERATION
card_event_joint_operation_cam1.text: Deal damage to target enemy equal to 1 plus the number of unit types you control.

card_event_reinforcements_cam1.name: card_event_reinforcements_cam1
card_event_reinforcements_cam1.title: REINFORCEMENTS
card_event_reinforcements_cam1.text: Fully repair all friendly units and draw a card.

card_location_british_scen1_ai.name: card_location_british_scen1_ai
card_location_british_scen1_ai.title: TEBOURBA
card_location_british_scen1_ai.text: Tebourba was a strategically important town in Tunisia, controlling the central route to Tunis City.

card_location_british_scen2_ai.name: card_location_british_scen2_ai
card_location_british_scen2_ai.title: DJEDEIDA
card_location_british_scen2_ai.text: The town of Djedeida is the central base guarding the route to Tunis City and the main air base.

card_location_british_scen3_ai.name: card_location_british_scen3_ai
card_location_british_scen3_ai.title: KASSERINE
card_location_british_scen3_ai.text: The town of Kasserine sits at the entrance to the Kasserine Pass.

card_location_british_scen4_ai.name: card_location_british_scen4_ai
card_location_british_scen4_ai.title: MATEUR
card_location_british_scen4_ai.text: The town of Mateur is one of the main bases for Axis units in Tunisia.

card_location_british_scen5_ai.name: card_location_british_scen5_ai
card_location_british_scen5_ai.title: TUNIS CITY
card_location_british_scen5_ai.text: Tunis City is the capital of Tunisia and the last bastion of Axis forces in North Africa.

card_unit_panzer_iii_j_early.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_j_early
card_unit_panzer_iii_j_early.title: PANZER III-J EARLY
card_unit_panzer_iii_j_early.flavorText: The Panzerkampfwagen III-J was a Panzer III variant, a German medium tank produced from 1939 to 1943. It was manufactured by Daimler-Benz and was used in all major theaters by the Germans and the Axis powers. The Panzer III-J had a main armament of a 1x 5 cm KwK 38/39 gun and a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner).

card_unit_panzer_iv_h_vet.name: card_unit_panzer_iv_h_vet
card_unit_panzer_iv_h_vet.title: PANZER IV-H
card_unit_panzer_iv_h_vet.text: Your ground units with 4 or more attack have Blitz.

card_unit_panzer_i_brothers_vet.name: card_unit_panzer_i_brothers_vet
card_unit_panzer_i_brothers_vet.title: PANZER I-B
card_unit_panzer_i_brothers_vet.text: When this unit becomes Veteran, add a PANZER I-B to your hand.

card_unit_stuka_brothers_vet.name: card_unit_stuka_brothers_vet
card_unit_stuka_brothers_vet.title: STUKA 87G
card_unit_stuka_brothers_vet.text: The enemy discards a card when you attack and destroy a ground unit.

card_event_exploit_the_gap.name: card_event_exploit_the_gap
card_event_exploit_the_gap.title: EXPLOIT THE GAP
card_event_exploit_the_gap.text: If you control the frontline, draw 1 of 3 top units of your deck. Give it Blitz and set cost to 0. Put rest on bottom.
card_event_exploit_the_gap.flavorText: Penetrating the defensive lines of an enemy, and exploiting the gap it creates, is generally called a “breakthrough” in military terms.

card_event_pursuit.name: card_event_pursuit
card_event_pursuit.title: PURSUIT
card_event_pursuit.text: Target unit must retreat. Your units operate for 1 less this turn.
card_event_pursuit.flavorText: The North African Campaign was a back and forth pursuit and clashes between the Axis and Allies forces, from the deserts of Libya to Egypt and everything in between. The campaign took 2 years, 11 months and 3 days, with long intermissions due to lack of supplies and extreme weather conditions.

card_event_reich_defenders.name: card_event_reich_defenders
card_event_reich_defenders.title: AFRIKA KORPS
card_event_reich_defenders.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite German units to add to your hand.
card_event_reich_defenders.flavorText: The Africa Corps was the German expeditionary force in North Africa during WWII and was active between 1941 and 1943. It was called Africakorps for the first 6 months but went through several name changes after that, from Panzerarmee Afrika to Deutsch-Italienische Panzerarmee and finally to Heeresgruppe Afrika (Army Group Africa). The force was most famously commanded by Erwin Rommel, and consisted of both German and Italian forces, both infantry and armored divisions.

card_event_root_out_the_enemy.name: card_event_root_out_the_enemy
card_event_root_out_the_enemy.title: ROOT OUT THE ENEMY
card_event_root_out_the_enemy.flavorText: Flamethrowers were first used during WWI for clearing out trenches and buildings, and during WWII their use was greatly increased. The Flammenwerfer 35, or FmW 35, was the name of the flamethrower used by the Wehrmacht and it weighed almost 36 kg. In 1944 the Wehrmacht introduced a lighter and more compact version called Einstossflammenwerfer 46.

card_unit_361_light_regiment.name: card_unit_361_light_regiment
card_unit_361_light_regiment.title: 361. AFRIKA REGIMENT
card_unit_361_light_regiment.text: When this unit moves into the frontline, deal 3 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_361_light_regiment.flavorText: The 361st Afrika Regiment was made up of 300 Germans who had served with the French Foreign Legion prior to WWII and despite being considered disreputable soldiers they were allowed to serve in the Wehrmacht due to the need for extra troops. The 361st Regiment was part of the 90th Light Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht Afrika Corp and served in North Africa, Sardinia and Italy. The division played a major role in the North African Campaign where it fought against the British 8th Army, but after the Tunisian Campaign in 1943 it surrendered to the Allies. The division was reorganized that same year and deployed in Sardinia and later moved to Italy where it was listed as destroyed in 1944.

card_unit_panzer_iii_g_desert.name: card_unit_panzer_iii_g_desert
card_unit_panzer_iii_g_desert.title: PANZER III-G
card_unit_panzer_iii_g_desert.flavorText: The Panzer III-G was one of many versions in the Panzer III medium tank series. Similar to the previous models of the G series it had a main armament of a 3.7 cm KwK 36 gun, although later productions had a 5 cm KwK 38 L/42 gun, and for secondary armament it had 2–3 x 7.92 mm Maschinengewehr 34. It was very similar to the F series, which was the first mass produced model, except the gun mantlet had extra armor. The Panzer III-G had a crew of 5 (commander, gunner, loader, driver, radio operator/bow machine-gunner) and 594 units of this model were produced.

card_unit_wespe_desert.name: card_unit_wespe_desert
card_unit_wespe_desert.title: WESPE
card_unit_wespe_desert.text: Has +1 attack if you control a tank.
card_unit_wespe_desert.flavorText: The Sd.Kfz. 124 Wespe (German for wasp) was a German made self-propelled gun on a Panzer II chassis used during WWII. The gun was produced from early 1943 to June 1944 and 676 units were manufactured, including 159 without the gun to serve as ammunition carriers. The Wespe was first used in combat on the Eastern-Front and it’s reliability and mobility made it a great addition to the artillery formations of the Panzer divisions. The Wespe was also used in the North Africa campaign and proved very valuable for the Afrika Korps that operated in the inhospitable desert. The Wespe had a maximum speed of 40 km/h (25 mph), a crew of 5 (commander, driver and 3x gunners) and a main armament it had a 10.5 cm leFH 18/2 L/28 gun.

card_event_alpenfestung.name: card_event_alpenfestung
card_event_alpenfestung.title: ALPENFESTUNG
card_event_alpenfestung.text: Set your HQ's defense to 25. Remove the top 10 cards of your deck.
card_event_alpenfestung.flavorText: The "Alpenfestung" was a German national redoubt planned by Reichsführer-SS Heinrich Himmler in November and December 1943. The plan was to establish a fortified "Alpine Fortress" in the mountainous regions of southern Germany and Austria as a final stand against the advancing Allied forces. However, it remained more of a symbolic idea born out of desperation rather than a practical or concrete plan. As the war progressed and the German military situation deteriorated, the actual implementation of the Alpine Fortress was not feasible due to resources shortages, the overwhelming Allied advance and the chaos within the German command structure. The alleged “Alpine Fortress” did affect the Allied planning during their advance towards Berlin, but when US forces entered Bavaria and western Austria in April 1945, not much organized resistance was met and it revealed the "National Redoubt" concept as a myth.

card_event_focused_attack_ger.name: card_event_focused_attack_ger
card_event_focused_attack_ger.title: FOCUSED ATTACK
card_event_focused_attack_ger.text: Your infantry and tanks get +1+1 for each unit type you control.
card_event_focused_attack_ger.flavorText: The Battle of Kasserine Pass was fought in February 1943 in Tunisia between the Allied forces, comprising primarily inexperienced US troops, and the seasoned German and Italian forces. It marked the first major confrontation between the Western Allies and the Axis forces in North Africa. The US forces, under the command of General Lloyd Fredendall, encountered significant difficulties due to lack of experience, inadequate leadership, and poor coordination among their units. The Germans, led by General Erwin Rommel, capitalized on these weaknesses, employing effective combined arms tactics and demonstrating their superiority in maneuver warfare. For the US Army, the battle served as a learning experience. It revealed its deficiencies in command, logistics and tactics, leading to improvements in the US Army training, leadership and coordination which contributed to their growing strength in the later stages of the war.

card_event_mountain_offense.name: card_event_mountain_offense
card_event_mountain_offense.title: MOUNTAIN OFFENSIVE
card_event_mountain_offense.text: Add a random 1-cost, 2-cost and 3-cost unit with Alpine to your support line.
card_event_mountain_offense.flavorText: In July 1942 Germany launched Operation Edelweiss, named after the mountain flower, which was an offensive into the mountainous region of Caucasus in the Soviet Union. The ensuing Battle of Caucasus lasted from 1942 to 1944 and involved intense combat in the rugged and challenging terrain of the Caucasus Mountains. The primary German objective was to secure the oil-rich regions in the area, particularly the Baku oil fields. German forces, including mountain troops and other divisions, faced not only the harsh natural conditions but also fierce resistance from Soviet forces. Despite initial gains, the Germans ultimately faced setbacks and by 1943 they started to withdraw from the region. However, it wasn’t until 1944 that the Soviet forces managed to get full control of the Caucasus.

card_event_pummel.name: card_event_pummel
card_event_pummel.title: PUMMEL
card_event_pummel.text: Suppress target unit, then destroy it if it costs 3 or less.
card_event_pummel.flavorText: The German Dover Strait coastal guns were a part of Hitler's ambitious Atlantic Wall defense system which aimed at fortifying the occupied coasts against a potential Allied invasion during WWII. Positioned along the French coast and operated by the German navy and army, these powerful artillery batteries, including heavy guns such as the 40.6 cm SK C/34 guns, nicknamed "Adolf Guns",  were strategically placed to guard the narrowest point of the English Channel, primarily aimed at hindering Allied naval movements. The batteries located at Calais and Cap Gris-Nez posed a significant threat to shipping and naval operations in the Dover Strait. Though intimidating, these coastal defenses faced challenges, including aerial bombardment by Allied forces and the necessity to relocate several guns due to sustained bombing raids. Despite their presence, they played a limited role in the actual conflict during the war, as the anticipated Allied invasion through the Dover Strait did not occur.

card_unit_139_gebirgsjager.name: card_unit_139_gebirgsjager
card_unit_139_gebirgsjager.title: 139. GEBIRGSJÄGER
card_unit_139_gebirgsjager.text: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ when you add or deploy an Alpine unit.
card_unit_139_gebirgsjager.flavorText: The 139th Gebirgsjäger Regiment was a unit of the 3rd Mountain Division of the Wehrmacht, raised from the Austrian Army following the Anschluss, the German annexation of Austria, in 1938. The division participated in the Invasion of Poland in 1939 as part of Army Group South but was later redeployed to garrison the Siegfried Line before the campaign ended. In 1940 the 139th Gebirgjäger Regiment was sent to Northern Norway to secure the Arctic port of Narvik, but there they faced heavy resistance from the Allies, and were on the brink of surrendering when the Allies decided to abandon Narvik due to the German invasion of France. In 1941 the regiment rejoined the 3rd Mountain Division and moved into Lapland to participate in Operation Silver Fox, which was an attack on the Soviet Arctic aimed at capturing Murmansk. The operation failed to achieve its main objectives and in 1942 the division was sent to the Eastern Front. There it engaged in combat near the town of Velikiye Luki, and then moved south to help in relieving Stalingrad. Following the German defeat at Stalingrad, the division fought in the southern theaters of the Eastern Front, retreating through Ukraine, Hungary, Slovakia, and eventually surrendering to the Red Army in Silesia when the war ended in 1945.

card_unit_13_gebirgsjager.name: card_unit_13_gebirgsjager
card_unit_13_gebirgsjager.title: 13. GEBIRGSJÄGER
card_unit_13_gebirgsjager.text: Gets +1+1 when you add or deploy an Alpine unit.
card_unit_13_gebirgsjager.flavorText: The 13th Gebirgsjäger-Regiment was a unit of the 4th Mountain Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was activated in October 1940, and in 1941 it participated in the Balkans Campaign, before joining Army Group South in Operation Barbarossa, the German invasion of the Soviet Union. In 1942 the division took part in Operation Edelweiss, which was a failed German offensive that aimed at securing the oil fields in the Caucasus, particularly in Baku. This was done to meet Germany's growing fuel needs and to cut off a crucial supply for the Soviet Union. Following the operation’s failure, the division was on the defensive and pushed back, first to the Crimean Peninsula, Ukraine, then to Hungary, Slovakia, and finally it surrendered to the Red Army in May 1945 near the Czech city of Olomouc.

card_unit_20_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_20_panzergrenadier
card_unit_20_panzergrenadier.title: 20. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_20_panzergrenadier.text: Deployment: Add a PANZER 35(t) and a COMBINED ARMS to your hand.
card_unit_20_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 20th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 10th Panzergrenadier Division, formally known as the 10th Infantry Division, of the German Wehrmacht. Prior to being redesignated as a panzer division in 1943, the division participated in the invasion of Poland in 1939 and the Invasion of France in 1940. In 1943 the Panzergrenadier Division was sent to the southern regions of the Eastern Front where it fought in a series of defensive battles against the advancing Red Army. In August 1944 the division was destroyed during the second Jassy–Kishinev offensive, a Soviet offensive against Axis forces which took place in Eastern Romania. In 1945 the division was formed again, but it was destroyed a second time shortly after in Poland. From February 2, 1945, the 10th Panzergrenadier Division was re-established as a combat group near Görlitz, and in March 1945 it fought north of the Neisse in Oberschlesien, before surrendering to the Red Army when the war ended.

card_unit_432_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_432_infantry_regiment
card_unit_432_infantry_regiment.title: 432. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_432_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 432nd Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 131st Infantry Division of the German Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in 1940 and participated in Operation Barbarossa in 1941 as part of Army Group Center, in the Battle of Białystok–Minsk and the Battle of Kiev, but it was pushed back by the Soviet counter offensive during the Battle of Moscow. The division was transferred to Velikiye Luki in 1943 and participated in the Battle of Nevel that same year. In 1944, the division was ordered to hold the line at the town of Vitebsk, in what is now Belarus, but after continuous fighting it was driven into the Heiligenbeil Pocket in East Prussia (now part of Russia) where the division was destroyed by the Red Army forces in March 1945.

card_unit_64_panzergrenadier.name: card_unit_64_panzergrenadier
card_unit_64_panzergrenadier.title: 64. PANZERGRENADIER
card_unit_64_panzergrenadier.text: Becomes Veteran if it starts your turn in the frontline.
card_unit_64_panzergrenadier.flavorText: The 64th Panzergrenadier Regiment was a unit of the 16th Panzer Division of the Wehrmacht during WWII. The division was formed in 1940 and participated in Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, where it fought in the Battle of Dubno and the Battle of Kiev. In 1942 they took part in the Second Battle of Kharkov and Case Blue, the German summer offensive in southern Russia. After Operation Uranus, the Soviet offensive in November 1942, the division was trapped in Stalingrad where most of its men were either killed or captured by the Red Army. The division was formed again in 1943 and sent to Italy to defend against the advancing Allied forces. In November 1943 it was sent to the Eastern Front where it participated in an attempt to break the encirclement of Axis troops caught in the Korsun-Cherkassy Pocket. In 1944 the division found itself trapped in the Kamenets-Podolsky pocket, but they managed to break out with the 1st Panzer Army and from there they  retreated to Poland. The 16th Panzer Division finally surrendered to Soviet and US forces in Czechoslovakia in May 1945.

card_unit_h39_swg.name: card_unit_h39_swg
card_unit_h39_swg.title: H39 sWG
card_unit_h39_swg.text: Suppress units attacked by this unit.
card_unit_h39_swg.flavorText: The Schweres Wurfgerät 40 was a multiple rocket launcher used by the German Wehrmacth during WWII. 28 or 32 cm rockets could be fired from packing cases in the groups of four mounted on wooden or metal launch frames.The packing cases of the rockets could also be mounted on frames attached to the sides of Sd.Kfz. 251/1 half-tracks or various captured French vehicles, such as the Hotchkiss H35 tank. The Schweres Wurfgerät 40 was nicknamed Stuka-zu-Fuß (Stuka on foot) and it was first introduced after the Battle of France in 1940 and used in service throughout the war.

card_unit_jet_protoype_a.name: card_unit_jet_protoype_a
card_unit_jet_protoype_a.title: JET PROTOTYPE
card_unit_jet_protoype_a.text: Deployment: Remove 6 cards from your deck. -1 operation cost for each with even cost.
card_unit_jet_protoype_a.flavorText: During WWII, Germany developed jet propulsion technology with notable aircraft like the Messerschmitt Me 262 and Arado Ar 234, marking significant advancements in aviation. These jet-powered aircraft had impressive speed and capabilities but faced challenges due to the lack of resources and the war's late stage. Despite their technical achievements, German jet planes had limited impact on the war's outcome, and issues like fuel shortages and Allied bombings hindered their effectiveness. However, the technology and expertise influenced post-war jet aviation development globally, as many German engineers and scientists played key roles in advancing jet and rocket technology in the United States and the Soviet Union.

card_unit_panther_d_winter.name: card_unit_panther_d_winter
card_unit_panther_d_winter.title: PANTHER D
card_unit_panther_d_winter.text: When this unit attacks, the damage it deals is also dealt to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_panther_d_winter.flavorText: The Panther tank, officially known as Panzerkampfwagen V Panther or PzKpfw V, was a German medium tank that was used from 1943 until the end of the war in 1945. The first production Panther tank was the Ausf.D, not the Ausf.A. This confuses many people since in the past German tank versions started with the letter A and then went on to B, C, D, etc. The Panther tank was developed for the purpose of countering the T-34 and to replace the Panzer III and Panzer IV tanks. It is by some considered the best tank of WWII, but it was rushed to the Battle of Kursk in 1943 even though it still had many known technical issues. As a result, many tanks broke down during the battle. They managed to fix most of these problems by the end of 1943 and early 1944, but new issues arose, such as the bombings of the tank factories, shortages of high-quality materials for important parts, a lack of fuel to train new crews, and the new tank crews not being as skilled as they should be. All of these things made the Panther tank less effective in combat. Around 6,000 Panther tanks were built, including quite a few variants, and approximately 842 of these were Panther Ds.

card_event_bypass.name: card_event_bypass
card_event_bypass.title: BYPASS
card_event_bypass.text: Deal damage to target HQ equal to the total cost of your German tanks in the frontline.
card_event_bypass.flavorText: German military tactics during WWII focused on maneuverability, with combined air and mechanized and armored ground attacks at the center stage. In the opening battles of World War II, German forces ran over, through and around every enemy defensive position in their way. Today their military doctrine is known under the term “Blitzkrieg”, but this term was rarely used by the Germans at the time as the tactic was based on Bewegungskrieg (maneuver warfare), a traditional military tactic that was known to be used by Hannibal the Great and the Romans. This tactic focuses on defeating the enemy by incapacitating their decision-making through shock and disruption.

card_event_case_yellow.name: card_event_case_yellow
card_event_case_yellow.title: CASE YELLOW
card_event_case_yellow.text: Deal 1 damage. Your units get +1+0. The enemy discards a card.
card_event_case_yellow.flavorText: Case Yellow (German: Fall Gelb), also known as the Manstein Plan or Operation Sichelschnitt, was the German war plan during the Battle of France in 1940. Erich Von Manstein, who was chief of staff of Army Group A of the Wehrmacht, had first formulated the plan for the invasion of France and the Low Countries in October 1939. The plan went through several revisions before it was executed and one of the reasons was that in January 1940 a German aircraft carrying documents with parts of the plan crashed in Belgium and the documents were captured by the Allies in the so-called Mechelen Incident. By this time Manstein took planning and the final version of the plan was devised by Franz Halder who was chief of staff of the Army High Command (OKH). Finally the invasion plan was executed on May 10 1940, and although it was considered risky and opposed by many generals, it led to a swift victory which surprised everyone, even the Germans.

card_event_eagle_day.name: card_event_eagle_day
card_event_eagle_day.title: EAGLE DAY
card_event_eagle_day.text: Put a German air unit into play with Blitz. Return it to your hand at the end of the turn.
card_event_eagle_day.flavorText: Eagle Day (Adlertag) marked the first day of Operation Eagle Attack, (Unternehmen Adlerangriff), the codename of a military operation by the German Luftwaffe in 1940, with the intention of destroying the British Royal Air Force (RAF). This was done in preparation for Operation Sea Lion (Unternehmen Seelöwe), the German plan for the invasion of Britain, and the goal was to prevent the RAF from attacking the invasion fleet and to cripple the air defense of the Royal Navy Home Fleet. The operation was postponed several times due to bad weather, but was finally carried out on 13 August 1940. Hermann Göring, the commander in chief of the Luftwaffe, had promised Hitler that the RAF would be destroyed in a matter of days. However, the operation failed its objectives and the Germans never managed to gain air superiority in British airspace. This caused Operation Sea Lion to be postponed indefinitely.

card_event_harass.name: card_event_harass
card_event_harass.title: HARASS
card_event_harass.text: Send a unit to hand. Convert it into a random unit of same cost if you have an air unit.
card_event_harass.flavorText: Between March 1942 and June 1943, the Luftwaffe launched persistent low-level bombing raids against Britain’s southern coast. Known to the British as “tip and run” attacks, these missions were flown by fast single-seat fighter-bombers, initially Bf 109s and later Fw 190s, from Jagdgeschwader 2 and Jagdgeschwader 26. These aircraft struck coastal towns, radar sites, airfields and shipping with surprise and speed, often avoiding detection until bombs had already been dropped. Despite never having more than 28 aircraft at a time, these units inflicted considerable disruption. British radar struggled to detect low-flying raiders and early warning systems proved inadequate. Anti-aircraft defenses expanded rapidly in response, from just 43 light guns in March 1942 to over 500 by the end of the year. Major attacks hit strategic targets like the Telecommunications Research Establishment at Worth Matravers and town centers from Torquay to Eastbourne. A single raid on Canterbury in October 1942 involved over 60 Fw 190s. While RAF Typhoons eventually claimed some successes, most losses occurred after the bombs had already been dropped. The campaign ended abruptly in June 1943 as German aircraft were redeployed to face the Allied threat in the Mediterranean. These attacks forced Britain to commit large resources for minimal German effort.

card_event_scatter_tactics.name: card_event_scatter_tactics
card_event_scatter_tactics.title: SCATTER TACTICS
card_event_scatter_tactics.text: When a unit attacks, give enemy units on the battlefield -2 attack until end of turn.
card_event_scatter_tactics.flavorText: The German blitzkrieg tactics, which proved so successful during the early stages of WWII, were in fact based on their old standard tactical doctrine of a “war of maneuver” and “concentration of forces”. Although there was much focus on armored and mechanized warfare, the Wehrmacht used many aspects of their stormtrooper tactics from 1918 and only 18% of the army was mechanized in 1940-41, the rest was dependent on horse drawn wagons and carts. It is true that German tanks had a lot more radios that they used effectively and their infantry and artillery anti-tank tactics were very effective. However, tank on tank warfare was never a thing and the so-called Panzer Blitzkrieg was a myth created by the German propaganda machine. In hindsight it can be said that the German onslaught through the Ardennes was a huge gamble and could have been easily countered by competent generals. But at the time the Allied armies were ill prepared, their political and military leadership was in turmoil and they didn’t heed the warning signs of what was coming for them.

card_unit_989_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_989_infantry_regiment
card_unit_989_infantry_regiment.title: 989. INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_989_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Gets +2+2 if this is your only unit.
card_unit_989_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 989th Grenadier Regiment was a unit of the 277th Infantry Division of the Wehrmacht. The regiment was formed in 1943 in Croatia, and shortly after it was relocated to France, along with the 277th Division. In August 1944 the division participated in the Battle of Normandy where it was destroyed, but reformed in September 1944 and sent to defend against the Allied advance in Northern France and Rhineland. After that the regiment participated in the Ardennes Offensive where it fought with the 12th Volksgrenadier Division in an attempt to capture the Belgian towns of Rocherath-Krinkelt and Elsenborn, in what is now known as the Battle of the Bulge. During the battle the regiment suffered heavy losses and was forced to retreat into Germany where it continued fighting, mostly with new and inexperienced recruits, and by the end of March in 1944 the regiment had been defeated.

card_unit_fieseler_156.name: card_unit_fieseler_156
card_unit_fieseler_156.title: FIESELER FI 156
card_unit_fieseler_156.text: At the end of your turn, activate a random Countermeasure in hand.
card_unit_fieseler_156.flavorText: The Fieseler Fi 156 Storch (e. stork) was a German liaison aircraft that was used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. The aircraft was designed to be versatile; it didn’t need a long runway and it had foldable wings which made it easy to transport by trailers or by being towed by vehicles. During WWII it was used by the Luftwaffe in all major theaters and perhaps most famously during the daring German commando rescue of Benito Mussolini in 1943. Over 2,900 Fi 156 Storch were built between 1937-1945, including variants, and the production for private use continued in France and Czechoslovakia after the war. Around 60 FI 156 were captured by the Allies during the war and one was assigned to Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery as his personal transport.

card_unit_heinkel_he_111_waw.name: card_unit_heinkel_he_111_waw
card_unit_heinkel_he_111_waw.title: HEINKEL HE 111
card_unit_heinkel_he_111_waw.text: After this unit attacks, deal damage to the enemy HQ equal to the number of unit types you control.
card_unit_heinkel_he_111_waw.flavorText: The Heinkel He 111 was a German medium bomber that was produced between 1935-1944 and used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. The He 111 was the most numerous medium bomber aircraft of the Luftwaffe at the start of the war, but its weak armament was exposed during the Battle of Britain, and despite constant modifications and upgrades it became obsolete during the latter stages of the war. The He 111 was used in most theaters of the war and used in various roles, such as strategic bomber, torpedo bomber, medium bomber and a transport aircraft. A total of 5,656 Heinkel He 111 were produced, including many variants.

card_unit_henschel_he_129.name: card_unit_henschel_he_129
card_unit_henschel_he_129.title: HENSCHEL HS 129
card_unit_henschel_he_129.text:
Has +2 attack against ground targets.
Deployment: Fight target enemy unit.
card_unit_henschel_he_129.flavorText: The Henschel Hs 129 was Germany’s primary ground-attack aircraft during WWII. It was designed in response to the Condor Legion’s experiences in Spain and focused on heavy armor and low-level attack capability. The cockpit was protected by a steel “bathtub” and 75 mm armored glass but offered poor visibility. The initial models used underpowered Argus As 410 engines, resulting in sluggish performance and handling issues. To address these problems, later versions were equipped with captured French Gnome & Rhône 14M engines, which offered better power and eliminated torque imbalance. The improved Hs 129 B-1 entered service in 1942, followed by the B-2. Both models were mostly used on the Eastern Front, mainly to attack tanks and transport columns. Armament upgrades included 30 mm MK 101 and MK 103 cannons, and later a 37 mm BK 3.7 gun. The final variant, the B-3, mounted a 75 mm BK 7.5 cannon with an autoloader and hydraulic recoil system. Though capable of destroying any Allied tank, its performance suffered from the weapon’s weight. Production ceased in 1944 after roughly 870 Hs 129s had been produced.

card_unit_king_tiger_ii.name: card_unit_king_tiger_ii
card_unit_king_tiger_ii.title: KING TIGER
card_unit_king_tiger_ii.text: Gain 2 kredits for each of your German units after this unit is deployed or operated.
card_unit_king_tiger_ii.flavorText: The King Tiger (German: Königstiger), official designation Panzerkampfwagen Tiger Ausf. B, was a German heavy tank that first entered service in 1944. The tank saw action on the Eastern Front and in Europe and its 8.8cm KwK 43 gun and armor made it a formidable weapon. It could knock out any Allied tank that came up against it and its thick armor made it almost impenetrable for any Allied weapon. The main problem with King Tiger was its reliability and many crews were forced to abandon the tank when it either broke down or ran out of fuel. Luckily for the Allies the tank was produced late and under the most difficult circumstances, both the bombing of German factories and lack of materials caused a series of delays and limited the production capabilities. Only 489 King Tigers were manufactured.

card_unit_me_bf_110_waw.name: card_unit_me_bf_110_waw
card_unit_me_bf_110_waw.title: BF 110 C ZERSTÖRER
card_unit_me_bf_110_waw.text: Increase operation cost by 1 after each time this unit attacks.
card_unit_me_bf_110_waw.flavorText: The Messerschmitt Bf 110C Zerstörer (Destroyer) was a German heavy fighter, fighter-bomber and night fighter, used by the Luftwaffe during WWII. The Bf 110 served successfully in the early campaigns in Poland, Norway and France as a heavy fighter, but less so when it took on the bomber-escort role during the Battle of Britain. However, during the latter stages of the war the Bf 110 would become one of WWII's most successful night fighter. The Bf 110 C was the first version of the Bf 110 and it had two DB 601A engines, capable of providing 1,100 hp and could reach up to 349 mph, which meant it could outrun almost any Allied fighter. However, the drawback was that it could only reach maximum speed at an altitude of 22,295 ft, so when it had to escort bombers at a lower altitude it became increasingly vulnerable to British and American fighters.

card_unit_salamander.name: card_unit_salamander
card_unit_salamander.title: SALAMANDER
card_unit_salamander.text: Remove from the battlefield after it attacks until the start of your next turn.
card_unit_salamander.flavorText: The Heinkel He 162 Volksjäger, codename Salamander, was a jet-powered fighter developed at the end of WWII as Germany’s desperate answer to Allied air superiority. Built under the Emergency Fighter Program, it was constructed largely from wood in order to conserve metals. The compact aircraft had a top-mounted BMW 003 engine and a tricycle landing gear. Though designed to be simple enough for young pilots, its high speed and flight characteristics required experienced hands. Its development was rushed. The first prototype flew just 90 days after the design was selected in September 1944. Early flights exposed structural flaws due to poor adhesives used in wooden parts, leading to fatal accidents and design improvements. The He 162 entered limited service in 1945 with Jagdgeschwader 1. Operational use was brief and plagued by fuel shortages, structural failures and pilot inexperience. Of nearly 1,000 units put into production, only about 120 were delivered, and even fewer saw combat. Despite its shortcomings, test pilots, including some Allied ones, praised its flight handling. Production ended with Germany’s surrender in May 1945. Surviving aircraft were captured for testing, and several remain in museums today.

card_event_air_escort.name: card_event_air_escort
card_event_air_escort.title: AIR ESCORT
card_event_air_escort.text: Trigger non-targeting deployment effects on friendly units on the battlefield.
card_event_air_escort.flavorText: During WWII, Italy’s Regia Aeronautica employed air escort tactics focused on protecting both  bombers and convoys, both in the Mediterranean and the African campaigns. Fighters such as the Macchi C.202 Folgore were often used in escort roles, but coordination was frequently hampered by limited radio technology and other problems such as fuel scarcity, short fighter ranges, and reliance on German Luftwaffe support for joint missions. By 1943, with the Allied invasion of Sicily, the Regia Aeronautica's ability to conduct effective escort missions was severely diminished.

card_event_air_strips.name: card_event_air_strips
card_event_air_strips.title: AIR STRIPS
card_event_air_strips.text: Add BREDA Ba.65 to hand and RM ROMA on top of your deck.
card_event_air_strips.flavorText: Throughout WWII, the Italian Regia Aeronautica relied heavily on improvised forward air strips to support fast-moving campaigns and overcome infrastructure limitations. In North Africa, Italian forces constructed temporary runways across Libya and into Egypt, often using materials like packed sand or metal matting to support operations in harsh desert conditions. These air strips allowed bombers and fighters to stay close to the front but were vulnerable to dust, heat and enemy attacks. In the Balkans, Italy used both captured and newly built airfields in Albania, Greece, and Yugoslavia to maintain air superiority and support occupation forces. Many of these sites were hastily prepared, relying on local labor and limited resources. Across Mediterranean islands like Pantelleria, Sardinia and Sicily, airfields served both as defensive positions and springboards for offensive sorties. These were frequently targeted by Allied raids, especially in 1943 during the lead-up to Operation Husky. On the Eastern Front, Italian air units operated from crude, often muddy fields in southern Russia, struggling with poor weather and logistics. Despite challenges, these air strips enabled continued support for Axis ground operations in every major theater where Italian forces fought.

card_event_attack_in_the_colonies.name: card_event_attack_in_the_colonies
card_event_attack_in_the_colonies.title: ATTACK IN THE COLONIES
