card_event_attack_in_the_colonies.text: Deal 3 damage to an enemy. Your HQ gains +5 defense.
card_event_attack_in_the_colonies.flavorText: Following the footsteps of their German ally, Italy declared war on Britain in June 1940. Their goal was to occupy British and French colonies in Africa as well as seizing control of the Suez Canal from the British. Initially the Italian forces managed to seize control of the upper Nile Valley in Sudan and British Somaliland. More troops were sent to capture the Northern part of the British colony of Kenya and to advance into Egypt in the hopes of reaching the Suez Canal. However, by this time the British managed to execute three counter offensives, and with great help from the RAF they managed to push back the Italians. What followed was a series of battles for control of Libya and regions of Egypt, and despite being reinforced by the Germans, the last Italian troops in East Africa were defeated at the Battle of Gondar in November 1941. However, several thousand Italian troops continued to wage a guerrilla war until September 1943, when Italy surrendered to the Allies.

card_event_betasom.name: card_event_betasom
card_event_betasom.title: BETASOM
card_event_betasom.text: Develop a Navy card. The top card of your deck has the Navy type until the end of your next turn.
card_event_betasom.flavorText: BETASOM, an acronym for "Bordeaux Sommergibile", was an Italian submarine base established in Bordeaux, France, during WWII. Operational from August 1940 to September 1943, it served as the headquarters for Italian naval operations in the Atlantic. The base housed up to thirty submarines and included facilities such as dry docks and interconnected basins. Approximately 1,600 personnel were stationed there, including a guard unit from the San Marco Regiment. Under the command of Admiral Angelo Parona and later successors, Italian submarines launched patrols targeting Allied shipping lanes. Despite initial challenges, including design limitations of their submarines, Italian forces adapted and achieved notable successes. By August 1943, they had sunk 109 Allied ships, totaling over 590,000 tons. However, coordination with German U-boat operations was limited, and the Italians often operated independently. Following Italy's armistice in September 1943, the base ceased operations. Some Italian submarines were scuttled, while others were taken over by German forces. Today, the former BETASOM base serves as a cultural venue, preserving its historical significance.

card_event_brute_force.name: card_event_brute_force
card_event_brute_force.title: BRUTE FORCE
card_event_brute_force.text: Deal 1 damage to target enemy for each unit you control above the enemy.
card_event_brute_force.flavorText: The occupation of Albania by Italy took place in April 1939 during the early stages of WWII. Italy, under the leadership of Benito Mussolini, sought to expand its influence in the Balkans and establish a puppet state in Albania. The invasion and subsequent occupation were swift and relatively uncontested. The Italian forces, led by General Alfredo Guzzoni, launched a combined air, land, and naval assault on Albania. The Italian military employed overwhelming force, including aerial bombardments, naval shelling, and ground offensives, to quickly overpower the Albanian defenses which only had 8,000 soldiers, 5 aircraft and 3 torpedo boats at their disposal. Facing overwhelming odds, the Albanian army, led by King Zog I, was unable to mount a significant defense and was forced to retreat. Following the occupation, Italy installed a puppet regime led by Shefqet Vërlaci, who was declared the Prime Minister of Albania. However, the Italian occupation of Albania was met with resistance from various Albanian nationalist and communist groups. The National Liberation Movement, led by Enver Hoxha, emerged as a significant force opposing the Italian occupation. The Italian occupation of Albania lasted until September 1943 when Italy surrendered to the Allied forces. After Italy's capitulation, Germany took control of Albania and continued the occupation until the end of the war. The occupation had a significant impact on Albania's political and social landscape, fueling nationalist sentiments and setting the stage for the country's subsequent struggle for independence and communist rule under Enver Hoxha.

card_event_colonial_dreams.name: card_event_colonial_dreams
card_event_colonial_dreams.title: COLONIAL DREAMS
card_event_colonial_dreams.text: The player with the most units in hand draws 2 cards.
card_event_colonial_dreams.flavorText: In 1940 the Italians joined the war on Germany’s side in the hopes of expanding their territories. They thought they had joined the winning side and that the war in Europe was almost over, but to the contrary it became their downfall. Prior to 1940 the Kingdom of Italy had colonized Albania, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Libya, Somalia and debatably China (Tientsin), Greece (Dodecanese Islands) and Yugoslavia (Croatia and Slovenia). However, all the aforementioned colonies were lost during WWII.

card_event_convoy_attack.name: card_event_convoy_attack
card_event_convoy_attack.title: CONVOY ATTACK
card_event_convoy_attack.flavorText: The Italian Navy, or Regia Marina, was primarily focused on protecting its own convoys from Allied attacks, rather than attacking Allied convoys. However, on a few instances it took offensive actions against Allied shipping, especially during the Battle of the Mediterranean (1940-43). During this period the Italian Regia Aeronautica and Regia Marina sometimes attacked the Allied ships together with the German Luftwaffe and Kriegsmarine.

card_event_dagger_has_struck.name: card_event_dagger_has_struck
card_event_dagger_has_struck.title: THE DAGGER STRIKES
card_event_dagger_has_struck.text: Pin target unit, then destroy it if it has the single highest attack on the battlefield.
card_event_dagger_has_struck.flavorText: One notable example of an Italian victory solely involving Italian troops during WWII was the Italian invasion of British Somaliland in August 1940. The Italian forces successfully invaded and occupied this strategic territory in the Horn of Africa,outmaneuvering and overwhelming the British defenders. This victory was the greatest success of the Italians in the East African campaign and demonstrated the Italian army's capability to conduct successful military operations without direct assistance from their German allies.

card_event_decisive_defense.name: card_event_decisive_defense
card_event_decisive_defense.title: DECISIVE DEFENSE
card_event_decisive_defense.text: When a unit attacks your HQ, add a 6th ALPINI REGIMENT next to it defending.
card_event_decisive_defense.flavorText: The First Battle of Bir el Gubi was fought in Libya in November 1941, between the Italian and Commonwealth forces. The battle was fought during Operation Crusader which was an Allied attempt to bypass Axis defenses on the Egyptian-Libyan frontier and to relieve the Siege of Tobruk. The battle ended with an Italian victory and this was the first tank battle in North Africa where the Italians armored forces were victorious. A couple of weeks later the Commonwealth forces made another attempt to capture Bir el Gubi, in what is known as the Second Battle of Bir el Gubi, but again the Italian forces managed to repel the attacks. The Axis forces would later retreat from Bir el Gubi after continuous Allied attacks.

card_event_desert_push.name: card_event_desert_push
card_event_desert_push.title: DESERT PUSH
card_event_desert_push.text: Fully repair target ground unit. If it is pinned, remove pin.
card_event_desert_push.flavorText: The Desert War took place in the desert of Egypt and Libya and was the main theater of the North African campaign during WWII. It started with the Italian invasion of Egypt in 1940, where the Italians were lightly opposed and managed to advance 100 km to a town called Sidi Barrani, where they stopped and started entrenching themselves. In 1942 the Axis in Northern Africa were under the control of Erwin Rommel who almost managed to kick the British out of Egypt. However, at the First Battle of El Alamein Rommel’s advance was halted by the British only 140 km from Alexandria, the capital of Egypt. From there on it was downhill for the Axis and an Allied victory in Northern Africa was completed in May 1943.

card_event_eastern_front.name: card_event_eastern_front
card_event_eastern_front.title: EASTERN FRONT BOUND
card_event_eastern_front.text: Give your Alpine units +1+1. Draw an Alpine unit from your deck.
card_event_eastern_front.flavorText: After the German invasion of the Soviet Union, Mussolini decided to show solidarity with his German ally by sending Italian troops to fight on the Eastern Front. From 1941 to 1943 the Italian Royal Army maintained two army units on the Eastern Front, the Italian Expeditionary Corps in Russia (Corpo di Spedizione Italiano in Russia, or CSIR) and the Italian 8th Army. In total the Italians maintained 3 corps on the Eastern front, a total of 229,000 men, 22,000 vehicles, and 1,340 artillery pieces. Many of the Italian troops were Alpini mountain troops, and although they were elite troops they lacked experience and equipment to fight on the vast and flat Russian steps. By the end of February 1943 about 30,000 Italians had been killed and another 54,000 would later die in captivity.

card_event_italian_human_torpedo.name: card_event_italian_human_torpedo
card_event_italian_human_torpedo.title: HUMAN TORPEDO
card_event_italian_human_torpedo.text: Destroy target enemy unit in the support line.
card_event_italian_human_torpedo.flavorText: A human torpedo is a type of diver propulsion vehicle on which the diver rides. They were used as secret naval weapons in WWII and the name is commonly used to refer to the weapon that Italy and later Britain deployed in the Mediterreanean and used to attack and sink enemy ships in the harbor.

card_event_lion_for_a_day.name: card_event_lion_for_a_day
card_event_lion_for_a_day.title: LION FOR A DAY
card_event_lion_for_a_day.text: Destroy target unit with 4 or more attack.
card_event_lion_for_a_day.flavorText: The quote “It is better to live one day as a lion than 100 years as a sheep” has by some been attributed to Benito Mussolini, but many believe it was borrowed by him.

card_event_mare_nostrum.name: card_event_mare_nostrum
card_event_mare_nostrum.title: MARE NOSTRUM
card_event_mare_nostrum.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. If your HQ has more defense than the enemy HQ, deal 3 damage.
card_event_mare_nostrum.flavorText: Mare Nostrum, means “Our Sea'' in Latin, and was a Roman name for the Mediterranean Sea. This term was much used by Mussolini and by the fascist propaganda machine and reflected the dream of an Italian Empire, similar to the Roman Empire, that would dominate the Mediterranean Sea. In 1940, following the fall of France, Mussolini started attacking British possessions in the Mediterranean. What followed was the Battle of the Mediterranean, which was one of the largest naval campaigns in WWII, and ended with Allied victory.

card_event_med_raid.name: card_event_med_raid
card_event_med_raid.title: MEDITERRANEAN RAID
card_event_med_raid.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit. If you control more units than the enemy, deal 4 instead.
card_event_med_raid.flavorText: The Italian Royal Navy could not match the strength of the British Royal Navy in the Mediterranean Sea and due to this they avoided large scale confrontations at sea. Instead they found other ways to attack the British ships, the most successful involved the use of submarines, frogmen and manned torpedoes (human torpedoes) to raid ships in the harbor. These attacks were primarily carried out by the Italian 10th Light Flotilla. From 1940 to 1942 they managed to sink and damage 28 Allied ships, including the battleships Valiant and  HMS Queen Elizabeth, along with 113,317 tons of merchant shipping.

card_event_naval_engagement.name: card_event_naval_engagement
card_event_naval_engagement.title: NAVAL ENGAGEMENT
card_event_naval_engagement.text: Fully repair all units in your support line. Destroy all units in the enemy support line.
card_event_naval_engagement.flavorText:
Although the Italian Navy (Regia Marina) was outmatched by the British fleet in the Mediterranean during WWII, there were a few instances where they achieved success. 

In the Battle of Cape Spartivento in November 1940, Admiral Inigo Campioni led the Italian Navy in a confrontation with the British Mediterranean Fleet. Italian cruisers and destroyers successfully attacked a British convoy bound for North Africa, causing damage to British ships. The Italian Navy managed to escape without significant losses.

In the Second Battle of Sirte, which took place in March 1942, the Italian Navy, once again under Admiral Angelo Iachino's command, attacked a convoy of supply ships en route to North Africa. Engaging British warships, the Italian fleet damaged the cruiser HMS Cleopatra and sank the destroyer HMS Kingston.

However, during the Allied Invasion of Sicily in 1943, the Italian Navy was overwhelmed by the superior Allied naval forces. The Italian fleet was largely neutralized, with several ships being captured or scuttled by their own crews to prevent them from falling into enemy hands. This led to the eventual surrender of the Italian Navy to the Allies in September 1943. Subsequently, the Italian fleet was either disarmed or incorporated into Allied naval operations for the remainder of the war.

card_event_pact_of_steel.name: card_event_pact_of_steel
card_event_pact_of_steel.title: PACT OF STEEL
card_event_pact_of_steel.text: Both players draw a card. Discard the lower cost card. Repeat 3 more times.
card_event_pact_of_steel.flavorText: The pact of steel was known formally as the Pact of Friendship and Alliance between Germany and Italy. It was a military and political alliance between Italy and Germany, signed in 1939 in Berlin.

card_event_regia_aeronautica.name: card_event_regia_aeronautica
card_event_regia_aeronautica.title: REGIA AERONAUTICA
card_event_regia_aeronautica.text: Deal damage to each enemy equal to friendly air units.
card_event_regia_aeronautica.flavorText: The Regia Aeronautica was established in 1923, following the creation of the Kingdom of Italy's unified air force. Over the years, it developed into a key component of Italy's military forces, participating in various conflicts, including the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939). During WWII the air force played a vital role in supporting the country's military campaigns from 1940 to 1943. Initially, it was well-equipped with modern aircraft, such as the Macchi C.200 and Fiat G.50 fighters, but it struggled later against superior Allied forces. In the Mediterranean theater, it battled British and Commonwealth forces, particularly during the North African Campaign, where it provided air support for ground operations in Libya and Egypt. Despite its strengths in some areas, the Regia Aeronautica faced critical issues, including outdated training, inferior aircraft later in the war, and a lack of coordination with the Italian Army and Navy. The air force's initial successes were overshadowed by heavy losses due to the technological superiority of Allied aircraft like the Spitfire and P-40. After Italy's surrender in 1943, the Regia Aeronautica was split, with some units joining the Allies (forming Kingdom of Italy’s Co-belligerent Air Force) and others aligning with the German Luftwaffe (forming Italian Social Republic’s National Republican Air Force).

card_event_regia_marina.name: card_event_regia_marina
card_event_regia_marina.title: REGIA MARINA
card_event_regia_marina.text: Draw the highest cost card in your deck. Repeat if it did not start there.
card_event_regia_marina.flavorText: The Regia Marina was the Royal Italian Navy, serving the Kingdom of Italy from 1861 until 1946. It entered WWII as a large and modern force on paper, with battleships, cruisers, destroyers, torpedo boats, submarines, and many fast attack craft. Its main task was to control the central Mediterranean, protect supply routes to North Africa, and challenge British naval forces based in Gibraltar, Malta, and Alexandria. Italian warships were often fast and well-armed, but the fleet faced serious limits. It lacked a true fleet air arm, had few radar-equipped ships, and suffered from fuel shortages. These problems hindered its performance in the night battles and convoy actions that dominated the Mediterranean campaign. Heavy losses at Taranto and Cape Matapan showed the danger of British air power, radar and intelligence. Nevertheless, the Regia Marina still achieved some important successes. Italian frogmen badly damaged HMS Queen Elizabeth and HMS Valiant at Alexandria in 1941, while surface forces and aircraft helped disrupt convoys around Malta in 1942. Its submarines also fought in the Atlantic, and Italian small craft served as far away as the Black Sea and Lake Ladoga, in Karelia.

card_event_rm_bersaglieri.name: card_event_rm_bersaglieri
card_event_rm_bersaglieri.title: RM BERSAGLIERE
card_event_rm_bersaglieri.text: Draw a card from your deck that did not start there. Give your HQ defense equal to its cost.
card_event_rm_bersaglieri.flavorText: The Italian destroyer Bersagliere was a Soldati-class vessel commissioned in 1939. Named after the elite Italian light infantry, she embodied speed and firepower. With a top speed of 34 knots and a crew of 206, Bersagliere was equipped with twin 120 mm guns, a dedicated star shell gun for night combat and anti-aircraft defenses. She operated primarily in the Mediterranean, serving in escort and fleet operations during Italy's naval campaigns. Part of the first batch of Soldati-class destroyers, Bersagliere featured several improvements over previous designs, including enhanced stability and fire control. These destroyers were vital in countering Allied convoys and supporting Axis operations across North Africa and beyond. On 7 January 1943, while anchored in the port of Palermo, Bersagliere was struck by Allied aircraft. A direct hit caused a catastrophic explosion, likely from her own torpedoes or depth charges, which destroyed the vessel. The blast split the ship in two, killing 59 crewmen. Her sinking reflected the growing dominance of Allied air power in the Mediterranean by 1943.

card_event_rm_roma.name: card_event_rm_roma
card_event_rm_roma.title: RM ROMA
card_event_rm_roma.text: Deal 4 damage to an enemy. The top card of your deck has the Navy type until the end of your next turn.
card_event_rm_roma.flavorText: The Roma, commissioned in June 1942, was the third and final Littorio-class battleship of Italy's Regia Marina. Equipped with nine 15-inch guns and advanced armor, she was among the most formidable warships of her time. However, Italy's fuel shortages and strategic constraints limited her operational use. On September 9, 1943, following Italy's armistice with the Allies, Roma led a fleet departing La Spezia, intending to surrender at Malta. While navigating near Sardinia, the fleet was attacked by German Dornier Do 217 bombers deploying Fritz X radio-controlled glide bombs. Roma was struck twice: the first bomb caused significant flooding and power loss and the second detonated a forward magazine that resulted in a catastrophic explosion. The ship broke apart and sank, leading to the deaths of 1,393 crew members, including Admiral Carlo Bergamini. Roma's sinking marked the first instance of a battleship destroyed by a precision-guided weapon, signaling a shift in naval warfare. Her wreck was located in 2012 off Sardinia's coast at a depth of approximately 1,000 meters.

card_event_spirit_of_rome.name: card_event_spirit_of_rome
card_event_spirit_of_rome.title: SPIRIT OF ROME
card_event_spirit_of_rome.text: Target friendly infantry unit gets +1+1 for every defense your HQ has over the enemy HQ.
card_event_spirit_of_rome.flavorText: The Italian Fascists under Mussolini often drew similarities between themselves and the legacy of ancient Rome, and this was both found in their ideology, symbols and propaganda. Fascists claimed that modern Italy was the heir to ancient Rome and that their history supported the creation and expansion of an Italian Empire.

card_event_spring_offensive.name: card_event_spring_offensive
card_event_spring_offensive.title: SPRING OFFENSIVE
card_event_spring_offensive.text: Draw 2 cards. Gain 2 kredits for each unit with 4 or more attack drawn.
card_event_spring_offensive.flavorText: In March 1941, Italy launched a major offensive in Greece during the Greco-Italian War. After several months of stalemate and setbacks following their initial invasion in October 1940, Italian forces attempted to break through Greek defenses in the Epirus region. Despite a large-scale effort and reinforcements, the offensive failed to achieve its objectives, and Greece held its ground until Germany intervened in April 1941.

card_event_vanguard_ita.name: card_event_vanguard_ita
card_event_vanguard_ita.title: VANGUARD
card_event_vanguard_ita.text: A friendly Alpine unit gets Blitz and "Damage dealt by this unit adds equal defense to your HQ."
card_event_vanguard_ita.flavorText: In military terms, a "vanguard" refers to the forward element or the leading part of a military formation or operation. The vanguard typically consists of troops or units that are at the forefront of an advance and its primary purpose is to scout, secure, and potentially engage with the enemy or any potential threats ahead of the main force. The vanguard's role is crucial in providing critical information to the commanding officers about the enemy's strength, position, and terrain conditions. The concept of a vanguard is not limited to ground forces; it can also be applied to naval and aerial operations. In the context of naval operations, the vanguard might refer to ships or submarines at the front of a fleet or task force. In aerial operations, it could apply to fighter or reconnaissance aircraft that lead the way in an air campaign. The vanguard is an essential component of military strategy and tactics, as it helps ensure the safety and success of the larger force by providing critical intelligence and early engagement capabilities.

card_event_campaign_alamein1_through_the.name: card_event_campaign_alamein1_through_the_wire
card_event_campaign_alamein1_through_the.title: THROUGH THE WIRE
card_event_campaign_alamein1_through_the.text: Target enemy unit loses Guard. Friendly Italian units get +1+1.

card_event_campaign_alamein3_spring_the_.name: card_event_campaign_alamein3_spring_the_reserves
card_event_campaign_alamein3_spring_the_.title: SPRING THE RESERVES
card_event_campaign_alamein3_spring_the_.text: Italian units in your hand cost 0 to deploy this turn.

card_event_desert_push_cam1.name: card_event_desert_push_cam1
card_event_desert_push_cam1.title: DESERT PUSH
card_event_desert_push_cam1.text: Fully repair target ground unit. If it is pinned, remove pin.

card_unit_18th_bersaglieri.name: card_unit_18th_bersaglieri
card_unit_18th_bersaglieri.title: 18th BERSAGLIERI
card_unit_18th_bersaglieri.text: Deployment: Shuffle 9th BERSAGLIERI into your deck.

card_unit_33rd_livorno_cam1.name: card_unit_33rd_livorno_cam1
card_unit_33rd_livorno_cam1.title: 65th VALTELLINA REGIMENT
card_unit_33rd_livorno_cam1.text: Reduce attack of this unit by 1 each time it is attacked, to a minimum of 1.

card_unit_125th_la_spezia.name: card_unit_125th_la_spezia
card_unit_125th_la_spezia.title: 125th LA SPEZIA
card_unit_125th_la_spezia.text: Deployment: Draw a card if you control an air unit.
card_unit_125th_la_spezia.flavorText: The 125th Infantry Regiment "La Spezia" was part of the 80th Infantry Division "La Spezia", an Italian airborne division formed in 1941. Originally supposed to take part in the invasion of Malta, the division was instead deployed to Libya after the operation was canceled. It participated in the Second Battle of El Alamein in October 1942, won by the Allies. Following the defeat, the division retreated to Tunisia, where it took part in the Battle of Medenine in March 1943, followed shortly after by the Battle of the Mareth Line, both of which resulted in Allied victories. During these battles, the division lost half of its strength, and the remaining troops, along with the rest of the Axis forces, retreated to Enfidaville (currently Enfidha) in northeastern Tunisia. By May 1943, the remaining Italian forces in Enfidaville were surrounded, and soon after, approximately 80,000 Italian troops surrendered to the British. The 80th Infantry Division "La Spezia" was officially lost on 13 May 1943.

card_unit_185th_folgore.name: card_unit_185th_folgore
card_unit_185th_folgore.title: 186th FOLGORE
card_unit_185th_folgore.text: When you deploy an Alpine unit, it gains Blitz.
card_unit_185th_folgore.flavorText: During WWII the 186th Paratroopers Regiment Folgore was part of the 185th Paratroopers Division Folgore of the Italian Army. The division was formed in 1941 and was sent to North Africa where it fought with the Axis in the Western Desert Campaign. While in Africa the 185th Division Folgore fought in several battles and operations, such as the First Battle of El Alamein (where the whole divisions was awarded a Gold Medal of Military Valor), Battle of Alam el Halfa, Operation Braganza and the Second Battle of El Alamein. After the armistice in 1944, soldiers from the division formed the Combat Group "Folgore" which fought with the Allies for the remainder of the war. After the war the name was changed to the Mechanized Division "Folgore", which was disbanded in 1986.

card_unit_185th_folgore_cov.name: card_unit_185th_folgore_cov
card_unit_185th_folgore_cov.title: 185th FOLGORE
card_unit_185th_folgore_cov.text: Costs 1 more to deploy if you started the battle.
card_unit_185th_folgore_cov.flavorText: The 185th Paratroopers Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Regiment "Folgore" (Italian: 185° Reggimento Paracadutisti Ricognizione Acquisizione Obiettivi "Folgore", abbreviated as 185º RRAO) was an elite Italian airborne unit during WWII. Initially formed with the intention of participating in the planned invasion of Malta, the "Folgore" instead found themselves defending Sicily and mainland Italy from Allied landings. Despite being under-equipped and facing overwhelming odds, the paratroopers demonstrated exceptional bravery and resilience in battles like the Battle of Primosole Bridge, where they held off superior British forces for several days. After the Italian armistice in 1943, some elements of the "Folgore" joined the Allies, fighting alongside them against the Germans.

card_unit_1st_san_marco.name: card_unit_1st_san_marco
card_unit_1st_san_marco.title: 1st SAN MARCO
card_unit_1st_san_marco.text: Deployment: Gets +2+2 and Blitz if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_unit_1st_san_marco.flavorText: The 1st San Marco Regiment is the Italian Navy’s elite marine infantry unit, with roots dating back to 1713. At the start of WWII the regiment was composed of two battalions, but it was later expanded to seven. Its first engagement was during the invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941, where the regiment carried out successful landings on several islands in the Adriatic and seized ports against minimal resistance. The 3rd Battalion of the San Marco Regiment gained fame and its nickname "Tobruk" during the British commando raid on the night of 13-14 September 1942, repelling the attack and capturing 200 enemies. In spring 1943, the San Marco Regiment fought hard in Tunisia to defend the Mareth Line, especially during the Battle of Wadi Akarit, where the Tobruk Battalion was destroyed.  German General Hans-Jürgen von Arnim, the last commander of Axis forces in North Africa, later commented that the San Marco Marines were "the best soldiers I ever commanded".  Following Italy’s surrender in September 1943, most San Marco troops joined the Allies, while the 4th Battalion continued fighting for the Axis until 1945. Known for their discipline and combat effectiveness, the San Marco Regiment proved itself as one of Italy’s most formidable units in WWII.

card_unit_2nd_alpini.name: card_unit_2nd_alpini
card_unit_2nd_alpini.title: 2nd ALPINI REGIMENT
card_unit_2nd_alpini.text: Deployment: If you control another Alpine unit, draw a card.
card_unit_2nd_alpini.flavorText: The 2nd Alpini Regiment was a light infantry regiment of the Italian Army that specialized in mountain warfare. During WWII the regiment was attached to the "Cuneense" division of the Italian Army which fought in France, the Italian attack on Greece and the invasion of Yugoslavia. In 1942 the division fought with the German Sixth Army on the Eastern Front in the Battle of Stalingrad where it ended up being encircled and almost annihilated by the Red Army. In February 1943 the division counted as few as 5,206 men, 206 of them being men of the 2nd Alpini Regiment, who by then had walked 200 km, fought in 20 battles and spent 11 nights camped out in the middle of the Russian Steppe. After the signing of the Italian armistice with the Allies in September 1943, the regiment was disbanded.

card_unit_33rd_livorno.name: card_unit_33rd_livorno
card_unit_33rd_livorno.title: 33rd LIVORNO REGIMENT
card_unit_33rd_livorno.text: Reduce attack of this unit by 1 each time it is attacked, to a minimum of 1.
card_unit_33rd_livorno.flavorText: During WWII the 33rd Livorno Regiment was part of the 4th Infantry Division Livorno, a mountain infantry division of the Italian Army. The division fought in France in 1940 and in 1943 it was located in Sicily where it fought against the invading Allied forces. After heavy fighting the Livorno Division was forced to retreat through the Sicilian towns of Agira and Regalbuto where it suffered heavy losses. Due to total lack of supplies the division was forced to evacuate to mainland Italy, suffering further losses on the way. Only 4200 men of the initial 13000 where evacuated, and following the armistice between Italy and the Allies in 1943, the remainder of the division surrendered to the German forces who had by then occupied Italy.

card_unit_39th_bologna.name: card_unit_39th_bologna
card_unit_39th_bologna.title: 39th BOLOGNA REGIMENT
card_unit_39th_bologna.text: If in your hand, this unit costs 1 more each time you lose a unit.
card_unit_39th_bologna.flavorText: During WWII the 39th Bologna Regiment was part of the 25th Infantry Division Bologna of the Italian Army. In 1941 the division was sent to Libya where it participated in the siege of Tobruk. In 1942 it was ordered to reinforce the El Alamein front, but lacking vehicles the troops had to march 400 miles, and after 46 days of marching the division reached the town of Alam el Halfa (south of El Alamein) where it linked up with the German-Italian Panzer Army in the Battle of Alam el Halfa, which ended in an Axis defeat. The division was forced to retreat and finally surrender to the Allies. Some detachments managed to escape to Tunisia and were merged to other units, but the remainder of the Bologna Division was officially dissolved in November 1942.

card_unit_3rd_alpini.name: card_unit_3rd_alpini
card_unit_3rd_alpini.title: 3rd ALPINI REGIMENT
card_unit_3rd_alpini.flavorText: During WWII the 3rd Alpini Regiment was part of the Alpini Corps of the Italian Army and specialized in mountain warfare. In 1940 the regiment was part of the Taurinense Division that fought in the Italian attack on Greece (Greco-Italian War). In 1941 the division was stationed on garrison duty in Montenegro where it stayed until the armistice with the Allies was signed in 1943. In 1944 the regiment was recreated, and with the 4th Bersaglieri Regiment it formed the 1st Italian Brigade of the Italian Liberation Corps, which fought with the Allies. After suffering heavy casualties the brigade was merged into a single infantry regiment of the Polish II Corps and fought its last engagements with the British 8th Army near the river Idice in Italy.

card_unit_49th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_49th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_49th_infantry_regiment.title: 49th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_49th_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Your HQ gets +4 defense if you control another unit with 4 or more attack.
card_unit_49th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 49th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 49th Infantry Division "Parma" of the Italian Royal Army during WWII. Initially, it took part in the Greco-Italian War in 1940, where it faced challenging combat conditions and strong Greek resistance in mountainous terrain. Following this campaign, the division was sent to Yugoslavia in 1941, where it carried out occupation duties in Montenegro and Albania and engaged in anti-partisan operations against local resistance forces. After Italy signed an armistice with the Allies in September 1943, the division was disbanded by German forces occupying the region. Some members of the division joined partisan groups or the Italian Co-belligerent Army to continue the fight.

card_unit_4th_alpini_regiment.name: card_unit_4th_alpini_regiment
card_unit_4th_alpini_regiment.title: 4th ALPINI REGIMENT
card_unit_4th_alpini_regiment.text: Deployment: Add a 4th ALPINI REGIMENT to your deck for every 10 cards in it.
card_unit_4th_alpini_regiment.flavorText: The 4th Alpini Regiment was one of the Royal Italian Army’s long-established mountain infantry units. By the outbreak of WWII, it formed part of the 1st Alpine Division “Taurinense” and fielded the Alpini battalions “Ivrea,” “Aosta,” and “Intra.” In June 1940, the regiment took part in the invasion of France, before serving on occupation duty in southern France. Elements of the regiment later fought in Albania during the Greco-Italian War, where the “Intra” Battalion and the regiment’s ski troops earned decorations for their actions. In October 1941, the regiment reformed the Skiers Battalion “Monte Cervino”, which was sent to the Eastern Front in early 1942. There, it served with the Italian 8th Army and was effectively destroyed during the Soviet Operation Little Saturn, later receiving a Gold Medal of Military Valor for its bravery and sacrifice. Meanwhile, the main regiment deployed to Montenegro with the “Taurinense” Division. After the Italian armistice in September 1943, the division fought German forces while attempting to reach the coast. By early October, its surviving elements were forced to surrender.

card_unit_5th_bersaglieri.name: card_unit_5th_bersaglieri
card_unit_5th_bersaglieri.title: 5th BERSAGLIERI
card_unit_5th_bersaglieri.text: Destruction: Shuffle 18th BERSAGLIERI into your deck.
card_unit_5th_bersaglieri.flavorText: The 5th Bersaglieri Regiment was part of Italy’s elite light infantry, known for its mobility and marksmanship. During WWII, it was assigned to the 131st Armored Division "Centauro", first seeing action in the Greco-Italian War. Operating in the rugged terrain of Epirus and Albania, the regiment engaged in tough mountain warfare where its agility proved valuable. In late 1942, the division was transferred to North Africa as part of the Axis response to British advances. Arriving in Libya, the 5th Bersaglieri fought in the Tunisian campaign, the final phase of the North African conflict. It took part in delaying actions and defensive battles under increasingly difficult conditions, facing Allied superiority in air power and armor. In May 1943, the regiment, along with the rest of the Centauro Division, was destroyed during the collapse of Axis forces in Tunisia. The 5th Bersaglieri had a long lineage dating back to the 19th century and earned several decorations, including the Military Order of Italy and medals for valor. It was one of the last Bersaglieri regiments to fight in North Africa before the Italian surrender in that theater.

card_unit_6th_alpini_regiment.name: card_unit_6th_alpini_regiment
card_unit_6th_alpini_regiment.title: 6th ALPINI REGIMENT
card_unit_6th_alpini_regiment.flavorText: The 6th Alpini Regiment is a regiment of the Italian Army’s mountain infantry. The regiment was formed in 1882 and has participated in many conflicts since then, including WWI and WWII where it distinguished itself in combat. In 1940 regiment fought with the Tridentina Division in France and was after that sent to Albania where it participated in the Italian attack on Greece. In 1942 the Tridentina joined the Italian Army in Russia and fought on the Eastern Front alongside the Germans. The Tridentina Division along with two other Alpini divisions were deployed along the Don River where they covered the left flank of the German Sixth Army during the Battle of Stalingrad. After the encirclement of the Sixth Army, the Red Army turned to the Alpini divisions and after 12 days of heavy fighting the Alpini divisions were almost annihilated. However, remnants of the Tridentine Division managed to break the encirclement and 4250 survivors managed to reach German lines in January 1943. The 6th Alpini Regiment was dissolved in 1943 after the signing of the Italian armistice with the Allies.

card_unit_76th_napoli.name: card_unit_76th_napoli
card_unit_76th_napoli.title: 76th NAPOLI
card_unit_76th_napoli.text: Deployment: Gets +1 attack for each defense your HQ has over the enemy HQ.
card_unit_76th_napoli.flavorText: The 76th Infantry Regiment “Napoli” of the 54th Infantry Division "Napoli" was a military unit of the Royal Italian Army during WWII. The division was formed in Sicily in 1939 and later deployed to focus on coastal defense in the southern part of the island in preparation for the anticipated Allied invasion. On 10 July 1943, the Napoli division engaged in fighting south of Noto, while its northern group fought at Lentini and Brucoli. The British captured Floridia and the entirety of the 75th Infantry Regiment on 12 July as it attempted to withdraw from the town. The division managed to stabilize the frontline at Palazzolo Acreide-Solarino-Priolo Gargallo by 13 July, but the new Allied landing north of Augusta outflanked the division and inflicted heavy casualties in the following days. The remnants of the Napoli division were absorbed into the incoming Panzer Division "Hermann Göring" and fought some small rearguard battles between 16-24 July. The division was disbanded on 14 August 1943 after it was unable to reform and its remaining personnel were ordered to evacuate to Southern Italy. For its conduct between 10 July and 1 August 1943 the 76th Infantry Regiment was awarded a Silver Medal of Military Valour.

card_unit_7th_alpini.name: card_unit_7th_alpini
card_unit_7th_alpini.title: 7th ALPINI REGIMENT
card_unit_7th_alpini.text: Damage dealt by this unit adds equal defense to your HQ.
card_unit_7th_alpini.flavorText: The 7th Alpini Regiment was first formed in 1887 and has since participated in the Italo-Turkish War, WWI and WWII. At the start of WWII the regiment was raised to four battalions and some would later serve in different theaters, but in 1940 the whole regiment was sent to the Western Alps to participate in the Italian invasion of France. That same year three of the regiment battalions participated in the Greco-Italian War, while one battalion (Val Cismon) was sent to Albania where Italian forces were suffering heavy casualties. In 1942 battalion Val Cismon was sent with the 3rd Alpine Division to the Eastern Front where it was annihilated during the Soviet Operation Little Saturn (1942-43). Meanwhile the Uork Amba battalion was fighting in the East African Campaign where it distinguished itself during the Battle of Keren. After the armistice between Italy and the Allies in 1943 remnants of the 7th Alpini Regiment surrendered to the German forces in France after a brief resistance.

card_unit_80th_pasubio.name: card_unit_80th_pasubio
card_unit_80th_pasubio.title: 80th PASUBIO
card_unit_80th_pasubio.text: Damage dealt by this unit adds equal defense to your HQ.
card_unit_80th_pasubio.flavorText: The Italian 80th regiment of the 9th Infantry Division Pasubio was a military unit that served during WWII. It was formed in 1939 and was part of the Pasubio division, which was named after the Pasubio massif, a mountain range in the Italian Alps. The 80th regiment saw action in several theaters of the war, including North Africa, the Balkans, and the Eastern Front. It was known for its bravery and determination, particularly during the Battle of Gazala in 1942, where it played a key role in the defense of Tobruk against the British forces. In 1943, the 80th regiment was sent to the Eastern Front, where it took part in the Battle of Kursk and the subsequent retreat of German and Italian forces. Despite suffering heavy losses, the regiment continued to fight until the end of the war. After the war, the 80th regiment was disbanded and its personnel were demobilized.

card_unit_93rd_messina.name: card_unit_93rd_messina
card_unit_93rd_messina.title: 93rd MESSINA
card_unit_93rd_messina.text: Units that did not start in your deck cost 2 less to deploy.
card_unit_93rd_messina.flavorText: The 93rd Infantry Regiment “Messina” was one of the two infantry regiments of the Italian 18th Infantry Division “Messina”. Its headquarters were located in Ancona, like the divisional headquarters, while the sister 94th Infantry Regiment was based in Fano. The regiment’s lineage went back to the Brigade “Messina”, formed in 1884 with the 93rd and 94th Infantry Regiments. The division was named after the city of Messina but recruited mainly in the Marche region. It remained stationed in Italy during the invasion of France, then moved to Albania in 1941 for the invasion of Yugoslavia. After crossing into Montenegro with XVII Army Corps, the Messina division captured Bar, Cetinje, and Kotor, where much of the Royal Yugoslav Navy was located. It then advanced to Podgorica and remained in the region on occupation duty. In 1942, the division was transferred to Croatia, where it later took part in Operation Alfa around Prozor. After the 1943 armistice, the division refused demands to surrender. The 93rd Regiment and the 108th CC.NN. Legion “Stamira” escaped by sea to southern Italy, while the rest of the division was disbanded by German forces.

card_unit_9th_bersaglieri.name: card_unit_9th_bersaglieri
card_unit_9th_bersaglieri.title: 9th BERSAGLIERI
card_unit_9th_bersaglieri.text: Destruction: Shuffle 18th BERSAGLIERI into your deck.
card_unit_9th_bersaglieri.flavorText: Formed in 1871, the 9th Bersaglieri Regiment was an elite infantry unit of the Italian Army, known for its speed and aggressive tactics. After serving on the Italian front during World War I, it was disbanded following heavy losses at Caporetto in 1917. The regiment was reconstituted in 1919 and saw combat again during WWII. Assigned to the Western Desert campaign, the 9th Bersaglieri deployed to North Africa alongside other units of the Italian Army. It fought as part of the Axis effort to control the region, facing British and Commonwealth forces across the harsh desert terrain. In October 1942, during the Second Battle of El Alamein, the regiment was overwhelmed. Under relentless Allied artillery fire and air attacks, it suffered severe losses and was ultimately destroyed. This battle marked a turning point in the North African campaign, forcing Axis forces into a long retreat. Decorated for valor in earlier conflicts, the 9th Bersaglieri maintained a reputation for resilience and discipline, even in the face of defeat. The regiment was officially disbanded on 5 November 1942 following its destruction.

card_unit_breda_ba_65.name: card_unit_breda_ba_65
card_unit_breda_ba_65.title: BREDA Ba.65
card_unit_breda_ba_65.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to each enemy.
card_unit_breda_ba_65.flavorText: The Breda Ba.65 was an Italian multirole combat aircraft developed in the 1930s and used during the Spanish Civil War by the Aviazione Legionaria, as well as in the early stages of World War II. The aircraft was a single-engine, all-metal monoplane designed for ground-attack, reconnaissance, and light bombing missions. It was powered by a Fiat A.80 radial engine, had a top speed of 430 km/h (267 mph), was armed with four machine guns and embarked up to 1,000 kg (2,200 lbs) of bombs. Its robust design featured a retractable landing gear and an enclosed cockpit, but its heavy armament often strained its performance. The Ba.65 first saw action in the Spanish Civil War, where it performed effectively in ground-attack roles but proved to be vulnerable to enemy fighters. When WWII broke out, the aircraft was already outdated and struggled against more advanced Allied planes and anti-aircraft defenses. It saw limited use in North Africa before being phased out due to its slow speed, mechanical issues and poor combat effectiveness. A total of 218 Ba.65s were manufactured between 1935 and 1939, with the majority serving in the Regia Aeronautica. However, 55 were exported and used by the air forces of Iraq, Chile and Portugal.

card_unit_cannone_da_47.name: card_unit_cannone_da_47
card_unit_cannone_da_47.title: CANNONE DA 47
card_unit_cannone_da_47.text: Takes 1 damage at the end of your turn unless you control more units than the enemy.
card_unit_cannone_da_47.flavorText: The Cannone Da 47/32 mod. 1935 was an Italian artillery gun that was used extensively by the Italian Army during WWII, both as an infantry gun and an anti-tank gun. The gun was effective against light and medium tanks but was ineffective against heavy tanks. Its drawbacks were that the axle spindles and shanks tended to break when it was being towed by tractors or tankettes, and it didn’t have any gun shield. The Italian soldiers called the gun “elefantino” (e. Little elephant) due to its shape.

card_unit_caproni_ca_133.name: card_unit_caproni_ca_133
card_unit_caproni_ca_133.title: CAPRONI CA.133
card_unit_caproni_ca_133.text: Your HQ gets +2 defense when you deploy or add a unit.
card_unit_caproni_ca_133.flavorText: The Caproni Ca.133 was a rugged, three-engine transport aircraft and light bomber which served as the backbone of the Italian Regia Aeronautica from the mid-1930s through the early years of WWII. First flown in 1934 and introduced a year later, it was originally designed as a civilian airliner before being adapted for military service, a transition where its simplicity and reliability proved invaluable. Constructed with a mix of wood, steel tubing, and fabric, the Ca.133 was built to endure harsh, remote environments. This durability made it ideal for colonial warfare. It saw extensive action in Italian East Africa during the Second Italo-Abyssinian War, performing bombing, strafing, reconnaissance, and transport missions, often in the absence of significant air opposition. While armed with defensive machine guns and a respectable bomb load, the Ca.133 was equally vital as a utility aircraft, with variants configured for troop transport or as air ambulances. Although slow and vulnerable to modern fighters, its versatility ensured a long career, with over 500 units built and active service continuing throughout Africa and the Mediterranean during WWII.

card_unit_fiat_br_20.name: card_unit_fiat_br_20
card_unit_fiat_br_20.title: FIAT BR.20
card_unit_fiat_br_20.text: Deployment: Add two 3rd ALPINI REGIMENT to your support line.
card_unit_fiat_br_20.flavorText: The Fiat BR.20 “Cicogna” (Italian for Stork) was an Italian twin-engine medium bomber, developed by the Fiat aircraft company, and used by the Regia Aeronautica (Italian Royal Air Force) and other air forces. The Fiat BR.20 is the first all-metal Italian bomber.It entered service in 1936 and flew its first combat mission in 1937 when it was used in support of Franco’s Nationalist forces during the Spanish Civil War. The aircraft was also used by the Imperial Japanese Air Force during the Second Sino-Japanese war in 1937. In June 1940, Italy declared war on France and the UK, and it was used successfully during the short lived campaign against France. However, during The Battle of Britain the BR.20 showed its limitations for the first time. The harsh climate conditions over the channel made them vulnerable to mechanical failure, plus their defensive armaments were insufficient against the British fighters. The Fiat BR.20 also saw use in North Africa, where the desert environment also caused mechanical problems for the aircraft. The aircraft saw limited use in the Soviet Union, Malta, Albania and Greece, but the BR.20’s role in major operations diminished as the war progressed. This was both due to the shortcomings of the aircraft and because the Italian industry struggled to produce enough aircraft to meet the demand. However, some units continued to use the BR.20 throughout the war, but mainly for reconnaissance and transport missions. A total of 500 Fiat BR.20s were built, including a few variants. None of the aircraft remain today.

card_unit_fiat_cr_32.name: card_unit_fiat_cr_32
card_unit_fiat_cr_32.title: FIAT C.R.32
card_unit_fiat_cr_32.text: When your HQ gains defense, fully repair a random friendly unit.
card_unit_fiat_cr_32.flavorText: The FIAT C.R.32 was an Italian biplane fighter aircraft that saw significant use during the interwar period and the early years of WWII. It was designed by the Italian manufacturer FIAT and entered service with the Regia Aeronautica (Italian Royal Air Force) in 1933. During the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939), the FIAT C.R.32 gained its reputation as one of the best biplane fighters of its time. It demonstrated excellent maneuverability and agility, making it highly effective in aerial combat. Its robust construction and good diving capabilities also added to its combat ability. However, by the outbreak of WWII in 1939, the FIAT C.R.32 was already becoming outdated compared to the monoplane fighters that other nations were deploying. It was gradually phased out of frontline service in the Regia Aeronautica, being replaced by more modern aircraft like the Macchi C.200 and C.202. During the early stages of the war, the FIAT C.R.32 continued to see limited use by Italy and its allies and it was used in various combat theaters, including North Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Balkans. By the mid-1940s, the FIAT C.R.32 was mostly relegated to secondary roles, such as training, reconnaissance, and ground-attack missions. It was gradually phased out of service as more advanced aircraft became available. Nonetheless, it is worth noting that a few C.R.32s remained in use until the end of the war in 1945.

card_unit_fiat_cr_42.name: card_unit_fiat_cr_42
card_unit_fiat_cr_42.title: FIAT C.R.42
card_unit_fiat_cr_42.text: Deployment: Gets +1 attack if you control more units than the enemy.
card_unit_fiat_cr_42.flavorText: The Fiat CR.42 Falco (e. falcon) was an Italian, single seated sesquiplane fighter, developed and manufactured by Fiat Aviazione and used by the Italian Royal Air Force in WWII. The CR.42 entered service in 1939 and was the last of the Fiat biplane fighters to enter frontline service. The fighter was used in bomber escort missions in Southern France in 1940, and later in raids on Britain, but was considered too vulnerable against British fighters and too slow to keep up with the rest of the air fleet. As the Allies started using more modern designs, the CR.42s were relocated to North Africa where they were still used in reconnaissance and ground attack roles. In total 1819 aircraft were manufactured and they were last used in 1948 by the Spanish Air Force.

card_unit_fiat_g50.name: card_unit_fiat_g50
card_unit_fiat_g50.title: FIAT G.50
card_unit_fiat_g50.text: Damage dealt by this unit adds equal defense to your HQ.
card_unit_fiat_g50.flavorText: The Fiat G.50 Freccia (e. arrow) was an Italian fighter aircraft that was used during WWII by the Regia Aeronautica (e. Italian Royal Air force) and the Axis air forces. The aircraft was first introduced in 1938 and proved its worth in the Spanish Civil War. The early Fiat G.50s were used as interceptors in the Battle of Britain but they turned out to be too slow and short ranged. Later variants performed better and the Fiat G.50 was the most common fighter used by the Axis during the Italian Campaign, but it was still inferior to Allied fighters such as the Hawker Hurricane. From 1935 to 1943 683 Fiat G.50s had been produced, including a few variants,  but by the time the Italians surrendered in 1943 very few of them were still in service.

card_unit_fiat_g55.name: card_unit_fiat_g55
card_unit_fiat_g55.title: FIAT G.55
card_unit_fiat_g55.text: Deployment: +2+2 if your HQ has 5 or more defense than the enemy HQ.
card_unit_fiat_g55.flavorText: The Fiat G.55 Centauro (e. centaur) was an Italian fighter aircraft used by the Italian Royal Airforce during WWII. The Centauro entered service in 1943 and was retired only two years later, but in this short period it proved to be Italy's best fighter aircraft of the era. During its short service time it proved to be an excellent interceptor at high altitude and it performed very well against modern Allied fighters in combat. It is claimed that the German Luftwaffe considered the Fiat G.55 to be the best Axis fighter after doing comparative testing with the Messerschmitt Bf 109G and the Focke-Wulf 190. Even so, only 300 aircraft had been built by the end of WWII.

card_unit_italian_cavalry.name: card_unit_italian_cavalry
card_unit_italian_cavalry.title: SAVOIA CAVALLERIA
card_unit_italian_cavalry.flavorText: The Savoia Cavalleria Regiment (3rd) is one of the oldest cavalry regiments of the Italian Army, dating back to the 17th century. During WWII the Savoia Cavalleria Regiment was attached to the 3rd Fast Division "Principe Amedeo Duca d'Aosta" of the Italian Expeditionary Corps in Russia. The regiment earned its fame in what’s now called the Izbushensky Charge, which was a clash between the regiment and Soviet infantry. Col. Bettoni Cazzago, commander of the regiment ordered a cavalry charge with sabers drawn and hand grenades against two entrenched battalions of the 812th Siberian Infantry Regiment. The clash ended with an Italian victory, but there were heavy losses on both sides, and the outcome didn’t have much bearing on the Eastern Front. This event is however remembered as the last cavalry charges in history and it had great propaganda resonance in Italy at the time.

card_unit_l6_40.name: card_unit_l6_40
card_unit_l6_40.title: L6/40
card_unit_l6_40.flavorText: The Fiat L6/40 was a light tank designed and produced by Fiat-Ansaldo and used by the Italian Army and the German Wehrmacht from 1940 and throughout WWII. The tank was used by the Italians in the North African Campaign and on the Eastern Front, and later in the Balkans Campaign and during the defence of Sicily in Italy. The L6/40 had a crew of two (commander/gunner and driver), a main armament of a 20 mm Breda 35 gun and a secondary armament of an 8 mm Breda 38 machine gun. The tank was produced until 1944 and a total of 283 units were built. A few variants were made, such as a flame tank, command tank, ammunition carrier, armed only with a single 8 mm Breda machine gun, and finally a Semovente 47/32 which was a self-propelled gun.

card_unit_la_decima.name: card_unit_la_decima
card_unit_la_decima.title: LA DECIMA
card_unit_la_decima.text: Deployment: Destroy target unit in the enemy support line.
card_unit_la_decima.flavorText: The Decima Flottiglia MAS, also known as La Decima, was an Italian flotilla of the Regia Marina that specialized in commando raids. The flotilla was composed of specially trained frogmen and used Manned Torpedoes, Explosive Motorboats and frogmen to carry out their raids. La Decima was active from 1941 to 1943 and participated in numerous daring raids on Allied shipping during that time. In 3 years members of the flotilla single handedly managed to sink or disable 5 Allied warships and 20 merchant ships. The La Decima units also earned a good reputation fighting on the frontline against the Allies at Anzio and on the Gothic Line.

card_unit_m13_40.name: card_unit_m13_40
card_unit_m13_40.title: M13/40
card_unit_m13_40.text: Deployment: Gains Blitz if you control an infantry.
card_unit_m13_40.flavorText: The Carro Armato M13/40 was an Italian medium tank that was used during WWII. The tank was influenced by the British Vickers 6-tonne tank and its Italian predecessor the M11/39. It was used in 1940 in the Greek Campaign and in the North African Campaign in 1941. The tank lacked firepower and from 1942 the Italians deployed it alongside a Semovente 75/18 self-propelled gun in order to make up for it. The M13/40 had a crew of 4 (commander, driver, gunner, loader), a main armament of a 47 mm cannone da 47/32 AT gun and a secondary armament of 4 x 8 mm Breda mod. 38 machine guns.

card_unit_macchi_c202.name: card_unit_macchi_c202
card_unit_macchi_c202.title: MACCHI C.202
card_unit_macchi_c202.text: Takes 2 damage at the end of your turn if your HQ has less defense than the enemy HQ.
card_unit_macchi_c202.flavorText: The Macchi C.202 Folgore (e. thunderbolt) was an Italian fighter aircraft developed and manufactured by Macchi Aeronautica and used during WWII by the Regia Aeronautica (Royal Italian Air Force). According to some the Folgore was one of the best wartime fighters to serve in large numbers with the Italian Air Force and it was superior to many of the older British fighters in the North African conflict. With its Daimler-Benz engine it could reach a top speed of 600 km/h and it was adequately armed four machine guns and two 160kg bombs. In total 1,150 aircraft were built and it was in use until 1951.

card_unit_macchi_c205.name: card_unit_macchi_c205
card_unit_macchi_c205.title: MACCHI C.205
card_unit_macchi_c205.flavorText: The Macchi C.205 Veltro (Italian: Greyhound) was an Italian WWII fighter aircraft from the Aeronautica Macchi manufacturer and a development of the earlier Macchi C.202 Folgore. Together with the Reggiane Re. 2005 and Fiat G. 55, the Macchi C. 205 belonged to the trio of "Serie 5" Italian fighter aircraft which were centered around the Daimler-Benz DB 605 engine, which was also used in the German Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighter, and the Bf 110 and Me 210C heavy fighters. The Macchi C.205V was introduced into active service in February 1943, and soon earned recognition as one of the finest Italian aircraft during WWII. It boasted an impressive top speed at around 640 km/h (400 mph), and was armed with twin 20 mm cannons and 12.7 mm Breda machine guns. It downed numerous Allied bombers and was an equal match to the more advanced Allied fighters, such as the North American P-51D Mustang. Nonetheless, the C.205V entered service late in the conflict, resulting in only a limited production before the war’s end. A total of 262 Macchi C.205’s were manufactured, including a few variants.

card_unit_macchi_c_200.name: card_unit_macchi_c_200
card_unit_macchi_c_200.title: MACCHI C.200
card_unit_macchi_c_200.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 for each other friendly air unit.
card_unit_macchi_c_200.flavorText: The Macchi C.200 Saetta ("Lightning") was an Italian fighter aircraft in service in the Regia Aeronautica during WWII from its introduction in 1939. It was designed and manufactured by Aeronautica Macchi, featured an all-metal construction and was powered by a Fiat A.74 radial engine. The aircraft was considered reliable despite having limited speed compared to its Allied counterparts. Its agility and sturdy airframe made it effective in dogfights, even though it was lightly armed with two 12.7mm Breda-SAFAT machine guns, and early models had open cockpits (later enclosed). The C.200 operated across multiple theaters, including the Mediterranean, North Africa, the Balkans and the Eastern Front. It excelled in ground-attack roles and close air support thanks to its durability, but it struggled against faster, more heavily armed adversaries like the Spitfire. From 1941-42, it was gradually replaced by the improved C.202 Folgore. Despite its underpowered engine and modest armament, the Saetta was respected for its maneuverability and played a key role in Italy’s early wartime campaigns. It was considered the best early-war Italian fighter.

card_unit_obice_da_75_13.name: card_unit_obice_da_75_13
card_unit_obice_da_75_13.title: OBICE DA 75/13
card_unit_obice_da_75_13.text: Your Alpine units can move and attack during the same turn.
card_unit_obice_da_75_13.flavorText: The Da 75/13 Modello 15 was a mountain gun from Austria-Hungary, originally known as the Skoda 75mm Model 15, but designated as the Obice da 75/13 in Italy. The Italians captured large numbers of these guns in WWI and they were distributed among the Italian Alpini divisions who found them very useful in mountain terrain. It was therefore decided to reproduce the Obice da 75/13 in 1933 and many of them were still in service when WWII started and they were still in use when the war ended.

card_unit_semovente_75_18.name: card_unit_semovente_75_18
card_unit_semovente_75_18.title: SEMOVENTE DA 75/18
card_unit_semovente_75_18.flavorText: The Semovente da 75/18 was an Italian self-propelled gun manufactured by Fiat-Ansaldo and used in WWII from 1942 to 1944. The idea was to build a self-propelled gun similar to the German StuG III and initially an M13 chassis was used, but later models used an M14 chassis. The gun had a crew of 3 (commander/gunner, driver, loader/radio operator), a main armament of a 75 mm obice da 75/18 model 34 gun and for secondary armament it used an 8 mm Breda model 38 or a 6.5 mm Breda model 30 machine gun. 262 units were built during the war, including a few variants.

card_unit_sm_79.name: card_unit_sm_79
card_unit_sm_79.title: SAVOIA-MARCHETTI SM.79
card_unit_sm_79.text: Deployment: Trigger a non-targeted deployment effect on a friendly unit.
card_unit_sm_79.flavorText: The Savoia-Marchetti SM.79 Sparviero (e. sparrowhawk) was an Italian medium bomber, developed and manufactured by the Savoia-Marchetti company. Its first flight was in 1934 and it was initially intended as an eight-passenger transport aircraft, but after one speed record after the other the Italian government soon saw its potential as an armed combat aircraft. The SM.79 first saw combat in the Spanish Civil War and due to its speed it initially operated without fighter escort. During WWII it was primarily used by the Italian Royal Air Force, first as a transport aircraft and medium bomber, but later as a torpedo bomber and a special drone version was made that was flown by remote control. The SM.79 liked by its crew, and due to its distinctive looks it was nicknamed  “il gobbo maledetto” (e. damned hunchback).

card_unit_trento_division.name: card_unit_trento_division
card_unit_trento_division.title: TRENTO DIVISION
card_unit_trento_division.text: Deployment: Destroy an enemy unit if you control another unit with 4 or more attack.
card_unit_trento_division.flavorText: The 102nd Motorised Division Trento was an Italian Army division that served during WWII, primarily in North Africa as part of the Army of the Po (Italian: Armata del Po). Formed in 1935, the Trento Division was motorized for improved mobility.Its core units included the 61st and 62nd Infantry Regiments, the 7th Bersaglieri Regiment  and the 46th Artillery Regiment, with additional support units for anti-tank, engineering, and signals capabilities. The Trento Division was deployed to North Africa in 1941, where it participated in several major campaigns and battles, most notably the Siege of Tobruk and the First and Second Battles of El Alamein. During these operations, the division fought alongside German units from Rommel's Afrika Korps. Despite its efforts, the Trento Division was hampered by logistical difficulties, equipment shortages, and the harsh desert conditions. During the Second Battle of El Alamein in 1942, the division suffered significant casualties, and after the subsequent Axis retreat from North Africa, the Trento Division was declared lost.

card_unit_wolves_of_tuscany.name: card_unit_wolves_of_tuscany
card_unit_wolves_of_tuscany.title: WOLVES OF TUSCANY
card_unit_wolves_of_tuscany.text: While this unit is in the frontline, your air units have +2 attack.
card_unit_wolves_of_tuscany.flavorText: The 7th Infantry Division, nicknamed "Lupi di Toscana" (e. Wolfs of Tuscany), was a division of the Royal Italian Army in service during WWII. During the war, the division first participated in the Italian invasion of Albania in 1939; and remained stationed there until June 1940 when it returned to Italy and served as part of the army reserve during the Italian invasion of France. Then, the 7th Infantry Division was deployed to Albania in January 1941 as reinforcements during the Greco-Italian War, where it engaged in fierce fighting near Taronine and suffered heavy losses, including the annihilation of one regiment. After regrouping, the division returned to the front in March 1941, participating in defensive and offensive operations, capturing villages and advancing to the Greek-Albanian border by April 1941. Following its return to Italy in October 1941, the division performed coastal defense duties in Calabria and Liguria, and took part in the Axis invasion of Vichy France in November 1942. After the armistice between Italy and the Allied forces in September 1943, the division resisted German forces in Rome for a short while before being disbanded.

card_event_desperate_measures.name: card_event_desperate_measures
card_event_desperate_measures.title: DESPERATE MEASURES
card_event_desperate_measures.text: Deal 2 damage to all enemies. You lose a kredit slot.
card_event_desperate_measures.flavorText: In 1944 most Japanese politicians and military commanders had realized that they would not gain the victory they had hoped for at the start of the war. However, many militarists wanted to continue the fight, even after the atomic bombs were dropped, in the hopes that they could negotiate the terms for peace and keep some of their conquered territories in Asia. They hoped that a continued loss of American and Allied lives would persuade the Americans to negotiate for a truce. Japanese soldiers were ordered to fight to the last while defending the remaining islands in the Pacific, and in October 1944, the first kamikaze attack took place. What followed was a wave of suicide attacks on Allied targets and the bloodiest battles of WWII.

card_event_elusive_force.name: card_event_elusive_force
card_event_elusive_force.title: ELUSIVE FORCE
card_event_elusive_force.text: The enemy cannot give orders next turn.
card_event_elusive_force.flavorText: At the start of WWII the Imperial Japanese Navy had one of the world's most powerful submarine fleet. It was a varied fleet, from manned torpedoes to the Sentoku I-400-Class, which was the largest submarine of WWII. The fleet also included a number of fleet submarines, which many could carry an aircraft, and the Sentaka I-200-Class that reached the highest submerged speed of WWII. Despite having an advanced submarine fleet they were built in relatively small numbers and they were less effective than German submarines. The reason was the Japanese naval doctrine which focused on large and decisive fleet battles, and consequently the submarines were used against warships rather than merchant ships, but primarily they acted as scouts and attrition units.

card_event_for_glory.name: card_event_for_glory
card_event_for_glory.title: FOR GLORY
card_event_for_glory.flavorText: Although Japanese commanders glorified kamikaze pilots for their courage and sacrifice, the same did not apply to “normal” combat pilots, at least not when it came to keeping scores of air victories. The Japanese focused on honoring team efforts as official records show they kept count of victories of air groups and not individual scores. However, the Japanese did have individual air aces. Their combat scores have been verified by historians through postwar examination of their personal claims, letters and diaries, as well as those of their comrades. According to the examination of these records the leading Japanese aces were navy pilots, and the top ranking Japanese ace of WWII was Warrant Officer Hiroyoshi Nishizawa (nicknamed Demon of Rabaul) with 87 claimed victories.

card_event_gunboat_hit.name: card_event_gunboat_hit
card_event_gunboat_hit.title: GUNBOAT HIT
card_event_gunboat_hit.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit in the enemy support line. Add a GUNBOAT RUN to your hand. Discarded end of turn.
card_event_gunboat_hit.flavorText: A gunboat is a small and fast ship with machine guns or mounted artillery that was mainly used in shallow coastal waters or rivers. During WWII the Imperial Japanese Navy had a number of gunboats in their service, some of them were captured from enemy fleets.

card_event_gunboat_raid.name: card_event_gunboat_raid
card_event_gunboat_raid.title: GUNBOAT RAID
card_event_gunboat_raid.text: Deal 3 damage to an enemy unit in the frontline. Add a GUNBOAT HIT to your hand.
card_event_gunboat_raid.flavorText: A gunboat is a small and fast ship with machine guns or mounted artillery that was mainly used in shallow coastal waters or rivers. During WWII the Imperial Japanese Navy had a number of gunboats in their service, some of them were captured from enemy fleets.

card_event_gunboat_run.name: card_event_gunboat_run
card_event_gunboat_run.title: GUNBOAT RUN
card_event_gunboat_run.text: Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ. Discarded end of turn.

card_event_honorable_death.name: card_event_honorable_death
card_event_honorable_death.title: HONORABLE DEATH
card_event_honorable_death.text: Destroy target unit with attack 3 or less. Owner of the unit draws a card.
card_event_honorable_death.flavorText: During WWII, and especially during the last stages of the war, it was considered more honorable to die rather than surrender or be captured by the enemy. In 1944 the first kamikaze attacks started, and on the Pacific islands, Japanese soldiers were ordered to fight to the last man, and many of them would commit suicide rather than be captured alive by the Americans. It is unclear if the soldiers really believed in the samurai code “Bushido” or if they were afraid of being killed by the Americans or by their own side for surrendering.

card_event_imperial_decree.name: card_event_imperial_decree
card_event_imperial_decree.title: IMPERIAL DECREE
card_event_imperial_decree.text: The next damage order you give this turn deals +1 damage.
card_event_imperial_decree.flavorText: In Imperial Japan, there was an official code for military personnel known as the "Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors," which symbolized the obedience and loyalty expected of service members. All military personnel were required to memorize the document and were sometimes called upon to recite it during ceremonies.

card_event_isolation.name: card_event_isolation
card_event_isolation.title: ISOLATION
card_event_isolation.text: Remove target unit from the battlefield. Return it at the start of your next turn.
card_event_isolation.flavorText: The military tactic to isolate an enemy is often referred to as encirclement, where the aim is to surround the enemy force and cut it from the supply route and/or the logistical base. This was a common tactic in WWII, utilized both on a grand scale and in smaller skirmishes.

card_event_sneak_maneuver.name: card_event_sneak_maneuver
card_event_sneak_maneuver.title: SNEAK MANEUVER
card_event_sneak_maneuver.text: Give target infantry or tank with 0 operation cost +2 attack.
card_event_sneak_maneuver.flavorText: During WWII the Japanese military had prepared against a large scale Soviet attack. The Japanese knew that they could never match the Soviet forces, both in manpower and equipment, and trained their soldiers in tactics that could counter these advantages, for example, by attacking at night, in the evening or in the early morning. The Soviet forces never executed a large scale attack on Japan but the Japanese could nevertheless use these tactics to their advantage against the Allies in the Pacific War.

card_event_to_the_last_man.name: card_event_to_the_last_man
card_event_to_the_last_man.title: TO THE LAST MAN
card_event_to_the_last_man.flavorText: From October 1944 and until the Japanese surrendered in August 1945, approximately 2,800 kamikaze pilots managed to sink 47 Allied ships and damaged 368 others. The last kamikaze attack was carried out some hours after the Japanese had announced their surrender and one of the pilots was Vice Admiral Matome Ugaki, the commander of the 5th Navy Air Fleet.

card_unit_144th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_144th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_144th_infantry_regiment.title: 144th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_144th_infantry_regiment.text: Destruction: Deal damage to the enemy HQ equal to the kredit slots you have lost this battle.
card_unit_144th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 144th Infantry Regiment was attached to the 55th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. In 1941 the regiment became part of the South Seas Detachment, a brigade sized force used to seize the islands of Guam. After a failed attempt to seize Wake Island the 144th Regiment was sent back to rejoin the 55th Division for the New Guinea Campaign where it fought in several battles and campaigns. That last major engagement was a failed offensive against the British and Commonwealth forces in what became known as the Battle of the Admin Box and took place in Myanmar. After that the division was on retreat and was located in Cambodia when Japan surrendered in 1945.

card_unit_1st_yokosuka.name: card_unit_1st_yokosuka
card_unit_1st_yokosuka.title: 1st YOKOSUKA
card_unit_1st_yokosuka.text: Deployment: Receives +1 attack for each friendly unit with 0 operation cost.
card_unit_1st_yokosuka.flavorText: The 1st Yokosuka was part of the Imperial Japanese Navy Land force and were marine troops that participated in numerous battles and campaigns in the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Pacific War. The 1st Yokosuka were parachute trained and were part of the Land Force of the Yokosuka Naval Base. The unit was last deployed during the attack on Celebes and the Battle of Manado, and were disbanded shortly afterwards.

card_unit_34th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_34th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_34th_infantry_regiment.title: 34th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_34th_infantry_regiment.text: At the end of your turn, draw and discard the top card of your deck.
card_unit_34th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The Tachibana Regiment (Shizuoka) was a unit of the Imperial Japanese Army. Before WWII, the regiment took part in several conflicts, including the Russo-Japanese War. During WWII, its parent division was considered an elite formation and took part in 16 major engagements and campaigns. The division was disbanded at the end of the war.

card_unit_a6m3_zeke.name: card_unit_a6m3_zeke
card_unit_a6m3_zeke.title: A6M3 ZEKE
card_unit_a6m3_zeke.text: Enemy countermeasures cost 2 more to activate.
card_unit_a6m3_zeke.flavorText: The Mitsubishi A6M3 Type 0 Model 32, better known as Zero, was a variant that was first introduced in 1941. It came with a new Sakae 21 engine that gave it more power and was designed for better altitude performance. This made the aircraft heavier than its predecessor, and even though it increased the speed by 11 km/h the range was 1,000 km less, which meant that it was only suitable for shorter range missions and interception. The Allied reporting name for the aircraft was Zeke 32. Only 343 A6M3’s were built.

card_unit_d4y_suisei.name: card_unit_d4y_suisei
card_unit_d4y_suisei.title: D4Y SUISEI
card_unit_d4y_suisei.text: Deployment: Pin target enemy unit and its adjacent units.
card_unit_d4y_suisei.flavorText: The Yokosuka D4Y Suisei (e. comet) was a Japanese two seated, carrier-based dive bomber used during WWII by the Imperial Japanese Navy. The D4Y came into service in 1942, and although it was initially designed as a dive bomber, it also served as a night fighter, reconnaissance aircraft and lastly it was used for kamikaze attacks. The D4Y was the fastest dive bomber of WWII, but like many other Japanese aircraft it lacked armor which made it vulnerable in combat against Allied fighters. The D4Y was produced from 1942 to 1945 with 2,038 aircraft manufactured in total, including many variants.

card_unit_hayabusa.name: card_unit_hayabusa
card_unit_hayabusa.title: Ki-43 HAYABUSA
card_unit_hayabusa.text: Destruction: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_hayabusa.flavorText: The Nakajima Ki-43 Hayabusa was a single-engine land-based tactical fighter used by the Imperial Japanese Army Air Force in World War II. It was code named "Oscar" by the Allies, but often called the "Army Zero" by American pilots due to its resemblance to the Mitsubishi A6M Zero.

card_unit_kagoshima_regiment.name: card_unit_kagoshima_regiment
card_unit_kagoshima_regiment.title: KAGOSHIMA REGIMENT
card_unit_kagoshima_regiment.flavorText: The 45th Infantry Regiment (Kagoshima) was part of the 6th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The regiment fought with its division in the Second Sino-Japanese War. During the later stages of WWII the regiment fought in Bougainville Island in the Solomon Islands as part of the Japanese Seventeenth Army.

card_unit_ki_51_sonia.name: card_unit_ki_51_sonia
card_unit_ki_51_sonia.title: Ki-51 SONIA
card_unit_ki_51_sonia.text: When this unit attacks a Pinned unit, destroy that unit.
card_unit_ki_51_sonia.flavorText: The Mitsubishi Ki-51 (Allied code name "Sonia") was a light bomber/dive bomber used by the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II. The Ki-51 was also used as a ground-attack aircraft in the China-Burma-India theater, and a reconnaissance version Ki-51A was also built. 2,385 aircraft were constructed and by the end of the war the Japanese began using them in kamikaze attacks.

card_unit_ki_61_tony.name: card_unit_ki_61_tony
card_unit_ki_61_tony.title: Ki-61-II TONY
card_unit_ki_61_tony.text: Spend 7 kredits at the end of enemy turn and add it to the battlefield.
card_unit_ki_61_tony.flavorText: The Kawasaki Ki-61 Hien (e. flying swallow) was a Japanese fighter aircraft used by the Imperial Japanese Air Service during WWII. It was first introduced in 1942 and used in front line service throughout the war. It took some time for the Allied pilots to identify the aircraft, first they mistook it for the German Messerschmitt Bf 109s and later the Italian Macchi C.202 which led to the Allied codename “Tony”. The Ki-61-II variant was introduced in 1943 and had a more powerful engine than its predecessor. Later variants would focus on increasing the speed and firepower. A total of 3,078 aircraft were built.

card_unit_osaka_regiment.name: card_unit_osaka_regiment
card_unit_osaka_regiment.title: OSAKA REGIMENT
card_unit_osaka_regiment.flavorText: The 8th Infantry Regiment Osaka was part of the 4th Infantry Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. Prior to WWII the regiment and its division had participated in several engagements in the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1941 the division participated in Battle of Changsha, but shortly after it was sent back to Japan to act as a reserve force. At the start of the Pacific War the division was assigned to the 14th Army and sent to the Philippines where it saw combat in the Battle of Bataan and later in the Battle of Corregidor. After the Phillipine Campaign the division performed security and garrison duties in the Japanese home islands and Sumatra, but was lastly transferred to Thailand where it was disbanded in 1946.
