card_event_diplomatic_attache.text: Deal 1 damage to target enemy, plus 1 for each previously played DIPLOMATIC ATTACHÉ.
card_event_diplomatic_attache.flavorText: The Tripartite Pact, signed in 1940, was a mutual defense treaty between Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and Imperial Japan. It aimed to establish a formal alliance and coordination among the Axis powers. The pact outlined principles of mutual assistance and collaboration in economic, political, and military matters. Germany sought support from Italy and Japan to expand the Axis alliance, Italy aimed to strengthen its position within the Axis and gain backing for its colonial ambitions, while Japan sought resources and influence in East Asia. The pact included provisions for mutual defense, consultation, and economic cooperation. However, the effectiveness of the pact was limited as each nation pursued its own strategic goals independently. While symbolically important, the pact did not lead to significant military coordination or joint planning among the signatories. Ultimately, the Tripartite Pact had a symbolic and diplomatic role, but its impact on the outcome of the war was limited as the fortunes of the Axis powers declined.

card_event_island_fighting.name: card_event_island_fighting
card_event_island_fighting.title: ISLAND DEFENSE
card_event_island_fighting.text: Draw a card if your HQ has 10 or less defense. Give your HQ +8 defense.
card_event_island_fighting.flavorText: During WWII, the Japanese employed various strategies to defend the islands in the Pacific. Their defensive tactics involved fortified positions, underground tunnels, guerrilla warfare, naval power, and kamikaze attacks. They constructed extensive fortifications, including bunkers and tunnels, to protect their troops and supplies. Guerrilla tactics such as hit-and-run attacks and ambushes were used in areas where direct defense was not possible. The Japanese Navy played a crucial role in coastal defense, using naval guns and vessels to repel enemy assaults. Kamikaze suicide attacks were also employed as a desperate measure. However, despite their efforts, the overwhelming resources of the Allied forces eventually led to the recapture of the Pacific islands from Japanese control.

card_event_japan_duty.name: card_event_japan_duty
card_event_japan_duty.title: DUTY IS A MOUNTAIN
card_event_japan_duty.text: Give your units: "Destruction effects on this unit trigger an extra time."
card_event_japan_duty.flavorText: The quote "Death is lighter than a feather, but Duty is heavier than a mountain" is commonly associated with the Japanese Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors (軍人勅諭, Gunjin Chokuyu). The Imperial Rescript was a document issued by Emperor Meiji in 1882, which outlined the principles and expectations for members of the Japanese military. It emphasized concepts such as loyalty, sacrifice, and unwavering dedication to duty. The Rescript played a significant role in shaping the mindset and moral code of Japanese soldiers and sailors during WWII. The quote in question was later used by Robert Jordan in his book series The Wheel of Time.

card_event_jungle_warfare.name: card_event_jungle_warfare
card_event_jungle_warfare.title: JUNGLE WARFARE
card_event_jungle_warfare.text: Give a unit: "Destruction: Deal 2 damage to a random enemy." Trigger its Destruction effects.
card_event_jungle_warfare.flavorText: During WWII, the Japanese forces were generally considered to have an advantage over the Allies in jungle warfare. The Japanese had extensive experience fighting in jungles due to their prior military campaigns in China and Southeast Asia, which gave them a deep understanding of the terrain and tactics suited for jungle warfare. They employed guerrilla tactics, utilized camouflage effectively, and were skilled in navigating the dense vegetation. They excelled at ambushes, infiltrating enemy positions, and conducting surprise attacks. In contrast, the Allied forces initially faced challenges adapting to the unique demands of jungle warfare. They lacked experience and training specific to these environments, and the dense foliage, limited visibility, difficult terrain, and tropical diseases posed significant obstacles. However, as the war progressed, the Allies learned valuable lessons and developed effective countermeasures. The Allies improved their jungle training, equipment, and tactics. They utilized superior firepower, air support, and artillery to offset the Japanese advantages. They also developed techniques for jungle patrolling, anti-guerrilla operations, and utilizing native guides for intelligence gathering. Over time, the Allies adapted and developed successful strategies to combat the Japanese in jungle environments. Campaigns such as Guadalcanal, New Guinea, and Burma showcased the Allies growing proficiency in jungle warfare and their ability to overcome Japanese resistance.

card_event_on_the_horizon.name: card_event_on_the_horizon
card_event_on_the_horizon.title: ON THE HORIZON
card_event_on_the_horizon.text: This turn, your units are immune to damage and have "Cannot attack the enemy HQ."
card_event_on_the_horizon.flavorText: At the start of WWII the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN), held a significant advantage over the Allied navies in the Pacific. They had a larger number of battleships, including the Yamato and Musashi, which were the largest ever built. The Japanese Navy also possessed more aircraft carriers, such as the Akagi and Kaga, and had a well-trained naval aviation force. Their submarines were effective in offensive operations. However, as the war progressed, the Allied navies, particularly the United States Navy, improved their capabilities and eventually gained the upper hand. The Battle of Midway marked a turning point where the U.S. Navy dealt a severe blow to the Japanese carrier force. Despite the initial advantage, the Japanese Navy faced increasing challenges from the growing strength of the Allies.

card_event_shinano.name: card_event_shinano
card_event_shinano.title: IJN SHINANO
card_event_shinano.text: Distribute damage randomly to enemies equal to the number of units on the battlefield.
card_event_shinano.flavorText: IJN Shinano was a Yamato-class aircraft carrier of the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN) during WWII. It was the largest aircraft carrier ever built at the time. Initially, Shinano was laid down as a third Yamato-class battleship, but due to the increasing need for aircraft carriers, it was converted into an aircraft carrier during construction. Shinano had an impressive size and displacement, with a length of over 244 meters (800 feet) and a full load displacement of approximately 72,000 tons. It was equipped with a powerful propulsion system, capable of reaching speeds of up to 27 knots. The carrier was intended to play a crucial role in Japan's naval operations, but it was completed late in the war. Shinano embarked on its maiden voyage in November 1944, but it was unfortunately sunk by a submarine, USS Archerfish, on November 29, 1944, just ten days after its commissioning. The sinking of Shinano was a significant blow to Japan's naval capabilities, as it lost its largest and most advanced aircraft carrier. The ship's fate remains an interesting episode in naval history, representing the brief operational period of a formidable carrier that never had the opportunity to fulfill its intended role in combat.

card_event_stealth_mission.name: card_event_stealth_mission
card_event_stealth_mission.title: STEALTH MISSION
card_event_stealth_mission.text: Give a friendly unit: "Remove from the battlefield at the start of your turn to gain 6 kredits and draw 3 cards."
card_event_stealth_mission.flavorText: Five Japanese submarines, known as the "midget submarines", were part of the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Their objective was to penetrate the harbor defenses and launch torpedoes at American ships. These submarines were relatively small, crewed by only two or three men, and carried two torpedoes each. The midget submarines encountered various challenges during their mission. One of them, Ha-19, became entangled in an anti-submarine net and was eventually scuttled by its crew, and submarine Ha-20, was sunk by the USS Helm. While the midget submarines did not cause significant damage to American warships, their presence added to the chaos and confusion during the attack. Their role in the attack highlights the Japanese Navy's strategy of employing various naval assets, including submarines, to maximize the impact of their operations. It is worth noting that Japanese submarines conducted numerous other missions throughout WWII, including patrols, reconnaissance, and attacks on enemy ships. However, the attack on Pearl Harbor remains one of the most notable examples of Japanese submarine operations during the war.

card_event_under_fire_japan.name: card_event_under_fire_japan
card_event_under_fire_japan.title: UNDER FIRE
card_event_under_fire_japan.text: Deal 1 damage to target enemy unit and to adjacent enemies. Pin units damaged.
card_event_under_fire_japan.flavorText: During WWII, Japanese soldiers demonstrated remarkable resilience and tenacity under fire. They were known for their discipline, dedication, and willingness to sacrifice themselves for their country. Japanese soldiers were trained to be highly aggressive and were often willing to engage in close-quarters combat, which sometimes resulted in fierce and brutal fighting. They were skilled in camouflage, infiltration, and ambush tactics, allowing them to surprise and overwhelm their opponents. Additionally, the Japanese soldiers had a strong sense of honor and loyalty to their superiors and country that drove them to fight fiercely, even when facing overwhelming odds. While Japanese soldiers were known for their courage and willingness to engage in fierce combat, it is important to acknowledge that their bravery was not always the best strategy, and it sometimes led to devastating losses.

card_unit_24th_cavalry_regiment.name: card_unit_24th_cavalry_regiment
card_unit_24th_cavalry_regiment.title: 24th CAVALRY REGIMENT
card_unit_24th_cavalry_regiment.text: Destruction: Draw a 24th CAVALRY REGIMENT from your deck.
card_unit_24th_cavalry_regiment.flavorText: The 24th Cavalry Regiment was a regiment of the 8th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army and played a significant role during the pre-war and during WWII. Initially, the 4th Brigade of the division participated in the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931. The division arrived in Manchukuo in 1932 and served as a garrison force. It was later subordinated to the Kwantung Army in 1937. In 1939, the division underwent reorganization and became a triangular division. During the Pacific War, the 8th Division remained in Manchukuo until February 1944 when a detachment was sent to Poluwat due to worsening conditions in the Pacific. In July 1944, the division was reassigned to the Philippines and faced heavy losses during the Battle of Leyte and the Battle of Manila. The remnants of the division surrendered in September 1945. The division was officially dissolved in December 1947. Notably, Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese holdout, belonged to the 8th Division and did not surrender until 1974.

card_unit_56th_recon.name: card_unit_56th_recon
card_unit_56th_recon.title: 56th RECON
card_unit_56th_recon.text: Destruction: Deal 1 damage to each enemy unit.
card_unit_56th_recon.flavorText: The 56th Reconnaissance Regiment was a motorized unit of the 56th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army which was active between 1940-1945. Initially, the 56th Division was intended as reinforcements for the Japanese invasion of Malaya but was attached to the 25th Army and sent to Burma in March 1942. The Division played a significant role in the Battle of Toungoo, where it linked with the 55th Division, and forced the Chinese to evacuate the city, paving the way to the east. The 56th Division defeated the Chinese 6th Corps in several battles, including Mawchi, Bawlake, Bato, Taunggyi, and Loikaw. It advanced north through the Shan States, took the city of Lashio, and cut off much of the local Chinese Army from China, forcing the Allies to evacuate Burma. After May 1942, the 56th Division mostly performed garrison duties on the Yunnan border. In January 1944, the division participated in the Battle of Northern Burma and Western Yunnan campaign, where it played a significant role in shattering Merrill's Marauders in the Siege of Myitkyina and delaying the Chinese forces during the Battle of Mount Song. The Division suffered heavy losses and was removed from the front line in October 1944. On the day of the surrender of Japan, August 15, 1945, the division was stationed on the border between South Burma and Thailand.

card_unit_66th_independent.name: card_unit_66th_independent
card_unit_66th_independent.title: 66th INDEPENDENT
card_unit_66th_independent.text: Deployment: Destroy an enemy unit with two adjacent units.
card_unit_66th_independent.flavorText: The 66th Independent Infantry Brigade was a unit of the 47th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. At the start of the war the 46th Division was tasked with reinforcing the mainland defenses as part of the Western District Army. However, in October 1943, it was temporarily reassigned to the 16th Army and given orders to move south, except for the 46th Artillery Regiment which remained behind. In late November 1943, the Division's 123rd Regiment landed on Sumba Island in the Lesser Sunda Islands. Subsequently, the 46th Division was reassigned to the 19th Army. In February 1944, the 147th Regiment arrived on the nearby Sumbawa Island. The division set up its headquarters there. Unfortunately, the 145th Regiment was unable to be transported and was redirected from Saipan in June 1944 to Iwo Jima under General Kuribayashi’s command. It met its demise during the intense Battle of Iwo Jima in February to March 1945.

card_unit_ki_45_dragon_slayer.name: card_unit_ki_45_dragon_slayer
card_unit_ki_45_dragon_slayer.title: Ki-45 DRAGON SLAYER
card_unit_ki_45_dragon_slayer.text: Deployment: Becomes Veteran if this is the first Ki-45 DRAGON SLAYER you deploy this battle.
card_unit_ki_45_dragon_slayer.flavorText: The Ki-45, also known as "Nick" by the Allies, was a twin-engine fighter aircraft developed during WWII. Its official name was "Toryu," which means Dragon Slayer in Japanese. The Ki-45 was initially designed as a heavy fighter for the Imperial Japanese Army Air Service, intended to serve as both an interceptor and a bomber destroyer. It first flew in January 1939 and entered service in 1941. The usual weaponry of the Kawasaki Ki-45 Toryu included a 20mm cannon located in the nose, a 37mm cannon firing forwards from the fuselage, a 7.92mm machine gun that fired from the rear, and the capability to carry drop tanks or bombs under the wings. Other experimental armaments were also tested, such as the use of a 75mm cannon for assaulting ships. The Ki-45 was used in a variety of roles during the war, including as night fighter, interceptor, bomber escort, and fighter bomber aircraft. It was involved in many major battles, including the defense of the Japanese homeland during the Allied bombing campaign, as well as in the Pacific and Southeast Asia. Despite its formidable armament and performance, the Ki-45 suffered from a number of design flaws that limited its effectiveness and the aircraft's heavy armament and armor made it less maneuverable than other contemporary fighters. A total of 1,701 Ki-45’s were manufactured, including a few variants.

card_unit_ki_49_donryu.name: card_unit_ki_49_donryu
card_unit_ki_49_donryu.title: Ki-49 STORM DRAGON
card_unit_ki_49_donryu.flavorText: The Nakajima Ki-49 Donryu, also known as the "Storm Dragon," was a twin-engine heavy bomber used by the Japanese during WWII.  The Ki-49 was heavily armed and armored but had limited bomb-carrying, and was initially designed for daylight bombing missions without fighter escort. The Ki-49 saw service in China, New Guinea, and Australia, but faced challenges since it was underpowered and vulnerable against enemy fighters. Upgraded versions were developed, but production delays hindered further improvements. As losses mounted and fighter opposition increased, the Ki-49's role shifted to anti-submarine patrols, troop transport, and even kamikaze missions. Production ended in December 1944 after approximately 819 aircraft had been built.

card_unit_kokuras_sword.name: card_unit_kokuras_sword
card_unit_kokuras_sword.title: KOKURA'S SWORD
card_unit_kokuras_sword.text: Destruction: If it's the enemy turn, add a random Japanese ground unit to your support line and give it this ability.
card_unit_kokuras_sword.flavorText: The 12th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army was an infantry division that saw action during WWII. It played a role in various military campaigns, particularly in China during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Its code name was the Sword Division and it recruited primarily from the northern part of the island of Kyūshū. Its original headquarters were located in the Kokura castle, in the city of Kitakyushu. In 1940, the 12th Division underwent reorganization, becoming a triangular division with the transfer of its IJA 14th Infantry Regiment to the IJA 25th Division. Under the command of Lieutenant General Masakazu Kawabe, the division was permanently stationed in Manchukuo (now Manchuria) from July 1940, falling under the jurisdiction of the Japanese Third Army in Dongning. Its main tasks involved policing and anti-partisan operations. As the Pacific War took a turn for the worse for Japan in 1944, the 12th Division was relocated to Hsinchu, Taiwan, to reinforce the defenses of the 10th Area Army. Eventually, it became part of the 40th Army when it was stationed in Taiwan in early 1945. However, since the Allies bypassed Taiwan and landed on Okinawa instead, the 12th Division spent the remainder of World War II as a garrison force in Taiwan, without engaging in combat.

card_unit_matsumoto_regiment.name: card_unit_matsumoto_regiment
card_unit_matsumoto_regiment.title: MATSUMOTO REGIMENT
card_unit_matsumoto_regiment.text: Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ when a Destruction effect triggers.
card_unit_matsumoto_regiment.flavorText: The 50th Infantry Regiment (Matsuomoto) was a unit of the 29th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army, which was active from 1941-1945. From 1941 the 29th division was tasked with the defense of the Liaoyang area in Manchukuo state of Manchuria, but in 1944 the majority of the division was deployed to Guam island along with the 48th Independent Mixed Brigade, while smaller units were dispatched to Tinian and Rota islands. The Japanese garrison on Tinian consisted of approximately 9,000 soldiers, including the 50th Infantry Regiment and a 29th tank company, who were well-fortified and prepared for the American invasion. The Battle of Tinian began on July 24, 1944, with a massive bombardment of the island by the US Navy and Army Air Force. The Japanese defenders, however, remained dug in and refused to surrender despite overwhelming odds. By 30 July the remnants of the defenders were holed up in caves and ravines on the south portion of the island. Realizing the futility of further resistance, Colonel Ogata ordered his forces to launch a massive banzai charge. This desperate attempt resulted in heavy casualties for the Japanese, but the battle continued for a few more days until organized resistance was effectively crushed on 3 August 1944. Only about 200 men of the Japanese garrison survived the fighting.

card_unit_okayama_regiment.name: card_unit_okayama_regiment
card_unit_okayama_regiment.title: TOTTORI REGIMENT
card_unit_okayama_regiment.flavorText: The 53rd Infantry Regiment (Tottori) was part of the 17th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. During the Pacific War, the 17th Division consisted of the 53rd, 54th, and 81st Infantry Regiments, supported by various other units including artillery, engineers, transport, and tanks. In September 1943, the division was assigned to the Southern Expeditionary Army Group and sent to New Britain in the Islands Region of Papua New Guinea, operating under the command of the 8th Area Army based in Rabaul. The first two convoys arrived in New Britain safely in 1943. However, the third convoy was ambushed by the USS Grayback submarine, resulting in the sinking of the auxiliary cruiser Awata Maru and the loss of 1,087 men from the 17th Division. The remaining units, led by Lieutenant General Iwao Matsuda, participated in the Battle of Cape Gloucester and the Battle of New Britain, eventually being reduced to a few independent mixed regiments guarding hospital areas. The survivors of the 17th Division surrendered to Allied forces in New Britain by the end of the war on August 15, 1945.

card_event_air_land_sea.name: card_event_air_land_sea
card_event_air_land_sea.title: AIR, LAND & SEA
card_event_air_land_sea.text: Develop a card in your deck. Lose a kredit slot.
card_event_air_land_sea.flavorText: During WWII, Japan's military strategy was heavily reliant on its capabilities in the air, on land, and at sea. In the air, the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service (IJNAS) and Imperial Japanese Army Air Service (IJAAS) were initially powerful, achieving surprise attacks like Pearl Harbor and early victories in the Pacific. However, their aircraft, pilot training programs and manufacturing capabilities couldn't keep pace with the Allies and this led to their decline. On land, the Imperial Japanese Army (IJA) was known for its brutal tactics and initial successes in conquering territories in Southeast Asia and the Pacific. However, its overextended supply lines, the logistical challenges it faced, and the relentless attacks of Allied forces led to its eventual defeat.. At sea, the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN) was a powerful force, with a focus on aircraft carriers and innovative tactics. Early victories such as in the Indian Ocean Raid boosted their confidence, but their losses in crucial battles like the Battle of Midway and the Battle of the Philippine Sea turned the tide against them. Despite their initial successes, Japan's overconfidence, resource limitations, and strategic miscalculations ultimately led to their defeat in all three domains.

card_event_carrier_battle.name: card_event_carrier_battle
card_event_carrier_battle.title: CARRIER BATTLE
card_event_carrier_battle.text: Deal 3 damage. Add CARRIER BATTLE to the enemy hand with all numericals one higher.
card_event_carrier_battle.flavorText: The Imperial Japanese Navy's aircraft carriers were instrumental in early World War II victories, including the attack on Pearl Harbor and the sinking of British warships. However, their fortunes changed at the Battle of Midway, where four of their carriers were sunk. Despite this setback, they kept fighting with their remaining carriers in battles like the Philippine Sea and Leyte Gulf, but ultimately suffered heavy losses due to the growing strength of the US Navy. The Imperial Japanese Navy possessed a total of 18 aircraft carriers throughout the war, but 14 were lost. The majority were lost around the Philippines, three of those in the Battle of the Philippine Sea alone.

card_event_commit_the_reserves.name: card_event_commit_the_reserves
card_event_commit_the_reserves.title: COMMIT THE RESERVES
card_event_commit_the_reserves.text: Destroy target unit with attack equal or less than your kredit slots. Lose a kredit slot.
card_event_commit_the_reserves.flavorText: During WWII, the Japanese reserve system played a crucial role in mobilizing manpower for the war effort. The system consisted of several categories, including the first and second reserves, and the national guard, with an estimated total of 2.8 million men: approximately 1.3 million in the first reserve, 1 million in the second reserve, and half a million men in the national guard. Men who had completed their active duty service were assigned to these reserves and could be called up in times of need. However, as the war progressed and casualties mounted, the quality and training of reservists declined. Additionally, the Japanese military's focus on offensive tactics and its reluctance to rotate troops led to exhaustion and a lack of fresh reinforcements. This ultimately hampered Japan's ability to sustain its war effort and contributed to its eventual defeat.

card_event_grand_plans.name: card_event_grand_plans
card_event_grand_plans.title: GRAND PLANS
card_event_grand_plans.text: Choose and discard a card to draw a card with higher cost from your deck.
card_event_grand_plans.flavorText: Even though Japan had grand plans at the outbreak of WWII, they did not plan to bomb the mainland United States. However, they did carry out a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7th, 1941. This was a US naval base and territory at the time and the attack was intended to cripple the US Pacific Fleet and prevent interference with Japan's planned military actions in Southeast Asia. While there were some isolated events of Japanese balloon bombs reaching the mainland US, these were not part of a larger strategic bombing campaign.

card_event_great_expanse.name: card_event_great_expanse
card_event_great_expanse.title: THE GREAT EXPANSE
card_event_great_expanse.text: Set your kredit slots to equal the enemy kredit slots. Your units get +1 attack for each slot gained.
card_event_great_expanse.flavorText: The Japanese military's "Great Expanse" during WWII was a display of ambition and ruthlessness. Within a few short months their forces swept across the Pacific and conquered a vast territory stretching from Manchuria to the borders of India. This fast expansion of Japan was driven by a desire for resources and a belief in their divine right to rule Asia. From the Aleutian Islands in the north to the Solomon Islands in the south, the Japanese empire grew into a dominating empire across the Pacific. However, this overextension of their forces and the fierce resistance of Allied powers proved unsustainable and led to their eventual downfall.

card_event_one_roof.name: card_event_one_roof
card_event_one_roof.title: ONE ROOF
card_event_one_roof.text: Draw 2 cards. Gain 4 kredits if you have lost 2 or more kredit slots this battle.
card_event_one_roof.flavorText: During WWII, Japan often used ideological concepts to justify imperial expansion and aggression. These ideologies provided a legitimizing narrative for Japan's military actions and, under the banner of "liberating Asia from Western colonial rule," promoted the establishment of a new order led by Japan. They were also used to mobilize domestic support for the war, portraying it as a righteous cause through which Japan would fulfill its destiny. However, the brutality and atrocities of invasion and occupation stood in stark contrast to the idealized vision promoted by wartime propaganda.

card_unit_174th_independent.name: card_unit_174th_independent
card_unit_174th_independent.title: 174th INDEPENDENT
card_unit_174th_independent.text: After this unit attacks the enemy HQ, it gets +1+1 and you draw a card.
card_unit_174th_independent.flavorText: The 174th Independent Battalion was a unit of the 102nd Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was formed in 1944 as a security division, which meant that it was mainly composed of independent infantry battalions instead of regiments. The division was transferred to the Philippines where part of the division fought against the US forces in the Battle of Leyte and the Battle of the Visayas. Afterwards some sub-units managed to hold out in mountainous regions until Japan's surrender on August 15th, 1945. During the Invasion of Palawan in March-April 1945, two battalions of the 102nd Division were defeated by the US 186th Regimental Combat Team. On Panay, a single company from the division retreated to the mountains and remained relatively intact. On Cebu, the 102nd Division consisted of a single battalion and survivors from Leyte. They suffered heavy casualties during the Battle for Cebu City but managed to continue guerrilla warfare after the battle. On Negros island, approximately 4,000 personnel from the 77th Infantry Brigade of the 102nd Division also survived and engaged in guerrilla warfare against invading US forces from March 1945 until the end of the war.

card_unit_40th_cavalry_regiment.name: card_unit_40th_cavalry_regiment
card_unit_40th_cavalry_regiment.title: 40th CAVALRY REGIMENT
card_unit_40th_cavalry_regiment.text:
Deployment: Lose a kredit slot. 
Destruction: Reduce the cost of cards in your hand by 1.
card_unit_40th_cavalry_regiment.flavorText: The 40th Cavalry Regiment was a unit of the Imperial Japanese Army's 40th Division during WWII. The division was formed in 1939, initially intended as a garrison force, and was later deployed to the front. The regiment performed reconnaissance, security, and other mobile duties. In 1945, the division received new deployment orders, but the war ended while it was in transit. It was subsequently disbanded, and surviving personnel returned to Japan by May 1946.

card_unit_51st_recon.name: card_unit_51st_recon
card_unit_51st_recon.title: 51st RECON
card_unit_51st_recon.text: When the enemy HQ gains defense, this unit gets equal attack.
card_unit_51st_recon.flavorText: The 51st Reconnaissance Regiment was a unit of the 51st Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division was formed in 1940 and it was transferred to Guangdong in China in 1941. At the time a detachment was used for rearguard duties during the Battle of Hong Kong. In 1942 the 51st Division was transferred to Rabaul in Papua New Guinea as part of the 18th Army. In 1943 it was ordered to the city of Lae in New Guinea,  but on the way its convoy was intercepted by Allied aircraft and only 2,000 of 6,900 troops reached Lae. The division eventually regrouped in the Salamaua area, in the northern eastern coastline of Papua New Guinea. It took part in the Salamaua–Lae campaign which ended in a defeat against the US and Australian forces. The 51st Division retreated from Lae in September 1943 and experienced extreme hardship in the process, losing equipment and suffering from starvation. Lacking weapons and ammunition after their retreat, most of the remaining 51st Division soldiers were unable to participate in combat, except for one company from the 102nd Infantry Regiment which fought at Finschhafen. From 1944 to 1945, the 51st Division's primary struggle was against starvation, and only a small fraction of its soldiers survived until Japan's surrender in August 1945.

card_unit_5th_regiment.name: card_unit_5th_regiment
card_unit_5th_regiment.title: 5th REGIMENT
card_unit_5th_regiment.text: When you lose a kredit slot, this unit gets +2+1 if on the battlefield or -2 cost if in hand.
card_unit_5th_regiment.flavorText: The 5th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 8th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was formed in 1898 and participated in the Russo-Japanese War, the Japanese invasion of Manchuria and finally the Pacific War. On September 19th, 1941, the 8th Division was assigned to the 20th Army to defend the Soviet Union border alongside the 25th Division. It remained stationed in Manchukuo during the initial phases of the Pacific War. In July 1944 the 8th Division was moved to the Philippines and after its arrival the 5th Regiment was transferred to Leyte where it was destroyed during the Battle of Leyte against the US forces. The remainder of the division participated in the Battle of Manilla in January 1945, where it suffered heavy losses. The survivors stopped fighting on September 2nd, 1945 after the surrender of Japan.

card_unit_e13a_jake.name: card_unit_e13a_jake
card_unit_e13a_jake.title: E13A JAKE
card_unit_e13a_jake.text: When you lose a kredit slot, your units get +1+1.
card_unit_e13a_jake.flavorText: The Aichi E13A, codenamed "Jake" by the Allies, was a long range reconnaissance seaplane used by the Imperial Japanese Navy from 1941 to 1945. The Aichi E13A was operational throughout the war and took on a variety of roles including coastal patrols, attacks on enemy convoys, communication duties, transporting officers, rescuing downed pilots, and even serving as kamikaze aircraft in the final stages of the war. In China it operated from seaplane tenders and cruisers, but it was also deployed on the battleships Yamato and Musashi for reconnaissance purposes, launched from their onboard catapults.The E13A was used as a scout for the Attack on Pearl Harbor, and during the Battles of the Coral Sea and Midway. A total of 1,418 aircraft were built, including a few variants.

card_unit_e7k.name: card_unit_e7k
card_unit_e7k.title: KAWANISHI E7K
card_unit_e7k.text: Reveal: Gets +2 attack if it is your turn.
card_unit_e7k.flavorText: The Kawanishi E7K was a Japanese three-seat reconnaissance seaplane that was mainly used in the 1930s by the Imperial Japanese Navy. At the beginning of the Pacific War in 1941 it was mainly being used in second line duties. There were two variants: E7K1 with 183 built, and E7K2 with 350 built. The E7K2 variant was used in front line services up until 1943, and both versions were used during the final stages of the war for kamikaze operations. The E7K had a 3 man crew, an armament consisting of one Type 97 aircraft machine gun, two Type 92 machine guns and could carry up to 120 kg of bombs.

card_unit_kurume_regiment.name: card_unit_kurume_regiment
card_unit_kurume_regiment.title: KURUME REGIMENT
card_unit_kurume_regiment.flavorText: The 248th Infantry Regiment (Kurume) was a unit of the 112th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was active from 1944 to 1945 and was mainly composed of men from the 28th Division. It was stationed in the city of Hunchun, in the Jiandao area which is a border region between Northeastern China and Korea. In August 1945 the Soviet Red Army invaded Manchuria and the division was caught in heavy fighting against the advancing Soviets. Hunchun city was soon lost to Soviet forces but the division continued fighting until it was ordered to lay down arms on August 18th after the general surrender of Japan. Most of the remaining men of the 112th Division were taken prisoners by the Red Army.

card_unit_shoge_detachment.name: card_unit_shoge_detachment
card_unit_shoge_detachment.title: SHOGE DETACHMENT
card_unit_shoge_detachment.flavorText: The Shoge Detachment was a unit of the 41st Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division was formed in 1939 and its first deployment was in the Shanxi province in China, where they were put on garrison duty. At the outbreak of the Pacific War in 1941 the division was based in Qingdao in eastern China, and the plan was to transfer it to Guadalcanal. However, after attempts to reinforce the Japanese garrison on the island failed, the decision was made to send it to New Guinea. As part of the 18th Army the 41st Division participated in the New Guinea campaign from 1943 to 45 where it fought against Australian and US forces. However, in 1943 the Shoge Detachment, named after their commander Ryoichi Shoge, was sent to fortify positions at Lae where it participated in the Salamaua–Lae Campaign under grueling circumstances. After being defeated at Lae, the Japanese forces decided to retreat to a new defensive line in the Huon Peninsula. Around 9,000 Japanese troops withdrew, and during the difficult retreat, the Japanese suffered heavy losses, both in manpower and equipment. Those that managed to reach their destination participated later in the Huon Peninsula Campaign, which was a series of battles fought in north-eastern Papua New Guinea in 1943 and 1944.

card_unit_tsu_regiment.name: card_unit_tsu_regiment
card_unit_tsu_regiment.title: TSU REGIMENT
card_unit_tsu_regiment.text:
Deployment: Target a unit. 
Destruction: Destroy the unit targeted.
card_unit_tsu_regiment.flavorText: The Tsu Regiment, formally known as the 133rd Infantry regiment, was a unit of the 116th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was formed in May 1938. In June that year it was transferred to Shanghai, and then to the Dabie Mountains in China where it participated in the Battle of Wuhan against the Chinese forces. Between 1939 and 1944 the division participated in various battles and campaigns in China, including the Battle of Changde and the Battle of Changsha. In October 1944 the 133rd Division was transferred to the Twentieth Army to take part in the Battle of Hengyang as part of Operation Ichi-Go. After intense fighting the division suffered heavy losses, but the battle ended with the Japanese capture of the city. In 1945 the division participated in the Battle of West Henan–North Hubei, a Japanese victory. The division was stationed in the city of Hengyang when Japan surrendered on August 15th, 1945.

card_event_drive_into_the_sea.name: card_event_drive_into_the_sea
card_event_drive_into_the_sea.title: DRIVE INTO THE SEA
card_event_drive_into_the_sea.text: Remove a unit from the battlefield. At the start of your next turn, return it to hand.
card_event_drive_into_the_sea.flavorText: In early 1942, Japanese forces tightened their grip on the Philippines, forcing American and Filipino troops into a desperate defense on the island fortress of Corregidor. After months of aerial and naval bombardment, the final assault began on May 5th. Under cover of darkness and artillery fire, Japanese troops crossed Manila Bay and landed on Corregidor’s northeastern coast. Despite the defenders’ fierce resistance, the attackers pushed inland, overwhelming beach defenses and securing a critical foothold. US and Filipino units launched counterattacks through the night, but Japanese reinforcements steadily poured ashore. The defenders were low on ammunition, rations and medical supplies. Communications broke down. By the afternoon of May 6th, Japanese troops had breached the Malinta Tunnel area, the last major Allied stronghold. Facing total collapse, Lieutenant General Jonathan Wainwright surrendered all forces on Corregidor. The fall of the island marked the end of organized resistance in the Philippines. Of the roughly 11,000 Allied troops captured, many would face brutal conditions in captivity.

card_event_ijn_shirakumo.name: card_event_ijn_shirakumo
card_event_ijn_shirakumo.title: IJN SHIRAKUMO
card_event_ijn_shirakumo.text: Pin target unit. If it is already pinned, remove it instead. Your HQ gains +2 defense.
card_event_ijn_shirakumo.flavorText: Commissioned in 1928, Shirakumo was part of the Fubuki-class, a revolutionary class of Japanese destroyers which set new standards in firepower and speed. Assigned to Destroyer Division 12, she was active from the beginning of Japan’s war in China and supported landings in southern China and French Indochina. At the start of WWII, Shirakumo escorted invasion convoys to Malaya and British Borneo. In February 1942, she helped sink the British cable-laying ship Anking. Later that month, she took part in the Battle of Sunda Strait, where Japanese forces sank the Allied cruisers Perth and Houston, as well as the Dutch destroyer Evertsen. During the Guadalcanal campaign, Shirakumo ran Tokyo Express missions to reinforce Japanese positions. On 28 August 1942, a bomb hit her engine room during an air attack, putting her out of action until October. She resumed escort duties in Northern-Pacific waters in 1943 but was lost with all hands on 16 March 1944 when the submarine USS Harder torpedoed her off Hokkaido while she was escorting a convoy to the Kuril islands.

card_event_overpower.name: card_event_overpower
card_event_overpower.title: OVERPOWER
card_event_overpower.text: Destroy a unit with 2 or less attack and all other units with the same name on the battlefield.
card_event_overpower.flavorText: In the opening phase of the Pacific War, Japanese fighter pilots flying aircraft such as the Mitsubishi A6M Zero achieved a string of impressive successes against Allied air forces. According to one account, Japanese crews claimed nine victories with no losses in a single early engagement. In the campaign over China and across the Pacific from 1941 to 1942, many Japanese aces accumulated high tallies. For instance, Tetsuzō Iwamoto of the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service is credited with at least 80 aerial victories overall. While comprehensive statistics are elusive, some suggest Japanese air services lost around 38,000 aircraft during the entire war, of which roughly 17,000 were non‑combat losses. The early‑war “air superiority” earned by Japan derived from good pilot training, aircraft range and surprise, but the margin gradually narrowed as Allied air forces improved tactics, introduced newer fighters and expanded production.

card_event_swift_victory.name: card_event_swift_victory
card_event_swift_victory.title: SWIFT VICTORY
card_event_swift_victory.text: Deal 3 damage. Units in the enemy deck get +3 attack.
card_event_swift_victory.flavorText: In the first six months of the Pacific War, Japan achieved stunning victories across Asia and the Pacific. Its forces captured Hong Kong, Malaya, the Philippines, the Dutch East Indies, and Burma with speed and coordination. These offensives seized vital resources and dealt heavy blows to Allied morale.But the rapid expansion soon exposed deep logistical problems. Japan didn’t have enough ships or infrastructure to support its troops across such a wide area. Supply lines became overextended, and fuel and ammunition shortages grew worse. As Allied forces regrouped, Japanese soldiers in distant garrisons faced dwindling supplies and limited reinforcements. Their swift victory gave Japan a vast empire, but not the means to sustain it.

card_event_volunteer_corps_home.name: card_event_volunteer_corps_home
card_event_volunteer_corps_home.title: VOLUNTEER CORPS
card_event_volunteer_corps_home.text: Remove a unit from the battlefield until the end of turn.
card_event_volunteer_corps_home.flavorText: In 1945, with defeat looming, Japan mobilized its civilian population in an unprecedented effort to resist an expected Allied invasion. This last-ditch strategy led to the formation of the Volunteer Fighting Corps, or Kokumin Giyū Sentōtai. It was the Japanese equivalent of Germany’s Volkssturm, intended to bolster homeland defense through civilian militias. Initially established in March 1945 as unarmed civil defense units focused on firefighting and evacuation, the corps soon evolved into a militarized force. By June, a new law authorized prefectural governors to conscript nearly all able-bodied men aged 15 to 60 and unmarried women aged 17 to 40. Though training and weapons were often scarce, some units practiced basic combat and fulfilled support roles like building fortifications and transporting supplies. Commanders were usually retired officers or civilians with military experience. These hastily assembled militias never saw combat due to Japan's surrender in August 1945. Still, their formation reflected the desperate state of the empire in its final months and the extent to which it was prepared to sacrifice its civilian population in defense of the home islands.

card_event_way_of_subjects.name: card_event_way_of_subjects
card_event_way_of_subjects.title: WAY OF SUBJECTS
card_event_way_of_subjects.text: All Japanese cards in your deck get Bond and "Your HQ gets +1 defense when you play this card."
card_event_way_of_subjects.flavorText: Shinmin no Michi (The Way of Subjects) was a political guide published by Japan’s Ministry of Education in 1941. It was used in schools and the military to promote loyalty to the Emperor and support for Japan’s war efforts. The text claimed Japan was a divine nation with a duty to lead Asia and resist Western influence. It rejected ideas like liberalism, communism and individualism, calling them dangerous to national unity. Instead, it taught that people should obey the Emperor, respect their parents, and put the nation above themselves. The message was clear: every citizen’s role was to serve the Emperor and the country without question. Shinmin no Michi was a key part of Japan’s wartime propaganda, used to shape public thinking and justify military expansion during WWII.

card_unit_106th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_106th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_106th_infantry_regiment.title: 106th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_106th_infantry_regiment.text:
Deployment: Deal 1 damage to an enemy.
Destruction: If it's the enemy turn, add a copy to your hand.
card_unit_106th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 106th Infantry Regiment was part of the Japanese 49th Division, an infantry formation of the Imperial Japanese Army established on 6 January 1944 in Seoul. The division was formed using troops from the 64th Infantry Brigade and the headquarters of the 20th Division. It was known as the “Wolf Division”, and its personnel included around 2% of Korean locals. In May 1944, the 49th Division was assigned to the Burma Area Army and sent to reinforce Japanese positions in Burma. The deployment was costly: two transport ships were sunk en route, causing around 1,600 deaths. Once in Burma, the division was split across various fronts. The 106th Infantry Regiment, along with the divisional headquarters and artillery units, was involved in fierce battles to retake the critical communications hub of Meiktila in March 1945. Despite determined counterattacks, their efforts failed due to poor coordination with other Japanese units, and they suffered heavy casualties. Following the failed Meiktila offensive, the remnants of the division participated in defensive actions during the Battle of the Sittang Bend and were still holding positions on the Sittang River when Japan surrendered in August 1945.

card_unit_151st_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_151st_infantry_regiment
card_unit_151st_infantry_regiment.title: 151st INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_151st_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Develop AMPHIBIOUS ASSAULT, EXPANSION or FOR PROSPERITY.
card_unit_151st_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 151st Infantry Regiment was part of the Imperial Japanese Army's 53rd Division, which was activated in 1941 and nicknamed the “Peace Division.” Originally raised in Kyoto, the division's troops came from several nearby prefectures. Initially held in reserve, it was deployed to Southeast Asia in late 1943, moving through Taiwan and Saigon before arriving in Burma in May 1944. There, the 53rd Division joined the Japanese 33rd Army in the defense of northern Burma. In June, the 153rd Infantry Regiment was detached and nearly destroyed during the Battle of Imphal. The rest of the division fought bitterly against British Chindit forces near Indaw and later in the battle for Mogaung, suffering 1,600 casualties in that engagement alone. In early 1945, the division was drawn into the fighting around Meiktila and Mandalay. Though some regiments supported other Japanese units, the main force attempted to hold ground near Pyawbwe but was overrun by Allied tanks. The division endured heavy losses again at the Sittang Bend and finally ceased fighting on August 17, 1945, after Japan’s surrender.

card_unit_211th_tokyo.name: card_unit_211th_tokyo
card_unit_211th_tokyo.title: 211th TOKYO
card_unit_211th_tokyo.flavorText: The 211th Infantry Regiment was part of the Imperial Japanese Army's 32nd Division, which was formed in April 1939. Initially based in Kyoto, the division was organized as a standard triangular infantry division and drew many of its troops from the Kansai region. The 32nd Division was first deployed to China during the Second Sino-Japanese War. There, it served under the 11th Army and participated in the Battle of Zaoyang-Yichang in 1940. After returning to Japan, the division was later sent to the Pacific theater as the war expanded. In 1944, it was assigned to the defense of the Philippines, particularly on the island of Leyte. There, it became part of the Japanese 35th Army. During the Battle of Leyte, the 32nd Division was heavily engaged and suffered devastating losses while attempting to resist the American landings. Cut off and outnumbered, it was gradually destroyed in the mountainous heart of the island. Disease, hunger, and lack of supplies took a greater toll than combat. Very few soldiers of the division survived the campaign. The 32nd Division's experience in Leyte was typical of many Japanese units late in the war: isolated, under-supplied, and ordered to fight to the end. Its destruction marked one of many costly defeats for Japan in the Philippines.

card_unit_73rd_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_73rd_infantry_regiment
card_unit_73rd_infantry_regiment.title: 73rd INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_73rd_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Trigger the destruction effects of all friendly units destroyed since the start of your last turn.
card_unit_73rd_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 73rd Infantry Regiment was part of the 19th Division, an Imperial Japanese Army unit established in 1915 as a permanent garrison force in Korea. Headquartered at Ranam in North Hamgyong Province, the division initially faced challenges from disease and limited resources, delaying its full operational readiness until 1918. Known as the “Tiger Division”, it remained stationed in the region to guard the Empire’s northeastern frontier. In 1938, the division engaged Soviet forces in the Battle of Lake Khasan. This brief but intense clash near the Korean-Soviet border resulted in over 1,400 casualties for the division in less than a week. Following the battle, it returned to garrison duties in Korea. However, as Japan’s position in the Pacific deteriorated, the 19th Division was transferred to the Philippines in late 1944 under the Fourteenth Area Army. Deployed to defend Luzon’s mountainous interior against advancing US forces, the division was virtually annihilated by early 1945, ceasing to function as a coherent unit.

card_unit_9th_guards_regiment.name: card_unit_9th_guards_regiment
card_unit_9th_guards_regiment.title: 9th GUARDS REGIMENT
card_unit_9th_guards_regiment.text: Destruction: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ, give yours +2 defense.
card_unit_9th_guards_regiment.flavorText: Formed in 1944, the 9th Guards Regiment belonged to the 3rd Guards Division, one of the last Imperial Japanese Army units raised for homeland defense. Alongside the 8th and 10th Guards Regiments, it was composed of elite troops drawn from Japan’s prestigious Imperial Guard. Unlike earlier guards divisions that served in overseas campaigns, the 3rd Guards Division was never deployed abroad. Instead, it was tasked with protecting the Japanese home islands as the threat of Allied invasion grew in 1945. Stationed within Japan’s borders, the 9th Guards Regiment spent its brief existence preparing for a final stand. It did not see combat before Japan’s surrender in August 1945. Despite its short service and lack of battlefield experience, the regiment’s formation reflected the desperation of Japan during the final months of the war, when even elite units were kept in reserve to face potential landings on the mainland. The division was disbanded following the end of the war. As with other guards formations, the 9th Guards Regiment retained a ceremonial and symbolic association with the Emperor, though its role in the war remained limited to defensive preparations.

card_unit_japan_ki_67_peggy.name: card_unit_japan_ki_67_peggy
card_unit_japan_ki_67_peggy.title: Ki-67 PEGGY
card_unit_japan_ki_67_peggy.text: Deployment: Remove an enemy unit that has 3 or less attack.
card_unit_japan_ki_67_peggy.flavorText: The Mitsubishi Ki-67 Hiryū, codenamed "Peggy" by the Allies, was a twin-engine medium bomber introduced by Japan in 1944. Designed to replace the aging Nakajima Ki-49, the Ki-67 was highly maneuverable and well-armored, a rarity among Japanese aircraft of WWII. It featured self-sealing fuel tanks and could survive significant battle damage, allowing it to dive-bomb and perform low-level escape maneuvers. Powered by two 1,900 hp radial engines, it reached speeds of up to 537 km/h and carried a bomb load of 1,070 kg internally. It was equipped with 12.7 mm and 20 mm defensive guns and saw action across China, Okinawa, French Indochina and the Mariana Islands. A total of 767 units were built, with many deployed against US fleets and airbases in the final stages of the war. Some were modified for suicide missions, including the Sakura-dan variant which carried two 800 kg bombs. Some variants such as night fighters and anti-submarine aircraft were also developed. Its durability and agility made it one of Japan's most capable twin-engine bombers of WWII.

card_unit_kanazawa_regiment.name: card_unit_kanazawa_regiment
card_unit_kanazawa_regiment.title: KANAZAWA REGIMENT
card_unit_kanazawa_regiment.text: When an undestroyed unit leaves the battlefield, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ, give yours +2 defense.
card_unit_kanazawa_regiment.flavorText: The 283rd Infantry regiment (Kanazawa) belonged to the 128th Division, an infantry formation created by the Imperial Japanese Army in January 1945 as Japan braced for invasion. The division was assembled during the final stage of the war, with its regiments, including the 283rd Regiment, drawn from the Toyama region. Initially tasked with defending the Japanese coastline, the division was soon redirected to the Asian mainland. In August 1945, the 128th Division was stationed in Manchuria under the command of the Kwantung Army when the Soviet Union launched a massive invasion. During this brief but intense campaign, the division faced overwhelming Soviet armored and air assaults. Despite being under-equipped and hastily organized, units like the Kanazawa Regiment attempted to resist the Soviet advance across northeastern Manchuria. The fighting was short-lived. Japan surrendered within days of the Soviet attack, and the 128th Division ceased operations soon after. Many of its soldiers were taken prisoner and interned in Soviet labor camps. Though formed late and given little time to prepare, the division saw real combat in the final hours of Japan’s war effort.

card_unit_kawasaki_ki_10.name: card_unit_kawasaki_ki_10
card_unit_kawasaki_ki_10.title: KAWASAKI Ki-10
card_unit_kawasaki_ki_10.text: Gets +1 attack until end of turn after you attack with a Japanese unit.
card_unit_kawasaki_ki_10.flavorText: The Kawasaki Ki-10 was the last biplane fighter used by the Imperial Japanese Army. Designed by Takeo Doi, it entered service in 1935 and served during Japan’s early campaigns in China. A total of 588 units were produced. Though technically outdated compared to contemporary monoplanes, the Army favored the Ki-10 for its agility and handling, especially in dogfighting. The aircraft featured unequal-span biplane wings with a fabric-covered metal frame and was powered by an 850 hp Kawasaki Ha9-IIa V-12 engine. It was armed with two forward-firing 7.7 mm Type 89 machine guns and could reach a top speed of 400 km/h. Several variants were developed, with the Ki-10-II offering aerodynamic improvements and a slightly modified engine. In combat, the Ki-10 saw action in Manchukuo and during the early stages of the Second Sino-Japanese War. It was involved in escort and interception missions, notably during bombing raids over Taiyuan in 1937. It became largely obsolete by 1939, and was replaced by the more modern Ki-27, though the Ki-10 remained in service for training and patrol duties until early 1942.

card_unit_ki_61_i_tei.name: card_unit_ki_61_i_tei
card_unit_ki_61_i_tei.title: Ki-61-I-TEI
card_unit_ki_61_i_tei.text: Destruction: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ, give yours +2 defense.
card_unit_ki_61_i_tei.flavorText: The Ki-61-I-TEI was a late-war variant of the Kawasaki Ki-61 Hien fighter, distinguished primarily by its upgraded armament and design adjustments aimed at improving firepower and maintainability. Introduced in 1944, the TEI model replaced the two 12.7 mm Ho-103 machine guns in the wings with 20 mm Ho-5 cannons, giving it significantly more destructive capability. The Ho-5, a Japanese design derived from the American Browning M2, was relatively light and compact but offered a high rate of fire and a heavier shell. This made the TEI version more effective against increasingly durable Allied aircraft. The TEI retained the Ki-61’s inline, liquid-cooled Ha-40 engine, a licensed version of the German DB 601. While the engine was advanced for a Japanese fighter, it remained maintenance-heavy and vulnerable in combat conditions. The aircraft’s structure, which included self-sealing fuel tanks and some pilot armor, reflected a growing Japanese concern for survivability by 1944. Despite improvements, production and deployment of the TEI variant were limited due to engine shortages and Allied bombing of Japanese industrial centers. It saw service defending the Japanese home islands and in units deployed to Okinawa and the Philippines. Roughly 1,380 Ki-61-I-TEI aircraft were produced before production ended.

card_unit_kofu_regiment.name: card_unit_kofu_regiment
card_unit_kofu_regiment.title: KŌFU REGIMENT
card_unit_kofu_regiment.text: Destruction: Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ, give yours +1 defense.
card_unit_kofu_regiment.flavorText: The Kōfu Regiment was part of the 201st Division, one of the final infantry divisions raised by the Imperial Japanese Army in 1945. Known as the Musashi Division, it was organized as a triangular division and stationed in the Kantō region of Honshu as part of the 36th Army. Its creation was a direct response to the US landings on Okinawa and to Japan's growing fear of an Allied invasion of the home islands. The division’s 501st Infantry Regiment was based in Zama, while the 502nd and 503rd Regiments were stationed in Musashimurayama, close to Tokyo. Other units deployed near Gotemba, forming a second defensive perimeter around the capital. The division’s task was to reinforce inland defenses against an anticipated amphibious assault, if the Allied launched Operation Downfall. Although fully mobilized, the 201st Division never engaged in combat. Japan surrendered before Allied forces landed on the main islands, leaving the division’s soldiers, including those of the Kōfu Regiment, untested in battle. Nevertheless, their deployment reflected Japan’s urgent shift to homeland defense during the final months of the war.

card_unit_oita_regiment.name: card_unit_oita_regiment
card_unit_oita_regiment.title: ŌITA REGIMENT
card_unit_oita_regiment.text: Gets +1+1 when a Destruction effect triggers.
card_unit_oita_regiment.flavorText: The 47th Infantry Regiment was part of the 48th Division, one of the most mobile and combat ready formations in the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. Established in 1940, the 48th Division was formed from existing garrison and line units, including the 47th Regiment, which had become available after the reorganization of the 6th Division. In 1941, it was mechanized alongside the 5th Division, an uncommon upgrade that reflected its planned role in early Pacific campaigns. The division deployed to the Philippines in December 1941 as part of the 14th Army. It landed at Lingayen Gulf and advanced rapidly, capturing Manila in early January 1942. Soon afterward, the division was sent to Java in the Dutch East Indies, where it seized Surabaya and its critical oil infrastructure on 7 March 1942.The 48th was then transferred to Timor, where it fought against entrenched Australian and Dutch commandos in a difficult guerrilla campaign. Despite local resistance and challenging terrain, the Japanese secured the island by the end of 1942. Unlike many other units that were redeployed, the 48th Division remained on Timor as a garrison force for the remainder of the war, ultimately surrendering to Allied forces on the island in August 1945.

card_unit_sapporo_regiment.name: card_unit_sapporo_regiment
card_unit_sapporo_regiment.title: SAPPORO REGIMENT
card_unit_sapporo_regiment.text: Gain +1+1 and a random combat keyword when an undestroyed unit leaves the battlefield.
card_unit_sapporo_regiment.flavorText: The 25th Infantry Regiment (Sapporo) was part of the 88th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army, which was activated in February 1945 and based in Toyohara on Sakhalin island. This late-war triangular division was formed around the Karafuto Mixed Brigade and tasked with defending Japan’s northernmost territories in anticipation of a Soviet attack. The 88th Division was assigned to the 5th Area Army. Its main combat action came during the Soviet invasion of the South of Sakhalin in August 1945. The Soviet offensive began with the shelling of Poronaysk on 9 August. The division held firm in its defensive positions for several days. The 125th Infantry Regiment, in particular, put up strong resistance. Japanese defenders claimed to have inflicted heavy Soviet casualties and destroyed numerous tanks, though they also suffered over 500 dead. Despite the order to surrender after the fall of Poronaysk on 22 August, hostilities continued. Some sources suggest confusion from alleged "secret orders" may have led to continued resistance. In total, more than 18,000 troops from the 88th Division and the Koton Fortified Region were captured and sent to labor camps in Siberia or Sakhalin.

card_unit_storm_division.name: card_unit_storm_division
card_unit_storm_division.title: STORM DIVISION
card_unit_storm_division.text: Your other Japanese units have +2 attack.
card_unit_storm_division.flavorText: The 116th Division, known as the "Storm Division," was formed in Kyoto in May 1938 from the headquarters of the 16th Division. It was classified as a B-class square division and initially assigned to the Central China Expeditionary Army. After landing in Shanghai in June, it advanced through Anqing to take part in the Battle of Wuhan. Elements of the division later fought at Nanchang in early 1939. Following the Doolittle Raid in 1942, the division was involved in the Zhejiang-Jiangxi campaign. That same year, it was reorganized as a triangular division after the transfer of its 138th Infantry Regiment. It took part in the Battle of Changde in 1943 and was heavily engaged during the Battle of Changsha in 1944. As part of Operation Ichi-Go, the Storm Division participated in the prolonged siege of Hengyang, where it suffered major losses during a 40-day assault before capturing the city. In 1945, it took part in the Battle of West Henan–North Hubei with the support of the 86th Independent Mixed Brigade. The division was stationed in Hengyang when Japan surrendered in August 1945.

card_event_banzai_charge.name: card_event_banzai_charge
card_event_banzai_charge.title: BANZAI
card_event_banzai_charge.text: Destroy all units with 4 attack or less. End your turn.
card_event_banzai_charge.flavorText: The term "Banzai charge" was used by the Allies to describe human-wave attacks employed by Japanese troops as a last resort during the Pacific War. Japanese commanders typically ordered such attacks only when they believed defeat was inevitable. A notable example occurred at the Battle of Attu in 1943, when Japanese troops launched a final charge after their ammunition and supplies were nearly exhausted; almost all of them were killed.

card_event_calm_before_the_storm.name: card_event_calm_before_the_storm
card_event_calm_before_the_storm.title: CALM BEFORE THE STORM
card_event_calm_before_the_storm.text: Give your units +3+1. End your turn.
card_event_calm_before_the_storm.flavorText: During the course of the war Japan conquered other Asian nations, pursuing its own imperialist objectives for economic and military dominance in Asia. However, when the US embargoed oil and steel to Japan due to the aggression in China, their war aims were to grab control of necessary resources in the Southwest Pacific, particularly Borneo and Indonesia. However, Japan knew that they couldn’t get to these resources without US interference, because standing in the way of Japan and these resources was the Philippines, which was in US possession. Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor was an attempt to cripple the US fleet in the Pacific, which would buy Japan the time it needed to seize the resources it needed and consolidate their conquests in Asia before the US could respond. Japan was very much aware that they couldn’t win a long war against the US, but they believed that swift defeat of their fleet in the Pacific would force them to negotiate for peace. Little did they know.

card_event_dawn_operations.name: card_event_dawn_operations
card_event_dawn_operations.title: DAWN OPERATIONS
card_event_dawn_operations.text: Your air units operate for free this turn. Lose a kredit slot.
card_event_dawn_operations.flavorText: Throughout military history the wee hours of the day has been the preferred time to launch an attack. This is because it gives the attackers enough daylight to locate and navigate among the enemy troops, and although every capable commander expects to be attacked at dawn, it can give the element of surprise since the defenders may still be in a slumber or ill prepared. There is no coincidence that WWII began at the crack of dawn, at 5:20 am (Polish time), Friday, September 1, 1939.

card_event_diversion.name: card_event_diversion
card_event_diversion.title: DIVERSION
card_event_diversion.text: Give target non-Guard ground unit in a support line Smokescreen. Draw a card.
card_event_diversion.flavorText: Japanese tank tactics during WWII focused mainly on infantry support roles, and although they had a large tank force in 1940, they lacked medium and heavy tanks. And as the war prolonged they didn’t have the industrial capacity or technology to keep up with the competition. They had enough light tanks that served their purposes, they could easily be transported and used in rough terrain. These tanks were either used independently or in infantry support roles, but they were usually outclassed in tank vs tank combat and were easy targets for anti-tank weapons.

card_event_new_doctrine.name: card_event_new_doctrine
card_event_new_doctrine.title: NEW DOCTRINE
card_event_new_doctrine.text: Ignore "Cannot attack the enemy HQ" on target unit.
card_event_new_doctrine.flavorText: In 1945 the Japanese were losing control in the Pacific and their tactic was to take up defensive positions in the islands of the Pacific. In Iwo Jima and Okinawa their tactic was to build an elaborate system of underground tunnels and heavily fortified bunkers, and instead of attacking the Americans when they landed on the beaches, they did their best to conceal their positions, both from land and air. The Japanese knew that these battles could not be won, but their goal was to slow down the American advance and bleed their forces, giving them time to build up defenses in the Japanese homeland where they believed a final and decisive battle would take place. These tactics were effective and resulted in two of the bloodiest battles of the war, which nevertheless ended with the total annihilation of the defending forces.

card_event_redeployment.name: card_event_redeployment
card_event_redeployment.title: REDEPLOYMENT
card_event_redeployment.text: Shuffle all cards in your hand into your deck, then draw that many cards plus one.
card_event_redeployment.flavorText: In 1945 the Japanese planned Operation Ketsu-Go, which was an attempt to make a last stand defending the home islands and fight to the bitter end. The Japanese High Command planned to transfer many troops and munitions from the Asian continent and to the home islands, but this proved very difficult due to constant American assaults and followed by a drastic decrease in manpower. Getting the munition ready also proved to be a serious problem due to shortages of resources and technology. For this last stand the Japanese had reserved around 5000 conventional aircraft, 5,500 kamikaze aircraft, 1,300 suicide submarines, hundreds of piloted bombs, manned torpedoes, and variaty of suicide vehicles. In manpower they had raised 56 divisions and 38 brigades, involving around 2,000,000 men. However, the imminent American invasion never took place. Following the detonation of atomic bombs over the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Japanese surrendered to the Allies on August 15, 1945.

card_event_rule_the_skies.name: card_event_rule_the_skies
card_event_rule_the_skies.title: RULE THE SKIES
card_event_rule_the_skies.text: The enemy HQ gets: "If this HQ has taken 3+ damage this turn, give your air units +1+1."
card_event_rule_the_skies.flavorText: Although the Japanese did rule the skies over their conquered territories in the beginning of the war, their lead was short lived when the Allied forces gained foothold in the Pacific and had consistent land bases from where they could launch their air attacks from. The Japanese air doctrine was focused on offensive operations and this did not change throughout the war, even when they were on the defensive. On top of that they had insufficient numbers of aircraft, too few aircrews, no radar, and not enough fuel to keep their aircraft constantly in the air to be on the lookout enemy aircraft.

card_event_shock_attack.name: card_event_shock_attack
card_event_shock_attack.title: SHOCK ATTACK
card_event_shock_attack.text: When a friendly unit loses Smokescreen this turn it gets +2+2
card_event_shock_attack.flavorText: A shock attack, or shock tactics, is an offensive maneuver where the goal is to put the enemy under psychological pressure with a fully committed attack that will shock or surprise the defenders, with the aim of causing them to retreat. The Imperial Japanese Army was known for its use of human wave attacks during WWII, and the success of these attacks early in the war made them a standard tactic of their army. The Allied forces would quickly adapt to these tactics and their superior firepower and manpower would often result in heavy Japanese casualties and the failure of the attacks.

card_unit_54th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_54th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_54th_infantry_regiment.title: 54th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_54th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 54th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 17 Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. During the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1938 the division participated in the Battle of Wuhan, and afterwards it stayed there on garrison duty as part of the China Expeditionary Army. In 1943 elements of the division, including the 54th Regiment, were transferred to New Britain in the Islands Region of Papua New Guinea, where it defended against the invading Allied forces. The remaining survivors of the 17th Division surrendered to the Allies when the Pacific War ended in August 1945.

card_unit_aichi_b7a2.name: card_unit_aichi_b7a2
card_unit_aichi_b7a2.title: B7A2 RYUSEI
card_unit_aichi_b7a2.flavorText: The Aichi B7A Ryusei (Ryusei means "Shooting Star" in Japanese) was a Japanese carrier borne torpedo dive bomber that was produced during WWII for the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service. The B7A Ryusei was a big and powerful aircraft and was intended to be used on a new type of carrier (Taihō-class) which could handle larger aircraft. The problem was that once the B7A entered production and was ready for service in 1944, there was only one carrier modern enough to handle the aircraft: the Taihō. And to make matters worse, the Taihō carrier was sunk during the Battle of the Philippine Sea, before any of the B7A’s were embarked. After this, some of the B7A’s operated from land, but they saw limited service until the war ended in 1945. A total of 105 B7A2 Ryusei were produced, plus a handful of other variants.

card_unit_kikka_jet.name: card_unit_kikka_jet
card_unit_kikka_jet.title: KIKKA
card_unit_kikka_jet.text: Destruction: Shuffle 4 KAMIKAZE cards into your deck.
card_unit_kikka_jet.flavorText: The Nakajima Kikka, aka Kōkoku Nigō Heiki, was the first Japanese jet aircraft. It was developed late in the war for the Imperial Japanese Navy and intended for ground attacks and anti-shipping. The first flight tests took place in August 1945, and overall it performed well overall, but before it could ever be used in frontline service, the Japanese had surrendered to the Allies. The idea to develop the Kikka came after the Japanese military attaché in Germany witnessed the trials of the Messerschmitt Me 262 in 1942, so it’s no coincidence that the design is similar.

card_unit_ki_42_ii_ko.name: card_unit_ki_42_ii_ko
card_unit_ki_42_ii_ko.title: Ki-43-IIb OTSU
card_unit_ki_42_ii_ko.text: Has +2 attack on your turn if the enemy controls no air units.
card_unit_ki_42_ii_ko.flavorText: The Ki-43-IIb Otsu was a variant of the Nakajima Ki-43 Hayabusa, a Japanese fighter aircraft that was in service of the Imperial Japanese Army Air Force between 1941-1945. The Allied reporting name for the Ki-43 was “Oscar” and it soon earned a reputation for being a very good fighter, but the first variants lacked both armor and self sealing fuel tank which caused it to catch fire easily or break after a few hits. Nevertheless the aircraft gained air superiority early in the war, but the tables turned with the introduction of newer Allied aircraft such as the Hellcat, P-51 Mustang, F4U Corsair and Spitfire. The Ki-43-IIb variant first entered service in 1942 and was very similar to the Ki-43-IIa variant, which differed from its predecessors in many ways. It had armor protection installed for the cockpit, a self-sealing fuel tank, smaller wingspan and the capability of carrying 500 kg of bombs. The Ki-43-IIb had minor upgrades such as new radio equipment and the oil cooler and the carburettor intake were also modified. A total of 5,919 K-43’s that were produced throughout the war, including variants.

card_unit_matsue_regiment.name: card_unit_matsue_regiment
card_unit_matsue_regiment.title: MATSUE REGIMENT
card_unit_matsue_regiment.text: Deployment: Choose and discard a card. Gain attack equal to the cost.
card_unit_matsue_regiment.flavorText: The 63rd Infantry Regiment (Matsue) was a unit of the 10th Division (codenamed Iron Division) of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division fought in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905), the Second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945) and finally in the Pacific War (1941-1945). The division saw extensive combat in China from 1937 to 1944, before being transferred to Luzon in the Philippines in order to defend against the US advance in the Pacific. The division was annihilated in the Battle of Luzon in 1945 where it fought under the command of Japanese Fourteenth Area Army.

card_unit_nara_regiment.name: card_unit_nara_regiment
card_unit_nara_regiment.title: NARA REGIMENT
card_unit_nara_regiment.text: Ignore "Cannot attack the enemy HQ" on your units.
card_unit_nara_regiment.flavorText: The Nara Regiment was a unit of the 29th Division (call sign Thunder Division) of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division was active from 1941-1945 and was to begin with part of the Kwantung Army and tasked with the defense of the Liaoyang area in Manchukuo state. In early March 1944 the division was assigned to the 31st Army and sent to Guam to participate in the defense of the island together with the 48th Independent Mixed Brigade. From 21 July to 10 August 1944 the division participated in the Battle of Guam which ended in an American victory and the surrender of the remaining Japanese forces, although a few Japanese soldiers held out in the jungle for much longer. One of them, Sergeant Shoichi Yokoi, surrendered in 1972 after living alone in a cave for 27 years.

card_unit_p1y2_kasho.name: card_unit_p1y2_kasho
card_unit_p1y2_kasho.title: P1Y1 MODEL 11
card_unit_p1y2_kasho.text: When a friendly unit loses Smokescreen it gets +2+2.
card_unit_p1y2_kasho.flavorText: The Yokosuka P1Y Ginga was a Japanese land based medium bomber that was developed for the Japanese Imperial Navy and used during WWII. The P1Y’s came into service in 1944 and were intended as a replacement for the G4M “Betty” bombers, but due to problems in production the transition had just begun when the war ended. A total of 1,002 P1Y aircraft were built by Nakajima and Kawanishi aircraft companies and the first aircraft to reach the front were of the P1Y1 Ginga Model 11 series. Most of the aircraft built were bombers, but 97 night fighter variants were also built, the P1Y2-S Kyokko,  but due to poor performance they were converted into the P1Y2 Ginga bomber variant. The Allied reporting name for the P1Y was “Frances”.

card_location_baguio.name: card_location_baguio
card_location_baguio.title: BAGUIO
card_location_baguio.text: The Battle of Baguio in 1945 involved Japanese and Allied forces.
card_location_baguio.flavorText: The Battle of Baguio took place from March to April 1945 as part of the Philippines Campaign during WWII. Japanese forces, led by General Tomoyuki Yamashita, fortified Baguio’s mountainous terrain to make a final defensive stand. US and Filipino forces, including the 33rd Infantry Division and local guerrilla fighters, pushed through intense Japanese resistance, using artillery and air strikes to break through the entrenched positions. Despite challenging terrain and a determined Japanese defense, Allied forces advanced steadily, capturing key positions and driving the Japanese back. By late April 1945, Baguio was under Allied control, marking a significant victory in the Philippines Campaign.

card_location_changchun.name: card_location_changchun
card_location_changchun.title: TRUK
card_location_changchun.text: TRUK atoll was the main Japanese naval base in the South Pacific during WWII.
card_location_changchun.flavorText: The atoll of Truk in the Caroline Islands was used as a Japanese forward naval base prior to the war and during WWII it became the main Japanese naval base in the South Pacific. A large portion of the Japanese fleet was based in Truk and it hosted five airfields, several seaplane and torpedo boat bases, repair facilities and a radar station. In February 1944 the Truk base was destroyed by the American airpower and was cut off for the remainder of the war.

card_location_manila.name: card_location_manila
card_location_manila.title: MANILA
card_location_manila.text: Manila is the capital of the Philippines, captured by Japan in 1942.
card_location_manila.flavorText: Manila, the capital of the Philippines, was captured by the Imperial Japanese forces in January 1942. Despite having lost the capital, the US-Filipino forces continued to resist up until The Battle of Corregidor that took place in May 1942. The decisive battle is named after Corregidor Island where the US-Filipino forces made a last attempt to defend the Bay of Manila in an old Spanish fortress. Shortly after the fall of Corregidor the Commander of Allied forces in the Philippines announced their surrender over the radio under Japanese censor. The Philippines Campaign, (December 1941 - May 1942) is considered one of the worst military defeats of the US and marked the beginning of the Japanese occupation of the Philippines, which lasted over 3 years, or until it was recaptured by the Allies in 1945.

card_location_rangoon.name: card_location_rangoon
card_location_rangoon.title: RANGOON
card_location_rangoon.text: Rangoon, capital of the British colony of Burma, was captured by Japan in March 1942.
card_location_rangoon.flavorText: Rangoon, also known as Yangon, is the capital of the Yangon region and the largest city of Burma (also known as Myanmar).
