Burma was under British rule from from 1885 to 1948, but during WWII it became a major battleground between the Axis and Allied powers. Japan, in coalition with the Burma Independence Army, took control of Burma in 1942 and stayed in power until the Allied forces launched a series of offensives in 1944, and after intense fighting they managed to end the Japanese occupation. Many Burmese fought on the Allied side with the British Burma Army, and many that initially fought on the side of Japan switched allegiance to the Allied side as the war progressed.

card_location_ai_japan_unlock1.name: card_location_ai_japan_unlock1
card_location_ai_japan_unlock1.title: CHERBOURG
card_location_ai_japan_unlock1.text: Cherbourg was an important harbor for the Allies after D-Day.
card_location_ai_japan_unlock1.flavorText: Cherbourg was an important harbor for the Allies after D-Day. The Battle of Cherbourg was part of the Battle of Normandy during World War II. It was fought immediately after the successful Allied landings on June 6, 1944. Allied troops, predominantly American, isolated and captured the fortified port, which was considered vital to the campaign in Western Europe, in a hard-fought, month-long campaign.

card_event_dug_in.name: card_event_dug_in
card_event_dug_in.title: DUG IN
card_event_dug_in.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. Shuffle SHIFTING DOCTRINE into your deck.
card_event_dug_in.flavorText: As US forces advanced across the Pacific, Japanese defenders adapted with increasingly complex fortifications. Early in the war, Japanese doctrine stressed offensive action, but by 1943 the realities of Allied firepower and supply disruption forced a shift to static defense. On islands like Tarawa, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa, Japanese troops dug deep and built strong. Lacking concrete and steel, they turned to local materials. Coconut logs, coral blocks, oil barrels and sand-filled crates became bunkers, rifle pits and anti-tank obstacles. Positions were camouflaged with palm fronds or buried. On Iwo Jima, over 16 miles of tunnels connected hidden artillery and machine gun nests. Reverse slope defenses and dummy installations confused Allied spotters. The aim was not to stop landings at the beach but to kill the enemy after they landed. Each position was built to absorb artillery and protect crews from grenades, with overlapping fields of fire and concealed exits. These defenses stalled Allied attacks for weeks, inflicting high casualties. At Okinawa, over 60 miles of tunnels housed an entire army underground. Japan's dug-in strategy turned small islands into fortresses and made every yard of ground costly.

card_event_engage_range.name: card_event_engage_range
card_event_engage_range.title: ENGAGE AT RANGE
card_event_engage_range.text: Deal 2 damage to an enemy. Convert into ENGAGE UP CLOSE if put from your hand to deck.
card_event_engage_range.flavorText: The Type 93 torpedo, nicknamed the “Long Lance”, was a powerful and advanced Japanese naval torpedo used during WWII. It was introduced in the 1930s and was fueled by compressed oxygen, giving it a much longer range, higher speed, and bigger warhead than Allied torpedoes of the time. With a range of up to 40 km (25 miles) and a warhead weighing around 490 kg (over 1,000 lbs), the Type 93 was extremely deadly. It could travel at high speeds with minimal wake, making it hard to detect. It was mostly launched from Japanese cruisers and destroyers, giving them a significant edge in night battles. The torpedo was especially effective early in the war, contributing to Japanese victories at Savo Island, Guadalcanal, and other Pacific battles. However, its long-range capabilities were not always fully used due to poor Japanese communication and targeting systems. Despite these flaws, the Type 93 was the most advanced torpedo of its time and a major threat to Allied naval forces throughout the war.

card_event_ijn_akagi.name: card_event_ijn_akagi
card_event_ijn_akagi.title: IJN AKAGI
card_event_ijn_akagi.text: Shuffle your hand into your deck, then draw 3 cards. They cost 2 less to play this turn.
card_event_ijn_akagi.flavorText: The Japanese aircraft carrier Akagi was one of the Imperial Japanese Navy’s most important carriers in the early stages of WWII. Originally laid down as a battlecruiser, she was converted into an aircraft carrier and commissioned in 1927. Akagi became the flagship of the First Air Fleet and played a key role in developing Japan’s carrier strike doctrine, emphasizing coordinated mass air attacks. She was central to Japan’s early successes in the Pacific, in particular the attack on Pearl Harbor and operations in the Philippines, Rabaul, and the Indian Ocean. Akagi carried over 60 aircraft and had a unique three-tiered flight deck early in her career, later rebuilt into a more conventional full-length flight deck. Her powerful air group helped Japan dominate the seas early in the war. However, her success ended at the Battle of Midway in June 1942. While caught off guard by an American carrier aircraft, the Akagi was hit by bombs that caused uncontrollable fires and as a result she was eventually scuttled by Japanese destroyers. Akagi’s loss at Midway marked a turning point in the Pacific War, symbolizing the beginning of Japan’s decline in naval air power.

card_event_mikura.name: card_event_mikura
card_event_mikura.title: IJN MIKURA
card_event_mikura.text: Pin target unit. At the end of turn, draw an IJN MIKURA from your deck.
card_event_mikura.flavorText: The Mikura was the lead ship of the Mikura-class escort ships used by the Imperial Japanese Navy during WWII. She was launched in 1943 and designed for convoy escort and anti-submarine warfare. The Mikura was armed with depth charges, anti-aircraft guns and sonar equipment, and with her sister ships she was part of Japan’s effort to defend vital shipping lanes. She mainly operated around Japan and the East China Sea where she escorted supply convoys and hunted Allied submarines. Mikura was involved in several anti-submarine actions, claiming some successes, though records on confirmed kills are unclear. Like many Japanese escorts, she often faced overwhelming American submarine and air attacks, and on March 28, 1945, Mikura was sunk by US aircraft south of the Japanese Island Kyushu. Overall, Mikura was part of Japan’s late-war attempt to improve convoy protection, but despite her design and purpose, she operated under increasingly difficult conditions with limited impact on the overall course of the war.

card_event_shifting_doctrine.name: card_event_shifting_doctrine
card_event_shifting_doctrine.title: SHIFTING DOCTRINE
card_event_shifting_doctrine.text: Shuffle a random card in hand into your deck, then draw 2 cards.
card_event_shifting_doctrine.flavorText: As Allied forces reversed Japan’s early wartime gains, Japanese military strategy shifted dramatically after 1942. Following defeats at Midway and Guadalcanal, Japan abandoned offensive campaigns and adopted defensive attrition tactics, fortifying islands like Saipan and Iwo Jima to inflict heavy casualties. The desperate introduction of kamikaze attacks during the Battle of Leyte Gulf marked a turn to sacrificial warfare. On land, mobile tactics were replaced by last-stand defenses, with troops dug into caves, tunnels, and bunkers instead of fighting in open terrain. At sea, Japan resorted to decoy fleets, midget submarines, and asymmetric tactics as its navy weakened. Leaders like General Tadamichi Kuribayashi exemplified this approach where his defense of Iwo Jima focused on maximizing US losses rather than holding ground. The strategy no longer aimed for victory but tried to stall the American advance and pressure the Allies into a negotiated peace.

card_event_the_tide_turns.name: card_event_the_tide_turns
card_event_the_tide_turns.title: THE TIDE TURNS
card_event_the_tide_turns.text: Shuffle your hand into your deck, draw equal amount. Deal damage to all units equal to Navy cards shuffled in.
card_event_the_tide_turns.flavorText: After Japan's defeat at Midway in June 1942, the Imperial Navy's momentum in the Pacific collapsed. Four fleet carriers were lost in a single day along with hundreds of elite pilots. This disaster forced Japan to abandon its plan for a quick, decisive victory. Before Midway, naval doctrine focused on a massive showdown with the US fleet, named Kantai Kessen (English: naval fleet decisive battle). Instead, Midway turned into a trap. American codebreakers had discovered the Japanese plan and set up an ambush near Midway Atoll. Following this defeat, Japan shifted to a defensive strategy. It built new carriers like Taihō and focused on extending its island defenses. But its industrial base could not match the speed and scale of American shipbuilding. Even more critical was the loss of veteran pilots. Japan tried to speed up training programs, but the new crews lacked the skill and experience of those lost at Midway. From this point, Japan’s naval operations were mostly reactive. Midway did not just stop Japan's advance, it marked the moment when the tide of the Pacific War truly turned.

card_unit_10th_recon.name: card_unit_10th_recon
card_unit_10th_recon.title: 10th RECON
card_unit_10th_recon.text: Deployment: Choose a card in hand. Shuffle it into your deck, then draw a card.
card_unit_10th_recon.flavorText: The 10th Recon Regiment joined the Imperial Japanese Army’s 10th Division during its reorganization in 1940. The division, known as the "Iron Division," had a long history but was redirected to garrison duties in Manchukuo that year. Stationed in Jiamusi under the Kwantung Army, it guarded the Soviet border and took part in anti-partisan operations. In 1944, the division was reassigned as Japan shifted to a defensive stance in the Pacific. The 10th Division was originally slated for deployment to Taiwan but was redirected to the Philippines. On Luzon, it came under the Japanese Fourteenth Area Army and faced devastating losses during the US invasion. Its 39th Infantry Regiment distinguished itself in fierce combat, but the division was largely destroyed. Survivors fought on in guerrilla operations until Japan’s surrender in 1945, though disease and starvation took a greater toll than battle.

card_unit_3rd_kure_snlf.name: card_unit_3rd_kure_snlf
card_unit_3rd_kure_snlf.title: 3rd KURE SNLF
card_unit_3rd_kure_snlf.text: Reduce the operation cost by 1 until end of turn, when you shuffle your deck.
card_unit_3rd_kure_snlf.flavorText: The 3rd Kure Special Naval Landing Force (SNLF) was an elite naval infantry unit of the Imperial Japanese Navy, formed at the Kure Naval District. It was initially active in China during the late 1930s, but was reconstituted in 1942 to participate in key operations across the Pacific theater. In May 1942, approximately 400 troops from the 3rd Kure SNLF landed on Tulagi Island in the Solomon Islands, where they established a seaplane base and fortifications. However, on August 7, 1942, US Marines launched an assault on Tulagi, and despite fierce resistance, the Japanese garrison, including the 3rd Kure SNLF, was overwhelmed. Out of the 350 men stationed there, 307 were killed, and only a few were taken prisoner. Later that month, on August 29, 1942, elements of the 3rd Kure SNLF participated in the Battle of Milne Bay in Papua New Guinea. Under the command of Commander Minoru Yano, approximately 769 naval troops landed to support earlier Japanese forces. The operation faced strong Allied resistance, and by September 5, the Japanese were forced to evacuate after suffering significant casualties. The heavy losses at Tulagi and Milne Bay marked the decline of the 3rd Kure SNLF's combat effectiveness and the unit was disbanded soon after.

card_unit_3rd_mixed_regiment.name: card_unit_3rd_mixed_regiment
card_unit_3rd_mixed_regiment.title: 3rd MIXED REGIMENT
card_unit_3rd_mixed_regiment.text: Once per turn, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ when you shuffle your deck.
card_unit_3rd_mixed_regiment.flavorText: The 3rd Mixed Regiment was a unit of the 38th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was formed in 1939 and deployed in southern China before being redirected for operations across the Pacific and Southeast Asia. In December 1941 the 38th Division took part in the invasion of Hong Kong. It was involved in a rapid offensive launched from the mainland and played a major role in breaking British defenses on the Kowloon Peninsula. Subsequently, the division crossed the Kowloon Bay into Hong Kong Island, and after a week of intense fighting, the Allied garrison surrendered on Christmas Day. Following the fall of Hong Kong, the regiment was involved in garrison duties and regional security operations. Later, elements of the 38th Division, including the 3rd Mixed Regiment, participated in campaigns in the Dutch East Indies and the Philippines. Throughout the war the division suffered heavy casualties, and the remainder of the men capitulated following the Japanese surrender in August 1945.

card_unit_5th_sasebo_snlf.name: card_unit_5th_sasebo_snlf
card_unit_5th_sasebo_snlf.title: 5th SASEBO SNLF
card_unit_5th_sasebo_snlf.text:
Gets +1+1 when you play a Navy card.
Destruction: Shuffle your deck, then draw a card.
card_unit_5th_sasebo_snlf.flavorText: The 5th Sasebo Special Naval Landing Force (SNLF) was an elite infantry battalion of the Imperial Japanese Navy, formed at the Sasebo Naval District. As part of Japan’s marine infantry, the unit specialized in amphibious assaults and jungle warfare during WWII. In 1942, the 5th Sasebo SNLF took part in the invasion of Buna–Gona in Papua New Guinea. They landed as part of the Yokoyama Advance Force, supporting the Japanese push along the Kokoda Track toward Port Moresby. Approximately 450 troops from the unit were deployed in this operation. Later that year, during Operation Re, the 5th Sasebo SNLF participated in the Battle of Milne Bay. They were part of a 1,500-strong force that included units from the 3rd and 5th Kure SNLF and the 5th Yokosuka SNLF. The operation faced strong resistance from well-prepared Allied forces.The 5th Sasebo SNLF earned a reputation for their tenacity and discipline, often fighting to the last man. Their actions in New Guinea exemplified the aggressive tactics and high morale characteristic of Japan’s naval infantry during the early Pacific campaigns.

card_unit_gifu_regiment.name: card_unit_gifu_regiment
card_unit_gifu_regiment.title: GIFU REGIMENT
card_unit_gifu_regiment.text: Once per turn, gains Shock and you draw a card when you play a Navy card.
card_unit_gifu_regiment.flavorText: The 136th Mixed Regiment (Gifu) was part of the 43rd Division of the Imperial Japanese Army, formed in June 1943. In April 1944, the division was reorganized into a marine (mixed) division and assigned to the 31st Army. The division departed from Tateyama, in Chiba Prefecture, on May 14, 1944, and arrived in Saipan on May 19, 1944. Upon arrival, approximately 9,000 troops and 13 artillery pieces of the 43rd Division fortified positions around Mount Tapochau. They managed to add a line of trenches to existing defenses before the US invasion fleet arrived on June 13, 1944. The Battle of Saipan started the next day. The 43rd Division, alongside the 9th Armored Regiment of the 1st Tank Division, launched a counterattack and temporarily recaptured high ground around Hinashita Hill. However, US forces regained these positions shortly after. After weeks of fighting the division was reduced to four infantry battalions and a half battalion of artillery. After being denied evacuation and reinforcements the division faced imminent defeat. With approximately 4,000 men remaining, many already wounded, their commander decided to lead a final banzai charge on July 7. This assault resulted in the annihilation of the 43rd Division.

card_unit_kyoto_regiment.name: card_unit_kyoto_regiment
card_unit_kyoto_regiment.title: KYOTO REGIMENT
card_unit_kyoto_regiment.text: Deployment: Remove an enemy unit until this unit leaves the battlefield.
card_unit_kyoto_regiment.flavorText: The 51st Infantry Regiment (Kyoto) was a unit of the 15th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was established in 1905 during the Russo-Japanese War. It was disbanded in 1925 as part of military downsizing. The division was reactivated in 1938. In 1943, the 15th Division was reassigned to the 15th Army in Burma to participate in Operation U-Go, an offensive aimed at invading the British Raj. The division's objective was to cut the road between Imphal and Kohima at Kangpokpi. However, challenging terrain and logistical issues delayed their advance. The division faced stiff resistance from Allied forces, including unexpected tank assaults, leading to significant casualties. By mid-1944, it was forced to retreat after failing to achieve its objectives. In early 1945, the 15th Division, alongside the 53rd Division, was tasked with defending Mandalay against advancing Allied forces. Despite reinforcements, it was understrength and unable to hold the city. After intense fighting, the division withdrew from Mandalay in March 1945. The remnants retreated through difficult terrain back into Thailand, where they remained until Japan's surrender in August 1945.

card_unit_nakajima_b5n2.name: card_unit_nakajima_b5n2
card_unit_nakajima_b5n2.title: NAKAJIMA B5N2
card_unit_nakajima_b5n2.text: Gets +1+1 when you play a card with Intel.
card_unit_nakajima_b5n2.flavorText: The Nakajima B5N, nicknamed "Kate" by the Allies, was the Imperial Japanese Navy’s main torpedo bomber during the early years of WWII. It was first flown in 1937 and was considered modern and fast for its time. It was manned by a crew of three and had the ability to carry a torpedo or bombs. The B5N played a major role in early Japanese victories. It was used in the attack on Pearl Harbor, where it launched torpedoes and bombs against US battleships. It also saw action in battles such as the Coral Sea, Midway, and the Philippines, sinking or damaging several Allied ships. However, from 1943 the B5N had become outdated. It had poor armor and no self-sealing fuel tanks, making it vulnerable to enemy fighters and anti-aircraft fire. Despite this, Japan continued to use it due to delays in replacing it with the newer B6N “Jill”. The B5N remained in service until the end of the war, often used for training or in kamikaze roles. It was Japan’s most successful torpedo bomber during the war, largely due to its heavy use in the early campaigns.

card_unit_sabae_regiment.name: card_unit_sabae_regiment
card_unit_sabae_regiment.title: SABAE REGIMENT
card_unit_sabae_regiment.text: Once per turn, when you shuffle, distribute damage randomly to enemies equal to units in play.
card_unit_sabae_regiment.flavorText: The 136th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 109th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The 109th Division, nicknamed the "Courage Division", was formed in August 1937 and was first deployed to North China, participating in operations along the Beiping-Hankou Railway and garrisoning in Shanxi province until it was dissolved in December 1939. The division was reformed in May 1944 from island garrisons and new recruits. It was assigned to the 31st Army under General Kuribayashi, becoming the main Japanese force on the Bonin Islands, especially Iwo Jima and Chichi Jima, with about 47,000 troops spread across the island clusters. In February 1945, the 109th Division fiercely defended Iwo Jima against overwhelming US forces, employing deep tunnel systems and determined resistance. Despite their efforts, almost all defenders were killed. Only about 1,083 Japanese soldiers survived, with General Kuribayashi believed to have died leading a final counterattack. The division’s last stand at Iwo Jima became one of WWII’s most intense and symbolic battles, remembered for its desperate defense and heavy casualties.

card_unit_thunder_division.name: card_unit_thunder_division
card_unit_thunder_division.title: THUNDER DIVISION
card_unit_thunder_division.text: Once per turn, when you play an Intel card, your other units get +2+2.
card_unit_thunder_division.flavorText: The 29th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army, known as the Thunder Division, was established in 1941 in Nagoya. It initially served under the Kwantung Army in Manchukuo and included the 18th, 38th, and 50th Infantry Regiments. In 1944, the division was reassigned to the 31st Army and sent to defend the Mariana Islands, anticipating a major US assault. During its transfer, the transport ship Sakito Maru was torpedoed by the submarine USS Trout. Over half of the 18th Infantry Regiment perished in the attack. The surviving troops landed on Guam, joining the rest of the division to prepare defensive positions. From July 21 to August 10, 1944, the Thunder Division fought against US forces in the Battle of Guam. Despite strong fortifications and determined resistance, the division was eventually overwhelmed. The majority of its personnel were killed in the battle.

card_event_7075_aluminium.name: card_event_7075_aluminium
card_event_7075_aluminium.title: 7075 ALUMINIUM
card_event_7075_aluminium.text: Add three 0-cost A6M2 ZERO to your hand with: "Destruction: Add a 0-cost copy of this unit to your hand."

card_event_advanced_imperial_rnd.name: card_event_advanced_imperial_rnd
card_event_advanced_imperial_rnd.title: ADVANCED IMPERIAL R&D
card_event_advanced_imperial_rnd.text: Choose One - Add 7075 ALUMINIUM to hand OR add IMPERIAL WEAPON No. 2 to hand.

card_event_cruiser_scouts.name: card_event_cruiser_scouts
card_event_cruiser_scouts.title: CRUISER SCOUTS
card_event_cruiser_scouts.text: Pin a unit and Forecast. Also Intel 3 if you have 0 kredits.
card_event_cruiser_scouts.flavorText: Cruiser scouts were the eyes of the Imperial Japanese Navy’s long range task forces. Since Japanese carrier aircraft were usually kept for attack missions, much of the search work fell to floatplanes carried by cruisers. These aircraft were launched by catapult, then recovered from the sea after landing near their ships. The Tone class cruisers, Tone and Chikuma, were especially suited to this role. Their main guns were placed forward, leaving the stern free for a large aircraft-handling area. Chikuma could carry six floatplanes, giving the fleet a wider search screen. These scouts could shape an entire battle. Before the Pearl Harbor attack, Tone and Chikuma launched floatplanes for weather checks and patrols. In 1942 at Midway, their Aichi E13A floatplanes searched hundreds of miles for US ships. Chikuma’s aircraft later found USS Yorktown and shadowed her for hours. Cruiser scouts gave commanders vital information, but delays, mistakes, and fragile communications could turn even successful sightings into missed chances.

card_event_expanded_imperial_rnd.name: card_event_expanded_imperial_rnd
card_event_expanded_imperial_rnd.title: EXPANDED IMPERIAL R&D
card_event_expanded_imperial_rnd.text: Choose One - Add LONG LANCE to hand OR add ADVANCED IMPERIAL R&D to hand.

card_event_ferocious_assault.name: card_event_ferocious_assault
card_event_ferocious_assault.title: FEROCIOUS ASSAULT
card_event_ferocious_assault.text: Destroy target infantry. Lose a kredit slot if its attack was greater than your kredit slots.
card_event_ferocious_assault.flavorText: Japanese anti-tank assaults often demanded extreme self-sacrifice from infantrymen, who were sometimes forced to approach enemy tanks at dangerously close range with satchel charges or Molotov cocktails. Lacking weapons capable of reliably penetrating heavy armor, the Imperial Japanese Army relied on concealment, concentrated fire against supporting infantry, and aggressive close assaults. Japanese troops would remain hidden until tanks and infantry entered close range, then use rifles, machine guns, mortars, and anti-tank guns to separate the armor from its support. If the tanks continued forward, soldiers could rush the isolated vehicles, attempting to disable their tracks with explosives before destroying them at close range. These tactics reflected both Japanese doctrine and the army’s material disadvantages. They could be effective against isolated armor, but often came at a severe cost to the infantry carrying out the assault.

card_event_imperial_research.name: card_event_imperial_research
card_event_imperial_research.title: IMPERIAL RESEARCH
card_event_imperial_research.text: Choose One - Add BALLOON BOMBS to hand OR add EXPANDED IMPERIAL R&D to hand.
card_event_imperial_research.flavorText: Imperial Japanese research during WWII produced weapons and materials that ranged from practical battlefield improvements to desperate late-war projects. One of the most effective was the Type 93 torpedo, later known as Long Lance. It used compressed oxygen instead of compressed air, which gave Japanese cruisers and destroyers’ torpedoes longer range, higher speed, and a smaller visible wake than many Allied torpedoes. Japanese engineers also helped push aircraft materials forward. Sumitomo developed Extra Super Duralumin, an aluminium alloy related to what later became 7075 aluminium. It was adopted for the Mitsubishi A6M Zero because it offered high strength with low weight, though it also required careful protection against corrosion. Other projects illustrated Japan’s search for unusual strategic weapons. Fu-Go balloon bombs used high altitude winds to cross the Pacific and carry incendiary and explosive payloads toward North America. About 9,300 were launched, but the campaign achieved little military effect. Imperial Weapon No. 2 referred to the Nakajima Kikka, Japan’s first turbojet-powered aircraft. It first flew in August 1945, but arrived too late for operational service.

card_event_imperial_weapon_no_2.name: card_event_imperial_weapon_no_2
card_event_imperial_weapon_no_2.title: IMPERIAL WEAPON No. 2
card_event_imperial_weapon_no_2.text: Add four KIKKA on top of your deck. They cost 0 to deploy and operate.

card_event_last_ditch_force.name: card_event_last_ditch_force
card_event_last_ditch_force.title: LAST DITCH FORCE
card_event_last_ditch_force.text: Destroy all units. Players lose 6 kredit slots. Units in decks get +3 attack.
card_event_last_ditch_force.flavorText: By the summer of 1945, Japan was preparing a true last ditch defense of the Home Islands. Operation Ketsugō was designed to meet the expected Allied invasion with overwhelming resistance and inflict such heavy losses that the Allies might accept a negotiated end to the war. Japanese strategists correctly anticipated that southern Kyūshū would be the first major target and concentrated troops, aircraft and ammunition there. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers were deployed, while thousands of aircraft were prepared for kamikaze attacks against the invasion fleet. Midget submarines, manned torpedoes, suicide boats and specially trained divers were also ready to strike Allied ships approaching the beaches. The defense extended far beyond the regular armed forces. Millions of civilians were organized into the Volunteer Fighting Corps, often with little training and few modern weapons. Rifles, Molotov cocktails, swords and even bamboo spears were to be used in a final defense of Japanese territory. Operation Ketsugō was never carried out. Japan surrendered in August 1945 before the planned Allied invasion could begin.

card_event_long_lance.name: card_event_long_lance
card_event_long_lance.title: LONG LANCE
card_event_long_lance.text: Destroy target unit. Draw 2 cards if it had an attack of 3 or less.

card_event_out_of_the_sun.name: card_event_out_of_the_sun
card_event_out_of_the_sun.title: OUT OF THE SUN
card_event_out_of_the_sun.text: Give your air units -1 operation cost. If you played a Sunny card this turn, they get +2 attack as well.
card_event_out_of_the_sun.flavorText: Attacking with the sun at one’s back was a fundamental air combat tactic during WWII, employed by all major combatants across every theater of the war. By positioning the sun directly behind their aircraft, pilots forced their targets to scan the sky against a blinding glare, making the attacker nearly invisible until the strike was already underway.

card_event_shinyo_motorboats.name: card_event_shinyo_motorboats
card_event_shinyo_motorboats.title: SHINYO MOTORBOATS
card_event_shinyo_motorboats.text: Lose a kredit slot. Deal damage to target unit equal to kredit slots lost this battle plus 1.
card_event_shinyo_motorboats.flavorText: Shinyo motorboats were fast explosive suicide boats developed by Japan during WWII as part of the Special Attack Units program. Their name meant “Sea Quake”. The program began in 1944 after Japan’s situation in the war had worsened. Early plans used steel hulls, but shortages led to a switch to wooden construction. Production ran from April 1944 to June 1945, and 6,197 boats were completed for the Imperial Japanese Navy. The standard Shinyo was a small one-man craft powered by a Toyota Type B engine. Type 1 boats could reach about 26 knots, while the larger Type 5 could reach about 30 knots and was manned by a crew of two. Each boat carried a bow-mounted explosive charge of about 270 kilograms, with two anti-ship rockets mounted behind the driver. Shinyo boats saw their main use during the Philippines campaign, in 1944 and 1945. They sank or damaged several Allied vessels around Luzon, Corregidor and Okinawa. By the end of the war, hundreds had been sent to Okinawa, Formosa, Hong Kong, and the Japanese home islands.

card_event_special_attack.name: card_event_special_attack
card_event_special_attack.title: SPECIAL ATTACK
card_event_special_attack.text: Lose a kredit slot. Your units get: "Destruction: Deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ. Gain a kredit slot."
card_event_special_attack.flavorText: Japanese Special Attack Units were formations of the Imperial Japanese Navy and Imperial Japanese Army used for suicide missions during WWII. They became more prominent near the end of the Pacific War, when Japan prepared for the expected invasion of the home islands under the Ketsugo defense plan. The units included kamikaze aircraft, explosive motorboats, manned torpedoes, midget submarines, and suicide divers. Aircraft were the best known special attack weapons. Some were standard fighters or bombers adapted for this role, while the Yokosuka MXY 7 Ohka was purpose-built as a rocket-powered flying bomb carried near the target by a bomber. Once released, the pilot glided toward the enemy ship, then fired the rocket engine for a high-speed final dive. Some special attack weapons were also developed for naval warfare. Shinyo boats were one-man explosive motorboats that could reach about 30 knots. Kaiten were modified torpedoes guided by a pilot, while Kairyu midget submarines carried torpedoes and an internal warhead. Fukuryu divers were trained to walk underwater with explosive charges on poles. Many of these weapons were stored for homeland defense, but some saw combat in the Philippines, Okinawa, and Palau.

card_unit_1st_recon.name: card_unit_1st_recon
card_unit_1st_recon.title: 7th RECON
card_unit_1st_recon.text: Destruction: Draw a card if you know a card in the enemy hand.
card_unit_1st_recon.flavorText: The 7th Reconnaissance Regiment served as the reconnaissance element of Japan’s 7th Division, scouting ahead of the main force and reporting on enemy positions and movements. By 1941, it was listed among the division’s principal components alongside its three infantry regiments, artillery, engineers and support units. The 7th Division was known as the “Bear Division” and was one of the Imperial Japanese Army’s oldest formations. Based in Hokkaido, it had a long military history dating back to the late 19th century and remained closely associated with the defense of Japan’s northern territories. During the Pacific War, parts of the division were sent overseas. The 28th Infantry Regiment  fought on Guadalcanal, where it suffered catastrophic losses at the battles of Tenaru and Edson’s Ridge, while another detachment took part in the occupation of Attu in the Aleutian Islands. Most of the division, however, remained in Hokkaido, where it built defensive positions, preparing for a potential Allied invasion. It remained there until Japan surrendered in September 1945.

card_unit_238th_regiment.name: card_unit_238th_regiment
card_unit_238th_regiment.title: 238th REGIMENT
card_unit_238th_regiment.text: Deals double damage if you have 3 or fewer kredit slots.
card_unit_238th_regiment.flavorText: During WWII, the 238th Infantry Regiment was part of the 41st Division, an infantry formation of the Imperial Japanese Army. The division was raised in Utsunomiya in 1939 as a triangular division, with the 237th, 238th, and 239th Infantry Regiments as its main combat units. It also included mountain artillery, engineer, and transport regiments. The division’s call sign was River Division. In 1942, the 41st Division was first intended for Guadalcanal, but Japanese efforts to reinforce that island failed. The division was instead diverted to New Guinea. It arrived at Wewak in February 1943, where it joined the 18th Army. It fought through the New Guinea campaign against Australian and US forces. A detachment was sent to strengthen Lae and later took part in the Salamaua Lae campaign. By mid 1944, the 18th Army had been reduced mainly to the 41st Division. Its failed attack at the Driniumor River caused heavy losses. The survivors withdrew into the Prince Alexander Mountains, where disease and malnutrition caused further losses before Japan’s surrender in 1945.

card_unit_38th_independent.name: card_unit_38th_independent
card_unit_38th_independent.title: 38th INDEPENDENT
card_unit_38th_independent.text: Cannot attack or move. Suppress it if you have 4+ copies. Duplicate this unit when you lose a kredit slot.
card_unit_38th_independent.flavorText: The 38th Independent Mixed Brigade was an infantry brigade of the Imperial Japanese Army, formed in June 1944 from the 17th Division. It was attached to the 17th Army and placed under Major General Kesao Kijima. The brigade entered the Bougainville campaign at a time when Japanese forces were already under heavy pressure. Allied control of the air and seas made supply difficult, while Japanese units on the island were increasingly cut off from one another. The brigade is best known for its role in the Battle of Pearl Ridge. There, it opposed the Australian advance across steep and difficult jungle terrain. The fighting lasted three days and ended on 1 January 1945, when the brigade was defeated. After the battle, its intended retreat south toward Buin was refused. This left the formation isolated around Numa Numa on Bougainville Island’s east coast. It remained there until the end of hostilities, separated from the main Japanese concentration in the south.

card_unit_78th_yongsan.name: card_unit_78th_yongsan
card_unit_78th_yongsan.title: 78th YONGSAN
card_unit_78th_yongsan.text: Has +1 attack for each kredit slot the enemy has over you.
card_unit_78th_yongsan.flavorText: The 78th Infantry Regiment was part of the 20th Division, an Imperial Japanese Army formation based at Yongsan in Korea. The division carried the code name Morning Division and was originally raised as a Korean garrison force. During WWII, its role changed when it was sent to New Guinea as part of the Japanese Eighteenth Army. By that time, the division included the 78th, 79th, and 80th Infantry Regiments, along with artillery, reconnaissance, engineer, and transport units. In 1943, the 20th Division moved under Lieutenant General Shigemasa Aoki, but he soon died of malaria. Lieutenant General Shigeru Katagiri then led the division during the Huon Peninsula campaign. After Allied landings at Lae and Nadzab, Japanese troops marched about 200 miles to reinforce Finschhafen. They fought at Finschhafen and Sattelberg, then withdrew after being defeated in October 1943. Katagiri was later killed during the Battle of Hollandia. The division’s surviving troops fought in New Guinea under Masutaro Nakai until Japan’s surrender. Of about 25,000 men, only 1,711 survived the war.

card_unit_79th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_79th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_79th_infantry_regiment.title: 79th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_79th_infantry_regiment.text: When you play a Sunny card, give your units +2 attack and remove pin on them.
card_unit_79th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 79th Infantry Regiment served with the 20th Division, a formation known as the Morning Division. By the time the division was sent to New Guinea, the 79th fought beside the 78th and 80th Infantry Regiments, with artillery, reconnaissance, engineer, and transport units supporting them. In 1943, the 20th Division was transferred to the Japanese Eighteenth Army in New Guinea. Its troops faced a harsh campaign of jungle movement, disease, shortages, and Allied pressure. After Allied landings at Lae and Nadzab, Lieutenant General Shigeru Katagiri led the division on a difficult march of about 200 miles to reinforce Finschhafen. The division fought in the Huon Peninsula campaign and gathered around Sattelberg, but was forced back after defeat there in October 1943. Katagiri was later killed while moving from Madang to Wewak. The remaining troops, later known as Nakai Detachment, continued fighting Australian forces in the Markham, Ramu, and Finisterre campaigns. Of about 25,000 men in the 20th Division, only 1,711 survived the war.

card_unit_j2m_raiden.name: card_unit_j2m_raiden
card_unit_j2m_raiden.title: J2M RAIDEN
card_unit_j2m_raiden.text: Gets +1+1 and -1 operation cost when the enemy gives an order.
card_unit_j2m_raiden.flavorText: The Mitsubishi J2M Raiden, meaning “Lightning Bolt,” was a land-based interceptor developed for the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service. Designed by Jiro Horikoshi, who had also created the A6M Zero, the Raiden represented a different approach to fighter design. It was intended primarily to intercept high-altitude bombers, prioritizing speed, climbing ability, and heavy armament over the exceptional manoeuvrability associated with earlier Japanese fighters. Development was slowed by problems with engine cooling and the undercarriage, and combat units did not begin receiving the improved J2M3 in significant numbers until early 1944. The Raiden made its combat debut during the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944 and was later used chiefly in the defense of Japan against B-29 Superfortress raids. Armed with four 20 mm guns, it carried formidable firepower. Pilots used dive and zoom attacks to compensate for reduced performance at extreme altitude. Limited production and the American shift toward night-bombing further reduced its effectiveness. Nevertheless, Raidens were still fighting on 15 August 1945, only hours before Japan announced its surrender.

card_unit_kawanishi_h8k.name: card_unit_kawanishi_h8k
card_unit_kawanishi_h8k.title: KAWANISHI H8K
card_unit_kawanishi_h8k.text:
Draw a card when you Forecast.
Deployment: Forecast.
card_unit_kawanishi_h8k.flavorText: The Kawanishi H8K was a large four engine flying boat used by the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service during WWII. It was designed for long-range maritime patrol, reconnaissance, bombing, and transport missions over the Pacific. The first prototype flew in January 1941, and the type entered service in 1942. A total of 167 aircraft were built from 1941 to 1945. The Allies gave it the reporting name Emily. Early tests showed poor handling on water, but changes to the hull and nose spray strips solved many of these problems. The improved H8K2 became the main version, with more powerful engines, greater fuel capacity, and heavier defensive armament. It carried five 20 mm cannons, five 7.7 mm machine-guns, and could carry torpedoes, bombs, or depth charges. Its range of more than 7,000 kilometers made it useful for ocean patrols far from Japanese bases. The H8K first saw combat in 1942 during Operation K, a second raid on Pearl Harbor on 4 March 1942, which required submarine refuelling at French Frigate Shoals. The attack caused no significant damage due to poor visibility, but showed the aircraft’s unusual reach.

card_unit_murase_battalion.name: card_unit_murase_battalion
card_unit_murase_battalion.title: MURASE BATTALION
card_unit_murase_battalion.text: Once per turn, gain 3 additional kredits when you lose a kredit slot.
card_unit_murase_battalion.flavorText: The Murase Battalion was formally named 1st Battalion, 144th Infantry Regiment, and was led by Major Gohei Murase. The battalion belonged to the South Seas Detachment, a Japanese force sent into the Papuan campaign after earlier operations at Guam and Rabaul. In 1942, the unit took part in the fighting around the Kokoda Track and then withdrew across the Owen Stanley Range after its failed attempt to reach Port Moresby. By the time the battalion reached the northern coast of Papua, it had been badly weakened by combat, hunger, disease, and the harsh terrain. It then became one of the key Japanese formations defending the Sanananda and Giruwa area. Rather than deep trenches, the battalion relied on above-ground bunkers built from coconut tree logs and earth, because the water table was too high for normal fieldwork. These positions were difficult to detect and resisted small arms fire well. During the Allied advance in late 1942 and early 1943, the battalion held out under severe pressure. But by January 1943, it had largely ceased to exist as an organized unit.

card_unit_yokosuka_e14y.name: card_unit_yokosuka_e14y
card_unit_yokosuka_e14y.title: YOKOSUKA E14Y
card_unit_yokosuka_e14y.text: Deployment: Forecast. Draw a card if you have 0 kredits.
card_unit_yokosuka_e14y.flavorText: The Yokosuka E14Y was a submarine based reconnaissance seaplane used by the Imperial Japanese Navy during WWII. It first flew in 1939, entered service in 1941, and 126 were built. The aircraft was carried in a watertight hangar aboard large submarines such as I 25. Its wings could fold for storage, and it was launched by catapult when the submarine surfaced. After completing a mission, it landed on floats beside the submarine and was lifted back aboard. The E14Y, nicknamed Glen by the Allies, carried a crew of two and usually served as a scouting aircraft. In 1942, E14Ys flew reconnaissance missions over Melbourne, Wellington, Auckland, and Sydney. One flight preceded the Japanese midget submarine attack on Sydney Harbour. The aircraft is best known for the Lookout Air Raid in Oregon, when it was launched from a submarine and dropped two incendiary bombs in an attempt to start forest fires. The attack caused no serious damage, but it made the E14Y the only submarine-based aircraft to bomb the US mainland during WWII.

card_event_air_superiority_cam1.name: card_event_air_superiority_cam1
card_event_air_superiority_cam1.title: AIR SUPERIORITY
card_event_air_superiority_cam1.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. If you have an air unit on the battlefield, deal 3 damage.

card_event_amphibious_assault_cam1.name: card_event_amphibious_assault_cam1
card_event_amphibious_assault_cam1.title: AMPHIBIOUS ASSAULT
card_event_amphibious_assault_cam1.text: Destroy an enemy unit that has 3 or less attack.

card_event_campaign_philippines2_chase_t.name: card_event_campaign_philippines2_chase_them_down
card_event_campaign_philippines2_chase_t.title: CHASE THEM DOWN
card_event_campaign_philippines2_chase_t.text: Friendly units have +2 attack and Blitz this turn.

card_event_campaign_philippines2_the_hun.name: card_event_campaign_philippines2_the_hunt
card_event_campaign_philippines2_the_hun.title: THE HUNT
card_event_campaign_philippines2_the_hun.text: Destroy target unit in the support line.

card_event_campaign_philippines4_aerial_.name: card_event_campaign_philippines4_aerial_assault
card_event_campaign_philippines4_aerial_.title: AERIAL ASSAULT
card_event_campaign_philippines4_aerial_.text: Deal 2 damage to all units in the frontline.

card_event_campaign_philippines4_infiltr.name: card_event_campaign_philippines4_infiltration
card_event_campaign_philippines4_infiltr.title: INFILTRATION
card_event_campaign_philippines4_infiltr.text: Give target Japanese unit in the frontline +3+3.

card_event_sneak_maneuver_cam1.name: card_event_sneak_maneuver_cam1
card_event_sneak_maneuver_cam1.title: SNEAK MANEUVER
card_event_sneak_maneuver_cam1.text: Give target infantry or tank with 0 operation cost +2 attack.

card_event_target_acquired.name: card_event_target_acquired
card_event_target_acquired.title: TARGET ACQUIRED
card_event_target_acquired.text: Destroy target unit that was attacked this turn.
card_event_target_acquired.flavorText: During WWII the Japanese forces had several anti-aircraft artillery weapons at their disposal. However, Japanese heavy anti-aircraft guns and their anti-aircraft fire control directors relied on 1930s electromechanical analog computer technology which had several limitations and was far less advanced compared to what the Americans were using. Furthermore, the Japanese AAA still depended on conventional fuses while the Americans had adopted the proximity fuse which had a far more devastating effect.

card_location_japan_scen1.name: card_location_japan_scen1
card_location_japan_scen1.title: FORMOSA
card_location_japan_scen1.text: The main force attacking the Philippines came from the island of Formosa.

card_location_japan_scen2.name: card_location_japan_scen2
card_location_japan_scen2.title: SAN FERNANDO
card_location_japan_scen2.text: San Fernando sits at the junction between Lingayen Gulf, Manila and the Bataan Peninsula.

card_location_japan_scen3.name: card_location_japan_scen3
card_location_japan_scen3.title: HERMOSA
card_location_japan_scen3.text: Hermosa is a town in the northern part of the Bataan Peninsula.

card_location_japan_scen4.name: card_location_japan_scen4
card_location_japan_scen4.title: HERMOSA
card_location_japan_scen4.text: Hermosa is a town in the northern part of the Bataan Peninsula.

card_location_japan_scen5.name: card_location_japan_scen5
card_location_japan_scen5.title: MARIVELES
card_location_japan_scen5.text: Mariveles is a small port town on the south coast of the Bataan Peninsula.

card_location_usa_scen1_ai.name: card_location_usa_scen1_ai
card_location_usa_scen1_ai.title: TAIVU POINT
card_location_usa_scen1_ai.text: The Japanese landed at Taivu Point east of Henderson Field to attack it.

card_location_usa_scen3_ai.text: The Matanikau valley west of Henderson Field offers the easiest path towards the US base.

card_location_usa_scen4_ai.text: Mount Austen is the main stronghold of the Japanese forces on Guadalcanal.

card_location_usa_scen5_seahorse.text: Deal 2 damage to units attacking Mount Austen.

card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment_cam1.title: 1st TAIPEI REGIMENT
card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment_cam1.text: Destruction: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.

card_unit_cedar_division_vet.name: card_unit_cedar_division_vet
card_unit_cedar_division_vet.title: CEDAR DIVISION
card_unit_cedar_division_vet.text: Draw 2 additional cards if your hand is empty at the start of your turn.

card_unit_sally_cam1.name: card_unit_sally_cam1
card_unit_sally_cam1.title: Ki-21 SALLY
card_unit_sally_cam1.text: Deployment: If the enemy has no air units on the battlefield, give this unit Fury.

card_unit_type94_tk_cam1.name: card_unit_type94_tk_cam1
card_unit_type94_tk_cam1.title: TYPE 94 TK
card_unit_type94_tk_cam1.text: Deployment: Add a SURPRISE ATTACK to your hand.

card_event_feigned_retreat.name: card_event_feigned_retreat
card_event_feigned_retreat.title: FEIGNED RETREAT
card_event_feigned_retreat.text: Discard your hand. Your HQ gets: "When you deploy a unit this battle, draw a card."
card_event_feigned_retreat.flavorText: A feigned retreat is a military tactic where a military force pretends to withdraw in an attempt to lure the enemy into a position where they are more vulnerable or can be ambushed. This is a tactic that has been used from the early dawn of warfare, but a difficult maneuver to execute with larger military formations as it requires well trained and disciplined soldiers. Japanese military leaders of WWII, and military leaders of other nations, commonly used this tactic on land, air and sea.

card_event_outflank.name: card_event_outflank
card_event_outflank.title: OUTFLANK
card_event_outflank.flavorText: The Japanese army doctrine was focused on the offensive and to quickly close in on the enemy. The preferred offensive tactics used by the army commanders during WWII was a maneuver called Envelopment which had the primary goal of exploiting the enemies flanks. Usually this maneuver was accompanied with frontal pressure while the main force tried to outflank the enemy. Often a small force would try to attack the enemy rear.

card_event_scouting_party.name: card_event_scouting_party
card_event_scouting_party.title: SCOUTING PARTY
card_event_scouting_party.text: Add two 33RD RECON to your support line.
card_event_scouting_party.flavorText: Japanese reconnaissance regiments during WWII were small units, not more than 500 men, and most divisions had one of these units attached to it. The structure of these units changed throughout the war, but originally they were Cavalry Regiments that were tasked with combat scouting. Usually the units were a mixture of motorized infantry and light armored cars or tankettes attached to infantry divisions, but some tank divisions also had a reconnaissance regiment with light tank companies attached.

card_event_soul_of_old_japan.name: card_event_soul_of_old_japan
card_event_soul_of_old_japan.title: SOUL OF OLD JAPAN
card_event_soul_of_old_japan.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite Japanese units to add to your hand.
card_event_soul_of_old_japan.flavorText: "Ashihara" is a term derived from the imagery of the earthly realm in Japanese mythology. Such cultural symbols were originally used to describe Japanese characteristics and cultural values. During WWII, however, wartime propaganda increasingly used these symbols to promote obedience, sacrifice, and mass mobilization, fueling notions of Japanese racial superiority and the belief that Japan was destined to rule the world.

card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment.name: card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment
card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment.title: 1st TAIPEI REGIMENT
card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment.text: Destruction: Deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_1st_taipei_regiment.flavorText: The 1st Taipei Regiment was a subordinate of the 48th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army, and its call sign was the Sea Division. The 48th Division was initially part of the Taiwan Army, but reassigned to the 14th Army in 1941 and mechanized in preparation for the Pacific War. The division was one of the first forces to land in the Philippines and captured Manila, but then reassigned to the 16th Army in eastern Java and ordered to capture Surabaya and its oil fields. The division was then assigned to garrison duty on the island of Timor as part of the 19th Army where it stayed until the Japanese surrender in 1945.

card_unit_61st_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_61st_infantry_regiment
card_unit_61st_infantry_regiment.title: 61st INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_61st_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 61st Infantry Regiment was a subordinate unit of the 4th Infantry Division of the Imperial Japanese Army. In April 1942 the 4th Division was assigned to the 14th Army and shipped to the Philippines to participate in the Battle of Bataan. The division then played a major part in the Japanese victory in the Battle of Corregidor where units of the 61st Infantry Regiment were the first to land on the island. Despite heavy resistance the regiment managed to secure a beachhead until the reinforcements arrived and managed to drive the enemies away. After the Philippines Campaign of 1941–42 the division was returned home for security duties. The division did not see much combat after that and ended the war in Thailand where it was disbanded after the war.

card_unit_b6n_tenzan.name: card_unit_b6n_tenzan
card_unit_b6n_tenzan.title: B6N TENZAN
card_unit_b6n_tenzan.text: Deployment: Pin target enemy unit. Destroy it if already pinned.
card_unit_b6n_tenzan.flavorText: The Nakajima B6N Tenzan was a carrier-based torpedo bomber used by the Imperial Japanese Navy during WWII. The aircraft was first introduced in 1943 and was the successor to the B5N “Kate”, but it reached the frontline only in small numbers and came too late to make a difference. At the time the US Navy had already achieved air superiority while Japan had lost most of its carriers and was in desperate need of experienced pilots. A total of 1,268 B6N’s were built, including a few variants.

card_event_distant_front.name: card_event_distant_front
card_event_distant_front.title: DISTANT FRONT
card_event_distant_front.text: Remove target unit with attack 3 or less from the battlefield. Return it at the start of your next turn.
card_event_distant_front.flavorText: The Japanese occupation of the Aleutian Islands off the coast of Alaska during WWII marked a strategic but challenging expansion into American territory. Initiated with the unopposed landing on Attu and Kiska islands in June 1942, the occupation aimed to divert American attention away from the Pacific theater and threaten North America. While the capture provided a foothold on American soil, the harsh environmental conditions, logistical difficulties, and lack of a clear strategic advantage made the occupation challenging. The Japanese garrisons faced supply issues, extreme weather, and isolation. Despite efforts to fortify the islands and the initial success in taking American territory, the Aleutian occupation became a drain on Japanese resources without impacting the overall war effort. Eventually, in July 1943 an evacuation of the Japanese forces on Kiska island was conducted stealthily under the cover of fog and darkness, deceiving the US forces into believing that the Japanese were still present. As a result, the Americans launched an amphibious assault to retake Kiska on August 15th, 1943, only to discover that the Japanese had already left the island.

card_event_forced_surrender.name: card_event_forced_surrender
card_event_forced_surrender.title: FORCED SURRENDER
card_event_forced_surrender.text: Pin target unit. Enemy units currently pinned remain pinned for an extra turn.
card_event_forced_surrender.flavorText: The Battle of Singapore (February 8th-15th, 1942) and the following British surrender to Japanese forces marked a significant and devastating moment in the conflict for the Allied forces. After a rapid and aggressive advance by Japanese forces through Malaya, the British, along with their Commonwealth and Allied troops, found themselves outnumbered, outmaneuvered, and ultimately besieged. The fortified city of Singapore, considered an impregnable fortress, fell in what is often referred to as one of the most humiliating and shocking defeats in British military history. Under the command of Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival, the British and Allied forces were forced to surrender unconditionally to the Japanese. The surrender of Singapore resulted in around 80,000 Allied troops becoming prisoners of war, marking a significant turning point in the war in the Pacific and Southeast Asia theaters, impacting morale and strategy for the Allied powers.

card_event_on_the_ascend.name: card_event_on_the_ascend
card_event_on_the_ascend.title: ON THE ASCENT
card_event_on_the_ascend.text: Destroy and Salvage the unit(s) with the least attack on the battlefield.
card_event_on_the_ascend.flavorText: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, Japan significantly expanded its territorial control. The conflict, which began in 1937 and lasted until 1945, provided Japan with the opportunity to extend its territory across various regions in China. Within the first two years of the war, Japanese forces achieved rapid success, gaining control of most ports and major cities up to Hankow, and a large portion of the railway network. The expansion continued as Japanese forces moved further inland and took control of key areas such as Shansi, Inner Mongolia, and Canton. With control over key railways and the seas, along with superior air power which led to the destruction of the Chinese air force and widespread bombings of cities, the human cost for the Chinese was extremely high. Yet the Chinese forces did not yield and conquering all of China proved to be a much more difficult task than initially anticipated for the Japanese. This war eventually became part of the larger Pacific War, and Japan's focus shifted as the conflict expanded. Finally, the Second Sino-Japanese War ended with Japan's defeat in 1945.

card_event_out_of_the_mist.name: card_event_out_of_the_mist
card_event_out_of_the_mist.title: OUT OF THE MIST
card_event_out_of_the_mist.text: Deal 1 damage to target unit. If it is destroyed this turn, Salvage it.
card_event_out_of_the_mist.flavorText: The Bombing of Dutch Harbor took place in June 1942 when the Japanese Imperial Navy launched air raids on the US naval base at Dutch Harbor in the Aleutian Islands, off the coast of Alaska, during WWII. The surprise attack was aimed at diverting American attention from the Japanese occupation of Attu and Kiska islands in the Aleutians, and resulted in considerable damage to American installations, ships, and infrastructure. The Japanese targeted military facilities and assets, causing casualties and destruction, but failed to inflict significant long-term damage or completely disable the base. The attack prompted the reinforcement of American defenses in the region and marked one of the few occasions during the war when the United States was subjected to direct enemy assault.

card_event_take_liberty.name: card_event_take_liberty
card_event_take_liberty.title: TAKE LIBERTY
card_event_take_liberty.text: Each player shuffles their hand into their deck, then draws 4 cards.
card_event_take_liberty.flavorText: The last major country to join an alliance with Japan during WWII was Thailand. In 1942, after the successful Japanese invasion of Thailand in December 1941 and the subsequent signing of a military alliance, Thailand formally joined the Axis Powers by declaring war on the Allies. While Thailand formally joined the Axis and aligned with Japan, its military contributions to the war effort were relatively limited. However, for the Japanese the alliance was more about securing diplomatic support and a level of control over strategic territory, as their intention was to use Thailand as their military base to invade Burma and Malaya in the future.

card_unit_118_mixed_regiment.name: card_unit_118_mixed_regiment
card_unit_118_mixed_regiment.title: 118th MIXED REGIMENT
card_unit_118_mixed_regiment.flavorText: The 118th Mixed Regiment was a unit of the 43rd Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division, whose call sign was the Honor Division, was raised in 1943 and assigned to the Central District Army which was responsible for the defense of the Japanese home islands during the Pacific War. However, in 1944 it was assigned to the 31st Army and reorganized into a marine division. That same year the bulk of the division was shipped to Saipan and reached its destination. However, the 118th Regiment, which sailed later, lost two thirds of its men on the way when a US submarine attacked their convoy. In early June 1944 the division had established defensive positions on the island, waiting for imminent invasion by the US forces. On June 15th the Battle of Saipan began and the division suffered significant setbacks against the US forces, losing strategic locations like Hinashita hill. By late June, the division was significantly weakened, and facing defeat, the division commander requested reinforcements or evacuation. With their situation deemed hopeless, the division launched a final, suicidal banzai charge on July 7th, resulting in its complete annihilation. This charge inflicted casualties on US troops but marked the end of the 43rd Division.

card_unit_20th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_20th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_20th_infantry_regiment.title: 20th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_20th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 20th Infantry Regiment was a part of the 16th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division was raised in 1905 during the Russo-Japanese War but didn’t see any combat at that time. However, in 1937, open hostilities began with China, leading the division to participate in various campaigns. In December 1938, it was incorporated into the 11th Army, and it was demobilized in August 1939. The division was later reorganized, sent to Manchukuo in 1940, and played a role in the Philippines campaign. As the war situation worsened, they were ordered to Leyte Island in 1944, where they faced heavy losses, and of the 13,000 men of the division, only a few hundred survivors remained by the end of the war.

card_unit_3rd_maizuru_snlf.name: card_unit_3rd_maizuru_snlf
card_unit_3rd_maizuru_snlf.title: 3rd MAIZURU SNLF
card_unit_3rd_maizuru_snlf.text: When you add or deploy an Alpine unit, deal 1 damage to a random enemy. Pin it if a unit.
card_unit_3rd_maizuru_snlf.flavorText: The 3rd Maizuru SNFL (Special Naval Landing Force) was a naval infantry unit of the Imperial Japanese Navy that were part of the land forces. The SNFL was not a marine force but instead they were sailors who received basic infantry training and were deployed in landings during WWII. The 3rd Maizuru SNFL landed on Kiska Island in Alaska in June 1942 with a battalion-sized force of 550 men and occupied the island without any resistance. In the coming months, more units joined, and the occupying force gradually expanded to approximately 5,640 military personnel and 1,170 civilians. Despite the significant size of the force, it was not enough for the construction of an airfield, roads, accommodations, and defenses. Over the course of the fourteen-month occupation, the Japanese faced escalating attacks from American air and naval forces. Finally, on 28 July 1943 the occupation force withdrew from Kiska Island without attracting the attention of the Allied forces, and 18 days later an Allied force of 34,000 men invaded the deserted island.

card_unit_tsuruga_regiment.name: card_unit_tsuruga_regiment
card_unit_tsuruga_regiment.title: TSURUGA REGIMENT
card_unit_tsuruga_regiment.text: Destruction: Deal damage equal to its attack to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_tsuruga_regiment.flavorText: The 67th Infantry regiment (Tsuruga) was a regiment of the 15th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army which was active from 1905 to 1925, and 1938 to 1945. In 1943 the 15th Division was assigned to the 15th Army in Burma in preparation for an offensive against British India, codenamed Operation U-Go. In 1944 the division participated in the attack on Imphal, followed by the Battle of Meiktila and Mandalay. During these operations the 15th Division lost more than half of its men, both in combat and to disease, and was forced to retreat from Burma and into Thailand where it was officially disbanded in 1945, a few days before the war ended.

card_unit_type_97_te_ke.name: card_unit_type_97_te_ke
card_unit_type_97_te_ke.title: TYPE 94 TK EARLY
card_unit_type_97_te_ke.text: Gets +1 attack when it damages the enemy HQ.
card_unit_type_97_te_ke.flavorText: The Type 94 tankette, also known as TK (short for Tokushu Keninsha, meaning "special tractor"), was a small armored vehicle used by the Imperial Japanese Army in various conflicts, including the Second Sino-Japanese War, the Battles of Khalkhin Gol against the Soviet Union, and World War II. Although tankettes were commonly used for tasks such as transporting ammunition and providing support to infantry, they were primarily designed for reconnaissance rather than direct combat. The lightweight Type 94 tankette demonstrated its effectiveness in China, where the Chinese National Revolutionary Army had limited resources and only three tank battalions at their disposal. These battalions were equipped with a few British export models and Italian CV-33 tankettes. It's worth noting that, like most tankettes built in the 1920s and 1930s, the Type 94 had thin armor, making it very vulnerable to both artillery and machine gun fire.

card_unit_winter_regiment.name: card_unit_winter_regiment
card_unit_winter_regiment.title: WINTER REGIMENT
card_unit_winter_regiment.text: Fully repair this unit when it Salvages a unit.
card_unit_winter_regiment.flavorText: The 227th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 37th Division (nicknamed Winter Division) of the Imperial Japanese Army. Originally the division was a garrison force tasked with maintaining order in occupied northern China, but it swiftly transitioned to frontline combat duties due to the Second Sino-Japanese War, where it engaged the Chinese communist Eighth Route Army in Shanxi Province. The Winter Division was reassigned to the 12th Army in March 1944 and played a significant role in Operation Ichi-go, the Japanese offensive in China, where it advanced through Henan and Guangxi provinces, and eventually occupied Nanning. Further orders led the division south into French Indochina where it was made ready to counter any potential British invasion from Burma. The division survived the war relatively intact and gained recognition for its discipline and officer leadership. After being stationed in Thailand until the end of the war, the 37th Division's troops were transported back to Japan and the division was inactivated shortly afterwards.

card_unit_zero_a6m2_21.name: card_unit_zero_a6m2_21
card_unit_zero_a6m2_21.title: A6M2-21 ZERO
card_unit_zero_a6m2_21.text: The first card played by the enemy each turn costs double.
card_unit_zero_a6m2_21.flavorText: The Japanese Zero, officially known as the Mitsubishi A6M Zero, was a legendary aircraft that played a pivotal role in the early years of WWII. Known for its exceptional agility and long-range capabilities, the Zero was the pride of the Imperial Japanese Navy's Air Service and became widely recognized as a symbol of Japan's air strength during the war. The Model 21 variant first flew in 1941 and was introduced with folding wingtips, which allowed it to fit on aircraft carriers, and a 520 liters wing tank plus a 320 liters drop tank which improved its range significantly. A total of 740 Model 21 variants were built throughout the war which made it one of the most produced versions. Two other versions of Model 21 were built in smaller numbers, the Nakajima-built A6M2-N "Rufe" floatplane, and the A6M2-K two-seat trainer.

card_event_audacity.name: card_event_audacity
card_event_audacity.title: AUDACITY
card_event_audacity.text: Add an AICHI D3A-2 to your support line. Deal damage to a random enemy unit equal to its attack.
card_event_audacity.flavorText: Japanese bombing strategies during WWII demonstrated their aircrews complete disregard for casualties and obedience to commands. Even in the face of intense anti-aircraft fire or oncoming fighters, bombers would maintain their close formation as they approached their target. Finally, the bombs would be dropped at a height between 7,000 and 26,0000 feet in response to a signal from the leader. However, by 1943 the Japanese found themselves on the defensive in most theaters, which meant that they had to change their tactics. For most parts they abandoned daylight bombing and focused on dawn and dusk bombing by fighters and night bombing was done by medium, torpedo and dive bombers. Their dive bombing operations were far from effective, but they too exemplified the pilots courage and indifference to losses, and there were numerous Allied reports of damaged aircraft trying to complete their objectives by crashing into their targets as a last resort.

card_event_edge_of_the_empire.name: card_event_edge_of_the_empire
card_event_edge_of_the_empire.title: EDGE OF THE EMPIRE
card_event_edge_of_the_empire.text: Shuffle your hand into your deck. Draw 3 cards at the end of turn.
card_event_edge_of_the_empire.flavorText: The Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, also known as the “New Order in East Asia”, was a concept where the idea was to liberate Asia from the Western colonial powers and create a bloc of Asian nations which would be led by Japan. This concept served as a front for Japan's expansion in Asia during WWII, but the controversy was that Japan replaced the Western powers with a ruthless administration and drained the resources in most of their conquered nations in order to achieve their own imperial ambitions. At the height of WWII, the Empire of Japan was one of the largest in history, its sovereignty reached 8,510,000 km2 and its occupied regions and territories population accounted for 20% of the world's population. However, following Japan’s surrender to the Allies in September 1945 its governance was restricted to Japan and its islands and as a result the Co-Prosperity Sphere ceased to exist.

card_event_flight_to_oblivion.name: card_event_flight_to_oblivion
card_event_flight_to_oblivion.title: FLIGHT TO OBLIVION
card_event_flight_to_oblivion.text: Remove the top air unit of your deck. Distribute damage randomly to enemies equal to its attack.
card_event_flight_to_oblivion.flavorText: In the final months of WWII, Japan launched increasingly desperate kamikaze attacks against advancing Allied forces. By late 1944, Japan’s conventional military strength had been badly eroded, leading to the organized use of suicide tactics through units like the Tokubetsu Kōgekitai, or Special Attack Units. These missions were often carried out by young pilots flying outdated or lightly armed aircraft packed with explosives. The Battle of Okinawa in 1945 marked the peak of kamikaze activity. Japan launched more than 1,500 kamikaze aircraft during the campaign, sinking or damaging over 300 US and Allied ships. Some of these aircraft included the purpose-built Yokosuka MXY-7 Ohka, a rocket-powered bomb piloted by a single man, which was carried close to target areas by larger bombers. Many of these attacks were launched in the literal eleventh hour of Japan's war effort, when fuel, aircraft, and trained pilots were in critical short supply. Despite their tactical impact, the kamikaze missions could not alter the outcome of the war. These final strikes reflected the extent of Japan’s resolve and the dire strategic situation it faced in 1945.

card_event_southern_plan.name: card_event_southern_plan
card_event_southern_plan.title: SOUTHERN PLAN
card_event_southern_plan.text: Gain 1 extra kredit slot. The enemy loses a kredit slot.
card_event_southern_plan.flavorText: Imperial Japan’s ultimate goal was to conquer China, but they knew they couldn’t subdue this large country without clashing with other great powers, the Soviet Union in the north or the United States in the south. Several reasons led to the choice of the southern plan, that was led by the navy, over the northern plan that would rely on the army. One was the raw materials such as oil and rubber in the American, British and Dutch possessions in the Pacific and Southeast Asia. Another reason was the defeat of the Japanese Army in the Soviet–Japanese border conflicts in the 1930’s and the Japanese believed that the Soviet Union was too powerful to conquer. Last but not least was the trade embargo imposed by the Americans and the British that was intended to pressure Japan to withdraw from China. The Japanese southern plan worked great for the first 6 months, but once American industrial and military capabilities reached their full potential, and after the devastating defeats in the Battle of Midway and the Battle of Guadalcanal, the Japanese warmachine was fated to fail in its efforts.

card_unit_114th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_114th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_114th_infantry_regiment.title: 114th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_114th_infantry_regiment.text: When a friendly Destruction effect triggers, it triggers twice.
card_unit_114th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 114th Infantry Regiment was a regiment of the 56th Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. In 1942, during the Pacific War, the division was sent to Burma and landed in Rangoon as an attachment to the 25th Army. In Burma the division participated in the Battle of Toungoo in March 1942 where it defeated the defending Chinese forces. Later the division would advance to the Karenni States of Burma where it defeated the Chinese 6th Corps and forced them to retreat. From May 1942 the 56th Division mostly performed garrison duties on the Yunnan border to Burma, but in 1944 heavy fighting against the Allied forces resumed. During the fighting the 114th Infantry Regiment was credited with defeating Merrill’s Marauders during the Siege of Myitkyina and managed to delay and inflict heavy casualties to superior Chinese forces during the Battle of Mount Song. During these battles the 56th Division suffered heavy losses and was removed from the front line and ended the war on the border between South Burma and Thailand.

card_unit_3rd_yokosuka.name: card_unit_3rd_yokosuka
card_unit_3rd_yokosuka.title: 3rd YOKOSUKA
card_unit_3rd_yokosuka.text: Has +1 attack for each adjacent Japanese unit.
card_unit_3rd_yokosuka.flavorText: The 3rd Yokosuka was a unit of the Special Naval Landing Forces (SNLF or Rikusentai) of the Imperial Japanese Navy during WWII. The SNLF paratroopers were lightly armed and their main objectives were to assault coastal areas, support amphibious landings or attack other strategic objectives such as airfields. The SNLF was composed of three battalion sized formations, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Yokosuka, and although they were trained as paratrooper units they took little or no part in airborne operations throughout the war. The 1st Yokosuka carried out one airborne assault during the Battle of Manado, in the Netherlands East Indies in 1942. The 2nd Yokosuka never saw action as paratroopers, but instead they were part of an amphibious landing force in the Borneo Campaign from 1941. The 3rd Yokosuka participated in an airborne assault during the Battle of Timor and suffered heavy casualties. Later they took part in an unopposed landings on islands in the East Indies archipelago in 1942 and returned to Japan shortly after. Note that the SNLF paratroopers (Rikusentai) should not be confused with the Imperial Japanese Army paratroopers known as Teishin.

card_unit_kyushu_j7w3.name: card_unit_kyushu_j7w3
card_unit_kyushu_j7w3.title: KYUSHU J7W3
card_unit_kyushu_j7w3.text: Has +2 attack and Fury if undamaged.
card_unit_kyushu_j7w3.flavorText:
The Kyushu J7W Shinden was an experimental Japanese interceptor with an unusual canard layout and a pusher propeller. Designed in 1943 by Lieutenant Commander Masayoshi Tsuruno of the Imperial Japanese Navy, it aimed to counter B-29 raids over Japan. Flight tests of earlier canard-equipped gliders convinced the Navy to order a full prototype from Kyushu Aircraft.
Powered by a 2,130 hp Mitsubishi MK9D radial engine, the Shinden carried four nose-mounted 30 mm Type 5 cannons. This gave it formidable firepower for intercepting heavy bombers. Its layout promised high speed and agility, and a jet-powered variant was envisioned for the future. Construction delays and engine cooling problems meant the first prototype only flew on 3 August 1945. Tsuruno himself piloted the short test flights, which revealed torque and vibration issues. Plans called for over a thousand units to be produced by 1947, but Japan’s surrender ended the project. Only two prototypes were built. One was scrapped and the other shipped to the US, where it remains on display at the Smithsonian’s Udvar-Hazy Center.

card_unit_n1k1_kyofu.name: card_unit_n1k1_kyofu
card_unit_n1k1_kyofu.title: N1K1 KYOFU
card_unit_n1k1_kyofu.text: Deployment: Shuffle a IJN MIKURA into your deck.
card_unit_n1k1_kyofu.flavorText: The Kawanishi N1K1 Kyōfū, given the Allied reporting name “Rex”), was a floatplane fighter designed for Imperial Japanese Navy operations carried from locations without airstrips. Developed to support Japan’s early-war offensives, it entered service in 1943, by which time Japan had shifted to the defensive. Performance demands from the Navy were highly ambitious for a floatplane, and the Kyōfū fell short. Powered by a Mitsubishi MK4C Kasei 13 engine, it had a top speed of 489 km/h, well below the Navy’s 574 km/h requirement. The aircraft featured a large central float and two stabilizing wing-mounted floats, which added drag and reduced maneuverability. Armed with a heavy cannon and machine guns, it nonetheless struggled against faster US fighters. Only a small number were deployed, operating from Ambon, the Aru Islands and Penang. Kyōfūs also took part in the defense of Okinawa and flew late-war homeland defense missions from Lake Biwa under the Sasebo and Ōtsu Air Corps. Though it saw limited success in combat, its basic design led to the creation of the land-based N1K-J Shiden, a more effective fighter that shed the float and ultimately became one of Japan’s best late-war aircraft.

card_unit_sakura_regiment.name: card_unit_sakura_regiment
card_unit_sakura_regiment.title: SAKURA REGIMENT
card_unit_sakura_regiment.text: Has +2 attack if you have fewer cards in hand than the enemy.
card_unit_sakura_regiment.flavorText: The 57th Regiment Sakura was a regiment of the 1st Division of the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII. The division was sent to the Philippines to participate in the Pacific War in 1944 and was initially based in Manila before being shipped to Leyte to defend against the Filipino and US forces which had reoccupied the island. The 1st Division participated in fierce combat during the Battle of Leyte where it was nearly annihilated. Of the 11,000 soldiers only 800 managed to evacuate to Cebu island where they would participate in the Battle for Cebu City.

card_unit_sunrise_division.name: card_unit_sunrise_division
card_unit_sunrise_division.title: SUNRISE DIVISION
card_unit_sunrise_division.text: Deployment: Gets +6+6 if your HQ has 10 or less defense.
card_unit_sunrise_division.flavorText: The 23rd Division, aka Sunrise Division, of the Imperial Japanese Army was formed in 1938 during the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945). The division participated in the Battle of Khalkhin Gol against the Red Army in 1939, where it suffered a staggering loss of 12,000 men, which was about 80% of their combat strength. Following the devastating defeat the remnants of the division returned to Japan to assist with the border defense force, but was later reformed as a mechanized infantry division and sent to Taiwan for garrison duties in 1944. That same year the Sunrise Division was sent to the Philippines where it participated in the Battle of Luzon, against the US and Philippine Commonwealth forces, where it lost 24,508 men out of a total strength of 29,636 men. After the Battle of Luzon the Sunrise Division ceased to exist.

card_location_concrete_bunker_neutral.name: card_location_concrete_bunker_neutral
card_location_concrete_bunker_neutral.title: BUNKER
card_location_concrete_bunker_neutral.text: A bunker is a reinforced structure used for protection against heavy fire.
card_location_concrete_bunker_neutral.flavorText: A bunker is a fortified shelter built to protect soldiers and equipment from artillery and bombs. Most are underground or partly dug into the earth. In WWII, bunkers ranged from small concrete trench shelters to massive coastal gun positions with walls several meters thick.
