Reinforced concrete and heavy earth cover helped deflect blast waves and survive intense bombardment. Strong doors and ventilation were essential for prolonged defense.

card_location_flotilla_neutral.name: card_location_flotilla_neutral
card_location_flotilla_neutral.title: FLOTILLA
card_location_flotilla_neutral.text: A flotilla is a small group of naval vessels operating together.
card_location_flotilla_neutral.flavorText: Flotillas are compact naval formations composed of smaller vessels such as torpedo boats, submarines, and patrol craft. During WWII, all major navies organized flotillas to perform missions in coastal zones, rivers, and confined seas where larger ships could not operate effectively. The Kriegsmarine fielded both Schnellboot (e. fast boat) and U-boat flotillas. Schnellboote, named E-boats by the Allies, launched night raids in the Channel and North Sea, while U-boat flotillas, operating from Atlantic ports, waged an extended campaign against Allied shipping. The Royal Navy countered with motor torpedo boat flotillas and escort groups defending convoy routes and attacking Axis coastal traffic. The US Navy deployed PT boat flotillas in the Pacific, where they disrupted Japanese barge traffic, scouted invasion beaches, and ambushed supply convoys in island chains like the Solomons and Philippines. On inland waters, US river flotillas supported amphibious operations in Burma and China with shallow-draft gunboats and landing craft. Soviet flotillas along the Volga and Danube supported ground offensives, while Italian MAS boats and Japanese fast attack units challenged Allied control of narrow seas. Despite their small size, flotillas played decisive roles in local battles, often shaping broader strategic outcomes.

card_location_fortress_darwin_neutral.name: card_location_fortress_darwin_neutral
card_location_fortress_darwin_neutral.title: FORTRESS DARWIN
card_location_fortress_darwin_neutral.text: Fortress Darwin was a vital Allied outpost during WWII.
card_location_fortress_darwin_neutral.flavorText: By 1942, Darwin had changed from a small northern town into a crowded Allied base. Its pre-war population was only about 5,800, but its harbour, airfields, roads, and fuel stores made it vital for operations toward Timor, Java, and the Philippines. The defence works grew around the peninsula. East Point guarded the sea approaches with 6-inch coastal guns, while anti-aircraft positions covered Fannie Bay, East Arm, and the airfields. A 6 km boom net stretched across Darwin Harbour to block submarines and small surface craft. The fortress was still unfinished when Japan struck in 1942. Darwin had 18 heavy anti-aircraft guns, limited fighter strength, and no working radar warning system. On 19 February, carrier-based aircraft and land-based bombers hit the harbour, town, and airfields. MV Neptuna exploded at Stokes Hill Wharf, USS Peary was sunk, and RAAF Darwin was badly damaged. The raids exposed Darwin’s weakness, but they also forced a larger Allied air build-up across northern Australia.

card_location_iwo_jima_neutral.name: card_location_iwo_jima_neutral
card_location_iwo_jima_neutral.title: IWO JIMA
card_location_iwo_jima_neutral.text: Iwo Jima was a heavily fortified Japanese island during WWII.
card_location_iwo_jima_neutral.flavorText: Iwo Jima was a crucial part of Japan’s inner defensive line. In 1944, Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi abandoned traditional beach defenses, instead transforming the volcanic island into a fortress with 18 kilometers of underground tunnels, caves, and bunkers. This extensive network allowed his troops to survive heavy bombardments and reoccupy cleared positions. When US Marines landed on 19 February 1945, Kuribayashi withheld fire until the beaches were crowded with men and equipment, sparking a brutal five-week struggle against deeply entrenched defenders. Although Mount Suribachi fell on 23 February, fierce resistance continued across the northern defenses. The island was officially declared secure on 26 March, though Japanese holdouts remained hidden in the caves.

card_location_supply_train_neutral.name: card_location_supply_train_neutral
card_location_supply_train_neutral.title: SUPPLY TRAIN
card_location_supply_train_neutral.text: Rail transport was the backbone of military logistics in WWII.
card_location_supply_train_neutral.flavorText: Rail transport was essential to military logistics in WWII. All major powers used supply trains to move troops, weapons, fuel, food, and ammunition across vast distances. Germany’s blitzkrieg tactics relied on rail to sustain fast-moving forces. The Soviet Union used its network to shift armies and entire factories across thousands of kilometers. In the US, a vast rail system transported men and materiel from training bases to ports for overseas deployment. Trains delivered vital supplies to front-line units and were frequent targets for bombing and sabotage. Terrain, weather, and enemy action often disrupted operations, so armies built temporary tracks, used camouflage, and deployed mobile repair crews. Rail hubs became critical points of strategy, and some supply lines moved thousands of tons daily. In many campaigns, success depended on keeping the trains running.

card_event_act_on_the_intel.name: card_event_act_on_the_intel
card_event_act_on_the_intel.title: ACT ON THE INTEL
card_event_act_on_the_intel.text: Deal damage to target enemy equal to known cards in the enemy hand.
card_event_act_on_the_intel.flavorText: A notable example of how the Polish acted on the intelligence gathered during World War II is the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. The Polish underground resistance, known as the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), collected extensive intelligence on German military activities and plans in occupied Warsaw. With the intelligence indicating that the Soviet Red Army was approaching Warsaw, the Home Army decided to launch an uprising against the German occupiers on August 1, 1944. The uprising aimed to liberate the city and establish Polish authority before the Soviets arrived. The intelligence gathered by the Home Army helped in identifying German troop movements, supply routes, and defensive positions. This information allowed the Polish resistance fighters to plan targeted attacks, sabotage operations, and coordinated offensives against German forces. The intelligence also aided in the establishment of a makeshift radio network, which enabled communication between different units and with the outside world. This allowed the Home Army to relay valuable information about the situation in Warsaw to the Allies and the Polish government-in-exile. Although the Warsaw Uprising ultimately faced overwhelming German military power and Soviet reluctance to provide direct support, the intelligence gathered by the Polish underground played a crucial role in the initial stages of the uprising. It allowed the Home Army to launch surprise attacks, disrupt German supply lines, and control key strategic points within the city for a significant period of time.

card_event_agency_africa.name: card_event_agency_africa
card_event_agency_africa.title: AGENCY AFRICA
card_event_agency_africa.text: Add to hand a copy of a random known card in the enemy hand.
card_event_agency_africa.flavorText: Agency Africa was a Polish intelligence network in North Africa, run by a Polish Army Officer called Mieczysław Zygfryd Słowikowski codenamed “Rygor”. The agency was run under the cover of an oats factory and a sales and marketing chain which gave him and his agents permits to travel freely in Algeria, Morocco and France. This also gave them access to Axis military units, airports, naval bases and ports where they offered their commodities for sale. Not only was his business a commercial success, but it also gave “Rygor” and his agents access to vital information which they shared with the UK and US intelligence services. The information gathered by Agency Africa was used by the Allies to plan and execute Operation Torch, the successful amphibious landings in North Africa.

card_event_anders_army.name: card_event_anders_army
card_event_anders_army.title: ANDERS' ARMY
card_event_anders_army.text: Draw 2 cards. Deal 2 damage to your HQ.
card_event_anders_army.flavorText: Anders’ Army was the common name for the Polish Armed Forces in the East, formed in the Soviet Union in 1941 under General Władysław Anders. Its ranks came largely from Polish citizens released from Soviet captivity after the Sikorski-Mayski agreement restored relations between the Soviet Union and the Polish government-in-exile. Many recruits arrived weak from imprisonment, hunger, and forced displacement, yet they became the core of a new Polish force. The army first organized around Buzuluk and Totskoye, then expanded in Central Asia. By late 1941 it counted around 25,000 soldiers, but shortages of food, clothing, weapons and transport made training difficult. Polish civilians, including soldiers’ families and orphans, gathered around the camps and shared the same hardship. In 1942, Anders’ Army was evacuated through the Caspian Sea and overland routes into Iran. About 79,000 soldiers and 37,000 civilians left the Soviet Union. The army then moved through Iran, Iraq, and Palestine under British command. Many of its soldiers later formed the Polish II Corps, which fought in Italy, notably at Monte Cassino.

card_event_daring_strike.name: card_event_daring_strike
card_event_daring_strike.title: DARING STRIKE
card_event_daring_strike.text: Costs 2 less for each Exile unit you control. Deal 2 damage to any target.
card_event_daring_strike.flavorText: After the annexation of Poland there were a number of Polish pilots that fled to Great Britain and started fighting for the RAF in the Battle of Britain. The Polish recruits soon earned a reputation as extraordinary pilots that often showed total disregard for their own lives in their fight against the German Luftwaffe. Driven by vengefulness they would often put their lives at risk, just to inflict damage. When their ammunition ran dry they would continue their attacks by ramming the enemy or by using the propeller to slice into the enemy aircraft until it went down. Polish pilots were also known to maneuver above German bombers and use the body of their aircraft to force them down to the ground.

card_event_exiled_forces.name: card_event_exiled_forces
card_event_exiled_forces.title: EXILED FORCES
card_event_exiled_forces.text: Add a copy of target unit to your support line. Destroy it in 3 turns.
card_event_exiled_forces.flavorText: During WWII, thousands of Polish soldiers continued the fight from exile after Poland's defeat in 1939. These exiled forces regrouped in France, the United Kingdom, the Middle East, and later in Italy and Western Europe. Their resilience formed the backbone of the Polish Armed Forces in the West, a military force loyal to the Polish government-in-exile based in London. After the fall of France in 1940, many Polish troops evacuated to Britain. There, they rebuilt under British command, forming air, naval and ground units. Polish pilots played a key role in the Battle of Britain, especially in the famed No. 303 Squadron. On land, the 1st Armoured Division under General Stanisław Maczek distinguished itself in the Normandy campaign and the liberation of the Netherlands. In Italy, the 2nd Corps led by General Władysław Anders gained renown for its capture of Monte Cassino in 1944. Despite their sacrifices, many of these troops were barred from returning to postwar Poland, now under Soviet influence.

card_event_first_to_fight.name: card_event_first_to_fight
card_event_first_to_fight.title: FIRST TO FIGHT
card_event_first_to_fight.text: Give a friendly unit: "When this unit survives combat, add a LEGIONS to your support line."
card_event_first_to_fight.flavorText: Poland was the first country to fight against the expansion of Nazi Germany. Poland’s decision to resist the Germans in the summer of 1939, after Austria and Czechoslovakia had been annexed without a fight in 1938, was of historical significance. Poland’s resistance forced Britain and France to honor a security guarantee which eventually would forge the alliance that would eventually win the war.

card_event_frontal_defense.name: card_event_frontal_defense
card_event_frontal_defense.title: FRONTAL DEFENSE
card_event_frontal_defense.text: Give a friendly unit: "At the end of your turn, deal 1 damage to all units."
card_event_frontal_defense.flavorText: Poland’s Plan West was shaped by the need to defend its western industrial regions and the belief that retreating might lead Britain and France to negotiate peace with Germany, as in the Munich Agreement in 1938. Despite French advice to fall back behind natural barriers like the Vistula and San Rivers, Poland positioned its forces along the German-Polish border, which left them vulnerable to fast-moving German attacks. The plan aimed for a gradual retreat, in order to buy time for full mobilization and an eventual counteroffensive with Allied support. However, poor mobility and weak supply lines prevented such maneuvering and Polish forces struggled against superior German mechanized units. On top of that, civilian panic and misinformation disrupted the Polish defense efforts. While Poland expected a quick Allied intervention, the Western powers anticipated a prolonged war, leading to Poland’s rapid defeat in September 1939.

card_event_hammer_home.name: card_event_hammer_home
card_event_hammer_home.title: HAMMER HOME
card_event_hammer_home.text: Duplicate a friendly Exile unit, then give both +1+1 and -1 operation cost.
card_event_hammer_home.flavorText: Estimates suggest that around 200,000 to 250,000 Polish soldiers fought in exile during WWII. Many of these soldiers fled Poland following the German and Soviet invasions and occupation in 1939. They regrouped in various countries, forming units within the armed forces of those nations, such as the Polish Armed Forces in the West, including the Polish Air Force, Navy, and Army. The Polish forces in exile played a crucial role in various battles and campaigns alongside the Allied forces throughout the war. Furthermore, the Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa) had recruited 400,000 members by 1944 and was the largest underground resistance in Nazi-occupied Europe. The Home Army engaged in a wide range of activities, including sabotage, intelligence gathering, and armed uprisings, most notably the Warsaw Uprising in 1944, a heroic but ultimately unsuccessful attempt to liberate the city from German occupation.

card_event_hel.name: card_event_hel
card_event_hel.title: HEL
card_event_hel.text: Give a LEGIONS unit +6 defense and: "Your HQ is immune to damage."
card_event_hel.flavorText: The Hel Fortified Area was a set of fortifications that were constructed in 1936 in northern Poland. The Battle of Hel was fought in this area and it was the last place that Poland surrendered to the Germans in 1939. The Germans used the Hel naval base as a training facility for U-boat crews throughout the war.

card_event_hold_the_line.name: card_event_hold_the_line
card_event_hold_the_line.title: HOLD THE LINE
card_event_hold_the_line.text: When an enemy unit enters the frontline, pin and deal 1 damage to all units in the frontline.
card_event_hold_the_line.flavorText: The German invasion of Poland started on 1 September 1939, and on 17 September the Soviet forces invaded Eastern Poland. Facing overwhelming odds the Polish armed forces managed to resist both nations until early October, or for 5 weeks. The Polish plan against Germany was to delay them as long as possible as they expected France and Britain to come to their aid before the Germans overwhelmed their defenses. However, both Britain and France anticipated that Poland would hold out for 2-3 months, while Polish commanders expected them to hold out for 6 months. On 7 September 1939 the French started an offensive in the Saar region in an attempt to divert German forces from Poland, but their advance soon came to a halt without any significant number of German units being withdrawn. Meanwhile Britain was more focused on naval matters which did not do much to halt the German advance, and on 17 September the Royal Navy lost the aircraft carrier Courageous to a German u boat torpedo, which was a devastating psychological blow. That same day the Soviet Union declared war on Poland and that diminished any hopes that the Western Allies had of saving Poland from falling.

card_event_orp_blyskawica.name: card_event_orp_blyskawica
card_event_orp_blyskawica.title: ORP BŁYSKAWICA
card_event_orp_blyskawica.text: Copy a random order in the enemy deck. Gain HQ defense equal to its cost.
card_event_orp_blyskawica.flavorText: ORP Błyskawica (Lightning) was one of two Grom-Class destroyers that were built for the Polish Navy by the British company J. Samuel White and were among the most heavily armed and fastest destroyers of WWII. Two days before the war started the Błyskawica, its sister ship Grom, and the Burza destroyer escaped unhindered from the Baltic Sea to Britain from where it worked closely together with the Royal Navy's Home Fleet. Both Błyskawica and Grom participated in the Norwegian Campaign where the latter was sunk by an attacking Heinkel He 111 bomber.  The Błyskawica participated in Operation Dynamo, the evacuation of British troops from Dunkirk, but would for the remainder of the war take part in convoy and patrol duties in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. After the war the Błyskawica was used as a training ship for the Polish Navy, but was decommissioned in 1976 and has since then been on display as part of the Naval Museum in Gdynia.

card_event_orp_general_haller.name: card_event_orp_general_haller
card_event_orp_general_haller.title: ORP GENERAL HALLER
card_event_orp_general_haller.text: Convert target unit and adjacent units into ROUTED TROOPS.
card_event_orp_general_haller.flavorText: ORP General Haller was a Polish Navy gunboat originally constructed in 1916 at the Crichton-Vulcan shipyard in Turku, Finland, for the Imperial Russian Navy. After Poland regained independence in 1918, the vessel was acquired in 1921 and renamed in honor of General Józef Haller, a leading figure in the Polish military. The ship measured 55 meters long, displaced 342 tons, and was armed with two 76mm guns, four machine guns, and could carry up to 30 naval mines. During the interwar years, Generał Haller served mainly as a training ship and minelayer. By 1939, she formed part of Poland’s small coastal defense force. At the outbreak of WWII, she was stationed at Gdynia under the command of Captain Stanisław Mieszkowski. Following German air attacks, the gunboat moved to the Hel Peninsula where her weapons were stripped and used to strengthen land-based coastal defenses. On 6 September 1939, ORP General Haller was sunk by Luftwaffe bombing.

card_event_orp_orzel.name: card_event_orp_orzel
card_event_orp_orzel.title: ORP ORZEŁ
card_event_orp_orzel.text: Increase the cost of a known card in the enemy hand by 2.
card_event_orp_orzel.flavorText: ORP Orzeł was a submarine serving in the Polish Navy during WWII and is best known for the Orzeł incident, where it escaped capture from Estonia during the Soviet occupation of the Baltics in 1939. The crew sailed the ship to the United Kingdom where it was eventually brought into the service of the 2nd Submarine Flotilla of the Royal Navy and used for patrol missions in the North Sea. The Orzeł participated in the Norwegian Campaign where it managed to sink a German troop transport ship, killing hundreds of German troops on their way to invade Norway. A few weeks later, during its seventh patrol in May 1940, the submarine went missing and was presumed sunk.

card_event_pilot_escape.name: card_event_pilot_escape
card_event_pilot_escape.title: PILOT ESCAPE
card_event_pilot_escape.text: Develop an air unit of your main nation. It costs 1 less to deploy and operate.
card_event_pilot_escape.flavorText: After the collapse of Poland in 1939, thousands of Polish airmen began a determined effort to escape captivity and continue the fight. Many crossed into Romania and Hungary, where they faced internment. Despite the risk, hundreds managed to escape these camps, using false documents, bribery, or local support. Their goal was to flee occupied Europe entirely and reach France. By early 1940, over 1,200 Polish airmen had escaped to France. When France fell in June, they had to escape again. With the help of French and British forces, most Polish pilots crossed the Channel to reach Great-Britain. In total, more than 8,400 Polish air personnel escaped to the UK. Every successful escape was an act of courage and determination, and brought experienced airmen closer to battle. Many of them joined the Royal Air Force and formed units like No. 303 Squadron, which became one of the most performant fighter units during the Battle of Britain.

card_event_plan_west.name: card_event_plan_west
card_event_plan_west.title: PLAN WEST
card_event_plan_west.text: Add two LEGIONS to your support line.
card_event_plan_west.flavorText: Plan West (Polish: Plan Zachód) was a Polish military plan that predicted a German invasion from the west. The Polish Army came up with the plan in the late 1930s, but up to that moment most of their defensive measures had been focused on the Polish-Soviet border in the east. The plan correctly assumed the size and location of the German attacks, but it had several shortcomings such as never having undergone a military exercise and it greatly underestimated German mobility and the blitzkrieg strategy.

card_event_punish.name: card_event_punish
card_event_punish.title: PUNISH
card_event_punish.text: The enemy discards a random card. Draw a card if it was known.
card_event_punish.flavorText: In Poland, during the months prior to the outbreak of WWII, a number of volunteers came forward to pilot torpedoes directed against German warships. A Bureau of Living Torpedoes was established to coordinate and train these volunteers, and to procure suitable equipment. However, no sufficient progress was made before the German invasion and occupation occurred, but the volunteers were used for other combat tasks and special operations.

card_event_rapid_response.name: card_event_rapid_response
card_event_rapid_response.title: RAPID RESPONSE
card_event_rapid_response.text: Add a LEGIONS unit to your support line for each enemy unit in the frontline.
card_event_rapid_response.flavorText: An example of a prompt mobilization by the Polish army during WWII was during the defense of Wizna. In September 1939, during the German invasion of Poland, a small contingent of Polish soldiers, consisting of approximately 720 men led by Captain Władysław Raginis, defended the Wizna fortress against more than 40,000 Germans.The Polish defenders held their ground for three days, despite being heavily outnumbered and outgunned. They repelled numerous German assaults and inflicted significant casualties on the enemy. Although eventually overrun due to lack of ammunition and reinforcements, the determined resistance of the Polish soldiers at Wizna became a symbol of bravery and defiance during the early days of the war.

card_event_romanian_bridgehead.name: card_event_romanian_bridgehead
card_event_romanian_bridgehead.title: ROMANIAN BRIDGEHEAD
card_event_romanian_bridgehead.text: Give target unit +2+2 and Blitz. Destroy it in 2 turns.
card_event_romanian_bridgehead.flavorText: The Romanian Bridgehead was a strategic fallback plan for the Polish Army during WWII, designed as a last resort in case of a full-scale German and Soviet invasion. The plan involved retreating Polish forces to southeastern Poland, near the border with Romania, in a region that is now part of Ukraine. The area’s rugged terrain, rivers, and natural defenses were expected to slow enemy advances, allowing Poland to regroup and receive potential aid from Britain and France through Romanian ports. However, the Soviet invasion on September 17th, 1939, alongside the ongoing German offensive, made the plan impossible to execute effectively. As a result, many Polish government officials, military leaders, and troops crossed into Romania, where they were interned, but they later escaped to continue fighting with the Allies. Despite its failure, the Romanian Bridgehead remains a key part of Poland’s WWII defense strategy.

card_event_section_ii.name: card_event_section_ii
card_event_section_ii.title: SECTION II
card_event_section_ii.flavorText: The Second department of Polish General Staff of the Polish Army, also known as Section II, was responsible for military intelligence, cryptography and analysis of foreign affairs. The department existed officially from 1918-1939, but after the German invasion of Poland almost all commanders of Section II managed to escape the country and resumed their work with French and British intelligence agencies. After the fall of France the agency worked mostly from Britain, but had an elaborate network of agents who supplied information to the Allies throughout the war which made a significant difference in the war effort. Members of Section II also developed techniques to decipher the German Enigma enciphered messages that formed the basis of the Enigma decryption that was later developed by the British at  Bletchley Park.

card_event_stretch_the_line.name: card_event_stretch_the_line
card_event_stretch_the_line.title: STRETCH THE LINE
card_event_stretch_the_line.text: Add a LEGIONS to your support line then Intel equal to friendly LEGIONS.
card_event_stretch_the_line.flavorText: The Battle of Mokra, which took place on September 1st, 1939, was a significant engagement during the German invasion of Poland and marked one of the first major clashes between Polish and German forces during WWII. Situated near the town of Mokra in southern Poland, the battle unfolded as part of the broader defensive efforts against the German advance. Polish defenders, consisting of the Volhynian Cavalry Brigade and elements of the 7th Infantry Division, confronted two German panzer divisions and two infantry divisions. Despite being outnumbered and outgunned, the Polish forces skillfully employed anti-tank weapons, including 37mm anti-tank guns and improvised Molotov cocktails, to inflict significant casualties on the German armored units. By the end of the battle, the Poles had destroyed over 50 German tanks and inflicted 800 casualties in one of the only Polish victories of the war. The determined resistance at Mokra disrupted the German timetable and temporarily halted their advance, allowing Polish forces to regroup and reinforce their defenses in other sectors. While ultimately unable to prevent the German conquest of Poland, the Battle of Mokra demonstrated Polish resolve and ingenuity in the face of overwhelming odds.

card_event_stubborn_defense.name: card_event_stubborn_defense
card_event_stubborn_defense.title: STUBBORN DEFENSE
card_event_stubborn_defense.text: When a friendly unit is attacked, give it +1 defense before damage. Draw a card if your unit survives.
card_event_stubborn_defense.flavorText: The Battle of Westerplatte was fought between 1-7 September in 1939 in the Free City of Danzig, now Gdańsk, and is one of the first battles of WWII. The heroic Polish defense against the overwhelming German forces was at the time an inspiration for the Polish Army and is still considered a symbol of Polish fight for freedom in the 20th century. The battle ended with the surrender of the Polish forces, but during the course of the fight they managed to repel 13 assaults that were supported by dive bomber attacks and naval bombardment. Of the approximately Polish 200 defenders, 15 were killed and 40 wounded, the rest were captured. Approximately 200 Germans were killed in the battle and 150 were wounded.

card_event_underground_state.name: card_event_underground_state
card_event_underground_state.title: UNDERGROUND STATE
card_event_underground_state.text: Target enemy unit Retreats. Add a LEGIONS to your support line.
card_event_underground_state.flavorText: The Polish Underground State (Polish: Polskie Państwo Podziemne), also known as the Polish Secret State, was an organization that was built in secrecy in Poland during the Soviet and German occupation. The organization started to form in 1939, a few days before Poland surrendered, and was under the command of General Michal Tokarzewski-Karaszewicz. It was a complex organization, with its own administration, judiciary system, media, educational facilities, its own army and it worked closely together with the Polish Government in Exile. The main goal of the organization was to fight the occupation and to reestablish the Polish state through any means possible, such as armed resistance, sabotage, espionage, propaganda etc. Ultimately hundreds of thousands of people were directly involved with various agencies of the Underground State.

card_event_uprising.name: card_event_uprising
card_event_uprising.title: UPRISING
card_event_uprising.text: Deal damage to all units equal to Polish units destroyed this battle.
card_event_uprising.flavorText: The Warsaw Uprising was a major military operation that took place in the summer of 1944. The operation was led by the Polish resistance Home Army and the aim was to liberate Warsaw from German occupation. At the time the Soviet forces were at the gates of Warsaw and the goal was to keep up the fight until Soviet forces arrived. However, this never happened and the Soviet forces stood by and watched while the Germans defeated the Polish resistance. After getting air clearance from the Soviets, the British and Americans managed to supply the Polish resistance from air, but to no avail. Much of the supplies ended up in German hands, and even if everything had reached the intended recipients it is unlikely that it would have changed the outcome. After 63 days of fighting the Germans had crushed the resistance and it is believed that between 150-200,000 civilians died during the fight. A total of 16,000 resistance fighters were KIA, 6,000 wounded and 15,000 were taken prisoners. The exact numbers of German casualties are not known and the estimates differ widely depending on the source. 2,000-17,000 Germans were killed, 9,000 wounded, 0-7,000 MIA and 2,000-5,000 were taken prisoners.

card_event_zamosc_uprising.name: card_event_zamosc_uprising
card_event_zamosc_uprising.title: ZAMOŚĆ UPRISING
card_event_zamosc_uprising.flavorText: The Zamość uprising was an armed resistance movement from Polish partisans against German forces in the Zamość region of occupied Poland during WWII. It took place from 1942 to 1944 as the Germans attempted to clear the area of its Polish population to make way for German settlers as part of the "Lebensraum" (living space) policy. The local Polish resistance, primarily members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie) with support from Soviet partisans, fought back with sabotage, ambushes, and guerrilla tactics. Despite having limited resources, the partisans managed to disrupt the German plans and to protect many Polish civilians, until the Germans started to lose control of the region in the spring of 1943. The Zamość uprising became a symbol of Polish resistance against the German occupation.

card_event_lysander_pl.name: card_event_lysander_pl
card_event_lysander_pl.title: LYSANDER PL
card_event_lysander_pl.text: When the enemy plays a known card, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_event_lysander_pl.flavorText: The Westland Lysander was a British made cooperation and liaison aircraft that came into service in 1938 and was used by RAF and Allied air forces during WWII. The aircraft was mainly used for artillery spotting or message and supply drops, but was withdrawn from combat duties after the Battle of France due to high losses inflicted by German fighters. For the remainder of the war the Lysander served mainly in liaison and air-sea rescue roles. The aircraft was used to maintain contact with the French Resistance, for supply drops, delivering and retrieving agents or to rescue downed pilots that were sheltered in France. Several Lysander aircraft were used by the No. 309 Polish Fighter-Reconnaissance Squadron, but from 1942 the squadron started to transition to Mustangs. A total 1,786 Westland Lysander’s were built, including a few variants.

card_unit_12th_ulan.name: card_unit_12th_ulan
card_unit_12th_ulan.title: 12th UŁAN
card_unit_12th_ulan.flavorText: The 12th Podolian Uhlan Regiment was one of Poland’s most storied cavalry units, tracing its traditions back to Napoleonic times and fighting continuously for Polish independence and survival across generations. Officially re-formed in 1919, the regiment distinguished itself in the Polish–Soviet War, taking part in major cavalry actions such as the Battle of Komarów, one of the largest cavalry engagements of the 20th century. During the interwar years, the 12th Uhlans were stationed in Volhynia and became part of Poland’s mobile cavalry forces, combining traditional horsemanship with modern tactics. In September 1939, the regiment was mobilized as part of the Wołyń Cavalry Brigade and fought fiercely against German armored units during the opening battles of the invasion of Poland, including actions around Mokra. Though forced to destroy their regimental flag to prevent its capture after the Soviet invasion, the legacy of the 12th Uhlans endured. It was reformed later within the Polish forces fighting alongside the Allies, but by then the unit had been transformed into infantry. The regiment went on to fight in Italy, earning lasting renown at Monte Cassino in 1944. In October 1946, it embarked from Naples and was transported to Great Britain, where it was officially disbanded on May 6, 1947.

card_unit_15th_wolves_regiment.name: card_unit_15th_wolves_regiment
card_unit_15th_wolves_regiment.title: 15th WOLVES REGIMENT
card_unit_15th_wolves_regiment.text: Deployment: Convert target unit into ROUTED TROOPS. Draw 2 cards if it was friendly.
card_unit_15th_wolves_regiment.flavorText: The 15th Infantry Regiment, a unit of the Polish Army, belonged to the 28th Infantry Division at the start of WWII. It earned its "Wolves" nickname for its relentless combat style during the Polish-Soviet War (1919–21), and its badge featured four wolf heads. In the opening days of the German invasion of Poland, as part of the Łódź Army, the regiment engaged in fierce defensive battles near the Warta River, delaying the enemy’s advance. During the defense of Pabianice on September 7, the regiment held off assaults by the SS Division "Leibstandarte Adolf Hitler", inflicting heavy losses. A few hours later, while retreating toward Łódź, they suffered severe casualties during a German ambush. Elements of the regiment then participated in engagements near Stryków and Warsaw’s outskirts. By mid-September, remnants regrouped and helped defend the Modlin Fortress until its capitulation on September 29. After the fall of Poland, surviving members continued to fight within various formations. Some joined the Polish Underground State, fighting in the Home Army, while others escaped and served with Polish forces in exile. In July 1944, with Soviet support, the regiment was reformed as part of the 5th Infantry Division of the Polish People's Army. It fought in major eastern front battles, including the crossing of the Oder River and the Battle of Berlin.

card_unit_16th_tarnow_regiment.name: card_unit_16th_tarnow_regiment
card_unit_16th_tarnow_regiment.title: 16th TARNOW REGIMENT
card_unit_16th_tarnow_regiment.text: When you play an Intel card, add a LEGIONS to the support line and draw a card.
card_unit_16th_tarnow_regiment.flavorText: The 16th Land of Tarnow Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 6th Infantry Division of the Polish Army. The division was formed in 1918 and fought in the Polish–Soviet War between 1919-1921. In 1939 the division was part of the Kraków Army and during the invasion of Poland it defended against the German 5th Panzer Division in the villages of Brzezce and Wisla Wielkathat that are located in the south of Poland. During the battle the 6th Division suffered heavy casualties, but managed to hold its positions until ordered to withdraw. The division would continue the fighting near Biskupice Radłowskie and later in the Battle of Tomaszów Lubelski where it surrendered to the German forces on September 20.

card_unit_1st_grenadier_regiment.name: card_unit_1st_grenadier_regiment
card_unit_1st_grenadier_regiment.title: 1st GRENADIER REGIMENT
card_unit_1st_grenadier_regiment.text: Enemy units that damage anything but this unit are destroyed.
card_unit_1st_grenadier_regiment.flavorText: The 1st Grenadier Regiment was part of the Polish 1st Grenadier Division during WWII. The division was formed in France in 1939 after Poland’s defeat in the initial German invasion as a part of the Polish Army in France. The creation of Polish formations in France marked the beginnings of the Polish Armed Forces in the West. Composed of Polish soldiers who had fled to France and of Polish workers who had migrated to France before the war, the division was led by General Bronisław Duch and became the largest Polish unit in the French Army, with more than 16,000 members. The division saw significant action in the Battle of France in 1940, where it held defensive positions and inflicted losses on the advancing German forces. However, after suffering heavy casualties and facing encirclement, the division was ultimately ordered to disband and flee to prevent capture. During the Battle of France, the division lost approximately 5,200 men, but many of those who managed to escape would later join the Polish resistance or the British forces in Britain, where they continued the fight.

card_unit_24th_uhlan.name: card_unit_24th_uhlan
card_unit_24th_uhlan.title: 24th UŁAN
card_unit_24th_uhlan.text: Is dealt 1 damage at the end of your turn unless a unit was destroyed.
card_unit_24th_uhlan.flavorText: The 24th Ulan Regiment of the Grand Chancellor of the Crown Stanisław Żółkiewski was a cavalry unit of the Polish Army that fought during WWII, particularly in the Invasion of Poland in September 1939. Formed as part of Poland’s traditional uhlan (light cavalry) forces, the regiment belonged to the 10th Motorized Cavalry Brigade, which was one of the first Polish units to be fully motorized. During the German invasion, the 24th Uhlan Regiment fought in several key battles, using a mix of cavalry and mechanized tactics to delay the advancing German Wehrmacht. The regiment fought in the Battles of Jordanów and Wysoka, as well as in Łańcut, Rzeszów, and Radymno. On September 19th, 1939, it crossed into Hungary, avoiding capture by German or Soviet forces. In recognition of its soldiers' bravery, the unit was awarded the Virtuti Militari. In 1940, the regiment was reformed in France and later in England. From 1943 the regiment fought in Western Europe as part of the 10th Armoured Cavalry Brigade.

card_unit_28th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_28th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_28th_infantry_regiment.title: 28th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_28th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 28th Infantry Regiment “Kaniów Riflemen” was based in Łódź and formed part of the Polish Army’s 10th Infantry Division. Together with the 30th and 31st Infantry Regiments and the 10th Light Artillery Regiment, it made up the division’s main combat strength in 1939. The 10th Infantry Division had been created in 1919 from the former Polish 4th Rifle Division and was also headquartered in Łódź. At the outbreak of WWII, it belonged to the Łódź Army under General Franciszek Dindorf-Ankowicz and was tasked with defending the fortified area along the upper Warta River, near the German border. From the morning of 1 September 1939, the division came under heavy attacks by the German Eighth Army, supported by aircraft and artillery. It held its positions until 3 September, when it was ordered to withdraw toward Sieradz. Communication and organizational problems delayed the movement, allowing German troops to cross the Warta. After further fighting against the German 10th and 24th Infantry Divisions, the 10th Division was defeated and scattered by 8 September, although some survivors later crossed the Vistula near Otwock.

card_unit_2nd_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_2nd_infantry_regiment
card_unit_2nd_infantry_regiment.title: 2nd INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_2nd_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Get the combat keywords of a target unit.
card_unit_2nd_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 2nd Infantry Regiment was part of the 1st Tadeusz Kościuszko Infantry Division, the first Polish unit formed under Soviet command during WWII. Established in 1943 near the Oka River, this division marked the revival of Polish armed forces in the East. It was named in honor of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a national hero in both Poland and the US, where he fought in the American revolutionary war. Trained and equipped by the Red Army, the division included many Polish citizens released from Soviet labor camps and prisons. Soviet officers initially held most command positions. The unit saw its first combat during the Battle of Lenino in October 1943. Despite heavy casualties and mixed results, Lenino served as a symbol of Poland’s renewed military effort against Nazi Germany. The division grew into a full army corps and later formed the core of the Polish First Army. It took part in major operations, including the liberation of Warsaw and the storming of Berlin. By the end of the war, the division had become a significant force.

card_unit_35th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_35th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_35th_infantry_regiment.title: 35th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_35th_infantry_regiment.text: When an enemy unit moves into the frontline, your units get +1+1.
card_unit_35th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: At the outbreak of WWII  35th Infantry Regiment was part of the 9th Infantry Division, also known as the 9th Infantry "Wielkopolska" Division, and was one of the major divisions of the Polish Army during the war. The division was formed in 1919 and played a significant role in the defense of Poland during the German invasion in September 1939, including the Battle of Bzura, where it was defeated by the German forces. The 9th Infantry Division defended a 70-kilometer line in Polish Pomerania as part of the Pomorze Army. They faced attacks from three Wehrmacht divisions and withdrew to the Cekcyn area. The Germans broke their defense line, and the division retreated to the outskirts of Bydgoszcz after crossing the Brda River. The 35th Infantry Regiment defended against the German 2nd Motorized Infantry Division, while the 22nd Infantry Regiment faced the 32nd Infantry Division along the Brda River. Following their defeat, the 9th Infantry Division regrouped in the woodlands to the north of Bydgoszcz where they came under attack from the Luftwaffe. With no means to defend themselves and lacking air support, the division disintegrated and ceased to exist. The sole exception was the 35th Infantry Regiment, which managed to successfully break out of the German encirclement on September 5th. Later in the war, the 9th Infantry Division was reconstituted as part of the Polish Armed Forces in the West and participated in the Italian Campaign, contributing to the liberation of Italy.

card_unit_37mm_bofors_gun.name: card_unit_37mm_bofors_gun
card_unit_37mm_bofors_gun.title: 37mm BOFORS GUN
card_unit_37mm_bofors_gun.text: When an enemy unit moves into the frontline, deal 1 damage to it.
card_unit_37mm_bofors_gun.flavorText: The Bofors 37 mm was a Swedish anti-tank gun that was exported to several countries in the 1930s and many bought the license to produce it themselves. Poland bought 300 guns from Sweden and several hundred more were produced by SMPzA in Pruszków. At the start of WWII the Polish Army had around 1,200 pieces, including a tank variant that was designated wz.37. The 37mm Bofors gun was effective against early models of medium and light tanks but by 1941 it was considered obsolete.

card_unit_3rd_carpathian.name: card_unit_3rd_carpathian
card_unit_3rd_carpathian.title: 3rd CARPATHIAN
card_unit_3rd_carpathian.text: Deployment: Convert a friendly unit into 24th UŁAN.
card_unit_3rd_carpathian.flavorText: The 3rd Battalion of Carpathian Rifles was a unit of the Polish Independent Carpathian Rifle Brigade, formed on 12 April 1940 in French-controlled Syria as part of the Polish Army in France, comprising Polish soldiers who had escaped occupied Poland following the 1939 invasion. Under the command of General Stanisław Kopański, the brigade was modeled after a French mountain infantry unit and initially served under the French Armée du Levant. Following France's capitulation in June 1940, the brigade refused to align with the Vichy regime. On 30 June 1940, it relocated to British-controlled Palestine, integrating into the British Army and reorganizing as a motorized infantry brigade. In August 1941, the brigade was shipped to the besieged port of Tobruk in Libya. There, it played a significant role in the defense against Axis forces, particularly during Operation Crusader, which lifted the siege in December 1941. Alongside their Australian allies, they were nicknamed the "Rats of Tobruk" by German propaganda and reclaimed the name as a badge of pride. On 3 May 1942, it was reorganized into the 3rd Carpathian Rifle Division, forming a core component of the Polish II Corps.

card_unit_4tp.name: card_unit_4tp
card_unit_4tp.title: 4TP
card_unit_4tp.text: Destroy this unit after it attacks the enemy HQ.
card_unit_4tp.flavorText: The 4TP (also designated PZInż. 140) was a Polish light reconnaissance tank prototype developed in the mid-1930s as part of the efforts to modernize the country’s armored forces. The tank was designed by engineer Edward Habich at Państwowe Zakłady Inżynierii (PZInż) and his goal was to replace outdated TK-3 and TKS tankettes with a more capable vehicle featuring a rotating turret and enhanced firepower. It was inspired by British Vickers-Carden-Loyd designs, but incorporated Polish innovations such as a torsion bar suspension, a domestically built 95-horsepower PZInż. 425 engine, and a reversible periscope. With a top speed of 55 km/h and a range of 450 km, it was agile and suited for reconnaissance, despite its thin armor (8 to 17 mm) and weak proposed armament: a 20 mm autocannon and a 7.92 mm machine gun. The prototype underwent extensive trials from 1937 to 1939, covering over 4,300 km without major mechanical failures, proving its reliability. Despite plans to produce 480 units for infantry divisions and motorized brigades, the project was canceled in 1939.

card_unit_5th_legions_regiment.name: card_unit_5th_legions_regiment
card_unit_5th_legions_regiment.title: 5th LEGIONS REGIMENT
card_unit_5th_legions_regiment.flavorText: The 5th Legions Infantry Regiment was an infantry regiment of the Polish Army from 1918-1939. In 1939, during the defense of Poland the regiment was part of the 1st Legions Infantry Division. The division was part of Operational Group Wyszków and was tasked with defending the north of Warsaw against German attacks from East Prussia. The regiment would see some heavy fighting during the Battle of Kałuszy and the Battle of Seroczyn against Panzer Division Kempf, where they suffered heavy casualties. The remaining survivors of the 5th Regiment surrendered to the German forces on 23 September near the city of Zamość.

card_unit_5th_wilno_regiment.name: card_unit_5th_wilno_regiment
card_unit_5th_wilno_regiment.title: 5th WILNO BRIGADE
card_unit_5th_wilno_regiment.text: Deployment: Convert this unit into target unit.
card_unit_5th_wilno_regiment.flavorText: The 5th Wilno Brigade was part of the 5th Kresowa Infantry Division, a Polish unit formed in 1943 in the Middle East under British command. The division drew its manpower from Polish soldiers who had been released from Soviet labor camps after the Sikorski-Mayski Agreement. Composed mostly of men from Poland's eastern territories, the 5th Kresowa Infantry Division was trained and equipped by the British and became part of the Polish II Corps under General Władysław Anders. It first saw combat in the Italian Campaign, beginning in early 1944. It played a crucial role during the Fourth Battle of Monte Cassino, capturing the strategic Hill 593 while enduring heavy losses. After Cassino, the division continued its advance through Italy, participating in the battles of Ancona and for the Gothic Line. It was known for its determination and resilience despite limited reinforcements. By the end of the war, the 5th Kresowa had suffered over 5,000 casualties. The unit remained in Italy until 1946, then demobilized in the United Kingdom. Many of its soldiers stayed there, whether by choice or not.

card_unit_6th_infantry_brigade.name: card_unit_6th_infantry_brigade
card_unit_6th_infantry_brigade.title: 6th INFANTRY BRIGADE
card_unit_6th_infantry_brigade.text: Deployment: Has 0 operation cost this turn.
card_unit_6th_infantry_brigade.flavorText: The 6th Lwów Infantry Brigade was one of the main infantry brigades of the Polish 5th Kresowa Infantry Division. It served alongside the 5th Wilno Infantry Brigade, with the 4th Wołyń Infantry Brigade added in 1945. The brigade’s name recalled the city of Lwów and the lost eastern borderlands of the Second Polish Republic, a strong theme in the division’s identity. The 5th Kresowa Infantry Division was formed in the Middle East in March 1943 from Polish forces that had left the Soviet Union and regrouped under Allied command. It became part of General Władysław Anders’ Polish II Corps, serving with the British Eighth Army in the Italian Campaign. The division landed in southern Italy in February 1944 and entered combat the next month. In May, it fought in the final Battle of Monte Cassino, where it suffered a 15% casualty rate. It then took part in the Battle of Ancona, fought near the Gothic Line, and joined the final Allied offensive in 1945, advancing to Bologna. During its service in Italy, the division suffered 5,127 casualties, including 1,063 killed.

card_unit_74th_silesian_regiment.name: card_unit_74th_silesian_regiment
card_unit_74th_silesian_regiment.title: 74th SILESIAN REGIMENT
card_unit_74th_silesian_regiment.text: When an enemy unit moves into the frontline, pin it.
card_unit_74th_silesian_regiment.flavorText: The 74th Upper Silesian Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 7th Infantry Division of the Polish Army. In 1939 the division was attached to the Kraków Army which defended the southwest corner of Poland during the German invasion. The division was involved in heavy fighting before being forced to retreat and take up defenses near the town of Lelów. There the division was encircled by the German forces, and although elements of the 74th Regiment along with some cavalry and sappers managed to break out of the encirclement, the division surrendered as it had suffered such heavy casualties that it was no longer capable of fighting. During Operation Tempest (1944-1945), a series of uprising by the Polish Home Army against the German occupation, the 7th Infantry Division was recreated with the 74th and 27th Regiment. The division took part in heavy fighting against the Germans, but most men ceased fighting after central Poland had been taken over by the Soviets. Many of the men went back underground as they feared being arrested the Soviet NKVD due to their anti-Soviet and anti-communist sentiments.

card_unit_78th_steel_regiment.name: card_unit_78th_steel_regiment
card_unit_78th_steel_regiment.title: 78th STEEL REGIMENT
card_unit_78th_steel_regiment.text: Deployment: Gets +2+2 for each enemy unit in the frontline.
card_unit_78th_steel_regiment.flavorText: The 78th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 20th Infantry Division of the Polish Army which was formed in 1920. In the summer of 1939 it was part of the Modlin Army which was tasked with defending the area near the interwar border of Poland and East Prussia. Between September 1st and 3rd, 1939, during the September Campaign, the 20th Infantry Division defended positions in the Battle of Mława against the German I Army Corps, consisting of the 11th Infantry Division, 61st Infantry Division and the Panzer Division Kempf. The German forces failed in their first attacks and lost approximately 25 tanks. On September 2, the Germans tried and failed again, but subsequently they managed to organize a successful offensive and to break through Polish positions on September 3rd. An attempted counter-attack by the Polish 8th Infantry Division failed, resulting in a chaotic retreat. Given the challenging circumstances, the 20th Infantry Division was ordered to withdraw on the night of September 3rd. They were bombed by the Germans and reached the Płock area around September 7th, where remnants of the division entered Warsaw to participate in its defense. Finally the division surrendered along with the Warsaw garrison on September 28th.The German forces that faced the 20th Infantry Division at Mława nicknamed it the "Steel Division".

card_unit_7tp.name: card_unit_7tp
card_unit_7tp.title: 7TP
card_unit_7tp.text: Draw a card the first time a friendly unit survives combat each turn.
card_unit_7tp.flavorText: The 7TP was a Polish modification of the British Vickers 6-ton Mark E tank which was produced in Poland under license. Around 149 7TP tanks were produced from 1935-1939 and the tanks were used in the defense of Poland in 1939. The tank had a main armament of a 37 mm Bofors wz. 37 gun which gave it enough firepower to penetrate the armor of any German tank, but its light armor made it vulnerable, especially against air attacks. The 7TP had a secondary armament of a 7.92 mm Ckm wz.30 machine gun and was operated by a crew of 3 (commander, gunner, driver).

card_unit_danuta.name: card_unit_danuta
card_unit_danuta.title: DANUTA
card_unit_danuta.text: At the start of your turn, add a 4TP to your support line with Blitz. Destroy it end of turn.
card_unit_danuta.flavorText: The Danuta was a Polish armored train used during WWII, primarily in the Invasion of Poland in September 1939. Originally built in 1919, it was part of Poland’s small but effective fleet of armored trains, designed for troop support, and mobile defense. Following Poland’s mobilization in 1939, the Danuta armored train was attached to the Poznań Army. During the initial phase of the invasion, it provided support to Polish infantry units. On September 4th, the train came under attack by Luftwaffe bombers but sustained only minor damage. Later, it took part in the Battle of the Bzura, a major Polish counteroffensive. By 16 September, the Danuta successfully stalled the German 24th Infantry Division’s advance and attempted to retreat toward the Polish 16th Infantry Division. However, it was ambushed by German anti-tank artillery during the withdrawal. Severely damaged and with ammunition nearly exhausted, the train’s commander, Captain Korobowicz, ordered its destruction to prevent capture. The crew detonated the train, inflicting casualties on pursuing German infantry. Amongst the scouting tanks deployed from the train, five TKS tankettes escaped, while two obsolete FT-17 tanks were destroyed to avoid their capture by German forces.

card_unit_fairey_battle_elit.name: card_unit_fairey_battle_elit
card_unit_fairey_battle_elit.title: BATTLE Mk I PL
card_unit_fairey_battle_elit.text: When you deploy another Exile unit, give it +1+1.
card_unit_fairey_battle_elit.flavorText: The Fairey Battle was a British light bomber that was produced between 1937-1940 and used during WWII by the RAF and Allied air forces. At the start of the war the Fairey Battle was already obsolete but it remained in frontline service due to lack of replacements. The aircraft was considered easy to fly and it could take damage, but it was no match against the modern German fighters. At the start of the war the Battle was used for reconnaissance missions but later it would be called on for ground attack roles in an desperate attempt to stop the German advance. However, in 1940 most Fairey Battle aircraft had been pulled from frontline service. The Fairey Battle was used by four Polish bomber squadrons in the RAF.

card_unit_iron_division.name: card_unit_iron_division
card_unit_iron_division.title: IRON DIVISION
card_unit_iron_division.text: At the start of your turn, draw a card. Destroy this unit after the third time.
card_unit_iron_division.flavorText: The 1st Legions Infantry Division was formed in 1919 and saw extensive action during the Polish-Soviet War (1919–1921). During the German invasion of Poland in September 1939, the division, commanded by Col. Wincenty Kowalski, was deployed as part of the Modlin Army near the border with East Prussia. Fully mobilized after the invasion began, the division first engaged German troops on 4 September 1939 near Długosiodło. It successfully repelled a German assault near Brańszczyk, conducting delaying actions while retreating toward Kałuszyn. On 11 September, German forces captured the town, but the division recaptured it after intense night fighting. On 13 September, the division launched a counterattack in the Battle of Kałuszyn, breaking through multiple German defensive lines but suffering heavy casualties, losing most of its artillery and supplies. The remaining scattered troops regrouped, with the largest contingent under Gen. Kowalski, now reduced to only three infantry companies. They later joined Polish forces under Gen. Stefan Dąb-Biernacki and took part in the Battle of Falków on 22 September, securing a victory against the German 8th Infantry Division. Soon after, the division ceased to exist as a combat force. Despite its losses, it distinguished itself during the invasion of Poland and was regarded by Wehrmacht soldiers as the "Iron Division".

card_unit_legion_pol.name: card_unit_legion_pol
card_unit_legion_pol.title: LEGIONS
card_unit_legion_pol.text: Gets +1+1 when you play a card with Intel.

card_unit_lublin_r_xiii.name: card_unit_lublin_r_xiii
card_unit_lublin_r_xiii.title: LUBLIN R-XIII
card_unit_lublin_r_xiii.text:
Cards you play have Intel 1.
Deployment: Reveal target Covert unit.
card_unit_lublin_r_xiii.flavorText: The Lublin R-XIII was a reconnaissance and light bomber aircraft primarily used by the Polish Air Force during WWII, particularly in the early stages of the conflict. The Polish aircraft manufacturer Plage i Laśkiewicz built the aircraft in the 1930s and it proved to be an effective asset for its purpose. On the eve of the Invasion of Poland in 1939, the Polish Air Force had about 150 R-XIII at their disposal, but only 49 of them were combat ready. The rest were in reserve, used for training purposes or in repairs. The R-XIII turned out to be inferior to all Luftwaffe aircraft, including fighters, bombers, and reconnaissance planes, due to its slower speed and limited armament consisting of just one machine gun. However, it proved itself useful in close reconnaissance and liaison duties and was actively employed in these roles. A total of 273 Lublin R-XIII were built, including a few variants, and none have survived until today.

card_unit_p37los.name: card_unit_p37los
card_unit_p37los.title: PZL.37 ŁOŚ
card_unit_p37los.text: When a friendly Polish air unit is destroyed, add a random Polish exile card to hand.
card_unit_p37los.flavorText: The PZL.37 Łoś was a Polish twin engined medium bomber that was first introduced to service in 1938. When it was first introduced it was considered to be one of the most advanced operational bombers in the world. At the start of WWII the Polish air force had 86 PZL.37’s in their service, but less than half of those were operational, some were in maintenance, others were being held in reserve or used for training purposes. The PZL’s that were operational managed to inflict considerable damage upon advancing German columns, but many were lost in combat due to lack of fighter protection. By 1940 many of the PZL’s had been evacuated to Romania where they were later seized by the Romanian government and used by the Romanian Air Force against the Allies. Over 120 PZL.37 Łoś were manufactured from 1938-1939, including variants. No PZL.37 Łoś aircraft remain today.

card_unit_polish_hurricane.name: card_unit_polish_hurricane
card_unit_polish_hurricane.title: HURRICANE PL
card_unit_polish_hurricane.text: Deployment: Give another friendly Exile unit +1+1 and -1 operation cost.
card_unit_polish_hurricane.flavorText: After the fall of Poland, the Polish Fighter Squadrons that were flying for RAF were initially issued Hurricanes. The highest scoring Hurricane squadron during the Battle of Britain was the No. 303 Polish Fighter Squadron, with 126 claimed kills vs 18 losses in 6 weeks, which also was the highest kill-to-loss ratio during the battle. For comparison, one British pilot was killed for every downed enemy aircraft, but the Poles downed 10.5 enemy aircraft per pilot death. What gave the Poles the edge was the fact that they were older and more experienced, plus they had learned to fly on more primitive aircraft in Poland, which helped them to take advantage of the extra speed and manoeuvrability that the Hurricane gave them. But above all, the Poles were super-vigilant in their cockpits, always on the alert and ready to react.

card_unit_polish_sherman.name: card_unit_polish_sherman
card_unit_polish_sherman.title: M4 SHERMAN PL
card_unit_polish_sherman.text: Has Blitz and operates for free if you have played an Exile card this turn.
card_unit_polish_sherman.flavorText: Both the 1st Polish Armored Division and the Polish 2nd Armored Brigade saw extensive action against the Axis forces on the Western front from 1944 to 1945. Both units were equipped with armored vehicles that were supplied by the Americans and the British, many of these were Sherman tanks.

card_unit_pzl_11.name: card_unit_pzl_11
card_unit_pzl_11.title: PZL P.11
card_unit_pzl_11.flavorText: The PZL P.11 was a Polish fighter aircraft that was introduced in 1934 and used during WWII by the Polish Air Force. At the start of the war the Polish Air Force had around 160 PZL P.11’s  available and for most parts they were no match to the modern aircraft used by the German Luftwaffe. A third of the PZL P.11’s were armed with four machine guns, but the rest only had two, and most of the aircraft were not equipped with a radio. Nevertheless the PZL P.11’s were better in many ways than their German counterparts, they were durable, had a good climb rate and could withstand high speed dives without risking breaking the wings off. The P.11 suffered heavy casualties during the defense of Poland in 1939 but did manage to shoot down a large number German aircraft, even though the exact number can not be verified. A total of 325 PZL P.11 were built, including a few variants.

card_unit_pzl_23_karas.name: card_unit_pzl_23_karas
card_unit_pzl_23_karas.title: PZL.23 KARAS
card_unit_pzl_23_karas.text: At the end of your turn, add a SECTION II to your hand.
card_unit_pzl_23_karas.flavorText: The PZL.23 Karas was an all-metal Polish light bomber and reconnaissance aircraft that was developed in the 1930s and used during the defense of Poland in 1939. A total of 250 PZL.23’s were built from 1936 to 1939, but only 110 were combat ready when war struck. The primary role of the PZL.23’s was to fly reconnaissance missions, but some were used in successful bombing missions, both against industrial targets in Germany and against the advancing German armies. The PZL.23’s suffered heavy casualties during the defense of Poland, both because of the lack of fighter support and due to its light armor and low speed. There are no known PZL.23s survivors of the war.

card_unit_pzl_7.name: card_unit_pzl_7
card_unit_pzl_7.title: PZL P.7
card_unit_pzl_7.text: When an enemy unit moves into the frontline, retreat this unit.
card_unit_pzl_7.flavorText: The PZL P.7 was a Polish fighter aircraft that was first introduced in 1933 and approximately 150 aircraft were built between 1932-33. Despite being obsolete at the outbreak of WWII (most had been replaced by PZL P.11 in 1935) the aircraft was used in Poland's defense against the invading German forces. Although the PZL P.7 had better maneuverability than many of its counterparts, it lacked speed and armament and stood little chance in combat. Most PZL P.7 fighters owned by the Polish Air Force were destroyed in 1939, both in combat and on the ground. A few aircraft were withdrawn to Romania or captured by the German or Soviet forces and used for training purposes.

card_unit_sherman_firefly_pl.name: card_unit_sherman_firefly_pl
card_unit_sherman_firefly_pl.title: M4 FIREFLY PL
card_unit_sherman_firefly_pl.text: When a friendly unit is attacked, give it +1+1 before damage.
card_unit_sherman_firefly_pl.flavorText: During WWII, Polish forces in exile, as part of the Western Allies, made extensive use of Sherman tanks provided by the British and Americans. After the fall of Poland in 1939, Polish military units re-formed in the United Kingdom and the Middle East, and many of these units were equipped with Sherman tanks. Units such as the 1st Polish Armoured Division, under General Stanisław Maczek, used Shermans during pivotal campaigns, including the Normandy Invasion in 1944 and the subsequent battles in France, Belgium, and the Netherlands. The division played a crucial role in the Falaise Pocket, where they helped encircle and defeat German forces, as well as in the liberation of Belgium and the push into Germany. Additionally, forces of the 2nd Polish Corps, fighting in the Italian Campaign, also utilized Sherman tanks during significant battles such as the Battle of Monte Cassino in 1944.

card_unit_spitfire_mk_v_pol.name: card_unit_spitfire_mk_v_pol
card_unit_spitfire_mk_v_pol.title: SPITFIRE Mk V PL
card_unit_spitfire_mk_v_pol.text: Deployment: Give a friendly ground unit +1+1 and Guard.
card_unit_spitfire_mk_v_pol.flavorText: The Supermarine Spitfire was a British fighter aircraft that was used in WWII and the only fighter that was in service from the start of the war in 1939 and until it ended in 1945. The Mk V variant came in three versions and had several sub-variants, and was produced in 1941. It was equipped with a Merlin 45 series engine and had several improvements that increased the aircraft maneuverability. Several Spitfire Mk V variants were flown by the Polish fighter squadrons in the RAF, most famously by Squadrons No. 303 and No. 302 who had a distinguished combat record and received several battle honours.

card_unit_sturmovik_pol.name: card_unit_sturmovik_pol
card_unit_sturmovik_pol.title: IL-2M PL
card_unit_sturmovik_pol.text: When a friendly unit with Heavy Armor survives combat, give it +1+1.
card_unit_sturmovik_pol.flavorText: The Ilyushin Il-2, also known as Sturmovik, was a Soviet ground-attack aircraft that was produced in large numbers from 1941 to 1945 and used extensively during WWII. The aircraft was nicknamed “The Flying Tank” or “Flying Infantryman” due to its thick armor and firepower that could neutralize almost any ground target. The Air Force of the Polish Army was formed in the Soviet Union in 1943 and served as part of the Polish Armed Forces in the East. Hundreds of Ilyushin Il-2’s were issued to the Polish units which were mainly used for ground attack missions, but also for reconnaissance missions and sometimes air-to-air combat.

card_unit_tks.name: card_unit_tks
card_unit_tks.title: TKS
card_unit_tks.flavorText: The TKS was a Polish tankette that was produced from 1931 to 1939 and formed the bulk of the Polish armored forces at the outbreak of WWII. The TKS tankettes stood little chance against their German counterparts as they were very small and most were only armed with a single machine gun. Most were used for reconnaissance and infantry support, but a few were armed with a 20 mm gun which made them more effective against enemy tanks.

card_unit_t_34_pol.name: card_unit_t_34_pol
card_unit_t_34_pol.title: T-34 76 PL
card_unit_t_34_pol.flavorText: The T-34 was a Soviet medium tank that was produced and used during WWII by the Red Army and their Allies. Quite a few T-34 tanks were provided to the armored formations of the Polish Armed Forces in the East. For example, the 1st Armoured Brigade of the 1st Polish Army, also known as Berling’s Army, had many T-34 tanks in their service. This unit fought many hard battles, including the Warsaw Uprising and the Battle of Berlin.

card_unit_yak_9_pl.name: card_unit_yak_9_pl
card_unit_yak_9_pl.title: YAK 9 PL
card_unit_yak_9_pl.flavorText: The Yakovlev Yak-9 was a Soviet fighter aircraft that played a significant role in the Soviet Air Force during WWII. It was a development of the earlier Yak-7 and Yak-1 fighters, incorporating improvements and modifications based on combat experience.The Yak-9 was designed by Alexander Yakovlev and entered service with the Soviet Air Force in 1942. It was a versatile aircraft that saw action in various roles, including air superiority, ground attack, and escort missions. The aircraft was known for its agility, robustness, and adaptability. While the majority of the Polish Air Force was disbanded or incorporated into foreign air forces after the German and Soviet occupations of Poland, a significant number of Polish pilots managed to escape and join Allied air forces. Some of these Polish pilots, while serving in Soviet-controlled units, flew Soviet aircraft, including the Yak-9. The most notable example is the Air Force of the Polish Army which was created alongside the Polish People's Army, a subordinate to the Red Army. It was the primary Polish air force formation within the Polish Armed Forces in the East during WWII.

card_unit_zaza_division.name: card_unit_zaza_division
card_unit_zaza_division.title: ZAZA DIVISION
card_unit_zaza_division.text: When this unit takes damage, draw a card.
card_unit_zaza_division.flavorText: The Cavalry Division Zaza was a division of the Polish Army that was formed during the Invasion of Poland in 1939. It was formed out of units of the Podlaska Cavalry Brigade and Suwalska Cavalry Brigade which had escaped the German encirclement during the invasion. The Zaza Division saw heavy fighting around the city of Lublin and later it participated in The Battle of Knock, which was the final battle in the invasion of Poland. The division surrendered on October 5 to the German forces, 17 days after it had been formed.

card_event_bomber_cost.name: card_event_bomber_cost
card_event_bomber_cost.title: LAND OF THE FREE
card_event_bomber_cost.text: Reduce cost of the highest cost bomber in your hand by your max kredit slots.

card_event_bombing_run.name: card_event_bombing_run
card_event_bombing_run.title: BOMBING RUN
card_event_bombing_run.text: Choose and discard a bomber with cost 3 or less. Deal its attack in damage to the enemy HQ.

card_event_carrier_support.name: card_event_carrier_support
card_event_carrier_support.title: CARRIER SUPPORT
card_event_carrier_support.text: Destroy an enemy unit with an attack of 2 or less, or 3 or less if you control an air unit.

card_event_dogfight_usa.name: card_event_dogfight_usa
card_event_dogfight_usa.title: DOGFIGHT
card_event_dogfight_usa.text: Choose one - Target fighter gets +3+3 OR is dealt 6 damage.

card_event_flank_attack_sov.name: card_event_flank_attack_sov
card_event_flank_attack_sov.title: FLANK ATTACK
card_event_flank_attack_sov.text: Choose one - Add 214th AMUR OR T-34 1942 to your support line.

card_event_french_promo2.name: card_event_french_promo2
card_event_french_promo2.title: OVERLOAD
card_event_french_promo2.text: Give target unit +2+2 and pin it.

card_event_inspired_tactics.name: card_event_inspired_tactics
card_event_inspired_tactics.title: INSPIRED TACTICS
card_event_inspired_tactics.text: Add the top unit of your deck with "Cannot attack the enemy HQ." to your support line with Blitz.

card_event_last_ditch.name: card_event_last_ditch
card_event_last_ditch.title: LAST DITCH
card_event_last_ditch.text: When an enemy unit destroys a friendly unit, destroy the enemy unit.

card_event_ruthless_planning.name: card_event_ruthless_planning
card_event_ruthless_planning.title: RUTHLESS PLANNING
card_event_ruthless_planning.text: Destroy a friendly unit. Draw a unit with Destruction from your deck.

card_event_secret_service.name: card_event_secret_service
card_event_secret_service.title: SECRET SERVICE
card_event_secret_service.text: Target friendly unit gets: "When you play a card with Intel, deal 1 damage to a random enemy."

card_event_soviet_promo3.name: card_event_soviet_promo3
card_event_soviet_promo3.title: FORCED MARCH
card_event_soviet_promo3.text: Choose one - add 1 OR 3 random Soviet units to your support line. Damage your HQ equal to their defense.

card_event_top_deck_play_test.name: card_event_top_deck_play_test
card_event_top_deck_play_test.title: BEACHHEAD
card_event_top_deck_play_test.text: Draw a card. Put it into play if it is a unit.

card_event_usa_promo2.name: card_event_usa_promo2
card_event_usa_promo2.title: MELEE
card_event_usa_promo2.text: All units become 1/1 and lose Smokescreen, Ambush and Destruction.

card_unit_110th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_110th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_110th_infantry_regiment.title: 110th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_110th_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage. Destruction: Enemy HQ gains +4 defense.

card_unit_1st_pulk_piechoty.name: card_unit_1st_pulk_piechoty
card_unit_1st_pulk_piechoty.title: 1st PUŁK PIECHOTY
card_unit_1st_pulk_piechoty.text: When the enemy plays a known card, deal 2 damage to a random enemy.

card_unit_211th_basargino.name: card_unit_211th_basargino
card_unit_211th_basargino.title: 211th BASARGINO
card_unit_211th_basargino.text: Gets +2 attack when you discard a card.

card_unit_britain_promo1.name: card_unit_britain_promo1
card_unit_britain_promo1.title: KING'S OWN SCOTTISH
card_unit_britain_promo1.text: When this unit attacks the enemy HQ, deal 2 damage to the HQ.

card_unit_jager_regiment_75.name: card_unit_jager_regiment_75
card_unit_jager_regiment_75.title: 75. JÄGER REGIMENT
card_unit_jager_regiment_75.text: Deployment: Retreat an enemy unit in the frontline.

card_unit_japan_promo1.name: card_unit_japan_promo1
card_unit_japan_promo1.title: 1st GUARDS CAVALRY
card_unit_japan_promo1.text: Deployment: Deal damage to your HQ equal to the number of non-Japanese cards in your deck.

card_unit_m1_240mm_howitzer.name: card_unit_m1_240mm_howitzer
card_unit_m1_240mm_howitzer.title: M1 240mm HOWITZER
card_unit_m1_240mm_howitzer.text: Reduce operation cost by 1 each time unit moves or attacks, to minimum of 0.

card_unit_royal_sussex.name: card_unit_royal_sussex
card_unit_royal_sussex.title: ROYAL SUSSEX
card_unit_royal_sussex.text: When you attack with a British unit with attack of 1, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.

card_unit_soviet_promo1.name: card_unit_soviet_promo1
card_unit_soviet_promo1.title: 77th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_soviet_promo1.text: Your Soviet units with 5 or more attack cost 1 less to deploy.

card_unit_usa_promo1.name: card_unit_usa_promo1
card_unit_usa_promo1.title: 36th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_usa_promo1.text: Deployment: Shuffle a 32nd INFANTRY REGIMENT into your deck.

card_event_barrage.name: card_event_barrage
card_event_barrage.title: BARRAGE
card_event_barrage.text: Choose one - enemy units have -4 attack this turn OR deal 2 damage to a ground unit.
card_event_barrage.flavorText: A barrage is a concentrated artillery bombardment dispersed over a wide area. At the Battle of Seelow Heights, the Red Army opened the road to Berlin in 1945 with what is described as the largest artillery bombardment in history. With over 9000 guns and rockets, the Red Army fired at the enemy along a front of almost 30 km.

card_event_comrades.name: card_event_comrades
card_event_comrades.title: JUGGERNAUT
card_event_comrades.text: Give a friendly tank or infantry +2+1. It must attack each turn or it is destroyed.
card_event_comrades.flavorText: During WWII the Soviet Union had the largest army in the world, which at its peak had 12,500,000 enlisted men and women. The next in line was the US army with 12,364,000 enlisted personnel.

card_event_counter_offensive.name: card_event_counter_offensive
card_event_counter_offensive.title: COUNTER OFFENSIVE
card_event_counter_offensive.text: Target infantry or tank gets +2+1 for each damaged unit on the battlefield.
card_event_counter_offensive.flavorText: A counter offensive is an attack made in response to one from an enemy. The codename for one of the most famous Soviet counter offensives on the Eastern Front was Operation Uranus. This counter offensive was launched during the Battle of Stalingrad in the winter of 1942 and with it the Red Army won a decisive victory in the battle. As a result the Red Army managed to encircle the German 6th Army, the 3rd and 4th Romanian armies and portions of the German Fourth Panzer Army. This counter offensive turned the tide on the Eastern Front and after it the Axis forces were fighting a defensive war on all fronts.

card_event_men_of_steel.name: card_event_men_of_steel
card_event_men_of_steel.title: MEN OF STEEL
card_event_men_of_steel.text: Choose one - your units get +1 Heavy Armor OR add a THE HAMMER to your hand.
card_event_men_of_steel.flavorText: The Soviet Union design and production philosophy was to focus on quantity rather than quality. As an example, Soviet designers were very much aware that the T-34 tank had several design deficiencies, but rather than addressing the problem and slowing down production while they were at it, it was decided to mass produce them in such a high quantity that they could be replaced whenever needed. The only change made in the T-34 production line was conducted in order to make the manufacturing easier and cheaper. The initial cost of producing a T-34 tank went from 269,500 rubles in 1941 to 135,000 rubles in 1943.

card_event_mobile_defense.name: card_event_mobile_defense
card_event_mobile_defense.title: MOBILE DEFENSE
card_event_mobile_defense.text: Add two T-70 units to your support line. Destroy them at the end of your next turn.
card_event_mobile_defense.flavorText: Mobile defense is a military manoeuvre where the defender drives back attacks by using well planned counter attacks. These tactics are usually applied when the defender wants to avoid a pitched battle where a static defensive system would not suffice to halt an advancing enemy.

card_event_mud.name: card_event_mud
card_event_mud.title: MUD
card_event_mud.text: Enemy ground units cannot attack next turn.
card_event_mud.flavorText: Rasputitsa season happens twice a year in parts of Eastern Europe and cause very muddy conditions, either due to autumn rain or melting ice and snow during spring time. During WWII the Rasputitsa provided a great defensive advantage for the Red Army. Common nicknames for the Rasputitsa seasons are “Marshal Mud” or “General Mud”.

card_event_night_witches.name: card_event_night_witches
card_event_night_witches.title: NIGHT WITCHES
card_event_night_witches.text: Add three POLIKARPOV PO-2-II to your hand.
card_event_night_witches.flavorText: Night Witches, or “die Nachthexen”, was a German nickname for the female pilots of the 588th Night Bomber Regiment of the Soviet Air Force.
