card_unit_128th_rifles.title: 128th RIFLES
card_unit_128th_rifles.flavorText: The 128th Rifle Regiment was part of the 29th Rifle Division of the Red Army which was formed in 1920 during the Russian Civil War. In 1939 the division participated in the Soviet invasion of Poland and in  1941 it defended against the German invasion of Soviet Union in Operation Barbarossa. After being destroyed and reformed two times the division was ordered to Stalingrad where it joined the 64th Army in the defense of the city. After the Soviet victory at Stalingrad the division was redesignated the 72nd Guards Rifle Division for its distinguished service during the battle and the 128th Rifles Regiment became the 224th Guards Rifle Regiment. For the remainder of the war the division fought in several battles on the Eastern Front and lastly it participated in the Budapest Offensive where it ended the war in a captured area around the Slovakian city of Bruty near the Hungarian border. The division is still active today but was transferred to Ukraine after the fall of Soviet Union and is now known as the 72nd Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Army.

card_unit_222th_guard_rifles.name: card_unit_222th_guard_rifles
card_unit_222th_guard_rifles.title: 222nd GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_222th_guard_rifles.text: Pincer: At the end of your turn, fully repair this unit.
card_unit_222th_guard_rifles.flavorText: The 222nd Guards Rifle Regiment was part of the 72nd Guards Rifle Division, which previously was known as 29th Rifle Division, but raised to guards status in 1943 after an heroic performance in the Battle of Stalingrad. The division fought for the liberation of the city of Belgorod in 1943 and in 1944 it fought in the Budapest offensive. In 1944 the division was attached to the 24th Guards Rifle Corps and managed to capture an area around the village of Bruty in Slovakia where its advance was halted by the German 1st Battalion of Grenadier Regiment. After the war the division became the 7th Guards Rifle Brigade, and after the fall of Soviet Union it was transferred to Ukraine and is now the 72nd Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Army.

card_unit_25th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_25th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_25th_infantry_regiment.title: 25th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_25th_infantry_regiment.text: At the end of your turn, add a LIGHT INFANTRY to the same front.
card_unit_25th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 25th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 44th Rifle Division of the Red Army. The division was formed in 1918 during the Russian Civil war and participated in the Finnish Winter War and WWII. The division was destroyed during the Winter War in 1940 and recreated in 1941 and became part of the 13th Rifle Corps of the 12th Army. The division was once more wiped out in combat, but recreated again and fought throughout the war with the 54th Army of the Volkhov Front and later with the 67th Army of the Leningrad Front.

card_unit_35th_mountain_rifles.name: card_unit_35th_mountain_rifles
card_unit_35th_mountain_rifles.title: 35th MOUNTAIN RIFLES
card_unit_35th_mountain_rifles.text: If this unit is removed from your deck, it enters the battlefield instead.
card_unit_35th_mountain_rifles.flavorText: The 35th Mountain Rifles Regiment was a part of the 30th Mountain Rifle Division of the Red Army which was first formed during the Russian Civil War in 1918. In 1941 the division was renamed the 30th Rifle Division and in 1942, after participating in heavy fighting, the division was redesignated the 55th Guards Rifle Division. As the 55th Guards the division participated in numerous operations from 1942-1945, including the Kerch–Eltigen Operation, Operation Bagration, the East Prussian Offensive, the Battle of Berlin and the Prague Offensive.

card_unit_456th_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_456th_rifle_regiment
card_unit_456th_rifle_regiment.title: 456th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_456th_rifle_regiment.text: Gets +1+1 and Guard when your HQ takes damage.
card_unit_456th_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 456th Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 109th Rifle Division of the Red Army which was formed three times from 1939-1942. The 1st formation was short lived and the 2nd formation served for 6 months in 1942 in the defense of the fortress of Sevastopol where it was destroyed. The 3rd formation, mostly composed of redesignated NKVD regiments, distinguished itself in combat throughout the war. The division spent most time fighting in the Leningrad Oblast, but in 1944 the division was transferred north where they joined the 21st Army in the fight against Finnish forces in Karelia. After the capitulation of the Finnish forces the 109th Division was transferred to the 8th Army in Estonia where they assisted in clearing the Baltic coast and islands. The division was disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_57mm_m1943.name: card_unit_57mm_m1943
card_unit_57mm_m1943.title: ZiS-2
card_unit_57mm_m1943.flavorText: The Zis-2 was a 57mm Soviet anti-tank gun that was produced and used during WWII. ZiS stood for Zavod imeni Stalina (e. Factory named after Stalin), but the name of the factory which produced the gun was “Joseph Stalin Factory No. 92”. Production started in 1941 but was halted that same year with the explanation that it was too powerful as it penetrated weak German armor from one side to the other without doing internal damage. Another more plausible explanation was that the gun was too expensive to produce. However, when the German heavy Tiger and Panther tanks started to appear on the battlefield in 1942-43 a more powerful gun was needed and the production of ZiS-2 was started again. By the end of the war over 10,000 ZiS-2 guns had been produced.

card_unit_petlyakov_pe_2ft.name: card_unit_petlyakov_pe_2ft
card_unit_petlyakov_pe_2ft.title: PETLYAKOV Pe-2FT
card_unit_petlyakov_pe_2ft.flavorText: The Petlyakov Pe-2 “Peshka” (Russian: Pawn) was a Soviet Petlyakov dive bomber variant that was first introduced in 1941. It was an advanced aircraft for its time and came with a pressurized cabin and electrically actuated systems.The Pe-2FT was produced from 1942 to 1945 and was one of many Petlyakov variants, but the one that was produced in greatest numbers. It had an improved defensive armament, extra lower rear guns, dive brakes were removed and from early 1943 it was powered by PF or PF-2 engines. It had a 7.62 mm machine gun added in the dorsal turret to improve its defensive armament,  plus other upgrades.  A total of 11,427 Pe-2 aircraft were manufactured and this included variants such as the Pe-2FT bomber, the Pe-2R reconnaissance aircraft, the Pe-2UT trainer, the Pe-3bis fighter and other variants.

card_unit_t_28_pincer.name: card_unit_t_28_pincer
card_unit_t_28_pincer.title: T-28
card_unit_t_28_pincer.text: Pincer: When this unit is destroyed, put it on top of owner's deck.
card_unit_t_28_pincer.flavorText: The T-28 was a Soviet medium tank that was introduced in the early 1930s and used by the Soviet Union and other forces prior to and during WWII. The tank was intended for infantry support and many of them were deployed by the Red Army during the Winter War with Finland and the Soviet Invasion of Poland. At the start of Operation Barbarossa the Red Army had 411 T-28 tanks available, but most of them were lost during the first months of the invasion, either in combat or they were abandoned after mechanical breakdown. The T-28 had a crew of six, a main armament of a 76.2 mm KT-28 howitzer and secondary armament of 4-5 x 7.62 mm DT machine guns. A total of 503 tanks were produced, including variants, but very few were still in use after 1941.

card_unit_t_60.name: card_unit_t_60
card_unit_t_60.title: T-60
card_unit_t_60.text: Destruction: Add a T-34 1942 to your hand.
card_unit_t_60.flavorText: The T-60 scout tank was a Soviet light tank that was used by the Red Army during WWII. The T-60 came into service in 1941 and was designed to replace the obsolete T-38 tank which had been in service from 1937. The original T-60 design came with a main armament of a 12.7 mm machine gun that was later replaced with a 20 mm TNSh cannon, which proved quite inadequate against newer German tank armor. The T-60 was not liked by their crews, to say the least, and some called it "a brother's grave for two" due to its disastrous performance on the battlefield. From 1941 to 1943 approximately 6000 T-60 tanks, including some variants, were produced, but they had more or less been pulled from frontline service in 1943 and mostly used for reconnaissance, convoy duties and training purposes. An unknown number of T-60 were captured by the Axis, some were converted to the German Panzerkampfwagen T-60 743(r).

card_unit_yak_7.name: card_unit_yak_7
card_unit_yak_7.title: YAK 7
card_unit_yak_7.text: At the start of your turn, draw a card and deal 1 damage to your HQ.
card_unit_yak_7.flavorText: The Yakovlev Yak-7 was a Soviet fighter that was originally designed to be a two-seat trainer version of the Yak-1 fighter, but was modified to a single-seat fighter that proved to be superior to the Yak-1. The Yak 7 was first used in front line service in 1942 where it was mostly used as a fighter-bomber, but also as an interceptor and fighter. The Yak-7 was a very capable aircraft and 6,399 aircraft were produced throughout the war, including variants. In 1944 the aircraft was retired from combat service and resumed its role as a trainer.

card_event_ancestral_call.name: card_event_ancestral_call
card_event_ancestral_call.title: ANCESTRAL CALL
card_event_ancestral_call.text: Your units get +1 attack for each other unit in their front.
card_event_ancestral_call.flavorText: The Soviet Union made extensive use of propaganda during WWII, and a number of historical figures were used to promote various messages and agendas. Alexander Nevsky, a medieval prince who defeated Germanic knights in the 13th century. Another popular figure was Mikhail Kutuzov who was a Russian general who played a key role in defeating Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812. These two were often cited as heroic figures in Soviet propaganda during World War II, particularly in the context of defending the Motherland against invading forces.

card_event_enemy_at_the_gates.name: card_event_enemy_at_the_gates
card_event_enemy_at_the_gates.title: ENEMY AT THE GATES
card_event_enemy_at_the_gates.text: All units get +2 attack and are dealt 2 damage.
card_event_enemy_at_the_gates.flavorText: The movie Enemy at the Gates is based on real events that took place during the Battle of Stalingrad in WWII. The film tells the story of a young Soviet sniper named Vasily Zaytsev, who becomes a hero of the Soviet Union for his actions during the battle. The movie portrays the brutal fighting that took place in Stalingrad and the heroism of the Soviet soldiers who fought to defend the city. However, it is important to note that the movie takes some liberties with the historical facts and should not be considered a completely accurate portrayal of the events that took place. For example, the character of Major Erwin König, the German sniper who is Zaytsev's rival in the film, is a fictional creation and there is no evidence that he actually existed. Additionally, some of the details of Zaytsev's life and his role in the battle are also fictionalized for dramatic effect. Overall, while Enemy at the Gates is not a completely accurate historical representation, it is based on real events and serves as a powerful portrayal of the human cost of war and the bravery of those who fought in it.

card_event_gambit.name: card_event_gambit
card_event_gambit.title: GAMBIT
card_event_gambit.text: Both players add the unit with the highest cost in their hand to their support line.
card_event_gambit.flavorText: In a general sense, a "gambit" refers to a strategic move or maneuver, often in the context of a game or conflict, where a player or participant takes an initial risk or sacrifice to gain an advantage. The term originated from chess, where it describes an opening move in which a player willingly sacrifices a pawn or piece to secure a favorable position or surprise their opponent. One notable example of a gambit-like maneuver by the Red Army during World War II is the Battle of Stalingrad. In this critical engagement, the Red Army strategically chose to defend the city of Stalingrad against the German forces, essentially luring them into a protracted urban warfare situation. By sacrificing territory and initially allowing the enemy to advance, the Red Army created an opportunity to encircle and trap the German 6th Army within the city. This daring move involved significant risks, but it ultimately paid off, as the encirclement led to the decisive defeat of the German forces and marked a turning point in the war.

card_event_spearhead.name: card_event_spearhead
card_event_spearhead.title: SPEARHEAD
card_event_spearhead.text: Destroy a friendly unit and adjacent units. Your units get +X+X, where X is units destroyed.
card_event_spearhead.flavorText: In a military context, the term "spearhead" refers to a unit or force that leads an attack or an offensive operation. It is a metaphorical reference to the pointed head of a spear, which is used to penetrate and break through enemy defenses. The spearhead unit is typically composed of highly skilled and well-equipped troops, often armored or mechanized, and is tasked with the initial assault to achieve a breakthrough in the enemy's front lines. Operation Bagration and the Battle of Kursk were two significant WWII offensives conducted by the Red Army, both involving spearhead operations. The Battle of Kursk, which took place in July and August 1943, witnessed the Red Army launching a counteroffensive against German forces. Spearhead divisions, strategically concentrated and equipped with tanks and heavy artillery, led the assault, breaking through German lines and setting the stage for subsequent Soviet victories. Operation Bagration, launched in June 1944, was a massive Soviet offensive on the Eastern Front aimed at destroying German Army Group Center. Spearhead units comprising armored and mechanized divisions, supported by infantry and artillery, spearheaded the attack, rapidly advancing deep into enemy territory and encircling German forces.

card_event_stand_together_brothers.name: card_event_stand_together_brothers
card_event_stand_together_brothers.title: STAND TOGETHER
card_event_stand_together_brothers.text: Destroy a friendly infantry. Add a Soviet tank with the same cost. Give it Blitz.
card_event_stand_together_brothers.flavorText: The Soviet army and the US army met at the River Elbe in Germany on April 25, 1945, towards the end of WWII in Europe. The meeting of the Allied forces, known as Elbe Day, was significant as it effectively split Germany in half and signaled the near-end of the war in Europe. The Soviet and American soldiers celebrated the meeting, and many exchanged gifts and took photographs together. However, the formal alliance between the Soviet Union and the United States began to deteriorate soon after the end of the war.

card_event_the_mighty_fall.name: card_event_the_mighty_fall
card_event_the_mighty_fall.title: THE MIGHTY FALL
card_event_the_mighty_fall.flavorText: At the start of Operation Barbarossa (the German invasion of the Soviet Union), the Soviet Union and the Red Army had a huge disadvantage, militarily, productionally and technologically. However, at the start of 1943 they started gaining the upper hand in a series of significant turning points. This started with their victory in the Battle of Stalingrad in February 1943, followed by The Battle of Kursk in July 1943, and finally the Operation Bagration (June-August 1944). It's also important to note that the Soviet Union's ability to produce weapons and equipment on a massive scale, combined with its vast resources and manpower, was a crucial factor in their overall success. While Germany initially had the upper hand in certain technological aspects, the Soviet Union's determination, industrial capacity, and strategic planning allowed them to catch up and ultimately overcome Germany's technological and military advantages. Additionally, the lend-lease program played a significant role in bolstering the Soviet Union's war effort, providing crucial supplies, vehicles, and weaponry that greatly contributed to their ability to turn the tide of the war in their favor.

card_event_urban_fighting.name: card_event_urban_fighting
card_event_urban_fighting.title: URBAN FIGHTING
card_event_urban_fighting.text: Set the operation cost of target unit to 4. Destroy adjacent damaged units.
card_event_urban_fighting.flavorText: During WWII, the Battle of Berlin was a significant example of urban fighting involving the Red Army and remnants of the German forces. Taking place from April 16 to May 2, 1945, it was a crucial phase in the final stages of the war. The Red Army, led by Marshal Georgy Zhukov, faced determined resistance from heavily fortified German defenses and civilian militias. The battle involved intense urban warfare as Soviet troops fought through the streets, buildings, and strongholds of Berlin. They encountered formidable obstacles, such as fortifications, booby traps, and a complex network of trenches. The fighting was characterized by fierce street battles, close-quarters combat, and heavy artillery and tank engagements. Despite the challenging conditions, the Soviet army gradually advanced and captured key targets, including the symbolic Reichstag building. The Battle of Berlin ultimately led to the surrender of German forces and marked the end of the war in Europe.

card_unit_1357th_rifles.name: card_unit_1357th_rifles
card_unit_1357th_rifles.title: 1357th RIFLES
card_unit_1357th_rifles.text: When this unit takes damage or is fully repaired, it gets +2 attack.
card_unit_1357th_rifles.flavorText: The 1357th Rifles was a regiment of the 24th Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. The division participated in fighting from the early days of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 and up until the German surrender in 1945. In 1941 the division displayed heroic efforts in the Lidy area, and took part in the defense of Kyiv and engaged in heavy defensive fighting in Belarus as part of the 21st Rifle Corps and 13th Army. The division would later be under the control of various armies and actively participated in numerous military operations, including the Battle of Stalingrad, the Donbas offensive, the clearing of Left-bank Ukraine, the Zhytomyr–Berdychiv offensive, the Kamianets–Podilskyi pocket, the Lviv–Sandomierz offensive, the East-Carpathian and West-Carpathian operations, as well as the Moravia-Ostrava and Prague offensives. On June 24, 1945, the division concluded its combat actions, being 100 km away from Prague.

card_unit_14th_guards_rifles.name: card_unit_14th_guards_rifles
card_unit_14th_guards_rifles.title: 14th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_14th_guards_rifles.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of its third turn on the battlefield.
card_unit_14th_guards_rifles.flavorText: The 14th Guard Rifles was a regiment of the 7th Guards Rifle Division which served as an elite unit throughout the Great Patriotic War. Initially assigned to the Bryansk Front, it later joined the Western Front, actively participating in the early stages of the 1941 winter counteroffensive northwest of Moscow as part of the 16th Army . Early 1942 the division was moved under the command of the 1st Guards Rifle Corps and was deployed to the Northwestern Front and participated in fighting around Demyansk until the German II Army Corps evacuated in February 1943. Throughout the following year, the division engaged in battles within the Staraya Russa region, primarily under the command of the 1st Shock Army. In January 1944, the division was transferred to the 7th Guards Rifle Corps of the 10th Guards Army. During the summer and autumn operations in the Baltic states, the 7th Guards Division distinguished itself, earning a battle honor and the esteemed Order of the Red Banner. In March 1945, it joined the Courland Group of Forces of the Leningrad Front, overseeing the German forces encircled in northwest Latvia along the Baltic coast. After the German surrender, the division was relocated to Estonia and eventually disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_266th_guards_rifles.name: card_unit_266th_guards_rifles
card_unit_266th_guards_rifles.title: 266th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_266th_guards_rifles.text: Becomes Veteran if the enemy has no Veteran units at the start of your turn.
card_unit_266th_guards_rifles.flavorText: The 266th Guard Rifle Regiment was part of the 88th Guards Rifle Division during WWII. The 88th Division was reformed in April 1943 from the 1st formation of the 99th Rifle Division and became one of the most decorated rifle divisions in the Red Army. It played a significant role in the liberation of Zaporozhye and fought alongside the 3rd Ukrainian Front in battles near the Dnieper River. The division earned the Order of Suvorov for its actions along the Inhulets River and participated in the liberation of Odessa. It also broke the German defense west of Kovel during Operation Bagration and secured a bridgehead over the Vistula at Magnuszew. In the Vistula-Oder Offensive, the division's regiments were recognized for their successes in the advance into Poland. The division then contributed to the expansion of a bridgehead over the Oder River near Küstrin and took part in the final offensive on Berlin. It ended the war near the Zoological Garden and later served in occupation duty in the Soviet sector of Germany until disbanding in early 1947.

card_unit_49th_karachev.name: card_unit_49th_karachev
card_unit_49th_karachev.title: 49th KARACHEV
card_unit_49th_karachev.text: When an enemy unit becomes Veteran, deal 2 damage to it.
card_unit_49th_karachev.flavorText: During WWII the 49th Guards Rifle Regiment was part of the 16th Guards Rifle Division, which was a highly decorated and elite infantry division of the Red Army during Great Patriotic War. It was formed in February 1942 and served in various fronts throughout the war. It was initially assigned to Kalinin Front and later transferred to Western Front's 30th Army where it took part in the struggle for the village of Polunino. It then fought in various battles and operations and was eventually reassigned to the 11th Guards Army, with which it served for the rest of the war. During the summer offensive against the German-held salient around Oryol, it assisted in the liberation of Karachev and received its name as an honorific. The division participated in the liberation of key cities like Orsha, Minsk, and Königsberg (today known as Kaliningrad), and was highly decorated for its actions. It remained in the Kaliningrad Oblast well after the war until it was finally disbanded in September 1960.

card_unit_91st_astrakhan.name: card_unit_91st_astrakhan
card_unit_91st_astrakhan.title: 91st ASTRAKHAN
card_unit_91st_astrakhan.text: When this unit gets a Pincer effect, give it +1+2.
card_unit_91st_astrakhan.flavorText: The 91st Astrakhan was an infantry regiment of the 31st Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. At the start of the war, the division joined the newly formed 45th Army, guarding the Turkish border. After heavy losses in the Battle of Kiev and the Donbas, the division was sent north to fill the gap. It participated in the Battle of Rostov and the Mius defensive operations. During the German offensive of 1942, known as Case Blue, the division retreated into the Caucasus. It was later transferred to the 12th Army and then to the 18th Army of the North Caucasian Front. The division suffered significant losses in the defense of Tuapse but received reinforcements. As the German retreat from the Caucasus began, the division joined the 46th Army, advancing along the Black Sea coast. In 1943, the division was moved north and joined the Southwestern Front before becoming part of the 3rd Ukrainian Front. During the Battle of the Dnieper, it was transferred to the 4th Guards Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front. The division participated in the Second Jassy-Kishinev Offensive, advancing into Romania. It later fought in the Vistula-Oder Offensive and the Berlin Offensive. Throughout the war, the division received prestigious awards such as the Order of the Red Banner, the Order of Suvorov 2nd class, and the Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky 2nd class.

card_unit_beriev_be_4.name: card_unit_beriev_be_4
card_unit_beriev_be_4.title: BERIEV BE-4
card_unit_beriev_be_4.text: Your units cost 2 less to deploy. When you deploy a unit, Retreat this unit.
card_unit_beriev_be_4.flavorText: The Beriev Be-4, originally designated KOR-2, was a Soviet flying boat that was developed and used during World War II. It was primarily designed for maritime reconnaissance and bombing missions. The Be-4 was a twin-engine aircraft featuring a biplane configuration with a large central float and smaller stabilizing floats attached to the wings. One of the notable characteristics of the Be-4 was its ability to operate from both land and water. It had a crew of three and was equipped with defensive armament, including machine guns, and it was well-suited for a variety of missions, including coastal patrols, anti-submarine warfare, and reconnaissance over maritime areas. A total of 47 aircraft were produced and they were in service throughout the war, mainly in the Black Sea, Baltic Sea, and Arctic Ocean regions.

card_unit_bm_13n_us6.name: card_unit_bm_13n_us6
card_unit_bm_13n_us6.title: BM-13N US6
card_unit_bm_13n_us6.text: Retreat this unit before damage is applied when it is attacked.
card_unit_bm_13n_us6.flavorText: The BM-13N, also known as Katyusha, was a Soviet rocket launcher system used during WWII. It was usually mounted on a Soviet truck chassis, but this particular model was mounted on an American Studebaker US6, which was provided to the Soviet Union as part of the Lend-Lease program. The Katyusha rocket launcher system consisted of a series of rails or tubes mounted on the back of the truck. These rails held multiple unguided rockets that could be fired in quick succession, creating a devastating barrage of firepower. The rockets were typically 132 mm in diameter and had a range of around 5 to 8 kilometers. The Katyusha gained notoriety for its ability to bomb enemy positions with a large number of rockets simultaneously, causing chaos and demoralizing the opposing forces. Its distinctive sound, resembling a howling or screaming, led to its nickname "Stalin's Organ" among German troops.

card_unit_bt_7_1937.name: card_unit_bt_7_1937
card_unit_bt_7_1937.title: BT-7 1937
card_unit_bt_7_1937.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of its fourth turn on the battlefield.
card_unit_bt_7_1937.flavorText: The BT-7 1937 was a Soviet light cavalry tank that was used during WWII. It was an improved version of the BT series of tanks, which were known for their speed and mobility. The BT-7 1937 featured a new turret and sloped armor, providing more protection compared to its predecessors. It had a crew of three and was armed with a 45 mm main gun, as well as two 7.62 mm DT machine guns. During the early stages of World War II, the BT-7 1937 played a role in the Soviet Union's defense against the German invasion. Its speed and agility made it effective in maneuvering on the battlefield. It could achieve speeds of up to 50 km/h in off-road conditions, allowing it to rapidly exploit enemy weaknesses and do hit-and-run tactics. However, the BT-7 1937 had its limitations. Its armor was relatively thin, making it vulnerable to enemy anti-tank fire. The tank's 45 mm gun was effective against most early-war German tanks, but became increasingly inadequate against more heavily armored adversaries as the war progressed. Despite its shortcomings, the BT-7 1937 was used throughout the war. It was primarily employed for reconnaissance, infantry support, and exploitation of breakthroughs. However, as newer and more advanced tanks became available, such as the T-34 and KV series, the BT-7 1937 was gradually phased out of frontline service.

card_unit_tupolev_sb_2.name: card_unit_tupolev_sb_2
card_unit_tupolev_sb_2.title: TUPOLEV SB-2
card_unit_tupolev_sb_2.text: Pincer: It costs the enemy +2 kredits to target or attack this unit.
card_unit_tupolev_sb_2.flavorText: The Tupolev SB-2 was a Soviet light bomber variant of the Tupolev ANT-40, used mainly by the Soviet Air Force during WWII. It played a significant role in the early stages of the war, particularly during the Soviet Union's defense against the German invasion. Developed in the late 1930s, the SB  was one of the most modern bombers of its time, featuring a streamlined design and advanced construction techniques. B It had a crew of three and was armed with machine guns for self-defense. By 1941, 94% of bombers in the Soviet Air Force were SB’s and it was employed in large numbers and proved to be effective against ground targets, enemy troop concentrations, and infrastructure. However, as the war progressed and German air superiority increased, the SB faced challenges. Its light armor and inadequate defensive armament made it vulnerable to enemy fire and the more advanced German fighters further reduced the bomber's effectiveness. Despite its limitations, the SB-2 remained in service throughout the war in various roles. It was used for reconnaissance, night bombing, and partisan support missions. Later in the war, as newer bombers became available, the Tupolev SB was gradually phased out of frontline service. A total of 6.656 SB’s were built, including quite a few variants.

card_event_covert_operation.name: card_event_covert_operation
card_event_covert_operation.title: COVERT OPERATION
card_event_covert_operation.text: Add the top Covert unit of your deck to your support line. Duplicate it.
card_event_covert_operation.flavorText: Operation Berezino, also known as "Operation Scherhorn" was a covert operation undertaken by the Soviet NKVD during WWII.  The primary goal of the operation was to create the illusion of a substantial German military unit operating within Soviet-held territories. The aim was to exhaust Nazi intelligence assets by intercepting and eliminating field operatives that were sent to aid these fictitious forces. The NKVD orchestrated a simulated German "resistance pocket," led by Lieutenant-Colonel Heinrich Scherhorn, who was an actual German prisoner that was coerced into collaboration with the Soviets. In response, the Germans launched an operation, led by Otto Skorzeny, which aimed at helping the fake resistance pocket achieve their goals. However, when Skorzeny's commandos arrived to the rescue, they were promptly detained and coerced into participating in the Soviet deception. Although German support waned over time, the illusion of "Group Scherhorn" persisted until May 1945, as proved the maintained radio communications with German command.

card_event_field_recon.name: card_event_field_recon
card_event_field_recon.title: FIELD RECON
card_event_field_recon.text: Give target infantry or tank +2+2 for each unit with Covert you control.
card_event_field_recon.flavorText: Despite the Red Army's substantial manpower and equipment, their dedicated reconnaissance assets remained relatively modest. Initially, Soviet infantry divisions had a reconnaissance battalion with limited armored and motorized equipment. As the war progressed, they streamlined their reconnaissance units into smaller companies, emphasizing stealth and information gathering over firepower and communication. With minimal weaponry and communication tools, Soviet reconnaissance focused on avoiding detection and relied heavily on infantry patrols on foot, which meant that they could not move far from their parent unit. However, their focus on stealth over firepower proved very successful against the Germans.

card_event_respite.name: card_event_respite
card_event_respite.title: RESPITE
card_event_respite.text: Your units get +1+3. The enemy HQ gets +5 defense.
card_event_respite.flavorText: During WWII, the Red Army's retreat tactics were a complex mix of strategic withdrawals and desperate holding actions. Initially caught off guard by Operation Barbarossa, the Red Army suffered immense losses and was forced into chaotic retreats. However, they learned to utilize their vast territory to their advantage, trading space for time. The scorched earth policy denied the German invaders resources, while partisan warfare disrupted supply lines and communications. As the war progressed, the Red Army refined its defensive strategies and incorporated well-planned counterattacks and resilient defenses in key locations like Stalingrad. These tactics ultimately played a crucial role in exhausting the German forces and turning the tide of the war.

card_event_strategic_focus.name: card_event_strategic_focus
card_event_strategic_focus.title: STRATEGIC FOCUS
card_event_strategic_focus.text: Choose One - Deal 5 damage to all ground units OR air units.
card_event_strategic_focus.flavorText: The Red Army's strategic focus during WWII evolved as the conflict progressed. Initially, their doctrine emphasized on deep operations and mobile warfare, with the aim of penetrating the enemy lines swiftly and decisively. However, due to the recent purges of the Red Army officer corps, few soldiers had the required skills and the devastating losses of 1941 and 1942 forced a shift towards defensive tactics. As the war turned in its favour, the Red Army returned to offensive operations, leveraging their numerical superiority and artillery firepower to overwhelm the German forces. This proved very successful in offensives like Operation Bagration and the Battle of Berlin, where Soviet forces advanced relentlessly, encircling and destroying enemy units. Throughout the war, the Red Army's focus remained on achieving victory through attrition, wearing down the enemy through relentless attacks and exploiting their vast manpower reserves.

card_event_turmoil.name: card_event_turmoil
card_event_turmoil.title: TURMOIL
card_event_turmoil.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit. Deal 4 instead if it is damaged.
card_event_turmoil.flavorText: The Battle of Stalingrad was a brutal and pivotal clash during WWII. The city held significant strategic and symbolic importance for both Germany and the Soviet Union during WWII. For Germany, capturing the city would secure access to crucial oil fields and control of the Volga River which was a vital transportation route. For the Soviets, Stalingrad bore the name of their leader, Stalin, and its loss would be a major blow to their morale. The battle began in July 1942 with German forces, supported by the Luftwaffe, launching a massive offensive that reduced much of the city to rubble. The fighting soon turned into intense urban combat, with both sides pouring in reinforcements. By November, the Germans had pushed the Soviets back to the Volga River, but the harsh winter conditions hampered their progress. The Battle of Stalingrad ended on February 2, 1943, with the surrender of the remaining German forces trapped in the city after months of brutal urban warfare and a successful Soviet counteroffensive.

card_unit_101st_bezhitsa.name: card_unit_101st_bezhitsa
card_unit_101st_bezhitsa.title: 101st BEZHITSA
card_unit_101st_bezhitsa.text: At the start of your turn, your units get +2 attack and you lose 2 kredits.
card_unit_101st_bezhitsa.flavorText: The 101st Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 4th Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army. The division was formed in 1919 during the Russian Civil war, and in 1921 it fought in the Polish-Soviet war. In 1939 the 4th Division fought in the Winter War, notably at the Battle of Kelja. In 1942 it became part of the 12th Army and participated in the Battle of the Caucasus, but after heavy losses it was disbanded. The division was formed again in 1943, and as part of the 69th Army, it took part in numerous battles and operations, such as the Bryansk Offensive, the Lublin-Brest Offensive, the Warsaw-Poznan Offensive, and finally in the Berlin Offensive. In 1945 the name of "Bezhitsa" was inscribed on the divisional banner for the division's participation in the Bryansk Offensive in 1943.

card_unit_115th_separate_btn.name: card_unit_115th_separate_btn
card_unit_115th_separate_btn.title: 115th SEPARATE BTN
card_unit_115th_separate_btn.text: Reveal: Gets +2+1 for each friendly turn it ends as Covert.
card_unit_115th_separate_btn.flavorText: The 115th Separate Battalion was a unit of the 30th Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army during WWII. The division was formed in 1918, but reformed at the outbreak of WWII and stationed at the Soviet-Romanian border. In August 1941 the 30th Rifle Division was transferred to the Separate Coastal Army which was ordered to defend Odessa. The division was cut off before reaching its destination and forced to withdraw.  In 1942 the division was involved in numerous defensive battles in the southwest regions of the Soviet Union and for its meritorious actions it was transformed into the 55th Guards Rifle Division. Between 1943 and 1945 the division took part in the liberation of North Caucasus and the Taman Peninsula. It participated in the Kerch–Eltigen operation, landing on the beach in Danger, Yenikale, and fought on the Kerch Peninsula until April 1944. It was later involved in strategic operations in Belarus and eastern Poland, and in the East Prussian, Berlin and Prague offensives. The division was disbanded with the Northern Group of Forces during the summer of 1945.

card_unit_186th_recon_company.name: card_unit_186th_recon_company
card_unit_186th_recon_company.title: 186th RECON COMPANY
card_unit_186th_recon_company.text: When a friendly Covert unit is Revealed, give your units +1+1.
card_unit_186th_recon_company.flavorText: The 186th Reconnaissance Company was a unit of the 160th Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army during WWII. In 1941 the division faced near destruction during the Battle of Moscow and temporarily disappeared from the Red Army's order of battle. It re-entered combat within the 33rd Army in January 1942, but it was understrength and reinforced with two rifle regiments from other divisions. The division assumed minor roles during the Battles of Rzhev, but later played a more active part in the 1943 summer offensive toward Smolensk under the 33rd Army. Following the disbandment of the Western Front in early 1944, the division joined the 2nd Belorussian Front and served under the 70th Army, and later with the 114th Rifle Corps during Operation Bagration. The 160th Division earned the Order of the Red Banner and the honorific "Brest" for its role in liberating the city. Afterwards the division participated in the Vistula-Oder and East Pomeranian Offensives where some of its units earned the honorific "Gdańsk". During the advance towards Germany the division fought through the Oder River and northward to the Baltic, ending the war in northern Germany before being disbanded in June 1945.

card_unit_36th_cavalry.name: card_unit_36th_cavalry
card_unit_36th_cavalry.title: 36th CAVALRY
card_unit_36th_cavalry.text:
Deployment: Gets +3+3 and Blitz.
Destruction: Add two suppressed copies to your support line.
card_unit_36th_cavalry.flavorText: The 36th Cavalry Division was a unit of the Red Army formed sometime prior to 1939. At the start of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 it was stationed in Vawkavysk, Belarus. On June 22nd 1941, the division was ordered to counterattack alongside the 6th Mechanized Corps. However, just a day later, Luftwaffe airstrikes inflicted heavy casualties and the division was destroyed within 48 hours. It was officially disbanded on July 6th, 1941. Subordinate units of the 36th Cavalry Division were the 24th, 42nd and 102nd Cavalry Regiments and the 8th Tank Regiment.

card_unit_38th_guards_rifles.name: card_unit_38th_guards_rifles
card_unit_38th_guards_rifles.title: 38th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_38th_guards_rifles.text: Reveal: Add a T-34 1942 to your support line if this unit was Covert for 3 or more turns.
card_unit_38th_guards_rifles.flavorText: The 38th Guards Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 65th Rifle Division, which became the 102nd Guards Rifle Division in 1944. When Operation Barbarossa began in 1941, the division was caught in defensive battles near the town of Tikhvin, located near Leningrad. That same year it participated in the liberation of the town during a Soviet Counteroffensive. The division continued fighting near Leningrad and in 1944 it was involved in the Petsamo-Kirkenes Operation, which was a Soviet offensive that defeated the Wehrmacht's forces in the Arctic. In February 1945, shortly after being raised to Guards status, the division took part in the East Pomeranian Offensive with the 19th Army of the 2nd Belorussian Front. From late March to early April 1945, it played a role in securing the naval base and port of Gdynia while also freeing the "Polish Corridor". Following this success, the division engaged in operations aimed at containing and neutralizing enemy forces along the western coast of the Danzig Bay. After the war it performed occupation duty on the demarcation line of the Mecklenburg province until it was disbanded in 1947.

card_unit_392nd_rifles.name: card_unit_392nd_rifles
card_unit_392nd_rifles.title: 392nd RIFLES
card_unit_392nd_rifles.text: Give units you deploy +2 attack and deal them 1 damage. Becomes Veteran when it has dealt 4+ damage.
card_unit_392nd_rifles.flavorText: The 392nd Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 73rd Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army. The division was initially formed in the Siberian Military District in 1930. At the start of the German invasion into the Soviet Union, the division was assigned to the 20th Army and suffered heavy losses during the early German offensives. It was reformed but again devastated during the Battle of Moscow in 1941. Despite this setback, the 73rd Rifle Division was rebuilt yet again. This time, it participated in the capture of the city of Voronezh during the Voronezh-Kastornoye offensive, and later in the Soviet counteroffensives that followed the Battle of Kursk. The division continued fighting through the war, distinguishing itself in operations such as the crossing of the Dnieper River, and played a role in offensives across Ukraine and into Poland. It ended the war on the Baltic Coast.

card_unit_92nd_naval_brigade.name: card_unit_92nd_naval_brigade
card_unit_92nd_naval_brigade.title: 92nd NAVAL BRIGADE
card_unit_92nd_naval_brigade.text: Reveal: Lose 3 kredits at the start of your next turn.
card_unit_92nd_naval_brigade.flavorText: When Germany invaded the Soviet Union, several Red Army naval infantry brigades were formed. These units were not similar to marines in other navies but served mainly as ship crews gathered for shore combat duties or as landing parties. The 92nd Naval Brigade (Brigada Morskoi Pekhoty) was formed from the Volga Flotilla in September 1942. Its two battalions were rushed to the defense of Stalingrad, charged with holding the Grain Elevator south of the Mamayev Kurgan in the face of heavy attacks. The Brigade was disbanded once the city was recaptured.

card_unit_97th_rifles.name: card_unit_97th_rifles
card_unit_97th_rifles.title: 97th RIFLES
card_unit_97th_rifles.text: Destruction: Shuffle 414th RIFLES into your deck, then draw a card.
card_unit_97th_rifles.flavorText: The 97th Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 18th Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army during WWII. The division was formed in 1918 and took part in the invasion of Poland in 1920, where it was defeated at the Battle of Warsaw. From 20 November 1939 to March 1940, during the Winter War, the division was assigned to the 56th Rifle Corps of the 8th Army. It led the attack along the Lemetti-Koirinoja-Imphilathi-Sortavala road, where it again got defeated by the Finns. It was disbanded shortly after. The 18th Division was reestablished in 1939 and was stationed in the city of Kazan when Operation Barbarossa started. The division fought against the German advance east of the Dnieper River, where it was encircled and only a small part of the division managed to escape. The 18th Division was established again in September 1941 and participated shortly after in the Battle of Moscow, after which it was raised to Guards status for its actions and renamed 11th Guards Rifle Division. In 1943 the division broke through the German encirclement of Leningrad and joined the Leningrad Front. In 1944 it took part in the Karelian offensive against the Finnish forces and later that year it participated in the East Pomeranian Strategic Offensive Operation and fought at Danzig, Poland. After the end of the war the 18th Rifle Division was stationed on the Danish island of Bornholm before being withdrawn and disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_katalina.name: card_unit_katalina
card_unit_katalina.title: KATALINA
card_unit_katalina.text: Gets +2+2 when an enemy countermeasure triggers.
card_unit_katalina.flavorText: The Consolidated PBY Catalina was an American flying boat and amphibious aircraft that was first introduced in 1936. It was provided to the Soviet Union through the Lend-Lease program and served as their primary naval reconnaissance and bomber aircraft during and after WWII. It proved so successful that it remained in service long after the war, with planned replacements such as the Be-6 never fully taking over its role. The Soviet Union received 185 Catalinas, including both amphibious and tricycle landing gear variants, which were well regarded by Soviet naval pilots. These versatile aircraft continued to be used for bombing and rescue operations until they were finally retired from service between 1954 and 1957.

card_unit_su_100.name: card_unit_su_100
card_unit_su_100.title: SU-100
card_unit_su_100.flavorText: The SU-100 was a highly effective Soviet tank destroyer that played a crucial role in the latter stages of WWII. It was built on the chassis of the T-34-85 medium tank and had a powerful 100mm D-10S gun mounted in a fixed casemate. This gun gave it the ability to penetrate the armor of almost any German tank it encountered, including the Tiger and Panther tanks. The SU-100 had a crew of 4 (Commander/Radio Operator, Gunner, Loader and Driver), and crews favored the SU-100 for its powerful armament, relatively low profile, and sloped armor, which provided decent protection. It saw extensive combat in the final offensives against the German army, and was also used in the Battle of Berlin because its gun could deal with heavy fortifications. A total of 4,976 SU-100’s were manufactured and it was in service in the Red Army until 1947.

card_event_aid_to_the_front.name: card_event_aid_to_the_front
card_event_aid_to_the_front.title: AID TO THE FRONT
card_event_aid_to_the_front.text: Give a unit with two or more combat keywords +2+2.
card_event_aid_to_the_front.flavorText: On 23 August 1944, King Michael of Romania led a dramatic coup that reshaped the Eastern Front. With support from a coalition of opposition parties and the Romanian Communist underground, he ordered the arrest of the leader of the Romanian government, Marshal Ion Antonescu, and announced an immediate armistice with the Allies. The decision came as Soviet forces broke through Axis lines in northeastern Romania. The Red Army’s advance was swift. Romanian units, previously allied with Germany, began cooperating with Soviet troops. Within days, German forces faced coordinated resistance from their former Romanian allies. Over 130,000 German troops were taken prisoner during the subsequent operations. Romania’s defection allowed the Soviet Union to secure vital oil fields and open a direct path into the Balkans. It also forced Germany to divert resources at a critical moment. In return, the Soviets promised support to Romania’s new government, dominated by King Michael but increasingly influenced by communists. The coup in Bucharest was one of the most consequential political reversals of the war. It transformed Romania from an Axis ally into an active contributor to the Allied cause on the Eastern Front.

card_event_exposed.name: card_event_exposed
card_event_exposed.title: EXPOSED
card_event_exposed.text: Costs 1 less if you control a US unit. Deal 5 damage to a unit with no combat keywords.
card_event_exposed.flavorText: In the summer of 1944, German Army Group Centre held what was believed to be a strong defensive line in Belarus. However, its position had become dangerously exposed. Hitler expected a Soviet offensive in the south and refused to allow tactical withdrawals, leaving the central front undermanned and vulnerable. On June 22, the Soviets launched Operation Bagration with over two million men. Exploiting weak flanks and gaps in coordination between German units, Soviet forces used overwhelming artillery, armor and air support to punch through enemy defensive lines. German divisions were rapidly encircled and destroyed, unable to retreat or regroup. Entire corps vanished within days. Communications collapsed, and supplies ran out. Towns like Vitebsk, Orsha, and Mogilev fell in quick succession. By mid-July, Army Group Centre had lost around 350,000 men, dead, wounded or captured. This crushing defeat shattered the German front in the east and opened the road to Warsaw. Operation Bagration remains one of the largest and most successful offensives in military history. The exposed heart of the German defense was struck with devastating precision, and it never fully recovered.

card_event_forged_in_fire.name: card_event_forged_in_fire
card_event_forged_in_fire.title: FORGED IN FIRE
card_event_forged_in_fire.text: Give a unit a random combat keyword it doesn't have. Draw a card if it now has 2 or more.
card_event_forged_in_fire.flavorText: The Soviet Union’s Red Army emerged from the crucible of early WWII battles as a hardened and transformed force. In 1941, when Operation Barbarossa began, the Soviet military was poorly prepared for the scale and speed of the German invasion. Command structures were in disarray, equipment was insufficient or outdated, and morale plummeted as entire armies were encircled and destroyed. Yet by 1943, a different army stood on the Eastern Front. Harsh lessons learned from catastrophic defeats at Kiev, Vyazma, and Kharkov had forged new strategies, stronger leadership, and greater coordination between infantry, armor and artillery. Training improved rapidly. Factories relocated beyond the Urals churned out vast numbers of T-34 tanks, Il-2 aircraft, and Katyusha rocket launchers, overwhelming German forces with sheer volume. The pivotal battles of Stalingrad and Kursk were not only victories but demonstrations of a maturing military machine shaped by relentless struggle. Soviet soldiers, once hastily mobilized and under-equipped, became experienced and determined, capable of executing complex operations on a continental scale. The Red Army which drove into Berlin in 1945 was not the same force that had fled from Minsk in 1941. It had been forged in fire.

card_event_motherland_calls.name: card_event_motherland_calls
card_event_motherland_calls.title: MOTHERLAND CALLS!
card_event_motherland_calls.text: Add a Soviet unit with Destruction in your deck to the support line. Give it Blitz. Destroy it at end of turn.
card_event_motherland_calls.flavorText: Soviet posters were among the most powerful tools of mass communication during WWII. As the German invasion advanced in 1941, the Soviet government unleashed a vast visual campaign to mobilize the population. Artists, often working through press agencies like TASS, created bold images that were quickly reproduced and plastered across cities, factories, and barracks. Their messages ranged from calls to defend the homeland to reminders of duty, sacrifice and unity. These posters featured vivid colors, dramatic compositions, and easily recognizable symbols like the red star, hammer and sickle, and heroic figures of soldiers, workers, and peasants. Designed for immediate impact, they aimed to stir emotion and reinforce resolve. Some artists, like Viktor Koretsky and Irakli Toidze, became well known for their stirring and sometimes brutal imagery. Toidze’s famous work The Motherland Calls became iconic, but it was part of a much broader and continuous campaign. Soviet wartime posters used bold pictures and simple slogans to inspire people during the hardest times of the war. They didn’t just spread government messages, they reminded everyone what they were fighting for and helped keep the country united and determined to survive.

card_event_persian_corridor.name: card_event_persian_corridor
card_event_persian_corridor.title: PERSIAN CORRIDOR
card_event_persian_corridor.text: Give a friendly British or US unit: "Destruction: Trigger all Destruction effects of your Soviet units."
card_event_persian_corridor.flavorText: The Persian Corridor became the Soviet Union’s most reliable supply line after Germany cut off the northern and western routes. Beginning in 1941, British and American forces moved Lend-Lease materiel through the Persian Gulf and across Iran into the Caucasus. This route carried nearly 8 million long tons of cargo, over 40 percent of all US aid sent to the Soviets. Iran’s roads and railways, many in poor condition before the war, were rapidly upgraded by Allied engineers. New ports and depots were built, and thousands of trucks moved daily convoys through rugged terrain. British and Indian troops managed security in the south, while Soviet units operated in the north. Unlike the Arctic convoys, which were often stalled by German attacks or harsh weather, the Persian Corridor stayed open year-round. The supplies it delivered included tanks, aircraft, food and raw materials critical to Soviet operations on the Eastern Front. It also helped the Allies maintain influence in a strategically important region for the rest of the war.

card_event_the_peoples_army.name: card_event_the_peoples_army
card_event_the_peoples_army.title: THE PEOPLE'S ARMY
card_event_the_peoples_army.text: Fill your hand and support line with LIGHT INFANTRY. Give them all Blitz.
card_event_the_peoples_army.flavorText: As German forces drove deep into Soviet territory in 1941, the distinction between soldier and citizen effectively vanished. In cities like Leningrad, Moscow, and Stalingrad, millions of civilians were mobilized to fortify the motherland. Ordinary men and women took up shovels, picks, and axes to dig anti-tank ditches, assemble tank traps, and erect barricades. Students, factory workers, and pensioners labored around the clock, often under the direction of local party committees or driven by the sheer desperation of the approaching front. In Moscow alone, hundreds of thousands of civilians helped construct over 1,000 kilometers of defensive lines during the critical autumn of 1941. In besieged Leningrad, women and teenagers braved shellfire and bitter cold to repair roads, unload supplies, and tend to the wounded. This mass participation, often formalized as the People’s Militia, helped delay German offensives at key moments. Though untrained and often underfed, these civilians formed a vital support network, earning a reputation built not on rank or uniform, but on a shared resolve to survive.

card_unit_132nd_omsk.name: card_unit_132nd_omsk
card_unit_132nd_omsk.title: 132nd OMSK
card_unit_132nd_omsk.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 for each of your units with two or more combat keywords.
card_unit_132nd_omsk.flavorText: The 132nd Omsk Rifle Regiment was part of the 27th Rifle Division, a unit originally formed during the Russian Civil War and known for its key role in the capture of Omsk in 1919. This earned the division its honorary title and solidified its place in early Soviet military history. During WWII, the first formation of the 27th Rifle Division was deployed near Grodno in Belarus at the start of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Facing the German 9th Army, the division was encircled in the Białystok–Minsk pocket and effectively destroyed by mid-July. Its commander, Major General Aleksandr Stepanov, was killed while leading a breakout attempt on August 11, and the division was officially disbanded the following month. A second formation of the division was established in August 1941 in Arkhangelsk, initially under the name Rebolsky Direction Division. Renamed the 27th Rifle Division on September 24, it was assigned to the 26th Army of the Karelian Front and saw action against Finnish forces in the far north until late 1944. The division later joined the 2nd Belorussian Front and was awarded the Order of the Red Banner on April 5, 1945, for its role in capturing Stolp. It ended the war under the 19th Army in May 1945.

card_unit_178th_guard_rifles.name: card_unit_178th_guard_rifles
card_unit_178th_guard_rifles.title: 178th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_178th_guard_rifles.text: Destruction: Add 89th INFANTRY REGIMENT to your support line.
card_unit_178th_guard_rifles.flavorText: The 178th Guards Rifle Regiment served as a frontline unit of the 58th Guards Rifle Division, which was formed in December 1942 from the battle-hardened 1st Rifle Division. The division was raised to Guards status for its actions during the Soviet counteroffensive at Stalingrad and became part of the 64th Army, later redesignated as the 7th Guards Army. As part of the 58th Division, the 178th Regiment saw extensive combat across the Eastern Front. It fought in the brutal campaigns of 1943, including the battles for the Donbass and the Dnieper River. In 1944, the regiment took part in Operation Bagration, contributing to the liberation of Belarus and the destruction of the German Army Group Centre. The division’s advance continued through eastern Poland and into East Prussia in early 1945. It was decorated with numerous awards, including the Order of the Red Banner and the Order of Suvorov.

card_unit_199th_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_199th_rifle_regiment
card_unit_199th_rifle_regiment.title: 199th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_199th_rifle_regiment.text: Gets +1+1 when you deploy or add a British or US unit.
card_unit_199th_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 199th Rifle Regiment served in the 39th Rifle Division, a veteran formation from the Russian Far East region. Originally formed in 1922, the division operated under the Special Far Eastern Army and later became part of the 1st Red Banner Army. Stationed near Vladivostok, the 39th was tasked with guarding the border against Japanese incursions and played a defensive role throughout most of WWII. Its regiments, including the 199th, were seasoned in frontier operations and prepared for rapid deployment in the event of conflict with Japan. In August 1945, during the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, the 39th Rifle Division finally moved into action. Advancing from Primorsky Krai, it helped crush the Japanese Kwantung Army in one of the final offensives of the war. For its role, the division received several decorations, including the Order of the Red Banner and the Order of Kutuzov. After the war, it was reorganized into a motorized unit and later transitioned into a training formation, preserving the legacy of its regiments, like the 199th, well into the postwar era.

card_unit_289th_gatchina.name: card_unit_289th_gatchina
card_unit_289th_gatchina.title: 289th GATCHINA
card_unit_289th_gatchina.text: Destruction: Draw a card. Your HQ gains defense equal to its cost.
card_unit_289th_gatchina.flavorText: The 289th Rifle Regiment served as part of the 120th Rifle Division, a formation which saw extensive combat across several fronts in WWII. The division’s third and final formation was established in April 1943 and took part in the Leningrad-Novgorod Offensive, helping to liberate key areas from German control. For its role in the battle for Gatchina, the division received the city’s name as an honorific title. During the fighting around Leningrad, the 120th operated under difficult winter conditions and against fortified German positions. After breaking through the siege lines, it participated in operations pushing into Estonia, notably engaging in the Battle of Narva in 1944. As the war progressed, the division advanced westward with Soviet forces and was ultimately involved in the climactic Battle of Berlin. For its combat performance, the division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner.

card_unit_44th_silesia.name: card_unit_44th_silesia
card_unit_44th_silesia.title: 44th SILESIA
card_unit_44th_silesia.text: Deployment: Draw a card for each friendly unit with two or more combat keywords.
card_unit_44th_silesia.flavorText: The 44th Silesia was one of the regiments within the Soviet 15th Guards Rifle Division, a formation which earned numerous distinctions through intense combat across the Eastern Front during WWII. Originally formed as the 1st Rifle Division, it was redesignated 15th Guards Rifle Division in early 1942 following its performance during the defense of Moscow. The division fought in the counteroffensive that pushed German forces back from the capital, then participated in the grinding battles around Smolensk and the Dnieper line. In 1944, the 15th Division advanced during Operation Bagration, helping liberate Belarus by breaking through entrenched German positions. That summer, the division moved westward, reaching the outskirts of East Prussia. In January 1945, it joined the Vistula-Oder Offensive, helping to clear the path into Silesia, where regiments like the 44th earned their battle honor titles. The division continued pushing into Germany and ended the war near Prague. Its achievements were recognized with multiple awards, including the Order of Lenin and the Red Banner.

card_unit_55th_rifles.name: card_unit_55th_rifles
card_unit_55th_rifles.title: 55th RIFLES
card_unit_55th_rifles.text: Destruction: Gain 3 additional kredits at the start of your next turn.
card_unit_55th_rifles.flavorText: The 55th Rifle Regiment was part of the 17th Rifle Division, an infantry formation of the Soviet Red Army with a long lineage dating back to the Russian Civil War. Originally formed in October 1918, the division fought in multiple early Soviet conflicts including the Civil War, the Polish-Soviet War, and the Winter War against Finland. In WWII, the division was first deployed to the Vitebsk-Polotsk area as part of the 10th Army at the start of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Surrounded by German forces east of Minsk, the division was destroyed by the end of that month, though it was not officially disbanded until September 19, 1941. A new 17th Rifle Division was reformed in October 1941 from the 17th Moscow People's Militia Rifle Division. It was assigned to the 33rd and later the 43rd Army, participating in the defense of Moscow. From 1943 onward, the division was part of the 1st Belorussian Front, where it fought in major operations including the Orel Counteroffensive, Operation Bagration, and the East Prussian Offensive. It was honored with the Order of the Red Banner and participated in the liberation of Bobruisk. The division was disbanded in 1947 after a brief postwar service as a rifle brigade.

card_unit_573rd_rifles.name: card_unit_573rd_rifles
card_unit_573rd_rifles.title: 573rd RIFLES
card_unit_573rd_rifles.text: Destruction: Add two 16th RIFLES to your support line.
card_unit_573rd_rifles.flavorText: The 573rd Rifle Regiment served as part of the 195th Rifle Division, a unit of the Soviet Red Army which saw extensive combat throughout WWII. Initially formed in the Kiev Special Military District in 1941, the division was destroyed during the encirclement at Kyiv that same year in September. A new 195th Division was formed in December 1941, this time in the South Ural region, and included the 573rd Rifle Regiment as one of its core units. This reformed division first saw major action in Operation Little Saturn in late 1942, where it helped breach the Italian 8th Army lines along the Don River. It then took part in Operation Gallop, pushing into the Donbas before being stalled by German counterattacks. The 195th later participated in the Third Battle of Kharkov, and during the summer of 1943 helped liberate areas of eastern Ukraine, including Dniprodzerzhynsk (present-day Kamianske), for which it received the Order of the Red Banner. In 1944, the division advanced through Ukraine into Romania and Bulgaria, engaging in several key offensives and helping encircle German forces during the Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive. After the war, it served as part of the occupation forces in Bulgaria until it was disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_61st_kirkenes.name: card_unit_61st_kirkenes
card_unit_61st_kirkenes.title: 61st KIRKENES
card_unit_61st_kirkenes.flavorText: The 61st Kirkenes Regiment belonged to the 45th Rifle Division, which was originally raised during the Russian Civil War and fought extensively throughout WWII. After being destroyed in the Battle of Stalingrad, the division was reformed in May 1943 from the 67th Naval Rifle Brigade. It then joined the Karelian Front and operated in the Arctic regions near the Soviet-Finnish border. The 45th Rifle Division played a key role in the Petsamo-Kirkenes Offensive in October 1944, a Soviet campaign aimed at expelling German forces from northern Finland and northeastern Norway. Fighting in extreme Arctic conditions, the division advanced through rugged terrain and poor weather, helping capture the strategic Norwegian town of Kirkenes. This marked the first major Soviet operation on Norwegian soil and contributed to the collapse of the German defensive line in Lapland. For its role in this campaign, the division received the honorific title "Pechenga" after capturing that key area. It remained active until the end of the war, guarding the soviet northern frontier. The division’s operations demonstrated the Red Army’s ability to wage high-tempo offensives even in harsh and remote environments.

card_unit_740th_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_740th_rifle_regiment
card_unit_740th_rifle_regiment.title: 740th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_740th_rifle_regiment.text: Deployment: Develop ARCTIC CONVOY, BURNING SKY or THE HAMMER.
card_unit_740th_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 740th Rifle Regiment was part of the Soviet Union’s 217th Rifle Division, an infantry unit formed just months before the German invasion in 1941. Created at Voronezh, the division saw early action under 28th Army, then 50th Army, narrowly avoiding destruction during Operation Typhoon. It played a key role in the defense of Tula where it endured heavy losses, with one regiment replaced by a local militia unit. After months of holding defensive positions, the 217th joined the 11th Guards Army and advanced westward during Operation Kutuzov in 1943. It later earned the Order of the Red Banner for its contribution to the battle for Gomel. During Operation Bagration in 1944, it helped liberate Zhlobin and Bobruisk. The division then participated in the Vistula-Oder Offensive, capturing Mława and pushing into East Prussia. For these achievements, it received the Order of Lenin and the Order of Suvorov. By war’s end, the 217th was engaged in the East Prussian campaign, finishing near Königsberg.

card_unit_77th_guards.name: card_unit_77th_guards
card_unit_77th_guards.title: 77th GUARDS
card_unit_77th_guards.text: When you deploy or add a unit, give it a random combat keyword.
card_unit_77th_guards.flavorText: The 77th Guards Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 26th Guards Rifle Division, one of the Red Army’s elite infantry formations. Created in April 1942 from the experienced 93rd Rifle Division, the 26th Division was quickly thrown into heavy fighting in the Rzhev sector. It endured brutal losses during the First Rzhev–Sychyovka Offensive and Operation Mars, in battles that tested the limits of Soviet infantry under grueling conditions. In 1943, the division joined the newly formed 11th Guards Army and fought in Operation Kutuzov and the advance through Bryansk. During the 1944 summer offensive, it played a key role in the Vitebsk-Orsha and Minsk operations, helping to encircle and destroy large portions of Army Group Center. After forcing a crossing over the Berezina River, the division received the Order of the Red Banner. It continued advancing through Lithuania and into East Prussia, where it stormed Insterburg and later took part in the capture of Königsberg. For its role in these battles, it was awarded the Order of Suvorov and earned a place among the Soviet Union’s most decorated divisions.

card_unit_iosef_stalin_ii_1944.name: card_unit_iosef_stalin_ii_1944
card_unit_iosef_stalin_ii_1944.title: IS II 1944 EARLY
card_unit_iosef_stalin_ii_1944.text: Destruction: Add two 42nd RIFLES. Give one Guard, the other Shock.
card_unit_iosef_stalin_ii_1944.flavorText: Introduced in 1944, the IS-2 was the Soviet Union’s answer to heavily armored German tanks like the Panther and Tiger. Officially designated as the Iosif Stalin II, the tank featured a powerful 122 mm D-25T gun capable of knocking out enemy armor at long ranges. Unlike earlier Soviet tanks, the IS-2 emphasized armor and firepower over speed. Its frontal armor, up to 120 mm-thick and sloped, proved highly resistant to German anti-tank weapons. By mid-1944, IS-2 units were entering combat in significant numbers, particularly during the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive. Their arrival caused concern among German commanders who recognized the tank’s ability to breach fortified positions. The IS-2’s high-explosive shells were also devastating against bunkers and infantry, making it valuable in both tank duels and urban assaults. Around 2,252 IS-2 tanks were produced in the year 1944 alone, forming the backbone of Soviet breakthrough tank regiments for the rest of the war.

card_unit_kv_1s.name: card_unit_kv_1s
card_unit_kv_1s.title: KV-1S
card_unit_kv_1s.text: Your other units have +1 attack for each of their combat keywords.
card_unit_kv_1s.flavorText: The KV-1S was an improved version of the Soviet KV-1 heavy tank, introduced in 1942 to address the original design's flaws. Early KV-1s had earned a reputation for their thick armor but suffered from excessive weight and mechanical breakdowns. The KV-1S, with the "S" standing for "skorostnoi" or "fast," featured lighter armor, a redesigned turret, and a commander's cupola which improved visibility. These changes reduced the tank's weight by several tons, increasing its top speed to around 43 km/h. Although it sacrificed some armor protection, the KV-1S was more reliable and mobile on the battlefield. It remained armed with the same 76.2 mm gun as earlier models, which by 1943 was becoming less effective against newer German armor. As a result, the KV-1S was soon overshadowed by the S-series heavy tanks. Still, it saw service on multiple fronts through 1943 and into early 1944. Production of the KV-1S ended after 1,370 units were built. It marked the final major revision of the KV-1 before the Red Army shifted focus to more advanced designs like the IS-2.

card_unit_tupolev_tb_3.name: card_unit_tupolev_tb_3
card_unit_tupolev_tb_3.title: TUPOLEV TB-3
card_unit_tupolev_tb_3.text: Deployment: Add I-16 ISHAK on both sides of this unit.
card_unit_tupolev_tb_3.flavorText: The Tupolev TB-3 was a Soviet heavy bomber designed by Andrei Tupolev and introduced in 1932. It was one of the world's first all-metal four-engine monoplane bombers and served in the Soviet Air Force throughout the 1930s and into WWII despite being considered obsolete by 1939. The TB-3 featured corrugated metal construction, fixed landing gear, and could carry up to 5,000 kg of bombs. A total of 818 were produced. At the outbreak of the German invasion in 1941, the Soviet Air Force still had over 500 TB-3s available. The aircraft flew night bombing missions starting June 23 and participated in major battles through 1943, including Moscow, Stalingrad, and Kursk. Though vulnerable to enemy fighters and flak due to its slow speed and lack of armor, the TB-3's large bomb load and range kept it in frontline service longer than expected. It also played a vital role in transporting cargo and troops, including paratroopers. Additionally, the TB-3 was used in experimental roles such as carrying small tanks and launching parasite fighters in the Zveno project. One notable mission was the 1941 strike on the port of Constanța, Romania, where TB-3 motherships deployed I-16 fighters to bomb targets, without suffering losses. Though officially retired in 1945, a few TB-3s remained in use for transport duties even after the war ended.

card_event_deep_operation.name: card_event_deep_operation
card_event_deep_operation.title: DEEP OPERATION
card_event_deep_operation.text: Add two LIGHT INFANTRY to your hand, then give all such units in hand Blitz.
card_event_deep_operation.flavorText: Deep Operation, or Soviet Deep Battle, was a military theory that was developed by the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s.  In short, the Deep Operations doctrine is to exploit the depths of the battlefield and is achieved through using overwhelming superiority of men and material, and whatever the costs, find the weakest points in the enemy's territory and move all reserve units to these sectors. Before the war the Soviet military had abandoned the deep battle concept, but they relearned it and started to apply it during the strategic offensive at Stalingrad. After that, deep operation was used with a devastating effect.

card_event_five_year_plan.name: card_event_five_year_plan
card_event_five_year_plan.title: FIVE YEAR PLAN
card_event_five_year_plan.text: Draw 5 cards. Your HQ takes 5 damage.
card_event_five_year_plan.flavorText: The Five Year Plans were plans to develop the economy of the Soviet Union over limited periods. The first five year plan was implemented from 1928-1932 and focused on developing heavy industry and agriculture in the Soviet Union, the second from 1933-1937 focused on the same thing. The third was from 1938-1941 and focused on armament, the fourth focused again on armament as well as heavy industries. The Soviet Union was the first state to develop five year plans, but many other socialistic states would later follow in their footsteps.

card_event_partisans.name: card_event_partisans
card_event_partisans.title: PARTISANS
card_event_partisans.text: Take control of an enemy unit. At the end of turn, send it to owner's hand.
card_event_partisans.flavorText: The Soviet partisans fought a guerrilla war against the Axis forces on the Eastern Front during WWII. The partisans were coordinated and controlled by the Soviet government and covertly received arms, equipment, and orders from the Soviet forces fighting at the front. Their role was to operate in the rear and to harass, disrupt, sabotage, and to provide intelligence about German military and economic activities in the occupied territories. The Soviet Partisans movement grew from 90,000 men and women in 1941 to 550,000 in 1943 and managed to make a significant contribution to the Allied victory on the Eastern Front.

card_event_promotion.name: card_event_promotion
card_event_promotion.title: PROMOTION
card_event_promotion.text: Draw a random unit from your deck. It gets +2+2 when it is deployed.
card_event_promotion.flavorText: The Red Army officer corps suffered greatly in the military purges of 1937 and had in no way recovered when the German forces invaded Soviet Union. However, as the war prolonged the situation improved, many officers that had been decommissioned in the purge were reinstated, and a new Red Army officers corps emerged, which included men that had risen from the ranks or were drawn from civil life.

card_event_red_dawn.name: card_event_red_dawn
card_event_red_dawn.title: RED DAWN
card_event_red_dawn.text: Choose one - Deal 3 damage to a unit and your HQ OR add FROM THE PEOPLE to hand.
card_event_red_dawn.flavorText: The color of red is often associated with left wing politics and the red flag which symbolizes socialism dates back to  the 19th century. The red flag of Soviet Union, also known as The Red Banner or Hammer & Sickle,  first emerged during the Russian Revolution and the red color symbolizes the workers that have died in their struggle against Capitalism.

card_event_refit.name: card_event_refit
card_event_refit.title: UPGRADE
card_event_refit.text: Destroy a friendly tank. Add a tank from the same nation that costs 3 more.
card_event_refit.flavorText: At the start of WWII the Soviet Union only possessed 20,000 tanks. Throughout the war they manufactured 106,000 tanks, and on top of that they received 22,000 tanks from the US and the UK. During the war approximately 120,000 Soviet tanks went out of service, some were destroyed, others broke down and were not repaired, some were considered obsolete and withdrawn from service.

card_event_road_to_berlin.name: card_event_road_to_berlin
card_event_road_to_berlin.title: ROAD TO BERLIN
card_event_road_to_berlin.text: The enemy HQ gets: "If this HQ has taken 3+ damage this turn, give your HQ +3 defense."
card_event_road_to_berlin.flavorText: On 16 April 1945 the Soviet Red Army started the final offensive against the German capital. After fierce fighting the Battle of Berlin ended on 2 May when the commander of the Berlin Defense Area unconditionally surrendered the city to General Vasily Chuikov of the Red Army. Operation Barbarossa started on June 22 1941, and 1410 days later the tables had turned.

card_unit_125_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_125_rifle_regiment
card_unit_125_rifle_regiment.title: 125th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_125_rifle_regiment.text: When the enemy draws a card, deal 1 damage to the enemy HQ.
card_unit_125_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 125th Rifle Regiment was part of the 2nd formation of the 6th Rifle Division of the Red Army. The division fought numerous battles and campaigns on the Eastern Front, including Operation Barbarossa, 3rd Battle of Kharkov, Battle of Debrecen and finally the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. The division took part in the liberation of Ukraine, Romania, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia from German occupation and received several honorifics for its service, including the Order of the Red Banner. The 6th Rifle Division was disbanded in the fall 1945.

card_unit_152mm_howitzer_gun.name: card_unit_152mm_howitzer_gun
card_unit_152mm_howitzer_gun.title: 152mm HOWITZER GUN
card_unit_152mm_howitzer_gun.flavorText: The 152 mm howitzer-gun M1937, also known as ML-20, was a Soviet heavy howitzer gun that was produced from 1937 to 1947 and used by the Red Army during WWII. The gun was one of the most successful Soviet artillery pieces during WWII as it had better range than the 15 cm sFH 18 German heavy howitzer, which meant that it could fire from positions where it was immune to enemy artillery fire. It was also more lightweight, which meant it was easier to transport, and it was much cheaper to produce than its German counterpart. A total of 6,884 ML-20’s were produced.

card_unit_173rd_guard_rifles.name: card_unit_173rd_guard_rifles
card_unit_173rd_guard_rifles.title: 173rd GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_173rd_guard_rifles.text: Gets +1 attack when your HQ takes damage.
card_unit_173rd_guard_rifles.flavorText: The 173rd Guard Rifles was a regiment of the 1st Division of the Soviet Red Army. The division was formed from units stationed in Moscow and during the course of WWII it was reformed a few times. In 1940 the division was redesignated 1st Motorized Division and in 1942 it was raised to guard status. The division fought at Stalingrad in 1942 and by the end of the year it was redesignated 58th Guards Rifle Division.
