In 1944 the division became part of the 70th Army of the 2nd Belorussian, and that same year it participated in the Lublin-Brest Offensive, followed by the advance into Poland where it fought at Gdynia. The division was briefly a part of the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany before being disbanded in July 1945.

card_unit_175th_motorized.name: card_unit_175th_motorized
card_unit_175th_motorized.title: 175th MOTORIZED
card_unit_175th_motorized.text: Destruction: All your Soviet tanks in hand and deck cost 1 less to deploy.
card_unit_175th_motorized.flavorText: The 175th Motorized Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army. In 1940 the division took part in the Soviet occupation of the Baltic states, but in 1941, during Operation Barbarossa, it was called back to Moscow where it joined the 7th Mechanised Corps in defending against the German advance. That same year the division participated in heavy fighting near Smolensk, where it was encircled and annihilated, but reformed again later in the year and renamed to the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division. Throughout the war the division participated in numerous battles and operations, including the Moscow counteroffensive in 1942, the Battle of Rzhev, and Operation Kutuzov which was the first of two counteroffensives during the Kursk Strategic Offensive Operation in 1943. Finally, in April 1945, the division took part in storming and liberating the town of Baltiysk from German occupation.

card_unit_214th_amur.name: card_unit_214th_amur
card_unit_214th_amur.title: 214th AMUR
card_unit_214th_amur.text: Your T-34 units have +1 Heavy Armor and operate for 1 less.
card_unit_214th_amur.flavorText: The 214th Amur Order of the Red Star Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 12th Rifle Division of the Red Army. The division was formed twice and its first formation was active from 1918-1921 and fought in the Russian Civil War and the Polish-Soviet War. The division was formed again in 1923 and was stationed at Omsk in Siberia where it spent WWII. In 1945 the division participated in the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and was involved in capturing several Chinese cities as well as defeating the Japanese Kwantung Army. In 1945 the division was given the honorific “Amur” for its services.

card_unit_272nd_guards.name: card_unit_272nd_guards
card_unit_272nd_guards.title: 272nd GUARDS
card_unit_272nd_guards.text: Destruction: Add a IOSEF STALIN II to your support line.
card_unit_272nd_guards.flavorText: The 272nd Guards Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 90th Guards Rifle Division of the Red Army. The division was formed in 1943 from the 325th Rifle Division and raised to guards status for its actions. The division fought in numerous battles and campaigns, including the Battle of Kursk, Operation Bagration, the Baltic Offensive and finally the East Prussian Offensive. In recognition for its service during the war the division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner.

card_unit_2nd_marines_battalion.name: card_unit_2nd_marines_battalion
card_unit_2nd_marines_battalion.title: 2nd MARINES BATTALION
card_unit_2nd_marines_battalion.text: Combat damage dealt to this unit is doubled.
card_unit_2nd_marines_battalion.flavorText: The Red Army Marines performed a number of important landings during WWII and contributed to the defense of Odessa, Moscow, Leningrad, Sevastopol, Stalingrad, Novorossiysk and Kerch. The 2nd Battalion of the 2d Marine Regiment is best known for its participation in the Yevpatoria assault in 1942, which was an amphibious assault on Yevpatoria in Crimea where the aim was to divert German troops attacking Sevastopol and the Kerch peninsula. During the battle there was an uprising in the city of Yevpatoria and many citizens decided to join the fight against the Germans. The operation was a success since it managed to distract the German forces from Sevastopol, but it came at a very high cost. Of the 700 marines participating in the battle almost all lost their lives. The few remaining survivors along with 3000 civilians were taken prisoner by the Germans and executed.

card_unit_461st_rifles.name: card_unit_461st_rifles
card_unit_461st_rifles.title: 461st RIFLES
card_unit_461st_rifles.text: When this unit is dealt damage, your HQ gets equal amount of defense.
card_unit_461st_rifles.flavorText: The 461st Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 142nd Rifle Division of the Red Army. The division was formed in 1939 and participated in the Winter War against Finland, but didn’t see much combat until 1944 during the Soviet Vyborg–Petrozavodsk Offensive. In 1945 the division participated in the Vistula-Oder Offensive against the Germans, and later in the East Pomeranian Offensive, where they managed to capture the town of Graudenz in northern Poland. The division finished the war on the Baltic coast where it was disbanded in the summer of 1945.

card_location_bryansk_waw.name: card_location_bryansk_waw
card_location_bryansk_waw.title: BRYANSK
card_location_bryansk_waw.text: Bryansk was the center of partisan activity against the German invaders.
card_location_bryansk_waw.flavorText: The city of Bryansk was captured by the Germans in 1941 but during the occupation over 60,000 partisans operated in the region in and around the city, mainly from the Bryanskie Forests. The partisans managed to disrupt the German supply lines by blowing up railways and bridges as well as killing numerous German soldiers in combat. The city was finally liberated by the Red Army on 17 September in 1943.

card_location_kursk.name: card_location_kursk
card_location_kursk.title: KURSK
card_location_kursk.text: The Battle of Kursk was history's largest tank battle.
card_location_kursk.flavorText: The Battle of Kursk, fought from July 5th to August 23rd, 1943, was WWII's largest tank battle and a crucial confrontation on the Eastern Front. Following the Soviet victory at Stalingrad, the Germans launched Operation Citadel to encircle Soviet forces in the Kursk salient. However, the Soviets had fortified their defenses, effectively countering the German attacks. The battle resulted in heavy losses on both sides, but the Soviets emerged victorious, marking a turning point in the war. This defeat halted the German advance and allowed the Soviets to gain the initiative, leading to a series of offensives that pushed the Germans back.

card_location_moscow.name: card_location_moscow
card_location_moscow.title: MOSCOW
card_location_moscow.text: Moscow is the capital of the Soviet Union.
card_location_moscow.flavorText: The Battle of Moscow was a military campaign that took place during WWII, from October 2, 1941 to January 7, 1942, in the region surrounding the capital of Soviet Union. Moscow was one the primary military objectives of the Axis, but the Red Army managed to halt their offensive and execute a successful strategic counteroffensive that pushed back the Axis forces. The Battle of Moscow is considered to be one of the most important battles fought between Soviet Union and the Axis as it was the first time the Axis advance was stopped by the Red Army.

card_location_stalingrad.name: card_location_stalingrad
card_location_stalingrad.title: STALINGRAD
card_location_stalingrad.text: The Battle of Stalingrad is often identified as the turning point on the Eastern Front.
card_location_stalingrad.flavorText: The Battle of Stalingrad is often identified as the turning point on the Eastern Front. It was the largest confrontation of World War II, in which Germany and its Allies fought the Soviet Union for control of the city of Stalingrad (now Volgograd) in Southern Russia.

card_location_ai_soviet_unlock1.name: card_location_ai_soviet_unlock1
card_location_ai_soviet_unlock1.title: DANZIG
card_location_ai_soviet_unlock1.text: The Free City of Danzig was captured by German forces at the start of the war.
card_location_ai_soviet_unlock1.flavorText: The Battle of Westerplatte in the harbor of Danzig was one of the first battles in Germany's invasion of Poland, marking the start of World War II in Europe. Germany held the city until at the end of the war when it was liberated by Soviet forces.

card_event_extended_barrage.name: card_event_extended_barrage
card_event_extended_barrage.title: EXTENDED BARRAGE
card_event_extended_barrage.text: Deal 6 damage to target unit. Lose 2 kredits at the start of your next turn.
card_event_extended_barrage.flavorText: The Soviet Union placed immense value on artillery, calling it the “God of War,” and fielded more guns than any other nation in WWII. Their arsenal ranged from 76mm to massive 203mm siege howitzers. The 76mm ZiS-3 was the most widely used, with around 100,000 produced by 1945. Medium artillery included 122mm guns, while the powerful 152mm ML-20 served as heavy artillery. The Soviets also made extensive use of 82mm and 120mm mortars and the infamous Katyusha rocket launchers, known to the Germans as “Stalin’s Organs” due to their terrifying sound. By the war’s later years, Soviet artillery tactics had evolved significantly and massed and concentrated barrages were used to clear the way for advancing infantry and tanks. These tactics were key in battles like Seelow Heights and the final assault on Berlin.

card_event_honorifics.name: card_event_honorifics
card_event_honorifics.title: HONORIFICS
card_event_honorifics.text: Convert a friendly unit into your last destroyed unit.
card_event_honorifics.flavorText: During WWII, the Soviet Union used a wide system of honorifics to recognize heroism and exceptional service. The highest individual award was Hero of the Soviet Union, given to people who showed outstanding bravery, either in combat or civilian roles. Recipients got a Gold Star medal and were also awarded the Order of Lenin. Units that performed especially well in battle could be given the Guards title. This raised their status and gave them better equipment, priority in reinforcements, and higher pay. These units often led major offensives. Some cities were honored with the title Hero City for their defense and sacrifice. Cities like Moscow, Leningrad, Stalingrad, and Sevastopol received this title, commemorated with a monument. The Soviet military also gave out many other awards, such as the Order of the Red Banner and service medals. In terms of rank, senior leaders could be named Marshal of the Soviet Union, while Generalissimo was a special title given only to Joseph Stalin. This system helped reward loyalty and boost morale during the war.

card_event_orders_from_above.name: card_event_orders_from_above
card_event_orders_from_above.title: ORDERS FROM ABOVE
card_event_orders_from_above.text: Target a tank or infantry. Give it +1+1 for each damaged unit if friendly. Otherwise, deal 3 damage to it.
card_event_orders_from_above.flavorText: During WWII, the Soviet Union's highest military authority was the Stavka of the Supreme High Command, established on June 23, 1941, following the German invasion. Initially chaired by Marshal Semyon Timoshenko, leadership quickly transitioned to Joseph Stalin, who assumed the role of Supreme Commander-in-Chief from July 10, 1941. Key members included Georgy Zhukov, Vyacheslav Molotov, Kliment Voroshilov, Semyon Budyonny, and Admiral Nikolai Kuznetsov. The Stavka was responsible for strategic military planning and coordination for all Soviet Armed Forces. It oversaw the organization of campaigns, allocation of resources, and coordination between various military branches and partisan groups. The General Staff acted as its executive body, implementing the Stavka's directives. Throughout the war, the Stavka issued critical orders, such as Order No. 270, which mandated severe penalties for surrender, and Order No. 227, famously known as "Not One Step Back," aimed at preventing unauthorized retreats. Operating primarily from Moscow, the Stavka adapted to wartime conditions by relocating to more secure locations, including underground facilities, in order to maintain command continuity during air raids. Following the end of hostilities in Europe, the Stavka was disbanded in October 1945, concluding its role in directing the Soviet war effort.

card_event_rush.name: card_event_rush
card_event_rush.title: RUSH
card_event_rush.text: Deal 1 damage to a friendly unit. Deal 4 damage to a random enemy unit.
card_event_rush.flavorText: When the war reached Soviet cities in 1941, urban combat required new tactics. First developed by the 62nd Army's 13th Guards Rifle Division in Stalingrad, the Soviet shturmovye gruppy (English: assault groups) were elite shock troops assembled to clear and capture fortified buildings and locations through fast close-quarters attacks. These small, flexible units changed street fighting with their specialized three-group structure. The assault group consisted of 6 to 8 men carrying PPSh submachine guns, grenades and sharpened spades. Their standard tactic was to infiltrate as closely as possible, then sprint to the building under covering fire. The assault group would toss grenades into doors and windows, then head inside to finish off the stunned German defenders in hand-to-hand combat.  Right behind them came the reinforcement group with heavy machine guns, mortars, sniper and anti-tank rifles. They transformed captured buildings into strongholds to defend against German counterattacks. Finally, the reserve group provided critical support by laying down covering fire, delivering ammunition and reinforcing failed attacks when needed. The Shturmovye Gruppy encouraged individual initiative and teamwork by pairing soldiers. Unlike traditional mass assaults, these units exploited German weaknesses, especially their fear of night fighting and close combat. These units became very efficient tools for the Red Army in urban warfare, using speed, surprise and overwhelming force to clear buildings room by room. By the time of the Berlin offensive in 1945, Soviet assault groups tactics had been mastered and widespread.

card_event_surveil.name: card_event_surveil
card_event_surveil.title: SURVEIL
card_event_surveil.text: Choose a card in hand. Convert it into target unit.
card_event_surveil.flavorText: During WWII, Soviet reconnaissance tactics focused on close-range observation and aggressive patrolling. The Red Army often lacked the advanced aerial surveillance tools used by the Western Allies, so they relied heavily on ground-based scouting. These missions were typically carried out by Razvedchiki scouts, specialized reconnaissance troops trained to operate in small teams. These teams moved silently and used camouflage to blend into the terrain. Their primary tasks were to locate enemy positions, monitor troop movements, and report back quickly. They often crossed into enemy territory at night, sometimes crawling for hours to avoid detection. Capturing enemy soldiers for interrogation was a common objective. The Soviets also used armored scout cars such as the BA-64 and light tanks such as the T-70 for mobile reconnaissance, especially during fast-moving operations. On the aerial side, aircraft such as the Polikarpov Po-2 and the Yak-9R were used for photo-reconnaissance, though they had limited range and were vulnerable to enemy fighters. Despite these challenges, Soviet recon units provided essential intelligence that shaped frontline tactics and helped direct artillery fire with greater accuracy.

card_event_victory_banners.name: card_event_victory_banners
card_event_victory_banners.title: VICTORY BANNERS
card_event_victory_banners.text: Target a unit. Convert all units on the battlefield belonging to the owner into the targeted unit.
card_event_victory_banners.flavorText: Victory banners became powerful symbols for the Red Army across the Eastern Front. Units often raised red flags to celebrate major gains, from city centers to enemy fortifications. These banners, whether handmade or official, served to signal triumph and boost morale. By the final year of the war, they had become essential emblems of Soviet success. As the Red Army closed in on Berlin in April 1945, Soviet command prepared several Victory Banners to ensure a flag would be raised over the German Reichstag. The political significance of this act was so great that multiple flags were distributed to different assault groups, each tasked with storming the building. Soviet leadership feared that heavy resistance or chance could prevent one unit from reaching the rooftop. To guarantee the symbolic moment occurred, at least nine banners were made and assigned to front-line units. These flags were carried into intense combat as soldiers fought room by room through the Reichstag. The 150th Rifle Division, led by General Vasily Shatilov, received one such banner, which would later be recognized as the official Victory Banner. The team that ultimately raised the banner included Sergeant Mikhail Yegorov and Sergeant Meliton Kantaria. Their flag was hoisted on May 1, 1945, though the act was later restaged for photographs. Other units also claimed to have raised that banner first, reflecting the chaos and competition of the moment.

card_unit_220th_rifles.name: card_unit_220th_rifles
card_unit_220th_rifles.title: 220th RIFLES
card_unit_220th_rifles.text: Has +2 attack for each damaged unit on the battlefield.
card_unit_220th_rifles.flavorText: The 220th Rifle Regiment was part of the 4th Rifle Division, a Soviet formation with a long service history. During the division’s first formation, it fought in the Russian Civil War, the Polish-Soviet War, the 1939 invasion of Poland, and the Winter War against Finland. In WWII, it took part in the Barvinkove-Losowaja Operation and the Battle of Voronezh in 1942. The 220th, along with the rest of the division, suffered severe losses and the division was disbanded in November 1942. It was reformed in 1943 in the Moscow Military District. From April 1943 to May 1944, it served with the 11th Army on the Baltic Front, before being transferred to the 48th Army. In January 1945, it was part of the 25th Rifle Corps of the 69th Army and fought in the brutal battle for the Puławy bridgehead in Poland. Losses were heavy, reducing the division’s strength to just six battalions. It later fought in the final assault on Berlin in April 1945. The division was disbanded in the summer of 1945. Its personnel were reassigned to other formations under the Group of Soviet Occupation Forces in Germany.

card_unit_312th_novgorod.name: card_unit_312th_novgorod
card_unit_312th_novgorod.title: 312th NOVGOROD
card_unit_312th_novgorod.text: Add a 6th MOTOR RIFLES to your support line when you Convert one or more cards.
card_unit_312th_novgorod.flavorText: During WWII, the 312th Rifle Regiment, originally the 77th Rifle Regiment, served under the 26th Rifle Division, a formation created in 1918 during the Russian Civil War. At the onset of the German invasion in 1941, the division was shifted west to join the fight. It played a role in several major campaigns throughout the war, including the battles of the Demyansk Pocket, Leningrad, Riga, Königsberg, and Samland. These offensives were vital in breaking German lines and regaining lost Soviet territory. In early 1944, the 312th Rifle Regiment was awarded the honorific title "Novgorod" for its role in the Leningrad-Novgorod Offensive, where it helped liberate the historic city of Novgorod from German occupation.

card_unit_336th_guards_naval.name: card_unit_336th_guards_naval
card_unit_336th_guards_naval.title: 336th GUARDS NAVAL
card_unit_336th_guards_naval.text: Deployment: Choose a unit in hand with a cost of 3 or less. Add a copy to your support line.
card_unit_336th_guards_naval.flavorText: The 336th Guards Naval Infantry Brigade traces its origins to the 347th Rifle Regiment of the 308th Rifle Division, formed in March 1942. Comprising personnel from the Omsk Infantry School and recruits from the Omsk Region, Altai Territory and its capital city Gorno-Altaysk (southern Siberia), the division was deployed to the Stalingrad Front in September 1942. It engaged in intense combat near the Kotluban state farm and later within Stalingrad itself, particularly around the Barrikady Factory. For its actions during this period, the 308th Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner in June 1943. After rebuilding, it participated in Operation Kutuzov and was subsequently honored with Guards status, becoming the 120th Guards Rifle Division. The 347th Rifle Regiment was redesignated as the 336th Guards Rifle Regiment. The unit continued to distinguish itself in operations across Orel, Bryansk, and Gomel-Rechitsa. In August 1944, it was awarded the honorary title "Bialystok" for its role in liberating the city. Later, it received the Orders of Suvorov and Alexander Nevsky for its exemplary performance.

card_unit_51st_rifle_brigade.name: card_unit_51st_rifle_brigade
card_unit_51st_rifle_brigade.title: 51st RIFLE BRIGADE
card_unit_51st_rifle_brigade.text: Gets +1+2 when you Convert one or more cards.
card_unit_51st_rifle_brigade.flavorText: The 51st Rifle Brigade was formed in October 1941 from military students and training units in the Volga Military District. Deployed in December, it joined the reserves of the Northwestern Front. In January 1942, the brigade participated in the Toropets–Kholm Offensive as part of the 4th Shock Army, which operated behind German lines. After months of combat, it was withdrawn to Kalinin in April. On April 21, 1942, the 51st Rifle Brigade was reorganized into the 119th Rifle Division. This new formation made use of the brigade's experienced personnel, allowing for rapid training and deployment. By November 1942, the division was engaged in Operation Uranus, the Soviet counteroffensive at Stalingrad. It was positioned within the Serafimovich bridgehead across the Don River and played a crucial role in encircling Axis forces. For its exemplary performance during the Stalingrad campaign, the 119th Rifle Division was raised to Guards status on December 16, 1942, becoming the 54th Guards Rifle Division. It later participated in major offensives across southern Ukraine, including the liberation of Makeevka, and advanced into Poland and Czechoslovakia. By the end of WWII, the division had earned multiple honors, such as the Orders of Lenin,  the Red Banner, Suvorov, and Kutuzov, before being disbanded in 1946.

card_unit_676th_regiment.name: card_unit_676th_regiment
card_unit_676th_regiment.title: 676th REGIMENT
card_unit_676th_regiment.text: Gains +2 attack and Shock every time it takes damage.
card_unit_676th_regiment.flavorText: The 676th Rifle Regiment was an infantry unit of the Soviet Red Army which was active during WWII. At the beginning of the war, it was part of the 192nd Mountain Rifle Division, serving under the 12th Army. By early August 1940, the 192nd Division was trapped in the German encirclement near Uman. All of the division, apart from the 676th Regiment, was destroyed. The regiment subsequently joined the 15th Rifle Division and participated in defending the Donbas area until being transferred to the Bryansk Front's 13th Army in May 1942. The 15th Rifle Division took part in the defensive battle at Voronezh in the summer of 1942 and in the subsequent Voronezh-Kastornoye offensive to liberate the city in early 1943. It was later involved in the Battle of Kursk, occupying a defensive position in the northern sector, and in a series of soviet offensive operations, notably Operation Bagration and the liberation of Baranovichi in 1944, the East Pomeranian Offensive and finally the Battle of Berlin in 1945. The 676th Rifle Regiment was awarded the Order of the Red Banner and the Order of Suvorov for its actions during the war.

card_unit_6th_motor_rifles_sov.name: card_unit_6th_motor_rifles_sov
card_unit_6th_motor_rifles_sov.title: 6th MOTOR RIFLES
card_unit_6th_motor_rifles_sov.text: Deployment: Draw a card. Convert two cards in your deck into this unit.
card_unit_6th_motor_rifles_sov.flavorText: The 6th Motor Rifle Regiment was an infantry unit of the Soviet Red Army which was active during WWII. At the beginning of the war, it was part of the 127th Rifle Division, later renamed 2nd Guards Rifle Division for its distinguished combat service during the early stages of the German invasion. The division entered the war under the 19th Army’s 25th Rifle Corps. After surviving the chaotic retreats of 1941 near Smolensk and Yartsevo, it fought defensive battles in the Kursk area in October, before joining the Soviet counteroffensive toward Stary Oskol during the Winter Campaign of 1941-42. The 2nd Guards Rifle Division earned the title "Tamanskaya" after liberating Taman during the Novorossiysk-Taman offensive in September and October 1943. The next month, it took part in the Kerch-Eltigen Operation, where it spearheaded the landings on Crimea's eastern coast. In Spring 1944, it participated in the Crimean Offensive, capturing Alushta on 15 April 1944. Transferred to the Baltic front in July, the division fought in the Šiauliai Offensive and the Battle of Memel, before advancing into East Prussia in 1945. It ended the war on the Baltic coast near Primorsk.

card_unit_99th_kholm.name: card_unit_99th_kholm
card_unit_99th_kholm.title: 99th KHOLM
card_unit_99th_kholm.text: Deployment: Lose 1 kredit at the start of your next turn.
card_unit_99th_kholm.flavorText: The 99th Rifle Regiment was an infantry unit in service in the 33rd Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. The division participated in the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939 and in the occupation of Lithuania from June 1940. Stationed there when Germany invaded in June 1941, it fought desperate battles during the Baltic strategic defensive operation, ultimately retreating through Kaunas and across the Viliya River. During August 1941, the division fought offensive battles in the area east of Kholm, liberating a number of villages. However, in early September 1941, the Germans launched a powerful offensive and the division was forced to retreat. After being reduced to only 500 men, the division was reformed and fought in the Toropets-Kholm Offensive in early 1942, leading to the encirclement of the German forces in the Kholm pocket. Throughout 1942 and until September 1943, the division fought southeast of the city of Kholm. The 99th Rifle Regiment earned the title "Kholm" for its bravery during those combats. The 33rd Division later distinguished itself in key operations, notably the Leningrad-Novgorod Offensive, the Tartu Offensive and the liberation of Riga in 1944. In 1945, it advanced through Pomerania and played a crucial role in the Battle of Berlin, storming the city from the north and reaching the Reichstag. Postwar, it served in Germany as part of the occupation forces before being disbanded in 1947.

card_unit_ilyushin_il_2.name: card_unit_ilyushin_il_2
card_unit_ilyushin_il_2.title: ILYUSHIN IL-2
card_unit_ilyushin_il_2.text: Deployment: Choose a unit in hand with a cost of 3 or less. Put it into play.
card_unit_ilyushin_il_2.flavorText: The Ilyushin IL-2, also known as the Sturmovik, entered Soviet service in 1941 as a heavily armored single-seat ground-attack aircraft. Designed to support troops at the front, it featured a steel armored shell integrated into the fuselage to protect the pilot, engine, and fuel tanks. This innovative structure made the IL-2 more resilient than most aircraft of its time. Armed with 23 mm cannons, bombs, and unguided rockets, it became a key asset in the Soviet Union’s response to the German invasion. Despite its strong defensive design, the single-seat IL-2 had critical weaknesses. Lacking a rear gunner, it was highly vulnerable to enemy fighters. Inexperienced pilots and ground crews faced a steep learning curve, and early losses were severe. Nonetheless, the aircraft proved effective in battlefield roles, especially against convoys and soft targets. Soviet pilots developed tactics that emphasized sloped dive attacks and concentrated fire. Production was initially slow due to wartime factory relocations, but output increased rapidly after Stalin’s personal intervention. By late 1942, improvements began to appear, including the transition to a two-seat design. However, the original single-seat IL-2 set the foundation for what would become the most produced military aircraft design in history.

card_unit_kv_85.name: card_unit_kv_85
card_unit_kv_85.title: KV-85
card_unit_kv_85.text: Deployment: Convert a card in hand into your last destroyed unit. Lose 2 kredits at the start of your next turn.
card_unit_kv_85.flavorText: The KV-85 was a Soviet heavy tank developed in 1943 as an interim solution to counter advanced German armor such as the Tiger I. It combined the KV-1S chassis with a new turret designed for the IS-1, mounting an 85mm D-5T gun capable of penetrating the Tiger I's armor at 1,000 meters. This upgrade addressed the KV-1's inadequate firepower against newer German tanks. Production was limited to 148 units between August and October 1943, as the KV-85 was quickly superseded by the more advanced IS series. Despite its enhanced armament, the KV-85 retained the KV-1S's chassis, which suffered from mobility and armor limitations. Its armor, while improved, was still vulnerable to German 75mm and 88mm guns. The KV-85 saw combat in late 1943, notably in Ukraine, where it provided valuable experience that informed the development of the IS-1 and IS-2 tanks. While its service was brief, the KV-85 represented a crucial step in the evolution of Soviet heavy tank design during WWII.

card_event_advanced_soviet_research.name: card_event_advanced_soviet_research
card_event_advanced_soviet_research.title: ADVANCED SOVIET RESEARCH
card_event_advanced_soviet_research.text: Choose One - Add SLOPED ARMOR to hand OR add three STALIN'S ORGAN to hand.

card_event_aerosani.name: card_event_aerosani
card_event_aerosani.title: AEROSANI
card_event_aerosani.text: Deal 2 damage to an enemy ground target and adjacent enemies.

card_event_do_or_die.name: card_event_do_or_die
card_event_do_or_die.title: DO OR DIE
card_event_do_or_die.text: When a friendly unit is destroyed this turn, add a BLAST and a PRODUCTION to your hand.
card_event_do_or_die.flavorText: Pavlov’s House was a four-story apartment block in central Stalingrad, close to the Volga and overlooking 9th January Square. In late 1942, soldiers of the 42nd Guards Rifle Regiment, 13th Guards Rifle Division, took the building back from German forces and turned it into a fortified strongpoint. Its popular name came from Sergeant Yakov Pavlov, who led the small group that first seized it, though Lieutenant Ivan Afanasiev later commanded the position. The defenders mined the approaches, put barbed wire around the building, and placed machine guns and anti-tank rifles in windows and on upper floors. They broke holes through walls to move inside the building and dug a trench to connect with Soviet positions near the Volga. Supplies reached them through this trench or by boats crossing under fire. The garrison held the position for roughly two months, with soldiers and civilians sheltering in the same ruined structure. Some later accounts made Pavlov’s House more famous than wartime records suggest, but it remains one of the best known examples of Stalingrad street fighting.

card_event_expanded_soviet_research.name: card_event_expanded_soviet_research
card_event_expanded_soviet_research.title: EXPANDED SOVIET RESEARCH
card_event_expanded_soviet_research.text: Choose One - Add STANDARD AMMO to hand OR ADVANCED SOVIET RESEARCH to hand.

card_event_form_battle_line.name: card_event_form_battle_line
card_event_form_battle_line.title: FORM BATTLE LINE
card_event_form_battle_line.text: Choose One - Add three LIGHT INFANTRY to your support line with Blitz OR +1+1.
card_event_form_battle_line.flavorText: From 1943, the Red Army rarely fought from a single neat line. Its battle positions were usually built in depth, with forward troops, supporting weapons, reserves, and command posts spread across several layers. Rifle companies held trenches, foxholes, villages, woods, or reverse slopes. Behind them stood mortars, machine guns, anti tank rifles, field guns, and reserve groups ready to seal gaps or counterattack. As their battle experience grew, Soviet commanders became better at arranging these layers into a connected system. Engineers laid mines and built obstacles along likely routes of attack. Artillery was grouped to support the front lines and strike enemy assembly areas. Anti-tank strongpoints covered roads, open ground, and approaches to bridges. Tanks were not only used for attacks, but also kept in reserve to meet enemy armor that had broken through. This method reflected the hard lessons from 1941 and 1942, when thin defenses were often shattered by rapid German attacks. By later campaigns, Soviet battle lines were meant to slow the enemy, absorb pressure, and seize opportunities for a counterstrike.

card_event_irregular_recruits.name: card_event_irregular_recruits
card_event_irregular_recruits.title: IRREGULAR RECRUITS
card_event_irregular_recruits.text: Add a random combination of two LIGHT INFANTRY and/or BLAST to your hand.
card_event_irregular_recruits.flavorText: In 1941, the Soviet Union rushed to raise new forces as German armies advanced toward Moscow and Leningrad. In Moscow, twelve people’s militia divisions were formed in only a few days in July. Recruits came from factories, offices, schools, and institutes. The campaign was presented as voluntary, but local party and military officials also used lists from workplaces to fill the ranks quickly. This gave units strong local ties, yet it also caused some problems. Skilled workers, older men, students, and people with little military experience often ended up in frontline formations before proper screening and training could be completed. Leningrad followed a similar path. Its People’s Militia Army began forming in late June 1941 from workers, students, reserve officers, retired officers, and destruction battalions first meant to fight saboteurs and parachutists. Some militia units were later absorbed into regular Red Army formations. Alongside them, behind German lines, Soviet partisan recruits included civilians and escaped soldiers.

card_event_rasputitsa.name: card_event_rasputitsa
card_event_rasputitsa.title: RASPUTITSA
card_event_rasputitsa.text: Each unit is dealt damage equal to its operation cost.
card_event_rasputitsa.flavorText: Rasputitsa, literally the “season of bad roads”, describes the periods of deep mud that k strikes Russia, Ukraine and Bielorussia during the spring thaw and autumn rains. During WWII, melting snow, heavy rainfall and waterlogged soils could turn unpaved roads and open ground into near impassable swamps, trapping trucks, artillery and even tanks. Rasputitsa became an important feature of fighting on the Eastern Front. In the autumn of 1941, it severely hindered movement during Operation Typhoon, the German offensive toward Moscow. Vehicles became bogged down and supply routes deteriorated as the Wehrmacht advanced farther into Soviet territory. The mud was not purely a Soviet advantage, however, as Red Army movements and logistics suffered as well. Rather than single-handedly stopping the German advance, rasputitsa compounded existing problems of Soviet resistance, enormous distances to cover, and overstretched supply lines.

card_event_sloped_armor.name: card_event_sloped_armor
card_event_sloped_armor.title: SLOPED ARMOR
card_event_sloped_armor.text: Add a IOSEF STALIN II to your support line. It fights target enemy unit. Send it to hand at the end of turn.

card_event_soviet_military_research.name: card_event_soviet_military_research
card_event_soviet_military_research.title: SOVIET MILITARY RESEARCH
card_event_soviet_military_research.text: Choose One - Add AEROSANI to hand OR EXPANDED SOVIET RESEARCH to hand.
card_event_soviet_military_research.flavorText: Soviet military research in WWII often focused on practical answers to urgent battlefield problems. The T-34 illustrated this approach clearly. Its sloped armor did not make the tank invulnerable, but it increased effective protection without adding the weight of much thicker vertical plates. This helped the T-34 combine armor, speed, and a powerful gun in a design that surprised German forces in 1941. This idea was not invented in the Soviet Union, but Soviet engineers used it on a mass-produced tank with exceptional effect. Other wartime projects followed the same practical logic. Katyusha rocket launchers gave the Red Army a cheap and mobile way to deliver sudden heavy fire, able to move before enemy counterfire could respond. Aerosani (propeller-driven sledges) offered reconnaissance, transport, and light raiding ability in deep snow where normal vehicles struggled. Soviet weapons research didn’t stop at armor and artillery. For instance, the 7.62×39mm intermediate cartridge was designed in 1943 for a new family of infantry weapons, including carbines, automatic rifles, and light machine guns.

card_event_standard_ammo.name: card_event_standard_ammo
card_event_standard_ammo.title: STANDARD AMMO
card_event_standard_ammo.text: Reduce the deploy and operation cost of all units in your hand and deck by 1.

card_unit_102_rifles.name: card_unit_102_rifles
card_unit_102_rifles.title: 102nd RIFLES
card_unit_102_rifles.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of your turn. Destruction: Draw a card.
card_unit_102_rifles.flavorText: The 102nd Rifle Regiment served as part of the Soviet 41st Rifle Division. The division had been formed at Kryvyi Rih before the war and entered the German Soviet War in June 1941 with the 6th Army on the Southwestern Front. It was destroyed near Kiev during the disastrous defeat in September 1941. Recreated at Chapayevsk in March 1942, the 41st Rifle Division was wiped out again near Izyum during the Second Battle of Kharkov in May. A third formation followed in October 1942, built from the 118th Rifle Brigade. This incarnation survived to fight at Kursk, through Belarus and into Poland, including the Lublin-Brest Offensive. Serving with the 69th Army of the 1st Belorussian Front, the division later took part in the Battle of Berlin in April and May 1945. It was disbanded in summer.

card_unit_1081th_smolensk.name: card_unit_1081th_smolensk
card_unit_1081th_smolensk.title: 1081st SMOLENSK
card_unit_1081th_smolensk.text: When you play a BLAST, distribute 2 damage randomly between all enemies.
card_unit_1081th_smolensk.flavorText: The 1081st Rifle Regiment was one of the original rifle regiments of the Soviet 312th Rifle Division, alongside the 1079th and 1083rd. The division was first formed in July 1941 at Akyubinsk in Kazakhstan, with many Kazakh personnel in its ranks. It was sent north toward Leningrad, then urgently redirected toward Moscow during Operation Typhoon. Its regiments arrived in poor order and were thrown into combat near Maloyaroslavets almost straight from the trains. Within weeks, the first 312th Rifle Division was badly depleted and its remnants were absorbed into other units. A second 312th Rifle Division was formed in Siberia at the end of 1941. It fought near Moscow, then in the costly battles around Rzhev and Sychevka. In 1943, the division joined the advance during Operation Suvorov and entered Dorogobuzh before helping liberate Smolensk. For this action it received the honor name “Smolensk”. The division later fought through Belorussia, Poland, and toward Berlin, earning the Orders of the Red Banner, Suvorov, and Kutuzov before being disbanded in 1945.

card_unit_216th_guards.name: card_unit_216th_guards
card_unit_216th_guards.title: 216th GUARDS
card_unit_216th_guards.text: At the start of your turn, deal 2 damage to your HQ and draw a card. Becomes Veteran after the second time.
card_unit_216th_guards.flavorText: The 216th Guards Rifle Regiment began as the 1043rd Rifle Regiment of the 284th Rifle Division. Its Guards title was earned at the Battle of Stalingrad, where the division held positions around Mamayev Kurgan and parts of the city center against the German Sixth Army. In March 1943, the 284th was redesignated as the 79th Guards Rifle Division, and the 1043rd became the 216th Guards Rifle Regiment. The regiment later distinguished itself during the Vistula crossing in 1944. Near Magnuszew, the division forced the river crossing under pressure, and the 1st Battalion of the 216th Guards was among the first units to succeed. Its commander, Captain Yefim Tsitovsky, was named a Hero of the Soviet Union for his role in securing the bridgehead. The 79th Guards Rifle Division kept fighting westward through Ukraine, Poland, and Germany as part of the 8th Guards Army. It earned the honorific “Zaporozhye” after the capture of the city in 1943, then participated in the Battles of the Oder, Seelow Heights, and Berlin. In the final push, it crossed the Teltow Canal and helped capture Tempelhof Airfield.

card_unit_3rd_morskoi_pekhoty.name: card_unit_3rd_morskoi_pekhoty
card_unit_3rd_morskoi_pekhoty.title: 3rd MORSKOI PEKHOTY
card_unit_3rd_morskoi_pekhoty.text: Deployment: Add a LIGHT INFANTRY to your support line and a BLAST to your hand.
card_unit_3rd_morskoi_pekhoty.flavorText: The 3rd Naval Infantry Brigade of the Baltic Fleet was formed in July 1941, when the Soviet Union turned sailors and naval base personnel into infantry to meet the German and Finnish advance. Its first men came from forces based at Kronstadt, Peterhof, and Oranienbaum. The brigade entered combat almost at once in Karelia near the Vidlitsa River. These sailors fought far from ships, often in forests, river lines, and fortified positions along Lake Ladoga and the Svir. In September 1941, the brigade was pressed back toward Lake Ladoga and had to be evacuated by the Ladoga Military Flotilla. It later held a bridgehead on the north bank of the Svir for a long period. In 1944, during the Svir Petrozavodsk Offensive, the brigade landed behind Finnish lines as part of the Tuloksa landing. It later received the Order of the Red Banner and the honorific title “Pechenga”, then fought in northern Norway and Czechoslovakia before the war ended.

card_unit_511th_regiment.name: card_unit_511th_regiment
card_unit_511th_regiment.title: 511th REGIMENT
card_unit_511th_regiment.text: Defense of this unit cannot go lower than 1. Becomes Veteran after it takes damage.
card_unit_511th_regiment.flavorText: The 511th Rifle Regiment joined the 239th Rifle Division when that formation was converted from a motorized division into a regular rifle division in July 1941. The division was first formed in the Soviet Far East as part of the prewar mechanized buildup, then gave up its tank regiment and many vehicles during reorganization. The 511th became one of its three rifle regiments, alongside the 813th and 817th. The 239th Rifle Division was moved west in November 1941 as the German advance threatened Moscow. It arrived in Tula Oblast and was thrown into battle almost entirely against elements of the 2nd Panzer Army. The division was later encircled near Stalinogorsk, broke out, and joined the Soviet winter counteroffensive. In 1942 it fought in the costly Battle of Rzhev, then moved north to the Volkhov Front. There, it took part in operations to break the siege of Leningrad and helped drive German forces away from the city in 1944, earning the Order of the Red Banner. The 511th Regiment later received the Orders of Alexander Nevsky and Kutuzov for its actions in Latvia and Silesia.

card_unit_641st_rifles.name: card_unit_641st_rifles
card_unit_641st_rifles.title: 641st RIFLES
card_unit_641st_rifles.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of your turn if damaged.
card_unit_641st_rifles.flavorText: The 641st Rifle Regiment served in both formations of the Soviet 165th Rifle Division. In the first formation, the division moved from the North Caucasus Military District to the Kyiv front in 1941. There, the 165th fought south of the Ukrainian capital before being caught in the encirclement of the Southwestern Front, the largest encirclement in the history of warfare, and effectively destroyed. A new 165th Rifle Division was formed in the Ural Military District in early 1942, and the 641st Rifle Regiment was again included in its order of battle. The rebuilt division went north to the Leningrad sector, where it fought in difficult operations around Lyuban, Krasny Bor, and Mga. It later moved west, fought near Nevel, and joined the advance through Belorussia and Poland. In 1944, the division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner and received the honorific title “Siedlce” after helping capture the city. In 1945, the 641st Rifle Regiment earned its own Order of the Red Banner during the East Pomeranian offensive, before the division ended the war near the Baltic coast.

card_unit_75th_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_75th_rifle_regiment
card_unit_75th_rifle_regiment.title: 75th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_75th_rifle_regiment.text: Add a copy next to your HQ when targeted by an enemy effect.
card_unit_75th_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 75th Rifle Regiment served as part of the Soviet 31st Rifle Division, alongside the 177th and 248th Rifle Regiments. Formed near Stalingrad in 1925, the division spent the interwar years in the region before moving to the Caucasus in 1940 to strengthen the Iranian and Turkish borders. During WWII, the 31st Rifle Division fought at Rostov and later retreated into the Caucasus during Case Blue, suffering heavy losses in the defense of Tuapse. It returned to the offensive as German forces withdrew and later fought in the Battle of the Dnieper, the Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive and the Vistula–Oder Offensive. In 1945, the division took part in both the Berlin and Prague offensives, ending the war deep in Central Europe.

card_unit_866th_rifles.name: card_unit_866th_rifles
card_unit_866th_rifles.title: 866th RIFLES
card_unit_866th_rifles.text: Destruction: Add two BLASTS to your hand.
card_unit_866th_rifles.flavorText: The 866th Rifle Regiment was one of the original infantry regiments of the Soviet 287th Rifle Division, formed at Yelets in 1941. Its first campaign was brief and brutal. While still not fully ready for combat, the division was sent into the Bryansk Front reserve, then rushed by rail to Brasovo after German armor broke through Soviet lines. Between 3 and 5 October 1941, the 287th Division launched counterattacks near Bryansk, but the formation was trapped in the Bryansk pocket and almost completely destroyed by mid October. The regiment’s story did not end there. The 287th Rifle Division was rebuilt at Lipetsk in late 1941, from survivors who had escaped the pocket. With the same basic organization, including the 866th Rifle Regiment, it returned to the Bryansk Front and later fought under the 3rd, 63rd, 13th, 38th, and 3rd Guards Armies. By 1945, the division had fought into the Berlin Offensive and carried the honorific “Novograd Volynsky”, along with several other Soviet decorations.

card_unit_909th_roslavl.name: card_unit_909th_roslavl
card_unit_909th_roslavl.title: 909th ROSLAVL
card_unit_909th_roslavl.flavorText: The 909th Rifle Regiment was one of the original infantry regiments of the Soviet 247th Rifle Division. The division was first formed in 1941 from NKVD personnel, then placed under Red Army command. It first fought during the Battle of Moscow, but was caught in the Vyazma encirclement during Operation Typhoon. Survivors broke out in small groups, and the division was soon disbanded. A second 247th Rifle Division was formed in late 1941 with the 909th Regiment again in its order of battle. It fought through the hard battles around Rzhev, crossed the Vazuza River during Operation Mars and briefly gained ground before suffering heavy losses. In 1943, the division joined the Smolensk offensive. It advanced across the Desna River and helped liberate Roslavl in September, earning the honorific title “Roslavl”. The division later fought through Belorussia, Poland, and Germany. In 1945, the 909th Regiment received honors for its actions in Brandenburg and Berlin, while the division was decorated with the Order of the Red Banner.

card_unit_stz_5_katyusha.name: card_unit_stz_5_katyusha
card_unit_stz_5_katyusha.title: STZ-5 KATYUSHA
card_unit_stz_5_katyusha.text: When this unit deals combat damage, add equal amount of BLASTS to your hand.
card_unit_stz_5_katyusha.flavorText: The STZ-5 Katyusha combined the Soviet STZ-5 tracked artillery tractor with the powerful BM-13-16 multiple rocket launcher. Produced at the Stalingrad Tractor Factory, the STZ-5 was designed as a military prime mover and became the most numerous purpose-built Soviet artillery tractor of WWII, with more than 9,900 produced. In 1941, a small number of STZ-5 tractors were fitted with 132 mm BM-13-16 launchers. These rare vehicles saw action in the fighting around Moscow in 1941 and Stalingrad in 1942. The Katyusha itself became one of the Red Army’s most distinctive weapons. Its rockets were less accurate than conventional artillery, but a battery could unleash a devastating barrage within seconds and then quickly relocate before enemy batteries could respond. Katyushas were mounted on many different vehicles during the war, including trucks, tanks and artillery tractors, with the STZ-5 representing one of the earliest tracked platforms for the launcher.

card_unit_tupolev_tu_2.name: card_unit_tupolev_tu_2
card_unit_tupolev_tu_2.title: TUPOLEV TU-2
card_unit_tupolev_tu_2.text: Draw a random unit from your deck when a friendly unit becomes Veteran.
card_unit_tupolev_tu_2.flavorText: The Tupolev Tu-2 was a Soviet twin-engine medium bomber designed for speed, range, and a heavy bomb load. It first flew in 1941 and entered service in 1942. A total of 2,257 were built. The aircraft was created under difficult conditions, since Andrei Tupolev had been arrested during the Soviet purges but was still placed in charge of an aircraft design team because of his value to the war effort. The Tu-2 was intended to match the German Junkers Ju 88 as a fast daylight bomber and dive bomber. It could carry up to 1.5 tons of bombs internally, and 2.2 externally, while two forward-firing 20 mm cannons and defensive machine guns gave it useful protection. Crews valued it because it was fast, handled well, and could survive heavy damage. Its combat debut happened around Velikiye Luki in late 1942 with the 132nd Bomber Aviation Regiment. Production problems and engine changes slowed wider use, but some improved versions went into production in 1943. The Tu-2 became one of the Soviet Union’s most important twin-engine bombers, and played a key role in the Red Army’s final offensives.

card_event_assault_cam1.name: card_event_assault_cam1
card_event_assault_cam1.title: FRONTAL ASSAULT
card_event_assault_cam1.text: Give your LIGHT INFANTRY units +1+1. If you have none, add two to your hand.

card_event_bloody_sickle_cam1.name: card_event_bloody_sickle_cam1
card_event_bloody_sickle_cam1.title: BLOODY SICKLE
card_event_bloody_sickle_cam1.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit and your HQ. Draw a card.

card_event_campaign_frostbite.name: card_event_campaign_frostbite
card_event_campaign_frostbite.title: FROSTBITE
card_event_campaign_frostbite.text: Deal 1 damage to an enemy ground unit.

card_event_campaign_moscow1_retreat.name: card_event_campaign_moscow1_retreat
card_event_campaign_moscow1_retreat.title: RETREAT
card_event_campaign_moscow1_retreat.text: Target friendly unit is removed from the battlefield. Pin a random enemy unit.

card_event_campaign_moscow3_charge.name: card_event_campaign_moscow3_charge
card_event_campaign_moscow3_charge.title: CHARGE
card_event_campaign_moscow3_charge.text: Destroy a friendly unit. Destroy a random enemy unit.

card_event_campaign_moscow3_forward_pres.name: card_event_campaign_moscow3_forward_press
card_event_campaign_moscow3_forward_pres.title: FORWARD PRESS
card_event_campaign_moscow3_forward_pres.text: Deal damage to target unit equal to number of friendly units.

card_event_campaign_moscow3_toe_to_toe.name: card_event_campaign_moscow3_toe_to_toe
card_event_campaign_moscow3_toe_to_toe.title: TOE TO TOE
card_event_campaign_moscow3_toe_to_toe.text: Deal damage to target unit equal to highest attack among friendly units.

card_event_from_the_people_tut.name: card_event_from_the_people_tut
card_event_from_the_people_tut.title: FROM THE PEOPLE
card_event_from_the_people_tut.flavorText: The war against Nazi Germany was called the Great Patriotic War in the Soviet Union, and for a good reason. It was not only the Soviet soldiers on the battlefield that made great sacrifices, but also the millions of workers that were mobilized in the rear to work for the war effort. History shows that many of these workers suffered unimaginable deprivations, but despite this, all the evidence points to the fact that workers willingly endured these hardships for the sake of the motherland and for the struggle against the German occupation.

card_event_reserves_cam1.name: card_event_reserves_cam1
card_event_reserves_cam1.title: RESERVES
card_event_reserves_cam1.text: Add two LIGHT INFANTRY to your hand, plus one for each previously played RESERVES.

card_event_ural_factories_cam1.name: card_event_ural_factories_cam1
card_event_ural_factories_cam1.title: URAL FACTORIES
card_event_ural_factories_cam1.text: Destroy a friendly unit. Add a random unit from same nation that costs 1 more.

card_location_soviet_scen1.name: card_location_soviet_scen1
card_location_soviet_scen1.title: BRYANSK
card_location_soviet_scen1.text: Bryansk is an important town on the road towards Moscow.

card_location_soviet_scen2.name: card_location_soviet_scen2
card_location_soviet_scen2.title: KALININ
card_location_soviet_scen2.text: Kalinin is a city northwest of Moscow, at the northern edge of the Mozhaisk defense line.

card_location_soviet_scen3.name: card_location_soviet_scen3
card_location_soviet_scen3.title: KLIN
card_location_soviet_scen3.text: The town of Klin lies between Kalinin and Moscow, 85 km from the capital.

card_location_soviet_scen4.name: card_location_soviet_scen4
card_location_soviet_scen4.title: MOSCOW
card_location_soviet_scen4.text: The capital of the Soviet Union and the seat of the government.

card_location_soviet_scen5.name: card_location_soviet_scen5
card_location_soviet_scen5.title: MOSCOW
card_location_soviet_scen5.text: The capital of the Soviet Union and the seat of the government.

card_unit_1005th_rifles_cam1.name: card_unit_1005th_rifles_cam1
card_unit_1005th_rifles_cam1.title: 1005th RIFLES
card_unit_1005th_rifles_cam1.text: When the opponent targets 1005th RIFLES with an order, draw a card.

card_unit_102_rifles_vet.name: card_unit_102_rifles_vet
card_unit_102_rifles_vet.title: 102nd RIFLES
card_unit_102_rifles_vet.text: When this unit becomes Veteran, add a THE HAMMER to your hand.

card_unit_10th_guards_regiment_cam1.name: card_unit_10th_guards_regiment_cam1
card_unit_10th_guards_regiment_cam1.title: 918th GUARDS
card_unit_10th_guards_regiment_cam1.text: When 918th GUARDS receives damage, give it +1 attack.

card_unit_12th_guards_mechanised_vet.name: card_unit_12th_guards_mechanised_vet
card_unit_12th_guards_mechanised_vet.title: 12th GUARDS MECHANISED
card_unit_12th_guards_mechanised_vet.text: Draw 2 cards when this unit becomes Veteran.

card_unit_190th_guard_rifles_vet.name: card_unit_190th_guard_rifles_vet
card_unit_190th_guard_rifles_vet.title: 190th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_190th_guard_rifles_vet.text: Gains Shock at the start of your turn.

card_unit_216th_guards_vet.name: card_unit_216th_guards_vet
card_unit_216th_guards_vet.title: 216th GUARDS
card_unit_216th_guards_vet.text: Your other units and HQ get +3 defense when this unit becomes Veteran.

card_unit_252nd_RIFLES_vet.name: card_unit_252nd_RIFLES_vet
card_unit_252nd_RIFLES_vet.title: 252nd RIFLES
card_unit_252nd_RIFLES_vet.text: Cannot be pinned or suppressed. Takes 1 less combat damage from ground units.

card_unit_266th_guards_rifles_vet.name: card_unit_266th_guards_rifles_vet
card_unit_266th_guards_rifles_vet.title: 266th GUARD RIFLES
card_unit_266th_guards_rifles_vet.text: When you deploy a unit, it becomes Veteran if able.

card_unit_321st_rifles_cam1.name: card_unit_321st_rifles_cam1
card_unit_321st_rifles_cam1.title: 51st RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_321st_rifles_cam1.text: Destruction: Add a 1/1 LIGHT INFANTRY to the support line.

card_unit_414th_rifles.name: card_unit_414th_rifles
card_unit_414th_rifles.title: 414th RIFLES
card_unit_414th_rifles.text: Destruction: Shuffle 97th RIFLES into your deck. Draw 3 cards and deal 3 damage to your HQ.
card_unit_414th_rifles.flavorText: The 414th Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 18th Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. The division was formed in 1918 with troops from Arkhangelsk, Belsky and Kotlassky areas. In 1920 the division took part in the invasion of Poland, but was defeated in the Battle of Warsaw that same year. In 1939 the 18th Division participated in the Winter War in Finland, but was encircled near Lemetti and yet again defeated. The division was formed again in 1940 and, as part of the 20th Army, it defended against the invading German forces east of the Dnieper River in 1941, where the division was nearly wiped out and disbanded shortly after. Again in 1941 the division was reformed and fought at the Battle of Moscow, and was afterwards raised to Guards status for its actions, and renamed 11th Guards Rifle Division. In 1943 the division broke through the encirclement of Leningrad and joined the forces of the Leningrad Front. In late September 1944, it was stationed along the Soviet-Finnish border, southwest of Sortavala, and later assigned to the Stavka reserves. As part of the 19th Army's 132nd Rifle Corps, the unit participated in the Svir-Petrozavodsk Offensive. In mid-November 1944, the division and its higher headquarters were reassigned to the 2nd Belorussian Front, contributing to the East Pomeranian Strategic Offensive Operation, notably fighting in Danzig, Poland.

card_unit_511th_regiment_vet.name: card_unit_511th_regiment_vet
card_unit_511th_regiment_vet.title: 511th REGIMENT
card_unit_511th_regiment_vet.text: Your infantry with 1 defense have +2 attack.

card_unit_641st_rifles_vet.name: card_unit_641st_rifles_vet
card_unit_641st_rifles_vet.title: 641st RIFLES
card_unit_641st_rifles_vet.text: Destruction: Draw a card if this unit destroyed an enemy unit this turn.

card_unit_84th_infantry_cam1.name: card_unit_84th_infantry_cam1
card_unit_84th_infantry_cam1.title: 17th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_84th_infantry_cam1.flavorText: The 84th Infantry Regiment was attached to the 6th Rifle Division of the Red Army in WWII. In the opening stages of Operation Barbarossa the division was stationed in Brest in Belarus and took part in the defense of the Brest Fortress, which later became a symbol of Soviet resistance. The 6th Rifle Division took part in many military operations during WWII, including the Third Battle of Kharkov, the Battle of the Korsun Cherkassy Pocket, the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. The division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner twice and the Order of Suvorov 2nd Class for its valor in combat.

card_unit_95th_rifles_blank.name: card_unit_95th_rifles_blank
card_unit_95th_rifles_blank.title: 95th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_95th_rifles_blank.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to your HQ.

card_unit_bt_7_1937_vet.name: card_unit_bt_7_1937_vet
card_unit_bt_7_1937_vet.title: BT-7 1937
card_unit_bt_7_1937_vet.text: Each time the enemy draws a card, deal 2 damage to the enemy HQ.

card_unit_bt_7_cam1.name: card_unit_bt_7_cam1
card_unit_bt_7_cam1.title: BT-7
card_unit_bt_7_cam1.flavorText: The BT 7 was a light tank and was produced between 1935 and 1940. It was nicknamed “Betka and/or Betushka” and was the last one of the BT series of Soviet cavalry tanks. In 1940 the BT 7 was more or less replaced by the T-34 medium tank.

card_unit_katyusha_cam1.name: card_unit_katyusha_cam1
card_unit_katyusha_cam1.title: KATYUSHA
card_unit_katyusha_cam1.text: When KATYUSHA attacks, it deals 0-1 additional damage.

card_event_conscripts.name: card_event_conscripts
card_event_conscripts.title: CONSCRIPTS
card_event_conscripts.text: Shuffle a RESERVES into your deck for each enemy unit on the battlefield. Draw a card.
card_event_conscripts.flavorText: Soon after Operation Barbarossa started in 1941, the Soviet government passed a law that stated that all male citizens from the ages of 16 to 28 were liable for military service. This law was expanded in 1942 to all citizens in the liberated territories and it stated that all citizens from 17-30 years old who had not joined the fight already should be conscripted into the Red Army ranks. This meant that the Red Army grew into a diverse force, with military personnel from different ethnicities, languages, beliefs or political convictions (or lack thereof).

card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union.name: card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union
card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union.title: HEROES OF THE SOVIET UNION
card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite Soviet units to add to your hand.
card_event_heroes_of_the_soviet_union.flavorText: Hero of the Soviet Union was the highest distinction awarded for heroism in service of the state or society. It was first awarded in 1934 and the last one was in 1991. 12,777 people got the award, most of them for feats during WWII, and some received it more than once.

card_event_moat.name: card_event_moat
card_event_moat.title: STAND FAST
card_event_moat.text: Give target infantry or tank unit +5+5 and +5 operation cost.
card_event_moat.flavorText: A moat is a deep ditch dug for defensive purposes around a fortification, building or town. To prepare for the Germans that were closing in on Moscow, the city was fortified in a hurry. 250,000 women and elderly men were hastily recruited to build trenches and anti-tank moats around Moscow. It is estimated that they moved three million cubic meters of earth with handheld shovels and no mechanical help.

card_event_tractor_factories.name: card_event_tractor_factories
card_event_tractor_factories.title: TRACTOR FACTORIES
card_event_tractor_factories.text: Add two T-34 1942 to your support line.
card_event_tractor_factories.flavorText: In 1941, at the start of Operation Barbarossa, the majority of Soviet tank factories were evacuated to the Urals. A few of the factories were converted tractor plants, the most notable one was the Stalingrad Tractor Plant which was responsible for almost half of all T-34 production before it became a site of fierce fighting during the Battle of Stalingrad. At the start of the Battle of Moscow the Red Army had 22,000 tanks in their arsenal, which was four times more than the Germans and more than all the armies of the world combined.

card_event_ura.name: card_event_ura
card_event_ura.title: URA!
card_event_ura.text: This turn, your Soviet units get +3 attack and deal excess damage to the enemy HQ in combat.
card_event_ura.flavorText: "Ura!" has been used as a battle cry by Russian soldiers for over a century, at least since the Russo-Ottoman War in 1877. Soldiers of the Red Army frequently used it during WWII and it’s still being used by the Russian Ground Forces.

card_unit_1005th_rifles.name: card_unit_1005th_rifles
card_unit_1005th_rifles.title: 1005th RIFLES
card_unit_1005th_rifles.text: When the opponent targets 1005th RIFLES with an order, draw a card.
card_unit_1005th_rifles.flavorText: The 1005th Rifle Regiment was made a subordinate unit of the 279th Rifle Division in 1941 and fought with the 50th Army during the Battle of Bryansk, which took place at the early stages of the Moscow Campaign. During the Battle of Bryansk the 50th Army was encircled by the Germans, but the units continued to fight in order to delay the onslaught on Moscow. After almost 20 days of fighting the 279th Rifle Regiment was destroyed, but the only remaining unit was the 1005th Rifle Regiment which became a separate unit under the Bryansk Front. The 297th Rifle Division was officially disbanded by the end of 1941, but reformed  in 1942 and participated in numerous battles and campaigns on the Eastern Front after that. The division ended the war in the Courland Pocket in 1945.

card_unit_17th_rifle_regiment.name: card_unit_17th_rifle_regiment
card_unit_17th_rifle_regiment.title: 17th RIFLE REGIMENT
card_unit_17th_rifle_regiment.text: At the start of your turn, fully repair this unit and give it +1+1.
card_unit_17th_rifle_regiment.flavorText: The 17th Rifle Regiment served with the 32nd Rifle Division at the start of Operation Typhoon, the German strategic offensive of 1941 which marked the end of Operation Barbarossa and the beginning of the Red Army counteroffensive. The 32nd Rifle Division was transported to the Mozhaisk Defense Line, west of Moscow, where they set up defenses against the advancing German forces. The division had dug in on the Napoleonic battlefield of Borodino among other places west of Moscow, and the first battle took place in the Yelnya area where the 17th Rifle Regiment had set up defenses. The best the 32nd division could hope for was to slow down the two advancing German veteran divisions (10th Panzer Division and the 2nd SS Division Das Reich) which they managed to do for 5 days before Mozhaisk was lost. The heroic defense did not go unnoticed by Soviet officials and the 32nd Rifle Division was raised to guard status (29th Guards Rifle Division) and the 17th Rifle Regiment was awarded the Order of the Red Banner.

card_unit_503rd_motors.name: card_unit_503rd_motors
card_unit_503rd_motors.title: 503rd MOTORS
card_unit_503rd_motors.text: Deployment: Give your LIGHT INFANTRY units +1+1.
card_unit_503rd_motors.flavorText: The 503rd Motor Regiment fought with the 19th Motor Rifle Division as part of the 24th Army of the Western Front during the Battle of Moscow. Throughout WWII the division served under various formations and participated in numerous battles and campaigns, fighting its way from Moscow to Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and finally to Czechoslovakia where it ended the war in 1945. For their outstanding performance during the war the division was awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd degree.

card_event_claim_the_skies.name: card_event_claim_the_skies
card_event_claim_the_skies.title: CLAIM THE SKIES
card_event_claim_the_skies.text: Your air unit with the highest attack gets +1+1, then fights target enemy unit.
card_event_claim_the_skies.flavorText: At the beginning of WWII, the Soviet Air Forces faced shortcomings with outdated aircraft and less advanced technology compared to Western nations. Despite having the world's largest air force in 1938, their aeronautical capabilities were notably inferior and were no match to the German Luftwaffe. However, by 1943, the Soviet Union had transformed their air force and managed to secure air superiority over Germany on the Eastern Front. By then their air forces were equipped with excellent fighters and ground attack aircraft, and outpaced the Germans in both quality and quantity. At the same time, the Luftwaffe withdrew numerous fighter squadrons from the Eastern Front in order to defend against Western Allied bombing raids, leaving the Eastern skies vulnerable to relentless air attacks. In 1944 and 1945, the Luftwaffe faced further challenges from dwindling resources, especially after the loss of the crucial Romanian oil fields that were now in the hands of the Soviet Union. As a result, by the end of the war, many German aircraft were just sitting on airfields without enough fuel to fly them.

card_event_depths_of_winter.name: card_event_depths_of_winter
card_event_depths_of_winter.title: DEPTHS OF WINTER
card_event_depths_of_winter.text: Remove all units from the battlefield. Replace them with LIGHT INFANTRY units.
card_event_depths_of_winter.flavorText: The ushanka is a traditional Russian fur hat with distinctive ear-flaps that can be folded up and secured atop the hat's crown or fastened beneath the chin, offering protection against cold weather. During the Winter War against Finland, significant organizational failures and inadequate gear exposed many Soviet troops to harsh cold conditions, resulting in fatalities due to exposure. In contrast, the Finnish army possessed superior equipment, notably an ushanka-style fur hat known as the turkislakki M36, which was introduced in 1936. Just prior to the Winter War in 1939, an improved version, the turkislakki M39, was introduced and continues to be in use today. Following the Winter War, the Red Army overhauled its winter uniforms, replacing the Budenovka, a soft woolen hat historically associated with Communist uniforms since the Russian Revolution, with ushankas modeled after the Finnish design. Officers received fur ushankas, while lower-ranking personnel were issued plush or "fish fur" ushankas. German soldiers, faced with the severe Russian winter during events like the Battle of Moscow, adopted ushankas and other Soviet-style winter gear because their own uniforms did not adequately shield them from extreme cold conditions.

card_event_line_of_engagement.name: card_event_line_of_engagement
card_event_line_of_engagement.title: LINE OF ENGAGEMENT
card_event_line_of_engagement.text: Add two LIGHT INFANTRY units to the battlefield, one in the frontline if possible.
card_event_line_of_engagement.flavorText: In military terms, the "line of engagement" refers to an imaginary or actual line on the battlefield where opposing forces make contact and engage in combat with each other. The line of engagement during WWII was not a fixed or static line like the trench lines of World War I, but rather a dynamic and constantly shifting front line that varied greatly depending on the theater of operations and the specific time period during the war. WWII was characterized by a series of major campaigns, battles, and offensives that changed the course of the conflict. As a result, the line of engagement was highly fluid and moved as military forces advanced and retreated.

card_event_push.name: card_event_push
card_event_push.title: PUSH!
card_event_push.text: Your HQ takes 3 damage. Deal damage to target enemy equal to damage to your HQ this turn.
card_event_push.flavorText: Operation Bagration was the name of one of the biggest operations of WWII, with 2.3 million troops engaged, fought between 22 June and 19 August 1944 in Soviet Belarus. The Soviet Red Army launched the offensive just over two weeks after the start of Operation Overlord in the West, and this forced the Germans to fight on two major fronts at the same time. The Red Army managed to destroy 28 out of 34 divisions belonging to Army Group Centre, leading to the collapse of the Axis front line. This marked the largest defeat in German military history, resulting in approximately 450,000 German casualties, while an additional 300,000 German soldiers found themselves trapped within the Courland Pocket.

card_event_snowstorm.name: card_event_snowstorm
card_event_snowstorm.title: SNOWSTORM
card_event_snowstorm.text: All units have an operation cost of 4 until the start of your next turn.
card_event_snowstorm.flavorText: The Eastern Front, where Germany fought the Soviet Union, was known for its extreme weather conditions, with harsh winters being a significant factor in several battles. One of the most famous examples is the Battle of Moscow and the Battle of Stalingrad. These battles saw brutal winter conditions with heavy snowfall, freezing temperatures, and limited supplies, making the situation extremely challenging, especially for the German forces who were not equipped for the harsh winter conditions.

card_event_special_reinforcements.name: card_event_special_reinforcements
card_event_special_reinforcements.title: SPECIAL REINFORCEMENTS
card_event_special_reinforcements.text: Add a copy of your last destroyed unit to your hand.
card_event_special_reinforcements.flavorText: The Red Army Guards units were distinguished elite military formations within the Soviet Union, established during WWII to acknowledge and reward units that had demonstrated exceptional valor in combat. These units varied in quality depending on their specific composition and active period, but on the whole, they were regarded as highly effective and well-trained components of the Soviet armed forces. They were often entrusted with challenging and important missions on the battlefield and played a vital role in several of the Soviet Union's major victories in WWII, such as the Battle of Stalingrad and the Battle of Kursk. Comprising battle-hardened and seasoned soldiers, the Guards units received extensive training and support to ensure their effectiveness. They were also provided with access to the best available equipment and resources within the Soviet military at the time.

card_unit_122nd_korsun.name: card_unit_122nd_korsun
card_unit_122nd_korsun.title: 122nd KORSUN
card_unit_122nd_korsun.text: Costs 1 less to deploy for each of your units.
card_unit_122nd_korsun.flavorText: The 122nd Guards Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 41st Guards Rifle Division, an elite unit which was formed in August 1942 from the 10th Airborne Corps, and served extensively throughout WWII. The division fought at Stalingrad and suffered heavy losses, but afterwards it underwent significant rebuilding before engaging in various operations. It participated in numerous battles in regions such as Donbas, eastern Ukraine, and Hungary, earning multiple battle honors (including “Korsun”) and decorations. In 1945 the division was stationed in Vienna briefly, but later moved to lower Austria where it connected with US forces towards the end of the war. Eventually, in October 1945, the division was transformed into the 18th Guards Mechanized Division.

card_unit_146th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_146th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_146th_infantry_regiment.title: 146th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_146th_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Gets +1+2 if you control 3 or more units.
card_unit_146th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 146th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 44th Rifle Division of the Soviet Red Army during the Winter War and WWII. The division was involved in several significant conflicts. During the Finno-Russian Winter War, it was sent to reinforce another Soviet division but faced numerous challenges. The 44th Division, lacking ski troops and being road-bound in deep snow, was ambushed by Finnish forces who used their mobility and better weapons to break the division's movement. The Finnish troops successfully divided and defeated the entire division, causing significant casualties. After its destruction, the division was reformed but faced further losses and ultimately was wiped out in combat against the German forces in the Kirovograd and Uman region on the Eastern Front. It was reconstituted multiple times, participating in battles in northern Russia and Kurland. After the war, it was briefly reactivated and later disbanded in 1959, with some of its regiments transferring to another division.

card_unit_252nd_RIFLES.name: card_unit_252nd_RIFLES
card_unit_252nd_RIFLES.title: 252nd RIFLES
card_unit_252nd_RIFLES.text: Gains +1 attack when your HQ takes damage, then becomes Veteran if attack is 6+.
card_unit_252nd_RIFLES.flavorText: The 252nd Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 70th Rifle Division of the Red Army during the Winter War and WWII. It was initially established in 1934 at Samara but was later moved to the Leningrad Military District. The division participated in the Winter War and received the Order of Lenin for its role in breaching the Mannerheim Line. With the outbreak of Operation Barbarossa in 1941, the division relocated and engaged in counter attacks against the German invasion at Soltsy and later defending the Neva line during the Siege of Leningrad. After capturing the Nevsky Pyatachok bridgehead in the Sinyavino Offensive in 1942, the division was re-designated as the 45th Guards Rifle Division. It was reformed in April 1942 from the 47th and 146th Rifle Brigades, and engaged in battles such as the Battle of Smolensk and the advance into eastern Belarus. It played a significant role in Operation Bagration where it broke through German defenses and advanced towards the Baltic in the Riga Offensive. The 70th Division participated in battles in East Prussia, including the Battle of Memel, the Battle of Königsberg and the Samland Offensive until the end of WWII. Postwar, it undertook garrison duties in Pomerania before its disbandment in early 1947.

card_unit_334th_mountain_rifles.name: card_unit_334th_mountain_rifles
card_unit_334th_mountain_rifles.title: 334th MOUNTAIN RIFLES
card_unit_334th_mountain_rifles.flavorText: The 334th Rifle Regiment was a unit of the 47th Mountain Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. On 24 September 1941 the division was sent to participate in an attack on Poltava which had been occupied by the Germans a few days earlier. However, the Soviet forces were forced into a disorganized retreat from the area, where the 47th Division lost 23 artillery guns and 7 mortars. In May 1942, as part of the 6th Army, the division fought in the Second Battle of Kharkov, which resulted in an Axis victory, and where the 47th Mountain Rifle Division was wiped out. The division was reformed in July 1942, and in 1943 it fought in the Nevel Offensive as part of the 83rd Rifle Corps. Afterwards the 47th Division was awarded the honorific title “Nevel” for its part in capturing the town. The division was later awarded the Order of Suvorov and the Order of Lenin for its actions. It was disbanded after the war.

card_unit_67th_baranovichi.name: card_unit_67th_baranovichi
card_unit_67th_baranovichi.title: 67th BARANOVICHI
card_unit_67th_baranovichi.text: Your LIGHT INFANTRY units have Alpine.
card_unit_67th_baranovichi.flavorText: The 67th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 20th Rifle Division of the Red Army during WWII. The division was first formed during the Russian Civil War and fought with the Red Army between 1919 and 1921, and disbanded afterwards. In 1944 it was formed again and saw extensive combat in operations such as Operation Bagration, the East Prussian Offensive and Prague Offensive, and it ended the war near Berlin with the 28th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front. The division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner during the war, and received the honorific title "Baranovichi". It was also awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd class. The 20th Rifle Division was transferred to Lida with the 28th Army after the war and disbanded in July 1946.

card_unit_t_34_85_1944.name: card_unit_t_34_85_1944
card_unit_t_34_85_1944.title: T-34-85 1944
card_unit_t_34_85_1944.text: Has Blitz and Guard if you control 3 or more units.
card_unit_t_34_85_1944.flavorText: The Soviet T-34-85, introduced in 1943, was an upgraded version of the highly successful Soviet T-34 medium tank. The "85" in its designation refers to the new 85mm gun installed in the turret, a substantial improvement over the earlier 76.2mm gun. This tank was a response to the need for increased firepower and improved performance against the more heavily armored German tanks encountered on the Eastern Front. The T-34-85 boasted better anti-tank capabilities and increased accuracy, allowing it to effectively combat the newer German tanks, such as the Panther and Tiger. The T-34-85 had a more powerful engine, providing greater speed and mobility compared to its predecessors.
