card_event_women_at_work.text: Choose a US unit in hand. Reduce its cost by its operation cost.
card_event_women_at_work.flavorText: During WWII, women in the United States played a crucial role in the workforce as millions of men left to serve in the military. With labor shortages, women filled jobs traditionally held by men, particularly in industries such as manufacturing, aviation, and shipbuilding. The iconic figure of "Rosie the Riveter" symbolized their contribution in factories, where they produced essential war materials like aircraft, weapons, and ships. Women also worked in administrative roles, transportation, and as nurses in military services. Their participation in the workforce marked a significant shift in gender roles and paved the way for future changes towards gender equality in the workplace.

card_unit_1st_cavalry_troop.name: card_unit_1st_cavalry_troop
card_unit_1st_cavalry_troop.title: 1st CAVALRY TROOP
card_unit_1st_cavalry_troop.text: When you deploy a unit, add its operation cost as attack to this unit.
card_unit_1st_cavalry_troop.flavorText: The 1st Cavalry Reconnaissance Troop was a reconnaissance unit attached to the 1st Infantry Division, nicknamed the Big Red One, during WWII. This light mechanized unit was tasked with gathering intelligence on enemy positions, terrain, and movements. Throughout the war, the 1st Cavalry Reconnaissance Troop saw action in key campaigns, including the North African Campaign, the Allied invasion of Sicily, and the D-Day landings in Normandy. It continued its service for the 1st Infantry Division during the Allied push through France and Belgium, fighting in the Battle of the Hürtgen Forest and the Battle of the Bulge.

card_unit_2nd_michigan.name: card_unit_2nd_michigan
card_unit_2nd_michigan.title: 2nd MICHIGAN
card_unit_2nd_michigan.text: Gain 2 kredits when you operate a unit with 3 or more operation cost.
card_unit_2nd_michigan.flavorText: The 126th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “Second Michigan” is a unit of the Michigan Army National Guard, part of the United States Army. When the United States entered WWII the regiment was trained for war in Europe, but was redirected to the Pacific and it landed in Australia in April 1942. From there the regiment sailed to New Guinea where it participated in the Battle of Buna-Gona as part of the 32nd Infantry Division. During the battle the 2nd Michigan faced devastating losses, both in combat and due to disease, and of the 131 officers and 3,040 men, only 32 officers and 579 enlisted men were left. The regiment was sent back to Australia to refit and retrain, and there it received amphibious training and lessons in jungle warfare. As part of the 32nd Infantry Division the regiment landed in Papua New Guinea where it participated in the Western New Guinea campaign, and later they fought in Leyte and Luzon. During its service the 32nd Division logged a total of 654 days of combat during WWII, more than any other United States Army division.

card_unit_306th_regiment.name: card_unit_306th_regiment
card_unit_306th_regiment.title: 306th REGIMENT
card_unit_306th_regiment.text: Deployment: Draw a card if you control another unit with 4 or more attack.
card_unit_306th_regiment.flavorText: The 306th Infantry Regiment was a regiment of the 77th Infantry Division of the US Army during WWII. The division was ordered into active service in 1942 and trained in amphibious assaults and jungle warfare in preparation for the island-hopping campaigns against Japanese forces. The division saw major combat in battles such as Guam, Leyte, and Okinawa, where it fought in harsh conditions, often facing fierce resistance from entrenched Japanese positions. The 77th Division is especially famous for its role in the liberation of Guam in 1944, where it helped reclaim American territory occupied since 1941. Later, during the brutal Battle of Okinawa, the division continued to distinguish itself in one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific, pushing through tough terrain and heavily fortified enemy positions.

card_unit_511th_airborne.name: card_unit_511th_airborne
card_unit_511th_airborne.title: 511th AIRBORNE
card_unit_511th_airborne.text: Reduce operation cost by 3 after it Shock attacks.
card_unit_511th_airborne.flavorText: The 511th Parachute Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 11th Airborne Division during WWII. The division was activated in 1943 and trained for airborne assaults, jungle warfare, and amphibious operations. Its first major engagement came during the Philippines Campaign, where it was involved in intense fighting on Leyte in late 1944. It is particularly celebrated for its role in the liberation of Luzon in early 1945. In a famous raid, the 11th Airborne liberated over 2,000 Allied POWs from the Los Baños Internment Camp, a bold operation involving airborne and amphibious elements which caught the Japanese forces by surprise. The division continued to see action on Luzon until the Japanese surrender, earning a distinguished reputation for resilience and bravery in some of the toughest conditions of the Pacific campaign. After the war, the 11th Airborne Division served in the occupation of Japan, helping to maintain security and assisting in postwar reconstruction efforts until they were recalled to the United States in 1949.

card_unit_62nd_armored_infantry.name: card_unit_62nd_armored_infantry
card_unit_62nd_armored_infantry.title: 62nd ARMORED INFANTRY
card_unit_62nd_armored_infantry.text: Deployment: Your Shermans get +2+2. If you have none, add a M4 SHERMAN to your hand.
card_unit_62nd_armored_infantry.flavorText: The 62nd Armored Infantry Regiment was a regiment of the 14th Armored Division of the United States Army. The division was formed in 1942 and was officially nicknamed the "Liberators". Although it was inactivated in 1945, it remains eligible for reactivation whenever needed. The division landed in Marseilles, southern France, in November 1944 and participated in heavy combat as part of the U.S. 6th Army Group, and later, the U.S. Seventh Army. In December 1944, just before New Year's Eve, the 14th Division was caught in Operation Northwind, the last major German counteroffensive of the war. The division engaged in heavy defensive fighting in January 1945, and although the Germans achieved some success, the main thrust of Operation Northwind was halted by the 14th Armored Division. In March 1945, the division advanced into Germany, breaking through the Siegfried Line. It later participated in the Capture of Heilbronn and the Battle of Nuremberg. During the advance, the division liberated several POW camps, including Stalag XIII-C, Oflag XIII-B, and Stalag VII-A, the largest prisoner-of-war camp in Germany. Later, the men of the 14th Armored Division liberated several sub-camps of the Dachau concentration camp. The division earned its nickname, the "Liberators," during the final days of the war after freeing around 200,000 Allied prisoners of war from German prison camps. In September 1945, the division was inactivated.

card_unit_big_red_one.name: card_unit_big_red_one
card_unit_big_red_one.title: BIG RED ONE
card_unit_big_red_one.text: Cards in your hand cost 4 kredits.
card_unit_big_red_one.flavorText: The 1st Infantry Division, known for its iconic red "1" insignia and nicknamed "The Big Red One", was one of the most distinguished and experienced U.S. divisions in WWII. The division saw action in some of the most crucial battles in both North Africa and Europe. Its WWII service began in 1942 in North Africa with Operation Torch , where it engaged in fierce fighting against Vichy France troops, and the Tunisian Campaign against German and Italian forces. After the Allies successfully pushed the Axis out of North Africa, the 1st Infantry Division participated in Operation Husky, the Allied invasion of Sicily, in 1943. One of the division’s most famous roles came on D-Day, June 6, 1944, when it led the assault on Omaha Beach during the Normandy invasion. Despite facing intense German resistance and heavy casualties, the Big Red One ultimately secured the beachhead. The division kept fighting through France and Belgium, and was involved in the brutal Battle of the Hürtgen Forest, and later the Battle of the Bulge, helping to repel the last major German offensive in the Ardennes forest. At the end of the war, the Big Red One fought through Germany, liberating towns and concentration camps until the final victory in Europe.

card_unit_calliope.name: card_unit_calliope
card_unit_calliope.title: CALLIOPE
card_unit_calliope.text: Deployment: Distribute 2 damage randomly between the target and adjacent enemies.
card_unit_calliope.flavorText: The T34 Calliope was an American rocket launcher which was mounted on a M4 Sherman tank during WWII. It was designed to provide mobile artillery support for infantry and armored divisions and was named after the musical instrument, also known as a steam organ, because of its distinctive pipes. The Calliope was a 60-tube rocket launcher capable of firing 4.5-inch rockets in rapid succession, creating a devastating barrage effect against enemy positions, fortifications, and troop concentrations. Introduced in 1944 and first used in the European Theater, the T34 Calliope proved valuable for its ability to deliver mass firepower quickly, often in support of Allied advances. While it lacked precision compared to traditional artillery, its psychological impact and ability to saturate areas with explosive force made it an effective weapon for softening enemy defenses and disrupting German positions.

card_unit_cyclone_division.name: card_unit_cyclone_division
card_unit_cyclone_division.title: CYCLONE DIVISION
card_unit_cyclone_division.text: Deployment: Add a Sherman to hand. Becomes Veteran when you have deployed 2 Shermans.
card_unit_cyclone_division.flavorText: The 38th Infantry Division, known as the Cyclone Division, is a US Army division which was first formed in 1917, served in WWI, and in the Pacific Theater during WWII. The division earned its nickname due to the cyclone emblem on its insignia, symbolizing its force and resilience. After extensive jungle and amphibious warfare training, the Cyclone Division saw major combat during the Philippines Campaign. Its notable actions include intense fighting on Luzon in early 1945, where it played a critical role in pushing back entrenched Japanese forces. One of its most famous achievements was its involvement in liberating Bataan and Corregidor, earning it the title “Avengers of Bataan” in recognition of its success in reclaiming ground previously lost to Japanese forces in 1942. On 15 September 1945 the division returned to the United States and was demobilized.

card_unit_l4_grasshopper.name: card_unit_l4_grasshopper
card_unit_l4_grasshopper.title: L-4 GRASSHOPPER
card_unit_l4_grasshopper.text: Your Sherman units cost 1 less to deploy and have Blitz.
card_unit_l4_grasshopper.flavorText: The L-4 Grasshopper was a light and versatile observation and liaison aircraft used by the US military during WWII. Adapted from the civilian Piper J-3 Cub, it played key roles in artillery spotting, reconnaissance, and supply missions throughout the war. With its slow speed and excellent maneuverability, the L-4 could take off and land on short, rugged fields, making it ideal for frontline operations. For the most part, the L-4 was unarmed, often flying low enough to evade enemy radar and attacks while providing critical “eyes” on the battlefield. Some L-4s were fitted with improvised racks carrying pairs or quartets of infantry bazookas for ground-attack missions against German armored units. The most famous of these was “Rosie the Rocketer” piloted by Maj. Charles "Bazooka Charlie" Carpenter, who destroyed six enemy tanks and several armored cars, particularly during the Battle of Arracourt in 1944. The L-4 could even be launched from ships using the Brodie landing system, further extending its versatility. Its simplicity and effectiveness made the L-4 an invaluable asset throughout the war.

card_unit_m6.name: card_unit_m6
card_unit_m6.title: M6
card_unit_m6.text: Your HQ takes 1 less damage for each of your units with 4 or more attack.
card_unit_m6.flavorText: The Heavy Tank M6 was an American heavy tank developed during WWII, intended to provide the U.S. Army with a powerful, heavily armored vehicle capable of countering German tanks. Designed in 1940, the M6 featured thick armor and was armed with a 76 mm M7 gun and a 37 mm M6 gun in a single turret, along with multiple machine guns. It was one of the largest tanks produced by the United States at the time, weighing over 60 tons. Despite its impressive firepower and armor, the M6 faced significant drawbacks. Its large size and weight made it difficult to transport and maneuver, and by the time it was ready for production, U.S. military doctrine had shifted to prioritize medium tanks, like the M4 Sherman, which were more versatile, more reliable, cheaper, and much easier to transport. As a result, the M6 never saw combat, and only around 40 tanks were produced before the program was canceled in 1944.

card_event_advanced_us_research.name: card_event_advanced_us_research
card_event_advanced_us_research.title: ADVANCED US RESEARCH
card_event_advanced_us_research.text: Choose one - add PENICILLIN to hand OR add two MANHATTAN PROJECT to hand.

card_event_allied_research_effort.name: card_event_allied_research_effort
card_event_allied_research_effort.title: ALLIED RESEARCH EFFORT
card_event_allied_research_effort.text: Choose one - add a random US or British unit OR order with cost 7 or more to your hand.
card_event_allied_research_effort.flavorText: During WWII the Allies collaborated extensively in research and development of old and new technology in support of their military efforts. Most of the research was shared between Britain and the USA, but much of the military equipment that was developed was supplied to the Soviet Union and other Allied nations. Their joint effort ranged from the development and manufacturing of small arms to codebreaking, radar and aviation technology and the making of the atomic bomb.

card_event_bolster_the_ranks.name: card_event_bolster_the_ranks
card_event_bolster_the_ranks.title: BOLSTER THE RANKS
card_event_bolster_the_ranks.text: Give target unit plus attack and defense equal to its operation cost, then set it to 0.
card_event_bolster_the_ranks.flavorText: Perhaps one of the most timely American military reinforcement occurred during the Battle of the Bulge, which according to Winston Churchill “undoubtedly the greatest American battle of the war”. The Germans had pushed through the middle of the American line, which held, but created the “bulge” that gave the battle its name. In the Belgian town of Bastogne a combined force of the 101st Airborne and elements of the 10th Armored Division held on stubbornly for 5 days in spite of being outnumbered and desperately low on supplies while waiting to be relieved. Patton’s 3rd Army was more than 100 miles, but displayed one of his greatest military feats by racing his men in record time to Bastogne to fend off the German attack and break the siege.

card_event_campaign_trail.name: card_event_campaign_trail
card_event_campaign_trail.title: CAMPAIGN TRAIL
card_event_campaign_trail.text: Your units operate for 2 less this turn and are fully repaired at the end of the turn.
card_event_campaign_trail.flavorText: The USA conducted 44 military campaigns during WWII. Many of the campaigns were fought in Asia and the Pacific, some in Africa and the Middle East and one in the continental American territory, which mainly involved naval warfare. However, the main focus was on Europe where most of the American troops were deployed.

card_event_depth_charges.name: card_event_depth_charges
card_event_depth_charges.title: DEPTH CHARGES
card_event_depth_charges.text: Gain an extra kredit slot. Your HQ gains Smokescreen until your next turn.

card_event_expanded_us_research.name: card_event_expanded_us_research
card_event_expanded_us_research.title: EXPANDED US RESEARCH
card_event_expanded_us_research.text: Choose one - add PRESSURIZED CABIN to hand OR add ADVANCED US RESEARCH to hand.

card_event_overcast.name: card_event_overcast
card_event_overcast.title: OVERCAST
card_event_overcast.text: Forecast. All HQs get +2 defense. All players gain an extra kredit slot and draw a card.
card_event_overcast.flavorText: Through history the weather has always been a major factor in warfare and in WWII the weather played an even more crucial role. Meteorological intelligence became very important as it affected the routing of ships and convoys and military planning, especially since much of it involved combined use of forces on the ground, air and sea. F.ex. D-Day was delayed by one day due to an unfavourable weather forecast. In the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans the Axis and the Allies fought to gain control of weather data in what is known as the North Atlantic Weather War. The Germans set up secret weather stations in remote places in the Arctic, Jan Mayen, Spitsbergen and Greenland, and gathered weather data in trawlers disguised as fishing boats etc. However, with the cracking of Enigma in 1942, German weather data across Europe became accessible to the Allies.

card_event_penicillin.name: card_event_penicillin
card_event_penicillin.title: PENICILLIN
card_event_penicillin.text: Your units and HQ gain +6 defense. Draw 4 cards.

card_event_pressurized_cabin.name: card_event_pressurized_cabin
card_event_pressurized_cabin.title: PRESSURIZED CABIN
card_event_pressurized_cabin.text: Add a B-29 SUPERFORTRESS to hand. Destroy a random enemy unit.

card_event_sniped.name: card_event_sniped
card_event_sniped.title: SNIPED
card_event_sniped.text: When an enemy unit attacks, it becomes 2/2.
card_event_sniped.flavorText: During WWII, there were two major factors that contributed to a victory in tank vs. tank confrontations. Firstly, the tank who got the first shot at an opposing tank was more likely to win the confrontation. The second and probably the most important factor was timing and logistics, showing up to a battle at the right time, in the right place, and with the right amount of force. These two factors were much more important than armor thickness, speed, and firepower.

card_event_special_assignment.name: card_event_special_assignment
card_event_special_assignment.title: SPECIAL ASSIGNMENT
card_event_special_assignment.text: Choose a unit in hand and add it to the battlefield.
card_event_special_assignment.flavorText: The Doolittle Raid was an American air raid on the Japanese mainland, done in 1942 and served mainly as retaliation for the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. 16 B-25B Mitchell bombers flew without fighter escort from the aircraft carrier USS Hornet and the plan was to bomb Japanese military targets and then head to safety in China. The raid was a success although it caused minimal damage and 15 of the bombers managed to escape to safety, 14 in China and one in Vladivostok in Soviet Union. 77 crewmen survived the mission but 8 were captured by Japanese troops in Eastern China.

card_event_us_military_research.name: card_event_us_military_research
card_event_us_military_research.title: US MILITARY RESEARCH
card_event_us_military_research.text: Choose one - add DEPTH CHARGES to hand OR add EXPANDED US RESEARCH to hand.
card_event_us_military_research.flavorText: No war has been more affected by advances in science and technology than WWII, and not only did it affect the outcome of the war but it also had a great effect on the civilian population after the war. The American invention of a small device called the cavity magnetron, which generates microwaves, greatly improved radar technology and would change how Americans prepared and consumed food after the war. The first mass production of Penicillin was done by American pharmaceutical companies prior to D-Day and it would help reduce the number of deaths and amputations of Allied troops during WWII. American aviation technology would also take great leaps, f.ex. the American B-29 bombers became the first aircraft that was equipped with the pressurized cabin system which allowed them to fly at much higher altitudes than before.

card_unit_120mm_m1_gun.name: card_unit_120mm_m1_gun
card_unit_120mm_m1_gun.title: 120mm M1 GUN
card_unit_120mm_m1_gun.text: Deployment: Choose one - deals double damage to air units OR deals double damage to tanks.
card_unit_120mm_m1_gun.flavorText: The 120 mm M1 Gun was an American heavy anti-aircraft gun that was first introduced in 1924, but at the time it was considered too heavy to be deployed in combat and too expensive to build. In 1938 there became a need for such a heavy gun and the design was modernized and around 550 M1 guns were manufactured. They were mostly deployed on fixed mounts, mostly in the United States but a few were deployed in other countries, in Panama Canal Zone, UK and Northern Ireland. The gun had a maximum range of 25 km, maximum altitude of 17,5 km, and due to its high altitude capabilities it was nicknamed the “stratosphere cannon”. A typical 120mm battery had four guns, a crew of 13 men and many of the guns had radar fire control systems.

card_unit_32nd_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_32nd_infantry_regiment
card_unit_32nd_infantry_regiment.title: 32nd INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_32nd_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Draw a 32nd INFANTRY REGIMENT from your deck.
card_unit_32nd_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 32nd Infantry Regiment of the US Army was first formed in 1916 and has been active to the present day. During WWII the regiment was attached to the 7th Infantry Division which would play a major role in retaking the Attu Islands from the Japanese in 1943. In 1944 the division was one of the first to land on Leyte Island in the Philippines where they saw extensive combat in one of the bloodiest battles in the Pacific. The regiment participated in its last battle in Okinawa in 1945 and they would end the war in Korea where they received the surrender of Japanese troops.

card_unit_47th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_47th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_47th_infantry_regiment.title: 47th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_47th_infantry_regiment.text: Becomes Veteran at the start of your turn if you have 13 or more kredit slots.
card_unit_47th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 47th Infantry Regiment of the US Army was first formed in 1917 and fought in WWI. The regiment was disbanded in 1921 but reformed in 1940. In 1942 the regiment landed in French Morocco where it fought the Vichy French forces during Operation Blackstone. The regiment fought with the 9th Division in the Battle of El Guettar and the Battle of Sedjenane during the Tunisian Campaign. In 1943 the division was then sent to Sicily where it fought in the Battle of Troina. The regiment landed with the 9th Division in Normandy 4 days after D-Day and would from then on fight in numerous battles, including the Battle of Cherbourg and the Battle of the Bulge, and finally fighting German resistance in the Harz Mountains in Germany. After the German surrender the regiment conducted occupation duty in Germany until 1946.

card_unit_4th_marines.name: card_unit_4th_marines
card_unit_4th_marines.title: 4th MARINES
card_unit_4th_marines.flavorText: The 4th Marine Regiment was first formed in 1914 and has been more or less active to the present day. In 1942 the regiment was moved to Corregidor in the Phillipine Islands where a Japanese attack was imminent. At the time the defenders consisted largely of the 4th Marines and elements of several other units, both US and Filipino, and many of them were Navy and Army personnel with no ground combat training or experience. As soon as the Japanese soldiers landed on the island faced fierce resistance from the regiment's artillery batteries, but once the Japanese managed to get inland and overcome the batteries the fight was over and the 4th Marines Regiment was destroyed. The 4th Marine Regiment was reestablished in 1944 and would fight with the 6th Marine Division at Guam in 1944 and Okinawa in 1945.

card_unit_60th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_60th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_60th_infantry_regiment.title: 60th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_60th_infantry_regiment.text: When this unit is fully repaired, add a copy of it to your support line.
card_unit_60th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 60th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “Go Devils”, was a regiment of the US Army and was first formed in 1917 during WWI. The regiment was deactivated in 1921, but reactivated in 1940 and assigned to the 9th Infantry Division. In 1942 the 60th Regiment was sent to North Africa to take part in Operation Torch, which was the Allied invasion of French Morocco. In 1943 it participated in the Allied invasion of Sicily where the men of the regiment managed to infiltrate the German lines and clear out the last resistance. In 1944 the regiment was part of the Allied invasion of Normandy and would see heavy fighting during the Allied liberation of France and the lower countries. The regiment fought in the Battle of the Bulge and would later fight in various battles and operations in the Allied push towards Germany. The 60th would end the war in Germany where it was on occupation duty until it was deactivated in 1946, but reactivated shortly thereafter and has been active to the present day.

card_unit_75th_rangers.name: card_unit_75th_rangers
card_unit_75th_rangers.title: 75th RANGERS
card_unit_75th_rangers.text: Deployment: Reduce the operation cost of target unit to 0.
card_unit_75th_rangers.flavorText: During WWII the Rangers were special military units of the US Army, made up of volunteers only, and were tasked with carrying out raids in enemy occupied territory and spearheading invasions, much like the British Commandos. What would become the 75th Ranger Regiment was at the start of WWII composed of a single battalion, the 1st Rangers Battalion. In 1942 the battalion fought with British and Canadian commandos in France during an amphibious attack on the port of Dieppe and that same year they landed in Algiers where they carried out successful raids on Italian and Vichy-French military installations. In 1943 the Rangers were expanded to a full regiment, six battalions in total, 1st-5th were deployed in Europe and the 6th in the Pacific where they fought in the Philippines and New Guinea. The 1st, 3rd and 4th battalions were destroyed in a joint operation in the Italian Campaign, but the 2nd and 5th spearheaded the D-Day landings on Omaha beach and fought in several battles after that, such as the Battle for Brest and the Battle of the Hurtgen Forest. It’s noteworthy that the main characters in Steven Spielberg's film classic Saving Private Ryan were men of the 2nd Battalion.

card_unit_b_17_f.name: card_unit_b_17_f
card_unit_b_17_f.title: B-17F
card_unit_b_17_f.text: Cannot be targeted by enemy orders.
card_unit_b_17_f.flavorText: The Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress was an American heavy bomber that was developed in the 1930s and used by the USAAF and RAF in WWII. The B-17 had a reputation of being a tough aircraft and could take a lot of battle damage and still reach its target and bring the crew home safely. The B-17F was one of many variants, with 3,405 units built, one of them being the famous Memphis Belle  which was an aircraft of the Eighth Air Force and the first B-17 to complete 25 combat missions. A total of 12,731 B-17s were built and 46 of them still survive today.

card_unit_c47_skytrain.name: card_unit_c47_skytrain
card_unit_c47_skytrain.title: C-47 SKYTRAIN
card_unit_c47_skytrain.text: At the end of your turn, add a random 1-cost US infantry to your support line.
card_unit_c47_skytrain.flavorText: The Douglas C-47 Skytrain, also known as R4D transports and the C-47 Dakota, was an American military transport aircraft manufactured by the Douglas Aircraft Company and used by the US Army Air Forces and the Allies in WWII. The C-47 was based on the design of the civilian passenger airliner DC-3. The aircraft served in all theaters of the war and was used to airlift military supplies, to evacuate wounded from remote islands suchs as the Guadalcanal and to drop paratroopers. Over 10,000 aircraft were produced, including variants, and they were still in service during the Korean and Vietnam war.

card_unit_m10_destroyer.name: card_unit_m10_destroyer
card_unit_m10_destroyer.title: M10 WOLVERINE
card_unit_m10_destroyer.text: Enemy tanks damaged by this unit are destroyed.
card_unit_m10_destroyer.flavorText: The M10 Wolverine was an American tank destroyer that was used by the US Army and the Allies from 1943 until the end of the war. The M10 mounted a 3-inch (76.2 mm) gun M7 in a rotating turret on a M4 Sherman medium tank chassis and a .50 caliber (12.7 mm) Browning M2HB machine gun as secondary armament. It had an open top turret which gave the crew excellent visibility and made it easier to escape when it took a hit, but left them vulnerable to enemy fire, especially in the Pacific where the Japanese often used close-assault anti-tank tactics. The M10 tank destroyer performed well throughout the war and was effective against all Axis tanks. 6,406 units were built throughout the war, including a few variants.

card_unit_pby_catalina.name: card_unit_pby_catalina
card_unit_pby_catalina.title: PBY CATALINA
card_unit_pby_catalina.text: At the start of your turn, draw 2 cards, then put a card in hand on top of your deck.
card_unit_pby_catalina.flavorText: The Consolidated PBY Catalina was an American flying boat that was first introduced in 1936 and was the most widely used amphibious aircraft of WWII. Around 3,300 Catalinas were built, including variants, and it was used by every branch of the US Armed Forces and other Allied forces who used them in a wide variety of roles. Most commonly it was used in anti-submarine warfare, but also patrol bombing, search and rescue, convoy escort and cargo transportation. American aircrews called their Catalina the “Cat” in combat missions and “Dumbo” in search and rescue missions.

card_unit_usaaf_spitfire_ix.name: card_unit_usaaf_spitfire_ix
card_unit_usaaf_spitfire_ix.title: USAAF SPITFIRE IX
card_unit_usaaf_spitfire_ix.text: Deployment: Draw a random air unit from your deck.
card_unit_usaaf_spitfire_ix.flavorText: The Supermarine Spitfire was a British fighter aircraft that was used during WWII, mainly by RAF, but also by their allies. Around 600 Spitfires served in the US Army Air Force and the Navy and it was one of the few foreign aircraft to do so. The Spitfire Mk IX variant first entered service in 1941 and became very successful in countering the newly developed German fighter, namely the Focke-Wulf Fw 190, and such was the Mk IX’s success that it became the second most produced Spitfire during the war. The Mk IX usually had an armament of 2 × 20 mm Hispano II cannon, 2 × 0.50 or 4 x 0.303 Browning M2 machine guns and capacity of carrying 2 x 110 kg bombs in the wing racket and 1 x 230 kg bomb in the center racket.

card_event_asw_patrol.name: card_event_asw_patrol
card_event_asw_patrol.title: ASW PATROL
card_event_asw_patrol.text: Gain 3 extra kredit slots. If US is Ally, destroy a random enemy unit also.
card_event_asw_patrol.flavorText: During WWII, ASW Patrol (Anti-Submarine Warfare Patrol) operations were crucial in countering the threat of German U-boats. Their mission was to protect convoys, naval vessels, and supply lines from submarine attacks. ASW Patrols utilized a variety of assets such as destroyers, frigates, corvettes, patrol boats, and aircraft equipped with sonar systems, depth charges, and other anti-submarine weapons. Tactics included using sonar to detect underwater contacts, employing depth charges for attacks, and coordinating assaults with multiple vessels. ASW Patrols also provided escort duty to merchant convoys, deterring U-boats from attacking. Close cooperation between naval vessels, aircraft, and shore-based command centers was crucial for intelligence gathering and coordinated attacks. Technological advancements improved ASW capabilities, with more sophisticated sonar systems and weapons like hedgehog mortars and squid mortars. Allied success in countering U-boats turned the tide in the Battle of the Atlantic and secured vital supply lines which allowed for the transport of troops, equipment, and supplies to their military campaigns.

card_event_attrition.name: card_event_attrition
card_event_attrition.title: ATTRITION
card_event_attrition.text: Deal 2 damage to target unit. Retreat it also if it is Veteran.
card_event_attrition.flavorText: The Battle of Anzio (1944) is a notable example of a conflict of attrition where US forces were involved. The Allied amphibious landing at Anzio, Italy, faced strong resistance from German forces and the subsequent stalemate resulted in a prolonged attritional phase, with both sides engaged in intense fighting and enduring heavy losses. Finally the Allies won the Battle of Anzio by implementing strategic adjustments and reinforcing their troops. They shifted from a defensive stance to aggressive offensive operations, launching attacks to expand the beachhead and regain control. With their success and the German retreat, the Allies secured a decisive victory, allowing them to break out of the beachhead and advance towards Rome.

card_event_battle_valor.name: card_event_battle_valor
card_event_battle_valor.title: BATTLE VALOR
card_event_battle_valor.text: Target unit becomes Veteran if able, then gets +2+4.
card_event_battle_valor.flavorText:
While it is difficult to provide precise numbers, machine gunners in bombers did contribute to shooting down enemy aircraft, especially when engaged in defensive actions. The primary objective of bomber gunners was to deter and suppress attacks rather than achieving high numbers of aerial victories. However, heroic actions of USAF machine gunners during WWII are numerous and what follows is an example. 

Staff Sergeant Maynard Harrison Smith served as a ball turret gunner on a B-17 Flying Fortress during WWII. On May 1, 1943, his aircraft was attacked by numerous German fighters during a mission over France. Smith's aircraft sustained heavy damage, and the tail section was severed, leaving the plane in imminent danger of breaking apart. Despite this, Smith remained at his position and provided covering fire in order to protect the crew. He refused to abandon his post until ordered to do so as the aircraft began to disintegrate. Smith's dedication and selflessness earned him the Medal of Honor.

card_event_field_hospital.name: card_event_field_hospital
card_event_field_hospital.title: FIELD HOSPITAL
card_event_field_hospital.text: Fully repair each friendly unit. Draw a card for each unit repaired.
card_event_field_hospital.flavorText: During WWII, US field hospitals played a crucial role in providing medical care to wounded soldiers on the front lines. These field hospitals were mobile units designed to provide emergency medical treatment and stabilize injured personnel before they could be transported to more extensive medical facilities. The United States made several notable contributions and innovations in the field of military medicine during the war. For example the first trials of Mobile Army Surgical Hospitals (MASH) were conducted by the U.S. Army, which was a significant innovation. These mobile surgical hospitals brought advanced surgical capabilities closer to the front lines, reducing the time between injury and surgical intervention. Another innovation was Blood Plasma and Component Therapy which the US military played a crucial role in developing and implementing during the war. This development significantly improved the management of casualties and contributed to better outcomes. It's important to note that while the United States made significant contributions in these areas, other nations also made important advancements in military medicine during WWII. Also note that many medical professionals and researchers from various countries worked together and independently to improve the care and outcomes for wounded soldiers.

card_event_fortunes_of_war.name: card_event_fortunes_of_war
card_event_fortunes_of_war.title: FORTUNES OF WAR
card_event_fortunes_of_war.text: Trigger the Destruction effects on a target unit as if it was yours, then remove the effect if an enemy unit.
card_event_fortunes_of_war.flavorText: During WWII, American industries and businesses did experience significant economic growth and increased production due to the war effort. The war stimulated the American economy and created opportunities for various industries to supply goods and services needed for the war. The defense industry, in particular, saw substantial profits as it produced weapons, ammunition, vehicles, aircraft, and other military equipment. Companies involved in manufacturing, such as automobile manufacturers (f.ex. Ford, General Motors), steel producers (f. ex.US Steel), and aviation companies (f. ex. Boeing), were among those that benefited from increased government contracts and military production. Additionally, the war led to increased employment opportunities, higher wages, and expanded markets for various sectors of the economy. The increased demand for goods and services stimulated economic growth and helped lift the United States out of the Great Depression.

card_event_manpower.name: card_event_manpower
card_event_manpower.title: MANPOWER
card_event_manpower.text: Fully repair a friendly damaged unit. Add a copy of it to your support line.
card_event_manpower.flavorText: During WWII, the United States employed a combination of both conscription (draft) and voluntary enlistment to build its military forces. The majority of the US military personnel were drafted, but a significant number also volunteered. Approximately 10 million men were drafted into military service during the war, but at the same time, around 6 million men volunteered to serve in the US military. The combined number of draftees and volunteers resulted in a substantial military force that played a critical role in the Allied victory.

card_event_night_bombing.name: card_event_night_bombing
card_event_night_bombing.title: NIGHT BOMBING
card_event_night_bombing.text: Destroy target undamaged unit, then randomly rearrange enemy units on the battlefield.
card_event_night_bombing.flavorText: The US air force did conduct night bombing missions during WWII, but their focus was primarily on daylight precision bombing. The US Army Air Forces (USAAF) believed that daylight bombing allowed for greater accuracy and minimized the risk of friendly fire incidents. But as the war progressed, the USAAF recognized the need for night bombing capabilities to intensify the strategic bombing campaign against Germany. Therefore in 1943, the USAAF began conducting limited night bombing operations using B-17 Flying Fortress and B-24 Liberator bombers equipped with radar and improved navigational aids. However, it's important to note that night bombing remained a secondary aspect of the USAAF's overall bombing strategy, with daylight precision bombing missions continuing to be the primary focus.

card_unit_133rd_ironman.name: card_unit_133rd_ironman
card_unit_133rd_ironman.title: 133rd IRONMAN
card_unit_133rd_ironman.text: Reveal: Deal 3 damage to the enemy HQ for each turn spent in the frontline.
card_unit_133rd_ironman.flavorText: The 133rd Infantry Regiment, nicknamed Ironman, is a unit of the 34th Infantry Division of the US Army. During WWII the division saw its first combat in French Algeria in 1942 as part of the Eastern Task Force. From there, they engaged in numerous battles in Tunisia, including the Battle of Hill 609. Due to heavy losses in North Africa the division skipped the invasion of Sicily, but it would instead later participate in the attack on the Italian mainland, landing at Salerno on September 9, 1943, as part of Operation Avalanche. The division's bravery and resilience were showcased in numerous engagements, including the battles along the Mignano Gap and the assault on Monte Cassino. Despite suffering heavy casualties, the division continued to push forward, ultimately playing a pivotal role in the liberation of Italy and the Allied victory in Europe.

card_unit_158th_bushmasters.name: card_unit_158th_bushmasters
card_unit_158th_bushmasters.title: 158th BUSHMASTERS
card_unit_158th_bushmasters.text: When a unit is fully repaired, distribute the damage repaired between random enemies.
card_unit_158th_bushmasters.flavorText: The 158th Regiment, initially part of the 45th Division, played a significant role in various operations during WWII. After the US entered the war in 1941, the unit was sent to the Panama Canal Zone where it did security operations and jungle patrols, from which they were given the nickname "Bushmasters" after the venomous snake inhabiting the jungle. In 1942, the 158th Regiment was chosen to create and train a jungle platoon, which led to the prioritization of jungle warfare training. In 1943, the Bushmasters arrived in Australia and later moved to New Guinea, where they participated in Operation Chronicle to establish an airfield on Kiriwina Island. Later elements of the regiment were deployed to Arawe, New Britain, and later to Finschhafen, where it was redesignated as the 158th Regimental Combat Team. The team joined Task Force Tornado and engaged in intense battles with the Japanese in New Guinea. The regimental combat team fought in the Battle of Noemfoor and the invasion of Luzon in the Philippines. Lastly the Bushmasters then invaded the Bicol Peninsula in the Philippines in April 1945. The Bushmasters then participated in the occupation of Japan before being inactivated in January 1946. General MacArthur commended the Bushmasters, stating that no greater combat team had ever deployed for battle.

card_unit_179th_tomahawks.name: card_unit_179th_tomahawks
card_unit_179th_tomahawks.title: 179th TOMAHAWKS
card_unit_179th_tomahawks.text: Destruction: Add a copy of this unit to your support line. It becomes Veteran.
card_unit_179th_tomahawks.flavorText: The 179th Infantry Regiment (nicknamed Tomahawks) was part of the 45th Infantry Division of the US Army during WWII. In 1943, the 179th Infantry Regiment, along with the rest of the 45th Infantry Division, was deployed to Europe. The regiment arrived in Italy in June 1943 and participated in the Allied campaign to liberate Italy from Axis control. The regiment fought in various battles and engagements throughout Italy. One of the notable actions in which the 179th Infantry Regiment participated was the Battle of Anzio, which took place from January to May 1944. The battle was a critical operation which aimed at breaking the stalemate of the Italian campaign and advancing towards Rome. After the Italian campaign, the regiment played a significant role in the Allied advance through France and into Germany and participated in major operations such as the Battle of the Bulge and the crossing of the Rhine River.

card_unit_327th_pathfinders.name: card_unit_327th_pathfinders
card_unit_327th_pathfinders.title: 327th PATHFINDERS
card_unit_327th_pathfinders.text: Deployment: Deal 2 damage to a unit. If this destroys it, 327th PATHFINDERS becomes Veteran.
card_unit_327th_pathfinders.flavorText: The Pathfinders of the 327th Glider Infantry Regiment were a specialized unit within the US Army during WWII. They were responsible for landing ahead of the main airborne forces to prepare and mark the landing zones for subsequent paratrooper drops or glider landings. The Pathfinders were trained to jump from aircraft or gliders and make their way to the designated landing zones. They would then set up beacons, signal lights, and other markers to guide the incoming aircraft. This was a crucial task, as accurate and timely delivery of troops and equipment was essential for the success of airborne operations. The 327th Glider Infantry Regiment played a vital role in several important operations during WWII, including the D-Day invasion of Normandy, the airborne assault during Operation Market Garden, and the Rhine River crossing during Operation Varsity. Additionally, in December 1944, the 327th was part of the 101st Airborne Division, which was hastily deployed to the Ardennes during the German offensive, known as the Battle of the Bulge. One of the most notable actions of the 327th Pathfinders during the battle was the defense of the town of Bastogne. For its action during the defense the regiment got its nickname “Bastogne Bulldogs”.  After the Battle of the Bulge, the 327th Infantry fought in the Rhineland and Berchtesgaden offensives. Following the end of WWII, the regiment was deactivated on 30 November 1945.

card_unit_3_inch_m5.name: card_unit_3_inch_m5
card_unit_3_inch_m5.title: 3-inch M5
card_unit_3_inch_m5.text: Has +1 attack for each friendly unit in the frontline.
card_unit_3_inch_m5.flavorText: The 3-inch M5 gun was a US anti-tank artillery piece, derived from the British QF 17-pounder, and used during WWII by the US forces. In terms of effectiveness, the M5 gun demonstrated its capability against medium and select heavy tanks encountered during the war. Its armor-piercing rounds possessed the necessary penetration power to disable or destroy enemy tanks, contributing significantly to the U.S. Army and Marine Corps anti-tank capabilities and it saw service both in the European and Pacific theaters. As the war progressed, the M5 gun eventually gave way to the more powerful 90mm M3 gun, which became the primary anti-tank weapon for the US Army.

card_unit_48th_armored_infantry.name: card_unit_48th_armored_infantry
card_unit_48th_armored_infantry.title: 48th ARMORED INFANTRY
card_unit_48th_armored_infantry.text: Reduce damage to this unit by 2 for each adjacent unit.
card_unit_48th_armored_infantry.flavorText: The 48th Armored Infantry, nicknamed “Dragoons”, was a unit of the US Army during WWII. In 1942 the regiment was assigned to the 7th Armored Division which first saw combat in France during the Normandy Campaign in June 1944. In September 1944 the division was attached to the British Second Army in the Netherlands where it fought in Operation Market Garden, which was a failed attempt to outflank the German defenses of the Siegfried line and ensure a swift advance towards Berlin. Later that year, when the division was getting ready to advance into Germany, the German Ardennes Offensive began on 16 December 1944, also known as the Battle of the Bulge. The division was then ordered to the Belgian town of St. Vith, where it managed to stall the German advance during a week of heavy fighting. Finally the 7th Armored Division was forced to withdraw, but after a brief rest it managed to recapture the town of St. Vith by 23 January 1945. In February 1945 the 7th Armored advanced into Germany and participated in fighting near the Hürtgen Forest and later during the Allied encirclement of the Ruhr Pocket. After the war ended the division served in occupation duty in Germany, but returned to New York in October 1945 where it was inactivated. Later the 1st and 2nd Battalions of 48th Infantry were later assigned to the 3rd Armored Division in West Germany during the Cold War.

card_unit_6th_infantry_regiment_usa.name: card_unit_6th_infantry_regiment_usa
card_unit_6th_infantry_regiment_usa.title: THE REGULARS
card_unit_6th_infantry_regiment_usa.text: Becomes Veteran when it is fully repaired.
card_unit_6th_infantry_regiment_usa.flavorText: The 6th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “Regulars”, is a regiment of the US Army which has been active from 1812 to present day. During WWII, the regiment was a unit of the 1st Armored Division which played a significant role as one of the first American units to cross the Atlantic and engage the Axis powers. Departing from Fort Dix, New Jersey on April 11, 1942, they arrived in Northern Ireland on May 16, 1942. Intensively trained, they prepared for their first combat which was Operation Torch, the seaborne invasion of French North Africa. The 6th Armored Infantry Regiment, commanded by Colonel Claud E. Stadtman, faced challenges during this operation. While one battalion suffered heavy casualties in the assault on Oran, another battalion successfully captured the Tafaraoui airfield. Despite setbacks, the overall objective was achieved. The regiment then moved to Tunisia, where they confronted a German-Italian counterattack. In December 1942, the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 6th Armored Infantry bravely defended a critical defensive line against heavy enemy fire. They held their positions, contributing to the broader Allied effort. Subsequently, in October 1943, the regiment landed in Italy. Eventually, it underwent reorganization, with its elements being redesignated as parts of the 1st Armored Division.

card_unit_8th_marines.name: card_unit_8th_marines
card_unit_8th_marines.title: 8th MARINES
card_unit_8th_marines.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to adjacent units. They get +2 attack.
card_unit_8th_marines.flavorText: The 8th Marine Regiment played a significant role during WWII as part of the United States Marine Corps. The regiment was initially formed in 1917 but was disbanded after WWI. It was reactivated in 1940 and deployed to various theaters in the Pacific.After extensive jungle training the regiment began their wartime service by defending the Samoan Islands. They later sailed to Guadalcanal to reinforce the 1st Marine Division engaged in the grueling Battle of Guadalcanal. It was during this campaign that the regiment earned its first Presidential Unit Citation for its bravery and achievements. Following their time in Guadalcanal, the 8th Marines joined the 2nd Marine Division in New Zealand, where they prepared for the Battle of Tarawa. During the battle, the regiment played a vital role in capturing the island, which opened the door to the Japanese Empire. For their actions in Tarawa, the 8th Marine Regiment was awarded their second Presidential Unit Citation. After refitting in Hawaii, the regiment participated in the Marianas campaign, storming the beaches of Saipan and Tinian. These victories provided key bases for launching air attacks against Japan. Finally, the 8th Marines joined the 1st and 6th Marine Divisions in the Battle of Okinawa, where they faced fierce Japanese resistance. The regiment's involvement in Okinawa marked the last major battle of WWII.

card_unit_p51_b.name: card_unit_p51_b
card_unit_p51_b.title: P-51 B
card_unit_p51_b.text: Destruction: Give your units +2+2 and draw 2 cards.
card_unit_p51_b.flavorText: The P-51B was a single-seat fighter aircraft used by the United States during WWII. It was a variant of the P-51 Mustang, a long-range escort fighter primarily designed to accompany and protect Allied bombers during their missions. The P-51B was introduced in 1943 and featured improvements over its predecessors, including a more powerful Merlin engine which increased its speed and long-range capabilities, making it an effective escort fighter and a formidable opponent for enemy aircraft. The B and C models only had 4x .50 cal guns, but this would be increased to six in the D model line. The long-range capability of the P-51B was due in large part to the addition of external fuel tanks, and this enabled the aircraft to escort bombers deep into enemy territory. A total of 1,987 P-51B’s variants were produced and they remained in service until the end of the war. Quite a few of these variants were operated by the RAF as "Mustang III".

card_unit_seabees.name: card_unit_seabees
card_unit_seabees.title: SEABEES
card_unit_seabees.text: When a friendly unit is fully repaired, reduce its operation cost by 1 and give it +1 attack.
card_unit_seabees.flavorText: The Navy Seabees, officially known as the United States Naval Construction Battalions, were formed in 1942 during WWII. The Seabees were composed of skilled workers that were enlisted or drafted into the Navy, and they played a vital role in constructing and maintaining military bases, airfields, roads, bridges, and other infrastructure in support of Allied operations. In the Pacific theater, the Seabees were crucial in the island-hopping campaign, building facilities in hostile environments like Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa. They rapidly constructed airfields and bases, often under enemy fire. In Europe, they built temporary harbors and ports to support the Normandy invasion, including the innovative Mulberry harbors. The Seabees were known for their speed, efficiency, and motto "We build, we fight." During WWII they completed over 30,000 construction projects, including more than 400 advanced bases and airfields. Despite their primary construction role, they also engaged in combat, defending their sites and participating in offensive operations.

card_event_america_goes_to_war.name: card_event_america_goes_to_war
card_event_america_goes_to_war.title: AMERICA AT WAR
card_event_america_goes_to_war.text: Gain an extra kredit slot. Draw a card if you have 2 or more unspent kredits.
card_event_america_goes_to_war.flavorText: Before entering WWII, the United States were recovering from the Great Depression, and while they had a strong industrial base, it was not fully mobilized for wartime production. However, once the US entered the war, the government implemented massive mobilization efforts, including the conversion of civilian industries to war production, the expansion of the military and the implementation of rationing and other measures on the home front. This led to a significant increase in industrial output, employment and economic growth, transforming the United States into the "Arsenal of Democracy" and playing a crucial role in the Allied victory. Additionally, the war brought about some social changes, including increased opportunities for women in the workforce and advancements in civil rights as African Americans and other minority groups contributed to the war effort.

card_event_bomber_mafia.name: card_event_bomber_mafia
card_event_bomber_mafia.title: BOMBER MAFIA
card_event_bomber_mafia.text: Develop a US bomber. Deal 2 damage to all enemy units if you have 5 or more unspent kredits.
card_event_bomber_mafia.flavorText: The Bomber Mafia refers to a group of American military officers and strategists who advocated for precision bombing tactics during WWII. This stance led to their nickname "Bomber Mafia" from opposing voices within the military who were against prioritizing heavy bombers in strategic planning and funding. While the Bomber Mafia successfully pushed for the expansion of bomber fleets in the US military, their ambitions for precise targeting during WWII were not fully achieved. One key obstacle was the challenge of accurate targeting with the technology and tactics available at the time. However, bomber fleets played a significant role in the overall American war effort, but instead of using precision bombing tactics they employed area incendiary bombing to devastating effect. Despite the shortcomings of the precision bombing tactics during WWII, the strategic insights of the Bomber Mafia left a lasting impact on the mission and direction of the US Air Force and its Strategic Air Command.

card_event_firebomb.name: card_event_firebomb
card_event_firebomb.title: FIREBOMB
card_event_firebomb.text: Deal 5 damage to a unit, excess is dealt to random enemies if you have 2 or more unspent kredits.
card_event_firebomb.flavorText: Firebombs, also known as incendiary bombs, were used by both the Allied and Axis air forces during WWII. The United States used firebombing tactics as part of their strategic bombing campaign against Axis powers, particularly in Japan. Firebombing involved the use of incendiary bombs to create large-scale fires that inflicted widespread destruction on urban areas and industrial targets. The most notable example of this strategy was the firebombing raids conducted by the US Army Air Forces against Japanese cities, such as Tokyo, which resulted in devastating firestorms. These raids aimed at crippling Japan's industrial capacity, demoralizing the population, and hastening the end of the war.

card_event_furor.name: card_event_furor
card_event_furor.title: FUROR
card_event_furor.text: Fully repair a friendly damaged unit. Add an OUTRAGE to your hand.
card_event_furor.flavorText: During WWII, US submarines comprised less than 2% of the US Navy ships, but sank over 30% of Japan's fleet, including eight aircraft carriers. Furthermore, US submarines played a crucial role in severely crippling the Japanese economy by sinking nearly five million tons of shipping, accounting for 60% of the Japanese merchant marine. One notable example is the submarine USS Tang which sank the most tonnage of shipping in WWII for the US. In her short career Tang sank a total of 116,454 tons, from January 1944 until it was sunk by its own defective torpedo off the coast of China in October 1944.

card_event_hidden_plans.name: card_event_hidden_plans
card_event_hidden_plans.title: HIDDEN PLANS
card_event_hidden_plans.text: Choose One - Draw a Covert unit OR reveal a Covert unit and give it +1+1.
card_event_hidden_plans.flavorText: One notable example of USA’s hidden plans during WWII is the Manhattan Project, a top-secret initiative to develop nuclear weapons. Led by scientists such as J. Robert Oppenheimer, the project resulted in the successful creation of atomic bombs, which were ultimately used against Japan in 1945. The goal was to keep the entire atomic bomb program secret from Germany and Japan which Manhattan Project security officials accomplished successfully. They also tried to keep word of the atomic bomb from reaching the Soviet Union despite them being their allies. Secrecy in the Manhattan Project was so complete that many people working for the organization did not know what they were working on until they heard about the bombing of Hiroshima on the radio.

card_event_mayhem.name: card_event_mayhem
card_event_mayhem.title: MAYHEM
card_event_mayhem.text: Choose a unit in hand. Swap it with a friendly unit on the battlefield.
card_event_mayhem.flavorText: The Battle of Okinawa stands out as one of the most intense and chaotic engagements involving the USA during WWII. During the battle, US and Japanese forces exchanged relentless artillery fire. The US Tenth Army alone fired 1.1 million 105mm howitzer rounds, which is one of the largest barrages in WWII’s history. Combat was fierce and often hand-to-hand, and troops were engaged in intense fighting across hillsides, caves, trenches, bunkers, and pillboxes. XXIV Corps troops used 60-mm mortar tubes to launch 521,000 projectiles, fired nine million rifle bullets, consumed 16 million .30 caliber machine gun rounds, used 367,000 hand grenades, and fired 25,600 rifle grenades. Additionally, the US Navy fired approximately 600,000 rounds in support of ground operations. The human cost was immense, 12,520 US troops were killed or declared missing in action, 110,000 Japanese defenders were killed, and on top of that it is estimated that over 100,000 civilians lost their lives in the Okinawa Campaign.

card_event_yank_the_army_weekly.name: card_event_yank_the_army_weekly
card_event_yank_the_army_weekly.title: YANK
card_event_yank_the_army_weekly.text: Your HQ gets: "This battle, the first time you Develop each turn, also Develop a RETRIBUTION."
card_event_yank_the_army_weekly.flavorText: Yank, the Army Weekly was a weekly magazine published by the United States military during WWII. Yank was first published in 1942 and was made available to all serving members in the US military, with a circulation that exceeded 2.5 million in 41 countries with 21 editions. The last issue was published on December 28th, 1945. Each issue was edited in New York City and then sent to different locations worldwide for printing, where local editors added local stories. A popular “morale booster” among the troops was the inclusion of a pin-up girl in every issue, often dressed in swimwear or other alluring attire. These pin-ups featured famous actresses and stage performers.

card_unit_103rd_cavalry_recon.name: card_unit_103rd_cavalry_recon
card_unit_103rd_cavalry_recon.title: 103rd CAVALRY RECON
card_unit_103rd_cavalry_recon.text: Reveal: Your units get +1+1 if this unit was Covert for 2 or more turns.
card_unit_103rd_cavalry_recon.flavorText: The 103rd Cavalry Reconnaissance Troop was a mechanized unit of the 103rd Infantry Division, nicknamed “Cactus Division” of the US Army. The division served in the US Seventh Army of the 6th Army Group during WWII. It was ordered into active service in November 1942 to undergo training. In 1944, the division underwent significant changes as it lost 2,550 enlisted men through transfers, and refilled its ranks with personnel from various units and training programs. In October 1944 the 103rd Division arrived in Marseille, France, and what followed was intense combat. The division managed to capture the towns of Saint-Dié and Sélestat near the German border, and then penetrated the defenses of the Siegfried Line. Under the command of General Anthony "Nuts" McAuliffe, from January to July 1945, the division continued its offensive, liberating the Kaufering concentration camp in Landsberg and advancing through Germany and Austria. After the Armistice in Europe, the division assumed occupational duties until its return to the United States on September 10th, 1945, and inactivation on September 22nd, 1945.

card_unit_121st_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_121st_infantry_regiment
card_unit_121st_infantry_regiment.title: 121st INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_121st_infantry_regiment.text: Destruction: Add an OUTRAGE to your hand.
card_unit_121st_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 121st Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 30th Infantry Division of the US Army during WWII. When America entered the war in 1941 the division spent two years training in the US before being shipped to France where it landed at Omaha Beach five days after the D-Day landings. There the division participated in Operation Cobra, which was a successful attempt to break out of the Normandy beachhead and end the stalemate. That summer the division continued fighting in France, but after the liberation of Paris it advanced into Belgium and the Netherlands. The division later fought in the Battle of Hürtgen Forest and the Battle of the Bulge, facing fierce resistance from German forces in challenging terrain and harsh winter conditions. After crossing the Rhine the division helped to mop up enemy pockets of resistance. While capturing the city of Braunschweig the division freed 2,500 prisoners from Weferlingen, which was a camp of Buchenwald. The division then met up with the Soviet Red Army at Grunewald on the Elbe River in April 1945, and soon after the war was over.

card_unit_394th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_394th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_394th_infantry_regiment.title: 394th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_394th_infantry_regiment.text: Reveal: Gets +2+2 if in the frontline.
card_unit_394th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 394th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the 99th Infantry Division of the US Army during WWII. The regiment arrived in France in late 1944 and experienced a relatively quiet period before facing the brunt of the German Ardennes Offensive, also known as the Battle of the Bulge. The division fought fiercely in the harsh winter conditions, which eventually contributed to the Allied victory in the battle. Following the Battle of the Bulge, the 394th continued to advance through Germany, participating in various campaigns such as the capture of the Remagen Bridge and the final push into the heart of Germany. When the war ended the 394th was transferred back to the USA and inactivated in September 1945.

card_unit_blue_and_gray.name: card_unit_blue_and_gray
card_unit_blue_and_gray.title: BLUE AND GRAY
card_unit_blue_and_gray.text: When a friendly unit (including this) is destroyed, add an OUTRAGE to your hand.
card_unit_blue_and_gray.flavorText: The 29th Infantry Division, also known as the Blue and Gray Division, is a division of the US Army formed in 1917 during WWI. At the outbreak of WWII, the division was called into active service and in May 1942 it was sent to England where it began training for the invasion across the English Channel. In 1944 the division was finally put to action and it landed on Omaha Beach in Normandy on D-Day, June 6, where it suffered heavy losses. What followed was bitter fighting in the Normandy hedgerow country, and ultimately the division managed to capture the city of Saint-Lô. After a short rest they started pushing towards Germany, and would later participate in the Battle of Aachen, followed by Operation Grenade, a major offensive which involved the crossing of the Roer river between Roermond and Düren with the US Ninth Army. After the armistice in Europe in May 1945, the division was tasked with military occupation duties in the Bremen enclave, where it remained until the end of the year. In 1946 the Blue and Gray Division finally returned to the US where it was demobilized.

card_unit_grumman_goose.name: card_unit_grumman_goose
card_unit_grumman_goose.title: GRUMMAN GOOSE
card_unit_grumman_goose.text: Reveal: When the enemy HQ is attacked this turn, draw a card.
card_unit_grumman_goose.flavorText: The Grumman G-21, nicknamed “Goose”, was initially designed as an “air yacht” for wealthy New York businessmen, so they could commute from their homes on Long Island to their Manhattan offices. However, it soon found a market as an airliner, military transport, and utility aircraft. During WWII the Grumman Goose was primarily used by the US Navy, the US Coast Guard and USAAF, but also by the Royal Canadian Air Force. The aircraft was mainly employed for transport, reconnaissance, rescue, and training roles. A total of 345 Grumman Goose were produced by October 1945, including quite a few variants, but most were phased out of military service after WWII.

card_unit_m20_scout_car.name: card_unit_m20_scout_car
card_unit_m20_scout_car.title: M20 SCOUT CAR
card_unit_m20_scout_car.text:
Deployment: Target a unit. 
Destruction: It gets +1+1.
card_unit_m20_scout_car.flavorText: The M20 Armored Utility Car, also known as the M20 Scout Car, was a variant of the Greyhound armored vehicle. The M20 had the turret replaced by a low-profile armored open-top structure and an anti-aircraft ring mounting a .50 cal M2 heavy machine gun. To address its lack of anti-tank weaponry, the crew was equipped with a bazooka. The M20 was primarily used for command purposes and reconnaissance, but it also functioned as an armored personnel carrier and cargo transporter. The vehicle was known for its speed and maneuverability, and on top of that it offered some protection against small arms fire and shrapnel. When used in command roles it had additional radio equipment installed. Originally it was named the M10 Armored Utility Car, but it was later re-designated as the M20 to prevent confusion with the 3-inch Gun Motor Carriage M10. Ford produced a total of 3,680 M20’s during its two-year production period from 1943 to 1944.

card_unit_the_deuce.name: card_unit_the_deuce
card_unit_the_deuce.title: THE DEUCE
card_unit_the_deuce.text: Your Covert units cost 1 less to deploy.
card_unit_the_deuce.flavorText: The 502nd Parachute Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “The Deuce”, was an airborne unit of the US Army formed in 1942 which fought with the 101st Airborne Division during WWII. The 502nd were among the first paratroopers to drop behind enemy lines in Normandy on D-Day, where their job was to support the Allied amphibious attacks. The regiment continued fighting in Normandy until they returned to England for refitting at the end of June 1944. In September 1944 the regiment jumped again behind enemy lines, this time during Operation Market Garden. After successfully securing their objectives, the soldiers of the 502nd, alongside the rest of the 101st, advanced northward to occupy defensive positions on “The Island”, situated southwest of Arnhem. This location became the setting for some of the 101st's toughest battles during their operations in the Netherlands. In December 1944, during the Battle of the Bulge, the 502nd along with the 101st Airborne Division, played a crucial role in defending the town of Bastogne. As the war was nearing its end the regiment was moved to the Ruhr Pocket to help in mop-up operations, and on 5th of May they managed to secure Hitler's private residence in the town of Berchtesgaden. During the summer of 1945 the regiment was sent in Austria on occupation duty, before being shipped back to the US and deactivated in November.

card_event_rationing.name: card_event_rationing
card_event_rationing.title: RATIONING
card_event_rationing.text: Choose One - Remove Bond from cards in your hand OR give your HQ +4 defense.
card_event_rationing.flavorText: After the US entered WWII, the government introduced a large-scale rationing system to manage critical shortages and support the war effort. Overseen by the Office of Price Administration, rationing began with tires in early 1942 and soon expanded to include gasoline, sugar, coffee, meat and canned goods. More than 5,000 local boards, staffed mostly by volunteers, issued ration books to civilians, who exchanged stamps for limited quantities of goods. Some stamps featured symbols like airplanes or wheat but they did not always specify which item they applied to, which was later clarified in newspapers. The rationing system aimed to ensure fair distribution and prioritize military needs, with exemptions made for some industries or individuals with essential jobs. Housewives became key players in conserving food, encouraged to cook with substitutes and avoid waste. Victory gardens and “Meatless Mondays” became symbols of homefront patriotism. While the program faced complaints and black-market activity, it was generally respected and helped the US sustain a long and resource-consuming global conflict.

card_event_spars.name: card_event_spars
card_event_spars.title: SPARS
card_event_spars.text: Choose One - Draw the top unit of your deck OR give it Ambush and Shock.
card_event_spars.flavorText: SPARS was the women's reserve of the US Coast Guard during WWII, established in 1942. The name came from the Coast Guard’s motto: Semper Paratus (e. Always Ready). At a time when military branches were expanding women's roles, SPARS was created to free men for sea duty by placing women in shore-based positions. Over 11,000 women served in SPARS, including officers and enlisted personnel. SPARS filled a wide range of roles, from clerical and communications to more technical work like radioman, pharmacist's mate, and parachute rigger. Training initially took place at Oklahoma A&M for enlisted recruits and at the Coast Guard Academy for officers, later moving to Palm Beach and other locations. SPARS recruited primarily white women initially, but by late 1944, African American women were allowed to enlist following policy changes. SPARS units were never deployed overseas, but their work was vital. They handled logistics, intelligence, supply chains, and support roles that ensured the Coast Guard's wartime operations continued smoothly. Disbanded after the war in 1946, SPARS laid groundwork for integrating women more fully into the Coast Guard, which ultimately led to accepting women in 1973.

card_event_surging_power.name: card_event_surging_power
card_event_surging_power.title: SURGING POWER
card_event_surging_power.text: Give the top four units of your deck +1+1, +2+2, +3+3 and +4+4 respectively.
card_event_surging_power.flavorText: In January 1942, just weeks after the attack on Pearl Harbor, the US government established the War Production Board to direct the nation’s industrial mobilization. With factories still adjusting to the demands of global war, the Board’s mission was to prioritize military needs, allocate raw materials, and standardize production. It moved quickly, suspending civilian automobile manufacturing and redirecting steel, rubber, and aluminum toward tanks, ships, and aircraft. Although its early months were plagued by overlapping jurisdictions and logistical bottlenecks, the Board soon became the engine of American industrial power. It organized the mass production of everything from rifles to bombers, bringing thousands of civilian firms under military contracts. Giants like Ford, General Motors, and Chrysler successfully retooled their assembly lines for war. By the end of 1942, the results were undeniable. American factories were rolling out over 4,000 aircraft and nearly 1,500 tanks every month. This foundation, laid during the uncertain first year of the conflict, enabled a sustained industrial campaign that would eventually overwhelm the Axis powers with sheer material strength.

card_event_swift_response.name: card_event_swift_response
card_event_swift_response.title: SWIFT RESPONSE
card_event_swift_response.text: When a friendly unit is destroyed, your units get +1+1 and Shock.
card_event_swift_response.flavorText: On 23 December 1944, the skies over the Ardennes finally cleared after days of snow and fog. The German Ardennes Offensive, known as the Battle of the Bulge, had relied on poor weather to shield its forces from Allied aircraft. But with visibility restored, the US Eighth and Ninth Air Forces responded immediately. P-47 Thunderbolts and P-51 Mustangs scrambled from bases across France and Belgium, targeting German columns that had advanced deep into Allied lines. Many pilots were airborne within minutes of the order. Forward air controllers guided strikes with growing precision, directing aircraft to roads choked with vehicles. German tanks and trucks, often stuck in traffic or short on fuel, were ideal targets. By the end of the day, hundreds of sorties had hit supply lines, bridges, and convoys. The Luftwaffe, already depleted, was unable to contest the skies. The sudden and overwhelming air response crippled the momentum of the German offensive and the tide began to turn. This rapid arrival of air power not only halted further German advances but helped encircle key enemy formations. The 23 December counterstrikes marked a turning point in the battle, proving how quickly Allied air forces could exploit a change in weather to devastating effect.

card_event_the_big_three.name: card_event_the_big_three
card_event_the_big_three.title: THE BIG THREE
card_event_the_big_three.text: Each friendly unit gets +1+1 for each friendly unit not of the same nation.
card_event_the_big_three.flavorText: The Big Three were the principal Allied leaders of WWII: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the USA, Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and Joseph Stalin,General Secretary of the Soviet Union. From 1941, when the US entered the war, Roosevelt pushed for unity among the Allies despite differing political systems and postwar goals. His leadership helped shape the strategic alliance, particularly during the Tehran Conference in 1943 and the Yalta Conference in 1945. At Tehran, Roosevelt acted as a mediator between Churchill and Stalin, successfully advocating for Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion of France. He maintained a working relationship with Stalin, believing personal diplomacy could ease postwar tensions. By Yalta, the alliance was strained, but Roosevelt still hoped cooperation could guide the postwar order. Discussions focused on dividing Germany, establishing the United Nations, and securing Soviet participation in the Pacific War. Roosevelt died shortly after Yalta and was succeeded by Harry S. Truman, who joined Churchill and Stalin at Potsdam. Roosevelt’s role in the Big Three was pivotal, balancing military necessities with a vision for a stable postwar world. His diplomatic style emphasized pragmatism and unity, helping hold together a complex alliance until victory was within reach.

card_event_uss_sullivans.name: card_event_uss_sullivans
card_event_uss_sullivans.title: USS THE SULLIVANS
card_event_uss_sullivans.text: Target unit and the top unit of your deck each get +1+1. Draw a card.
card_event_uss_sullivans.flavorText: Commissioned in September 1943, USS The Sullivans (DD-537) was a Fletcher-class destroyer named in honor of the five Sullivan brothers who perished aboard the USS Juneau in 1942. It was the first US Navy ship named after more than one person. Assigned to the Pacific Fleet, The Sullivans participated in numerous key campaigns during WWII. She screened aircraft carriers in major operations including the Marshall Islands, the Battle of the Philippine Sea, and the Marianas campaign. In October 1944, she played a defensive role during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, engaging enemy aircraft and rescuing downed pilots. Later, during operations off Okinawa, the ship faced intense kamikaze attacks. On 27 April 1945, a kamikaze narrowly missed, crashing into the sea close aboard. Despite the hazards, she continued escort and rescue duties with distinction. Throughout her wartime service, The Sullivans rescued over 100 aviators and endured numerous air raids without serious damage. She earned nine battle stars for her actions in the Pacific. After the war, she served in various capacities before being decommissioned in 1965. Her legacy as a tribute to familial sacrifice and naval service continues today as a museum ship in Buffalo, New York.

card_event_victory_garden.name: card_event_victory_garden
card_event_victory_garden.title: VICTORY GARDEN
card_event_victory_garden.text: Each US unit in your deck gets: "Destruction: Give the top unit in your deck +1+1."
card_event_victory_garden.flavorText: During WWII, the US government urged civilians to plant Victory Gardens to bolster the nation’s food supply. These homegrown plots, often found in backyards, schoolyards and vacant lots, produced vegetables and herbs that supplemented rationed food. By 1943, an estimated 20 million gardens had been planted across the country, yielding nearly 9 million tons of produce. This effort not only alleviated pressure on commercial agriculture but also conserved vital resources like transportation and labor for the military. Victory Gardens became a symbol of civic duty, giving ordinary citizens a tangible way to contribute to the war effort. Government pamphlets, radio broadcasts and local campaigns provided practical gardening advice and encouragement. Children participated through school programs, and families often kept hens alongside their vegetable plots for fresh eggs. These gardens transformed neighborhoods into productive spaces and helped maintain morale during a time of scarcity.

card_unit_15th_engineers.name: card_unit_15th_engineers
card_unit_15th_engineers.title: 15th ENGINEERS
card_unit_15th_engineers.text: Deployment: Gain 1 extra kredit slot for each unit in the frontline. Your units gain equal amount of attack.
card_unit_15th_engineers.flavorText: Formed when the US entered WWI in 1917, the 15th Engineer Battalion began as the 5th Reserve Engineers. After multiple redesignations, it earned battle honors at the Battle of Saint-Mihiel and during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, before being demobilized in 1919. Reactivated in 1940 and assigned to the 9th Infantry Division, it was renamed the 15th Engineer Combat Battalion in 1942 and sent to North Africa. There, it supported operations against the Afrika Korps, then advanced with US forces through Sicily.
