In June 1944, the battalion landed in Normandy and began clearing mines and building bridges for the 9th Division’s drive across France. It helped enable the first US crossing of the Seine and joined brutal fighting in the Battle of Hürtgen Forest and the Battle of the Bulge. In March 1945, Company B earned a Distinguished Unit Citation for its role in the crossing at Remagen, where the battalion helped secure the Ludendorff Bridge and push deeper into Germany. The unit remained active until late 1946, after having supported every major 9th Division campaign in Europe.

card_unit_1st_defense_battalion.name: card_unit_1st_defense_battalion
card_unit_1st_defense_battalion.title: 1st DEFENSE BATTALION
card_unit_1st_defense_battalion.text: Deployment: Gets +1 attack if you have a US unit in the frontline.
card_unit_1st_defense_battalion.flavorText: The 1st Defense Battalion of the United States Marine Corps was formed in 1939 with the mission of providing coastal and air defense for key Pacific outposts. Although equipped for static defense, the Marines of this unit embodied the Corps’ principle that "every Marine is a rifleman." When called upon, they fought not just behind coastal guns, but in direct combat too. By December 1941, elements of the battalion were actively engaged at Johnston, Palmyra, and Wake Island, with the Wake detachment earning a legendary reputation. When Japanese forces launched their first amphibious assault on the island, the Marines responded with remarkable discipline. Their coastal batteries sank the destroyer Hayate and helped repel the landing force, the first major Japanese setback of the war. Despite being isolated and outnumbered, the Wake garrison held out for 15 days before finally being overrun. While the survivors endured years as prisoners of war, other detachments of the battalion continued to serve across the Pacific, later reorganized as antiaircraft units.

card_unit_1st_florida.name: card_unit_1st_florida
card_unit_1st_florida.title: 1st FLORIDA
card_unit_1st_florida.text: Destruction: A random friendly unit gets attack and defense equal to the attack of this unit.
card_unit_1st_florida.flavorText: Nicknamed “First Florida,” the 124th Infantry Regiment traces its roots to the Florida State Troops in the late 1800s. After service in the Spanish–American War and the Pancho Villa Expedition, the regiment was reorganized and activated for duty in both world wars. In WWI, it joined the 31st Division, but its soldiers were mostly used as replacements in France. In WWII, the 124th rejoined the 31st Infantry Division and trained at Camp Blanding, Florida. It deployed to the Pacific theater, participating in key campaigns in Dutch New Guinea and the Philippines. At the Battle of Morotai in 1944, the regiment helped establish a vital airbase against constant Japanese resistance. This operation enabled further Allied advances into the southern Philippines. Later, during the Mindanao campaign, the 124th saw some of its toughest fighting, clearing entrenched Japanese positions in dense jungle. For its actions, the regiment was awarded the Presidential Unit Citation and the Philippine Presidential Unit Citation. Throughout the war, the men of the 124th upheld their motto, “Florida and Country,” with distinction.

card_unit_41st_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_41st_infantry_regiment
card_unit_41st_infantry_regiment.title: 41st INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_41st_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Develop DEATH FROM ABOVE, UNITY IS STRENGTH or WE CAN DO IT!
card_unit_41st_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 41st Infantry Regiment was first activated in June 1917 at Fort Snelling, Minnesota. Though readied for deployment to France during World War I, the regiment never saw combat before the Armistice. After a series of reorganizations during the interwar years, it returned to active status before WWII. In 1942, the regiment was assigned to the 2nd Armored Division, becoming one of the first mechanized infantry units of its kind. It landed in North Africa during Operation Torch, then advanced through Sicily. From June 1944, it was involved in the Battle of Normandy, and spearheaded armored thrusts deep into Nazi-occupied Europe. The 41st fought in some of the toughest campaigns, including the Ardennes and the crossing of the Rhine into Germany. Throughout the war, its soldiers rode into battle in half-tracks, alongside tanks, supporting rapid advances and urban assaults. Their effectiveness in combined arms warfare earned them a reputation for discipline and aggression. After WWII, the regiment continued to serve in major conflicts including Desert Storm and operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.

card_unit_f6f_hellcat_home.name: card_unit_f6f_hellcat_home
card_unit_f6f_hellcat_home.title: F6F-5 HELLCAT
card_unit_f6f_hellcat_home.text: When this unit attacks, it and the top unit of your deck gets +1+1.
card_unit_f6f_hellcat_home.flavorText: The F6F-5 Hellcat, introduced in 1944, was the most advanced and numerous version of the Grumman F6F series. It improved on the earlier F6F-3 with a more powerful engine, strengthened airframe, and a redesigned engine cowling for better streamlining. Many were equipped with radar, making the F6F-5N a capable night fighter. Over 7,800 of this variant were produced out of a total 12,275 Hellcats built. Designed for carrier operations, the Hellcat was rugged, easy to fly, and lethal. It was specifically developed to counter the Mitsubishi A6M Zero and proved highly successful in doing so. With its 2,000 hp Pratt & Whitney R-2800 engine, the Hellcat had the speed, firepower and durability to dominate the skies. First seeing combat in 1943, the Hellcat quickly became the backbone of US Navy fighter squadrons in the Pacific. By the end of the war, it was credited with destroying 5,223 enemy aircraft, more than any other Allied naval plane. Its impact on air superiority was unmatched during the critical campaigns from the Gilbert Islands to Okinawa.

card_unit_m2a4.name: card_unit_m2a4
card_unit_m2a4.title: M2A4
card_unit_m2a4.text: Has Blitz if it has 3 or more attack.
card_unit_m2a4.flavorText: The M2A4 was the ultimate version of the M2 light tank series, marking a crucial turning point in American armor development just prior to the US entry into WWII. It featured a single turret armed with a 37mm M5 gun and a total of five .30 caliber machine guns, positioned in the turret, bow, sponsons, and an anti-aircraft mount. With armor thickness increased to a maximum of 25mm, it was powered by a 250 hp radial engine, allowing for a top speed of 36 mph and a range of 200 miles. Built by the American Car & Foundry Company, 375 units were produced between 1940 and 1942. Unlike earlier American light tanks which carried only machine guns, the M2A4 reflected hard lessons learned from the Spanish Civil War, where tanks without cannons had proven useless against enemy armor. Although mostly used for training, the M2A4 saw significant combat with the US Marine Corps during the Guadalcanal campaign in 1942. Deployed by the 1st Tank Battalion, these tanks supported infantry assaults, neutralized Japanese bunkers, and used canister rounds effectively in defensive actions. Though soon superseded by the improved M3 Stuart, the M2A4 bridged the gap between interwar designs and the modern combat vehicles of WWII.

card_unit_m3_lee_home.name: card_unit_m3_lee_home
card_unit_m3_lee_home.title: M3 LEE
card_unit_m3_lee_home.text: When this unit moves into the frontline, all units in your deck get +1 attack.
card_unit_m3_lee_home.flavorText: Introduced in 1941, the M3 Lee was an American medium tank developed rapidly to meet the urgent need for a 75 mm gun platform. Designed as a stopgap before the M4 Sherman was available, the M3 featured a distinctive layout with a sponson-mounted 75 mm gun in the hull and a smaller 37 mm gun in a turret above. Its tall silhouette and riveted armor were drawbacks, limiting its effectiveness in hull-down positions. Still, it offered strong firepower and reliable performance early in the war. A total of 6,258 units were produced between August 1941 and December 1942 by several manufacturers, including the Detroit Tank Arsenal and Baldwin Locomotive Works. In British service,  versions using the original US turret were called Lee, while those modified to British specifications were named Grant. The M3 first saw action in North Africa, where it initially outmatched the Panzer III and early Panzer IVs. However, by mid-1943 it was largely replaced in European theaters by the M4 Sherman. It continued to serve in the Pacific and with Allied forces, including the Soviet Union, through the Lend-Lease program. Despite its limitations, the M3 Lee played a vital role in bridging the gap to more advanced designs.

card_unit_magnificent_seven.name: card_unit_magnificent_seven
card_unit_magnificent_seven.title: MAGNIFICENT SEVENTH
card_unit_magnificent_seven.text: When this unit attacks, the top unit of your deck gets +1+1.
card_unit_magnificent_seven.flavorText: Nicknamed the “Magnificent Seventh”, the 7th Marine Regiment earned a fierce reputation during WWII as part of the US 1st Marine Division. Reactivated in early 1941, the regiment first deployed to Samoa before arriving on Guadalcanal in September 1942. Over four months of brutal combat, the 7th Marines fought in 42 engagements and killed over 6,000 Japanese soldiers. Many Marines fell to disease, fatigue, and wounds, yet the unit held its ground against repeated attacks. After Guadalcanal, the regiment continued its campaign across the Pacific, seeing action in New Guinea and New Britain before landing on Peleliu in September 1944. The battle became one of the bloodiest in Marine Corps history. In 1945, the 7th Marines landed on Okinawa, where they took Dakeshi Ridge and Wana Ridge at heavy cost. These battles, marked by stubborn Japanese resistance and grueling terrain, resulted in over 1,200 casualties. By the end of the war, the regiment had been involved in some of the most intense fighting in the Pacific. Its experience reflected the high toll that extended amphibious operations imposed on US forces.

card_unit_p_38_lightning_home.name: card_unit_p_38_lightning_home
card_unit_p_38_lightning_home.title: P-38H LIGHTNING
card_unit_p_38_lightning_home.text: Destruction: The top unit of your deck gets +3 attack and Blitz.
card_unit_p_38_lightning_home.flavorText: The Lockheed P-38 Lightning was a distinctive twin-engine fighter with a twin-boom design and a central nacelle for the pilot. Developed for high-altitude interception, it was the only US fighter in production from the beginning to the end of WWII. Over 10,000 were built, including around 600 P-38H variants. Introduced in mid-1943, the P-38H was powered by two Allison V-1710-89/91 engines and featured improved intercoolers and a stronger airframe. It carried a 20 mm cannon and four .50 caliber machine guns in the nose, allowing for concentrated fire without convergence issues. The H model could carry up to 3,200 pounds of bombs or drop tanks, making it highly versatile. The P-38 saw its greatest success in the Pacific, where its long range made it ideal for escort missions and island-hopping campaigns. It was flown by America’s top aces, including Richard Bong and Thomas McGuire. Though eventually overshadowed in Europe by the P-51 Mustang, the Lightning remained crucial in multiple roles, as fighter, bomber, pathfinder and reconnaissance aircraft. With its quiet engines and forgiving handling, the P-38H offered a balance of firepower, endurance and adaptability that proved vital in the air war.

card_unit_red_bull.name: card_unit_red_bull
card_unit_red_bull.title: RED BULL
card_unit_red_bull.text: At the start of your turn, double the attack of this unit.
card_unit_red_bull.flavorText: The 34th Infantry Division, nicknamed the “Red Bull” Division, was the first US division deployed to Europe in WWII. It shipped for Northern Ireland in early 1942, beginning a long journey that would carry it from North Africa to northern Italy. In the Tunisian campaign, the division engaged Axis forces in rugged terrain and helped secure the final Allied victory there in 1943. From September 1943, the Red Bull Division took part in the Allied invasion of mainland Italy. It advanced through Naples, Rome, and the Arno River valley before fighting in the Apennine Mountains. The division played a key role in breaching German defenses during the final push into the Po Valley in 1945. The 34th suffered heavy casualties during the Italian Campaign but developed a reputation for toughness. The division’s shoulder patch, a red steer skull over a black water jug, was inspired by a soldier’s design from its 1917 training days in New Mexico.

card_unit_the_professionals.name: card_unit_the_professionals
card_unit_the_professionals.title: THE PROFESSIONALS
card_unit_the_professionals.text: Destruction: All units in your deck get +2+3 and a random combat keyword.
card_unit_the_professionals.flavorText: Nicknamed "The Professionals," the 46th Infantry Regiment earned its reputation during WWII as the tip of the spear for the US 5th Armored Division. After reactivation in 1941 at Fort Knox, the unit trained intensively before landing in Normandy in 1944. It soon led the breakout through France, pushing rapidly across enemy lines during the Allied advance. The 46th was often the first element of the 5th Armored to make contact with German forces, securing key towns and road junctions. In one notable advance, they captured the strategic town of Domfront in Normandy in August 1944, forcing a hasty German retreat. The regiment continued its push through Luxembourg and into Germany, participating in five major campaigns. Their consistent frontline role and effectiveness in rapid, mechanized warfare earned them their other nickname: "Victory’s Spearpoint".

card_unit_thunderbolt.name: card_unit_thunderbolt
card_unit_thunderbolt.title: THUNDERBOLT
card_unit_thunderbolt.text: Deployment: Draw 2 cards. Then choose a card in hand and put it on top of your deck.
card_unit_thunderbolt.flavorText: After its activation in 1917, the 83rd Infantry Division saw limited action in WWI, but it would earn lasting recognition during WWII. Nicknamed the “Thunderbolt” Division, it landed at Omaha Beach in June 1944, a few weeks after D-Day, and quickly proved its mettle during the Allied breakout from Normandy. The 83rd advanced rapidly through France and into Luxembourg, often engaging in bitter combat. It gained a reputation for aggressiveness, especially during operations in the Normandy bocage and during the drive toward the German border. In late 1944, it took part in the Battle of the Bulge, helping blunt the German offensive. In 244 days of combat, the Thunderbolt Division liberated over 80,000 square kilometers and captured more than 150,000 prisoners. The division fought through Germany and was among the first American units to reach the Elbe River. There, they famously linked up with Soviet forces, marking a key moment in the final collapse of Nazi Germany.

card_event_fresh_recruits.name: card_event_fresh_recruits
card_event_fresh_recruits.title: FRESH RECRUITS
card_event_fresh_recruits.text: When a friendly unit is destroyed, give a random friendly unit +2+3.
card_event_fresh_recruits.flavorText: In 1939, the US military counted 356,000 men and women in its ranks. By the end of WWII, 16 million had been churned through the military recruiting process. It is safe to say that the US government managed to bolster the ranks in an incredible speed during the course of the war, starting with a skeleton force and ending with a military worthy of a superpower.

card_event_in_hour_of_need.name: card_event_in_hour_of_need
card_event_in_hour_of_need.title: IN HOUR OF NEED
card_event_in_hour_of_need.flavorText: A month after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt established the War Production Board. The purpose of the board was to convert peacetime industries into weapons and military factories. Another purpose was to conserve metal, petroleum, rubber, paper and plastic for the war effort, which meant strict rationing for civilians. F.ex. the US had manufactured 3 million civilian automobiles in 1941, but during the course of the war only 139 were manufactured.

card_event_island_hopping_elit.name: card_event_island_hopping_elit
card_event_island_hopping_elit.title: ISLAND HOPPING
card_event_island_hopping_elit.text: The enemy HQ gets: "If this HQ has taken 3+ damage this turn, a random friendly unit gets +2+2."
card_event_island_hopping_elit.flavorText: Island hopping, also known as Leapfrogging, was a military strategy employed by the Allies in the Pacific War against the Empire of Japan and the Axis powers during WWII. In short the strategy was about taking control of islands in the Pacific that were not heavily defended by the Japanese, and quickly constructing landing strips and small military bases. From there the target was set on the next island, and gradually the Allied forces moved closer to its final goal which was Japan. The island hopping strategy was very costly for the Allies, but ultimately it led to victory over the Japanese forces.

card_event_mass_deployment.name: card_event_mass_deployment
card_event_mass_deployment.title: MASS DEPLOYMENT
card_event_mass_deployment.text: Add 3 US units to your support line with total cost equal to your kredit slots.
card_event_mass_deployment.flavorText: Out of the more than 16 million Americans that served in WWII, approximately 11,7 million of them served overseas. Although the United States fought many campaigns in the Pacific, Asia and North Africa, their largest military deployment was in Europe.

card_event_stars_n_stripes.name: card_event_stars_n_stripes
card_event_stars_n_stripes.title: STARS & STRIPES
card_event_stars_n_stripes.text: Deal 1 damage to each unit in the enemy support line for each unit there.
card_event_stars_n_stripes.flavorText: Stars and stripes is a nickname used for the flag of the United States, but it’s also a name of a daily newspaper that reports on matters concerning the members of the US Armed Forces. During WWII the newspaper was printed and distributed in several operating theaters.

card_event_united_we_stand.name: card_event_united_we_stand
card_event_united_we_stand.title: UNITED WE STAND
card_event_united_we_stand.text: Deal 2 damage to a unit. If this destroys it, both players gain 1 extra kredit slot.
card_event_united_we_stand.flavorText: During WWII, the motto "United we stand, divided we fall", or simply “United we stand”, was a slogan that invoked not just American patriotism but unity among the Allied nations. In the US this motto could be seen written on posters, pinups, postcards, buttons, pins, matchbooks, and other artifacts from WWII that displayed wartime patriotism.

card_unit_1st_texas_infantry.name: card_unit_1st_texas_infantry
card_unit_1st_texas_infantry.title: 1st TEXAS INFANTRY
card_unit_1st_texas_infantry.text: Double attack and defense when you gain an extra kredit slot.
card_unit_1st_texas_infantry.flavorText: The 1st Texas Infantry, officially known as 141st Infantry Regiment, is a regiment of the US Army and traces its origin back to the Texas Revolution in 1836. They would later fight in the American Civil War for the Confederate States Army and in WWI. During WWII the regiment was assigned to the 36th Infantry Division of the US Army which fought several battles and campaigns on the Western Front, including the Italian Campaign, the Allied landings in Southern France, the Allied drive to the Rhine, and the push into Germany. The 1st Texas Infantry was first in doing several things. F.ex. it was among the first American troops to land in Europe, among the first Allied troops to enter Rome, the first infantry regiment to land on the coast of Southern France, and the first troops of the 36th Division to enter Germany.

card_unit_26th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_26th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_26th_infantry_regiment.title: 26th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_26th_infantry_regiment.text: Has +2 attack for each adjacent unit.
card_unit_26th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 26th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “Blue Spaders”, was formed in 1901 and is a unit of the US Army.  During WWII the regiment was assigned to the 1st Infantry Division, and in 1942 they participated in the first US led amphibious assault in North Africa and saw some heavy fighting at the Battle of Kasserine Pass, which was a series of battles during the Tunisian Campaign. The regiment would later participate in the Amphibious Battle of Gela, which was during the Allied invasion of Sicily, and in 1944 they landed at Omaha Beach in Normandy during D-Day. In 1944 the regiment participated in the Battle of Aachen, which became the first German city to fall into Allied hands. That same year the 26th defended against German attacks at Elsenborn Ridge during the Battle of the Bulge. The regiment ended the war in Czechoslovakia, but would later do occupation duties in Germany and serve as guards at the Nuremberg Trials.

card_unit_2nd_california.name: card_unit_2nd_california
card_unit_2nd_california.title: 2nd CALIFORNIA
card_unit_2nd_california.text: Combat damage dealt to this unit is reduced to 1.
card_unit_2nd_california.flavorText: The 184th Infantry Regiment, aka Second California, is a regiment of the US Army and has been active from 1924 to this day. When the US entered WWII the regiment took up defensive positions against an expected Japanese invasion on American soil. It wasn’t until 1944 that the regiment saw combat during the Battle of Leyte, and in 1945 it participated in the Battle of Okinawa. After the surrender of Japan, the 184th was sent to Korea in order to disarm the garrison and there it served as an occupation force until 1946.

card_unit_37mm_m1_aa_gun.name: card_unit_37mm_m1_aa_gun
card_unit_37mm_m1_aa_gun.title: 37mm M1 AA GUN
card_unit_37mm_m1_aa_gun.text: When this unit attacks, reset the attack of the defending unit.
card_unit_37mm_m1_aa_gun.flavorText: The 37 mm gun M1 was an American anti aircraft autocannon that was used by the US Army during WWII. There were two variants of the 37 mm AA gun, a towed variant, and one where the gun was mounted with two M2 machine guns on the M2/M3 half-track. The gun was also deployed in coast defense anti-motor torpedo boat batteries, usually there were two 37 mm guns alongside 90 mm guns in the batteries, but some batteries had four 37 mm guns. The 37 mm would later be replaced with the 40 mm Bofors gun M1.

card_unit_507th_pir.name: card_unit_507th_pir
card_unit_507th_pir.title: 507th PIR
card_unit_507th_pir.text: At the end of your turn, give a random friendly infantry unit +2 attack.
card_unit_507th_pir.flavorText: The 507th Parachute Infantry Regiment was an airborne regiment of the US Army. The regiment was formed in 1942 and during WWII it was a unit of the 82nd Airborne Division, and later the 17th Airborne Division. The regiment was shipped to Britain in 1943 where they started to train and prepare for the invasion of Normandy that was scheduled the year after. In June 1944, during D-Day, the 507th participated in the airborne landings in Normandy and were tasked with securing the Merderet River crossings. After the successful Allied landings in Normandy the regiment continued fighting in France until early 1945. Finally the 507th participated in Operation Varsity with the 17th Airborne Division, the airborne crossing the Rhine and the largest airborne operation in history. The regiment continued fighting with the 17th Airborne Division in Germany until the war ended in May 1945.

card_unit_pb4y_2_privateer.name: card_unit_pb4y_2_privateer
card_unit_pb4y_2_privateer.title: PB4Y-2 PRIVATEER
card_unit_pb4y_2_privateer.text: It costs the enemy +2 kredits to target or attack this unit.
card_unit_pb4y_2_privateer.flavorText: The Consolidated PB4Y-2 Privateer was an American patrol bomber that was introduced in 1943 and used by the US Navy during WWII. The Privateer flew its first missions in 1944 in the Pacific Theater and took on a variety of roles such as reconnaissance, search and rescue, anti-shipping, electronic countermeasures and communication relay. The aircraft looked very similar to the B-24 Liberator, except that it had a single vertical tail which increased its stability in low and medium altitudes. The Privateer was designed for a crew of 11, including a pilot and co-pilot, navigator, bombardier, five gunners and two radio operators. Its armament included 12 M2 Browning machine guns and it could carry up to 5800 kg of bombs, mines, or torpedoes. A total of 739 Privateers were built, including variants, some of which were produced after the war.

card_unit_p_40_k.name: card_unit_p_40_k
card_unit_p_40_k.title: P-40 K
card_unit_p_40_k.text: When a friendly bomber is destroyed, destroy a random enemy unit.
card_unit_p_40_k.flavorText: The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk was an American fighter and ground attack aircraft that was first introduced in 1938 and used during WWII by many Allied air forces. Due to a limited supply of Merlin engines that had powered previous Warhawks, the P-40K variant had it replaced with a new and more powerful Allison engine that had an automated boost control. The first 600 P-40k variants were produced in 1942 and shipped to China under Lend-Lease. The idea was to produce it in limited numbers as this would be the last P-40 series, the plan was to replace it with the P-60. However, problems with production of the P-60 meant that the production was increased to a total of 1,300 P-40k’s, including a few sub variants. Most P-40k’s served with the US air forces in Asia and the Pacific and with the Chinese Air Forces, but a few were sent to Britain under Lend-Lease and were redesignated as Kittyhawk III.

card_unit_red_devils.name: card_unit_red_devils
card_unit_red_devils.title: RED DEVILS
card_unit_red_devils.text: It costs the enemy +1 kredits to target or attack this unit.
card_unit_red_devils.flavorText: The 508th Parachute Infantry Regiment, aka Red Devils, is an airborne unit of the US Army that was formed in 1942. After extensive training the regiment participated in Operation Overlord in 1944 as part of the 82nd Airborne Division. The regiment saw heavy fighting and their contribution was considered decisive in helping the airborne meet its objectives at Normandy. Later that same year the regiment jumped into Holland as part of Operation Market Garden, where they maintained a defensive position over 11 km long against heavy German resistance, and prevented the demolition of the Nijmegen Bridge across the Waal River. In December 1944 the regiment moved into Belgium along with the 82nd Airborne and saw extensive action in the Ardenne Forest, in what is known as the Battle of the Bulge, where they defended their positions against the German Panzer Divisions. After the Battle of the Bulge the regiment saw little combat and in 1946 it returned to the US and deactivated.

card_unit_sb2c_helldiver.name: card_unit_sb2c_helldiver
card_unit_sb2c_helldiver.title: SB2C HELLDIVER
card_unit_sb2c_helldiver.text: When you gain an extra kredit slot, add a copy of this unit to your hand.
card_unit_sb2c_helldiver.flavorText: The Curtiss SB2C Helldiver was an American carrier based dive bomber that was in the service of the United States Navy in the Pacific theater during WWII. The Helldiver was meant to replace the Douglas SBD Dauntless, but it did not make a good first impression. The Helldiver was faster than the Dauntless and it also had folding wings that saved storage space on the carriers, but it had major faults such as being underpowered, with shorter range than the Dauntless and frequent maintenance problems. When the first SB2C Helldivers started to enter service in 1943 their poor performance led to many accidents, they either ran out of fuel or crashed during landing. Both its pilots and aircraft carrier crew took an instant dislike to the aircraft, so much that it earned the nickname “The Beast” and “Son of a bitch 2nd class”. However, in 1944 the SB2C-3 variant was finally introduced, it had an upgraded engine and a Curtiss four bladed propeller which solved its lack of power and ultimately the aircraft started to score some incredible success in the Pacific theater. The Helldiver made an important contribution in several battles over the Philippines, Iwo Jima, Okinawa and would play an important role in sinking the Japanese heavy battleships Yamato and Musashi, plus several regular sized battleships, aircraft carriers and other ships.

card_location_arracourt.name: card_location_arracourt
card_location_arracourt.title: ARRACOURT
card_location_arracourt.text: The Battle of Arracourt was a 1944 tank battle between US and German forces.
card_location_arracourt.flavorText: The Battle of Arracourt (September 18-29, 1944) was a key WWII tank battle in theLorraine region in France between US and German forces. The American 4th Armored Division, despite facing poor visibility and being outnumbered, used superior tactics, combined arms, and air support to counter the German Fifth Panzer Army’s attempt to halt the Allied advance in France. The Americans destroyed over 200 German tanks and assault guns while losing only about 55 of their own, marking a decisive victory that furthered the Allies' push toward Germany.

card_location_cherbourg.name: card_location_cherbourg
card_location_cherbourg.title: CHERBOURG
card_location_cherbourg.text: Cherbourg was an important harbor for the Allies after D-Day.
card_location_cherbourg.flavorText: Cherbourg was an important harbor for the Allies after D-Day. The Battle of Cherbourg was part of the Battle of Normandy during World War II. It was fought immediately after the successful Allied landings on June 6, 1944. Allied troops, predominantly American, isolated and captured the fortified port, which was considered vital to the campaign in Western Europe, in a hard-fought, month-long campaign.

card_location_guadalcanal.name: card_location_guadalcanal
card_location_guadalcanal.title: GUADALCANAL
card_location_guadalcanal.text: Guadalcanal is an island in the Solomon Islands, captured by the US in 1943.
card_location_guadalcanal.flavorText: Guadalcanal is an island in the Solomon Islands where a military campaign in WWII was fought between Japan and the United States. The Guadalcanal Campaign lasted from August 7, 1942 to February 9, 1943, and was the first Allied major land offensive against Japan and the first decisive victory won by the Allies in the Pacific.  What made the island a strategic place of importance was the Henderson Field air base which helped the Allies to control the sea lines of communications between Australia and the United States.

card_location_washington_waw.name: card_location_washington_waw
card_location_washington_waw.title: WASHINGTON
card_location_washington_waw.text: Washington DC played a vital role in the United States planning and preparation for WWII.
card_location_washington_waw.flavorText: Washington DC, the capital of the US, went through a drastic transformation during WWII. As the government grew during the war the population of the city nearly doubled and hundreds of new government facilities were built around the city. The majority of the new government workforce were women as the men were sent off to combat in Europe and the Pacific. Washington was never attacked during the war, and was never at risk, but the military did put up some anti-aircraft guns in the city just to be safe.

card_event_air_cover_us.name: card_event_air_cover_us
card_event_air_cover_us.title: AIR COVER
card_event_air_cover_us.text: Add two BREWSTER F2A to the battlefield, in the frontline if possible.
card_event_air_cover_us.flavorText: During WWII, the United States deployed a range of fighter aircraft to provide air cover for ground forces, naval convoys, and strategic locations. The Brewster F2A Buffalo, one of the Navy’s first monoplanes, was quickly outclassed by Japanese Zeros due to its poor speed and maneuverability. But despite heavy losses in early battles, it provided adequate defense until replaced by the Grumman F4F Wildcat. The F6F Hellcat was introduced in January 1943, and its superior range, firepower, and survivability helped secure Allied air superiority in the Pacific. The P-38 Lightning operated globally for the USAAF, while the P-47 Thunderbolt and P-51 Mustang dominated in Europe.

card_event_night_patrol.name: card_event_night_patrol
card_event_night_patrol.title: NIGHT PATROL
card_event_night_patrol.text: Draw 2 cards. Then choose a card in hand and put it on top of your deck.
card_event_night_patrol.flavorText: During WWII, the US Navy relied on several types of small, fast vessels for night patrols, especially in the Pacific and around contested coastal areas. The most famous were PT boats (Patrol Torpedo boats). They were mostly built of wood and powered by powerful engines, which made them fast and agile and ideal for hit-and-run attacks under cover of darkness. They carried torpedoes, machine guns, and depth charges, and were often used to ambush enemy ships or support amphibious landings. One of the most well-known PT boat commanders was John F. Kennedy, who commanded PT-109 in the Solomon Islands. In addition to PT boats, the Navy also used submarine chasers (SC boats) and patrol craft (PC boats) for night patrols, particularly for anti-submarine roles. These vessels were equipped with sonar and depth charges and were often used to protect convoys. Destroyer escorts (DEs) also played a role, especially on longer patrols. While larger ships used radar and sonar for night operations, it was the smaller boats that took the risks close to shore.

card_event_semper_fi.name: card_event_semper_fi
card_event_semper_fi.title: SEMPER FI
card_event_semper_fi.text: Convert 4 of the top 8 cards of your deck into 22nd MARINES. Give them the Navy type.
card_event_semper_fi.flavorText: "Semper Fi" is the abbreviation of the Latin phrase "Semper Fidelis," meaning "Always Faithful" in English. It's the motto of the United States Marine Corps, adopted in 1883, signifying a Marine's lifelong commitment to the Corps, the country, and their fellow Marines. It represents a dedication to loyalty and unwavering service. "Semper Fidelis" is also the title of the official march of the United States Marine Corps, composed by John Philip Sousa in 1889. On the United States Marine Corps Seal, the symbols of the Eagle, Globe, and Anchor emblem holds a ribbon emblazoned "Semper Fidelis".

card_event_strike_group.name: card_event_strike_group
card_event_strike_group.title: STRIKE GROUP
card_event_strike_group.text:
Show when drawn: Draw a random air unit from your deck.
Your air units get +1+1.
card_event_strike_group.flavorText: A carrier strike group is a type of battle group of the US Navy. During WWII, it was primarily referred to as a Fast Carrier Task Force, a powerful and flexible naval formation utilizing aircraft carriers to conduct offensive operations. Unlike traditional fleets built around battleships, these groups centered on fast aircraft carriers escorted by cruisers, destroyers, and submarines. This formation allowed for rapid, long-range strikes across the Pacific. Carrier groups such as Task Force 58 projected US air power deep into enemy territory. In campaigns such as the Gilberts, the Marshalls, and the Marianas, their aircraft neutralized airfields, bombed installations, and supported amphibious landings. At the Battle of the Philippine Sea in 1944, coordinated strikes from these groups overwhelmed Japanese airpower in what became known as the "Great Marianas Turkey Shoot". The mobility and concentration of air assets gave the US a decisive edge. Each carrier operated dozens of fighters, dive bombers, and torpedo aircraft. Their escorts screened against submarines and surface threats, while logistics ships kept them supplied at sea. These strike groups proved essential in turning the tide of the Pacific War. They bypassed strongpoints, isolated garrisons, and delivered sustained pressure on Japan’s shrinking perimeter.

card_event_uss_arcfish.name: card_event_uss_arcfish
card_event_uss_arcfish.title: USS ARCHERFISH
card_event_uss_arcfish.text: Destroy a random enemy unit. Repeat if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_event_uss_arcfish.flavorText: USS Archerfish (SS-311) was a US Navy Balao-class submarine commissioned in 1943. The submarine is probably best known for sinking the Japanese aircraft carrier Shinano, which is the largest warship ever sunk by a submarine. Archerfish operated in the Pacific during WWII, conducting patrols, laying mines and gathering intelligence. On 29 November 1944, off the coast of Japan, Archerfish launched six torpedoes at Shinano, which had only recently been commissioned and was on her maiden voyage. Four torpedoes struck, and despite her massive size and protective design, the carrier capsized and sank a few hours later. This marked one of the most significant submarine victories of the war. Archerfish completed five war patrols and earned seven battle stars. After the war she served in various roles including sonar testing and Arctic missions, before being decommissioned in 1968.

card_event_uss_fitch.name: card_event_uss_fitch
card_event_uss_fitch.title: USS FITCH
card_event_uss_fitch.text: Give your units +1+1. Give them +2+2 instead if there is a Navy card on top of your deck.
card_event_uss_fitch.flavorText: The USS Fitch (DD-462/DMS-25) was a Gleaves-class destroyer of the U.S. Navy which served with distinction during World War II. She was commissioned in 1942, and first operated in the Atlantic where she escorted convoys and participated in the invasion of North Africa (Operation Torch) in November 1942. Fitch then supported the Normandy landings in June 1944 where she provided naval gunfire support at Omaha Beach on D-Day and aided in minesweeping. She later participated in the invasion of southern France (Operation Dragoon) in August 1944. Afterward, she was converted to a high-speed minesweeper and redesignated DMS-25 in 1945. Fitch joined the Pacific Fleet near the end of the war and was present in Tokyo Bay during the Japanese surrender on September 2, 1945.

card_event_uss_missouri.name: card_event_uss_missouri
card_event_uss_missouri.title: USS MISSOURI
card_event_uss_missouri.text: Destroy target unit in the frontline. Retreat adjacent units.
card_event_uss_missouri.flavorText: The USS Missouri (BB-63) was the last battleship commissioned by the US Navy during WWII. She played a significant role in the Pacific Theater. Launched in January 1944, she was armed with nine 406mm (16-inch) main guns capable of striking targets over 32 kilometers away, along with twenty 127mm (5-inch) secondary guns and numerous anti-aircraft weapons. This powerful armament made her a formidable force in shore bombardments and fleet defense. After her launch, Missouri joined the Pacific Theater, where she provided anti-aircraft cover and naval gunfire support during major operations, including the Battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa. Her most iconic moment came on September 2, 1945, when she hosted the formal Japanese surrender ceremony in Tokyo Bay, officially ending WWII. Representatives of the Allied Powers, led by General Douglas MacArthur, and the Empire of Japan signed the surrender on her deck. Although she would serve in later conflicts, Missouri’s legacy is most closely tied to her role in the final chapter of WWII. Today, she is preserved as a museum ship at Pearl Harbor.

card_event_uss_yorktown.name: card_event_uss_yorktown
card_event_uss_yorktown.title: USS YORKTOWN
card_event_uss_yorktown.text: Add four BREWSTER F2A to the battlefield, in the frontline if possible.
card_event_uss_yorktown.flavorText: The USS Yorktown (CV-5) was the lead ship of her class and one of the US Navy's most important aircraft carriers during the early phase of WWII. Commissioned in 1937, she initially served in the Atlantic but was transferred to the Pacific shortly after the attack on Pearl Harbor. As the flagship of Task Force 17, Yorktown played a crucial role in several key battles. In May 1942, during the Battle of the Coral Sea, Yorktown's aircraft were instrumental in sinking the Japanese light carrier Shōhō and damaging the aircraft carrier Shōkaku. Although Yorktown was damaged in the battle, emergency repairs at Pearl Harbor were completed in just three days, allowing her to join the decisive Battle of Midway in early June. At Midway, Yorktown’s air groups helped sink the Japanese carriers Sōryū and Hiryū. However, she was struck by bombs and torpedoes from Hiryū-launched aircraft. Though initially kept afloat, Yorktown was later hit by torpedoes from the submarine I-168 while under tow and sank on June 7, 1942.

card_unit_175th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_175th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_175th_infantry_regiment.title: 175th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_175th_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Choose a card in hand. Put it on top of your deck.
card_unit_175th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 175th Infantry Regiment is a unit of the US Army, active since 1774, which makes it the seventh oldest regiment in the United States. It had already served in numerous conflicts before WWII, including the Revolutionary War and WWI. The regiment was mobilized in January 1941 and trained in the US before sailing to England in October 1942 aboard the RMS Queen Elizabeth. It spent months preparing for the invasion of Europe, training in Cornwall and conducting amphibious drills at Slapton Sands. The 175th regiment landed on Omaha Beach on 7 June 1944, a day after D-Day, as part of the 29th Infantry Division, tasked with capturing the village of Isigny. It fought its way through thick hedgerows toward Saint-Lô, meeting strong German resistance. At Hill 108, later known as "Purple Heart Hill," the 1st Battalion held its position while nearly surrounded. After securing Saint-Lô, the regiment joined the assault on Brest, targeting German submarine bases. In early 1945, it helped capture Jülich in western Germany, and later took part in the occupation of Mönchengladbach. On 2 May, a patrol from the 175th met Soviet troops near the Elbe River. The regiment remained in Germany with the 29th Division until January 1946, before returning home and reactivating later that year.

card_unit_22nd_marines.name: card_unit_22nd_marines
card_unit_22nd_marines.title: 22nd MARINES
card_unit_22nd_marines.text: Becomes Veteran and you draw a card when you play a Navy card.
card_unit_22nd_marines.flavorText: Activated in June 1942 in San Diego, the 22nd Marine Regiment was initially sent to defend islands in the Pacific, training in Samoa and Hawaii before entering combat. The regiment’s first major action came in February 1944 at Eniwetok in the Marshall Islands, where they captured key islands using new fire team tactics. Later, the 22nd Marines joined the 1st Provisional Marine Brigade for the invasion of Guam in July 1944, landing near Agat and fighting for three weeks to secure the island. After Guam, the regiment became part of the 6th Marine Division and took part in the fierce Battle of Okinawa in April 1945. Landing on the northern beaches, the 22nd Marines pushed across the island and played a key role in capturing Naha and Sugar Loaf Hill, suffering heavy casualties. After WWII ended, the regiment was sent to China to help oversee the surrender and repatriation of Japanese forces before being inactivated in March 1946.

card_unit_4th_alabama.name: card_unit_4th_alabama
card_unit_4th_alabama.title: 4th ALABAMA
card_unit_4th_alabama.text: Show when drawn: Give your units +1 attack until end of turn.
card_unit_4th_alabama.flavorText: The 167th Infantry Regiment, known as the "4th Alabama", is a unit of the US Army which has been active from 1836 to this day. During WWII, the regiment served with the 31st "Dixie" Division in the Pacific Theater. After deploying in March 1944, the regiment saw its first combat in July along the northern coast of New Guinea. In September, elements of the 167th participated in the amphibious assault on Morotai Island, securing key positions and eliminating remaining Japanese resistance by January 1945. Later, the regiment moved to the Philippines, landing on Mindanao in April 1945. There, the 167th faced challenging terrain and harsh conditions as it advanced through coastal areas near Davao Gulf and Sarangani Bay. The regiment's efforts contributed to the liberation of the island from Japanese control. For its service in the Pacific, the 167th Infantry Regiment received the Philippine Republic Presidential Unit Citation. The regiment remained in the southern Philippines until the end of the war, returning to the United States in December 1945.

card_unit_pb2y_coronado.name: card_unit_pb2y_coronado
card_unit_pb2y_coronado.title: PB2Y CORONADO
card_unit_pb2y_coronado.text:
Show when drawn: Add a BREWSTER F2A to the support line.
Your fighters have +1 attack.
card_unit_pb2y_coronado.flavorText: Consolidated PB2Y Coronado was a large, four-engine flying boat developed for the US Navy and introduced in 1940. It was designed for long-range patrol, bombing and transport roles, and intended as a heavy counterpart to the more famous PBY Catalina. While the Coronado saw limited frontline combat use, it became valuable in the Pacific for long-distance logistics, medical evacuation, and maritime reconnaissance. Early models carried heavy defensive armament and bomb loads, but as the war progressed, many were converted for cargo and troop transport. Some were also outfitted as flying hospital aircraft. Operating from remote island bases, Coronados supported amphibious invasions and strategic airlift across the vast ocean theater. A total of 217 PB2Ys were built, including all variants.

card_unit_sykes_regulars.name: card_unit_sykes_regulars
card_unit_sykes_regulars.title: SYKES REGULARS
card_unit_sykes_regulars.text: Draw 3 cards when this unit moves into the frontline.
card_unit_sykes_regulars.flavorText: The 20th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed "Sykes' Regulars" after Civil War General George Sykes, is a US Army unit established in 1861. During WWII, as part of the 6th Infantry Division, the regiment was engaged in bitter jungle and mountain fighting throughout the Pacific campaigns. They landed at Maffin Bay on 11 June 1944, and took part in the Battle of Lone Tree Hill, a decisive engagement in the Western New Guinea Campaign. In January 1945, they joined General MacArthur’s return to Luzon, in the Philippines, storming Blue Beach at Lingayen Gulf. There, they faced well-equipped Japanese troops entrenched in strong defensive positions, and the Pacific’s biggest armor concentration. They helped secure key strategic objectives, contributing significantly to the Allied victory in the Pacific. Later, they battled remaining enemy forces on Munoz Island until the 15 August 1945 ceasefire. The Sykes Regulars had 219 days of continuous combat and they were, along with other members of the 6th Division, the most heavily engaged unit in the United States Army during WWII.

card_unit_the_123s.name: card_unit_the_123s
card_unit_the_123s.title: 123s
card_unit_the_123s.text: When you deploy a unit, this unit is Converted into it and gains this ability.
card_unit_the_123s.flavorText: The 123rd Infantry Regiment, part of the Illinois Army National Guard, was reactivated in 1942 and assigned to the 33rd Infantry Division. Its motto, "1, 2, 3 Go!", reflects its designation and readiness for action. Initially trained in desert warfare in California, the regiment was later redirected to the Pacific Theater. After additional jungle warfare training in Hawaii, the 123rd landed at Maffin Bay, New Guinea, in September 1944. There, designated as "Task Force Tornado", they conducted extensive patrols to secure the Wakde airstrip and the Toem–Sarmi sector. Their operations effectively neutralized Japanese forces in the area, with over 4,000 enemy casualties reported. In February 1945, the regiment participated in the Luzon campaign in the Philippines. They advanced through challenging mountainous terrain, engaging in fierce battles to capture strategic positions, including the city of Baguio. Their efforts contributed significantly to the liberation of the Philippines from Japanese occupation. Following Japan's surrender, the 123rd Infantry Regiment served as part of the occupation forces in Japan until its demobilization in early 1946.

card_unit_the_american_guard.name: card_unit_the_american_guard
card_unit_the_american_guard.title: THE AMERICAN GUARD
card_unit_the_american_guard.text: Deployment: Choose a card in hand. Convert the top card of your deck into it.
card_unit_the_american_guard.flavorText: The 71st New York Infantry Regiment, known as the "American Guard," boasts a storied history that stretches back to its founding in 1850. As part of the New York State Militia, the regiment served in the Civil War, the Spanish-American War, and WWI. During WWII, the 71st attached to the 44th Infantry Division, deploying to Europe in 1944. The division landed in France at Cherbourg in September 1944 and entered combat near Lunéville in October, repelling heavy German attacks in the Parroy forest. Advancing through the Vosges Mountains, the division liberated Avricourt and Strasbourg alongside French forces. In December, the 44th helped assault and capture major Maginot Line fortifications, including Fort Simserhof. After defending the Sarreguemines area through early 1945, the division crossed the Rhine at Worms in March, took Mannheim, and later crossed the Main River. In April, they pressed into southern Germany, capturing towns such as Füssen and Wertach, and pushed into Austria. On May 2, 1945, they accepted the surrender of Wernher von Braun and other German scientists. After brief occupation duty in Austria, the 44th Division returned to the US in July and was inactivated in November 1945 following the end of the war.

card_event_naval_battle.name: card_event_naval_battle
card_event_naval_battle.title: NAVAL BATTLE
card_event_naval_battle.text: Choose One - Destroy all units with an odd cost OR even cost.
card_event_naval_battle.flavorText: The Battle of Sunda Strait was fought on the night of 28 February to 1 March 1942, as Japanese forces moved to invade Java in the Dutch East Indies. After the defeat in Battle of the Java Sea, the American heavy cruiser USS Houston and the Australian light cruiser HMAS Perth reached Tanjung Priok, then received orders to sail through Sunda Strait toward Tjilatjap. The Dutch destroyer HNLMS Evertsen followed behind. The Allied ships expected only friendly patrol craft in the strait. Instead, they ran into a large Japanese invasion convoy entering Bantam Bay, escorted by destroyers, cruisers, and other warships. The battle began after Perth challenged a ship near Saint Nicolaas Point and received the wrong reply. Japanese torpedoes and gunfire soon filled the night. Houston and Perth fought while trying to force a path westward, even firing into the transport group, but they were surrounded and badly outnumbered. Both cruisers were sunk after midnight. Some Japanese ships were also lost, several to friendly fire. Houston’s captain, Albert H. Rooks, was killed and received the Medal of Honor posthumously.

card_event_parachute_assault.name: card_event_parachute_assault
card_event_parachute_assault.title: PARACHUTE ASSAULT
card_event_parachute_assault.text: Fill your support line with 506th AIRBORNE. Give them Blitz and Shock.
card_event_parachute_assault.flavorText: US parachute tactics during WWII focused on surprise, disruption, and seizure of key terrain behind enemy lines. Paratroopers were dropped ahead of the main ground or amphibious force, often at night, with specific objectives such as bridges, road junctions, causeways, artillery positions, and routes needed by advancing troops. In Normandy, for example, the 82nd and 101st Airborne were dropped behind Utah Beach to secure exits from the beachhead and hinder German movements. Once on the ground, units were expected to assemble quickly, attack their objectives, disrupt enemy communications and reinforcements, and then hold until relieved. Because parachute drops frequently scattered units, small groups often had to improvise and continue toward objectives without their full formations. Heavy weapons, artillery, engineers, jeeps, and additional infantry followed in gliders.

card_event_quinine.name: card_event_quinine
card_event_quinine.title: QUININE
card_event_quinine.text: Target infantry gets +1+2 and -1 operation cost.
card_event_quinine.flavorText: Quinine was one of the most important anti-malaria drugs used by US forces in the Pacific during WWII. Jungle heat, heavy rains, swamps, mud, and mountain terrain made service difficult, but mosquitoes made it far worse. Malaria spread quickly in the South Pacific, often causing more casualties than combat itself, and weakening entire units before battle. The Army already knew basic prevention methods, including mosquito nets, careful camp placement, and regular quinine or Atabrine treatment. But in practice, supply shortages, long transport routes, and limited numbers of tropical diseases specialists made control difficult. Early estimates for anti-malaria supplies were far below real demand, and commanders warned that without enough quinine, many other supplies would lose much of their value. In the Philippines in 1942, about 24,000 of 75,000 American and Filipino defenders were estimated to be suffering from malaria. Across the South Pacific, many soldiers caught the disease at some point. Atabrine helped, but some men avoided it because it could turn skin yellow. Quinine remained a vital treatment when available, especially for troops already weakened by hunger, dysentery, and exhaustion.

card_event_surprise_engagement.name: card_event_surprise_engagement
card_event_surprise_engagement.title: SURPRISE ENGAGEMENT
card_event_surprise_engagement.text: Costs 2 less if Rain was played this turn. Destroy a random enemy unit. Draw the top unit of your deck.
card_event_surprise_engagement.flavorText: The Battle of the Driniumor River was one of the most brutal surprise infantry assaults of the New Guinea campaign. In 1944, US forces near Aitape were pushing westward while also guarding airfields and supply lines. Across the river stood elements of the Japanese 18th Army, already weakened by hunger and disease but still capable of a dangerous attack. In July 1944, Japanese infantry crossed the Driniumor at night and struck the forward positions of the US 32nd Infantry Division. The attack achieved surprise in several sectors. Outposts were overrun, communications broke down, and small groups of American infantry had to fight in isolation in thick jungle. For a time, the fighting became a confused struggle of patrol clashes, ambushes, and desperate local defenses. The Americans recovered by using artillery, mortars, and air support to break up Japanese attacks, then launched counterattacks to restore the line. As the battle continued, the Japanese offensive lost strength. The fighting around the Driniumor river showed how quickly a quiet jungle front could erupt into a brutal infantry battle at close range.

card_event_usaaf.name: card_event_usaaf
card_event_usaaf.title: USAAF
card_event_usaaf.text: Draw a US bomber and a US fighter from your deck.
card_event_usaaf.flavorText: The United States Army Air Forces, or USAAF, was created in June 1941 as the main land-based air arm of the U.S. Army. It rapidly expanded from the much smaller pre-war Air Corps into one of the largest military organizations of WWII, reaching more than 2.4 million personnel and nearly 80,000 aircraft at its peak in 1944. The USAAF fought across every major theater of the war. In Europe, the Eighth and Fifteenth Air Forces carried out the strategic bombing campaign against German industry, transportation and oil production, while tactical air forces supported Allied ground troops. In the Pacific, USAAF units operated from New Guinea, China and island bases across the Central Pacific. During the final stage of the war, the Twentieth Air Force used long-range B-29 Superfortress bombers to strike the Japanese home islands. By the end of WWII, the USAAF had effectively become an independent air service in all but name. Its wartime experience led to the creation of the independent United States Air Force in September 1947.

card_event_us_weather_bureau.name: card_event_us_weather_bureau
card_event_us_weather_bureau.title: US WEATHER BUREAU
card_event_us_weather_bureau.text: Choose One - Forecast OR draw a card.
card_event_us_weather_bureau.flavorText: The US Weather Bureau became an unexpected part of wartime security after the US entered WWII. Weather reports could help ships, aircraft and submarines plan movements, so the Office of Censorship restricted what newspapers and radio stations could share. Forecasts were shortened, weather maps disappeared, and broadcasters often needed permission before mentioning storms. This caused serious problems on the home front. On 16 March 1942, a powerful tornado outbreak struck the central and southern US. Near Memphis, radio station WREC knew doctors and nurses were needed in damaged communities, but censorship rules prevented it from giving clear public details until permission arrived from Washington hours later. A similar danger appeared in 1943, when a hurricane hit the Texas coast with little warning. Ships that normally sent weather reports from the Gulf of Mexico had stayed radio silent because of U-boats fear. The restrictions were intended to protect military operations, but they also weakened public trust in official forecasts. In October 1943, many limits on weather news were lifted after officials decided the cost to farming, aviation, shipping and public safety had become too high.

card_unit_116th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_116th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_116th_infantry_regiment.title: 116th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_116th_infantry_regiment.text: Deployment: Give a friendly infantry and all units with the same name in hand and deck +5+5.
card_unit_116th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 116th Infantry Regiment, part of the Virginia National Guard, served with the 29th Infantry Division during WWII. Its lineage goes back to the colonial era, but the regiment became especially famous for its role in the Normandy landings. On D-Day, 6 June 1944, the 116th led the assault on the western sector of Omaha Beach. Companies A, E, F, and G landed in the first wave and faced intense German fire. Company A, drawn largely from Bedford, Virginia, was hit particularly hard, with most of its men injured or killed. Despite severe losses, survivors pushed inland, helped open routes off the beach, and continued the advance through Normandy. The regiment later fought in the Battle of Saint-Lô, the capture of Brest, and along the Siegfried Line. It then advanced across western Germany, crossed the Roer, and took part in operations against the Ruhr Pocket. By late April 1945, the 116th had reached the Elbe, where the 29th Infantry Division linked up with Soviet forces shortly before Germany’s surrender.

card_unit_162nd_regiment.name: card_unit_162nd_regiment
card_unit_162nd_regiment.title: 162nd REGIMENT
card_unit_162nd_regiment.text: Combat damage dealt to your infantry is reduced to 2. Fully repair your infantry when you play a Rain card.
card_unit_162nd_regiment.flavorText: The 162nd Infantry Regiment was a unit of the Oregon National Guard with roots going back to the 3rd Oregon Infantry Regiment. During WWII it served with the 41st Infantry Division, known as the Jungleers. After earlier campaigns in the Pacific, the regiment took part in the southern Philippines operations in 1945. On Mindanao, the 162nd landed near San Mateo on 10 March. The assault faced only light resistance at the beach, and the regiment quickly secured Wolfe Field before pushing inland and west along the coast. The harder fighting came afterward, when Japanese forces withdrew into high ground covered by jungle, wire, mines, and hidden positions. The 162nd advanced in two columns toward Mount Capisan, supported by artillery and close air support. By late March, organized resistance in that sector had been broken. Elements of the regiment also fought on nearby Sibago Island, where a small Japanese garrison held a lighthouse overlooking Basilan Strait. The fight lasted several days despite the island’s small size. The 162nd later moved to eastern Mindanao, securing lines of communication and helping clear Japanese resistance, before preparing for the planned invasion of Japan.

card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment_us.name: card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment_us
card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment_us.title: 1st INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment_us.text: After you deploy or add an infantry unit, it operates for free this turn.
card_unit_1st_infantry_regiment_us.flavorText: The 1st Infantry Regiment, one of the oldest regiments in the US Army, served with the 6th Infantry Division during WWII. After training across the United States and later in Hawaii, the regiment deployed to New Guinea in February 1944. It took part in the New Guinea Campaign, including the assault at Sansapor, and received a Presidential Unit Citation for its actions at Maffin Bay. In January 1945, the 1st Infantry Regiment landed at Lingayen Gulf on Luzon as the 6th Infantry Division joined the campaign to liberate the Philippines. The regiment continued fighting across Luzon through the summer, remaining with the division for most of the campaign. Following Japan’s surrender, they moved to Korea in October 1945, where the 6th Infantry Division was tasked with occupation duties. The 1st Infantry Regiment remained there until its inactivation in 1949.

card_unit_6th_marine_regiment.name: card_unit_6th_marine_regiment
card_unit_6th_marine_regiment.title: 6th MARINE REGIMENT
card_unit_6th_marine_regiment.text: Has Blitz and 0 operation cost if Sunny or Rain was played this turn.
card_unit_6th_marine_regiment.flavorText: The 6th Marine Regiment, known as the Fighting 6th Marines, entered WWII as part of the 2nd Marine Division. After the US joined the war, the regiment first garrisoned Iceland before returning to the division and sailing for the South Pacific. It landed on Guadalcanal in January 1943 and joined the final American push from Kokumbona to Cape Esperance, helping clear the last organized Japanese forces from the island. Later that year, the regiment fought at the Battle of Tarawa, in the Gilbert Islands. The 6th Marines served as the division’s floating reserve, but fierce resistance on Betio forced its commitment early. The 1st and 3rd Battalions landed on Green Beach and pushed across the island, while the 2nd Battalion blocked the enemy on nearby Bairiki Island. The regiment suffered 355 casualties and received a Presidential Unit Citation for Tarawa. In 1944, the 6th Marines fought at Saipan and Tinian. Saipan was its costliest WWII battle, with 356 killed and 1,208 wounded. After Tinian, the regiment prepared for Okinawa and later the planned invasion of Japan, but the war ended before that landing happened.

card_unit_duck_us.name: card_unit_duck_us
card_unit_duck_us.title: DUCK
card_unit_duck_us.text: Gets +1+1 and you Forecast when you move it into the frontline.
card_unit_duck_us.flavorText: The Grumman J2F Duck was a single-engine amphibious biplane used by the US Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and Army Air Forces. It first flew in 1936 and was an improved version of the earlier JF Duck, with a longer central float and a stronger engine. A total of 584 J2F Ducks were built, including 330 produced by Columbia Aircraft after US entry into WWII increased demand. The Duck looked old-fashioned beside faster wartime aircraft, but its value came from versatility. Its large central float also held a retractable landing gear, allowing it to operate from both water and land. Crews used it for utility flights, light transport, scouting, mapping, photographic surveys, anti-submarine patrols, target towing, and air-sea rescue. It could carry two passengers or a stretcher inside the fuselage. One Duck made a notable escape from Bataan in 1942. After repairs using parts from another damaged aircraft, it departed after midnight on 9 April, carrying five passengers and pilot Roland J. Barnick. It was the last aircraft to leave Bataan before the Allied surrender there. Ducks later served at Guadalcanal in search and rescue missions.

card_unit_fifth_ohio.name: card_unit_fifth_ohio
card_unit_fifth_ohio.title: FIFTH OHIO
card_unit_fifth_ohio.text: Deployment: Destroy target enemy unit with combined attack and defense of 6 or less.
card_unit_fifth_ohio.flavorText: The Fifth Ohio, officially called 145th Infantry Regiment, entered federal service in 1940 with the 37th Infantry Division of the US Army, later known as the Buckeye Division. After training at Camp Shelby and taking part in the Louisiana Maneuvers, the regiment sailed to Fiji in 1942, before entering combat in the Solomon Islands. In New Georgia in 1943, the 145th fought in the Battle of Bairoko. Its troops moved through jungle, mud, and hidden Japanese defenses as Allied forces tried to cut supply routes to Munda. The fighting was slow and costly, with strong points often cleared one at a time. The regiment later fought on Bougainville, where the defense of Hill 700 became one of its hardest engagements. In 1945, the 145th joined the Luzon campaign. It helped take Clark Field, fought in Manila, and stormed intra muros through the Quezon and Parian Gates.

card_unit_kingfisher_us.name: card_unit_kingfisher_us
card_unit_kingfisher_us.title: KINGFISHER
card_unit_kingfisher_us.text: Forecast after this unit attacks the enemy HQ.
card_unit_kingfisher_us.flavorText: The Vought OS2U Kingfisher was the main shipboard observation seaplane used by the US Navy during WWII. First flown in 1938, it was a compact floatplane that could be launched by catapult from battleships and cruisers, then recovered from the sea by crane. A total of 1,519 Kingfishers were built. The aircraft was not fast, and its 450-horsepower engine gave it only modest performance. Its strength was reliability and usefulness. Kingfishers spotted gunfire for warships, scouted ahead of fleets, searched coastal waters, and supported shore bombardments. They could also carry small bombs or depth charges, and were armed with one fixed machine gun for the pilot, and another on a flexible mount for the observer. The Kingfisher became especially valuable in air-sea rescue. In 1942, one helped recover Eddie Rickenbacker and his crew after weeks adrift in the Pacific. In 1944, Lieutenant John A. Burns used a Kingfisher near Truk Lagoon to rescue downed airmen and taxi them to the submarine USS Tang. The US Coast Guard also used 76 Kingfishers for reconnaissance, anti-submarine patrol, and rescue missions.

card_unit_ruffians.name: card_unit_ruffians
card_unit_ruffians.title: RUFFIANS
card_unit_ruffians.text: Deployment: Gets +1+1 for each other infantry you control.
card_unit_ruffians.flavorText: “Ruffians” refers to Raff’s Ruffians, the nickname given to the 507th Parachute Infantry Regiment after Colonel Edson Raff took its command in Normandy. The regiment was formed at Fort Benning in 1942 and first assigned to the 82nd Airborne Division. It made its combat debut on D-Day. During Mission Boston, the 507th was dropped into Normandy to help secure crossings over the Merderet River. Its intended drop zone laid north of Amfreville, but clouds, anti-aircraft fire and confusion scattered many aircraft. Small groups of paratroopers had to fight their way through the flooded fields and hedgerows, often far from their planned objectives. The regiment suffered heavy losses in Normandy before returning to England in July 1944. It later joined the 17th Airborne Division, fought during the Battle of the Bulge and jumped again in Operation Varsity, the airborne crossing of the Rhine in 1945. After advancing into Germany, the 507th ended the war there in May, was shipped home and inactivated later that year.

card_unit_tropic_lightning.name: card_unit_tropic_lightning
card_unit_tropic_lightning.title: TROPIC LIGHTNING
card_unit_tropic_lightning.text: Draw a card the first time you gain an extra kredit slot. Your units get +2+2 the second time. Becomes Veteran the third time.
card_unit_tropic_lightning.flavorText: The 25th Infantry Division, nicknamed “Tropic Lightning”, was activated at Schofield Barracks in Hawaii in 1941. It was formed from Hawaiian garrison units just over two months before the attack on Pearl Harbor. After the Japanese air attack, the division moved into defensive positions around Honolulu and Ewa Point, then spent much of 1942 training for combat in the Pacific. The division entered battle on Guadalcanal in late 1942, relieving Marines near Henderson Field. In January 1943, it fought in the Mount Austen area and helped reduce the Japanese pocket there. Its advance toward Cape Esperance ended organized Japanese resistance on the island by February. Tropic Lightning soldiers next fought in the New Georgia campaign, where they moved through jungle and mud toward Bairoko Harbor and helped secure key islands in the central Solomons. After resting and training in New Zealand and New Caledonia, the division returned to combat on Luzon in the Philippines in 1945. It fought across the Central Plain, through the Caraballo Mountains, and captured Balete Pass, opening the route toward the Cagayan Valley.

card_unit_wolfhounds.name: card_unit_wolfhounds

card_unit_wolfhounds.text: Gets +1+1 when you deploy or add an infantry, then becomes Veteran if it has 6 or more attack.
card_unit_wolfhounds.flavorText: The 27th Infantry Regiment, known as the Wolfhounds, was part of the 25th Infantry Division during WWII. Its nickname came from its deployment to Siberia during the Russian Civil war, where the regiment’s determined pursuit tactics earned the respect of Bolshevik opponents. In 1941 the Wolfhounds were stationed in Hawaii, and some of them were among the first to fire back during the attack on Pearl Harbor. In the Pacific War, the regiment saw hard fighting on Guadalcanal. It took part in the Battle of Mount Austen, the Galloping Horse, and the Sea Horse, where the 25th Infantry Division fought through rough jungle terrain against strong Japanese defenses. The regiment was later engaged in the New Georgia campaign, advancing on the right flank toward Munda in the Solomon Islands. The Wolfhounds also served in the Philippines campaign, and in the occupation of Japan after the end of the war. There they earned another nickname, the Gentle Wolfhounds, through their support of the Holy Family Home orphanage in Osaka. What began as a Christmas visit in 1949 became a long relationship, with gifts, supplies, and medical help.

It was formed in 1813 and has been involved in nearly every military action undertaken by the United States since then. During WWII the 30th participated in numerous battles and military operations including Operation Torch, Operation Husky, Operation Avalanche, Operation Shingle and Operation Anvil. In the final stages of the war the 30th Regiment was attached to the XV Corps that was tasked as the Spearhead across the Rhine into Germany. Their motto is "Our Country Not Ourselves".

card_unit_f4f_3_wildcat_cam1.flavorText: The Grumman F4F Wildcat was an American carrier based fighter aircraft that was used during WWII by the US Navy and the Royal Navy. The aircraft was first used by the British in 1940 during the Battle of the Atlantic, and from 1941 to 1942 it was the only fighter available to the Marine Corps and the US Navy during the Pacific War. The aircraft was slower and less maneuverable than the Japanese Zero, but it had greater firepower and it was more durable and could withstand heavy battering without going down. A total of 7,885 Wildcats were manufactured, including quite a few variants, and most of them served on escort carriers.
