card_event_a_few_good_men.name: card_event_a_few_good_men
card_event_a_few_good_men.title: A FEW GOOD MEN
card_event_a_few_good_men.text: Choose 1 of 3 random elite US units to add to your hand.
card_event_a_few_good_men.flavorText: Shortly after the US Marines landed on Guadalcanal island their recon group was wiped out by the enemy during a patrol. Shortly after a barefoot man in tattered clothes reported to base, this was Major Martin Clemens British colonial administrator and soldier, and with him were his native scouts, and they would provide vital help with coordinating intelligence on Japanese activities on the island. His chief scout was Jacob C. Vouza, a retired Sergeant Major of the Solomon Islands Protectorate Armed Constabulary, but now back in service. On August 20, 1942, while Vouza was scouting for suspected Japanese outposts he was captured by the enemy. Having found a small American flag in Vouza's possession his capturers started torturing him for information. He was interrogated for hours, beaten, hanged upside down from a tree until he passed out, covered with red ants, but Vouza kept silent the whole time. Finally the Japanese soldiers bayoneted him seven times and left him to die, but once his captures departed Vouza chewed through his ropes and made it several miles to the American lines. Vouza managed to warn the Americans about an imminent attack, which gave them precious time to prepare for what is now known as the Battle of the Tenaru, where the Marines won a decisive victory. Vouza was rushed to the hospital where the doctors managed to save his life and after 12 days he returned to duty.

card_event_direct_hit.name: card_event_direct_hit
card_event_direct_hit.title: DIRECT HIT
card_event_direct_hit.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. If the unit has 0 operation cost, destroy it instead.
card_event_direct_hit.flavorText: The US Marines air force units operating from Henderson Field on Guadalcanal island were referred to as the “Cactus Air Force”, “Cactus” being the Allied code name for the island. Japanese aerial losses during the campaign have never been calculated, but the 15 Marine combat squadrons that operated from the island during this time suffered from 94 pilots killed or missing-in-action, with another 177 evacuated with wounds or with sickness (especially severe malaria). The US Marine Corp aviation units did not have aerial superiority during this time and it was a hard lesson learned for times to come.

card_event_high_altitude_bombing.name: card_event_high_altitude_bombing
card_event_high_altitude_bombing.title: HIGH ALTITUDE BOMBING
card_event_high_altitude_bombing.flavorText: High Altitude Bombing, also known as High Level Bombing is, as the name suggests, the tactic of dropping bombs on a target from a high altitude. At the start of WWII the US air forces used heavy bombers such as the B-17 and the B-24 Liberator for high altitude and the 1930s technology of gyroscope-stabilized optical bombsights helped them to strike their targets with more accuracy. The B-29 Superfortress was introduced in 1944 and it was designed for high altitude bombing and the technology exceeded all its predecessors.

card_event_patrol.name: card_event_patrol
card_event_patrol.title: PATROL
card_event_patrol.text: Target enemy unit loses Guard, Smokescreen and Destruction. Deal 2 damage to it.
card_event_patrol.flavorText: The Guadalcanal Campaign was a war of attrition which escalated over a period of 6 months. There were times when weeks or months would pass without the Americans encountering the enemy and much time was spent patrolling the island while trying to hunt down and eliminate the Japanese resistance.

card_event_special_delivery_us.name: card_event_special_delivery_us
card_event_special_delivery_us.title: SPECIAL DELIVERY
card_event_special_delivery_us.text: Discard all cards with cost 2 or less from hand, then draw 2 cards.
card_event_special_delivery_us.flavorText: Reinforcements and supplies for the starved and malaria-ridden Marines that had been on Guadalcanal island since early August 1942 finally started to arrive in October that same year. The first unit to arrive was the 164th Infantry Regiment of the Americal Division. By end of the year US forces were strong enough to begin the final offensive on the island.

card_unit_164th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_164th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_164th_infantry_regiment.title: 164th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_164th_infantry_regiment.text: Destruction: Give a random friendly unit +1+1.
card_unit_164th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: In 1942 the 164th Infantry Regiment along with the 182nd, 132nd Infantry Regiment plus artillery and support units formed the Americal Division of the US Army. In October 1942 the division landed on Guadalcanal as an emergency reinforcement to the 1st Marine Division and became the first US Army unit to engage in combat in the Guadalcanal Campaign. The 164th fought alongside the Marines on the island and saw fierce fighting, at first they managed to withstand repeated assaults by the Japanese and later they participated in jungle patroles in an attempt to eliminate resistance on the island. After the Battle of Guadalcanal the 164th Regiment had gained valuable experience in jungle warfare. The regiment fought in the Bougainville campaign as part of the 5307th Composite Unit (AKA Merrill’s Marauders) which was a special operations jungle warfare unit.

card_unit_2_5_marines.name: card_unit_2_5_marines
card_unit_2_5_marines.title: 2/5 MARINES
card_unit_2_5_marines.text: Deals double damage against units in the frontline.
card_unit_2_5_marines.flavorText: The 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines Regiment participated in the initial landings on Guadalcanal islands in August 1942 and stayed there until they were relieved in October. The 2/5th also fought in New Britain, Eastern New Guinea, Peleliu and Okinawa.

card_unit_p39_airacobra.name: card_unit_p39_airacobra
card_unit_p39_airacobra.title: P-39 AIRACOBRA
card_unit_p39_airacobra.text: Takes 2 less combat damage against ground units.
card_unit_p39_airacobra.flavorText: The Bell P-39 Airacobra was an American fighter aircraft that was introduced in 1941 and was used by the US air forces and their Allies during WWII. The aircraft saw combat in the Pacific, Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front. Some were used by the Cactus Air Force in the Battle of Guadalcanal and although it wasn’t on par with contemporary Japanese fighters it performed well in bombing runs and conducting strafing, especially when attacking Japanese ground forces on the island. A total of 9,588 Airacobra aircraft were manufactured from 1940 to 1944, including many variants.

card_event_duress.name: card_event_duress
card_event_duress.title: DURESS
card_event_duress.flavorText: Louis Zamperini's story during WWII is a tale of survival and resilience. He was an Olympic athlete that turned bombardier of the United States Army Air Force, but his aircraft crashed in the Pacific Ocean during a rescue mission in 1943. Along with two other crew members, Zamperini survived the crash and spent 47 days adrift in a life raft, battling starvation, dehydration, and shark attacks. After drifting over 2,000 miles, Zamperini and his surviving companion, Russell Phillips, were captured by the Japanese navy. Zamperini was taken as a prisoner of war and held in several Japanese prison camps where he endured brutal treatment, starvation, and physical and psychological torture for over two years until he was finally released. Zamperini’s biography “Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption” was published in 2010 and was adapted into a Hollywood film directed by Angelina Jolie in 2014.

card_event_grim_day.name: card_event_grim_day
card_event_grim_day.title: GRIM DAY
card_event_grim_day.text: Until your next turn, it costs +2 kredits for the enemy to target or attack your units.
card_event_grim_day.flavorText: The Battle for Convoy ONS-5 which took place in May 1943 is considered the turning point of the Battle of the Atlantic. The ONS-5 convoy consisted of 42 ships and 16 US and British escort vessels -bound from Liverpool to Halifax. On the opposing side were 40 U-boats under the command of Admiral Karl Dönitz which attacked the convoy relentlessly over the course of a week. During the battle the Germans managed to sink 13 ships totaling 63,000 tons, while the Allied escort vessels sunk 6 U-boats and caused significant damage to 7 more. This engagement served as clear evidence that the convoy escorts had honed their skills in safeguarding convoys. Their armaments and expertise not only enabled them to protect the convoys and fend off attackers, but also allowed them to deal heavy damages to the enemy. Following this encounter, the Allies achieved a string of victories and inflicted substantial casualties on the U-boat fleet, a period referred to by the German Kriegsmarine as "Black May." This ultimately led Admiral Karl Dönitz to withdraw his forces from the North Atlantic theater.

card_event_production_order.name: card_event_production_order
card_event_production_order.title: PRODUCTION ORDER
card_event_production_order.text: Choose One - add a B-24D OR a B-24J to your hand.
card_event_production_order.flavorText: The War Production Board (WPB) was established by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in January 1942 and served as the US government agency that oversaw wartime production during WWII. It was  tasked with directing the conversion of civilian industries to support the war effort, managing the allocation of critical resources, establishing material distribution priorities, and restricting nonessential production. The WPB implemented rationing measures for items like gasoline, heating oil, metals, rubber, paper, and plastics. The WPB was dissolved shortly after Japan's defeat in 1945 and succeeded by the Civilian Production Administration. From 1942 to1945, the WPB supervised the production of $183 billion worth of weapons and supplies, approximately 40 percent of the global munitions output, while maintaining civilian living standards, with one-fourth of the US output dedicated to warplanes and warships.

card_event_supply_priorities.name: card_event_supply_priorities
card_event_supply_priorities.title: SUPPLY PRIORITIES
card_event_supply_priorities.text: Choose One - deal 1 damage to all units OR fully repair all units.
card_event_supply_priorities.flavorText: During WWII the US Army had developed what’s called “Standard Tables of Organization and Equipment (TO&E)", still in use today. There was a TO&E for each type of unit, specifying the authorized personnel and equipment for that unit. These tables included information on the number of personnel, types of weapons, vehicles and other supplies required for a unit to function effectively. Military planners used these tables as a foundation to determine the basic supply needs for different types of units. Other nations in the conflict used also similar TO&E’s. As an example, during WWII an Armored Division of the US Army needed 30 tons of supplies daily when it was inactive, but about 700 tons a day when it engaged in heavy fighting. An infantry division needed 80 tons a day when inactive, but 1,100 tons during heavy fighting.

card_event_vicious_salvo.name: card_event_vicious_salvo
card_event_vicious_salvo.title: VICIOUS SALVO
card_event_vicious_salvo.text: Deal 3 damage to target unit. Suppress adjacent units.
card_event_vicious_salvo.flavorText: The term "salvo" refers to a simultaneous discharge of artillery, firearms, or other weapons. It is the act of firing a group of weapons, such as cannons, guns, or missiles, all at once or in rapid succession. A salvo is often used for a coordinated and concentrated attack or as a display of firepower. In naval warfare, a salvo can refer to the firing of all the guns on one side of a warship. It can also be used metaphorically to describe a simultaneous or collective action or event, not necessarily related to weapons.

card_event_victory_march.name: card_event_victory_march
card_event_victory_march.title: VICTORY MARCH
card_event_victory_march.text: Set the operation cost of your units to 0. Gain HQ defense equal to total cost reduced.
card_event_victory_march.flavorText: The Battle of the Bulge (December 16th, 1944 – January 16th, 1945), codenamed "Unternehmen Wacht am Rhein",  marked the last German offensive on the Western Front, and despite initial successes and complete surprise, the Germans could not gain the upper hand. Their Ardennes operation caused significant losses and delayed the Allied invasion of Germany by several weeks, but by February 1945, the Western Front lines were largely back to where they were in December 1944. The German casualties were severe, depleting their last reserves and damaging the Luftwaffe, and on top of that the Soviets began the Vistula-Oder Offensive where they conquered most of the pre-war Polish territory. After this, Germany’s defeat was only a matter of time.

card_unit_104th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_104th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_104th_infantry_regiment.title: 104th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_104th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 104th Infantry Regiment was a unit of the US Army.Its lineage traces back to 14 November 1639 and it stayed active until 2005. In January 1942 the 104th was put on coastal defense duty and their task was to secure landing bases in the North Atlantic and to prevent saboteurs landing on American beaches. In January 1943 the regiment received amphibious assault training, and finally on August 27th, 1944 the regiment, as part of the 26th Infantry Division, sailed to Cherbourg in France. The division entered combat in France in September 1944 when it landed at Cherbourg. The division was then assigned to the US Third Army under Lieutenant General George S. Patton, and after a few minor skirmishes it went on a full offensive in November. The division captured the towns Dieuze and Sarre-Union, and engaged in intense house-to-house combat before reaching the Maginot fortifications. It was then reassigned to III Corps and sent to Luxembourg in order to participate in the Battle of the Bulge. Later the division advanced into Austria and aided in the capture of Linz before overrunning the Gusen concentration camp before its destruction by German forces. The division halted its advance following the cease-fire order on May 4th, 1945.

card_unit_13th_engineers_battalion.name: card_unit_13th_engineers_battalion
card_unit_13th_engineers_battalion.title: 13th ENGINEERS BATTALION
card_unit_13th_engineers_battalion.text: Gain an extra kredit slot when you deploy a unit with 3 or more operation cost.
card_unit_13th_engineers_battalion.flavorText: The 13th Engineer Battalion traces its lineage back to the American Civil War and has remained active throughout numerous conflicts until it was deactivated in 1994. During WWII, the 13th Engineer Battalion was brought back to action in California on July 8th, 1940. In 1943, they were sent along with elements of the 7th Infantry Division to the Aleutian Islands where they helped establish a beachhead at Massacre Bay in Alaska on May 11th, 1943. Later the battalion participated in the Battle of Attu Island, where they stopped a Japanese banzai charge, resulting in 239 enemy casualties. In 1944, they moved from Attu to Kwajalein Atoll, where they cleared out bunkers, shelters, and gun positions in just six days. Later that same year the battalion landed on Leyte where one of its units, Alpha Company, received a special award for their exceptional work in keeping the main supply route open under tough conditions. On April 1st, 1945, the 13th Engineer Battalion was part of the first group to land on Okinawa. There they took part in some of the toughest fighting of WWII, sealing up almost 600 caves and destroying others. In September they sailed with the 7th Infantry Division to Korea to accept the surrender of the Japanese forces there. From 1948 the 13th was stationed in Japan, until 1950 when it participated in the Korean War.

card_unit_142nd_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_142nd_infantry_regiment
card_unit_142nd_infantry_regiment.title: 142nd INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_142nd_infantry_regiment.text: When this unit destroys an enemy unit, your HQ gains +2 defense.
card_unit_142nd_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 142nd Infantry Regiment is a unit of the US Army which has been active from 1917 to this day. In 1940 the regiment underwent extensive training in various locations across the United States before sailing from New York to North Africa in April 1943. As part of the 34th Infantry Division the regiment was involved in the Italian campaign, taking part in significant battles and operations, including the Naples-Foggia campaign, the assault on Monte Sambucaro, and the fighting at Anzio. After participating in the liberation of Rome, the division retrained in Paestum before making a third amphibious assault in Southern France in August 1944. Their actions included surrounding Livron, liberating Lyon, capturing Remiremont, and battling through the Vosges Mountains. The 142nd fought through various German strongholds, crossed the Rhine River, and continued to advance into Germany. Participating in the 34th Division's advance across the Lech River in April 1945. The regiment concluded the war in Austria and returned to the US in December 1945, marking the end of their active service at Camp Patrick Henry, Virginia.

card_unit_devils_brigade.name: card_unit_devils_brigade
card_unit_devils_brigade.title: DEVIL'S BRIGADE
card_unit_devils_brigade.text: Deployment: Deal 1 damage to an enemy. If it is a unit with Alpine, destroy it instead.
card_unit_devils_brigade.flavorText: The Devil’s Brigade, also known as The Black Devils or officially as the 1st Special Service Force, was an elite American–Canadian commando unit which was formed in 1942 and fought in WWII. The unit was known for its rigorous training in specialized skills like parachuting, skiing, rock climbing, amphibious operations, and other abilities that were crucial to their missions. The brigade saw combat in Italy and France between 1943 and 1944 and earned a reputation for audacious and effective missions behind enemy lines. Though unconfirmed, the unit was referred to as both the Black Devils and the Devil's Brigade by the Germans, with the latter being their preferred name. They were also known for having cards printed with their insignia and the message "Das dicke Ende kommt noch!" ("The worst is yet to come") written in red ink, which they left on deceased German soldiers to invoke psychological warfare. In December 1944, a combination of politics and a new military strategy caused the Devil's Brigade to be disbanded, but those who had survived filled in as replacements in Allied Airborne Divisions. However, despite its short lived service during WWII, the modern American and Canadian special operations forces trace their heritage to this unit.

card_unit_les_terribles.name: card_unit_les_terribles
card_unit_les_terribles.title: LES TERRIBLES
card_unit_les_terribles.text: When you deploy another unit with operation cost 3 or more, draw a card.
card_unit_les_terribles.flavorText: The 128th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed Les Terribles (the Terrifics in French), is a unit of the US Army which has been active since the American Civil War and has participated in many conflicts since then. In 1940, the 128th Regiment, as part of the 32nd Division, was sent to training in Louisiana, and then the unit was transported by convoy to Port Adelaide, Australia. From 1942 to 1944, the 128th achieved significant victories during various battles in the Pacific theater. They managed to break through Japanese lines at the Battle of Buna in New Guinea and defeated Japanese forces at Saidor and Aitape. In Leyte and Luzon they pierced through the Yamashita Line. The 32nd Division was still engaged in combat when the cease fire order came on 15 August 1945, and by then the division had been fighting for 654 days, which is more than any other US division in any war.

card_unit_m10_a1.name: card_unit_m10_a1
card_unit_m10_a1.title: M10A1
card_unit_m10_a1.flavorText: The M10 Wolverine served as a tank destroyer for the US Army and its Allied counterparts from 1943 until the conclusion of WWII. The M10A1 variant received a gasoline Ford engine and was based on the Sherman M4A3 chassis. Around 1,700 vehicles of all variants were produced ; most were armed with a M7 76.2 mm gun, but the last 300 received the new M1 76 mm (3-inch) gun which had a better muzzle velocity and could fire heavier ammunition. As of 1944, the M10 began encountering difficulties when facing the German Tiger and Panther tanks. It wasn't until the introduction of HVAP (High Velocity Armor Piercing) rounds that it regained a competitive edge, but even then it required precision in targeting weak points to effectively engage the German tanks.

card_event_battery.name: card_event_battery
card_event_battery.title: BATTERY
card_event_battery.text: Deal 4 damage to target unit, excess damage is dealt to the enemy HQ.
card_event_battery.flavorText: An artillery battery is a grouping of artillery, mortars, rocket artillery, multiple rocket launchers, and in later years surface-to-surface missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and other weapons designed to improve command and control of gunnery crews and their systems. General Patton often commented that the US artillery won the war for them, and one example of its importance was during the Battle of the Bulge. Due to bad weather Allied air superiority was out of the picture, which meant that the artillery had to fill the void. The US Army managed to amass around 350 guns of all calibers in the northern sector of the Bulge which was one of the largest concentrations of artillery in history. This massive firepower helped slow down the German advance and proved vital in the Allied defense of Elsenborn Ridge and Bastogne.

card_event_firewall.name: card_event_firewall
card_event_firewall.title: FIREWALL
card_event_firewall.text: Give target unit: "Cannot attack the enemy HQ."
card_event_firewall.flavorText:
The Battle of Midway was a major naval battle fought between the US and Japan in June 1942, six months after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. The battle took place near the Midway Atoll in the Pacific Ocean and was a turning point in the Pacific Theater of WWII.
The Japanese hoped to lure the American fleet into decisive battle and clear the seas for further attacks on Midway, Fiji, Samoa and Hawaii, but the Americans were able to intercept and decipher Japanese messages, giving them advance notice of the Japanese attack. The US Navy was able to position their ships and aircraft accordingly and launch a surprise attack on the Japanese carriers, sinking four of them. The Japanese were forced to retreat, and the battle resulted in a decisive victory for the United States. The victory at Midway was due to a combination of factors, including intelligence, strategic planning, superior technology, and skillful leadership. The battle marked a turning point in the Pacific Theater of WWII, as it weakened Japan's naval power and gave the Allies an advantage in the war.

card_event_screening_force.name: card_event_screening_force
card_event_screening_force.title: SCREENING FORCE
card_event_screening_force.text: Costs 1 less for each friendly BREWSTER F2A. Add two SBD 3 DAUNTLESS with Blitz to your support line.
card_event_screening_force.flavorText: During WWII, the concept of an aerial screening force became vital for the protection of bomber formations and advancing ground troops. The US employed dedicated fighter units to form protective barriers against enemy aircraft, especially over Europe where the skies were heavily contested. Escort fighters like the P-47 Thunderbolt and P-51 Mustang flew ahead or alongside bomber groups, intercepting German fighters before they could close in on the main formation. The US Ninth Air Force, operating in support of Allied ground advances, often coordinated with the British Second Tactical Air Force to neutralize enemy air threats. These formations patrolled likely approach routes, engaged enemy aircraft before they reached the front lines, and maintained air superiority over the battlefield. Screening extended beyond physical interception, with electronic warfare also playing a role. US aircraft equipped with jamming devices disrupted German radar and communications during large operations, such as the Normandy landings. These efforts prevented enemy fighters and Flak batteries from responding effectively. Screening forces, both physical and electronic, were essential to the success of Allied air and ground operations.

card_unit_112th_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_112th_infantry_regiment
card_unit_112th_infantry_regiment.title: 112th INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_112th_infantry_regiment.text: Has +2 attack for each adjacent unit.
card_unit_112th_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 112th Infantry Regiment of the US Army dates back to the American Civil war and has since participated in several conflicts, including WWI and WWII. During WWII the regiment landed in Normandy in 1944, after D-Day, where it became the 112th Infantry Regimental Combat Team (RCT). Apart from the infantry the RCT included several support units, the 229th Field Artillery Battalion, the 103rd Engineer Battalion, Company C, 447th Antiaircraft Artillery Battalion, and Company C, 630th Tank Destroyer Battalion. After Normandy the 112th participated in the liberation of Paris and later the Battle of Hürtgen Forest (19 September to 16 December 1944) where the regiment was at one point reduced to 300 men during an engagement. The US soldiers nicknamed the Battle for Hürtgen Forest “the meat grinder”, and for good reason since it is the longest single battle US forces have ever fought and one of the bloodiest. Following Hürtgen Forest the 112th RCT fought in the Battle of the Bulge, where it defended a sector of 100 km where 9 German divisions concentrated their attacks. During the Battle of the Bulge the 112th RCT managed to inflict 1600 casualties and destroy 18 enemy tanks, for which it received the Distinguished Unit Citation which is rewarded for extraordinary heroism in action.

card_unit_442nd_infantry_regiment.name: card_unit_442nd_infantry_regiment
card_unit_442nd_infantry_regiment.title: 442nd INFANTRY REGIMENT
card_unit_442nd_infantry_regiment.text: Destruction: If it is the enemy turn, add a copy of this unit to your hand.
card_unit_442nd_infantry_regiment.flavorText: The 442nd Infantry Regiment, or the 442nd Regimental Combat Team (RCT) was a fighting unit that was composed almost entirely of American soldiers of Japanese ancestry (Nisei). The unit was active from 1944 to 1946 and during that time it became the most decorated regiment of the US Army. The 442nd RCT was composed of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Infantry Battalions, 522nd Field Artillery Battalion, 232nd Engineering Company, an Anti-Tank Company, Services Company, Medical Detachment, and a Headquarters Company. From 1944 to 1945 the 442nd fought mainly in the European Theater, mostly in Italy, Southern France and Germany, and participated in numerous operations and campaigns during their brief service time. What is special about the regiment apart from its distinguished combat performance, is that they were all volunteers, and while they were fighting, many of their families were held in internment camps on US soil.

card_unit_5th_medical_battalion.name: card_unit_5th_medical_battalion
card_unit_5th_medical_battalion.title: 5th MEDICAL BATTALION
card_unit_5th_medical_battalion.text: Your other units have +1 attack and are fully repaired at the end of your turn.
card_unit_5th_medical_battalion.flavorText: A medical battalion was a divisional unit that offered medical support to the division in the field. Its main role was to conduct necessary evacuation and to administer medical care for the casualties of the division. The 5th Medical Battalion was attached to the 5th Infantry Division, aka “Red Devils”, of the US Army during WWII. In 1942 the division was shipped to Iceland, where the British occupation force was replaced by the US forces, but from there it was sent to England in 1943 to prepare for the Allied invasion of Europe. After two years of training the 5th Division landed in Normandy in 1944, over a month after the D-Day landings, and in the following months it participated in heavy combat during the Battle of France. In December 1944 the division was sent to reinforce the Allied southern flank in Belgium during the Battle of the Bulge. After that the division fought its way towards Germany along with the Allied forces and ended the war in Czechoslovakia in 1945.

card_unit_5th_rangers.name: card_unit_5th_rangers
card_unit_5th_rangers.title: 5th RANGERS
card_unit_5th_rangers.text: Deployment: Choose one - this unit has 0 operation cost OR it gets +4+4.
card_unit_5th_rangers.flavorText: The 5th Ranger Infantry Battalion was activated in 1943 and was one of seven Ranger Battalions that were raised during WWII. The 5th Rangers landed on Omaha Beach along with companies A, B and C of the 2nd Rangers, where elements of the 116th Infantry Regiment had been pinned down by heavy enemy fire from the heights above. Despite heavy casualties the Rangers managed to advance across the seawall and barbed wire and to knock out the enemy positions. The Rangers then managed to advance 6 km inland to the village of Vierville-sur-Mer and by doing so they opened the breach for the supporting troops to follow up and expand the beachhead. The 5th Ranger Battalion would later distinguish itself in numerous battles and operations in Europe, including the Battle for Brest, the Battle of Hürtgen Forest and the Battle of the Bulge.

card_unit_m4a2.name: card_unit_m4a2
card_unit_m4a2.title: M4A2
card_unit_m4a2.text: Deployment: Add a M4A2 to your support line.
card_unit_m4a2.flavorText: The Sherman M4A2 medium tank variant was nearly identical to the Sherman M4, but it had a diesel engine and came with a pair of vented armored grates on the rear hull deck. The variant saw limited combat with the US forces, some were in service of the US Marine Corps, but mostly it was used by the British forces. Some M4A2’s were shipped to the Soviet Union through the Lend-Lease program. The tank fitted the needs of the Red Army perfectly as they were using diesel tanks only. A total of 10,968 M4A2 tanks were produced from 1942 to 1945.

card_unit_p47d_25_waw.name: card_unit_p47d_25_waw
card_unit_p47d_25_waw.title: P-47D-25-RE
card_unit_p47d_25_waw.text: Deployment: Destroy a random enemy unit in the frontline.
card_unit_p47d_25_waw.flavorText: The P-47D-25-RE was a Republic P-47 Thunderbolt variant, an American fighter aircraft that was developed during WWII and used by the US States Army Air Forces (USAAF) and RAF. The P-47D-25-RE was the first Thunderbolt variant produced with a bubble canopy, a design that was based on the Hawker Typhoon. This improved the pilots rear vision, and so did the flatter rear fuselage needed to allow the new canopy to be installed. The P-47D series came first into service in 1943 and were used by the USAAF and RAF and were used in the roles of fighter-bombers, in ground-attacks and as short-to medium-range escort fighters. The P-47D’s came with an armament of eight 0.50 machine guns and could carry a 2,500lb bomb load, or ten 5-inch rocket projectiles. A total of 15,636 Thunderbolts were built, 385 of them were the  P-47D-25-RE variant.

card_unit_seagull.name: card_unit_seagull
card_unit_seagull.title: SEAGULL
card_unit_seagull.text: Your HQ cannot lose more than 4 defense each turn.
card_unit_seagull.flavorText: The Curtiss SO3C Seamew was an American aircraft that was developed for the United States Navy as its standard floatplane scout. The manufacturer called the aircraft the Seamew, but in 1941 the US Navy started calling it the Seagull, which was the name of the Curtiss SOC biplane it was supposed to replace. Those in service of the Royal Navy were still called Seamew and this caused some confusion. From the time it entered service the SO3C suffered serious flaws, both with in-flight stability and with the Ranger engine. The in-flight stability problem was solved to some extent, but the engine problem remained, and its poor performance led to the aircraft being withdrawn from front line service. In some cases the SO3C was replaced with the old SOC Seagull, the one it was supposed to replace. In 1945 the Curtiss SO3C Seamew was retired and by that time a total of 795 aircraft had been produced, including variants.

card_unit_seahawk.name: card_unit_seahawk
card_unit_seahawk.title: SEAHAWK
card_unit_seahawk.flavorText: The Curtiss SC Seahawk was a single-seat scout seaplane developed for the US Navy during WWII. The first prototype flew on 16 February 1944 in Columbus Ohio and production orders followed even before flight tests finished. It was designed to replace earlier types such as the Curtiss SO3C Seamew and the Vought OS2U Kingfisher and was regarded as likely America's best scout floatplane by the end of the war. A total of around 577 SC-1 aircraft were built, entering service in October 1944 aboard ships such as USS Guam. The Seahawk carried two Browning M2 12.7 mm machine guns in the wings and two small underwing racks capable of carrying radar gear or light bombs. A bunk in the rear fuselage allowed rescue or personnel transfer. Its main float design proved problematic for bomb storage so was later modified to carry extra fuel. The Seahawk first saw combat in June 1945 during operations around Borneo, though its late arrival meant limited wartime use. It continued flying postwar until around 1949, when helicopters replaced floatplanes for scouting on battleships and cruisers.

card_unit_tigercat.name: card_unit_tigercat
card_unit_tigercat.title: TIGERCAT
card_unit_tigercat.text: At the end of your turn, add a SBD 3 DAUNTLESS to your support line.
card_unit_tigercat.flavorText: The Grumman F7F Tigercat was a twin-engine heavy fighter designed for the US Navy. Developed in response to a 1941 demand for a fast, long-range aircraft with heavy armament, it first flew in 1943. The Tigercat was equipped with four 20 mm cannons and four 12.7 mm machine guns, along with underwing racks for bombs, rockets or torpedoes. It was one of the fastest piston-engine fighters of the war, significantly outpacing the F6F Hellcat at low altitude. Despite its performance, the Tigercat faced challenges. Its large size and heavy weight made it difficult to operate from standard aircraft carriers. Early models struggled with directional control on one engine and had problems with carrier landings. Only the final variant, the F7F-4N, was certified for carrier use, and very few were produced. The Tigercat arrived too late to see combat in WWII. Marine reconnaissance units used it for mapping invasion beaches in the Pacific in mid-1945. It later saw limited action during the Korean War, primarily in night fighter and ground attack roles. The aircraft remained in service with the Marine Corps until the early 1950s.
